editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: . . . so that you may read them at hand and be able to keep them safe. Now should writings be left to no one at all, or to some? If to none, what use are letters? But if to some, then either to the serious-minded or to those who are not. It would surely be absurd to reject the writing of the serious while approving the compositions of men who are nothing of the kind. Are we, then, to allow Theopompus and Timaeus to compose fables and slanders, and Epicurus besides, the founder of atheism, and Hipponax and Archilochus to write with such shamelessness, and yet forbid the man who proclaims the truth to leave behind a benefit for those who come after? It is a fine thing, I think, to leave good children behind for those who follow. Children of the body are offspring; words are the offspring of the soul. So we call our fathers those who instructed us; and wisdom is something shared and loving toward mankind. Solomon, at any rate, says: "My son, if you receive the saying of my commandment and hide it within yourself, your ear will hearken to wisdom." He means that the word, once sown, is hidden as in earth, in the soul of the learner; and this is a spiritual planting.

Next it would be in place to take up — since the Scripture called the Greeks thieves of the barbarian philosophy — how this is to be shown in brief. For we shall set forth that they not only record, by imitating, the marvellous things of those things recorded among us, but that they fabricate and falsify the most authoritative of the doctrines, our Scriptures being older, as we have demonstrated; and we shall convict them in the matters concerning faith, and concerning wisdom and knowledge and science and hope and faith, and concerning repentance and self-control, and indeed the fear of God (a very swarm of the virtues of truth, of which as many as the present treatment of the subject requires will be taken in); and that especially the hidden part of the barbarian philosophy, this symbolic and enigmatic kind, was emulated by those who in earnest philosophized the things of the ancients, as a thing most useful, or rather most necessary, to the knowledge of the truth.

The followers of Valentinus, who derive the conjugal pairs from above, from the divine emanations, approve of marriage; but the school of Basilides say that, when the apostles asked whether it might not be better not to marry, the Lord answered, "Not all can receive this saying; for there are eunuchs, some from birth, some by necessity." And they explain the saying in some such way as this: some men have from birth a natural aversion to women, and those who make use of this natural constitution do well not to marry. These, they say, are the eunuchs from birth; while the eunuchs by necessity are those theatrical ascetics who master themselves only because they are drawn on by the desire for fame; and those who have been mutilated by some misfortune have become eunuchs by necessity. Those, then, who are eunuchs by necessity are not eunuchs by reason. But those who for the sake of the eternal kingdom have made themselves eunuchs adopt this course of reasoning, they say, because of the things that result from marriage, fearing the distraction of providing for the necessities of life.

It seems right, I think, to treat next of martyrdom, and who the perfect man is; in which discussion there will be included, as the demands of what we are to say require, the things that go along with these, and how one must philosophize alike whether one be a slave or free, and whether one's kind be man or woman. And next, having more fully completed the discussion concerning faith and concerning inquiry, we shall set out the symbolic form, so that, having concluded the ethical discourse as in a rapid survey, we may present summarily the benefit that passed over to the Greeks from the barbarian philosophy. After this sketch will be delivered the setting forth, by way of epitome, of the Scriptures, both against the Greeks and against the Jews; and all that, in the Stromateis before this, we had purposed, at the very entry of the preface, to complete in a single notebook, but which, being of necessity in bondage to the multitude of matters, we could not encompass.

Having said this much about the gnostic, by way of a rapid survey, let us now proceed to what comes next; and faith, in its turn, must be examined again. For there are those who draw a distinction, holding that our faith has to do with the Son, but knowledge with the Father. They fail to notice that, in order truly to believe in the Son, one must believe that he is the Son, that he came, and how, and for what purpose, and concerning his passion; while it is necessary also to know who the Son of God is. Now neither is knowledge without faith, nor faith without knowledge; nor again is the Father without the Son, since the very name of Father implies a Son, and the Son is the true teacher concerning the Father. And in order that one may believe in the Son, he must know the Father, to whom the Son also belongs; and again, in order that we may come to know the Father, we must believe in the Son, because it is the Son of God who teaches. For we pass from faith to knowledge, and through the Son to the Father. The knowledge of the Son and the Father, which is according to the gnostic rule that is truly gnostic, is the apprehension and grasp of truth by means of the truth. We, then, are those who are believers in what is disbelieved, and gnostics in what is unknown — that is, gnostics in what is unknown and disbelieved by all, but believed and known by the few; gnostics not in word, registering deeds, but in contemplation itself.

The sixth, and along with it the seventh, of our gnostic notes according to the true philosophy, the Stromateis — having traced out, so far as may be, the ethical discourse here brought to its close, and having set forth what manner of man, in his life, the gnostic is — proceeds to show the philosophers that this man is in no way godless, as they have supposed, but is the only one truly god-fearing; setting forth, by way of summary, the manner of the gnostic's worship of God, so far as it is safe to commit to memoranda in writing. For the Lord enjoined us to work for the food that abides unto eternity, and somewhere the prophet says, "Blessed is he who sows beside every water, where the ox and the ass tread" — the people gathered out of the law and out of the Gentiles into the one faith. And "he who is weak eats herbs," according to the noble apostle. The Paedagogus, divided into three books, has already set forth our nurture and rearing from childhood — that is, the manner of life that grows up together with faith out of catechizing, and prepares the soul, virtuous, of those enrolled among men, for the reception of gnostic science. When, then, the Greeks shall have learned plainly from what is to be said by us in what follows, that they themselves act impiously in persecuting the man who loves God, then at last, as the notes go forward according to the character of the Stromateis, we must resolve the difficulties further raised against us, both by Greeks and by barbarians, concerning the Lord's coming.

It is now time to demonstrate to the Greeks that the gnostic alone is truly devout, so that the philosophers, learning what kind of person the true Christian is, may condemn their own ignorance—since they persecute the name at random and without cause, and idly call atheists those who have come to know the God who truly is. With the philosophers it is fitting, I think, to use clearer arguments, drawn from their own learning, so that, already trained, they may be able to follow, even if they have not yet shown themselves worthy of partaking in the power to believe. For the present we shall not appeal to the words of the prophets; later, at the appropriate places, we shall make use of the Scriptures, but for now we shall indicate summarily what they reveal, sketching Christianity in outline, so that we may not break the continuity of the argument by introducing the Scriptures—and that to those who do not yet understand their language. But once we have shown what is meant, then the testimonies too will be made plain to them, when they believe out of abundance. (And even if what we say should appear to some of the multitude to differ from the Scriptures of the Lord, let it be known that it draws its breath and life from there, and that, taking its starting points from them, it professes to set forth their sense alone, not their wording.) For elaboration carried too far, if it is not made at the right moment, would reasonably seem superfluous; and to have given no thought at all to what is pressing is utterly slothful and deficient. But "blessed indeed are those who search out the testimonies of the Lord; with the whole heart will they seek him"; and the Law and the prophets bear witness concerning the Lord.

. . . But not even the most ancient of the philosophers were carried away toward disputing and being at a loss; how much less, surely, should we be—we who cling to the truly true philosophy, to whom the Scripture plainly enjoins, for the sake of discovery, to search out by inquiring? For the younger of the philosophers among the Greeks, out of an empty and unfulfilled love of honour, are carried off, at once refutatively and contentiously, into useless babbling; but the barbarian philosophy, by contrast, casting out all strife, said: "Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened; ask, and it shall be given you." The reasoning that proceeds by question and answer, then, knocks at the door of truth as it appears, according to its inquiry; and when the obstacle is removed in the course of the search, scientific contemplation comes to be.

And so he adds: "And you will incline your heart to understanding; you will apply it for the admonition of your son." For soul, I think, joined to soul, and spirit to spirit in the sowing of the word, makes what is cast in to grow, and gives it life; and every son who is taught in obedience to the one who teaches is a son. "My son," he says, "do not forget my ordinances." But if knowledge does not belong to all, then writings are, for the many, "a lyre to an ass," as the proverb-makers say. Swine, at any rate, take more pleasure in mud than in clean water. "For this reason," says the Lord, "I speak to them in parables: because, seeing, they do not see, and hearing, they do not hear, nor do they understand" — not that the Lord causes their ignorance (it would be impious to think so), but that he reproves prophetically the ignorance already there, and declares that they will fail to understand what is said.

Upon this it is fitting, I think, to make a defence concerning the things for which the Greeks run us down, using a few Scriptures — if perhaps the Jew too, listening quietly, may be able to turn from the things in which he believed to him in whom he did not believe. And there will fittingly follow, for the noble of the philosophers, a refutation made in love, both of their life and of the discovery of their new doctrines — we not requiting our accusers (far from it, who have learned to bless those who curse, even if they vainly bring blasphemous words against us), but for the turning of those very men, if perhaps the all-wise might be ashamed, brought to soberness by a barbarian refutation, so as to be able, late at least, to discern what those studies are, on account of which they undertake their journeys overseas. For of what they are thieves — and indeed these things too must be demonstrated, once their self-love is taken away — and of what they, having searched, boast that they themselves found out — the refutation of these. And, as a consequence, we must run over also the so-called cyclic education, in how far it is useful, and over astrology and mathematics and magic and sorcery. For the all-Greeks pride themselves on these too as the greatest sciences. But he who reproves with frankness makes peace.

And "It is better to marry than to burn"—the apostle says this, they claim, so that you may not cast your soul into the fire, holding out night and day, and afraid that you may fall away from continence; for the soul that is set on holding out becomes divided in its hope. "Hold out, then," says Isidore in so many words in his Ethics, "against a contentious wife, that you may not be torn away from the grace of God; and when you have discharged the fire, pray with a good conscience. But when," he says, "your thanksgiving falls away into petition, and you ask henceforth not to do right but not to do wrong, then marry. But suppose a man is young, or poor, or downcast in spirit, and is unwilling to marry as reason directs—let such a one not separate from his brother. Let him say, 'I have entered into the holy place, I can suffer no harm.' But if he has some misgiving, let him say, 'Brother, lay your hand upon me, that I may not sin'; and he will receive help both for the mind and for the senses. Let him only will to accomplish the good, and he will attain it."

After this, when the sketch concerning the matters before us has been completed as fully as possible, we must give a full account of what has been treated, concerning first principles, in natural philosophy by the Greeks and the other barbarians, whose opinions have come down to us, and we must take in hand the most authoritative of the things devised by the philosophers. Following upon these, it would be fitting, after the survey of theology, to treat of the things handed down concerning prophecy; so that, having shown that the Scriptures in which we have believed are authoritative by the authority of the Almighty, we may be able to proceed through them in due connection, and from this point to show, against all the heresies, one God and Lord Almighty, who was genuinely proclaimed through the law and the prophets, and besides through the blessed gospel. And many controversies against the heterodox await us, as we attempt both to resolve in writing the things they bring forward, and to persuade them even against their will, convicting them out of the Scriptures themselves.

Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear; and faith is the ears of the soul. It is this faith that the Lord hints at when he says, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" — that, by believing, one may understand what he says, and as he says it. Indeed Homer too, the most ancient of poets, in using "hearing" for "perceiving" — the particular for the general — writes most pointedly, "and they themselves heard it." For, taken as a whole, the concord and harmony of the faith on both sides comes to one and the same end, salvation. We have for our unerring witness the apostle, who says: "For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, so that you may be strengthened" — that is, "that I may be encouraged together in you, through our mutual faith, both yours and mine." And again, a little further down, he adds: "For the righteousness of God is revealed in it, from faith to faith." So the apostle plainly proclaims a twofold faith — or rather one faith, admitting of growth and perfecting. For common faith lies underneath like a foundation; thus, to those who longed to be healed and were moved by faith, the Lord would say, "Your faith has saved you." But the special faith, built up upon it, is brought to perfection together with the believer, and is rounded off along with that faith which comes through learning, and through fulfilling the commandments of the Word — such as the apostles were, of whom it was said that faith can move mountains and transplant trees.

As in a meadow the flowers blooming in variety, and in a garden the planting of fruit-trees, are not separated according to their several kinds from those of another kind — and accordingly some men, studious of learning, gathered together Meadows and Heliconian collections and Honeycombs and Robes, variously flowered — so too, since the things that come to memory are taken as they chance, and are neither cleared up in their order nor in their phrasing, but are scattered on purpose, mixed together, the sketch of our Stromateis is variegated after the manner of a meadow. And, being of this sort, they would be to me memoranda for kindling embers; and to him who is fit for knowledge, if he should chance to light upon them, inquiry will come about, with sweat, toward what is profitable and useful. For it is just to reckon the toil, not only of food, but much more of knowledge, the lot of those who are conveyed through the truly narrow and straitened way of the Lord to the everlasting and blessed salvation. And our knowledge, and the spiritual garden, is our Saviour himself, into whom we are planted, transferred and transplanted into the good land out of the old life; and the change of planting contributes to good fruitfulness. The Lord, then, into whom we have been transplanted, is light and the true knowledge.

Our task, then, is to demonstrate that the gnostic alone is holy and devout, worshipping the true God in a manner worthy of God; and upon what is worthy of God there follow the being beloved of God and the love of God. He holds everything that excels to be honourable according to its worth: among objects of sense, rulers and parents and every elder are to be honoured; among objects of instruction, the most ancient philosophy and the most venerable prophecy; among objects of thought, that which is eldest in origin—the timeless and unoriginate Beginning and First-fruit of all that is, the Son. From him we may learn the cause beyond, the Father of all things, the most venerable and most beneficent of all, no longer handed down by speech, but to be revered by veneration and silence with holy awe—reverend and to be worshipped in the highest degree; spoken of, indeed, by the Lord as far as those who were learning could grasp, but apprehended only by those chosen out for knowledge by the Lord—"by those," as the Apostle says, "whose senses have been trained by exercise."

To those who knock in this way, I think, that which is sought is opened; and to those who in this way ask their questions according to the Scriptures, there comes, from God, the goal upon which they advance—the gift of God-given knowledge, apprehensively, through the inquiry that truly shines out by reason. For it is not possible to find without seeking; nor to seek without searching; nor to search without unfolding and laying open, by way of question, what is sought, leading it into clearness; nor again, having passed through the whole examination, not to receive at last the prize—the knowledge of the thing sought. But it is possible for the one who has sought to find, and he will seek if he first supposes that he does not know. Led, then, from here by longing toward the discovery of the noble, he seeks fair-mindedly, without contention, without love of glory—both asking and answering, and besides examining the very things said. For it befits those who hold fast not only to the divine Scriptures, but also to the common notions, to make their inquiries with discovery ending in some profitable conclusion. For another place and crowd awaits the turbulent among men and their vulgar word-mongering; but the lover and disciple of truth ought to be peaceable, even in his inquiries, approaching, through scientific demonstration, without self-love and with love of truth, toward apprehensive knowledge.

Already, indeed, the Saviour himself shows abundantly that, having distributed his goods to the servants according to the capacity of each — a capacity that must be increased by practice — he returns again to settle accounts with them. Then, having welcomed those who had increased his money, the faithful in little, and having promised to set them over much, he bade them enter into the joy of their Lord. But to the one who had hidden away the money entrusted to him for lending, and who gave back idle the very sum he had received, he said, "Wicked and slothful servant, you ought to have put my money with the bankers, and at my coming I would have recovered my own"; and so the useless servant is cast into the outer darkness. "Be strong, then," says Paul also, "in the grace that is in Christ Jesus; and what you have heard from me through many witnesses, commit these things to faithful men, who will be competent to teach others also." And again: "Be diligent to present yourself approved to God, a workman who need not be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth."

We have said already many times that we have neither studied nor practise speaking elegant Greek; for this is enough to lead the many away from the truth. But the true philosophizing will profit those who attend to it, not in the tongue but in the judgment. And one must, I think, who cares for truth, not compose his phrasing by design and pains, but try only to name, as he can, what he wishes. For from those who cling to the phrases and busy themselves about these, the matters slip away. It belongs to the husbandman to take, unharmed, the rose that grows among thorns, and to the craftsman to find out the pearl buried in the flesh of the oyster. And they say that birds too have the most pleasant quality of flesh when, no plentiful food being set before them, they themselves, scratching with their feet, pick out their food with toil. So if anyone, a contemplator of the like, longs that the true should be found, hidden among the many plausible and Greek things — as the true face beneath the masks — he will hunt it down by busying himself. For the power that appeared to Hermas in the vision says: "Whatever can be revealed to you will be revealed."

But sometimes with the mouth we say, "We do not wish to sin," while the mind is set upon sinning. Such a man does not do what he wishes only out of fear, so that the punishment may not be reckoned against him. Now humanity has certain things that are both necessary and natural, and others that are natural only. Clothing is both necessary and natural; but sexual intercourse is natural, yet not necessary. I have set down these utterances to refute those Basilidians who do not live rightly, on the supposition either that they have license to sin because of their perfection, or that in any case they will be saved by nature even if they sin now, because of their innate election—since not even the founders of their doctrines allow them to do the same things. Let them not, then, while creeping under the name of Christ and living more licentiously than the most unrestrained of the heathen, fasten blasphemy upon that name; for such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, whose end shall be according to their works.

When, then, our whole purpose has been completed, in those notebooks in which, if the Spirit will, we serve the pressing need (for great is the necessity of the things that must be said first concerning the truth), then indeed we shall pursue the truly gnostic natural philosophy, being initiated into the lesser mysteries before the greater, so that nothing may stand in the way of the truly divine teaching of holy things, the things that must be related and handed down beforehand having been already purified and prefigured. Now the natural philosophy, or rather the contemplation, according to the rule of the truth of the gnostic tradition, hangs upon the discussion concerning cosmogony, ascending from there to the theological kind. Hence with good reason we shall make the beginning of the tradition from the prophesied generation, setting down in part the doctrines of the heterodox too, and trying as far as we are able to resolve them. But this shall be written, if God will and as He inspires; for the present we must pass on to what lies before us, and complete the ethical discourse.

Hence, perceiving the greatness of the power, they asked that faith be added to them — that faith which, like a grain of mustard seed, bites into the soul to its profit and grows mightily within it, so that upon it may rest our reasonings about things on high. For if a man knows God by nature, as Basilides supposes — calling the special faith intelligence, and at once a kingdom, and the creation of beautiful things, and worthy of the substance of its maker, existing close to him — interpreting it as substance and not as a thing in his own power, as nature and as hypostasis, the boundless beauty of an undeferred creation, and not as the rational assent of a soul that has freedom of will, then the commandments, both those of the old covenant and those of the new, are superfluous, since one is saved by nature, as Valentinus would have it, and is by nature faithful and elect, as Basilides thinks. In that case nature would have been able, at some time or other, even without the Saviour's coming, to shine out of itself. But if they say that the Lord's sojourn was necessary, then the special properties of nature have departed from them, since election is saved by learning and purification and the doing of good works, and not by nature. For Abraham, who believed by hearing the voice that under the oak in Mamre promised, "To you I give this land, and to your seed" — was he elect or not? If he was not, how did he believe at once, as it were by nature? But if he was elect, their hypothesis is undone, since election is found even before the Lord's coming, and is indeed saved; for "it was reckoned to him for righteousness."

And in another way too knowledge is said to be twofold: the one common, the understanding and apprehension that is in all men alike, shown forth publicly in the recognizing of each of the things that lie before us — in which not only the rational powers but perhaps the irrational also will share, and which I for my part would never call knowledge, since it is by nature apprehended even through the senses; the other, named knowledge in the special sense, is characterized from the resolve and the reason, in respect of which the rational powers alone become knowledges, applying themselves purely to the things of mind by the bare activity of the soul. "A good man," says David, "is he who pities those who are perishing in error, and lends, of the imparting of the word of truth" — not haphazardly, but "he will order his words in judgement," with deep reckoning; "this man scattered, he gave to the poor."

The service of God, then, for the gnostic is the unbroken care of his soul and his occupation with the divine through love that never ceases. For of the service rendered to men, one kind is that which improves, the other that which ministers. Medicine improves the body, philosophy the soul. From children to parents, and from subjects to rulers, there comes a ministering benefit. Likewise in the Church the presbyters preserve the image of that which improves, and the deacons that which ministers. Both these forms of service are rendered to God by the angels in the administration of earthly things, and by the gnostic himself, who ministers to God and displays to men the contemplation that improves, so that he may be appointed to teach for the correction of mankind. For he alone is devout who serves God well and irreproachably in human affairs. For just as the best tending of plants is that by which the fruits are produced and gathered through skill and agricultural experience, furnishing men with the benefit derived from them, so the devotion of the gnostic, taking up into itself the fruits of the men who through him have come to believe—as more and more are brought to recognition and so are saved—accomplishes through experience the best of harvests. And if godliness is a settled disposition preserving what is fitting toward God, then he alone who is godly is beloved of God; and this would be the man who knows what is fitting both in knowledge and in life, knowing how he ought to live who is to become, and is already being made, like to God.

If, then, both proclaim the word — the one by writing, the other by the living voice — how are they not both to be welcomed, since they have made their faith active through love? As for the cause of one who fails to choose the better part, God is not to blame. To lend out the word is the work of the one; to test it and either choose it or not is the work of the other, and the judgment is decided within themselves. The science of heralding is already, in a manner, angelic, in whichever way it works — by the hand or by the tongue — for it brings benefit. "He who sows to the spirit will of the spirit reap eternal life; and let us not grow weary in doing the good." For the very greatest gifts are conferred, by divine providence, on whoever happens upon the word: a beginning of faith, an eagerness for the right way of life, an impulse toward truth, a movement that seeks, a trace of knowledge — in a word, it gives the occasions of salvation. And those who have been genuinely nourished on the words of truth, having received provision for the eternal life, take wing toward heaven. Most admirably, then, the Apostle says: "In everything commending ourselves as servants of God, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing yet possessing all things; our mouth is open to you." And, writing to Timothy, he declares: "I charge you, before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels, that you keep these things without prejudice, doing nothing out of partiality."

Continence, then, is contempt of the body, in accordance with the confession we make to God. For continence has to do not only with sexual matters but with the other things too which the soul wrongly desires, not being satisfied with what is necessary. There is continence with respect to the tongue, to possessions, to their use, and to desire. It does not merely teach self-control; it actually furnishes us with self-control, since it is a power and a divine grace. So we must say what our people think on the matter set before us. We count blessed both celibacy and those to whom this has been granted by God; but we admire monogamy and the dignity of a single marriage, saying that we ought to share another's suffering and to bear one another's burdens, lest anyone who seems to stand firmly should himself also fall. And concerning a second marriage, the apostle says, "If a man burns, let him marry."

If anyone, daring to follow Marcion, should say that the Creator saves the man who believes in him with a salvation proper to himself, the power of the Good will be outdone by it, coming late and after the Creator they so applaud, and itself only then setting about to save, either by teaching or by imitation of the other. But even if the Good thus saves, according to them, he does so neither over his own creatures nor with the consent of him who made the creation, but by force or by guile. And how is he still good, who is thus and is later? But if his place differs, and the abode of the Almighty falls short of the abode of the Good God, still the will of him who saves does not fall short of the Good, since it was that which made the beginning. Foolish, then, are the unbelievers, as is shown from what we have already gone through; for "their paths are crooked, and they do not know peace," says the prophet. "Foolish and unlearned questionings avoid," the inspired Paul exhorted, "because they breed quarrels." And Aeschylus has cried out: "Do not toil in vain at things that bring no profit."

In this way, then, he is first a lover of God. For as he who honours his father is a lover of his father, so he who honours God is a lover of God. And it appears to me that there are three results of the gnostic faculty: first, to know things; second, to perform whatever reason dictates; and third, to be able to hand on, in a manner worthy of God, the things hidden in the truth. He, then, who is persuaded that God is almighty and has learned the divine mysteries from his only-begotten Son—how is this man an atheist? For the atheist is he who does not believe that God exists; the superstitious man is he who fears the daemonic powers, who deifies everything—wood and stone and spirit—and enslaves the man who does not live according to reason.

Both of these men, then, must necessarily test themselves: the one, whether he is worthy to speak and to leave records behind; the other, whether he is fit to listen and to read — just as some, distributing the thanksgiving, allow each man of the people, as is the custom, to take his own portion. For conscience is the best guide to the exact choosing and avoiding; and its firm foundation is an upright life together with fitting instruction. And to follow those already tested and proved is best, both for grasping the truth and for carrying out the commandments. So "whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup."

For we know that the inquiry which proceeds together with faith, building upon the foundation of faith the magnificent knowledge of the truth, is the best of all. We know, too, that what is plain is not inquired into (as whether it is day, when it is day), nor what is obscure and will never become plain (as whether the stars are even or odd in number), nor again what admits of opposite arguments — and those things admit of them which can be argued with equal force by those who handle the contrary position, as whether the unborn child is a living being or not. There is a fourth kind, when from one of these two sides an irrefutable and indissoluble argument is put forward. If, then, the ground for inquiry is removed in every one of these ways, faith is made firm; for we set before them that irrefutable proposition, namely that it is God who speaks, and who, concerning each one of the matters I am investigating, supplies the answer in Scripture.

It would be fitting, then, for one who has taken up the task of benefiting his neighbours to consider whether he has rushed rashly into teaching, out of rivalry with others; whether his sharing of the word is a thing of vanity; whether he reaps this reward alone — the salvation of his hearers; and whether he speaks not to please men. For the man who speaks through written records has escaped the reproach of flattery and of taking bribes alike. "For we were never found using words of flattery," says the Apostle, "as you know, nor a pretext for greed — God is witness — nor did we seek glory from men, neither from you nor from others, though we might have stood on our weight as apostles of Christ; but we were gentle in your midst, as a nurse cherishes her own children." In the same way, those who partake of the divine words must be watched: whether they come to this point merely out of curiosity, to inspect, as men inspect the buildings of cities; or whether they approach for some worldly advantage, having learned that those consecrated to Christ are generous with what they have. As for the hypocrites — let them be. But if anyone wishes not merely to seem just but to be so, it befits him to be conscious within himself of the noblest things.

Who, then, is so godless as to disbelieve God, and to demand of God proofs as one demands them of men? Again, of inquiries, some require sense-perception — as if one asks whether fire is hot or snow white; some require admonition and rebuke, as Aristotle says, like that question, whether one ought to honour one's parents. And there are some that deserve punishment, such as demanding proofs whether there is providence. Providence, then, existing, it is impious to hold that the whole work of prophecy and of the dispensation concerning the Saviour did not come about according to providence; and perhaps one ought not even to attempt to prove such things, since the divine providence is manifest both from the sight of all visible things, which are works of skill and wisdom — some of them coming to be in order, others manifested in order — and from the fact that he who gave us being and life gave us also reason, wishing us to live rationally and well. For the Word of the Father of all is not this uttered word, but the wisdom and most manifest goodness of God, and again a power all-mastering and truly divine, not incomprehensible even to those who do not confess him — an all-sovereign will.

If, then, the harvest is great but the labourers few, it is right indeed to pray that we may have as great an abundance of labourers as possible. And husbandry is twofold: the one unwritten, the other written. In whichever way the labourer of the Lord sows the noble grain, and makes the ears grow and reaps them, he will show himself a truly divine husbandman. "Labour," says the Lord, "not for the food that perishes, but for that which abides unto eternal life." And nourishment is taken either by food or by words. And truly, "blessed are the peacemakers" — those who teach anew the men here in this life who are warred upon by their wandering and by ignorance, and who lead them over into the peace that is in the word and in the life lived according to God, and who feed those who hunger after righteousness by the distribution of bread. For there are souls too that have their own nourishment: some growing by recognition and knowledge, others grazing upon Greek philosophy, of which, as of nuts, not the whole is edible. "He who plants and he who waters," being servants of him who gives the increase, "are one" in their service; "and each will receive his own wage according to his own labour. For we are fellow-workers of God; you are God's tillage, God's building," according to the Apostle.

But since some are unbelievers and some contentious, not all attain to the perfection of the Good. For neither is it possible to attain it without choice, nor again does the whole rest upon our own resolve — as, for instance, the outcome. For by grace we are saved — yet not without good works, but we must, being by nature disposed toward the Good, acquire a certain zeal for it; and we must possess a sound resolve, unrepenting in the pursuit of what is noble, for which above all we have need of the divine grace, of right teaching, of pure docility, and of the drawing of the Father toward himself. For, being bound to this earthly body, we apprehend the things of sense through the body, but lay hold of the things of mind through the rational faculty itself. And if anyone expects to grasp all things by sense, he has fallen far from the truth. Spiritually, then, the apostle writes concerning the knowledge of God: "For now we see as through a mirror, but then face to face." For to few is the vision of the truth given. So Plato too says in the Epinomis: "I do not say it is possible for all men to become blessed and happy, except a few — as long, that is, as we live; this I lay down. But there is a good hope that, when one has died, he may attain all things." The same is the purport of the words in Moses: "No one shall see my face and live." For it is plain that no one can, during the time of this life, grasp God clearly; but "the pure in heart shall see God," when they have come to the final perfection. For since the soul was too weak to apprehend the things that are, we had need of a divine teacher. The Saviour is sent down, both teacher and supplier of the acquisition of the Good, the holy token of the great and unutterable providence.

We must not, then, allow the hearers to form their judgment by comparison, nor hand over the word for cross-examination to men reared in the arts of every kind of discourse and in the inflated powers of clever argument, whose souls are already preoccupied and not first emptied. But when a man, out of faith, chooses to feast, he stands firm for the reception of the divine words, having gained faith as a reasoned judgment; and there follows from this an abundant conviction. This, indeed, was that prophetic saying: "Unless you believe, neither will you understand." "So then, as we have opportunity, let us work the good toward all, but especially toward those of the household of faith." And let each of these, after the manner of blessed David, sing with thanksgiving: "You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow. You will make me hear joy and gladness; the bones that have been humbled shall rejoice. Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inmost parts. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the gladness of your salvation, and uphold me with a guiding spirit."

"Where, then, is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?" he says. And again: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will bring to nothing" — meaning, plainly, these would-be wise men and these contentious ones. Beautifully, then, does Jeremiah say: "Thus says the Lord: Stand upon the ways and ask for the everlasting paths, which is the good way, and walk in it, and you shall find purification for your souls." "Ask," he says, and learn from those who know, without contentiousness and without strife. And having learned the way of truth, let us walk it straight, without turning back, until we light upon what we long for. With reason, then, did the king of the Romans — Numa was his name — being a Pythagorean, first of all men found a temple to Faith and Peace. And to Abraham, who believed, righteousness was reckoned. He, while pursuing the lofty philosophy of things in the air, and the sublime study of the motions of the heavens, was called Abram, which is interpreted "lofty father"; but afterwards, when he looked up to heaven — whether he saw the Son in the Spirit, as some explain it, or a glorious angel, or in some other way came to know a God greater than the creation and than all the order within it — he takes on the alpha, the knowledge of the one and only God, and is called Abraham, having become, instead of a natural philosopher, wise and a lover of God. For it is interpreted "elect father of sound." For the audible word resounds; and the father of this is the mind, and the mind of the earnest man is what is chosen out.

The man who speaks to those present both tests them by time and judges by discernment, and distinguishes from the rest the one who is able to hear, watching his words, his ways, his character, his life, his movements, his bearing, his glance, his speech — the crossroads, the rock, the trodden path, the fruitful earth, the land overrun with weeds, the rich and good and cultivated ground that can multiply the seed many times. But the man who speaks through written records makes his consecration to God, crying out these things in writing: not for gain, not for vainglory, not to be overcome by partiality, not to be enslaved by fear, not to be lifted up by pleasure — but to enjoy only the salvation of his readers, in which he has no share even now, but which he awaits in hope, expecting the recompense that will surely be paid by him who has promised to pay the labourers their wage according to their worth. Yet neither should the man enrolled among men aim at a return. For has not the one who has boasted of his good deed already received his recompense in the good repute it brought? And the man who does anything of his duty for the sake of a return — whether, as a benefactor, hastening to be repaid, or, as an evildoer, steering clear of recompense — is he not caught in worldly custom? But one must imitate the Lord so far as one can. And this would be the man who serves the will of God, having received freely and giving freely, taking as his worthy wage the very citizenship itself. "The hire of a harlot shall not enter the holy place," he says.

And I am moved very greatly to praise the poet of Acragas, who sings the praises of faith in some such fashion as this: "O friends, I know indeed that truth is in the words I shall declare; but very grievous it is to men, and the onset of faith upon the mind is full of envy." For this reason the apostle too exhorts us, that our faith may be "not in the wisdom of men" — of those who profess to persuade — "but in the power of God," which alone, even without demonstrations, by bare faith, is able to save. "The most approved knows how to guard against what is merely believed; and moreover justice will lay hold of the framers and witnesses of falsehoods," says the Ephesian. For he too, having learned from the barbarian philosophy, knows of the purification by fire of those who have lived ill — which the Stoics afterwards called conflagration; in accordance with which they teach that the individual man will rise again, thus paying court to the resurrection. Plato says that the earth is at certain times purified by fire and water, somewhat thus: "Many and various destructions of men have come to pass, and will come to pass — the greatest by fire and water, and others, lesser, by countless other means." And a little after he adds: "But the truth is, there is a shifting of the bodies that move about the earth and through the heavens, and at long intervals there comes a destruction of things upon the earth by a great fire." Then concerning the deluge he goes on: "But when, in turn, the gods purge the earth with waters and flood it, the herdsmen and shepherds in the mountains are preserved, while those in the cities among us are swept by the rivers into the sea.

It is forbidden, then, to bring "the price of a dog" to the altar. But whoever has had the eye of his soul blunted, by bad nourishment and bad teaching, against its native light — let him walk toward the truth that makes plain in writing the unwritten things. "You who thirst, go to the water," says Isaiah; and "drink water from your own vessels," Solomon advises. In the Laws, indeed, Plato — that philosopher sprung from the Hebrews — bids the farmers neither to draw water for irrigation nor to take it from others, unless they have first dug for themselves down to the so-called virgin soil and found the ground without water. For it is just to relieve want, but not good to provision idleness; and so Pythagoras said that it is reasonable to help a man take up a burden, but not to help him lay it down. And the Scripture kindles together the spark of the soul and strains its native eye toward contemplation, perhaps even implanting something — as the husbandman who grafts — but rousing up what is already there. "For many among us," according to the divine Apostle, "are weak and sickly, and a good number sleep. But if we examined ourselves, we would not be judged."

We have shown, in the first book of the Stromateis, that the philosophers of the Greeks are called thieves, as having taken the most authoritative of their doctrines from Moses and the prophets without acknowledgement. To these things we shall add this also: that those angels who had obtained the lot above, slipping down into pleasures, told out the secrets to the women — as much of them as had come to their knowledge — while the other angels concealed them, or rather kept them for the Lord's coming. From that source flowed the teaching of providence, and the revelation of things on high. And when prophecy had already been spread abroad among the poets of the Greeks, the dogmatic treatment of the philosophers came into being — in part true, when they fell upon the truth by conjecture, in part going astray, when they failed to understand what was hidden in the prophetic allegory. This it is our purpose to mark out briefly as we run through the more pressing matters.

This treatise is not a piece of writing artfully made for display; rather, these are memoranda stored up for my old age, a remedy against forgetfulness, simply an image and shadow-sketch of those vivid and living words, and of the blessed and truly memorable men, whom I was counted worthy to hear. Of these, one was in Greece, the Ionian; others were in Greater Greece — one of them from Coele Syria, another from Egypt; and others were across the East, the one of that region from among the Assyrians, the other in Palestine, a Hebrew by descent. But when I met with the last (though in power he was the first), I found rest, having tracked him down where he lay hidden in Egypt. A Sicilian bee in truth, plucking the flowers of the prophetic and apostolic meadow, he begot in the souls of his hearers a pure and undefiled thing of knowledge. These men, preserving the true tradition of the blessed teaching directly from Peter and James, from John and Paul, the holy apostles — son receiving from father (though few are like their fathers) — came, by God's will, down even to us, to deposit those ancestral and apostolic seeds.

We say, then, that faith must go forward not idle and alone, but together with inquiry. For I do not say this, that one should not inquire at all; for "Seek, and you shall find," he says. "What is sought is to be caught, but what is neglected slips away," according to Sophocles. And Menander the comic poet says the like: "All things that are sought, the wisest say, have need of care." But one must stretch out the discerning part of the soul toward the discovery, and clear away the obstacles, and cast away utterly contentiousness and envy, and strife itself, that worst of things, which shall most miserably perish from among men. For most beautifully does Timon of Phlius write: "Strife, the bane of mortals, goes about with empty din, sister and handmaid of man-slaying Quarrel; and blind she rolls about over all things, and then fixes herself upon a mortal's head and casts him down from hope." Then, a little further on, he adds: "Who set these to fight in deadly strife? The rabble that runs in the train of Echo; for, angered at their silence, it stirred up against men a chattering disease." And many perished over the argument that denies falsely, and the horned argument, and the hidden one, and the crocodile, and the sorites, and the veiled one, and over ambiguities and sophisms.

And I know well that they will rejoice — I mean not that they take pleasure in this exposition itself, but only in the keeping of the tradition according to these notes. For such an outline is, I think, the work of a soul that longs to keep the blessed tradition unfading. "A man who loves wisdom will gladden his father." Wells that are drawn from yield clearer water; but what no one shares turns to corruption. Use too keeps iron cleaner, while disuse breeds rust upon it. In a word, regular exercise produces a healthy condition both in spirits and in bodies. "No one lights a lamp and puts it under the bushel, but on the lampstand, that it may shine for those counted worthy of the same feast." For what use is wisdom that does not make wise the man able to hear? Moreover, the Saviour saves always and works always, "as he sees the Father." And in teaching a man learns more, and in speaking he often hears along with those who listen to him; for there is one Teacher of both speaker and hearer, who pours forth upon both the mind and the word.

But to inquire about God, if it tends not to strife but to discovery, is salutary. For it is written in David: "The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their heart shall live for ever and ever." For those who seek according to the true seeking, praising the Lord, shall be filled with the gift that comes from God — that is, with knowledge — and their soul shall live; for the soul is allegorized as the heart that supplies the life, since through the Son the Father is made known. Yet we must not give over our ears unreservedly to all who speak and write, since cups too, when taken hold of by many by the handles and so befouled, lose their handles, and, falling besides, are themselves broken. In the same way those who have befouled the pure hearing of the faith with many trivialities, becoming at last deaf to the truth, prove useless and fall to the ground.

And so the Lord did not forbid us to "keep sabbath" from the good, but allowed us to share the divine mysteries and that holy light with those able to receive them. He did not, mark you, reveal to many what did not belong to many, but to the few, to those whom he knew it befitted, those able to receive and to be shaped to them. The unspeakable things, like God himself, are entrusted to the word, not to writing. And if anyone should say it is written, "Nothing is hidden that shall not be made manifest, nor anything covered that shall not be uncovered," let him hear from us too that to the man who listens in secret the secret will be made manifest — this is what was foretold through that oracle — and to the man able to receive in a veiled way what is handed down, the veiled and the truth will be revealed; and what is hidden from the many will become manifest to the few. For why do not all know the truth? Why is righteousness not loved, if righteousness belongs to all? But the mysteries are delivered mystically, that they may be in the mouth of the one who speaks and of the one to whom it is spoken — or rather, not in the voice, but in the understanding. "And God has set in the Church first apostles, then prophets, then evangelists, then pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ."

Not without reason, then, do we bid little children, taken hold of by the ears, to kiss their relatives — hinting, surely, by this, that the fellow-feeling of love comes to birth through hearing. And God is love, who is known to those who love, as God is faithful, who is delivered to the faithful through learning. And we must make ourselves at home with him through the divine love, that we may behold like with like, hearkening to the word of truth guilelessly and purely, after the manner of children obedient to us. And this is what was hinted at by whoever it was that inscribed over the entrance of the temple at Epidaurus: "Pure must he be who goes within the fragrant shrine; and purity is to think holy thoughts." "Unless you become as these little children," he says, "you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." For here is the temple of God, founded upon three foundations — faith, hope, and love.

The writing of these memoranda of mine is, I know well, weak compared with that gracious spirit which we were counted worthy to hear; yet it would be an image recalling the archetype to the man "struck by the thyrsus." "Speak to a wise man," it says, "and he will be wiser; and to him who has, it shall be added." And it does not promise to interpret the unspeakable things adequately — far from it — but only to bring them to mind, whether for when we have forgotten, or so that we may not forget at all. Much, I know well, has slipped past us through length of time, falling away unrecorded. And so, easing the weakness of my memory, providing for myself a saving reminder, a systematic exposition of the chief points, I have of necessity made use of this outline. There are, indeed, some things we have not even recalled (for great was the power in those blessed men); there are also things which, remaining unrecorded, have now escaped with time; and others that were quenched within the very mind as they faded — for such a service is not easy for those not approved. These things, reviving by these notes, I willingly pass over some, selecting with knowledge, afraid to write what I guarded against even speaking — not from grudging (for that would not be lawful), but fearing for my readers, lest somewhere they should stumble in another direction, and we be found, as the proverb-makers say, holding out a sword to a child. For it is not possible that what has been written should not fall out, even if it has remained unpublished by me; rolling on forever, using only the one written voice, it answers nothing more than what is written to the one who questions it further. For it necessarily needs a helper, either the one who wrote it or some other who has stepped into the same track.

There are also things at which my writing will hint; some it will set forth plainly, others it will only mention; it will try to speak while hiding, to disclose while concealing, and to point while keeping silent. It will set out the teachings dogmatized by the notable heresies, and will answer them with all that ought to be arranged beforehand for the knowledge that comes by the higher contemplation — a knowledge which will advance for us, as we proceed according to the glorious and venerable rule of the tradition from the genesis of the world, setting out first the things that must be grasped before the contemplation of nature, and clearing away beforehand the obstacles that stand in the way of the sequence; so that our ears may be ready for the reception of the gnostic tradition, the ground having first been cleansed of thorns and of all the weeds, as a husbandman clears it for the planting of a vineyard. For there is a contest, and a preliminary contest; and there are mysteries before the mysteries. Nor will these notes of ours shrink from using the noblest things of philosophy and of the rest of the preliminary education. "For not only for the Hebrews and those under the Law," according to the Apostle, "is it reasonable to become a Jew, but also, for the sake of the Greeks, a Greek, that we may gain all." And in the Epistle to the Colossians he writes: "admonishing every man and teaching in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ."

The grace of contemplation suits the outline of these memoranda in another way too. The abundance of good learning is like a seasoning mingled in with the athlete's diet — not the diet of one given to luxury, but of one who, through honourable ambition, takes a good appetite. So in singing we relax the over-high pitch of solemnity with melody. And just as men who wish to address a crowd often do so through a herald, that what is said may be the better heard, so here too — for the discourse before the tradition itself is addressed to many — we must set out the familiar opinions and sayings that ring loud among them at every turn, by which the hearers will the more be turned. And, in a word (for in the many small pearls there is the one, and in the great catch of fish the finest fish), with time and toil the truth will shine out, if a good helper is at hand; for it is through men that most of God's benefits are bestowed.

All of us, then, who use our eyes behold what falls before them, but different men for different ends. The cook and the shepherd do not behold the sheep alike: the one is busy whether it is fat, the other watches it for good breeding. Let one man milk the sheep, if he needs nourishment; let him shear the wool, if he needs covering. So let the fruit of Greek good-learning come forward for me. For I do not think anyone holds any writing so fortunate that no one will contradict it; rather, that writing must be reckoned reasonable which no one will contradict reasonably. And so too one must accept that action and that choice — not the one that is blameless, but the one that no one will reasonably blame. Nor does it follow that if a man does not do a thing as his primary aim, he does it from circumstance; rather, managing something with godly wisdom and adapting himself, he will act. For the man who has virtue needs no further road to virtue, nor does the strong man need recovery. And just as farmers first water the ground, so we too, with the drinkable part of the discourse among the Greeks, first water their earthly element, that it may receive the spiritual seed cast into it and be able to nourish it with ease.

The Miscellanies will contain the truth mingled with the doctrines of philosophy, or rather veiled and hidden within them, as the edible kernel within the shell of the nut; for it is fitting, I think, that the seeds of truth be kept only for the husbandmen of faith. I am not unaware of the things harped on by certain ignorant and timid men, who say that one must busy oneself with what is most necessary and holds faith together, and pass over what is external and superfluous, since it wears us out to no purpose and detains us about things that contribute nothing to the end. Others even suppose that philosophy entered life for evil, to the harm of mankind, brought in by some wicked inventor. But I, throughout the whole of the Miscellanies, will show that wickedness has an evil nature and could never become the husbandman of anything good, hinting somehow that philosophy too is a work of divine providence.

What other method, then, could be better or clearer for the beginning of such teaching than to go through, in discourse, the name proposed, so plainly that all who speak the same tongue can follow? Is, then, the name "demonstration" such a thing as "blityri"—a mere sound signifying nothing? And how is it that neither the philosopher, nor the orator, nor indeed the judge, brings forward "demonstration" as a meaningless name, nor does any of those at law fail to know its signification, that it does not exist? Indeed, the philosophers procure demonstration as something substantial, one in one way and another in another. Concerning everything sought, then, if one should rightly determine the matter, one would refer the discourse to no other beginning more agreed upon than that which is signified, out of its name, by common consent among all those of the same race and the same tongue. Then, setting out from here, one must inquire whether the thing signified, concerning which the discourse is, exists or not; and next, if it should be shown to exist, one must inquire exactly into its nature, of what sort it is, and whether perhaps it oversteps the rank assigned to it.

"And be not lifted up in your own wisdom," the Proverbs say, "but in all your ways make her known, that she may set straight your ways; and your foot shall not stumble." For by these things it wishes to show that the works must be in accordance with the word; but also that we must show that we have the useful, chosen out of all education. And the ways of wisdom are various that set straight toward the way of truth, and the way is faith. "And let not your foot stumble" — it speaks of certain things that seem to oppose the one and divine providential administration. Whence it adds: "Be not prudent in your own eyes" — according to the godless reasonings that set themselves against the dispensation of God — "but fear the only powerful God," upon which it follows that nothing is opposed to God. And besides, the addition teaches plainly that the divine fear is a turning away from evil; for it says: "And turn away from every evil." This is the discipline of wisdom; "for whom the Lord loves he disciplines," making him grieve unto understanding, but restoring him to peace and incorruption.

Let our notebooks, as we have often said, on account of those who read them carelessly and without skill, be variously, as the name itself indicates, spread out like a patchwork, passing continually from one thing to another, and indicating one thing by the connection of words while pointing to something else. For those who seek gold, says Heraclitus, dig up much earth and find little; but those who are truly of the golden kind, mining what is akin to them, will find the much in the little; for the Scripture will find one man who understands it. The Stromateis of these notebooks aid both toward recollection and toward the manifestation of the truth, for the man able to inquire with reason. And we too must work further at these and find out other things besides, since, for those going on a road they do not know, it is enough merely to point out the way that leads there;

But before setting hand to what lies before us, we must, by way of preface, render in addition what is wanting to the end of the fifth book of the Stromateis. For since we have set forth that the symbolic kind is ancient, and that not only the prophets among us used it, but also the more part of the ancient Greeks, and not a few of the other barbarians among the nations; and since we ought to have gone over the mysteries of those initiated — these things I postpone to make clear when we come, in going over the doctrines about first principles current among the Greeks, to refute them; for we shall show that the mysteries too hold to this contemplation; but having set forth that the showing-forth of the Greek mind was irradiated by the truth given to us through the Scriptures, and having shown, by the way the borrowing of the truth passed over to them — if it is not harsh to say it — come, let us set the Greeks forth as witnesses of the theft against themselves. For those who thus downright steal their own things from one another make sure of being thieves, and yet, even against their will, plainly show that they appropriate our truth in secret among their fellows. For those who will not keep their hands off their own will hardly keep them off ours.

And since it does not suffice merely to state one's opinion about the thing sought (for it is open to the opponent equally to declare in turn what he wills), but one must confirm what is said: if the judgement of it should be referred to something likewise disputed, and that again likewise to another disputed thing, the matter will go on to infinity and will be indemonstrable; but if the confirmation of the thing not agreed upon should be referred to something agreed upon by all, that must be made the beginning of the teaching. Every name proposed, then, must be taken over into a discourse agreed upon and clear to those who share in the consideration—a discourse that will be the beginning of the teaching, and that will explain the discovery of the things sought. Come, then, let the name "sun" be proposed. The Stoics, then, say that this is "an intelligent kindling out of the waters of the sea." Is not their definition more obscure than the very name, needing another demonstration whether it is true? Better, then, to say, in common and clear discourse, that the sun is named "the brightest of the things that move through heaven"; for this discourse is more trustworthy, I think, and clearer, and equally agreed upon by all.

The barbarian philosophy, then, which we follow, is in truth perfect and true. So it says in Wisdom: "For he himself gave me an unerring knowledge of the things that are, to know the constitution of the world," and the rest, down to "and the powers of roots." In all these it has comprehended the natural contemplation, that concerning the world of sense, of all the things that have come to be. And next it hints also at the intelligible things, by what it adds: "And whatever is hidden and manifest I came to know; for wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me." You have, in brief, the promise of our philosophy. And the learning of these things, practised together with right conduct of life, leads up, through the wisdom that is the artificer of all things, to the Ruler of the universe — a thing hard to catch and hard to hunt, ever retreating and standing far off from the pursuer. Yet the same, being far off, has come very near — an unspeakable wonder. "I am a God who draws near," says the Lord — far off in essence (for how could the generated ever come near the ungenerated?), but very near in power, by which all things are enfolded in his bosom. "If anyone does anything in secret," he says, "shall I not see him?" And indeed the power of God is ever present, touching us by the power that beholds and benefits and educates.

Those who trace their descent from Carpocrates and Epiphanes hold that women should be common property; and from them the greatest blasphemy has flowed against the name of Christ. This Epiphanes, whose writings are still in circulation, was the son of Carpocrates and of a mother named Alexandria; on his father's side an Alexandrian, on his mother's a Cephallenian. He lived in all seventeen years, and is honoured as a god at Same in Cephallenia, where a temple of dressed stone, with altars, sacred precincts, and a shrine of the Muses, has been built and consecrated to him; and the Cephallenians, gathering at the temple at the new moon, offer sacrifice to celebrate his apotheosis as his birthday, pour libations, feast, and sing hymns. He was educated by his father both in the ordinary curriculum and in the doctrines of Plato, and was the founder of the monadic knowledge, from which the sect of the Carpocratians took its origin.

and after this, one must already walk on, and find out for oneself the rest of the way—just as, they say, when a certain man who once had a slave asked what he might do to please his master, the Pythia answered, "You will find if you seek." It is truly hard, it seems, to find out a good that is hidden, since the sweat of virtue is set before us, and
long and steep is the path to her, and rough at first; but when one reaches the summit, then it is easy, hard though it was before.

For truly narrow and pressed is the way of the Lord, and the kingdom of God is for those who use force; whence He says, "Seek, and you shall find," holding to the truly royal road and not running off from it.

And I will pass over the doctrines of philosophy in silence, since those who divided up the heresies confess in writing — that they may not be convicted of ingratitude — that they took the most authoritative of their doctrines from Socrates. But using the testimonies of a few of the much-talked-of and reputable men among the Greeks, and having convicted their thievish kind, taking the periods indifferently, I will turn to what follows. When Orpheus, then, had written, "Thus nothing was more cursed nor more chilling than woman," Homer says outright, "Thus there is nothing more dread nor more cursed than woman." And when Musaeus had written, "As ever skill is far better than strength," Homer says, "Surely the woodcutter is better by skill than by force." Again, when Musaeus had written, "And in the same way too the grain-giving field puts forth leaves: some die away among the ash-trees, others it puts forth; so too it whirls round the generation and tribe of men," Homer transcribes, "As of leaves, some the wind sheds upon the ground, but the wood, flourishing, puts forth others, and the season of spring comes on; so of the generation of men, one springs up and another passes away." Again, when Homer had said, "It is not holy to exult over slain men," Archilochus and Cratinus write — the one, "For it is not noble to mock at men once dead"; and Cratinus in the Spartans, "A fearful thing is this for men, to boast greatly over slain warriors."

Faith, then, in the knowledge of God is the first thing, together with the Saviour's teaching the conviction that to do wrong in no way whatever—this is what one must hold to be fitting to the knowledge of God. By this the most devout man is the most powerful being on earth, and the angel the most powerful in heaven, as being nearer in place and already partaking more purely of the eternal and blessed life. But most perfect and most holy and most sovereign and most ruling and most kingly and most beneficent is the nature of the Son, which is nearest to the one Almighty. This is the greatest pre-eminence, which orders all things according to the will of the Father and steers the whole most excellently, working all things with untiring and unwearied power, looking through the things by which it acts upon the hidden thoughts. For the Son of God never departs from his watch-tower, not being divided, not severed, not passing from place to place, but being everywhere always and contained nowhere—wholly mind, wholly the Father's light, wholly eye, seeing all things, hearing all things, knowing all things, searching the powers with power. To him is subject the whole host of angels and of gods—to the paternal Word who has taken up the holy administration "because of him who subjected" all to him, on whose account also are all his men: but some "by recognition," others not yet; and some as friends, others as faithful household servants, others simply as servants. This is the Teacher who trains the gnostic by mysteries.

Hence Moses, persuaded that God would never be known by human wisdom, says: "Show me yourself," and forces his way into the darkness where the voice of God was — that is, into the unapproachable and formless conceptions concerning Being. For God is not in darkness or in a place, but above both place and time and the property of the things that have come to be. Wherefore he is never found in a part, neither containing nor contained, either by some limit or by cutting off. "For what kind of house will you build me?" says the Lord. But he did not build even for himself, being uncontainable; and though heaven be called his throne, not even so is he contained, but he rests, delighting in his creation. It is plain, then, that the truth has been hidden from us — which has already been shown from one example, and a little later we shall present it through more.

This man, then, says in his work On Justice that the justice of God is a kind of community based on equality. The heaven, stretched out equally on every side, encircles the whole earth in a ring; the night displays all the stars alike; and the sun, the cause of the day and the father of light, God poured out from above equally upon all who have the power to see, and they all see in common, since He makes no distinction between rich and poor, commoner and ruler, foolish and wise, female and male, free and slave. Nor does He do anything contrary to this even among the irrational creatures, but pouring Himself out from above in common and equally upon all living things, He establishes justice for the good and the bad alike, since no one is able to have more or to deprive his neighbour, so as to double his own light at that neighbour's expense. The sun causes common food to spring up for all living things; the common justice is given to all alike; and toward such ends the race of oxen comes into being in the same way as the oxen, the race of swine as the swine, the race of sheep as the sheep, and so with all the rest; for in them justice is shown to be community. Then, in accordance with this community, all things are sown alike according to their kind, and common food is set forth, growing on the ground, for all the cattle and for all alike, controlled by no law, but present in harmony for all by the bounty of Him who gives and commands.

With good reason, then, much is the fertile power in the small seed of the doctrines contained in this work, like "the all-herb of the field," as the Scripture says. Hence the Stromateis of these notebooks bear an apt title, plainly culled like that ancient offering of which Sophocles writes:

For there was wool of sheep, and there was from the vine a libation and a grape well stored away, and there was within all kinds of fruit mixed with barley-grains, and the fatness of olive-oil, and the most varied wax-fashioned work of the yellow bee.

And again, Archilochus, transferring that Homeric line, "I was blinded, nor do I myself deny it; in exchange for many," writes somewhat thus: "I went astray, and this ruin has overtaken some other too"; just as, indeed, that verse too, "Common is the War-god, and he slays the slayer," he himself, altering it, brought out somewhat thus: "I will do it; for in truth the War-god is common to men." And again, paraphrasing this, "Of victory for men the bounds lie with the gods," he is plainly its author by this iambic line: "And take heart, young men; the bounds of victory lie with the gods."

He trains the believer by good hopes, and the hard of heart by corrective discipline through the action upon the senses. From this comes providence, in private and in public and everywhere. That there is a Son of God, and that he is the Saviour and Lord whom we proclaim, the divine prophecies plainly set forth. In this way the Lord of all, both Greeks and barbarians, persuades those who are willing; for he does not compel one who is able to receive salvation from him by choosing and by fulfilling all that comes from him toward laying hold of the hope. This is he who gives philosophy also to the Greeks through the inferior angels; for by ancient and divine command angels are distributed among the nations. But "the Lord's portion" is the glory of those who believe. For either the Lord does not care for all men—and this would come about either through inability, which is not permissible, for it is a sign of weakness, or through unwillingness while able, but the suffering is not the mark of a good being; nor is he slothful through luxury, who for our sakes took on suffering flesh—or else he cares for all alike, which indeed befits him who has become the Lord of all. For he is a Saviour, not of some and not of others; but to each in proportion to his fitness he distributes his benefit—to Greeks and barbarians, and to those among them who are foreordained and, in their own due season, called as faithful and elect.

And how are they not worthy of acceptance, both those who wish to learn and those who are able, according to Solomon, "to know wisdom and discipline, and to understand words of prudence, and to receive turnings of words, and to understand true righteousness" (as though there were also another not taught according to the truth, by the laws of the Greeks and the other philosophers) "and to set judgments straight" — not the judicial, but he indicates that we must have the criterion within us sound and unwandering — "that he may give to the harmless cunning, and to the young child perception and notion." For having heard these things, the wise man — the one persuaded to obey the commandments — will be wiser in knowledge, "and the man of understanding will gain guidance, and will understand a parable and a dark saying, the words of the wise and riddles." For the discourses inspired from God are not counterfeit, nor are those who traffic from them, nor yet are they snares, with which the many of the sophists entangle the young, busying themselves about nothing true. Rather, those who possess the Holy Spirit "search the depths of God" — that is, they become partakers of the hidden meaning concerning the prophecies. But to give the holy things to the dogs is forbidden, so long as they remain beasts; for it is never fitting to pour out for the envious and disturbed and still unbelieving characters, shameless in their barking inquiry, the divine and pure stream, the living water.

Nor has procreation any written law (for it would have been transcribed otherwise); rather, all sow and beget alike, having an inborn community given them by justice. To all alike the Maker and Father of all, having laid down justice as His own law, has granted in common the eye to see, making no distinction between female and male, rational and irrational—nothing whatever between any; but distributing sight equally by equality and community, He has bestowed it on all alike at a single command.
