But the laws of men, he says, being unable to punish ignorance, have taught men to transgress; for the particularity of the laws has cut up and gnawed away the community of the divine law—not understanding the saying of the apostle, who says, "Through the law I came to know sin." "Mine" and "thine," he says, crept in through the laws, so that the earth and possessions, and even marriage, are no longer enjoyed in common; for God made the vines for all alike, and they refuse neither sparrow nor thief; and the grain likewise, and the other fruits. But community, being violated, together with equality, gave birth to the thief of cattle and crops.
So our Stromateis, like the farmer in Timocles the comic poet, yield as revenue
figs, olive-oil, dried figs, honey,
as from an all-bearing plot. For which good harvest he adds:
You are speaking of a harvest-wreath, not of farming.
For the Athenians used to cry out:
The harvest-wreath bears figs and rich loaves, and honey in a cup, and oil to anoint oneself.
We must, then, often, as in winnowing-fans, shake and toss the mixture of seeds, and pick out the wheat.

Again, when Homer had said, "with unwashed feet, sleeping on the ground," Euripides in the Erechtheus writes, "On an unspread floor they sleep, nor wet their feet in springs." And when Archilochus had likewise said, "But one man's heart is gladdened by one thing, another's by another," after the Homeric, "For one man delights in one kind of works, another in another," Euripides in the Oeneus says, "But one man delights more in one way of life, another in another." And I have heard Aeschylus saying, "He who is rightly happy must stay at home — and he who fares ill, let him too stay at home"; and Euripides crying the like upon the stage, "Blessed is he who, faring well, stays at home"; and Menander too playing the comedian somewhat thus: "One ought to stay at home, and to stay free, or else be no longer rightly happy."

He, then, who has called all alike, but has assigned special honours to those who have believed in a special way, would never envy any; nor would the Lord of all ever be hindered by another, especially since he ministers to the will of the good and almighty Father. But neither does envy touch the Lord, who came into being without beginning and is free from passion. Nor indeed are the affairs of men such as to be objects of the Lord's envy. The one who envies is another, one whom passion has touched. And it cannot be said that through ignorance the Lord is unwilling to save mankind, on the ground that he does not know how each is to be cared for. For ignorance does not touch the Son, who before the foundation of the world was the Father's counsellor. For this was the Wisdom "in which" the Almighty God "rejoiced"; for the Son is the "power of God," being the most sovereign Word of the Father before all things that have come to be, and rightly would he be called his "Wisdom" and the Teacher of those who were fashioned through him. Nor again, drawn aside by any pleasure, would he ever abandon the care of mankind, who indeed took up the flesh, which is by nature subject to passion, and trained it into the disposition of freedom from passion. And how could he be Saviour and Lord, if he were not Saviour and Lord of all? Rather, he is Saviour of those who have believed, because they have willed to know, and Lord of the disobedient, until, being able to confess, they obtain through him a benefit suited and proportioned to them. And every activity of the Lord has its reference to the Almighty, and the Son is, so to speak, a kind of paternal energy.

"Let not waters overflow for you outside your spring, but let your waters pass through into your streets." "For the many do not understand such things as they meet with, nor, having learned, do they know them, but seem so to themselves," according to the noble Heraclitus. Does it not seem to you that he too blames those who do not believe? "But my just man shall live by faith," the prophet has said. And another prophet too says: "Unless you believe, neither will you understand." For how could the soul ever hold the contemplation of these things, surpassing nature, with the unbelief about learning fighting within? But faith — which the Greeks slander, reckoning it empty and barbarian — is a voluntary anticipation, an assent of godliness, "the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen," according to the divine Apostle; "for by this especially the elders were witnessed to." And "without faith it is impossible to please God."

God, then, having made all things in common for man, and having brought the female together with the male in common, and having joined all the living creatures in the same way, declared justice to be community joined with equality. But those who have come into being in this way have denied the community that brought them together, and say: "Let the man who has married one woman keep her, although all can share in common, just as he has shown the rest of the animals do." Having said this in so many words, he then adds again in the very same words: "For He implanted in the males a strong and more vehement desire for the continuance of the kinds, which neither law nor custom nor anything else that exists can do away with; for it is a decree of God." And how can this man any longer be examined in our reckoning, when he openly abolishes through these arguments both the law and the gospel? For the one says, "You shall not commit adultery"; and the other says, "Everyone who looks with desire has already committed adultery." For the saying of the law, "You shall not covet," shows the one God proclaimed through the law and the prophets and the gospel; for it says, "You shall not covet your neighbour's wife." Now the neighbour is not the Jew to the Jew, for they are brothers and of the same Spirit; what remains, then, is that "neighbour" means a man of another nation. For how is he not a neighbour who is able to share in the Spirit? For Abraham is father not of the Hebrews only, but also of the Gentiles.

Again, when Theognis had said, "There is for the fugitive no friend and faithful comrade," Euripides has made, "Every friend flees the poor man out of his way." And when Epicharmus had said, "O daughter — alas for your fortune! — you who, being older, dwell with one who is young," and added, "For the one takes another young woman, and she in turn seeks out some other man for herself," Euripides writes, "An evil thing it is to yoke a young woman to a young man; for the one longs to take another's bed, and she, being in want of this, plots evil." Again, when Euripides in the Medea had said, "For the gifts of an evil man bring no benefit," Sophocles in the Ajax the scourge-bearer says that iambic line, "Gifts of foes are no gifts, and bring no profit." And when Solon had written, "For satiety breeds insolence, when much wealth follows," Theognis writes outright, "Satiety breeds insolence, when wealth follows an evil man." Whence Thucydides too in the Histories says, "Most men are wont, when unlooked-for prosperity comes to them suddenly and at the least cost, to turn to insolence." And Philistus likewise imitates the same, saying thus: "For those who, beyond expectation and unlooked-for, fare well, are wont above all to turn to insolence."

The Saviour, then, could never be a hater of men, who through his surpassing love of mankind did not disdain the weakness of human flesh, but put it on and came for the common salvation of men; for the faith of those who choose it is common. Nor would he ever neglect his own work, since to man alone of all living creatures the conception of God was instilled at his creation. Nor could there be for God any better or more harmonious ordering of mankind than the one appointed. For it is always fitting that the better should by nature rule the worse, and that to the one able to administer something well should be assigned the management of that other. And the true ruler and governor is the divine Word and his providence, which surveys all things and overlooks the care of none of its own. These would be those who have chosen to be his own—those who through faith are being perfected. Thus the Son is established, by the will of the almighty Father, as the cause of all good things, the first author of motion, a power not to be grasped by sense. For he was not seen as what he was by those unable to receive him because of the weakness of the flesh; rather, taking on flesh perceptible to sense, he came to show what is possible for men through obedience to the commandments. Being therefore the paternal power, he easily prevails over whatever he wills.

And others have rendered faith to be an assent of the mind to an unseen matter, just as, of course, demonstration is a manifest assent to a matter that was unknown. If, then, faith is a choice, being a kind of appetite for something, the appetite is here intellectual; and since choice is the beginning of action, faith is found to be the beginning of action, the foundation of an intelligent choice, when someone demonstrates beforehand to a man, through faith, the demonstration. And to follow willingly what is advantageous is the beginning of understanding. So an undistracted choice gives a great inclination toward knowledge. Indeed, the practice of faith becomes knowledge, propped upon a firm foundation. For the sons of the philosophers define knowledge as a state not to be shaken by reason. Is there, then, any other such state of true godliness itself, of which the Word alone is the teacher? I think not. And Theophrastus says that perception is the beginning of faith; for from this the beginnings extend toward the reason in us and the understanding. He, then, who has believed the divine Scriptures, having a firm judgment, receives as an irrefutable demonstration the voice of God who has granted the Scriptures. So faith is no longer fortified by demonstration. "Blessed, then, are those who have not seen and yet have believed." For the enchantments of the Sirens, displaying a superhuman power, astounded those who came near them, making them ready, almost against their will, for the reception of what was said.

And if the woman who has committed adultery and the man who has fornicated with her are punished with death, it is surely plain that the commandment which says, "You shall not covet your neighbour's wife," speaks of the Gentiles, so that the man who, according to the law, has kept himself from his neighbour's wife and from his sister, may hear plainly from the Lord, "But I say, You shall not covet." And the addition of the word "I" shows the more pressing force of the commandment, and that both Carpocrates and Epiphanes fight against God—Epiphanes, who, in that very much-talked-of book, On Justice I mean, adds something like this in so many words: "Hence the saying of the lawgiver, 'You shall not covet,' is to be taken as if spoken in jest, and still more ridiculous is the addition, 'your neighbour's'; for the very one who gave desire, as that which holds together the things of generation, commands that it be taken away, though He takes it from no animal; and the words 'your neighbour's wife,' which force community into private ownership, are still more ridiculous."

Again, when Euripides had written, "From a father and mother who toil out a hard manner of living, the offspring are better," Critias writes: "I begin with a man from his very birth: how would he become best in body and strongest? If he who begets him should exercise and eat with vigour and harden his body, and if the mother of the child that is to be should make her body strong and exercise it." And again, when Homer upon the shield wrought by Hephaestus had said, "On it he made the earth, and on it the heaven, and on it the sea; and on it he set the great strength of the river Ocean," Pherecydes of Syros says, "Zas makes a robe, great and beautiful, and on it he embroiders earth and Ogenos and the halls of Ogenos." And when Homer had said, "Shame, which greatly harms men and greatly helps them," Euripides in the Erechtheus writes, "And I myself am hard put to judge concerning shame; for one has need of it, and yet again it is a great evil."

He leaves not the least part of his administration uncared for; otherwise the whole would no longer have been well wrought by him. But it is, I think, the mark of the greatest power that the examination of all the parts, even to the smallest, should proceed with exactness—all things looking toward the first Governor of the universe, who by the Father's will steers the salvation of all, while others are appointed under others as rulers, until one comes at last to the great High Priest. For from one Beginning above, which works according to the will, depend the first and second and third orders; then at the summit of the visible world is the blessed company of angels; and so on down even to us, some set under others, out of one and through one being saved and saving, are they ordered in their ranks. As, then, even a far-distant piece of iron is moved together by the breath of the Heraclean stone, drawn out through many iron rings, so too those drawn by the Holy Spirit—the virtuous are made akin to the first abode, and the rest in turn down to the last—while those who are evil through weakness, having fallen into a bad condition through unjust greed, neither holding nor being held, are swept away, entangled by the passions, and fall to the ground. For this is the law from above: that whoever wills should choose virtue.

Such, then, are the doctrines of these noble Carpocratians. They say that these men, and certain others who are zealous for similar evils, gather together for their banquets (for I would not call their assembly an agape), men and women together; and when they have eaten their fill—"in fullness, as they say, comes Cypris"—they overturn the lamps so as to put out the light that would shame their fornicating justice, and unite as they wish with whomever they please. Having practised this community in such an "agape," they then by day demand from whatever women they wish obedience to the Carpocratian law—I dare not call it the law of God. Such things, I think, Carpocrates ought to have legislated for the lusts of dogs and swine and goats. He seems to me also to have misheard Plato, who in the Republic says that the women are common to all—meaning that those who have not yet married are common to those who would ask for them, just as a theatre is common to all the spectators, but that each woman, once a man has secured her first, belongs to that man, and the married woman is no longer common.

And you might take the passages of the theft side by side, even from those who flourished at the same time and contended with one another in such things — from Euripides, out of the Orestes, "O dear charm of sleep, helper against sickness," and from Sophocles out of the Eriphyle, "Go away; you stir sleep, the healer of sickness"; and from Euripides out of the Antigone, "In name the bastard is to be blamed, but his nature is equal," and from Sophocles out of the Aleadae, "All that is good has an equal nature"; again from Euripides out of the Temenus, "For God too lends a hand to him who toils," and from Sophocles in the Minos, "Fortune is no ally to those who do not act"; yes, and from Euripides out of the Alexander, "And time will show you; by which token, learning, I shall know you to be either good or bad," and from Sophocles out of the Hipponous, "Therefore hide nothing, for all-seeing and all-hearing time unfolds all things."

Therefore the commandments, both those under the Law and those before the Law—not laid down for the lawful (for "the law is not laid down for the just")—appointed that the one who chooses life should receive eternal life and a blessed reward; and that the one, again, who delights in evil should be granted to dwell with those he has chosen; and again, that the soul which is at every point being improved into the recognition of virtue and the increase of righteousness should receive a better rank in the universe, "stretching forward" at each advance toward the disposition of freedom from passion, until it "arrives at the perfect man," the pre-eminence of knowledge and of inheritance together. These saving revolutions are apportioned according to the order of the change, by times and places and honours and kinds of knowledge and inheritances and ministries—each according to each—up to the higher and immediate contemplation of the Lord in eternity. For what is lovely draws toward the contemplation of itself everyone who has wholly set himself, by the love of knowledge, upon contemplation.

Xanthus, in his work entitled Magica, says: "The Magi consider it lawful to have intercourse with their mothers and daughters and sisters, and that the women are common—not by force and in secret, but with the consent of both, when one man wishes to marry another's wife." Concerning these and similar sects, I think, Jude spoke prophetically in his epistle: "Likewise also these men, dreaming (for they do not lay hold of the truth waking), even to the point that their mouth speaks swelling words."

But let us run over those passages too in like manner. For when Eumelus had made, "Nine maidens of Mnemosyne and Olympian Zeus," Solon begins his elegy thus: "Splendid children of Mnemosyne and Olympian Zeus." Again, paraphrasing the Homeric line, "Who are you, of what men? Where is your city and your parents?", Euripides uses these iambics in the Aegeus: "What land shall we say you have left, to be a guest in this city? What is the boundary of your fatherland? Who is he that begot you? Of what father are you declared?" And again — when Theognis had said, "Wine drunk in plenty is bad; but if one use it with knowledge, it is no evil but a good," Panyassis writes, "Wine to mortals is the best gift of the gods, drunk in measure, but overmuch it is worse."

Therefore the Lord too, drawing from one fountain the commandments which he gave, both the earlier and the later, neither overlooked those before the Law as lawless, nor again permitted those who did not heed the barbarian philosophy to break free unbridled. For giving commandments to the one and philosophy to the other, he "shut up" unbelief until the coming; whence everyone who has not believed is without excuse. For from either kind of advance, the Greek and the barbarian, he leads on to the perfection that is through faith. And if any of the Greeks, passing over the preliminary stage of Greek philosophy, has set out at once for the true teaching, this man, even though unschooled, has outrun the rest, having chosen the short road to salvation through faith unto perfection.

And again, when Hesiod had said, "And to you, in place of fire, I will give an evil thing, in which all may delight," Euripides makes, "For in place of fire another fire, greater and harder to fight, sprang up — women." Besides this, when Homer had said, "But there is no way to glut the greedy belly, the accursed, which gives men many ills," Euripides makes, "The wretchedly perishing belly conquers me, from which all evils come." Again, when Callias the comic poet had written, "They say all must alike go mad among the mad," Menander in the Husbandmen runs even with him, saying, "Not everywhere does the presence of prudence fit; and in some things one must go mad along with the rest." And when Antimachus of Teos had said, "For out of gifts come many ills to men," Agias made, "Gifts beguile the mind of men, and their deeds too."

Everything, then, that did not hinder a man's choice from being voluntary, God both made and showed to be helpful toward virtue, so that in some way, even to those who can discern but dimly, the one truly almighty God might be shown to be good, saving from age to age through the Son, but in no way and by no means the cause of evil. For toward the salvation of the whole all things have been ordered by the Lord of the universe, both in general and in particular. It is therefore the work of saving righteousness ever to lead each forward to the better, as far as may be. For with a view to the salvation and continuance of the higher, even the lesser things are administered in proportion to their characters. Thus all that is virtuous passes over into better dwellings, having for the cause of its change the choice of knowledge, which the soul held as its own sovereign possession. But the necessary chastisements, through the goodness of the great Judge who watches over all, both through the angels who are near and through varied prior judgements and through the final judgement, compel to repentance those who have grown more "callous."

And when Hesiod had said, "For a man wins no better prize than a woman — a good one; but than an evil there is nothing more chilling," Simonides said, "A man wins no possession better than a good woman, nor more chilling than an evil." Again, when Epicharmus had said, "Think as one who will live both a long time and a short," Euripides writes, "Why, having set our foot on an unsure prosperity, do we not live most sweetly, free of grief?" Likewise, when the comic poet Diphilus had said, "Changeable is the life of men," Posidippus says, "No man has passed his life unpained, being a man; nor, being unfortunate, has remained so to the end." And in keeping with these, Plato says, writing of man as a creature given to change. Again, when Euripides had said, "O much-toiling life of mortals, how slippery you lie in all things, and now you increase, now you waste away; and there is no fixed bound for mortals to attain, except when the chill end of death, sent from Zeus, shall come," Diphilus writes, "There is no life that has not possessed evils — griefs, cares, plunderings, rackings, diseases. Of these, death, appearing like a physician, has given respite, laying those who have them to rest in sleep."

We have set down sufficient testimonies, then, from the writings of the Greeks concerning faith. But that we may not wander on at excessive length, ambitious to gather together very much also concerning hope and love, it is enough to say only this: that in the Crito Socrates, setting living well and dying above mere living, thinks he has some hope of another life after his end. For in the Phaedrus, too, saying that the soul, becoming by itself alone, is able to share in true wisdom, a wisdom higher than human power, when the love of this world has given it wings toward heaven, he says that, coming through philosophic love to the goal of hope, it receives the beginning of another, everlasting life.

And again, when Euripides had said, "Many are the forms of things divine, and the gods accomplish many things unhoped-for," the tragedian Theodectes likewise writes, "that the fortunes of mortals are not secure." And when Bacchylides had said, "To few of mortals has the spirit granted, faring well at the right moment through all their time, to come to grey-templed old age before they meet with calamity," Moschion the comic poet writes, "But he is most blessed of all who, living to the end, has practised an even life." And you may find too, when Theognis had said, "A young wife is no use to an old man; for she obeys not the rudder like a boat," Aristophanes the comic poet writing, "A shameful thing — an aged man with a young wife." For when Anacreon had made, "I am minded to sing of delicate Love, blossoming with garlands of many flowers; he is the lord even of the gods, he tames mortals too," Euripides writes, "For Love comes not upon men alone, nor again upon women, but troubles the souls of the gods above and goes over the sea."

And in the Symposium he says that there is mingled in all a natural love for the begetting of like to like — in men, of men only; in the earnest man, of his counterpart. But it is impossible for the earnest man to do this, unless he has the virtues in perfection, by which he will instruct the young who come to him, and, as he says in the Theaetetus, will beget and bring forth men. For some are pregnant in body, some in soul; since among the barbarian philosophers too, to instruct and to enlighten is called regenerating. "And I begot you in Christ Jesus," the good apostle says somewhere. Empedocles reckons love also among the first principles, conceiving a certain combining affection: "this do you behold with the mind, and sit not amazed with the eyes." And Parmenides too, in his poem, hinting at hope, speaks thus: "Yet behold things absent as firmly present to the mind; for you shall not cut off what is from clinging to what is, neither scattering itself wholly in every way throughout the world, nor drawing together."

But that the discourse may not go on too long, while we are ambitious to display the proneness of the Greeks to theft in their words and doctrines, come, let us set before us Hippias the sophist of Elis, downright bearing witness to us, who comes to the same argument upon the matter I have set before me, speaking somewhat thus: "Of these things, perhaps, some were said by Orpheus, some by Musaeus, briefly, one in one place and another in another; some by Hesiod, some by Homer, some by the rest of the poets; and of those in prose, some by Greeks, some by barbarians. But I, from all these, putting together the things most akin, will make this discourse, new and of many kinds."

And that we may not let philosophy, history, and rhetoric too go without the like refutation, it is reasonable to set down a few of these as well. For when Alcmaeon of Croton had said that it is easier to guard against an enemy than a friend, Sophocles made, in the Antigone, "For what wound could be greater than an evil friend?" and Xenophon has said, "No one could harm his enemies in any other way than by seeming to be a friend." And in the Telephus, when Euripides had said, "Being Greeks, shall we be slaves to barbarians?", Thrasymachus in the speech on behalf of the Larisaeans says, "Shall we, being Greeks, be slaves to Archelaus, a barbarian?"

And when Orpheus had made, "There is water for the soul, and death is the change to waters; and out of water comes earth, and out of earth again water; and from this the whole soul, changing, passes into the aether," Heraclitus, putting together his words out of these, writes somewhat thus: "For souls it is death to become water, and for water death to become earth; and out of earth comes water, and out of water soul." Indeed, when Athamas the Pythagorean had said thus, "The unbegotten beginning of all things, and the four roots there are — fire, water, air, earth; for out of these are the comings-into-being of the things that come to be," Empedocles of Acragas made, "First hear the four roots of all things: fire and water and earth, and the boundless height of aether; for out of these is all that was and shall be and is." And when Plato had said, "For this reason too the gods, who know the things of men, the more quickly release from life those whom they hold most precious," Menander made, "Whom the gods love dies young."

And when Euripides in the Oenomaus writes, "We conjecture the unseen from things present," and in the Phoenix, "The unseen is fairly caught by tokens," Hypereides says, "But the things that are unseen, those who teach them must of necessity inquire into by tokens and probabilities." And again, when Isocrates had said, "We must conjecture the things to come from those that have come before," Andocides does not shrink from saying, "For one must use the things that have happened before as tokens concerning the things that shall be." Again, when Theognis had made, "The ruin of counterfeit gold and silver is bearable, Cyrnus, and easy for a wise man to detect; but if the mind of a friendly man lies hidden in his breast, being false, and he has a treacherous heart in his breast, this God has made the most counterfeit thing for mortals, and to know it the most grievous of all," Euripides writes, "O Zeus, why have you given to men sure tokens of the gold that is counterfeit, but on the body of men, by which one should discern the bad, no mark is set?" And Hypereides himself too says, "There is no mark of the mind set upon the face of men."

Now, concerning these memoranda, which at the necessary points take in Greek opinion, I say this much to the fault-finders. First: even if philosophy were useless, if establishing its uselessness is useful, then it is useful. Next: it is not possible to condemn the Greeks while using only a bare statement of what they have dogmatized, without entering into the detailed examination of each point until one reaches understanding. For the refutation that comes with experience is most trustworthy, since the most perfect proof is found to be the knowledge of the things condemned. And indeed many things that do not contribute to the end still adorn the craftsman. Besides, wide learning helps to recommend the man who sets out the most authoritative of the doctrines for the persuasion of his hearers, and, breeding admiration in those being instructed, commends them toward the truth.

Again, when Stasinus had made, "Foolish is he who, slaying the father, leaves the sons," Xenophon says, "For I seem now to have done the like as if one, having slain a father, should spare his children." And when Sophocles in the Antigone had made, "Now that mother and father are in Hades, there is no brother who could ever spring up," Herodotus says, "Mother and father being no longer alive, I shall have no other brother." Besides this, when Theopompus had made, "Old men are children twice, by a right account," and before him Sophocles in the Peleus, "Peleus son of Aeacus, alone as housekeeper I tend in his old age and rear like a child again; for the man who grows old becomes a child once more," Antiphon the orator says, "For the rearing of the old is like the rearing of children"; and the philosopher Plato too: "So, as it seems, the old man would become a child twice over."

Such a winning of souls is worthy of trust — by which lovers of learning receive the truth in veiled form — so that neither do they seem to think philosophy corrupts life, being the maker of false things and base deeds, as some have slandered it (whereas it is a clear image of truth, a divine gift given to the Greeks), nor are we ourselves drawn away from faith, as though bewitched by some deceitful art; but, so to speak, by using a fuller covering we somehow furnish a kind of demonstrative exercise of faith. Indeed, the joining of doctrines through their comparison woos the truth, by which knowledge has followed — philosophy having entered not as the primary cause, but our taking, through the fruit that comes from knowledge, a firm conviction of true apprehension by the science of things that are inferred. For I say nothing of the fact that the Miscellanies, embodied by their wide learning, mean to hide artfully the seeds of knowledge.

Yes, and when Thucydides had said, "to have alone faced the danger at Marathon," Demosthenes said, "By those who faced the danger at Marathon." Nor will I pass over these: when Cratinus in the Pytine had said, "The preparation, perhaps, you know," Andocides the orator says, "The preparation, men of the jury, and the eagerness of my enemies, almost all of you will know." Likewise too Nicias, in the speech against Lysias concerning a deposit, says, "You see, men of the jury, the preparation and the eagerness of my adversaries"; and after him Aeschines says, "You see the preparation, men of Athens, and the array." Again, when Demosthenes had said, "How great, men of Athens, is the zeal and canvassing that has arisen about this trial, almost all of you, I think, have perceived," Philinus likewise: "How great, men of the jury, the zeal and array that has come about over this trial, not one of you, I think, is ignorant."

As the man eager for the hunt finds his quarry by seeking, searching, tracking, and coursing with hounds, so the truth, when sought and won by toil, appears full of sweetness. Why, then, did it seem good to arrange these memoranda in this way? Because there is great danger in dancing out the truly secret discourse of true philosophy before men who unsparingly wish to contradict everything, and not justly, and who hurl away all names and words in no orderly fashion, deceiving themselves and bewitching those who cling to them. "For the Hebrews ask for signs," as the Apostle says, "and the Greeks seek wisdom."

Again, when Isocrates had said, "as being kin to his money, but not to him," Lysias in the Orphans' speeches says, "And it has become plain that he was kin not to their persons, but to their money." Since, too, when Homer had made, "Friend, if, having fled this war, we were going to be ageless and immortal for ever, I would neither fight myself among the foremost nor send you into the battle that brings men glory; but now, since the fates of death stand over us in their thousands, which no mortal can flee or escape, let us go, whether we shall give glory to some man, or some to us," Theopompus writes, "For if it were possible, having fled the present danger, to live the rest of one's time without fear, it would be no wonder to be a lover of life; but as it is, so many fates beset our life that death in battle seems the more to be chosen." And again — when Chilon the wise had spoken his apophthegm, "Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand," Epicharmus brought forth the same thought under another name, saying, "Ruin is the daughter of a pledge, and a pledge the daughter of loss."

But also, when the physician Hippocrates had written, "One must look, then, to season and country and age and diseases," Euripides in a certain hexameter saying says, "Whoever knows how to heal well must look to the diets of those who dwell in a city, having seen the land, in considering the diseases." Again, when Homer had made, "I say that no man of mortals has escaped his fate," Archinus says, "To all men it is owed to die, either earlier or later"; and Demosthenes, "For to all men the end of life is death, even if one shut himself up and keep watch in a little house."

And again, when Herodotus in the account of Glaucus the Spartan had said that the Pythia declared that to make trial of the god and to do the deed came to the same thing, Aristophanes said, "For thinking has equal power with doing"; and before him Parmenides the Eleatic: "For to think is the same thing as to be." And — when Plato had said, "We might perhaps say, not absurdly, that the beginning of love is sight, that hope lessens the passion, that memory nourishes it, and that habit preserves it," Philemon the comic poet writes, "All first see, then marvel, then gaze further, then fall into hope; thus from these comes love." But also, when Demosthenes had said, "To all of us death is owed," and the rest, Phanocles in his Loves, or Beautiful Ones, writes, "But the thread of the Fates is not to be undone, nor can any of us who feed upon the earth ever flee it."

And you might find too, when Plato had said, "For the first sprouting of every plant, well started toward excellence, is most authoritative in setting upon its own nature its fitting end," Ephorus the historian writing, "But none even of the wild plants is by nature to be tamed once they have passed their younger age." And that saying of Empedocles, "For ere now I have been a boy and a girl, a bush and a bird, and a mute fish in the sea," Euripides in the Chrysippus transcribes, "Nothing of the things that come to be dies, but being parted, one from another, it shows forth another form." And when Plato in the Republic had said that women should be common, Euripides in the Protesilaus writes, "For the bed of women should be common." But when Euripides had written, "Since what suffices is enough for the temperate," Epicurus says outright, "Self-sufficiency is the richest of all things." Again, when Aristophanes had written, "You shall have a secure life, being just; and apart from tumult and fear you shall live well," Epicurus says, "The greatest fruit of righteousness is freedom from disturbance."

The kinds, then, of the Greek theft in thought, set forth as a clear example for one able to discern, let these suffice. And by now they have been caught, not only filching the thoughts and the phrases and paraphrasing them, as has been shown, but they shall also be convicted of having the stolen things downright whole; for they have brought out the things of others, taken outright, as their own — as Eugammon of Cyrene took the book on the Thesprotians, whole, from Musaeus; and Peisander of Cameirus the Heracleia of Peisinus of Lindus; and Panyassis of Halicarnassus the Capture of Oechalia from Creophylus of Samos.

And you might find too the great poet Homer transferring word for word those verses, "Like a shoot that a man rears, a flourishing shoot of olive," and the rest, from Orpheus, out of the destruction of Dionysus. And in the Theogony it is made by Orpheus, concerning Cronos, "He lay, bending aside his thick neck, and sleep, the all-subduer, seized him" — and these things Homer transferred to the Cyclops. And Hesiod makes, concerning Melampus, "Sweet too it is to learn how much the immortals have appointed for mortals, a clear token of base men and noble," and the rest, taking it word for word from Musaeus the poet. And Aristophanes the comic poet in the first Thesmophoriazusae transferred the verses out of Cratinus' Men on Fire. And Plato the comic poet and Aristophanes in the Daedalus filch from one another. And the Cocalus, written by Araros the son of Aristophanes, Philemon the comic poet, altering it, brought on the stage as comedy in the Hypobolimaeus. And the things of Hesiod, Eumelus and Acusilaus the historiographers turned into prose and brought out as their own. For Gorgias of Leontini and Eudemus of Naxos, the historians, stole from Melesagoras; and besides these, Bion of Proconnesus, who also transcribed, abridging them, the things of the ancient Cadmus; and Amphilochus and Aristocles and Leandrius and Anaximenes and Hellanicus and Hecataeus and Androtion and Philochorus; and Dieuchidas of Megara took the beginning of his discourse from the Deucalioneia of Hellanicus.

And I say nothing of Heraclitus of Ephesus, who took the most part from Orpheus. And from Pythagoras Plato derived that the soul is immortal — and Pythagoras from the Egyptians. And many of Plato's school have composed writings in which they show that the Stoics, as we said at the beginning, and Aristotle too, took the most and most authoritative of their doctrines from Plato. And Epicurus too has contrived his leading doctrines out of Democritus. So much, then, for these things; for life will fail me, if I should choose to go through each one, convicting the self-loving Greek theft, and how they appropriate the discovery of the noblest doctrines among them, which they have taken from us.

Likewise too all men would agree that demonstration is a discourse procuring conviction, for things disputed, out of things agreed upon. And not only demonstration and conviction and knowledge, but foreknowledge too is spoken of in two ways—the one scientific and firm, the other merely conjectural. In the strictest sense, then, that is called demonstration which implants scientific conviction in the souls of those who learn; the other is conjectural—just as a man, the one is truly a man who possesses the common faculties, while the other is wild and beastlike. So indeed the comic poet said: "How charming a thing is a man, when he is a man." And of an ox and a horse and a dog the same account holds, with reference to the virtue or vice of the animal. For looking toward the perfection of the genus, we come to the strictest of the things signified. Indeed, we conceive that man to be a physician who lacks nothing of the medical power, and that man a gnostic who lacks nothing of scientific knowledge.

And indication differs from syllogism in this: that the thing indicated is the disclosing of one thing, being itself one—as we say that being with child is an indication that one is no longer a virgin—while the thing taken by syllogism, being one, follows upon several—as, say, that Python betrayed the Byzantines, if so it chanced. Not one thing, but several, are taken as disclosing it. And to draw a conclusion from things agreed upon is to syllogize; but to conclude something from true premisses is to demonstrate; so that the benefit of demonstration is, as it were, a composite thing—both from taking, with reference to the things sought, premisses that are true, and from the conclusion's following upon them. But if either the former should not be the case, or the latter should not follow upon it, one has not demonstrated, but has syllogized. For to bring in the proper conclusion upon the premisses is to syllogize only; but for each of the premisses to be true is not to syllogize only, but also to have demonstrated. And to conclude is, as is plain from the word itself, to lead to the end; and the end, surely, in every discourse is the thing sought, which is also called the conclusion. And no simple and primary discourse is named a syllogism, even if it be true; but it is at the least composed of three such things—two as premisses, and one as conclusion. And either all things stand in need of demonstration, or some are trustworthy of themselves.

But if the former, then, demanding a demonstration of each demonstration, we shall go on to infinity, and so demonstration will be overturned; but if the latter, then these very things that are trustworthy of themselves will become the beginnings of demonstrations. Indeed the philosophers agree that the beginnings of the universe are indemonstrable. So that, if there is such a thing as demonstration, it is altogether necessary that there be first something trustworthy of itself, which is called primary and indemonstrable. To indemonstrable trustworthiness, then, all demonstration is referred back. And there would be also other beginnings of demonstrations, after the fountain that is from faith—the things that appear plainly to sense and to thought. For the things that fall to sense are simple and indissoluble; but the things relative to thought are simple and rational and primary; and the things begotten of them are composite, yet no less plain and trustworthy and more rational than the primary things. The natural power of distinguishing the consequent and the contradictory, which is proper to reason, all of us possess by nature. If, then, there should be found such a discourse as is able to procure, out of things already trustworthy, conviction for things not yet trustworthy, we shall say that this very thing is the substance of demonstration. And it has been said that the kind both of faith and of demonstration is twofold: the one producing only persuasion in the souls of the hearers, the other producing knowledge. If, then, one should begin from the things plain to sense and to thought, and then bring in the proper conclusion, he truly demonstrates; but if from things merely held in repute, yet not primary—that is, plain neither to sense nor to thought—then, if he bring in a proper conclusion, he will syllogize, but will not make the demonstration scientific; and if not a proper one, he will not even syllogize at all.
Now the many have a disposition like the condition of a stormy season, unsettled and unreasoning.
Many good things has unbelief done, and faith evil things.

And Epicharmus says, "Remember to be distrustful: these are the joints of the mind." So then, to distrust the truth brings death, as to believe brings life; but, on the contrary, to believe falsehood and to distrust the truth drags one down to destruction. The same account holds of continence and incontinence. For to be continent toward good works is the work of vice; but to abstain from injustice is the beginning of salvation. So the Sabbath, by abstinence from evils, seems to me to hint at continence, and at what it is by which man differs from beasts. And again, the angels of God are wiser than this: "You made him a little lower," it says, "than the angels"—for they do not take the Scripture as referring to the Lord (and yet He too bore flesh), but to the perfect and gnostic man, who is made lower than the angels in respect of time and of his clothing. I say, then, that wisdom is something other than knowledge, since it does not differ from life; for the common possession of mortal nature—that is, of man—with the being deemed worthy of immortality is life, the habit of contemplation and of continence being what differs.

And demonstration differs from analysis. For each of the things demonstrated is demonstrated through certain things demonstrated, these too having been previously demonstrated by others, until we run back to the things trustworthy of themselves, or to the things plain to sense and thought—which is called analysis. But demonstration is when one arrives from the primary things at the thing sought, through all the things in between. The demonstrative man, then, must take much forethought for the truth of the premisses, but make no anxiety about the names—whether one wishes to call them axioms, or propositions, or premisses. Likewise, too, of what being laid down what is concluded, he must take much forethought; but whether one wishes to name his discourse concluding, or conclusive, or syllogistic, let him be least concerned. For these two things, I say, the demonstrative man must keep in all cases: to take true premisses, and to bring in upon them a consequent conclusion—which some also call the inference: the thing inferred upon the premisses. Concerning everything sought, in each particular problem, there is need of differing premisses, but proper to the thing proposed; and it is necessary to take over the thing proposed itself into a discourse, and this discourse must be agreed upon by all. But if the premisses be taken not proper to the problem, it is not possible to find out anything well concerning it, the whole nature of the problem—which is also called the question—being unknown. In all things sought, then, there is something previously known (which, being wholly trustworthy of itself, is believed without demonstration), which one must make the starting-point of the inquiry into them, and the criterion of the things that seem to have been found.

So Pythagoras too seems to me to say that God alone is wise (since the apostle in the epistle to the Romans writes: "made known unto the obedience of faith to all the nations, to the only wise God through Jesus Christ"), and that he himself, on account of his friendship toward God, is a philosopher. "God conversed with Moses," it says, "as a friend with a friend." Now the truth is plain to God. He, then, at once begets truth; and the gnostic loves truth. "Go to the ant, O sluggard," says Solomon, "and become a disciple of the bee." For if the proper work of each thing according to its own nature is one, both of the ox and likewise of the horse and of the dog, what shall we say is the proper work of man? He seems to me like a centaur, a Thessalian fiction, composed of a rational and an irrational part, of soul and body; but the body works the earth and hastens toward the earth, while the soul is stretched out toward God—the soul that, educated through true philosophy, hastens toward its kindred above, having turned away from the desires of the body, and from these toward toil and fear too; although we have shown that endurance and fear are good. For if through the law comes the knowledge of sin, as those who run down the law say, and "until the law sin was in the world," yet "apart from the law sin is dead," we answer them. For when you take away the cause of fear, which is sin, you have taken away fear, and much more punishment, when that which is by nature given to desire is absent; "for the law is not laid down for the righteous," the Scripture says.

Here those about Basilides hold faith to be natural, in which sense they also set it down under the head of election, as finding the studies without demonstration by an intellectual apprehension. But those from Valentinus, assigning faith to us, the simple, but knowledge to themselves, wish it to be inherent, by the advantage of a superior seed, in those who are saved by nature — knowledge far separated from faith, as they say the spiritual is from the natural. Further, those from Basilides say that faith, together with election, is proper to each interval; and that, as a consequence of the supramundane election, the worldly faith of every nature follows, and that the gift of faith is correspondent to the hope of each.

Well, then, does Heraclitus say, "They would not have known the name of justice if these things did not exist"; and Socrates, that the law would not have come into being for the sake of the good. But the accusers did not even know this, that, as the apostle says, "he who loves his neighbour works no evil; for 'You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal,' and if there is any other commandment, are summed up in this one saying, 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself.'" So, then, "You shall love the Lord your God," it says, "with your whole heart, and your neighbour as yourself." If, then, he who loves his neighbour works no evil, and every commandment is summed up in this, in loving one's neighbour, the commandments that hang fear over us produce love, not hatred.

So faith is no longer a right achievement of choice, if it is an advantage of nature; nor will he who has not believed, being without responsibility, meet with a just recompense, nor he who has believed be responsible; and the whole property and difference of faith and unbelief would fall under neither praise nor blame, for those who reckon rightly, since it has, as its primary cause, a natural necessity that has come from the One who is able to do all things. And, we being drawn like puppets, after the manner of lifeless things, by natural activities, the voluntary and the involuntary are dragged along, and the impulse that leads these. And I, for one, no longer conceive of this as a living being, whose impulse has been allotted necessity, moved by a cause from outside. And where, any more, is the repentance of the once unbelieving, through which is the forgiveness of sins? So that neither is baptism any longer reasonable, nor the blessed seal, nor the Son, nor the Father; but God, I think, is found by them to be the distribution of natures, not having the foundation of salvation, the voluntary faith.

Fear, then, of which the law is the begetter, is not a passion. So the law is holy and truly spiritual, according to the apostle. We must, it seems, having inquired curiously into the nature of the body and the substance of the soul, grasp the end of each, and not regard death as evil. For "when you were slaves of sin," says the apostle, "you were free in regard to righteousness. What fruit, then, did you have at that time? The things of which you are now ashamed; for the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord."

Now if Plato himself and the Pythagoreans, like the followers of Marcion later, had supposed generation to be evil (though Plato was far from holding women to be common), still the Marcionites suppose nature to be evil, made of evil matter and by a just Demiurge. By this reasoning, not wishing to fill up the world made by the Demiurge, they wish to abstain from marriage, setting themselves against their Maker and hastening toward the Good who called them—not, as they say, toward the God who is otherwise. Hence, wishing to leave nothing of their own here, they become continent not by free choice, but out of enmity toward their Maker, unwilling to use what He created. But these men, having departed from natural reasoning by their impious war against God, and despising the long-suffering and kindness of God—even if they do not wish to marry—still use the food He created and breathe the air of the Demiurge, being His works and remaining among His things; and they proclaim, as they say, a strange knowledge, though even in this respect they owe thanks to the Lord of the world, in that here they have received the good news.

It seems, then, to have been shown that death is the communion of the soul, while sinful, with the body, and life is the separation from sin. But many are the stakes and trenches of desire at our feet, the pits of wrath and passion, which the man who is no longer to behold the knowledge of God through a mirror must leap over, and flee from every dismantling of the plots laid for him;
for far-seeing Zeus takes away half of a man's virtue, when the day of slavery comes upon him.

And the Scripture knows as slaves those who are under sin and sold to sins, the lovers of pleasure and lovers of the body, and as beasts rather than men those who have been made like the cattle, "horses mad for the female, neighing after their neighbours' wives"; the licentious man is an insolent ass, the covetous a savage wolf, and the deceiver a serpent. So the separation of the soul from the body, practised throughout life by the philosopher, fashions in him a gnostic readiness easily to bear the death of nature, which is the loosing of the bonds of the soul toward the body. For "to me the world has been crucified, and I to the world," he says; "and I now live, though in the flesh, as one whose citizenship is in heaven."

But against these men, when we treat the discussion concerning first principles, we shall argue most precisely. As for the philosophers we mentioned, from whom the Marcionites, having impiously learned that generation is evil, give themselves airs as over their own doctrine—they do not hold it to be evil by nature, but evil to the soul that has perceived the truth; for they bring down the soul, which is divine, into this world here as into a place of punishment, and it is fitting, according to them, that souls embodied here should be purified. And this doctrine belongs no longer to the Marcionites, but to those who hold that souls are put into bodies, bound again into them, and decanted from one body to another—against whom there will be another occasion to speak, when we treat of the soul.

"But concerning the rest I am silent," glorifying the Lord. Yet of those gnostic souls I do speak—souls which by the magnificence of their contemplation surpass the polity of each holy order, in accordance with which the blessed dwellings of the gods are distinguished and allotted; souls counted holy among the holy, transferred whole out of whole, arriving at better places out of better, no longer embracing the divine contemplation in mirrors or through mirrors, but feasting, as much as may be, on the vision clear and most exactly pure—a vision insatiable to souls that love it with a more than natural love—reaping eternally an eternal gladness, all honoured to remain in the sameness of pre-eminence. This is the comprehending contemplation of "the pure in heart." This, then, is the activity of the perfected gnostic: to hold communion with God through the great High Priest, being made like to the Lord, so far as may be, through all his service toward God—a service that reaches out to the salvation of men by care for the benefit done to us, and again by ministry, by teaching, and by well-doing in deeds. Yes, the gnostic both founds and fashions himself, and besides adorns those who give heed to him, being made like to God, by likening to freedom from passion—so far as may be—the freedom from passion gathered through discipline to that which possesses it by nature; and this while holding communion and dwelling with the Lord "without distraction." Gentleness, I think, and love of mankind and magnificent godliness are the standards of gnostic assimilation.

Heraclitus, at any rate, plainly disparages generation when he says: "When they are born, they wish to live and to have their deaths"—or rather, to find rest—"and they leave children behind to become deaths in their turn." Empedocles too plainly agrees with him when he says:
I wept and wailed when I beheld the unfamiliar place.
And again:
For out of living things he made dead, changing their forms.
And again:
Alas, wretched race of mortals, deeply ill-fated: out of such strifes and groans you were born.
The Sibyl too says:
Mortal men and made of flesh, who are nothing,
like the poet who writes:
Earth nurtures nothing feebler than a man.

These virtues, I say, are "an acceptable sacrifice" with God—the unproud heart with right knowledge, which Scripture calls "a whole burnt offering to God," when the whole man who has been taken up into holiness is enlightened into undivided union. For both the Gospel and the Apostle command us to take ourselves captive and to slay our own selves—putting to death "the old man, corrupted according to its desires," and raising up "the new man" from the death of the old perversion—laying aside the passions and becoming free from sin. This, then, was what the Law too hinted at when it commanded the sinner to be put to death: the passing over from death to life, the freedom from passion that comes of faith. Not understanding this, the teachers of the Law, taking it as a thing for contention, have furnished occasions to those who try in vain to slander it. For this reason we reasonably do not sacrifice to God, who is in need of nothing, who has furnished all things to all; but the one who was offered up for us we glorify by offering up ourselves—from that which is needless of nothing into needing nothing, and from that which is free of passion into freedom from passion. For God rejoices in our salvation alone. Reasonably, then, to him who is not conquered by pleasures we offer no sacrifice down here—not even as high as the densest clouds, but far short even of these, while the steam of smoke reaches only as far as it reaches.
Yes, and Theognis too shows generation to be evil, when he speaks in some such way as this:
In agreement with these the tragic poet Euripides writes:

We ought, when a man is born, to gather together and mourn for him, in view of all the evils he goes to meet; but the dead, freed at last from his toils, we ought to send forth from his house rejoicing and with words of good omen.
And again he says the like:
Who knows whether to live is to be dead, and to be dead is to live?

The Divine, then, is neither in need, nor a lover of pleasure, nor a lover of gain or of money; being full, and furnishing all things to every created and needy thing, it is not charmed by sacrifices nor by votive offerings nor by glory and honour, nor is it led aside by any such things. Rather it shows itself like good and noble men, who would never betray the just—whether through fear of a threatened danger or by the promise of greater gifts. But as many as have not perceived the self-determined and unenslaved character of the human soul as regards its choice of life, being vexed at the things done through the injustice that comes of want of education, do not believe that God exists. Of the same opinion are those who, falling into the incontinence of pleasures and into excessive griefs and unwilled misfortunes, and giving way under their calamities, say that there is no God, or that, if he exists, he does not oversee all things. Others again are persuaded that those reckoned as gods can be won over by sacrifices and gifts, lending their aid, so to speak, to the men's own excesses; and these are not even willing to believe that the only true God exists—he who abides in the sameness of just goodness.

Herodotus too plainly does the same when he makes Solon say: "O Croesus, every man is a creature of calamity." And his story of Cleobis and Biton clearly intends nothing else than to blame generation and to praise death.
As is the generation of leaves, so too is that of men,

says Homer. And Plato, in the Cratylus, attributes to Orpheus the doctrine that the soul is punished in the body, saying thus: "For some say that the body [sōma] is the tomb [sēma] of the soul, as though it were buried in the present life; and because the soul signifies whatever it signifies by means of the body, it is for this reason rightly called a 'sign' [sēma]. But it seems to me that the followers of Orpheus chiefly established this name, on the ground that the soul pays the penalty for whatever it pays the penalty."

For he who hopes, like him who believes, sees with the mind the things of mind and the things to come. If, then, we say that something is just, and say also that something is beautiful, and speak too of a truth, yet have never beheld any such thing with the eyes but only with the mind — and the Word of God says, "I am the truth" — then the Word is to be contemplated by the mind. "And whom do you call the true philosophers?" he asked. "Those," said I, "who love the contemplation of the truth." And in the Phaedrus Plato, speaking of truth as an idea, will make it plain . . . And the idea is a thought of God, which the barbarians have called the Word of God. The words run thus: "We must dare to speak the truth, especially when speaking about truth; for the substance that is truly existent, colourless and shapeless and intangible, is to be seen by the pilot of the soul, the mind, alone." And the Word, coming forth, became the cause of creation; and afterwards he begets even himself, when the Word became flesh, that he might also be seen. The just man, then, will seek the discovery that comes of love, and, hastening toward it, is happy; for "to him who knocks," he says, "it shall be opened. Ask, and it shall be given you." For those who take the kingdom by violence are said to force their way, not by contentious arguments, but by the perseverance of a right life and by unceasing prayers, wiping out the stains of their former sins. "And one may choose evil in crowds. But for him who toils, God also lends a hand. For not in the midst do the unconquerable gifts of the Muses lie, for the chance comer to bear away."

The gnostic, then, is devout—he who cares first for himself, and then for his neighbours, that we may become as good as possible. For the son too gives delight to a good father by showing himself diligent and like his father, and the subject to the ruler; for to believe and to obey lies in our power. The cause of evils one might take to be the weakness of matter and the unwilled impulses of ignorance and the irrational necessities that come of want of learning. The gnostic, having through learning risen above these as above wild beasts, and imitating the divine purpose, does good to those of mankind who are willing, so far as he can. And if ever he comes into a position of rule, like Moses, he will govern for the salvation of the governed, and will tame what is wild and unpersuaded, honouring the best and chastising the wicked—chastisement being inscribed, in accordance with reason, for instruction. For above all things the soul of a just man is a divine image and like to God, in which, through obedience to the precepts, there is enshrined and set up the Ruler of all things mortal and immortal, the King and Begetter of all that is noble—who is in truth law and ordinance and eternal Reason, being one Saviour both to each privately and to all in common. This is he who is truly only-begotten, the express character of the glory of the all-ruling and almighty Father, who stamps upon the gnostic the perfect contemplation according to his own image—so that there is now a third divine image, made like, as far as may be, to the second cause, to the true Life, through which we live the true life—copying out, as it were, the gnostic stamp that has become ours, conversant with things firm and wholly unchanging.

It is worth recalling also the saying of Philolaus; for the Pythagorean says thus: "The ancient theologians and seers bear witness that, because of certain punishments, the soul has been yoked to the body and buried in it as in a tomb." Pindar too, speaking of the Eleusinian mysteries, adds:

Plato likewise, in the Phaedo, does not hesitate to write in some such way as this: "And those who established the rites for us were no ordinary men... [the soul] will dwell with the gods." And what of it when he says: "As long as we have the body, and our soul is commingled with such an evil, we shall never sufficiently attain that which we desire"? Does he not hint that generation is the cause of the greatest evils? And in the Phaedo he bears witness: "For it is likely that all who rightly lay hold of philosophy are unnoticed by others in that they practise nothing else than to die and to be dead."

The recognition of one's own ignorance, then, is the first lesson for him who walks according to reason. Being ignorant, a man sought; and seeking, he finds the teacher; and finding him, he believed; and believing, he hoped; and loving, he is thenceforth made like to the beloved, striving to be that which he first came to love. Such a method Socrates points out to Alcibiades, who asks thus: "Do you not think I could know about the just in any other way?" "Yes, if you should find it out." "But do you not hold that I could find it out?" "Most certainly, if you should seek it." "Then do you not think I would seek it?" "I do, if you should think you did not know." In this way too the lamps of the prudent virgins, lit by night in the great darkness of ignorance — which night the Scripture hinted at — are the prudent souls, pure as virgins, who, perceiving themselves set in worldly ignorance, kindle the light and rouse the mind and illumine the darkness and drive out ignorance and seek the truth and await the appearing of the teacher. "A multitude of philosophers," said I, "is impossible." "Many are the bearers of the wand, but few are the bacchants," according to Plato; for "many are called, but few chosen." And "not in all," says the apostle, "is knowledge." "And pray that we may be delivered from absurd and wicked men; for faith is not for all." And the philosophic poetry of Cleanthes the Stoic writes the like, somewhat thus: "Look not to opinion, wishing to become wise on a sudden, nor fear the undiscerning and shameless opinion of the many. For the multitude has no understanding judgement, whether of just things or of noble; only among few men shall you find it."

Ruling, then, over himself and his own, possessing a firm grasp of the divine knowledge, he comes near to the truth in genuine fashion. For the knowledge and firm grasp of things intelligible may rightly be called science; its work concerning things divine is to consider what the first cause is, and what it is "through which all things were made and without which nothing has come to be"; and again, what things are, as it were, pervading, and what containing; what are conjoined, and what disjoined; and what rank each of these holds, and what power and what office each contributes. And again, among human things, to consider what man himself is, and what is for him according to nature or contrary to nature; how he ought to act or to be acted upon; what his virtues are, and what his vices; and the questions of goods and evils and things intermediate, and all that concerns courage and prudence and temperance, and that perfect virtue which crowns them all, righteousness. But prudence and righteousness he uses toward the acquisition of wisdom; and courage not only in enduring adverse circumstances, but in mastering pleasure and desire, grief and anger as well, and, in general, in setting himself against everything that allures us, whether by violence or by some deceit. For one must not endure vices and evils, but thrust them away; and one must endure things fearful. Useful, therefore, even pain is found to be, in medicine and in teaching and in chastisement; and through it characters are set right for the benefit of mankind.

And again: "Does not then, even here, the soul of the philosopher most of all dishonour the body and flee from it, and seek to be by itself, alone?" And does this not chime with the divine apostle, who says: "Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?"—unless he is figuratively calling "the body of death" the like-mindedness of those who have been dragged down into vice. Even before Marcion, Plato is plainly turning away from intercourse, the beginning of generation, in the first book of the Republic. For, praising old age, he adds: "Know well that, for my part, the more the other pleasures of the body fade away, the more do the desires and pleasures concerning discourse increase"; and when sexual pleasure is mentioned: "Hush, man! I most gladly escaped it, as one escapes a raging and savage master."

More sententiously the comic poet says, in brief: "It is shameful to judge of noble things by the loud din." For they have heard, I think, that beautiful Wisdom that says to us: "In the midst of the witless, watch your opportunity; but in the midst of the thoughtful, persevere." And again: "The wise will hide knowledge." For the many demand demonstration as a pledge of the truth, not content with the salvation that comes by bare faith. "But to evil men it is altogether natural to disbelieve those who hold sway over the truth; but as our Muse bids you to give pledges, learn, now that the argument has been cloven within your inward parts." For to evil men it is habitual, says Empedocles, to wish to master the truth through disbelieving it. But that our things are reputable and worthy of belief, the Greeks shall come to know as the argument is more closely examined in what follows; for by the like we are taught the like. "Answer," says Solomon, "the fool out of his folly." Therefore to those who ask after their own kind of wisdom we must hold out what is proper to them, so that as easily as may be, through what is their own, they may with good reason arrive at faith in the truth. For "to all I became all things," he says, "that I might gain all"; since the rain of the divine grace too is sent down upon just and unjust. "Or is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also, if indeed God is one," cries the noble apostle.

The forms of courage are steadfastness, greatness of mind, magnanimity, liberality, and magnificence. For this reason the gnostic is touched neither by the blame nor by the ill repute that comes from the many, nor is he subject to opinions or to flatteries; and in enduring toils, while at the same time accomplishing something of what befits him, and rising courageously above all circumstances, he shows himself a true man among the rest of men. And again, preserving prudence, he is temperate in the quietness of his soul, receptive of the noble things that are promised as his own, in the turning away from base things as alien—becoming orderly and above the world, doing all things in order and arrangement and erring in nothing anywhere; rich, indeed, in the highest degree, by desiring nothing, since he has few needs and is in the abundance of every good through the knowledge of the Good. For the first work of his righteousness is to pass his life in love with his own kind, and to dwell with them both on earth and in heaven.

Again in the Phaedo, disparaging generation, he writes: "Now the doctrine spoken about these things in secret, that we men are in a kind of guard-post." And again: "But those who are reckoned to have lived in an exceptionally holy way are those who, set free and released from these places in the earth as from prisons, attain to the pure dwelling above." Yet, even so disposed, he perceives that the world is well administered, and says: "One must not, then, set oneself free from this and run away." And, to put it briefly, he gave Marcion no occasion to reckon matter evil, since he himself spoke reverently about the world as follows: "From the one who composed all things it has acquired everything good; but from its former condition it has whatever is harsh and unjust that comes to be in heaven—these it both has from that condition itself and works into the living creatures."

In this way he is also liberal in giving, when he has the means, and a lover of mankind, being the bitterest hater of wickedness through his perfect turning away from all evil-doing. He must learn, then, to be faithful both to himself and to his neighbours and obedient to the commandments. For this is "the servant of God"—he who is willingly led by the commandments. But he who now, not for the commandments' sake but for the sake of knowledge itself, is "pure in heart"—this man is "the friend of God." For neither are we born possessing virtue by nature, nor does it come to us by nature afterwards, once we are born, as do certain other parts of the body (since then it would no longer be voluntary or praiseworthy); nor again is virtue perfected, as language is, out of the things that befall us and the habit thereby formed (for it is in nearly this way that vice arises). Nor does knowledge come about from any art, whether of those that provide a livelihood or of those that tend the body; nor yet from the ordinary cycle of education—it is enough if these can but prepare and serve the soul. For the political laws can perhaps restrain wicked acts;

And still more clearly he adds: "The cause of these things for it is the bodily element of its mixture, the companion of that ancient nature, because it partook of much disorder before it came into the present order of the world." No less, in the Laws, does he lament the race of men, speaking thus: "The gods, taking pity on the race of men, whose nature is born to toil, ordained for them, as rest from their labours, the recurring round of festivals." And in the Epinomis he runs through the causes of his pity and says this: "How, from the very beginning, it is hard for every living thing to come into being—first to share in the condition of those in the womb, then to be born, and still to be reared and educated: all this comes about through countless toils, as we all agree."

but neither they themselves, nor persuasive arguments, being superficial, could provide a scientific and abiding hold upon the truth. Greek philosophy, as it were, purifies the soul beforehand and prepares it for the reception of faith, upon which the truth builds up knowledge. This is he—this is the true athlete in the great stadium, the fair world, who is crowned with the true victory over all the passions. For the president of the games is the almighty God, the umpire is the only-begotten Son of God, and the spectators are angels and gods; and the all-contending struggle is "not against blood and flesh," but against the "spiritual powers" of inordinate passions that work through fleshly things. Prevailing over these great adversaries, and having contended as in certain contests against the tempter who hangs over him, he wins the prize of immortality. For the verdict of God toward the most just judgement cannot be deceived. The theatre, then, is summoned to the contest, and the athletes contend in the stadium; and out of these he prevails who has become obedient to his trainer. For all things lie equally before all from God, and he himself is blameless; but the one who is able will choose, and the one who has willed will prevail. For this reason too we have received mind, that we may know what we do; and the "Know thyself" means, here, to know to what end we have come to be. And we have come to be in order to be obedient to the commandments, if we choose to will our own salvation. This, perhaps, is Adrasteia—the inevitable—by which there is no escaping God.

And what? Does not Heraclitus too call generation death, in agreement with Pythagoras and the Socrates of the Gorgias, when he says: "Death is all that we see when awake; sleep, all that we see asleep"? But enough of these things; and when we treat of first principles, then we shall also examine these contraries which the philosophers hint at and the school of Marcion lay down as doctrine. Only, I think it has been shown by us not obscurely that Marcion took the starting-points of his strange doctrines from Plato, both ungratefully and ignorantly.

The human work, then, is ready obedience to God, who has proclaimed a manifold salvation through commandments; and well-pleasing is acknowledgement. For the benefactor takes the first step in well-doing, and he who receives it readily, with the due reflections, and keeps the commandments, this man is faithful; and he who, as far as he is able, requites the well-doing with the well-doing of love, is now a friend. There is one chief requital on the part of men: to do those things that are pleasing to God. And just as the Teacher and Saviour receives the benefits done to men, and their correction, as though they were his own offspring and a kind of kindred result, reckoning them to his own favour and honour—just as he reckons the injuries done to those who have believed in him as his own ungratefulness and dishonour (for what other dishonour could touch God?)—so it is that there is no other requital worthy of so great a salvation that one could render in return for the benefit from the Lord. But as those who do harm to property insult the masters, and as those who harm soldiers harm their commander, so the maltreatment of those consecrated to the Lord is disregard of the Lord himself. For just as the sun illuminates not only heaven and the whole world, lighting up earth and sea, but also through windows and a small chink sends its ray into the innermost chambers, so the Word, poured out everywhere, looks upon even the smallest acts of life.

Great is this crowd. Some of them, enslaved to pleasures, willing to disbelieve, laugh at the truth that is worthy of all reverence, setting down as a plaything what is "barbarian"; while certain others, exalting themselves, force themselves to find slanders against the words, devising contentious inquiries — hunters of little phrases, zealots of paltry arts, "wranglers and twisters of thongs," as that man of Abdera says: "For twisting is the tongue of mortals; in it are many tales, and a wide pasture of words of all kinds, this way and that"; and: "Whatever word you speak, such you will hear in return." Exalting themselves, then, by this art, the wretched sophists, prattling in their own quibbling, toiling all their life about the distinction of names and the particular composition and entanglement of phrases, show themselves more talkative than turtle-doves — scratching and tickling, not in manly fashion, as I see it, the ears of those itching to be scratched, a sheer river of words but a mere dripping of sense. Indeed, like old shoes, all the rest of them is weak and falls apart, and only the tongue is left.

Let our discussion concerning continence go forward. We were saying that the Greeks, suspecting the difficulty involved, uttered many things against the begetting of children, and that the followers of Marcion, taking these up impiously, are ungrateful to the Demiurge. For tragedy says:

It were better not to come to be than to be born, for mortals. And then I bear children amid bitter pains; and having borne them, if I bear them foolish, I groan in vain, beholding them base; and if I lose the good ones, if any are saved, I melt my wretched heart in dread.
