What good is this? Is it not enough to vex one single soul, and then to have toils upon it?
And again likewise:
To me it seems, now as long ago,
that men ought never to beget children, seeing into what toils we beget them.
And in what is said next he plainly traces the cause of evils back to first principles, speaking thus:

O you who were born to be wretched and to fare ill, you became a man, and a wretched life you took from there, whence for all began to give nourishment this air, breathing breath into mortals; do not, then, being mortal, presume against mortal things.

Most nobly the Athenian Solon inveighs and writes: "You look to the tongue and to the words of a wheedling man; each one of you walks in the tracks of a fox, but in all of you together there is an empty mind." This is what that saving voice hints at: "The foxes have holes, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." For upon the believer alone, I think — wholly distinguished from the rest of the beasts named by the Scripture — the sum of all things finds rest: the good and gentle Word, "who catches the wise in their own craftiness; for the Lord alone knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are vain" — the Scripture calling "wise," of course, the sophists who are over-curious about phrases and arts.
And again he renders the like as follows:
And then again:
Alas, alas, how many are the chances of mortal woes, and how many their shapes; one could not name their limit.
And still likewise:
For of things among mortals there is nothing happy through to the end.

Hence the Greeks themselves have called those who are over-busy about anything whatever both "wise" and "sophist," using the derived word. Cratinus, at least, in the Archilochi, after listing the poets, said: "What a swarm of sophists you have rummaged out." And Iophon likewise, as the comic poet does in the Flute-Singing Satyrs, says of rhapsodes and certain others: "For indeed a crowd of many sophists has come in, fully equipped." Of these and the like — all who have practised empty words — the divine Scripture says most nobly: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will set aside."

For this reason, they say, the Pythagoreans too abstained from sexual relations. But to me they seem rather to marry for the sake of begetting children, and to wish to master the pleasure of sex after the begetting of children. For this reason they mystically forbid the eating of beans—not because the pulse is wind-producing and hard to digest and makes dreams troubled, nor again because the bean is likened to a human head, as in that little verse,
It is all one to eat beans and the heads of one's parents,

but rather because beans, when eaten, make women barren. Theophrastus, at any rate, in the fifth book of his Causes of Plants, records that the husks of beans, placed about the roots of newly planted trees, dry up what is growing; and the domestic fowl, by feeding on them continually, become barren.

And by now they are convicted, not only of filching their doctrines from the barbarians, but also, besides, of mimicking the things wrought among us, from above by the divine power through those who have lived in holiness for our turning toward God, marvellously — telling wonders by Greek mythology. And indeed we shall ask them whether these things they record are true or false. But false they would not say (for they would not willingly cast against themselves a vote of the greatest silliness, that of writing falsehoods); and true they must of necessity confess them to be. And how, then, do the things wonderfully shown forth through Moses and the other prophets still appear unbelievable to them? For God the Almighty, caring for all men, turns some toward salvation by commandments, some by threats, some by wondrous signs, and some by gentle promises. But indeed the Greeks — when a drought once was for a long time wasting Hellas and a barrenness of crops held it fast, the survivors, they say, coming as suppliants by reason of the famine to Delphi, asked the Pythia how they might be rid of the evil. And she gave them one help for their calamity, if they should use the prayer of Aeacus. Persuaded by them, then, Aeacus went up onto the Greek mountain, and stretching out his clean hands to heaven, calling on God as the common Father, prayed him to take pity on Hellas, worn down. And as he prayed, an extraordinary thunder pealed, and all the air round about was overcast, and violent and unceasing rains, breaking out, filled the whole land; whence a plentiful and rich fruitfulness was brought to perfection, husbanded by the prayers of Aeacus.

"And Samuel," it says, "called upon the Lord, and the Lord gave voices and rain in the day of harvest." Do you see that he who rains upon just and unjust, through the powers set beneath him, is one God? And our whole Scripture is full of God's hearing the prayers of the just, and accomplishing each of their requests. Again, the Greeks record that, when the Etesian winds once failed, Aristaeus in Ceos sacrificed to Zeus Icmaeus; for there was great destruction, since all things were being burned up with the heat, and especially since the winds that were wont to cool the crops were not blowing; and he easily called them back. And the Delphians, when Xerxes was marching against Hellas, the Pythia having proclaimed, "O Delphians, pray to the winds, and it shall be the better," having made an altar and a sacrifice to the winds, had them as helpers; for blowing strongly about the headland of Sepias they shattered the whole equipment of the Persian fleet.

And Empedocles of Acragas was surnamed "Wind-stayer." It is said, then, that from the mountain of Acragas, a wind once blowing heavy and sickly upon the inhabitants — and the cause too of barrenness in their women — he stopped the wind; wherefore he himself writes in his verses, "And you shall stay the might of the unwearied winds, which, rushing upon the earth, waste with their blasts the fields of mortals; and again, when you will, you shall bring back the winds in requital." And he said that there followed him "some who craved divinations, and some, long pierced by grievous diseases." So plainly they have believed, from our Scriptures, that the just accomplish healings and signs and wonders. For even if certain powers move the winds and dispense the rains, yet let them hear the psalmist: "How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts." This is the Lord of the hosts and the principalities and the powers, concerning whom Moses says, that we may understand him: "And you shall circumcise the hardness of your heart, and you shall no longer harden your neck; for the Lord your God, he is Lord of lords and God of gods, the great God, and strong," and the rest. And Isaiah says, "Lift up your eyes on high and see: who has shown forth all these things?"

Some say, then, that plagues and hail and storms and the like are wont to come about not from material disorder alone, but also according to some wrath of spirits or of angels who are not good. For instance, they say that the Magi at Cleonae, watching the heavens, turn aside, by songs and sacrifices, the threat of the wrath of the clouds that are about to hurl hail. Indeed, if at any time a want of a victim should overtake them, they make their own finger bleed, and are content with that sacrifice. And Diotima the Mantinean, the Athenians having sacrificed before the plague, made a ten-year postponement of the disease for them; just as the sacrifices of Epimenides the Cretan put off for them the Persian war for the same length of time. And they think it makes no difference whether we call these souls gods or angels. For instance, those experienced in the matter, in their consecrations, in many of the temples and almost all, set up the graves of the departed, calling their souls spirits, and teaching that they are to be worshipped by men, as having received power, through the purity of their life, by the divine providence, to go about the region of the earth in the ministry to men; for they knew that some souls are by nature held fast by the body.

But about these things we shall treat in due season, in the discourse about angels, as the writing goes forward. And Democritus, foretelling many things from the observation of things on high, was surnamed "Wisdom." For instance, when his brother Damasus had welcomed him kindly, conjecturing from certain stars that there would be a great rain, he foretold it. So those who were persuaded by him gathered in their crops (for it was the season of summer, and they were still on the threshing-floors); but the rest lost everything, when an unexpected and heavy rain broke out. And how will the Greeks any longer disbelieve the divine manifestation about Mount Sinai, when fire was burning, consuming nothing of the things that grew about the mountain, and a sound of trumpets was borne, breathed forth without instruments? For that which is called the descent of God upon the mountain is an appearing of the divine power, pervading the whole world and proclaiming the unapproachable light. For such is the allegory according to the Scripture. But indeed the fire was seen, as Aristobulus says, by all that multitude — not fewer than a hundred myriads, besides those under age — assembling round the mountain, the circuit about the mountain being not less than five days' journey.

In every place, then, of vision, the fire was seen by all of them, burning round about, as by men encamped, so that the descent was not local; for everywhere is God. And those too who composed the histories say that about the British island there is a cave lying beneath a mountain, and on the summit a chasm; when, then, the wind falls into the cave and dashes against the recesses of the hollow, a sound is heard as of cymbals beaten in rhythm. And often too, as the leaves are moved through the woods by a sudden onset of wind, a sound falls upon the ear like the song of birds. But those who composed the Persian histories record that in the highlands, in the country of the Magi, three mountains lie in a row in a long plain; and those who pass through the place, coming to the first mountain, hear a sound as of a confused crowd, like that of not a few myriads shouting, as in array of battle; coming to the middle, they catch a tumult at once greater and more distinct; and at the end they hear, as of men singing the paean, like men who have conquered. And the cause, I think, of every such sound is the smoothness of the places and their cavernous nature; for the wind that has entered, being thrown back and going again into the same place, resounds the more violently.

And let these things be so. But for God the Almighty it is possible, even with nothing lying beneath, to engender a voice and an impression in the hearing, showing forth his own majesty by what has a natural sequence beyond the wonted course, unto the turning of the soul that does not yet believe, and the reception of the commandment given. And a cloud being present, and a high mountain, how is it not possible for a varied sound to be heard, as the wind is moved by the working cause? Wherefore the prophet too says, "You heard the voice of words, and a likeness you did not see." Do you see how the Lord's voice is the Word without shape? For the power of the Word, a luminous word of the Lord, the truth come down from heaven above upon the gathering of the church, wrought through a luminous and immediate ministry.

For every inquiry is conducted out of a knowledge previously existing. And it is possible for the knowledge that exists beforehand to be: sometimes of the substance bare, the works of the thing being unknown—as of stones, plants, animals, whose activities we do not know; or of their affections, or powers, or, in a word, of one of the things belonging to existing things. And sometimes one of these powers or affections, or some of these, is known—as the desires and passions of the soul—but the substance is unknown and sought. And in many cases, our very thought supposing all these things to itself, the inquiry is to which of the substances such a thing would belong. For having grasped in the understanding the conceptions of both—of the substance and of the activity—we thus come to the inquiry. And there are cases in which, knowing the activities together with the substances, we are ignorant of the affections. The method of discovery, then, is this: one must begin from the very recognition of the problems. For often the form of the expression deceives, and confounds and disturbs the understanding, so that it is not easy to find from what difference it is—as, for example, whether the thing conceived in the womb is an animal. For having some notion both of an animal and of the thing conceived, we inquire whether being an animal belongs to the thing conceived; and this is, whether to the conceived substance belongs the power to be moved and, further, to perceive. So that the inquiry is of activities and affections upon a substance previously known.

Straightway, then, one must put the question back to the one who proposes it: what, after all, does he call an animal? For this must especially be done when we see the name being led into different uses; and one must search out whether the thing signified by the name is disputed or agreed upon by all. For if he should say that he calls an animal whatever grows and is nourished, we shall again ask in turn whether he holds that plants too are animals; and then, if he says so, one must already show the thing conceived to be growing and nourished. For Plato calls plants too animals, as partaking of "the third kind of soul" alone, the appetitive; but Aristotle thinks that plants partake of the vegetative and nutritive soul, yet does not think fit to call them animals already; for he thinks that only what partakes of the other soul, the perceptive, deserves to be called an animal. The Stoics, however, do not name the vegetative power a soul at all. But if the one who proposes the question denies that plants too are animals, we shall show him saying things that contradict himself. For having defined the animal by being nourished and growing, but having declared that the plant too is not an animal, he seems to say nothing else than that the thing nourished and growing both is an animal and is not an animal. Let him say, then, what he wishes to learn: whether the thing in the womb grows and is nourished, or whether it has some share of perception or of self-impelled motion. For according to Plato the plant is ensouled and an animal; according to Aristotle, not yet an animal, for it lacks perception, but already ensouled. For with him the animal is an ensouled, perceptive substance. But according to the Stoics the plant is neither ensouled nor an animal; for the animal is an ensouled substance.

If, then, the animal is ensouled, and the soul is a perceptive nature, it is plain that the ensouled thing is already perceptive. If, then, the one who asked whether the thing in the womb is an animal, on being asked back, should say that he calls an animal that which is nourished and grows, he has his answer. But if he should declare that this is what he is seeking—whether the thing conceived is already perceptive, or is in some way self-impelled to motion—then the investigation of the matter becomes clear, the deceit about the name no longer remaining. But if he does not answer the counter-question, nor wishes to say what after all he means, or to what thing he is applying the name "animal" when he made his proposition, but bids us ourselves draw the distinction, he would be recognized as a wrangler. And if, there being two modes—one by question and answer, the other by continuous exposition—he refuses the one, let him give ear to all the things we go through into the problem; then, when we have finished, it will be open to him to take up each particular point in turn.

But we, who have received, through the Scriptures, that choice and avoidance have been given to men with a self-determining authority from the Lord, let us rest upon faith as an unwavering criterion, having shown the spirit ready, in that we have chosen life and have believed God through his voice. And he who has believed the Word knows the matter to be true; for the Word is truth. But he who has disbelieved the one who speaks has disbelieved God. "By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen has not come from things that appear," says the Apostle. "By faith Abel offered a fuller sacrifice than Cain, through which he was witnessed to be just, God bearing witness over his gifts; and through it, having died, he yet speaks" — and the rest, down to "than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin." These, then, even before the Law, faith justified and made heirs of the divine promise.

But if he should attempt to break in upon the examination by interrupting with questions, he plainly does not even wish to listen. But if he chooses to answer, first of all one must ask him to what thing he is applying the name "animal"; and when he has answered this, one must ask again what after all he signifies by "the thing conceived" or "the thing in the womb"—whether he wishes "the thing in the womb" to signify the things not yet fully formed and the seed itself once cast in, or only the things articulated and already fully formed, which are called embryos. And when he has answered this too, one must then conclude the matter in hand in order and teach it. But if he wishes us to speak, himself not answering, let him give ear: since you will not say with reference to what signification you say the thing you proposed (for in that case I would not have been making my discourse about things signified, but should already have been considering the very things themselves)—know that you have done something like what you would have done had you proposed the question whether the dog is an animal. For reasonably I would say: what dog? For I shall go through the land-dog and the sea-dog and the star in heaven called the Dog, and also Diogenes and the rest of the dogs in turn. For I could not divine whether you are asking about all, or about one. What, then, you will do later—to learn now about which you are inquiring—say plainly. But if you turn about names, the thing conceived—this very name—is plainly, to everyone, neither an animal nor a plant, but a name and a sound and a body and a being and a something, and anything rather than an animal. And if this is what you proposed, you have your answer.

Why, then, should I still set out testimonies of faith, gathering them from the history among us? For the time would fail me to recount Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, and David and Samuel and the prophets, and what follows upon these. And of the four things in which the true resides — perception, mind, knowledge, assumption — by nature the mind is first, but to us and in relation to us perception is first; and out of perception and mind is constituted the essence of knowledge, and the evident is common to mind and perception. But perception is a stepping-stone of knowledge, while faith, having journeyed through the things of sense, leaves behind assumption, and hastens toward the unerring things and abides in the truth. And if anyone should say that knowledge is demonstrative with reason, let him hear that the first principles too are indemonstrable; for they are known neither by art nor by prudence. For the one is concerned with things that can be otherwise, and the other is productive only, not also contemplative.

Hence with good reason the gnostic, when called, obeys readily, and to the one who asks for his poor body he hands it over willingly, and his passions too, stripping these off beforehand from his fleshly frame, not insulting the tempter but, I think, instructing and convicting him:
from what honour and what length of bliss,

as Empedocles says, having come hither, he dwells among mortals. This man truly bears witness for himself that he is a genuine believer toward God; and for the tempter, that he has striven in vain against the man faithful through love; and to the Lord, his god-given persuasion toward the teaching, from which he will not depart through fear of death. Indeed, he confirms by deed the truth of the preaching, showing that the God toward whom he hastens is able. You would wonder at his love, which he plainly teaches as he is united thankfully to what is akin to him; and moreover he abashes the unbelievers by his precious blood.

Nor indeed is the thing signified by the name "conceived" an animal; rather, that is incorporeal, and a thing-said, and a matter, and a notion, and anything rather than an animal. And the nature of the animal would be something else; for it was plainly being shown of the very thing sought—I mean, of what sort the nature of the embryo is, this being a different problem from the one about the things signified by the name "animal." I say, then: if you call an animal that which is able to perceive and to be moved of its own impulse, then not simply that which is moved of its own impulse and perceives is an animal; for it is able also to sleep, or, when the objects of sense are not present, not to perceive. Rather, that which is able either to be impelled or to perceive by nature is the mark of an animal. For something of this sort is signified by these terms. First, whether the thing conceived is already able to perceive or to be moved of its own impulse—which is what is proposed for consideration; and second, whether the thing conceived will ever be able to perceive or to be moved of its own impulse—in which signification no one inquires, it being plain. But it was inquired whether the embryo is already an animal or still a plant. And then the name "animal" was taken over into a discourse, that it might be clear. Having found it differing from the non-animal by perception and self-impelled motion, we again distinguished this from the things lying near it, saying that one thing is that which is such in potency—which is not yet perceiving and being moved, but will at some time be such—and another is that which is already such in actuality; and of this, one is already in act, and the other is able to act but is at rest or sleeping. And this last is the thing sought. For one must not say that the embryo is an animal from its being nourished—which is of the substance—departing from the thing sought and attending to the things that otherwise belong to it.

By faith alone, then, is it possible to reach the principle of the universe. For all knowledge is teachable; and the teachable is from what is foreknown. But the principle of the universe was not foreknown to the Greeks — neither to Thales, who took water for the first cause, nor to the other natural philosophers in succession; since even if Anaxagoras first set mind over things, yet not even he preserved the efficient cause, depicting certain senseless whirls together with the inactivity and senselessness of mind. Wherefore the Word says: "Call no one your teacher upon the earth." For knowledge is a demonstrative state, but faith is a grace that brings up, from the indemonstrable, to the universal the simple — which is neither with matter, nor matter, nor under matter.

This man, then, will not, out of fear, turn aside from denying Christ for the sake of the commandment, so as to become a martyr through fear; nor again, selling his faith in hope of rewards prepared, but out of love toward the Lord he will most gladly be released from this life—giving thanks, perhaps, both to the one who furnished the cause of his departure hence and to the one who contrived the plot, since he has received a reasonable pretext, which he did not himself supply, of showing himself for what he is: to the one through endurance, but to the Lord through love, by which he was already shown forth to the Lord, who knew, even before his birth, the purpose of the one who would bear witness. Taking courage, then, he goes to the Lord as to a friend, for whom he has willingly given up his body, and besides, as the judges expected, his soul too; having heard, in the words of the poet, "dear brother" from our Saviour, on account of the likeness of his life. So at once we call martyrdom "perfection," not because the man received the end of his life as the rest do, but because he displayed a perfect work of love. And the men of old among the Greeks too praise the death of those who died in war—not counselling a violent death, but because the man who dies in war is released, free from fear of dying, cut off from the body, having neither toiled beforehand in soul nor grown soft, as men do in their sicknesses; for they pass away made womanish and yearning for life.

And common to all the things said to be discovered is demonstration, which is a discourse confirming, out of certain things, some other thing. And the things out of which the thing sought must be confirmed must be agreed upon and known to the one who learns. And the beginning of all these is that which is plain to sense and to thought. The first demonstration, then, is composed out of these; but that which, from the things already shown to have been demonstrated through this, concludes again something else, is no less trustworthy than the former, yet cannot be named primary, because it is not concluded from primary propositions. The first kind of the difference among the things sought, there being three, has been shown—I mean, that (the substance being known) some of its works or affections are unknown; and the second difference of problems was that in which we all know the works and affections, but are ignorant of the substance—as, in what part of the body is the ruling faculty of the soul.

But the unbelievers, as it seems, drag all things down from heaven and the invisible to earth, "simply grasping rocks and oaks with their hands," according to Plato. For laying hold of all such things, they affirm that this alone is, which offers some collision and contact, defining body and essence as the same. But those who dispute against them defend themselves very cautiously from above, from some invisible quarter, contending that certain intelligible and incorporeal forms are the true essence. "Behold, I make new things," says the Word, "which eye has not seen nor ear heard nor has come up upon the heart of man" — with a new eye, a new hearing, a new heart, all that is visible and audible and apprehensible through faith and understanding, the disciples of the Lord speaking, hearing, doing spiritually. For there is an approved coin and another counterfeit, which deceives the laymen no less, but not the money-changers, who know, having learned, to separate and distinguish the counterfeit from the approved. So the money-changer says to the layman only this of the coin, that it is counterfeit; but the how, the why, only the banker's familiar and the one trained for this learns. And Aristotle says that the judgment that follows upon knowledge — that this thing is true — is faith. Faith, then, is more authoritative than knowledge and is its criterion.

For this reason they do not even release the soul pure, but carrying with itself the desires like leaden weights—unless some of these have become noteworthy for virtue. And there are those too who die in war along with their desires, and these are in no way different than if they had withered away in sickness. If, then, confession toward God is martyrdom, every soul that has lived purely with the knowledge of God, that has obeyed the commandments, is a martyr both in life and in word, however it is released from the body—pouring out faith like blood throughout the whole of life, and at its departure too. For at once the Lord says in the gospel: "Whoever shall leave father or mother or brothers," and so on, "for the sake of the gospel and my name, is blessed"—indicating not the simple martyrdom but the gnostic one, of the man who has conducted himself according to the rule of the gospel through love toward the Lord. For the knowledge of the name and the understanding of the gospel signify knowledge, not the bare appellation . . . to leave behind the worldly kindred, and to leave behind substance and all possession, in order to live without passionate attachment. For the fatherland and nurse are allegorized as the mother, and fathers as the civic laws; which the high-minded righteous man must thankfully despise, for the sake of becoming a friend of God and attaining the right-hand portions of the sanctuary, as the apostles too did.

And conjecture counterfeits faith, being a weak assumption, as the flatterer counterfeits the friend and the wolf the dog. But since we see that the carpenter, having learned, becomes a craftsman, and the pilot, educated in the art, will be able to steer — reckoning that to wish to become noble and good is not enough — it is necessary, then, being persuaded, to learn. And to be persuaded by the Word, whom we proclaimed teacher, is to believe in him in nothing opposing. For how is it possible to set oneself against God? Faithful, then, is knowledge, and knowable is faith, by a certain divine sequence and reciprocal sequence. Indeed, even Epicurus, who especially preferred pleasure to truth, supposes faith to be an anticipation of the mind; and he renders anticipation an application to something evident and to the evident conception of the thing; and that no one can either inquire or be at a loss, or even form an opinion, nor indeed refute, without an anticipation.

Then Heraclitus says, "Gods and men honour those slain in war"; and Plato writes in the fifth book of the Republic: "Of those who have died on campaign, whoever ends his life having earned a good name—shall we not first say that he is of the golden kind? Most certainly." And the golden kind is among the gods in heaven and the fixed sphere, who chiefly have the leadership of providence over men. But some of the heretics, having misheard the Lord, impiously and at the same time cowardly love life, saying that the true martyrdom is the knowledge of the truly existent God—which we too confess—but that the man who confesses through death is a murderer and a slayer of himself, and bringing forward other such sophisms of cowardice. To these we shall speak when the occasion demands; for they differ from us about first principles.

And how could anyone, not having an anticipation of what he reaches after, learn about what he inquires into? And he who has learned makes the anticipation already an apprehension. And if the learner does not learn without an anticipation receptive of the things said, he himself has ears that can hear the truth. And "blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear"; just as, of course, blessed is also he himself, of his obedience. And to hearken is to understand. If, then, faith is nothing other than an anticipation of the mind concerning the things said, and this is called both obedience and understanding and persuasion, no one will learn without faith, since neither without anticipation. And, being true beyond anything, that is demonstrated which was said by the prophet: "Unless you believe, neither will you understand." This too Heraclitus of Ephesus, paraphrasing the oracle, has said: "Unless he hope for the unhoped-for, he will not find it out, it being unsearchable and without passage."

But we too blame those who leap upon death; for there are some, not ours, partners only in the name, who hasten to give themselves up out of hatred toward the Demiurge, the wretches, with a death-wish. These, we say, take themselves off as no martyrs, even if they are publicly punished. For they do not preserve the character of the faithful man's martyrdom, not having known the truly existent God, but give themselves over to an empty death, just as the gymnosophists of the Indians give themselves to a vain fire. But since these falsely-named men slander the body, let them learn that the good proportion of the body too contributes to the mind toward good natural endowment.

But Plato the philosopher too, in the Laws, says that the man who is to become blessed and happy must, from the very beginning, be a partaker of the truth, that he may live as long a time as possible being true; for he is faithful. But the unfaithful is he to whom voluntary falsehood is dear; and he to whom it is involuntary is without sense; and neither of these is to be envied. For everyone who is unfaithful and unlearned is without a friend. And perhaps it is this that he calls, in a hidden way, the "kingly wisdom" in the Euthydemus. So in the Statesman he says, word for word: "So that the science of the true king is kingly, and he who possesses it, whether he be a ruler or a private man, will, at all events, according to the art itself, be rightly called kingly." So those who have believed in Christ both are and are called good (chrestoi), as those who are truly kingly are those cared for by a king. For as the wise are wise by wisdom, and the lawful lawful by law, so by Christ the king the Christians, the kingly ones of Christ. Then, going on, he adds clearly: "The right would be lawful, and law, being by nature, is right reason, and not in writings nor in other things." And the Eleatic stranger declares the kingly and statesmanlike man a living law.

For this reason Plato said in the third book of the Republic—he whom they most invoke as their witness in disparaging generation—that one must care for the body for the sake of the soul's harmony, through which it is possible to live and to live rightly, proclaiming the message of the truth; for it is by living and through health that we make our way and learn knowledge. But for the man to whom it is not even possible to come a little way up to the heights without being among the necessities and through them doing all that conduces to knowledge—how is the good life not to be chosen by him? In living, then, the good life is set right, and the man who through the body has practised good living is sent forward into the habit of eternity.

And such is he who fulfils the law and does the will of the Father, but is plainly inscribed upon a certain lofty wood, set forth as an example of divine virtue to those able to discern. And the Greeks know the dispatch-staves of the ephors in Lacedaemon, on which the law was inscribed on wood; but my law, as has been said, is both kingly and living, and is right reason: "Law, the king of all, both mortals and immortals," as the Boeotian Pindar sings. For Speusippus, in the first book against Cleophon, seems to write the like to Plato through this: "For if kingship is a serious thing, and the wise man alone is king and ruler, then the law, being right reason, is serious" — which it indeed is. With these the Stoic philosophers dogmatize in agreement, attaching kingship, priesthood, prophecy, legislation, wealth, true beauty, nobility, and freedom to the wise man alone — who, however, is very exceedingly hard to find, as is confessed even by them.

But since they are not willing to believe, with right reason, either in the Good or in knowledge unto salvation, we ourselves, reckoning their own things to be ours — because all things are God's, and especially since what is noble came to the Greeks from us — set our hand to them as they are by nature able to hear. For the great mob does not judge what is intelligent, or what is just, out of the truth, but out of whatever pleases it. And it would be pleased by none more than by those like itself. For so much of a man as is still blind and deaf, having no understanding, nor the undaunted and keen-sighted vision of a soul that loves to behold — which the Saviour alone implants — must, like one uninitiated at the rites or unmusical in the dance, being not yet pure nor worthy of the holy truth, but discordant and disorderly and material, stand still outside the divine choir; "for we compare spiritual things with spiritual." For this reason, indeed, the manner of concealment, being truly divine and most necessary to us on account of the holy Word that lies stored away in the sanctuary of truth, was hinted at by the Egyptians through what they call their inner shrines, and by the Hebrews through the veil; through which it was permitted to enter only to those who were consecrated — that is, to those dedicated to God, who had circumcised the desires of their passions through love toward the divine alone. For Plato too agreed that it is not lawful for the impure to touch the pure.

Hence the prophecies and the oracles are spoken through riddles, and the rites are not shown to all who come unreservedly, but with certain purifications and forewarnings: "For the Muse was not yet greedy of gain in those days, nor a hireling; nor were sweet, honey-voiced songs, soft of utterance, sold by Terpsichore with silvered faces." Take, for instance, those who are educated among the Egyptians: first of all they learn the method of the Egyptian letters called epistolographic; second, the hieratic, which the sacred scribes use; and last and finally the hieroglyphic, of which one kind, by means of the primary elements, is literal, and the other symbolic. Of the symbolic, one kind is literal by imitation, another is written as it were figuratively, and another is downright allegorical by means of certain riddles. Thus, wishing to write "sun," they make a circle, and "moon" a crescent shape, according to the literal kind. But figuratively, transferring and shifting things according to affinity, and altering some and reshaping others in manifold ways, they engrave them.

Thus the praises of their kings they hand down in myths treated as theology, and inscribe by means of reliefs. Of the third kind, according to riddles, let this be a specimen: the other stars, on account of their oblique course, they likened to the bodies of serpents, but the sun to that of the beetle, since it moulds a round shape out of ox-dung and rolls it facing it. And they say that this creature lives six months under the earth, and the other part of the year above the earth, and that it sows its seed into the ball and brings forth young, and that no female beetle comes into being. All those, then, so to speak, who have treated of theology, both barbarians and Greeks, hid away the first principles of things, and handed down the truth in riddles and symbols, and again in allegories and metaphors and such-like devices — like the oracles among the Greeks; and the very Pythian Apollo is called Loxias, "the oblique."

Yes, and the apophthegms of those called among the Greeks the wise men show forth, in a few words, the unfolding of a greater matter — such as, doubtless, "Spare time": either because life is short, and one ought not to spend this time in vain; or, in the opposite sense, "Spare expense" in private outlay, so that, even if you live many years, the necessaries of life may not fail you.

But the Greeks suppose their gods to be, like men, both in form and in passion; and as each people paint their forms like to themselves—as Xenophanes says, "the Ethiopians black and snub-nosed, the Thracians red-haired and grey-eyed"—so too they fashion the souls of their gods like to their own. The barbarians, accordingly, make them beastlike and savage in character, and the Greeks gentler, yet still subject to passion. For this reason it is reasonable that the wicked should have base conceptions about God, and the good the best; and on this account he who is truly "kingly in soul," and is gnostic and devout and free from superstition, is persuaded that the only God is honourable, august, magnificent, well-doing, beneficent, the author of all good things, but in no way the cause of evils. And concerning Greek superstition we have, I think, set things forth sufficiently in our treatise entitled the Exhortation, making free use of the relevant history as need pressed. There is no call, then, "to tell over again as a tale what has been clearly said."

In the same way "Know yourself" points to many things: both that you are mortal, and that you were born a man; and further, in comparison with the other excellences of life, that you are of no account — calling oneself glorious, or rich, or, on the contrary, that, though rich and glorious, you pride yourself on no abiding advantage. And "Know for what you came into being," he says, "and whose image you are, and what is your substance, and what your fashioning, and what your kinship with the divine," and the like. The Spirit says too, through Isaiah the prophet, "I will give you treasures dark and hidden." And the treasures of God, and the wealth that does not fail, is wisdom hard to track down.

Yet, as far as to take note of it while we are upon the subject, a few points out of many will suffice—and these alone serve to show that those who liken the Divine to the worst of men are atheists. For either the gods are harmed by men, and are shown by us to be worse than men in being harmed by them; or, if not this, then how is it that, in cases where they are not harmed, they grow bitter—like some irascible old woman provoked to anger—as men say that Artemis was wroth with the Aetolians on account of Oeneus? For how did she not reason, being a goddess, that Oeneus had not despised her, but had either forgotten, or had neglected the matter as though he had already sacrificed? Well too does Auge plead her cause against Athena for being angry with her because she had given birth in the temple, saying: "You rejoice to look on the spoils that destroy mortals, and the wreckage of the dead, and these are not defilement to you; but if I have given birth, you count this a dreadful thing." And yet the other animals too, giving birth in the temples, do no wrong.

But the poets too, taught their theology by these prophets, philosophize much by way of hidden meaning — I mean Orpheus, Linus, Musaeus, Homer, and Hesiod, and those who are wise in this way. The persuasive charm of their poetry is to them a veil before the many. Dreams and symbols are all the more obscure to men, not out of envy — for it is not lawful to think of God as subject to passion — but in order that inquiry, slipping in toward the meaning of the riddles, may run up to the discovery of the truth. Thus Sophocles, the poet of tragedy, says somewhere: "And I know God to be such as this: ever to the wise a propounder of oracles in riddles, but to the dull a poor teacher, and that in few words" — using "poor" for "simple."

Reasonably, then, the superstitious, becoming credulous about those easily moved to anger, take all that befalls them to be signs and causes of evils. If a mouse should dig through an altar that is made of clay, or, having nothing else, should gnaw through a bag; if a fowl that is being reared should crow at evening—they set this down as a sign of something. Menander mocks just such a man in his Superstitious Man: "May some good thing befall me, O most honoured gods! For as I was putting on my shoe I broke the strap of my right sandal." "Reasonably, you babbler; for it was rotten, and you, being mean, would not buy a new pair." Charming is the saying of Antiphon. When a man took it for an omen that a sow had eaten her piglets, Antiphon, seeing that she had been wasted by hunger through the meanness of the one who fed her, said: "Rejoice at the omen, that, being so hungry, she did not eat your children." "And what is there to wonder at," says Bion, "if the mouse gnawed through the bag, finding nothing to eat? For it would have been a wonder if—as Arcesilaus jestingly suggested—the bag had eaten the mouse."

Homer too calls a craftsman "wise," and concerning the Margites — if indeed it is his — he writes somewhat thus: "Him the gods made neither a digger nor a ploughman, nor in any other way wise, but he missed every art." Hesiod, calling the lyre-player Linus "skilled in every kind of wisdom," does not shrink from calling a sailor too "wise," writing of one "in no way made wise in seamanship." And Daniel the prophet says: "The mystery which the king asks — it is not in the power of wise men, magi, enchanters, Gazarenes, to declare it to the king; but there is a God in heaven who reveals it." And indeed he calls the men of Babylon "wise." That the Scripture, by the same name, calls "wisdom" all worldly knowledge or art — and there are many such, devised by human reasoning in combination — and that the inventive and wise contrivance is from God, will be clear if we set down this passage: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with a divine spirit of wisdom and understanding and knowledge in every work, to devise and to be master-builder, to work gold and silver and bronze, the blue and the purple and the scarlet, and the stone-cutting and the carpentry of wood, to work in all manner of work."

Of those who are led by heresy, we have mentioned Marcion of Pontus, who, because of his opposition to the Demiurge, refuses the use of worldly things. The cause of his continence—if indeed this is to be called continence—is the Demiurge Himself, against whom this giant who fights with God supposes himself to stand, and so is continent against his will, running down both the creation and the thing fashioned. And even if they make use of the saying of the Lord to Philip, "Let the dead bury their own dead, but follow me," let them consider this: that Philip too bears the same fashioning of the flesh, and yet had no defiled corpse. How then, having a body of flesh, did he have no corpse? Because he had risen from the tomb when the Lord put the passions to death, but lived to Christ. We have mentioned also the lawless community of women according to Carpocrates; but, having discussed the saying of Nicolaus, we passed over this. They say that he had a beautiful wife, and after the Saviour's ascension, being reproached by the apostles for jealousy, he brought his wife into the midst and gave leave for anyone who wished to marry her. For this act, they say, agrees with that saying, "One must abuse the flesh"; and accordingly, following both the deed and the saying simply and without examination, those who pursue his sect fornicate without restraint.

Plainly, at any rate, concerning all our Scripture it is written in the Psalms that it is spoken as in a parable: "Hear, my people, my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter problems from of old." And the noble apostle says the like, somewhat thus: "We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age that come to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God foreordained before the ages unto our glory, which none of the rulers of this age has known; for had they known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." The philosophers, indeed, were not empowered to outrage the Lord's coming; it remains, then, that the apostle is rebuking the conceit of the wise among the Jews. Therefore he adds: "But we preach, as it is written," he says, "things which eye has not seen and ear has not heard, and which have not entered into the heart of man, the things which God has prepared for those who love him. For to us God has revealed them through the Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God." For he knows the spiritual man, the gnostic, to be the disciple of the Holy Spirit supplied by God, which is the mind of Christ. "But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit; for to him they are foolishness."

Well too did Diogenes say to the man who marvelled that he had found the serpent coiled about the pestle: "Do not marvel; for that would have been the stranger thing, had you seen the pestle coiled about the upright serpent." For the irrational animals too must run and dart, fight, bring forth, and die—things which, being according to nature for them, could never be contrary to nature for us. "And many birds beneath the sun's rays go to and fro." The comic poet Philemon too mocks such things: "Whenever I see," he says, "a man watching closely who sneezed or who spoke, or who it is that goes before him, scanning it all—I sell that man at once in the market-place. Each of us walks for himself, and speaks and sneezes; things come to pass for us in the city according to their nature." Then, sober, men ask for health; but, gorging themselves and rolling in drunkenness at the festivals, they draw diseases upon themselves.

Then he adds a general statement: "And to everyone understanding in heart I have given understanding" — that is, to the man able to receive it by toil and training. And again, expressly in the name of the Lord, it is written: "And you, speak to all the wise in understanding, whom I have filled with the spirit of perception." The wise in understanding have a certain native property of nature, but they receive a twofold "spirit of perception" from the most authoritative Wisdom, when they have made themselves fit. For those who pursue the mechanical arts enjoy a surplus in the region of the senses: in hearing, the man commonly called the musician; in touch, the modeller; in voice, the singer; in smell, the perfumer; in sight, the engraver of the impressions on seal-stones. And those who spend their time on education are supplied with a perceptiveness by which the poets grasp metres, the sophists phrasing, the dialecticians syllogisms, and the philosophers the contemplation that belongs to them. For this perceptiveness is inventive and ingenious, persuading us to make a plausible attempt; and training toward knowledge increases the application.

But I myself have learned that Nicolaus had relations with no other woman than the one he married; that of his children the daughters grew old as virgins, and the son remained unmarried and undefiled. Such being the case, the bringing of the wife of whom he was jealous into the midst of the apostles was the casting off of passion; and the continence with respect to the most eagerly pursued pleasures taught the meaning of "abusing the flesh." For he did not wish, I think, to serve two masters at once—pleasure and God—against the Saviour's commandment. They say, at any rate, that Matthias too taught thus: to fight against the flesh and to abuse it, yielding nothing to it for unrestrained pleasure, but to increase the soul through faith and knowledge.

Thus the apostle, to set the common faith over against gnostic perfection, calls it in one place a foundation, in another milk, writing in this fashion: "Brethren, I could not speak to you as to spiritual men, but as to fleshly, as to babes in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able. But neither even now are you able, for you are still fleshly. For where there is among you jealousy and strife, are you not fleshly, and walking after the manner of men?" The objects of choice belong to the sinful among men; but those who have abstained from these set their minds on the things of God and partake of gnostic food. "According to the grace," he says, "given to me, as a wise master-builder I have laid a foundation, but another builds upon it gold and silver and precious stones." These are gnostic structures upon the base of faith in Jesus Christ; but stubble are the additions of the heresies, and wood and hay. "Of what sort each man's work is, the fire shall test." The gnostic edifice he hints at also in the Epistle to the Romans, saying: "For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift, to the end that you may be strengthened." But it was not possible to write of such gifts openly.

Many fear also the inscriptions that are set up. Very neatly did Diogenes, finding written over the house of a worthless man, "The glorious victor Heracles dwells here; let no evil enter in," say: "And how then shall the master of the house come in?" These same men, worshipping every piece of wood and every stone, as the saying goes—anointing them—stand in dread of red wool and lumps of salt and torches, of squill and brimstone, being bewitched by the sorcerers with their unclean purifications. But God—the God who truly is—knows only the character of the just as holy, just as that of the unjust and wicked is accursed. One may indeed see that the eggs of birds that have undergone such purifications, if warmed, are still quickened into life; and this would not happen if they had taken up the evils of the one purified. Charmingly too the comic poet Diphilus mocks the sorcerers in these lines: "Purifying the daughters of Proetus, and their father Proetus son of Abas, and a fifth, an old crone besides—with one torch and one squill, for so many bodies of men—with brimstone and bitumen and the loud-roaring sea, from gently-flowing, deep-flowing Ocean. But, blessed Air, send through the clouds for hellebore, that I may make this bug into a drone."

With reason, then, the Apostle has called the wisdom of God "manifold," showing forth its own power "in many parts and in many ways" — through art, through knowledge, through faith, through prophecy — for our benefit, "since all wisdom is from the Lord, and is with him for ever," as the wisdom of Jesus says. "For if you call upon prudence and perception with a loud voice, and seek her as treasures of silver, and eagerly track her out, you will understand the fear of God and will find a divine perception" — the prophet has spoken thus by way of contrast with the perception that belongs to philosophy, which he teaches us to search out greatly and magnificently for our advance toward the fear of God. He has, then, set over against it the perception that is in the fear of God, hinting at knowledge, and saying this: "For God gives wisdom from his own mouth, and perception together with prudence, and stores up help for the just" — for to those justified by philosophy help is stored up, and the perceptiveness that is toward the fear of God.

There are some who proclaim the vulgar Aphrodite to be a mystical communion, insulting even the name; for "to do" something is called "to work" something evil, just as "to do" something good is also called by the same name "to work" it. So likewise communion is good in the sharing of money and food and clothing; but these men have impiously called any sort of sexual intercourse "communion." They say, at any rate, that one of them approached a beautiful young virgin of our company and said, "It is written, 'Give to everyone who asks of you.'" But she, very gravely, not understanding the man's lewdness, answered, "Concerning marriage, talk with my mother." O the godlessness! Even of the Lord's sayings these partners in lewdness make false use—these brothers in lust, a reproach not only to philosophy but to all human life, who falsify the truth, or rather demolish it as far as in them lies. For these thrice-wretched men celebrate as a sacred mystery the carnal and copulatory communion, and think that this leads them up into the kingdom of God.

Well too says Menander: "If you had some real evil, Phidias, you would need to seek a real remedy for it; but as it is, you have none. Find then an empty remedy for the empty trouble, and think that something does you good. Let the women wipe you all round in a circle and burn incense about you; sprinkle yourself with water from three springs, having thrown in salt and lentils." Pure is everyone who is conscious of no evil in himself. Tragedy, accordingly, says: "Orestes, what disease destroys you?" "The consciousness—that I know I have done dreadful things." For in truth purity is nothing else than abstinence from sins. Well, then, does Epicharmus say: "If you keep your mind pure, you are pure in your whole body." So too we say that one must first purify the souls from base and wicked doctrines through right reason, and then, in that way, turn to the recollection of the chief points set forth before. For even before the delivery of the mysteries they think it right to bring certain purifications to those who are about to be initiated, since one must lay aside the godless opinion and turn to the true tradition.

Into the brothels, then, does such a communion lead; and swine and goats would be their fellow-partners; and among them the foremost place in their greater hopes would belong to the prostitutes who keep the roof, receiving without restraint all who wish to come. But you did not so learn Christ, if indeed you have heard Him and have been taught in Him, as the truth is in Christ Jesus: to put off, in regard to your former conduct, the old man who is corrupted according to the desires of deceit; and to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and to put on the new man, who is created according to God in righteousness and holiness of the truth, after the likeness of the divine. Be therefore imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, even as Christ also loved you and gave Himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour. But fornication and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be named among you, as becomes saints; nor filthiness nor foolish talking. For, teaching us to be pure even in our speech, the apostle writes: "This you know, recognizing that no fornicator," and so on, down to "but rather even reprove them."

Their doctrine flowed from a certain apocryphal book, and I will set down the passage that is the mother of their lewdness. And whether they themselves are the authors of the book (consider the madness, if they lie even against God out of incontinence), or whether they came upon others and conceived this fine doctrine after hearing it in a distorted way, the words of the passage are as follows: "All things were one; but since its unity did not seem good to be alone, there went forth from it an inspiration, and it had communion with it and made the Beloved; and from this there went forth from it an inspiration, with which it had communion and made powers that could neither be seen nor heard"—down to "each by its own name." For if these men, like the followers of Valentinus, posited spiritual communions, perhaps one might accept their supposition; but to refer the communion of carnal outrage to holy prophecy is the act of one who has given up all hope of salvation.

Such are the doctrines of the followers of Prodicus also, who falsely proclaim themselves "gnostics," saying that they are by nature sons of the first God; and, abusing their nobility and their freedom, they live as they please—and they please to live in a manner devoted to pleasure, holding that they are to be mastered by no one, as lords of the Sabbath, and as royal children born above every race; and to a king, they say, there is no written law. But, first of all, they do not do all that they wish, for many things will hinder them even when they desire and attempt them; and the things they do, they do not as kings but as runaway slaves, for they commit adultery in secret, fearing to be caught, shunning condemnation, and afraid of punishment. But how is incontinence and foul speech freedom? For "everyone who sins," he says, "is a slave"—the apostle says.

But how does the man who has given himself over to every desire conduct himself according to God, when the Lord has said, "But I say, You shall not covet"? Does a man willingly choose to sin, and lay it down as a doctrine to commit adultery, to indulge in pleasure, and to ruin the marriages of others—when we pity even others who sin against their will? And even if they have come into a strange world, if they do not prove faithful in what is another's, they will not possess what is true. Does a stranger insult the citizens and wrong them, instead of, like a sojourner, using what is necessary and living without offence to the citizens? How is it that, doing the same things as those who are hated by the nations because they do not do what the laws enjoin—that is, the unjust, the incontinent, the covetous, and the adulterers—they alone claim to have known God? For they ought, even when present among strangers, to live well, that they might truly display their royal character.

But indeed these men, having undertaken to live lawlessly, are hateful both to human lawgivers and to God. The man, at any rate, who pierced through the fornicator is shown in the book of Numbers to be blessed by God. "And if we say," says John in his epistle, "that we have communion with Him"—that is, with God—"and walk in darkness, we lie and do not do the truth; but if we walk in the light, as He is in the light, we have communion with Him, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from sin."

Whence, then, are those who do such things better than worldly men, when they are like the worst of worldly men? For those who are alike in their deeds are, I think, alike also in their natures. But those over whom they claim to excel in nobility, they ought also to surpass in character, so that they may escape being shut up in prison. For truly, as the Lord said, "Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of God." And concerning continence in foods, it is shown in Daniel. And, to put it briefly, concerning obedience David says in his psalm: "Wherein shall a young man set straight his way?" And at once he hears: "By keeping your word with his whole heart." And Jeremiah says: "Thus says the Lord: Do not walk in the ways of the nations."

From this point certain other defiled and worthless men, taking their start, say that man was fashioned by different powers, and that the parts down to the navel are of a more godlike craft, and the parts below of an inferior one—for which reason, they say, men desire intercourse. But it has escaped them that the upper parts also crave food, and in some men lust as well. And they oppose Christ too, who said to the Pharisees that the same God made both the outer man and the inner one. Moreover, appetite belongs not to the body, even though it arises through the body. There are certain others, whom we call Antitactae, who say that the God of the universe is by nature our Father, and that all that He has made is good; but that one of those who came into being from Him sowed the tares, having begotten the nature of evils, in which he wrapped us all, setting us against the Father. For this reason, they say, we too set ourselves against him to avenge the Father, working against the will of the second one. Since, then, this one said, "You shall not commit adultery," we, they say, will commit adultery, to abolish his commandment.

We would say to these men also that we have received that false prophets and all who counterfeit the truth are known from their works. But your works are slandered; how then will you say that you cling to the truth? For either there is no evil, and the one whom you blame as set against God is no longer worthy of blame, nor has he become the maker of any evil (for the tree is destroyed together with its fruit); or, if wickedness exists in fact, let them tell us what they say the given commandments concerning righteousness, continence, endurance, and forbearance, and the like, really are—whether base or noble. And if the commandment, forbidding most of the shameful deeds, were base, then wickedness will be legislating against itself for its own abolition, which is impossible; but if it is good, then by setting themselves against good commandments they confess that they set themselves against the good and do evil.

And we might find yet another testimony to the confirmation of the point, that the best of the philosophers, having appropriated the noblest doctrines from us, boast of them as their own — namely, that they have culled some things even from the other barbarians, things bearing upon each school, and most of all from the Egyptians: among other things, the doctrine of the transmigration of the soul. For the Egyptians pursue a certain philosophy of their own; and this their august worship makes most plain above all. First there goes before the singer, carrying one of the symbols of music. They say that he must take up two books out of those of Hermes, of which one contains hymns of the gods, the second a reckoning of the kingly life. And after the singer comes the horoscopist, having in his hand a horologe and a palm, the symbols of astrology. He must always have on his lips the astrological books of Hermes, four in number: of which one is about the ordering of the apparently fixed stars, another about the position of the sun and moon and the five planets, another about the conjunctions and illuminations of sun and moon, and the rest about their risings.

Moreover, the Saviour Himself, whom alone they claim to obey, forbade hatred and reviling, and says, "When you go with your adversary, try to be reconciled to him while you are his friend." Either, then, they will deny even Christ's exhortation by setting themselves against the one who is set against them, or, becoming friends with him, they will not contend against him. And what? Do you not know, my good men (for I would speak as if to people present), that by fighting against good commandments you are resisting your own salvation? For it is not the things rightly enjoined, but yourselves, that you overturn. The Lord said, "Let your good works shine"; but you make your lewdnesses conspicuous. Besides, if you wish to abolish the lawgiver's commandments, why is it that you try to abolish "You shall not commit adultery" and "You shall not corrupt boys" and whatever conduces to continence, on account of your own incontinence, but do not abolish the winter that He made, so as to make summer while it is still mid-winter, nor make the earth navigable and the sea passable, as those who composed the histories say the barbarian Xerxes wished to do?

Next comes the sacred scribe, having feathers on his head and a book in his hands and a rule, in which are the writing-ink and the reed with which they write. He must know what are called the hieroglyphics, concerning cosmography and geography, the position of the sun and moon and the five planets, the description of Egypt and the drawing of the Nile, the appointing of the temples and the regions consecrated to them, and the measures and the things useful in the sacred rites. Then the keeper of the robes follows those before mentioned, having the cubit of justice and the libation-vessel. This man knows all the things called educative and the "calf-sealing"; and there are ten which pertain to the honour of their gods and contain the Egyptian piety — about sacrifices, first-fruits, hymns, prayers, processions, festivals, and the like.

And why do you not set yourselves against all the commandments? For when He said, "Increase and multiply," you who set yourselves against Him ought to make no use at all of intercourse; and when He said, "I have given you all things for food and enjoyment," you ought to enjoy nothing. And when He says, "An eye for an eye," you ought not to repay opposition with opposition; and when He commanded the thief to repay fourfold, you ought even to give more to the thief. Likewise again, setting yourselves against the commandment "You shall love the Lord," you ought not to love even the God of the universe; and again, when He said, "You shall not make a graven or molten image," it would follow that you should worship graven images. How then are you not impious, setting yourselves, as you say, against the Demiurge, yet emulating the deeds of prostitutes and adulterers? And how do you not perceive that you are making greater the one whom you regard as weak, if what he wishes comes to pass, and not what the Good one willed? For, on the contrary, your "father," as you call him, is shown by your very selves to be weak.

And after all comes the prophet, bearing in his bosom in open view the water-vessel, whom follow those who carry the loaves to be sent forth. This man, as president of the temple, learns the ten books called hieratic (and they contain things about laws and the gods and the whole training of the priests); for the prophet, among the Egyptians, is also the overseer of the distribution of the revenues. There are, then, two-and-forty books altogether necessary to Hermes; of which the thirty-six, containing the whole philosophy of the Egyptians, those before mentioned learn; the remaining six the bearers of the sacred robes learn, being medical, about the constitution of the body, and diseases, and instruments, and drugs, and about the eyes, and lastly about the things of women.

These men too gather words culled out of certain prophetic passages and badly stitched together, taking literally what was said allegorically. For they say it is written, "They resisted God and were saved." And some add "the shameless God," and they receive this oracle as a command given them, and reckon it salvation to resist the Demiurge. Now "the shameless God" is not written; but even if it were so, understand, you fools, that the one called the devil is meant as "shameless," either as slandering man, or as accuser of those who sin, or as apostate. The people, at any rate, concerning whom the passage is spoken, being chastised for their sins, and bearing it heavily and groaning, murmured this saying, that the other nations transgress and are not punished, while they alone are checked at every turn—just as Jeremiah said, "Why does the way of the impious prosper?" Like this is the saying in Malachi, the one mentioned above: "They resisted God and were saved." For the prophets, receiving oracles, are shown not only to hear certain things from God, but also themselves to report, by way of objection, the things commonly said by the people, raising them as certain questions on behalf of men—from which the saying before us happens to derive.

And the things of the Egyptians, to speak briefly, are such. But the philosophy of the Indians too is noised abroad. For Alexander the Macedonian, having taken ten of the Indian gymnosophists who were thought the best and most concise in speech, set them problems, threatening to put to death the one who did not answer to the point, and bidding one, the eldest of them, to be the judge. The first, then, being examined whether he thought the living or the dead more numerous, said, "The living; for the dead are not." The second, whether the land or the sea nourishes greater beasts, said, "The land; for the sea is a part of it." The third, what creature is the most cunning, said, "That which up to now has not been known — man." The fourth, being questioned by what reasoning they had stirred up Sabbas, who was their ruler, to revolt, answered, "Wishing him either to live well or to die well." The fifth, asked whether he thought day or night had come into being first, said, "Night, by one day; for of insoluble questions the answers too must of necessity be insoluble." The sixth, asked how one might be loved most, said, "If, being most powerful, he is not fearsome." The seventh, asked how one might become a god out of a man, said, "If he should do what it is not possible for a man to do." The eighth, asked what is stronger, life or death, said, "Life, which bears so many ills." The ninth, examined how long it is good for a man to live, said, "As long as he does not think dying better than living." And when Alexander bade the tenth too say something (for he was the judge), he said, "One spoke worse than another." And when Alexander said, "Then shall you too die first, judging so?", he said, "And how, O king, would you be truthful, having said you would kill first the one who answered worst?"

And does not the apostle, aiming at these men, write in his epistle to the Romans: "And not, as we are blasphemed, and as some say that we say, 'Let us do evil that good may come'—whose condemnation is just"? These are they who, in their reading, by the pitch of the voice distort the Scriptures to suit their own pleasures, and by transposing certain accents and stops do violence to what is prudently and beneficially enjoined, bending it toward their own indulgences. "You who provoke God by your words," says Malachi, "and you say, 'In what have we provoked Him?'—in your saying, 'Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and in them He has taken pleasure'; and, 'Where is the God of justice?'"

And the same attempt at demonstration holds also for the third problem. Some, then, say that it is not possible for there to be several beginnings of one animal. Now, of beginnings of the same kind, it is not possible that there be several for one animal; but that there be beginnings differing in their kinds is nothing absurd. Against the Pyrrhonists. If suspension of judgement says that nothing is firm, it is plain that, beginning from itself, it will first annul itself. Either, then, it grants that something is true and that one should not suspend judgement about all things; or it stands fast, saying that nothing is true—and then it is plain that it itself will not be speaking truth before all else. For either it speaks truth, or it does not. But if it speaks truth, it grants, unwillingly, that something is true; and if it does not speak truth, it leaves true the very things it wished to do away with. For in that whereby the annulling suspension is shown false, therein the things annulled are shown true—like the dream that says that all dreams are false. For being destructive of itself, it becomes confirmatory of the others. And altogether, if it is true, it will make its beginning from itself, being suspension of judgement not about anything else, but first about itself. And further, if a man apprehends that he is a man, or that he is suspending judgement, he plainly is not suspending judgement. And how would he even at the outset have come into the dispute, suspending judgement about all things? And how would he answer the thing asked? For about this very matter he is plainly not suspending judgement. Indeed, he even declares that he is suspending judgement; for which reason, even if one ought, in obedience to them, to suspend judgement about all things, we shall first suspend judgement about suspension itself—whether one ought to be persuaded by it or not.

Further, if this very thing is the truth—not to know the truth—then not even at the outset is anything true granted by him. But if he shall say that even this is disputable, namely, the being ignorant of the truth, then in this very thing he grants that the truth is knowable, in that he appears not to confirm the suspension of judgement about it. A school of thought is an inclination toward doctrines; or, as some say, an inclination toward many doctrines that have consistency with one another and with the appearances, tending toward living well. And a doctrine is a kind of rational apprehension; and apprehension is a settled disposition and assent of the understanding. And not only the suspenders of judgement, but every dogmatist too, is wont in certain matters to suspend judgement—either through weakness of mind, or through the unclearness of things, or through the equal strength of the arguments. The approaches and beginnings of inquiries are about these things and in these things.

It is worth wondering at the Stoics too, certain of whom say that the soul is not at all affected by the body—neither toward vice by sickness nor toward virtue by health—but that both these things are indifferent. And yet Job too, by surpassing continence and excellence of faith, having become poor from rich, dishonoured from honoured, ugly from comely, and sick from healthy, is set down for us as a good example, abashing the tempter, blessing his Maker, bearing the latter state as he had borne the former, teaching very well that the gnostic can in all circumstances make good use of them. And that the right deeds of old are set forth as images for our own correction, the apostle shows when he says: "So that my bonds became manifest in Christ in the whole praetorium and to all the rest, and that the more of the brothers, having become confident in the Lord by my bonds, are far more bold to speak the word of God fearlessly," since the martyrdoms too are gloriously sanctified examples of conversion. "For whatever was written," he says, "was written for our instruction, that through the endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have the hope of encouragement."

All the aforesaid doctrines, then, appear to have been handed down to the Greeks from Moses the great. That all things belong to the wise man, he teaches through these: "And because God has had mercy on me, I have all things." And he shows him to be dear to God, saying: "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob." For the one is found called outright a friend, and the other is shown renamed as one who sees God; and Isaac, allegorized as a consecrated victim, he chose out for himself as a type to be for us of the saving dispensation. And among the Greeks too Minos is sung as "the nine-year king, the familiar of Zeus," they having heard how God conversed with Moses "as if one were to speak to his own friend."

The soul, when pain is present, seems somehow to incline away from it and to count precious release from the present suffering. Indeed, at such a time it grows slack toward learning, when the other virtues too are neglected. And we do not, of course, say that virtue itself suffers (for virtue does not fall sick), but that the man who has shared in both, virtue and sickness, is pressed by what bears down on him; and unless he should be high-minded, the man who has not yet acquired the habit of continence is unsettled, and is found to be on a par—since not to endure is the same as to flee.

Moses, then, was wise, king, legislator; but our Saviour surpasses all human nature. He is beautiful, so as to be loved by us alone who long for the true beauty, for he was "the true light"; and king he is shown to be, proclaimed both by children still untaught and by Jews unbelieving and ignorant, and heralded by the prophets themselves; and rich to such a degree that he disdained all the gold above and below the earth, together with all the glory, given to him by the adversary. Why need it be said that he alone is high priest, the only one who knows the service of God, the king of peace, Melchizedek, the most competent of all to lead the race of men? And legislator, in that he gives the law in the mouth of the prophets, most clearly enjoining and teaching what is to be done and what not.

The same account holds of poverty too, since this also forces the soul away from what is necessary—I mean from contemplation and pure freedom from sin—compelling the man who has not wholly dedicated himself to God through love to spend his time on the getting of provisions; just as, on the contrary, health and abundance of necessities keep the soul free and unhindered, the soul that knows how to make good use of what is present. "For such men will have affliction in the flesh," says the apostle, "but I spare you; for I wish you to be without anxiety, for what is seemly and waits well upon the Lord without distraction."

And who could be of nobler birth than he, whose only father is God? Come, let us present Plato too, lighting upon the same doctrines.
