He has called the wise man rich in the Phaedrus, saying: "O dear Pan, and whatever other gods are here, grant me to become beautiful within; and as for what I have without, let it be friendly to what is within. And may I count the wise man rich." And the Athenian stranger, blaming those who think that the rich are those who have acquired much money, says thus: "But that those should be both very rich and good is impossible — those, that is, whom the many reckon rich; and they call rich those who have, among few of mankind, possessions worth the most money, which even a bad man may have acquired." "To the faithful belongs the whole world of riches," says Solomon, "but to the unfaithful not even an obol." Much more, then, must we be persuaded by the Scripture which says that a camel will pass through the eye of a needle sooner than a rich man philosophize; and, on the contrary, it blesses the poor, as Plato understood, saying: "Poverty is to be reckoned not the making of one's substance less, but the making of one's insatiability more. For it is never the smallness of property, but insatiability, from which the good man, being free, would also be rich." And in the Alcibiades he calls vice slavish, and virtue freeman-like. "Take from yourselves the heavy yoke," it says, "and take the gentle one," says the Scripture, just as the poets too call a yoke "slavish." And the "You were sold for your sins" agrees with what was said before. "Everyone, then, who does sin is a slave; and the slave does not abide in the house forever. But if the Son frees you, you will be free," and "the truth will free you." And again, that the wise man is beautiful, the Athenian says thus: "As if one should affirm that the just, even if they happen to be ugly in their bodies, are, by their most just character, in this respect altogether beautiful — scarcely would anyone speaking thus seem to speak amiss." And "his form was failing beyond all the sons of men," the prophecy foretold. And Plato has called the wise man king, in the Statesman, and the passage lies before us.

These things, then, are to be held to, not for their own sake but for the sake of the body, and the care of the body is for the sake of the soul, to which the reference is made. For in this the man who conducts himself in a gnostic way must of necessity learn what is fitting, since it has been agreed that pleasure is not the good, from the fact that some pleasures are bad. And next, if we choose some pleasures and flee others, not every pleasure is good. The same account holds likewise of pains, of which we endure some and flee others, and the choice and avoidance come about according to knowledge; so that knowledge is the good, not pleasure—on account of which we shall sometimes even choose a particular pleasure.

These things, then, being shown, let us run back again to the discourse concerning faith. Indeed, with all demonstration Plato presents that there is everywhere need of faith, somewhat thus, while at the same time hymning peace: "For a man faithful and sound in factions could not come to be without the whole of virtue. But of the mercenaries there are very many who are warlike and willing to die in war, of whom most become rash and unjust, insolent and senseless, except, indeed, some very few. If, then, these things are rightly said, every legislator who is of even small use will lay down his laws looking above all to the greatest virtue. And this is faithfulness, of which we have need at every time, both in peace and in every war and in the whole of the rest of life. For it seems, having gathered them, to contain the others." And the best is neither war nor faction; for it is to be deprecated to have need of these; but peace toward one another, and at the same time kindliness, is the strongest. From these it appears that the greatest prayer is to have peace, according to Plato, and that the greatest mother of the virtues is faith.

So at once the martyr chooses the pleasure that comes through hope, through the present pain. But if pain is conceived in connection with thirst, and pleasure in connection with drinking, then the pre-existing pain becomes productive of the pleasure; and evil could not be productive of good, so neither of them is evil. Simonides, then, like Aristotle, writes:
To be healthy is best for a man,
and:
second, to be born comely in form, third, to be rich without deceit.
And Theognis of Megara:
One must flee poverty, even into the deep-monstered sea to hurl oneself, Cyrnus, and down the sheer rocks.
But on the contrary Antiphanes the comic poet says: "Wealth, taking men who see more than the other, makes them blind."

With reason, then, it is said in Solomon, "wisdom is in the mouth of the faithful," since Xenocrates too, in his work On Prudence, says that wisdom is the knowledge of the first causes and of the intelligible essence, holding prudence to be twofold, the one practical, the other contemplative, which last is human wisdom. Wherefore wisdom is prudence, but not all prudence is wisdom. And it has been shown that the knowledge of the principle of the universe is faith, but not demonstration. For it is absurd that the emulators of Pythagoras of Samos, declining the demonstrations of the things inquired into, should hold the "He himself said it" to be faith, and be content with this voice alone for the confirmation of what they have heard; but that the lovers of beholding the truth, undertaking to disbelieve a trustworthy teacher, the only Saviour God, should demand from him tests of what is said. But "he that has ears to hear, let him hear," he says. And who is this? Let Epicharmus tell: "Mind sees and mind hears; the rest is deaf and blind." That some are unbelieving Heraclitus says, rebuking them: "Not knowing how to hear or how to speak" — helped, no doubt, by Solomon: "If you love to hear, you will receive; and if you incline your ear, you will be wise."
So at once by the poets a man is proclaimed blind from birth:
And she bore him a son, who never saw the cock,
says Euphorion the Chalcidian.
It was then a bad education for manliness— wealth for men, and excessive luxuries,
Euripides has written in the Alexander. And it has been said:
Poverty obtained wisdom, because of their kinship.
And:
The love of money would take not Sparta only, but every city.
It is not, then, only white silver or gold that is currency, but virtue too for mortals,
as Sophocles says.

Take, for instance, the Pythagorean symbols, which hang very closely upon the barbarian philosophy in a hidden way. The Samian, then, counsels not to keep a swallow in the house — that is, not to receive a chattering, whispering, ready-tongued man, who cannot keep within him the things he is given a share in. "For the swallow and the turtle-dove, the sparrows of the field, have known the seasons of their comings," says the Scripture; and one ought never to dwell together with idle talk. Indeed the turtle-dove, murmuring, showing forth the thankless slander of reproach, is with reason expelled the house: "so do not sit by me and mutter, one from this side, one from that." But the swallow, by which the myth of the son of Pandion is hinted at, is worth abominating because of the sufferings noised abroad concerning her, of which we have received that Tereus partly suffered and partly wrought. And it pursues the musical cicadas; whence he who is a pursuer of the Word is rightly thrust away. "Yes, by Olympus-watching, sceptred Hera, I have a faithful storehouse upon my tongue," says the poetry. And Aeschylus: "I too have a key, a guard upon my tongue." Again, Pythagoras enjoined, when the pot was lifted from the fire, not to leave behind the imprint in the ashes, but to confound it; and to disturb and stir up the bedclothes upon rising from sleep. For he was hinting that one ought not only to make conceit vanish, but to leave behind not even a trace of anger — that, when it has boiled up and ceased, it should settle, and wipe out all remembrance of wrong. "Let not the sun go down upon your wrath," says the Scripture; and he who said "You shall not covet" took away all remembrance of wrong; for anger is found to be an impulse of desire in a gentle soul, set above all upon defence, irrationally.

Before the coming of the Lord, then, philosophy was necessary to the Greeks for righteousness; and now it becomes useful toward the fear of God, being a kind of preliminary education for those who reap faith through demonstration. "For your foot," it says, "shall not stumble," if you refer good things to providence, whether they be Greek or our own. For God is the cause of all good things — but of some as primary, as of the Old Covenant and the New, and of others as consequent, as of philosophy. Yet perhaps philosophy too was given primarily to the Greeks then, before the Lord called the Greeks also; for it too was a schoolmaster bringing the Greek mind, as the Law brought the Hebrews, toward Christ. Philosophy, then, prepares the way beforehand, paving the road for the man who is being perfected by Christ. "Fortify wisdom," says Solomon, "and she will exalt you; with a crown of delight she will shield you" — since you too, fortifying her with the parapet of philosophy and of right magnificence, will keep her unassailable by the sophists.

In the same way too the bed is bidden to be disturbed, so that one may no longer keep in mind any nocturnal emission, nor any sleep by day, nor even the pleasure of the night. And perhaps he was also hinting that the murky imagination must be confounded by the light of the truth: "Be angry, and sin not," David says, teaching that one ought not to give assent to the impression, nor to bring on the deed that ratifies the wrath. Again, "Do not sail on land" is a Pythagorean symbol, and it shows that the taxes and the like, the wages of hire, being troublesome and unstable, ought to be declined. For this reason, indeed, the Word says that the tax-gatherers are hardly saved. Again, Pythagoras enjoins not to wear a ring, nor to engrave on it images of the gods — just as Moses long before plainly laid down in law that one must make no carved or molten or moulded or painted statue and likeness, that we may not cleave to things of sense, but pass over to the things of mind. For the familiarity that comes of having the sight ready to hand cheapens the majesty of the divine; and to worship the intelligible substance through matter is to dishonour it through sense. Hence the wisest of the Egyptian priests set apart the seat of Athena unroofed and open to the sky, as the Hebrews founded the temple without an image. And there are some who, worshipping God, make a likeness of the heaven that encompasses the stars, and bow down to it.

For is it not nobly and truly that we neither circumscribe in a place the Uncontainable, nor shut up in shrines "made with hands" that which contains all things? What holy work could belong to builders and stone-cutters and the mechanic's craft? Are not those better than these who have judged the air and the encompassing—nay rather the whole world and the universe—worthy of the pre-eminence of God? It would indeed be ridiculous, as the philosophers themselves say, that man, being "the plaything of God," should fashion God, and that God should become a game of art. For the thing produced is the same as, and like to, that out of which it is produced: the ivory thing is of ivory, and the golden of gold. But the statues and shrines wrought by mechanic men come into being out of inert matter, so that they too would be inert and material and profane; and even if you perfect the art, it has shared in the mechanic's labour. No longer, then, are the works of the art holy and divine. And what could be set up at all, when nothing is unestablished, since all things are in a place? But the thing established by another is established as having previously been unestablished. If, then, God is established by men, he was once unestablished, and so did not exist at all.

One, then, is the road of truth; but into it, as into an ever-flowing river, the streams flow in from one place and another. With inspiration, then, it is said: "Hear, my son, and receive my words," it says, "that the ways of your life may be many; for I teach you the ways of wisdom, that the springs may not fail you" — the springs that gush from the same earth. He has not only reckoned up many saving ways for some one just man, but adds the many ways of the many just, indicating thus: "The ways of the just shine like the light." And the commandments and the preliminary studies too would be ways and starting-points of life. "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often did I wish to gather your children, as a hen her chicks." And "Jerusalem" is interpreted "vision of peace." He shows, then, prophetically, that those who in peace have looked upon things have been led by a schoolmaster in many ways to their calling. What then? He wished, but was not able. How often, or where? Twice: through the prophets, and through the coming. So "how often" indicates the manifoldness of wisdom; and in each single mode, of quality and of quantity, she certainly saves some, both in time and in eternity, "for the spirit of the Lord has filled the world." And if anyone, forcing the sense, should say — "Do not give heed to a worthless woman, for honey drips from the lips of a harlot" — that this means Greek learning, let him listen to what follows: "which for a season greases your throat," it says — but philosophy does not flatter. Whom, then, does it hint at as the woman who has played the harlot? It adds expressly: "For the feet of folly bring those who use her down to Hades with death, and her tracks are not firmly set. Make your way far, then, from foolish pleasure; do not stand at the doors of her house, lest you give over your life to others." And it bears witness: "Then you will repent in old age, when the flesh of your body is worn away" — for this is the end of foolish pleasure. So much for that. But when it says, "Be not much with a strange woman," it advises us to use worldly learning, but not to spend our time and remain in it; for it educates beforehand for the discourse of the Lord the things given, at the appointed seasons, to each generation for its benefit. For some, already, lured by the charms of the handmaids, have made light of the mistress, philosophy, and have grown old, some of them in music, others in geometry, others in grammar, and most of them in rhetoric.

Indeed, since the Scripture says, "Let us make man after our image and likeness," I think it worth while to set down also the saying of Eurytus the Pythagorean, which runs thus. In his work On Fortune, having said that the Creator made man using himself as a pattern, he goes on: "And the body is like the rest, as being come of the same matter, but wrought by the best of craftsmen, who fashioned it using himself as an archetype." And, in a word, Pythagoras and his followers, together with Plato above the rest of the philosophers, had very close converse with the Lawgiver, as one may gather from their very doctrines. And, by some happy hitting of a divining utterance, not without God they fell together upon certain prophetic words; and grasping the truth in parts and kinds, they honoured it with names not without light, nor going outside the showing-forth of the things — having taken an impression of their kinship with the truth. Whence the Greek philosophy is like the gleam from a wick, which men kindle, stealing the light skilfully from the sun; but when the Word was proclaimed, all that holy light shone forth. Then in the houses the stolen fire is of use by night; but by day the fire is outshone, and all the night is lit up by so great a sun of the intelligible light.

For that would be unestablished which is not—since everything that is not is established; but that which is could not be established by that which is not, nor indeed by another that is, for it too is. It remains, then, that it should be established by itself. But how shall a thing beget itself? Or how shall Being itself establish itself in being? Did it, being previously unestablished, then establish itself? But it would not even have existed, since that which is not is unestablished; and how should that which is reckoned to have been established—having already possessed being—afterwards make itself? And that of which all beings are—how should this stand in need of anything? But if the Divine were of human form, it would need the same things as man: food and shelter, a house and all that follows. For those of like shape and like passions will need a like manner of life. And if the sacred is understood in two ways—both God himself and the structure raised for his honour—how shall we not most properly call the Church, which has become holy unto the honour of God by recognition of him, a temple of God, the thing of great worth and not built by the mechanic's craft, nor decked out by a charlatan's hand, but made into a shrine by the will of God? For it is not the place but the assembly of the elect that I call the Church. This is the better temple for the reception of the greatness of God's worth. For the living being of great worth is consecrated, through surpassing holiness, to him who is worth the whole, or rather worth more than all things. And this man would be the gnostic, of great worth and precious to God, in whom God is established—that is, the knowledge of God is consecrated. Here too we should find the image, the divine and holy statue, in the just soul, when it is itself blessed, as having been purified beforehand, and blessed in performing blessed deeds. Here too is both that which is established and that which is being established: the one in those already gnostic, the other in those capable of becoming so, even if they are not yet worthy to receive the knowledge of God. For everyone who is going to believe is already faithful to God, and is consecrated, a virtuous statue set up unto honour, dedicated to God.

But as the cycle of studies contributes to philosophy, their mistress, so philosophy itself works together toward the acquisition of wisdom. For philosophy is the pursuit of wisdom, and wisdom is the knowledge of things divine and human and of their causes. Wisdom, then, is mistress of philosophy, as philosophy is of the preliminary education. For if philosophy promises self-control of tongue and belly and the parts below the belly, and is to be chosen for its own sake, it will appear the more venerable and authoritative if it is pursued for the honour and knowledge of God. The Scripture will furnish testimony of what has been said through these words: Sarah was once barren, the wife of Abraham. Bearing no child, Sarah entrusts to Abraham, for the bearing of children, her own handmaid, Hagar the Egyptian by name. Wisdom, then, who dwelt with the faithful man (and Abraham was reckoned faithful and just), was still barren and childless in that generation, having borne nothing virtuous to Abraham; and she rightly thought it fitting that the man who already had the season for advance should first lie with worldly education (and Egypt is allegorized as the world), and afterward come to her too, according to divine providence, and beget Isaac.

Take, for instance, how Pythagoras has made an epitome of what was said by Moses concerning righteousness, saying "Do not step over the yoke-beam" — that is, do not go beyond what is equal in the distributions, honouring the justice that ever binds friends to friends, cities to cities, allies to allies; for "the equal is by nature lawful among men, but the lesser is ever set in enmity to the greater, and begins the day of hatred," as the poetry gracefully has it. For this reason the Lord says, "Take up my yoke," because it is kindly and without weight. And to the disciples who quarrelled about precedence he enjoins equality with simplicity, saying that they must become as the little children. In the same way the apostle too writes that in Christ there is no slave or free, no Greek or Jew; for the creation in Christ is new, free from contention and from greed, and is a just equality. For envy stands outside the divine choir, and jealousy and grief — wherefore the initiates also forbid eating the heart, teaching that one ought never, by heavy moods and griefs over things that befall against our will, to bite and devour the soul. Wretched, then, is that man whom Homer too speaks of as wandering alone, "devouring his own heart."

Philo interprets Hagar as "sojourning" (for here it is said: "Be not much with a strange woman"), and Sarah as "my sovereignty." It is possible, then, for one who has been educated beforehand to come to the most sovereign wisdom, from which the race of Israel is increased. From this it is shown that the wisdom which Abraham pursued is teachable — passing from the contemplation of heavenly things to faith and righteousness according to God. Isaac signifies the self-taught; and therefore he is found a type of Christ. He was the husband of one woman, Rebecca, whom they translate "endurance." Jacob is said to have come together with several, being interpreted "the exerciser" (and the exercises are by many and differing doctrines); whence he too is renamed Israel, the truly clear-sighted one, as being of much experience and given to exercise. There might be something else signified by the three forefathers: that the seal of knowledge is sovereign, composed of nature, learning, and exercise. You may also have another image of what has been said in Tamar, who sat at the crossroads and gave the appearance of a harlot, whom the learning-loving Judah (and "Judah" is interpreted "mighty"), leaving nothing unexamined and unsearched, looked upon and turned aside to her, keeping his confession toward God.

Again, since the Gospel and the apostles, like all the prophets, set down two ways, and call the one — that which is hedged about by commandments and prohibitions — narrow and straitened, and the opposite one, which leads to destruction, broad and wide, unhindered by pleasures and by passion; and since they say, "Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners"; the myth of Prodicus of Ceos concerning Virtue and Vice comes forward in like manner, and Pythagoras does not shrink from forbidding men to walk the public roads, enjoining that one ought not to follow the opinions of the many, which are undiscerning and inconsistent. And Aristocritus, in the first book of his Replies to Heracleodorus, mentions a certain letter that runs thus: "Atoeas, king of the Scythians, to the people of the Byzantines: Do not harm my revenues, lest my mares drink your water." For the barbarian was symbolically signifying the war that was about to be brought upon them. In like manner too the poet Euphorion brings in Nestor saying: "And we had not yet watered our Achaean mares at the Simoeis." For this reason, indeed, the Egyptians set up sphinxes before their temples, as showing that the discourse about God is full of riddles and obscure — and perhaps also that one ought both to love and to fear the divine: to love it as gentle and kindly toward the holy, but to fear it as inexorably just toward the unholy. For the sphinx hints at the image of a beast and a man together.

For this reason Abraham too, when Sarah was jealous of Hagar for outshining her — choosing, as it were, only the useful part of worldly philosophy — said, "Behold, the handmaid is in your hands; deal with her as is pleasing to you," showing that "I welcome worldly education both as the younger and as your handmaid, but I honour and revere your knowledge as the perfect mistress." "And Sarah ill-treated her" — the same as to say, she brought her to her senses and admonished her. Well, then, it is said: "My son, do not make light of the discipline of God, nor grow faint when reproved by him; for whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and scourges every son whom he receives." Examined in other passages, however, the Scriptures cited present themselves as indicating other mysteries. We say, then, plainly in bare speech, that philosophy has its quest concerning truth and the nature of the things that are (and this is the truth concerning which the Lord himself said, "I am the truth"); and that the preliminary education for the rest that is in Christ exercises the mind and rouses the understanding, breeding a quickness that seeks, through true philosophy. Having found this — or rather, having received it from the Truth herself — the initiates possess it.

And that the Greeks are caught as thieves of every Scripture, has, I think, been shown sufficiently through many proofs. But that they do not know God by recognition, but by periphrasis — the most reputable of the Greeks, that is — Peter says in the Preaching: "Know, then, that there is one God, who made the beginning of all things, and has power over their end"; and: "the invisible, who sees all things; the uncontainable, who contains all things; the unneedy, of whom all things have need and through whom they are; the incomprehensible, the everlasting, the incorruptible, the uncreated, who made all things by the word of his power" — that is, of the Son. Then he adds: "Worship this God, not after the manner of the Greeks" — clearly, then, the reputable men among the Greeks worship the same God as we, but not by perfect recognition, not having learned the tradition that comes through the Son. "Do not, then," he says, "worship" — he did not say "the God whom the Greeks worship," but "not after the manner of the Greeks" — changing the manner of the worship of God, not proclaiming another God.

So that we may not, by clawing further at this topic, recall yet more absurd heresies, nor again, being forced to speak against each one severally, both be ashamed on their account and prolong these notes to the utmost length, come, let us divide all the heresies into two classes and answer them. For either they teach men to live indifferently, or, striking too high a note, they proclaim a continence based on impiety and on love of enmity. Let us first treat the former class. If it is permitted to choose every kind of life, then plainly the life of continence too; and if every life is without danger to the elect, then plainly the life of virtue and prudence is far more without danger. For if license has been granted to the lord of the Sabbath such that, even if he live licentiously, he is unaccountable, much more will the man who conducts himself decently not be liable. For "all things are permitted, but not all things are profitable," says the apostle. And if all things are permitted, then plainly to be prudent is permitted too.

What, then, is "not after the manner of the Greeks," Peter himself will make plain by adding: "Because, being carried about by ignorance, and not knowing God as we do by the perfect knowledge, having shaped things over which he gave them power for their use — wood and stones, bronze and iron, gold and silver — forgetful of their matter and use, they set up the things that are slaves to their being, and worship them; and the things which God gave them for food — the birds of the air and the swimming things of the sea and the creeping beasts of the land, with the four-footed cattle of the field, and weasels and mice and cats and dogs and apes — and their own foods they sacrifice as victims to things eatable, and offering dead things to the dead as to gods, they are ungrateful to God, by these things denying that he is."

As, then, the man who has used his license to live according to virtue is praiseworthy, so much more is He who gave us license, free and sovereign, and granted us to live as we wish, to be revered and worshipped, in that He did not leave our choices and avoidances enslaved by necessity. But if both have freedom from fear—both he who has chosen incontinence and he who has chosen continence—still the dignity is not the same. For the one who has run aground on pleasures gratifies the body, while the prudent man frees from the passions the soul, which is mistress of the body. And though they say we have been called to freedom, let us only not make our freedom an occasion for the flesh, as the apostle says. But if we are to gratify desire, and to count the disgraceful life a matter of indifference, as they say, then either we must obey all the desires—and if so, we must do all the most lewd and unholy deeds, following those who urge us on; or we shall avoid some of the desires, and then we are no longer to live indifferently, nor to be slaves without restraint to the basest parts of us, the belly and the genitals, men who flatter our dead self for desire's sake. For desire, when ministered to for enjoyment, is fed and brought to life, just as, when curtailed, it withers away.

And that they have known the same God, both we ourselves and they, though not in the same way, he will go on to show again, somewhat thus: "Nor after the manner of the Jews, though not in the same way: for they, thinking that they alone know God, do not know him, serving angels and archangels, the month and the moon. And if the moon does not appear, they do not keep the sabbath called the first, nor keep the new moon, nor the feast of unleavened bread, nor the feast, nor the great day." Then he adds the coping-stone of the matter sought: "So that you too, holily and justly learning the things which we deliver to you, keep them, worshipping God newly through Christ. For we have found in the Scriptures, as the Lord says, 'Behold, I make with you a new covenant, not as I made with your fathers in Mount Horeb.' A new one he made with us; for the things of the Greeks and the Jews are old, but we who worship him newly, in a third manner, are Christians." For he has plainly, I think, shown forth the one and only God, known by the Greeks in a Gentile manner, by the Jews in a Jewish manner, but newly and spiritually by us.

And how is it possible for a man who has been overcome by the pleasures of the body to be made like the Lord, or to have knowledge of God? For desire is the beginning of every pleasure, and desire is a kind of pain and anxiety, reaching out for something through want. So those who have chosen this manner of life seem to me to do nothing other than, as the saying goes,
to suffer in vessels turned to shame,

choosing for themselves an evil drawn down upon them, both now and afterward. If, then, all things were permitted, and there were no fear of failing of one's hope through evil deeds, perhaps they would have some pretext for living wickedly and pitiably. But since a blessed life has been shown to us through commandments, which all must hold to, not disregarding any of the things said nor making light of what is fitting, even the least, but following wherever reason leads—and if we fall away from it, we must of necessity fall into an immortal evil, but if we follow the divine Scripture, by which believers make their way, we are made like the Lord as far as we are able—we must not live indifferently, but must keep ourselves pure of pleasures as far as we are able, and take care of the soul, which must be devoted to the divine alone. For the mind, being pure and freed from all wickedness, is in a way receptive of the power of God, the divine image rising up within it. "And everyone who has this hope set on the Lord," he says, "purifies himself, even as He is pure."

And besides, that the same God is the supplier of both covenants, the giver too of Greek philosophy to the Greeks, through which the Almighty is glorified among the Greeks, he has set forth. And it is plain from this too. For out of Greek learning, and out of the learning of the law, are gathered into the one race of the people that is saved those who accept the faith — the three peoples not being divided by time, that one might suppose three natures, but trained by different covenants of the one Lord, . . . being of one Lord by his word. For just as God willed to save the Jews, giving them prophets, so too, raising up the most reputable of the Greeks as prophets of their own in their own tongue, in so far as they were able to receive the benefaction from God, he distinguished them from the common run of men — as Paul the apostle will show, beside the Preaching of Peter, saying:

But for those still led by the passions it is impossible to receive the knowledge of God; nor then to attain the hope, having acquired no knowledge of God. And of the man who fails of this end, ignorance of God seems to be the accusation, while the conduct of his life makes plain his ignorance of God. For it is altogether impossible at once to be a man of knowledge and not to be ashamed of pampering the body. Nor can the saying "Pleasure is the good" ever harmonize with the truth that the honourable alone is good, or that the Lord alone is honourable, and God alone good and alone to be loved. "In Christ you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, in the putting off of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ. If, then, you were raised together with Christ, seek the things above, set your minds on the things above, not the things on the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God"—not the fornication that they practise. "Put to death, therefore, your members that are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, on account of which the wrath comes." Let them too, then, put away wrath, anger, malice, blasphemy, foul speech out of their mouth; having put off the old man with his desires, and having put on the new man, who is renewed unto knowledge after the image of Him who created him.

"Take the Greek books too, recognize the Sibyl, how she shows forth one God and the things that shall be; and taking Hystaspes, read, and you shall find the Son of God written of far more luminously and plainly, and how many kings shall set their array against Christ, hating him and those who bear his name and his faithful ones, and his patience, and his coming." Then in one word he asks of us: "And the whole world, and the things in the world — whose are they? Are they not God's?" For this reason Peter says that the Lord said to the apostles: "If, then, anyone of Israel, having repented, should be willing to believe in God through my name, his sins shall be forgiven him. And after twelve years go out into the world, lest anyone say, 'We did not hear.'"

For their manner of life clearly convicts those who have known the commandments, since as is a man's reason, so is his life; and the tree is known from its fruits, not from its flowers and leaves. Knowledge, then, comes from the fruit and the conduct, not from the word and the flower; for we do not say that knowledge is bare reasoning, but a kind of divine science, that light which has come to be in the soul out of obedience to the commandments, which makes plain all things in the world of becoming, and prepares a man to know himself and teaches him to come into possession of God. For what the eye is in the body, that knowledge is in the mind. And let them not call slavery to pleasure "freedom," as though bile were sweet; for we have learned that freedom which the Lord alone gives us, releasing us from the pleasures and desires and the other passions. "He who says, 'I have known the Lord,' and does not keep His commandments, is a liar, and in him the truth is not"—John says.

One must set forth first, both for definitions and for demonstrations and for divisions, in how many senses the thing sought is spoken of; and the homonyms must be handled, and the synonyms set in order clearly according to their significations. Then one must inquire whether the thing proposed is among the things considered in relation to others, or is taken in itself. Besides these: whether it is, what it is, what has befallen it; or thus: whether it is, what it is, why it is. And toward the contemplation of these, the knowledge of particulars and that of universals contributes, together with the prior things and the divisions of them into their differences. Induction, then, brings the universal and the definition; the divisions bring the species and the essence and the individual; the contemplation of "in how many senses" brings the grasping of the proper; and the workings-through of difficulties bring the differences within them, and the demonstrations, and in other ways increase the contemplation, and the things consequent upon it. And out of all these, knowledge and truth are established. Again, the thing summed up out of division becomes a definition; for the definition is taken both before division and after it: before, when it is conceded or proposed; after, when it is demonstrated. And in respect of sense, too, the universal is summed up out of the particular; for the beginning of induction is sense, and the end is the universal. Induction, then, does not show what a thing is, but that it is or is not; division sets forth what a thing is; and definition, like division, teaches the substance and what a thing is, but not whether it is; while demonstration makes clear all three—whether it is, and what it is, and why it is. And there are some definitions that include the cause as well.

And since one knows scientifically when one sees the cause, and the causes are four—the matter, the moving cause, the form, the end—definition will be fourfold. One must take, then, first the genus, in which are the nearest of the things above; after this, the immediate difference. And the continuity of the differences, being cut and divided off, fills out the essence. And it is not necessary to state all the differences of each thing, but the species-making ones. Geometrical analysis and synthesis are like dialectical division and definition; and from division we run up to the simpler and more original things. For we divide the genus of the thing sought into the species existing in it—as, in the case of man, we divide the animal, being a genus, into the species appearing in it, the mortal and the immortal; and so, ever cutting the things that seem to be composite genera into the simpler species, we come to the thing sought, which no longer admits of division. For having divided the animal into the mortal and the immortal, and then the mortal into the land and the water animal, and again the land into the winged and the footed, and so, dividing the species nearest to the thing sought, which also includes the thing sought, we shall arrive, cutting, at the simplest species, which includes nothing else, but only the thing sought. For again we divide the footed into the rational and the irrational; and then, choosing out the species nearest to man among those taken from the division, and putting them together into one discourse, we render the definition of man, which is: an animal, mortal, land-dwelling, footed, rational.

Whence division holds, with respect to the definition, the rank of matter, searching out the simplicity of the name; while the definition holds the rank of the craftsman and maker, putting together and constructing and presenting the knowledge of the thing. And definitions are neither of the things themselves nor of the ideas, but, rather, of the things of which we have universal conceptions—of these conceptions we say that the definitions are the interpretative discourses; for of these conceptions the divisions too are made. And of divisions, one divides the thing divided into species, as a genus; another into parts, as a whole; and another into the accidents. The division of the whole into the parts is for the most part conceived in respect of magnitude; but the division into the accidents can never be wholly grasped, since indeed a substance too must by all means belong to each of the things that exist. Whence both these divisions are unapproved, and only the cutting of the genus into species is approved—by which is characterized both the sameness according to genus and the otherness according to the specific differences. The species is always contemplated in some part; not, however, conversely—if anything is a part of something, that thing will also be a species. For the hand is a part of man, but is not a species. And the genus exists within the species; for the animal is both in man and in ox; but the whole does not exist within the parts, for man does not exist in the feet. Therefore the species is more proper than the part; and whatever things are predicated of the genus, all these will be predicated of the species too.

Best, then, is it to divide the genus into two species; but if not, into three. The species, then, divided in a more generic way, are characterized by the same and the other; and then, divided through the generic significations, they are characterized. For each of the species is either a substance (as when we say: of existing things, some are bodies, others incorporeal), or a quantity, or a quality, or a relative, or a where, or a when, or to lie, or to have, or to do, or to be affected. He who is scientifically acquainted with anything whatever will render the definition of it as well; so that he who is unable to grasp and define anything in discourse could never be scientifically acquainted with it. And out of ignorance of the definition arise both the many disputes and the deceptions. For if the one who knows the thing has, in his understanding, the knowledge of it, and is able also to make clear in discourse what he conceives, and the interpretation of the conception is a definition—then it is necessary that the one who knows the thing be able to render its definition too.

And the difference is taken in addition to definitions, holding the rank of a sign in the definition. Thus, to the definition of man, the "capable of laughter" being added, makes the whole: an animal, rational, mortal, land-dwelling, footed, capable of laughter. For the things brought in by way of difference to the definition are signs of the proper things, but do not display the nature of the things themselves. Indeed they say that the difference is the giving of a property. And inasmuch as the thing that has the difference differs from all the rest by it—which belongs to it alone and is counter-predicated of the thing in the definitions—it is necessary to take over the first genus as foremost and substantial. In the longer definitions, then, there is the multitude of species found out through the ten categories; but in the shortest, the leading ones of the nearest species, being taken, signify the substance and nature of the thing. And the shortest is composed of three—the genus and two of the most necessary species. And this comes about for the sake of brevity. We say, then, man is the rational, laughing animal. And the thing especially belonging to the thing defined must be taken in addition—either its proper virtue, or its proper work, and certain other such things. The definition, then, being explanatory of the substance of the thing, is unable to grasp exactly the nature of the thing, but through the most proper species makes the disclosure of the substance; and the definition has the substance, as it were, in quality.

"Lord, who has believed our report?" says Isaiah. "For faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of God," says the Apostle. "How, then, will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? And how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without one preaching? And how will they preach, unless they are sent? As it is written: 'How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good tidings of good things.'" You see how he brings faith up, through hearing and the preaching of the apostles, to the word of the Lord and the Son of God? Do we not yet understand that the word of the Lord is a demonstration? Just as playing at ball does not depend only on the one who, by skill, sends the ball, but also needs the one who receives it gracefully, that the exercise may be carried out according to the rules of ball-play, so it has come about that teaching too is trustworthy, when the faith of the hearers — being, so to speak, a kind of natural art — contributes toward the learning.

Our holy Saviour ranked both poverty and wealth, and the like, in the realm of the spiritual and of the perceptible alike; for in saying, "Blessed are those who have been persecuted for the sake of righteousness," He plainly teaches us to seek the martyr in every circumstance. He who is poor for the sake of righteousness bears witness that the righteousness which he loved is good; and he who hungers or thirsts for the sake of righteousness bears witness that righteousness is the best thing.

So earth too, being fruitful, works together toward the casting in of the seeds. For there is no use in the best education without the receiving of the learner, nor indeed of prophecy, when the ready obedience of the hearers is not present. For the dry chips, being ready to receive the burning power, are the more easily kindled; and the much-talked-of stone draws iron through kinship, as the amber too attracts chips and the electron stirs up bits of chaff; and the things drawn obey them, drawn by an unspeakable breath, not as causes but as joint causes. Vice, then, being twofold in kind — the one leading on with deceit and by stealth, the other forcing and carrying off — the divine Word has cried out, calling all together, knowing well, indeed, even those who will not be persuaded; yet, since it lies with us to be persuaded or not, that none may have ignorance to plead, it has made the calling just, and demands from each according to his power. For to some, together with the willing, the being able is present, who have increased this by exercise and are cleansed; and others, even if they cannot yet, already have the willing. And to will is the work of the soul, but to do is not without the body. Nor are matters measured by the end alone, but are judged also by each man's choice — whether he chose readily, whether he repented of the things in which he sinned, whether he gained understanding of the things in which he stumbled, and changed his mind, which is to know afterward; for repentance is a slow knowing, but the first knowledge is sinlessness.

Likewise too the man who weeps and mourns for the sake of righteousness bears witness that the best law is good. As, then, He calls those who have been persecuted blessed, so too those who hunger and thirst for the sake of righteousness—He who accepts the genuine longing, which not even hunger had power to break off. And if they hunger after righteousness itself, they are blessed; and blessed too are the poor, whether in spirit or in substance, for the sake of righteousness, that is plain. So then it is not simply the poor, but those who have willed to become poor for the sake of righteousness, whom He counts blessed—those who have looked down on the honours here for the sake of acquiring the good; and likewise the noble in character and in body through purity, and the well-born and renowned, those who through righteousness have pressed on into adoption and through this have received authority to become children of God, and to walk upon serpents and scorpions, and to have lordship over demons too and over the army of the adversary.

Repentance, then, is also a right achievement of faith. For unless one believes that what he was held by before is a sin, he will not change; and unless he believes that punishment hangs over the offender, but salvation over the one who lives according to the commandments, he will not, even so, change. And hope too is composed of faith. So those from Basilides define faith as an assent of the soul to something of those things that do not move the perception because they are not present. And hope is the expectation of the acquisition of a good; and the expectation must be faithful. And faithful is he who keeps inviolably the things entrusted; and there are entrusted to us the discourses concerning God and the divine words, the commandments, together with the carrying out of the precepts. This is the faithful servant, the one praised by the Lord. And when one says "God is faithful," he indicates that one ought to believe him when he declares; and his Word declares, and God himself would be faithful. How, then, if to believe is to suppose, do the philosophers think the things from them firm? For an assumption is not a voluntary assent before demonstration, but an assent to something strong.

And in general the Lord's discipline leads the soul away from the body thankfully, if indeed the soul itself draws itself off by transposition. For "he who finds his soul shall lose it, and he who loses it shall find it," if only we cast our perishable part upon the incorruption of God. Now the will of God is the knowledge of God, which is the communion of incorruption. He, then, who recognizes, according to the doctrine of repentance, that his soul is sinful, will lose it to the sin from which it has been drawn off, but having lost it he will find it, according to the obedience that lives again to faith but has died to sin. This, then, is to find the soul—to know oneself.

And who would be stronger than God? But unbelief is a weak, negative assumption of the opposite, just as distrust is a state hard to receive faith. And faith is a voluntary assumption and a kindly anticipation before apprehension, and an expectation of what is to come; while the expectation of other things is an opinion of the uncertain; and confidence is a firm conviction about something. Wherefore we believe in him in whom we have placed confidence, unto divine glory and salvation; and we have placed confidence in the only God, whom we know that he will not transgress the things well promised to us, and made and granted to us by him out of goodwill. And goodwill is the willing of good things for another for that one's own sake. For the one is without need; but to us the beneficence and the favour from the Lord come down, being divine goodwill, and goodwill that is toward doing good. And if to Abraham, believing, it was reckoned for righteousness, and we are the seed of Abraham through hearing, then we too must believe. For we are Israelites who are obedient not through signs, but through hearing. "Therefore be glad, you barren one who do not bear; break forth and cry," it says, "you who do not travail; for many are the children of the desolate, more than of her who has the husband." "You lived within the enclosure of the people; your children were blessed into the tents of the fathers." And if the same dwellings are announced by prophecy to us and to the patriarchs, one God is shown for both covenants.

The turning toward divine things the Stoics say comes about from a change, the soul changing into wisdom; but Plato, by the soul's taking a turning toward the better and a conversion from a kind of nocturnal day. And at once the philosophers too concede a reasonable departure from life to the earnest man, if something should so deprive him of action that there is no longer left to him even the hope of action. But the judge who has forced a man to deny the one he loves seems to me to test who is a friend of God and who is not. Here no comparison is any longer left—which one might rather choose, a human threat or the love of God; and somehow the abstinence from evil deeds is found to be a diminution and quenching of vices, the activity of them being taken away through inaction. And this is, "Sell your possessions and give to the poor, and come, follow me"—that is, follow the things spoken by the Lord.

So it adds more clearly: "You have inherited the covenant of Israel" — speaking to the calling from the nations, once barren of this husband, who is the Word, once desolate of the bridegroom. "But the just shall live by faith" — the faith according to the covenant and the commandments — since these two, in name and in time, given according to age and advance dispensationally, being in power one, the one old, the other new, are supplied through the Son from one God. So the Apostle too, in the Epistle to the Romans, says: "For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith" — teaching the one salvation, perfected from prophecy into the Gospel through one and the same Lord. "This charge I commit to you, child Timothy, according to the prophecies that went before upon you, that you may war in them the good warfare, having faith and a good conscience, which some, having thrust away, have made shipwreck concerning the faith," because they defiled with unbelief the conscience that came from God.

Some say that He meant by "possessions" the things in the soul that are alien to it; and how these are distributed to the poor, they cannot say. But God distributes all things to all according to merit, the dispensation being just. "Despising, then," He says, "the possessions which God distributes, through your greatness of soul, follow the things spoken by me," hastening toward the ascent of the spirit, justified not by abstinence from evils alone, but moreover perfected by doing the Lord's good. So at once He convicted the man who boasted of having perfectly fulfilled the commands from the law of not having loved his neighbour; and love, which is lord of the Sabbath by a gnostic ascent, professes beneficence. And one ought, I think, to have come to the saving word neither from fear of punishment nor through any promises of a gift, but for the sake of the good itself.

With reason, then, faith is no longer to be slandered as ready-to-hand, easy, and common, and besides of chance people. For if it were a human pursuit, as the Greeks supposed, it would have been quenched; but it grows, and there is no place where it is not. I say, then, that faith — whether it was founded by love or even by fear, as the accusers say — is something divine, neither torn apart by another worldly friendship nor dissolved by fear when present. For love makes the faithful by the friendship that is toward faith; and faith, the seat of love, brings in beneficence in return, when even the schoolmaster fear of the law is believed in by those who believe. And it is believed that fear too is; for if in acting the being is shown, then he who is to come and threatens, but does not act or come present, is believed even to be; and, being believed to be, he is not himself the begetter of faith, being judged trustworthy by it.

Such men stand at the right hand of the sanctuary; but those who think to exchange the things of incorruption through the giving of corruptible things are called, in the parable of the two brothers, "hired servants." And does not here too the "according to the likeness" and "image" come to the surface, so that some live as fellow-citizens according to the likeness toward the Saviour, while those standing on the left live according to the image of these? . . . There are, then, three things from the truth, the one root being laid under both, but the choice not equal—or rather the difference according to the choice not equal. For it differs, I think, to choose according to imitation from one who chooses according to knowledge, as the thing made fiery and the thing illumined differ from the fire and the light. So Israel is the light of the likeness according to the Scripture, but the other is the image. And what does the parable of Lazarus mean to the Lord, showing the image of a rich man and a poor man? And what is "No one can serve two masters, God and mammon"—the Lord so naming the love of money?

As, then, God is not circumscribed in a place, nor ever imaged in the shape of a living creature, so neither is he subject to passion nor in need, as created things are—as to desire sacrifices, in the manner of food, through hunger. Things that passion touches are all corruptible; and to offer food to one who needs no nourishment is vain. And that comic poet Pherecrates, in his Deserters, has charmingly represented the gods themselves blaming men over their sacrifices: "When you sacrifice to the gods, first of all you set apart for the priests their customary portion, and then for yourselves; and then—shame to tell it—having stripped the two thighs clean to the groin, you devour all the flesh and the loin clean bare, and the rest—the very vertebra—you scour as with a file, and then portion it out to us as if to dogs; and then, ashamed before one another, you hide it under heaps of barley-cakes." And Eubulus, himself also a comic poet, writes thus somewhere about sacrifices: "To the gods themselves you sacrifice only the tail and the thigh, as though to pederasts." And bringing on Dionysus in his Semele, he has made him expostulate: "First of all, whenever any sacrifice to me, they sacrifice blood, the bladder, the liver, the heart, and the surface membrane; for I myself eat neither sweetmeats nor thigh-pieces."

Divine, then, is so great a change, that one becomes faithful out of unfaithful and believes by hope and by fear. And indeed the first inclination toward salvation appears to us as faith, after which fear and hope and repentance, together with self-control and endurance, advancing, lead us on both to love and to knowledge. With reason, then, the Apostle Barnabas says: "From what I received I was eager to send to you a part, little by little, that together with your faith you might have also perfect knowledge." "The helpers of our faith, then, are fear and endurance; and the things that fight with us are long-suffering and self-control. While these," he says, "abide in purity toward the Lord, there rejoice together with them wisdom, understanding, science, knowledge." Since, then, knowledge has as its elements the aforesaid virtues, it has come about that faith is more elementary still — being as necessary to the gnostic as breathing is to living for the one who lives in this world; and as without the four elements it is not possible to live, so without faith it is not possible for knowledge to follow. This, then, is the foundation of truth.

So at once, at the call to the supper, the lovers of possessions, though invited, do not come—not because of possessing, but because of possessing with passionate attachment. "The foxes, then, have holes." He called the malicious and earth-born men, those who spend their time about the wealth that is mined and dug out of the ground, "foxes." Likewise too, concerning Herod: "Go, tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and accomplish cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected." For He called "birds of heaven" those who, in heaven, are distinguished from the other birds—the truly pure, those who are able to fly toward the knowledge of the heavenly Word. For indeed not only of wealth and glory and marriage, but also of poverty, are there countless cares for the man who cannot bear it; and perhaps it was these cares that He hinted at in the parable of the fourfold sowing, when He said that the seed of the Word, falling among thorns and hedges, was choked by them and could not bear fruit.

Menander too has represented the loins' end and the gall: "Laying upon the gods the inedible bones," he says, "they themselves consume the rest." Or is not the steam of whole burnt offerings to be shunned even by wild beasts? And if the steam is in truth a privilege of the gods of the Greeks, they would do well to deify their cooks as well, who are reckoned worthy of the same happiness, and to worship the very oven, which comes nearer to the much-prized steam. And Hesiod somewhere, regarding a division of meats by which Zeus was deceived by Prometheus, says that Zeus took "the white bones of an ox, by a cunning art" covered "with white fat"; and that thereafter "the tribes of men upon earth burn white bones to the immortals upon the fragrant altars." But they say that in no way is God nourished by being harmed through a desire arising from want. So then they will make him like a plant, nourished without appetite, and like beasts that lie hidden in their lairs. For they say these creatures grow harmlessly, fed either by the thickness of the surrounding air or by the very exhalation of their own bodies. And yet, if the Divine is nourished by them without need, what further need has the needless of nourishment? But if, being by nature in need of nothing, he rejoices in being honoured, then not unreasonably do we honour God through prayer, and send up this best and holiest sacrifice with righteousness, doing homage by the most righteous Word, through whom we receive knowledge, and through him glorifying the one we have learned. There is, then, among us this altar here below, the earthly one—the assembly of those who are dedicated to prayers, having, as it were, one common voice and one mind. And nourishments through the sense of smell, even if they are more divine than those through the mouth, are still signs of breathing. What, then, do they say about God?

It is necessary, then, to learn how one must deal with each of the things that befall, so as to be trained, through gnostic good living, into the habit of eternal life. "I saw," it says, "the impious man exalted exceedingly and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by," says the Scripture, "and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found. Guard innocence and behold uprightness, for there is a remnant for the man of peace." This would be the man who unfeignedly believes from the whole heart and is calm with his whole soul. For "the other people honour me with their lips, but their heart is far off from the Lord. With their mouth they bless, but with their heart they curse; they loved Him with their mouth and with their tongue they lied to Him; but their heart was not upright with Him, nor were they faithful in His covenant."

It would be a long task to go through all the prophetic and legal sayings that are spoken in riddles, picking them out one by one; for nearly the whole Scripture utters its oracles in some such way. It is enough, I think, for one who has understanding, by way of demonstration of what is set before us, that a few examples be put forward. Take, for instance, how the concealment is owned by the reference, recorded among the Hebrews, of the seven enclosures about the ancient temple, and by the arrangement of the high priest's robe reaching to the feet, which through its varied symbols related to things visible hints at the whole framework that stretches from heaven to earth. And the covering and the veil were variegated with hyacinth and purple and scarlet and fine linen, hinting that the nature of the elements holds the revelation of God: for the purple is from water, the fine linen from earth, the hyacinth is likened to the air, being dusky, as the scarlet to the fire.

Does he breathe out and in, like the race of daemons? Or does he only breathe in, like creatures of the water by the opening of their gills? Or does he breathe round about, like insects by the contraction of the body through the pressure of the wings? But they would liken God to none of these, if they were of sound mind. For all things that breathe draw in the air by the contraction of the lungs against the chest. Then, if they were to assign to God entrails and arteries and veins and nerves and members, they will be introducing him as in no way differing from these. But the breathing-together is rightly spoken of in regard to the Church. For the sacrifice of the Church is the word sent up as a fragrant offering from holy souls, while at the same time, together with the sacrifice, the whole mind is laid open to God. But they say that the most ancient altar in Delos was held to be pure, and that to it alone Pythagoras drew near, not defiled by slaughter and death—and will they disbelieve us when we call the just soul the truly holy altar, and the holy prayer that rises from it the incense? But sacrifices, I think, were devised by men under pretext of eating flesh; for it was possible, even otherwise, without such idolatry, for whoever wished to partake of meats. For the sacrifices according to the Law allegorize our piety, just as the turtle-dove and the pigeon offered for sins indicate to God the acceptable purification of the irrational part of the soul. But if any of the just does not burden his soul with the eating of meats, he uses a reasonable principle—not the one with which Pythagoras and his followers dream of the transmigration of the soul. Xenocrates, treating the subject specially in his work On Nourishment from Animals, and Polemon in his treatises On Life according to Nature, seem clearly to say that nourishment through flesh is unprofitable, since, being already worked over, it assimilates to the souls of the irrational creatures.

Readiness to see what is needful is much helped by preliminary training. And the objects of thought would be an exercise for the mind. Their nature is threefold, contemplated in quantities, magnitudes, and things expressed in speech. For the reasoning that comes from demonstrations sets exact conviction in the soul of the man who follows it, so that he cannot think the thing demonstrated could be otherwise; and it does not let us fall before those who steal up on us for deceit. In these studies, then, the soul is cleansed of the things of sense and rekindled, that at some time it may be able to discern the truth. For good nourishment and good education, when preserved, make good natures; and good natures, taking hold of such education, become better than before, both in other respects and in begetting — as in the case of the other animals too. Therefore it says: "Go to the ant, you sluggard, and become wiser than it, which lays up in the harvest much and varied nourishment against the threat of winter; or go to the bee, and learn how she is a worker — for she too, grazing over the whole meadow, brings forth a single honeycomb."

"Therefore let the deceitful lips be made dumb, that speak lawlessness against the righteous." And again: "May the Lord utterly destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue, those who said, 'We will magnify our tongue; our lips are our own; who is lord over us? From the misery of the poor and the groaning of the needy I will now arise,' says the Lord; 'I will set them in safety; I will speak boldly in him.'" For Christ belongs to the humble-minded, not to those who exalt themselves over His flock. "Lay not up, then, for yourselves treasures upon the earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break through and steal"—perhaps the Lord says this rebuking the lovers of possessions, perhaps too those who are simply anxious and full of care, and indeed the lovers of the body too. For loves and sicknesses and base reckonings break through the reasoning and the whole man; but our true treasure is where the kinship of the mind is. He hands down, further, the social aspect of righteousness, showing that we must give back to the habit of the old way of life the things acquired for us by it, and run back to God, asking for mercy. This is truly a purse not growing old, the provision of eternal life, an unfailing treasure in heaven, because "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy," says the Lord.

And between the covering and the veil, where the priests were permitted to enter, lay the altar of incense, a symbol of the earth set in the middle of this world, from which come up the exhalations. And that place was midway between the inner part within the veil, where it was permitted to the high priest alone to enter on stated days, and the outer enclosing court, open to all the Hebrews. Therefore they say it is the very midmost of heaven and earth; while others say it is a symbol of the intelligible and the sensible world. The covering, then — a hindrance to the unbelief of the laity — was stretched before the five pillars, keeping back those in the enclosure. Thus, most mystically, five loaves are broken by the Saviour and multiplied for the multitude of the hearers. For great is the number of those who cleave to the things of sense as though these alone existed. "Look round about, and take heed," says Plato, "lest one of the uninitiated overhear." And these are they who think that nothing else exists except what they can lay firm hold of with both hands, but who do not admit actions and processes of becoming and everything invisible as having a share in being; for such are they who cleave to the pentad of the senses alone. But the apprehension of God is not to be trodden by the ears, nor by those of like kind.

For this reason, indeed, the Jews especially abstain from swine's flesh, as though this beast were unclean, since beyond the rest it roots up and destroys the crops. But if they say that the animals are given to men, we too agree—only not by all means for food, nor indeed all of them, but those that are useless for work. Therefore not amiss does the comic poet Plato say in his play The Feasts: "Of four-footed beasts we ought henceforth to kill none but swine; for their flesh is most pleasant, and nothing comes from the pig but bristles and mud and squealing for us." Whence too Aesop said, not amiss, that swine squeal loudest when they are dragged off, knowing in themselves that they are good for nothing else but sacrifice. For which reason Cleanthes too says that they have soul instead of salt, that their flesh may not rot. Some, then, eat them as useless; others abstain as from a thing destructive of the crops; and others do not eat them because the creature is prone to coupling. In this way too the Law does not sacrifice the goat, except in the single rite of the sending-away of evils, since pleasure is the metropolis of vice. And indeed they say that the eating of goat's flesh contributes to epilepsy. They say also that the greatest distribution arises from swine's flesh, and therefore it is useful to those who train the body, but no longer to those who labour to increase the soul itself, on account of the sluggishness that comes from flesh-eating.

And if you pray in your closet, as the Lord taught, worshipping in spirit, your stewardship would no longer be only about the house, but also about the soul: what is to be apportioned to it, and how, and how much; what is to be laid up and treasured within it, and when these things are to be brought forth, and to whom. For not by nature but by learning do men become noble and good, like physicians and pilots. We all alike, at least, behold the vine and the horse; but the farmer will know whether the vine is good for bearing fruit or bad, and the horseman will easily distinguish the spiritless from the swift. And that some are better endowed by nature for virtue than others shows that certain pursuits of those so endowed surpass others; but it does not charge any of the better-endowed with perfection in virtue, since both those poorly endowed for virtue, when they have met with the fitting education, have for the most part attained nobility, and, on the other hand, those well endowed have become bad through neglect. By nature, again, God has fashioned us social and just.

He says these things also to those who wish, for the sake of righteousness, to be poor; for they have heard through the commandment that "broad and spacious is the road that leads to destruction, and many are they who go through it." He discourses about nothing else than profligacy and love of women, love of glory, love of rule, and the like passions; for "fool," He said thus, "this night they require your soul of you; and what you prepared for it, whose shall it be?" And the words of the commandment run, word for word, thus: "Guard yourselves, then, against all covetousness, for a man's life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions. For what does a man profit if he gain the whole world but suffer the loss of his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? Therefore I say: Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall put on; for the soul is more than food and the body than clothing." And again: "For your Father knows that you need all these things; but seek first the kingdom of heaven and righteousness, for these are great, and the small things and those about this life shall be added to you."

Hence the Son is called the face of the Father, having become the bearer of flesh through the pentad of the senses — the Word who is the announcer of the Father's distinctive being. "And if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit. We walk by faith, not by sight," the good apostle says. Within the covering, then, the priestly ministry was hidden, and it keeps off from those within it many that are without. Again, the veil of the way into the holy of holies — there four pillars stood, a token of the holy tetrad of the old covenants. And the mystic name of four letters was set upon those to whom alone the inner sanctuary was to be trodden; it is pronounced Iaoue, which is interpreted, "he who is and who shall be." And indeed among the Greeks too the name "God" contains a tetrad of letters. And into the intelligible world the Lord alone, having become high priest, enters, slipping in through the sufferings to the knowledge of the unspeakable, withdrawing above every name that is made known by the voice. Indeed the lamp-stand too lay on the south side of the altar of incense, by which were shown the motions of the seven light-bearers that make their circuits to the south. For three branches grow from each side of the lamp-stand, and upon them the lamps; since the sun too, like the lamp-stand, set in the midst of the other planets, gives of its light to those above it and to those below it, according to a kind of divine music.

And now: land animals and birds, breathing the same air as our souls, are nourished by it, having a soul akin to the air; but they say that fishes do not breathe this air, but that other one which was mingled with the water straightway at the first creation, as it was with the rest of the elements—which is also a token of their material permanence. One must, then, "offer to God sacrifices that are not costly, but dear to God." And that compound incense in the Law, made up of many tongues and voices in prayer—or rather that which is prepared out of diverse nations and natures by the gift of the covenants "into the unity of faith," and gathered together in praises, with a pure mind, with a just and upright polity, out of holy works and righteous prayer. For who is so foolish, in the words of the poet's grace, and so utterly slack and credulous of men, as to hope that the gods take delight in bones without flesh and in burning gall—things not even edible to hungry dogs—and that all of them obtain this as a privilege, and pay back a return of thanks to those who do it, even if they happen to be pirates or robbers or tyrants? But we say that the fire sanctifies not the flesh, but sinful souls—meaning by fire not that which devours all and is mechanic, but the prudent fire, that which "pierces through the soul" that passes through the fire.

Hence it must not be said that the just is manifest from nature alone; rather, we must understand that the good of our creation is rekindled by the commandment, the soul being educated by learning to be willing to choose the noblest. But just as we say it is possible to be faithful even without letters, so we confess that it is not possible, without learning, to understand the things said in the faith. For to admit what is well said and not to admit what is foreign is not the work of faith simply, but of faith concerned with learning. And if ignorance is at once want of education and want of learning, teaching sets in the knowledge of things divine and human. But just as it is possible to live rightly in poverty of life, so it is also possible in abundance; and we confess that, with preliminary education, one might hunt down virtue more easily and more quickly — though it is not unattainable even without these things, except that even then it is for those who have learned and have exercised their faculties of perception. "Hatred," says Solomon, "stirs up strife; but education guards the ways of life," that one be not deceived, that one be not robbed by those who have practised evil craft to the harm of their hearers. "And education unexamined goes astray," he says; and we must take part in the refuting kind, for the sake of beating back the deceitful opinions of the sophists.

Does He not exhort us outright to pursue the gnostic life, and urge us to seek the truth in deed and in word? Christ, who educates the soul, reckons a man rich not by his giving but by his purpose. So Zacchaeus—but some say it was Matthias—the chief tax-collector, when he had heard the Lord deeming him worthy to come to him, said: "Behold, the half of my possessions I give as alms, Lord; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore fourfold." Of whom the Saviour too said: "The Son of Man, coming today, has found that which was lost." And again, watching at the treasury, He said that the rich man cast in proportionally to his wealth, but the widow had cast in more than all—two coppers—for the one contributed from his abundance, but she out of her want.

The golden lamp-stand has yet another riddle, of the sign of Christ — not by its shape alone, but also by its casting light in manifold ways and in many parts upon those who believe in him and hope and look toward him through the ministry of the first-created. And they say that the seven eyes of the Lord are the seven spirits resting upon the rod that flowers from the root of Jesse. And on the north side of the altar of incense the table had its place, on which lay the setting-out of the loaves, because the things of the north are the most nourishing of the spirits. And there might be certain abodes of churches breathing together into one body and one assembly. And the things recorded upon the holy ark signify the things of the intelligible world, hidden away and shut off from the many. Indeed, those golden figures too, each of them six-winged, whether they show forth the two Bears, as some would have it, or rather the two hemispheres — and the name Cherubim means "much knowledge" — but both together have twelve wings, and by the zodiacal circle and the time that is borne along it they show forth the world of sense.

Well, then, does Anaxarchus the Eudaemonic write in his work On Kingship: "Much learning helps greatly, but greatly harms the one who has it: it helps the man who is adroit, but harms the man who readily utters every word in every assembly. One must know the measures of the right moment; for this is the boundary of wisdom. But all who sing outside the door, even if they sing something prudent, are not reckoned among the wise, but have a mind of folly." And Hesiod: "Of the Muses, who make a man of many counsels inspired and clear-voiced" — for he calls the man of many counsels "well-supplied in words," the clear-voiced man "formidable," and "inspired" the man of experience and philosophy and knowledge of the truth.

And that He referred everything to the education of the soul: "Blessed," He says, "are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth." The meek are those who have brought to rest the truceless battle in the soul, of wrath and desire and the kinds subordinate to these. And He praises those meek by choice, not by necessity.
