For with the Lord there are both rewards and many mansions, according to the proportion of lives; for "whoever receives," He says, "a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet's reward; and whoever receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man's reward; and whoever receives one of these little disciples shall not lose his reward." And again, the differences according to merit, the noble recompenses of virtue—through the unequal hours, and besides through the equal wage given to each of the workmen (that is, salvation, which the denarius hints at), He has indicated the equal justice toward those who worked during unequal hours.

Concerning these things, I think, tragedy too, philosophizing on nature, says: "Unwearying Time goes round, full with ever-flowing stream, begetting itself; and the twin Bears, with the swift-wheeling rushings of their wings, keep watch over the Atlantean pole." And Atlas, the pole that does not suffer, may be the fixed sphere, but better perhaps it is to be understood as the unmoved age. But I think it better that the ark, called by the Hebrew name thēbōtha, signifies something else; it is interpreted "one in place of all places." Whether, then, the Ogdoad and the intelligible world is signified, or the God who comprehends all things, shapeless and invisible, let it be set aside to say now; except that it indicates rest in the company of the glorifying spirits, which are hinted at by the Cherubim. For he who had charged that not even a carved idol be fashioned would never himself have figured a statue of holy things; nor is there at all in heaven any such composite and sensible living creature. But the face is a symbol of the rational soul, and the wings are the lofty ministries and operations of the powers on the right and on the left together, and the voice is the thankful glory in unceasing contemplation.

They will work, then, in the mansions proportionate to the rewards of which they were deemed worthy, fellow-workers of the ineffable dispensation and ministry. And those who are reckoned to have been preferred toward living a holy life, says Plato, "are those who, set free and released from these places in the earth as from prisons, attain to the pure dwelling above"; and again, by clearer terms, he says the same thing in some such way: "Of these themselves, those who have been sufficiently purified in philosophy live altogether without bodies for all time"—although he gives them certain forms, to some airy, to others fiery. He adds further: "And they come to dwellings still fairer than these, which it is neither easy to show nor is the time sufficient at present." Hence with good reason "blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." For those who have repented of the evil life they led before will be present at the call; for this is to be comforted. And there are two ways of the man who repents: the more common, fear over the things done; and the more particular, the soul's shame before itself out of conscience—whether here or also elsewhere, since no place is idle of the beneficence of God.

Let it be enough to have carried the mystic interpretation thus far. The high priest's robe reaching to the feet is a symbol of the sensible world: of the seven planets, the five stones and the two carbuncles, for Cronos and the Moon. For the one is southern and moist and earthy and heavy, the other is airy; whence Artemis is called by some "the air-cleaver," being a kind of being, and the air is dusky. And the powers set over the planets, which co-operate in the generation of things here according to the divine providence, he with reason represents as set upon the breast and the shoulders, through which the generation-producing action, the first hebdomad, comes about; and the breast is the dwelling-place of the heart and the soul. And in another way too the variegated stones might be modes of salvation, set, some among the higher, some among the lower parts of the whole body that is being saved. And the three hundred and sixty bells hung from the robe are the year's time, "the acceptable year of the Lord," proclaiming and announcing the greatest appearing of the Saviour. And the golden plate, lifted up, signifies the kingly authority of the Lord, since the Saviour is the head of the church.

Again He says: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy." Now mercy is not, as some of the philosophers have supposed, grief over others' misfortunes, but rather something noble, as the prophets say: "I desire mercy and not sacrifice." And He wishes us to be merciful not only by doing mercy but also by willing to show mercy, even if we cannot, to whom the doing is present according to purpose. For sometimes we wish, through the giving of money or through bodily zeal, to do mercy—to aid the needy, or to serve the sick, or to stand by one fallen into difficulty—and we are not able, whether through poverty or sickness or old age (for this too is a natural sickness), to minister to the purpose toward which we set out, being unable to bring to completion what we had willed. The willing, then, will share in the same honour with those who were able, of whom the purpose is equal, even if others have the advantage in abundance.

The plate above the head, then, is a sign of a most commanding rule; for we have heard, as it is said, that "the head of Christ is God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." Indeed the breast-piece is made up of the shoulder-piece, which is a symbol of work, and of the oracle-pouch — and this hints at the Word — and it is an image of heaven, which came to be by the Word, lying beneath the head of all things, Christ, and moving in the same way and after the same fashion. The shining emerald stones, then, upon the shoulder-piece signify the sun and the moon, the fellow-workers of nature. And the shoulder, I think, is the beginning of the hand. And the twelve set in four rows upon the breast describe for us the zodiacal circle according to the four turns of the year. And it was fitting, besides, that the law and the prophets should be set beneath the Lord's head, through which the righteous of both covenants are shown forth; for in saying that the apostles are both prophets and righteous men we should speak well, since one and the same Holy Spirit works through all. And as the Lord is above the whole world — or rather beyond the intelligible world — so too the name written upon the plate was held worthy to be above every rule and authority; and it is written by reason of the written commandments and of the sensible presence. And it is called the name of God, since, as the Son beholds the goodness of the Father, he works, being called God the Saviour, the beginning of all things, which was figured first, before the ages, from the invisible God, and has stamped all things that came to be after it.

And since there are found to be two ways that lead to the perfection of salvation—works and knowledge—He called blessed the pure in heart, for they shall see God. And indeed, if we look at the truth, knowledge, by which the purification of the soul's ruling part comes about, is also a good activity. Some goods, then, are good in themselves, others by sharing in the goods, as we say of noble deeds; but apart from the intermediate things, which hold the place of matter, neither good nor bad deeds come about—I mean such as life and health and the other necessary or circumstantial things. He wishes, then, that those who arrive at the knowledge of God be pure in respect of bodily desires and holy in their reasonings, so that the ruling part may have nothing spurious set before its own power.

Indeed the oracle-pouch signifies the prophecy that cries aloud and proclaims by the Word, and the judgement that is to come; since it is the same Word that prophesies and that at once judges and distinguishes each thing. And they say that the garment, the robe reaching to the feet, prophesies the dispensation according to the flesh, by which he was more nearly seen in the world. Thus the high priest, having put off the consecrated tunic — for the world, and the creation in the world, has been consecrated by him who agreed that the things made were good — bathes and puts on the other tunic, a holy of holy, so to speak, which goes in with him into the inner sanctuary; showing forth, as I think, the Levite and the gnostic, as ruler over the other priests, those others having been washed with water and clothed with faith alone and awaiting their own abode, while he himself has distinguished the things of mind from the things of sense, and, by an ascent above the other priests, hastens to the passage into the intelligible, being washed of the things here no longer with water, as before he was purified when he was being enrolled into the Levitical tribe, but now by the gnostic Word.

Whenever, then, a man dwells in contemplation, conversing purely with the divine, the one who gnostically shares in the holy quality comes more closely into the habit of an impassive identity, so as no longer to have knowledge and to possess understanding, but to be understanding and knowledge. Blessed, then, are the peacemakers. Those who have tamed and made gentle the law that wars against the mind of our intellect—the threats of wrath and the lures of desire and the other passions, all that wage war against the reasoning—and who have lived their lives with knowledge and good works and true reasoning, shall be restored to the most beloved adoption. And the perfect peacemaking would be that which keeps the peaceful state unchanged whatever befalls, calling the dispensation holy and good, established in the knowledge of divine and human things, through which it reckons the contraries in the world to be the fairest harmony of creation. And they make peace also for those here who are warred upon by the stratagems of sin, teaching them to pass over to faith and peace.

Pure, then, in all his heart, having ordered his whole conduct most excellently to the highest, having grown beyond the priest to something greater, downright purified both in word and in life, having put over himself the brightness of glory, having received the unspeakable inheritance of that spiritual and perfect man — which eye has not seen and ear has not heard and which has not entered into the heart of man — having become a son and a friend, he is now filled, face to face, with the insatiable contemplation. There is nothing like hearkening to the Word himself, who gives the mind more by means of the Scripture. For it says thus: "And he shall put off the linen robe, which he had put on when he entered into the holy place, and shall leave it there. And he shall bathe his body with water in a holy place, and shall put on his robe." In another way, I think, the Lord puts off and puts on, coming down into sense; in another way he who has believed through him puts off and puts on over himself, as the apostle also showed, the consecrated robe. Hence, after the image of the Lord, the most approved of the consecrated tribe were chosen as high priests, and those elected to kingship and to prophecy were anointed.

The summary, I think, of every virtue is what the Lord teaches us, namely, that one must, in a more gnostic way, despise death out of love toward God. "Blessed," He says, "are those who have been persecuted for righteousness' sake, for they shall be called sons of God"; or, as some who alter the gospels have it: "Blessed are those who have been persecuted for the sake of righteousness, for they shall be perfect; and blessed are those who have been persecuted for my sake, for they shall have a place where they shall not be persecuted. And blessed are you when men hate you, when they separate you, when they cast out your name as evil for the sake of the Son of Man"—if, plainly, we do not loathe our persecutors and endure the punishments from them, not hating them, considering that we have been tested more slowly than we expected, but knowing this too, that any trial whatever is an occasion of martyrdom.

But as the preaching has come now in season, so in season the law and the prophets were given to the barbarians, and philosophy to the Greeks, accustoming their ears to the preaching. The Lord, then, who redeemed Israel, says: "In an acceptable time I heard you, and in a day of salvation I helped you, and I gave you for a covenant of the nations, to settle the earth and to inherit the inheritance of the wilderness, saying to those in bonds, 'Come out,' and to those in darkness, 'Be uncovered.'" For if the Jews were in bonds — to whom too the Lord said, "Come out from your bonds," those who willed — meaning those willingly bound, who had laid upon themselves burdens hard to bear by human meddling, plainly those in darkness would be those who, in idolatry, had their ruling part buried. For to the just according to the law there was lacking faith, wherefore the Lord, healing these too, said, "Your faith has saved you"; but to the just according to philosophy there was lacking not only faith in the Lord, but also the standing apart from idolatry. For instance, when the truth was revealed, these too repent of their former deeds; wherefore the Lord preached the good news even to those in Hades.

To those who, with a fair name, are impious through continence, both against the creation and against the holy Demiurge, the Almighty and only God, and who teach that one must not accept marriage and the begetting of children, nor introduce into the world others destined to be unfortunate, nor supply nourishment to death—to these we must say the following. First, the saying of the apostle John: "And now many antichrists have come, whence we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us." Next, we must refute them by resolving the things they bring forward, in some such way as this. To Salome, when she asked, "How long shall death have power?" the Lord said—not that life is evil and the creation wicked—"As long as you women bear children," teaching the natural sequence; for upon generation there always follows decay.

The Scripture, at any rate, says: "Hades says to Destruction, 'His form indeed we did not see, but his voice we heard.'" It was not, surely, the place that, taking a voice, spoke the foregoing, but those ranked in Hades, who had given themselves over to destruction, as men who from some ship had willingly cast themselves into the sea; these, then, are they who heard the divine power and voice. For who, being right-minded, would suppose that in one condemnation are both the souls of the just and those of sinners, pouring out injustice upon providence? And do not these things make plain that the Lord preached the good news both to those who perished in the flood — or rather were fettered — and to those held in prison and ward? And it has been shown, in the second book of the Stromateis, that the apostles, following the Lord, preached the good news even to those in Hades. For it was fitting, I think, as here, so there too, that the best of the disciples should be imitators of the teacher, that the one might bring to conversion those of the Hebrews, and the others the Gentiles — that is, those who had lived in righteousness according to the law and according to philosophy, but not perfectly, having ended their life sinfully. For this befitted the divine dispensation, that those who had held more worthily in righteousness and lived chiefly so, and had repented of their stumblings, even if they chanced to be making confession in another place, being among those of God the Almighty, should be saved, each according to his own knowledge.

The law, then, has chosen to lead us out from luxury and all disorder, and this is its purpose, to lead us up out of unrighteousness into righteousness, choosing prudent marriages and the begetting of children and a civic life. And the Lord did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfil it—to fulfil it not as one defective, but in that, by His coming, the prophecies of the law were brought to completion; since even before the law the things of right conduct were proclaimed through the Word to those who lived justly. Now the many, not knowing continence, conduct themselves in the body, not in the spirit; but the body without the spirit is earth and ashes. And indeed the Lord judges adultery from the intention. For what? Is it not possible to use marriage with continence, and not to try to dissolve what God has joined together? Such things are taught by those who divide the marriage union, on whose account the name is blasphemed. And these men, who say that intercourse is defiled, having themselves received their own existence from intercourse—how are they not defiled?

And the Saviour too works, I think, since to save is his work; which indeed he has done, drawing to salvation those who were minded to believe in him through the preaching, wherever they chanced to have been. If, then, the Lord went down to Hades for nothing else than to preach the good news, as he went down, he preached it either to all, or to the Hebrews only. If, then, to all, all who believed shall be saved, even if they chance to be of the Gentiles, having made confession already there; since the chastisements of God are saving and instructive, leading to conversion and choosing the repentance rather than the death of the sinner — and this the more, since souls released from bodies are able to see more purely, even though darkened by passions, because no longer hindered by the flesh. But if he preached the good news to the Jews only, who lacked the recognition and faith that come through the Saviour, plainly, since God is no respecter of persons, the apostles too, as here, so there preached the good news to those of the Gentiles fit for conversion. And it is well said in the Shepherd: "They went down with them into the water, but these went down living and came up living, while those, the previously fallen asleep, went down dead, but came up living."

But of those who have been sanctified, I think the seed too is holy. Now not only the spirit, but also our character and life and body, ought to be sanctified by us; for on what ground does the apostle Paul say that the wife is sanctified by the husband, or the husband by the wife? And what is it that the Lord said to those who asked Him about divorce, whether it was lawful to put away a wife, since Moses had permitted it? "For your hardness of heart," He says, "Moses wrote this; but have you not read that to the first-formed man God said, 'You two shall be one flesh'? So that he who puts away his wife, except for the cause of fornication, makes her commit adultery." "But after the resurrection," he says, "they neither marry nor are given in marriage." And indeed it is said of the belly and of foods: "Foods for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will bring to nought both this and these"—rebuking those who think they should live like boars and goats, that they may eat and copulate without fear.

Yes, and the Gospel says too that many bodies of those fallen asleep arose, plainly transferred into a better order. There came about, then, a certain universal movement and transference according to the dispensation of the Saviour. The just man, then, in so far as he is just, does not differ from the just man, whether he be one under the law or a Greek; for God is Lord not of the Jews only, but of all men, and more nearly the Father of those who have known him. For if to live well is to live lawfully, and to live reasonably is to live according to law, and those who lived rightly before the law were reckoned to faith and judged to be just, plainly those too who lived outside the law, by the peculiar quality of their soul, having lived rightly — even if they chanced to be in Hades and in ward — having heard the Lord's voice, whether his own or that working through the apostles, would quickly turn and believe. For we remember that the Lord is the power of God; and power could never be weak. Thus, I think, it is shown that God is good, and the Lord able to save with righteousness and equality toward those who turn, whether here or elsewhere. For not here only does his working power reach; it is everywhere and ever works.

If, then, they have already received the resurrection, as they say, and for this reason reject marriage, let them neither eat nor drink; for the apostle said that the belly and foods are brought to nought in the resurrection. How then do they hunger and thirst and suffer the things of the flesh, and the other things that he who through Christ has received the perfect resurrection that is hoped for will not suffer? But indeed even those who worship idols abstain from both foods and sex. "The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking," he says. Note that even the Magi take care to abstain from wine and from animal food and from sex, while serving angels and demons. And as humility is meekness, not the maltreatment of the body, so too continence is a virtue of the soul, which is not in the open but in secret.

For instance, in the Preaching of Peter the Lord says to the disciples after the resurrection: "I chose you twelve, having judged you disciples worthy of me, whom the Lord willed; and reckoning you faithful apostles, I send you out into the world to preach the good news to the men throughout the inhabited earth, that they may know that there is one God, declaring, through faith in me, Christ's faith, the things that shall be; that those who hear and believe may be saved, and those who do not believe, having heard, may bear witness, having no defence to say, 'We did not hear.'" What then? Has not the same dispensation come about even in Hades? — so that there too all the souls, having heard the preaching, might either show forth repentance, or confess the chastisement to be just, by which they did not believe. It would have been a piece of no common covetousness for those who had gone out before the Lord's coming, not having had the good news preached to them, nor having furnished of themselves the ground for believing or not, to partake either of salvation or of chastisement. For it is surely not lawful that some should be condemned uncondemned, and that only those after the coming should have enjoyed the divine righteousness. And to all souls from above, the rational ones, it was said: "Whatever anyone of you did in ignorance, not knowing God clearly, if, having recognized him, he repent, all his sins shall be forgiven him." "Behold," it says, "I have set before your face death and life; choose life" — God saying that he has set them for the comparison of choice, not that he made both.

There are some who openly call marriage fornication, and lay it down as doctrine that it was given by the devil; and these great boasters say that they imitate the Lord, who neither married nor possessed anything in the world, boasting that they have understood the gospel better than others. But the Scripture says to them: "God sets Himself against the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Then they do not know the reason why the Lord did not marry. For first, He had His own bride, the Church; and next, He was not a common man, that He should have need of some helper after the flesh; nor was it necessary for Him to beget children, since He abides eternally and was born the only Son of God. And this same Lord says: "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder." And again: "As it was in the days of Noah—they were marrying, being given in marriage, building, planting—and as it was in the days of Lot, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man." And, to show that He does not speak to the Gentiles, He adds: "When the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on the earth?" And again: "Woe to those who are with child and to those who give suck in those days." Yet these things too are spoken allegorically. For this reason He did not even fix the times which the Father has set in His own authority, so that the world might continue through the generations.

And in another Scripture he says: "If you hear me and are willing, you shall eat the good things of the earth; but if you do not hear me, nor are willing, a sword shall devour you; for the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." And again David says outright — or rather the Lord, in the person of the holy one (and this one, from the foundation of the world, is everyone who at different times has been saved or shall be saved through faith): "My heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; and moreover my flesh shall dwell in hope," he says, "for you will not leave my soul in Hades, nor will you give your holy one to see corruption. You have made known to me the ways of life; you will fill me with gladness with your countenance."

As for "Not all receive this saying; for there are eunuchs who were so born, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven; let him who can receive it, receive it"—they do not know that, after the saying about divorce, when some asked, "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not profitable for a man to marry," then the Lord said, "Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it is given." For this is what those who asked wished to learn: whether, when a wife has been condemned for fornication and cast out, He permits a man to marry another. They say, too, that not a few athletes abstain from sex, practising continence for the sake of bodily training—such as Astylus of Croton and Crison of Himera. And Amoebeus the harper, though newly married, abstained from his bride. And Aristotle of Cyrene alone overlooked Lais, who was in love with him.

As, then, the people is precious to the Lord, so the whole holy people is, together with the Jew, also he of the Gentiles who turns, who was prophesied as the proselyte. With reason, then, the Scripture says that the ox and the bear shall be in the same place; for the Jew is called the ox, from the animal judged clean under the law and under the yoke, since the ox both parts the hoof and chews the cud; but the Gentile is shown forth by the bear, an unclean and savage beast; and this animal brings forth flesh unshapen, which it shapes into the likeness of the beast by its tongue alone. For by the Word the Gentile who turns is shaped into being tamed from his beastlike life, and being now domesticated, he too is purified like the ox. The prophet says, for instance: "The Sirens shall bless me, and the daughters of the sparrows, and all the beasts of the field." Of the unclean animals are the beasts of the field — that is, of the world — known; since he calls those who come to faith savage and filthy in their life, not yet cleansed by the righteousness of the law, "beasts." But having changed from being beasts through the Lord's faith, they become men of God, advancing from the first willing to change, into the becoming so. For the Lord exhorts some, but to those who have already set their hands he stretches out a hand and draws them up; for the Master of all does not withdraw before any face, nor will he reverence greatness, since he himself made small and great alike, and provides for all in like manner.

Having sworn to the courtesan that he would take her away to his homeland if she would help him in something against his rivals, when he had accomplished it, gracefully fulfilling his oath, he had a most lifelike image of her painted and set it up at Cyrene—as Ister relates in his work On the Peculiarities of Contests. So that not even celibacy is virtuous, unless it comes about through love toward God. Concerning those who loathe marriage, the blessed Paul says: "In later times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and to teachings of demons, who forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods." And again he says: "Let no one disqualify you in self-imposed worship, in humility, and in unsparing treatment of the body." And the same man writes this also: "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be loosed. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife." And again: "Let each man have his own wife, lest Satan tempt you."

And David says: "If the Gentiles were fixed in the destruction which they made, in this snare which they hid their foot was caught; but the Lord became a refuge to the poor man, a helper in good season and in affliction." Fittingly, then, the good news was preached to those who were in affliction. And for this reason it says: "Declare among the nations his doings, that they be not judged unjustly." If, then, for this reason he preached the good news to those in the flesh, that they should not be condemned unjustly, how should he not also, for the same cause, have preached it to those who went out before his coming? For "the Lord is just, and loved righteousness; his countenance saw uprightness." But "he who loves injustice hates his own soul."

And what? Did not the ancient righteous men too partake of the creation with thanksgiving? Some of them even begot children, marrying with continence. And to Elijah the ravens brought food, bread and meat. And the prophet Samuel, having reserved a thigh from what he was eating, brought and gave it to Saul to eat. But these men, who claim to surpass them in conduct and in life, will not be able even to be compared with their deeds. "Let not him who does not eat despise him who eats, and let not him who eats judge him who does not eat; for God has received him." But indeed the Lord, speaking of Himself, says: "John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, 'He has a demon.' The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, 'Behold, a man gluttonous and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax-collectors and sinners.'" Or do they reject the apostles too? For Peter and Philip begot children, and Philip even gave his daughters to husbands.

If, then, in the flood all sinful flesh perished, the chastisement having come to them for their instruction, first we must believe that the will of God, being instructive and active, saves those who turn; and next that the finer part too, the soul, could never suffer anything dread from the coarser-grained water, not being held by it, by reason of its fineness and simplicity, in respect of which it is also called incorporeal. But whatever is coarse-grained, having been thickened by sin, this is cast away together with the fleshly spirit that lusts against the soul. And already even Valentinus, the chief of those who profess community, in his homily On Friends, writes word for word: "Many of the things written in the public books are found written in the church of God; for these common things are the words that come from the heart, the law written in the heart; this is the people of the Beloved, that is loved and that loves him."

And Paul does not hesitate, in a certain epistle, to address his own consort, whom he did not carry about with him because of the convenience of his ministry. He says, then, in a certain epistle: "Have we not the right to take about a sister, a wife, as the other apostles do?" But these men, fittingly to their ministry, gave their undistracted attention to the preaching, and took the women about not as wives but as sisters, to be fellow-ministers to the women who kept the house, through whom the teaching of the Lord made its way without reproach even into the women's quarters. For we know also all that the noble Paul ordains concerning women deacons in the other epistle to Timothy. Yet this same man has cried aloud that the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, nor indeed abstinence from wine and meat, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. Which of them goes about wearing a sheepskin and a leather belt, as Elijah did? Which has clothed himself in sackcloth, otherwise naked and unshod, as Isaiah did? Or wears only a linen loincloth, as Jeremiah did? And the gnostic firmness of John's life—who will imitate it? Yet even living thus, the blessed prophets gave thanks to the Creator.

For whether he means the Jewish Scriptures or those of the philosophers by "public books," he makes the truth common. And Isidore too, son and at the same time disciple of Basilides, in the first book of his Expositions of the Prophet Parchor, himself also writes word for word: "The Attics say that something was signified to Socrates by a spirit that attended him, and Aristotle says that all men have spirits which accompany them through the time of their being in the body." This prophetic teaching he took and laid down in his own books, not confessing whence he filched this saying. And again, in the second book of the same work, he writes somewhat thus: "And let no one think that what we say is proper to the elect was said beforehand by certain philosophers; for it is not their discovery, but appropriating it from the prophets they ascribed it to the man accounted wise among them." And again, in the same: "For it seems to me that those who pretend to philosophize, in order to learn what is the winged oak and the embroidered robe upon it — all that Pherecydes theologized by allegory — took the theme from the prophecy of Ham . . ."

The justice of Carpocrates, and of those who like him pursue the unrestrained community, is overthrown in some such way as this. For just after saying, "Give to him who asks of you," He adds, "And from him who would borrow do not turn away"—teaching this kind of community, not the lecherous kind. For how can there be one who asks and receives and borrows, unless there is one who has and gives and lends? And what of it when the Lord says, "I was hungry and you fed me, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you took me in, I was naked and you clothed me"? And then He adds: "Inasmuch as you did it to one of these least, you did it to me." Does He not lay down the same things in the Old Testament too? "He who gives to the poor lends to God," and "Do not withhold from doing good to the needy," it says.

And again: "Let not acts of mercy and faith forsake you," He said. "Poverty humbles a man; but the hands of the manly make rich." And He adds: "Behold a man who did not give out his money at interest"—he is acceptable; and "a man's own wealth is reckoned the ransom of his soul." Does He not make it plain outright? As, then, the world is composed of opposites—of hot and cold, dry and wet—so too of those who give and those who receive. And again, when He says, "If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor," He reproves the man who boasted that he had kept all the commandments from his youth; for he had not fulfilled "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." And it was then that, being brought to completion by the Lord, he was taught to give a share out of love.

He did not, then, forbid being rich rightly, but only being rich unjustly and insatiably; for a possession hastened on with lawlessness becomes the less. For there are some who, by sowing, gain the more, and some who, by gathering, are diminished. Concerning whom it is written: "He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness abides for ever." For the one who sows and gathers more is he who, through earthly and temporary giving, acquires the heavenly and eternal things; but the other is he who shares with no one, but heaps up vainly upon the earth, where moth and rust destroy—of whom it is written: "Gathering his wages, he gathered them into a bag full of holes." It is of this man that the Lord says in the gospel that his land bore well; and then, wishing to store up the fruits and to build greater barns, he said to himself, by way of impersonation: "You have many good things laid up for many years; eat, drink, be merry." "You fool," He said, "this very night they require your soul of you. The things you have prepared, whose shall they be?"

The causes that produce suspension of judgement are two, the highest: one, the manifold and unstable character of human judgement, which is by nature productive of discord—either of men with one another, or of themselves with themselves; the second, the discord in existing things, which also has reasonably become productive of suspension of judgement. For, being able neither to believe all impressions because of their conflict, nor to disbelieve all (because the statement that says that all are untrustworthy, being itself one of all, is circumscribed together with all), nor to believe some and disbelieve others because of their equality, we have been brought down to suspension of judgement. And of these very most original causes of suspension, the instability of the understanding is productive of discord, and discord is the immediate cause of suspension; whence life is full of law-courts and council-chambers and assemblies, and, in general, of the choosing and shunning of the so-called goods and evils—which are tokens of an understanding at a loss and shifting before the equal strength of the opposing things. And the chests of books are full, and the treatises and works of those who are in discord in their doctrines and have persuaded themselves that they know the truth in things.

But those who accuse fear run down the law; and if the law, then plainly the God too who gave the law. For these three things necessarily exist about the subject matter: the administrator, the administration, the thing administered. If, then, by hypothesis they should take away the law, then necessarily each man who is led by desire, gratifying pleasure, will neglect what is good, despise the divine, and be at once impious and unjust, leaping away fearlessly from the truth. "Yes," they say, "fear is an irrational avoidance and a passion." What do you say? And how could this definition still hold for you, the commandment having been given me through reason? And the commandment forbids, hanging fear over us, for the education of those who can thus be admonished. Fear, then, is not irrational, but rather rational; for how is it not, when it advises, "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness"? But if they quibble about the names, let the philosophers call the fear of the law "caution."

As being a reasonable avoidance. These men Critolaus of Phaselis, not amiss, called "word-fighters." Already, then, the commandment has appeared elegant and most noble to those who accuse us, when understood by a change of name. Caution, then, is shown to be rational, being an avoidance of what harms, from which springs the repentance of former sins. "For the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and good understanding is to all who do it." He calls "doing" of wisdom that which is the fear of God paving the way to wisdom. And if the law is productive of fear, the beginning of wisdom is the knowledge of the law, and there is no wise man without law. Without sense, then, are those who decline the law, upon which it follows that they are reckoned godless. "And education is the beginning of wisdom. But the impious will despise wisdom and education," says the Scripture.

Let us see what fearful things the law announces. If they are the things between virtue and vice — such as poverty and disease and ill repute and low birth, and the like — these the laws of the city too are praised for setting forth; and to the men of the Peripatos, who introduce three kinds of goods and reckon their opposites to be evils, this opinion is harmonious. But to us the given law commands to flee the things that are truly evil — adultery, lasciviousness, pederasty, ignorance, injustice, disease of soul, death — not the death that dissolves soul from body, but that which dissolves soul from truth; for these vices and the activities from them are truly terrible and fearful. "Not unjustly are nets stretched out for the winged," say the divine oracles; "for they themselves, sharing in blood, treasure up evils for themselves." How, then, is the law any longer said not to be good, by certain heresies that cry out the Apostle's saying, "for through the law is knowledge of sin"? To whom we say: the law did not make, but showed, the sin; for, having commanded what is to be done, it convicted what is not to be done. And it belongs to the good both to teach the saving thing and to point out the poisonous, and to counsel the use of the one and command the avoiding of the other.

So the Apostle, whom they do not understand, said that knowledge of sin was made manifest through the law, not that it received its existence. And how is the law that educates not good, the schoolmaster given for Christ, that we may turn, being directed by fear in educative fashion toward the perfecting that is through Christ? "I do not wish the death of the sinner," he says, "so much as his repentance." And the commandment makes repentance, being preventive of the things not to be done, and promising the beneficences. By "death," I think, he means ignorance. And "he who is near the Lord is full of scourges" — that is, he who draws near to knowledge enjoys dangers, fears, griefs, afflictions, on account of the longing for the truth. "For an educated son turned out wise, and a son of understanding was saved from burning; and a son of understanding will receive commandments." And Barnabas the Apostle, having set first, "Woe to those who are prudent in themselves and knowing in their own eyes," added: "Let us become spiritual, a perfect temple to God. As far as is in us, let us practise the fear of God and strive to keep his commandments, that we may rejoice in his ordinances." Whence "the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom" is divinely said.

We are commanded to reverence and honour the Word, being persuaded that he is Saviour and Ruler, and through him the Father—not on chosen days, as some others do, but doing this continually through the whole of life and in every way. Indeed "the elect race," it is said, "Seven times in the day have I praised you," being justified according to the commandment. Whence the gnostic honours God neither in a fixed place, nor in a chosen shrine, nor on certain festivals and appointed days, but through his whole life, in every place—whether he happens to be alone by himself, or has with him some who have believed as he has: that is, he gives thanks for his knowledge and for his manner of life. And if the presence of one good man, through the shame and reverence it inspires, ever shapes the one who meets him toward the better, how shall not the man who is ever present, through knowledge and life and thanksgiving, with God unceasingly, with good reason be at every point better than himself in all things—in his deeds, his words, and his disposition? Such is he who is persuaded that God is present everywhere, and does not suppose him shut up in certain fixed places, so that, thinking himself sometimes apart from God, he might indulge in licence by night and by day. Keeping festival, then, through the whole of life, persuaded that God is present everywhere and on every side, we till the ground praising him, we sail singing hymns, and in the rest of our conduct we move skilfully. The gnostic comes nearer to being made the household of God, being grave and at the same time cheerful in all things—grave on account of his turning toward the Divine, cheerful on account of his reckoning up of the human goods which God has given us. The prophet sets forth the excellence of knowledge in this way:

"Goodness and discipline and knowledge teach me"—exalting the leading faculty of perfection by a gradual ascent. This man, then, is in truth the kingly man; this is the holy priest of God. Which thing even now is preserved among the most learned of the barbarians, who advance the priestly race to kingship. This man, then, in no way gives himself over to the rabble-rout that lords it in the theatres; the things said and done and seen there for the sake of dissolute pleasure he does not admit even in a dream—neither these pleasures of the spectacle nor the varied delights of the rest of the enjoyments: the costliness of incense that bewitches the sense of smell, the contrivings of dishes, the relishings of various wines that entice the taste, nor the many-flowered and fragrant garlands that effeminate the soul through the senses. But referring the august enjoyment of all things ever to God, of his food and his drink and his anointing he offers first-fruits to the Giver of all, acknowledging the favour both of the gift and of its use, through the Word given to him. He rarely comes to banquets and drinking-parties, except when the prospect of friendship and concord that the gathering holds out should urge him to go. For he is persuaded that God knows and hears all things—not only the voice, but the very thought; since hearing in us, though it works through bodily passages, receives its apprehension not through bodily power, but through a certain perception of the soul, and through the understanding that discriminates the voices which signify anything.

The Greek preliminary education, then, together with philosophy itself, appears to have come from God to men, not as the primary thing, but in the way the rains break down upon the good earth and upon the dunghill and upon the housetops. Grass and wheat spring up alike; and a fig tree grows even on the tombs, and any of the more shameless trees, and the things that grow on these come up as a type of the true, because they have enjoyed the same power of the rain, but have not had the same grace as the things that grow in the rich soil, being either withered or torn up. And here too the parable of the seed, which the Lord interpreted, is of use. For there is one husbandman of the soil that is in men, who from above sows from the foundation of the world the nourishing seeds, who has rained down the Lord, the Word, at each season; but the seasons and the receptive places have bred the differences. Besides, the husbandman sows not only wheat (though even of this there are several kinds), but also the other seeds — barley and beans and peas and vetch and the garden seeds and the flowering seeds. And of the same husbandry is the planting of trees: to work all that pertains to the nurseries and to the gardens and the orchards, and, in general, the nature and nourishment of trees of every kind. Likewise, not only herding sheep, but also herding cattle and breeding horses and dogs and keeping bees are all arts; and, in a word, the keeping of flocks and the rearing of animals differ from one another in the more and the less, but all are useful for life. And by philosophy I do not mean the Stoic, nor the Platonic, nor the Epicurean and Aristotelian, but whatever has been well said by each of these schools, teaching righteousness with reverent knowledge — this whole eclectic body I call philosophy. But whatever they have cut off from human reasonings and falsified, this I would never call divine.

God, then, is not of human form, for this end—that he may hear; nor does he need senses, as the Stoics held, especially hearing and sight, on the ground that he could not otherwise apprehend. Rather, both the responsiveness of the air and the keenest joint-perception of the angels, and the power of the conscience that touches the soul, by a certain unspeakable power and apart from hearing through the senses, knows all things together with the thought. And even if one should say that the voice does not reach to God, but rolls below about the air, yet the thoughts of the saints cut through not only the air, but the whole world. And the divine power, like light, reaches through to discern the whole soul. What then? Do not the purposes also reach to God, sending forth their own voice? And are they not borne onward by the conscience? And for what voice would he wait who knows beforehand, according to his purpose, the elect one even before his birth, and what will be as though it already were? Or does not the light of his power shine everywhere into the depth of the whole soul, "searching the storehouses," as Scripture says, "with the lamp" of his power? For God is wholly hearing and wholly eye—if one may use these names.

And let us consider this too: that if ever those who do not have knowledge live well — for they have fallen into well-doing — and some even hit upon the discourse concerning truth through understanding, yet Abraham was justified not by works but by faith. There is, then, no benefit to them after the end of life, even if they are now doers of good, unless they have faith. For this reason the Scriptures were translated into the speech of the Greeks, so that they might never be able to put forward ignorance as an excuse, being able to listen to our things too, if only they will. One man speaks of truth in one way; truth interprets herself in another. The guess at truth is one thing, truth is another; likeness is one thing, the being itself another; and the one is gained by learning and exercise, the other by power and faith. For the teaching of godliness is a gift, but faith is a grace. "For in doing the will of God we know the will." "Open, then," says the Scripture, "the gates of righteousness, that, entering through them, I may confess to the Lord." But the ways toward righteousness are many and varied — God saving in manifold ways, for he is good — and they lead to the sovereign way and gate. But if you seek the kingly and authentic entrance, you will hear: "This is the gate of the Lord; the just shall enter through it." Of the many gates that stand open, then, this gate in righteousness was the one in Christ, in which blessed are all who have entered and have set their journey straight in gnostic holiness. So Clement, in his Epistle to the Corinthians, says, word for word, setting out the distinctions of those approved in the Church: "Let one be faithful, let one be able to declare knowledge, let one be wise in the discernment of words, let one be vigorous in deeds."

In general, then, the conception of God that is unfitting, whether in hymns or in words, or even in writings or in doctrines—but which turns aside into low and unseemly notions and suppositions—preserves no godliness at all. Whence the praise of the many differs in no way from blasphemy, through ignorance of the truth. The prayers of men are of the same things as their appetites and desires and, in a word, their impulses. For this reason no one desires drink, but the drinking of the draught; nor an inheritance, but to inherit; and just so, not knowledge, but to know; nor even right citizenship, but to live as a citizen. The prayers, then, are of those things of which there are also requests, and the requests of those things of which there are also desires; and to pray and to reach out is done correspondingly toward having the goods and the benefits that accompany the possession. Always, then, the gnostic makes his prayer and request for the truly good things, those that concern the soul, and prays, working at the same time himself as well, to come into a settled disposition of goodness—so as no longer to have the good things laid up beside him, like certain lessons learned, but to be good.

Therefore it befits especially these men to pray—those who both know the Divine as they ought and have the virtue suited to him, who know what the truly good things are, and what one ought to ask, and when, and how, in each case. But it is the height of ignorance to ask things of those who are not gods as though they were gods, or to ask things that do not profit, asking evils for oneself under an appearance of goods. Whence, reasonably, since the good God is one, we pray—both we and the angels—that from him alone some of the good things may be given and others may abide. Yet not in like manner. For it is not the same thing to ask that a gift may abide, and to be eager to receive the beginning of it. And the turning away of evils is a kind of prayer. But this kind of prayer must never be used toward the harm of men—unless the gnostic, contriving the turning of the unjust toward righteousness, should so frame his request for those who have grown "callous." Prayer, then, is, to speak somewhat boldly, converse with God. And even if, whispering, not so much as opening our lips, we speak in silence, yet within we cry aloud; for God unceasingly hears all the inward converse.

For this reason too we lift up the head and raise the hands to heaven, and rise upon the feet at the closing utterance of the prayer, following the eagerness of the spirit toward the intelligible essence; and, striving to lift the body from the earth together with the word, we make "the soul winged" by longing for the better things, and force our way toward "the holy places," counting as nothing the bond of the flesh. For we know well that the gnostic makes voluntarily his going-out from the whole world—just as the Jews did from Egypt—showing plainly, more than by anything else, that he will be as near as possible to God. And if some assign also fixed hours to prayer—as the third, say, and the sixth and the ninth—yet the gnostic prays throughout his whole life, striving through prayer to be with God, and to leave behind, to speak briefly, all that is of no use to him once he has come to be there: as one who has already received here below the perfection of the conduct that springs from love. And the divisions of the hours into three, honoured with equal prayers, are known also to those who recognize the blessed Triad of the holy abodes.

Hence the Egyptians too did not commit their mysteries to the chance comer, nor carry out the knowledge of divine things to the profane, but only to those who were about to advance to the throne, and to those of the priests judged to be most approved, by reason of their nurture and education and birth. Like the Hebrew riddles, then, in their concealment are those of the Egyptians too. Some of the Egyptians show the sun upon a ship, others upon a crocodile. And they signify that the sun, making its course through the sweet and moist air, begets time, which is hinted at by the crocodile by reason of some other priestly story. Indeed, in Diospolis of Egypt, upon what is called the sacred portal, there is figured a child, a symbol of coming into being, and an old man, of decay, and a hawk, of God, and a fish, of hatred, and again, by another signification, a crocodile, of shamelessness.

Having come to this point, I was reminded of the doctrines introduced by certain heterodox men concerning the supposed needlessness of prayer—that is, by those of the school of Prodicus. Lest, then, they should be puffed up over this godless cleverness of theirs as though it were a strange new sect, let them learn that it was anticipated by the philosophers called Cyrenaics. Nevertheless this unholy knowledge of theirs, falsely so named, shall meet with refutation at the proper time, so that it may not now, slipping into these notes—being no small thing, this onslaught of theirs—break the continuity of the argument in hand, while we are showing that he alone is truly holy and devout who is in truth gnostic according to the rule of the Church, to whom alone the request is assigned according to the will of God, both when he asks and when he merely thinks it. For as God is able to do all that he wills, so the gnostic "receives all that he asks." For God knows in general both those who are worthy of good things and those who are not; whence he gives to each what befits them. Therefore he would often not give to the unworthy who ask, but would give to those who are plainly worthy. Yet the request is not idle, even if the good things are given apart from the asking. So then both thanksgiving and the request for the conversion of one's neighbours is the work of the gnostic. In this way the Lord too prayed, giving thanks for the things in which he completed his ministry, and praying that as many as possible might come to recognition, that among those being saved, through the salvation that comes of recognition, God might be glorified, and that the only Good and only Saviour might be recognized through the Son from age to age. And yet faith too, that one will receive, is a kind of prayer laid up gnostically within.

Then the man who has lied, and shown himself faithless, and gone over to the army of the devil—in what evil, do we think, is he? He lies, then, against the Lord—or rather, he has cheated himself of his own hope—who does not believe God. And he does not believe who does not do what He has commanded. And what? Does not the man who denies the Lord deny himself? For he takes away the master from his lordship, who deprives himself of his intimacy with Him. He, then, who denies the Saviour denies life, since the life was the light. He does not call these men "of little faith," but "faithless" and "hypocrites," who have the name inscribed but deny the being faithful; for both a slave and a friend are called faithful. So that if anyone loves himself, he loves the Lord and confesses salvation,

The whole symbol, then, when put together, appears to declare this: "O you who are born and pass away, God hates shamelessness." And the makers, fashioning ears and eyes out of costly material, consecrate them to the gods, dedicating them in the temples — hinting, surely, that God sees and hears all things. Besides this, the lion is to them a symbol of strength and might; just as the ox, surely, of earth itself and of husbandry and of food, and the horse of courage and boldness, and again the sphinx of might together with understanding, having the whole body of a lion, but the face of a man. In like manner to these, hinting at understanding and memory and power and skill, man is engraved by them upon the sacred things.

But if prayer becomes an occasion of converse with God, then no occasion of approach to God must be let slip. Indeed, when the holiness of the gnostic is interwoven with the blessed providence, through the voluntary confession it displays the perfect benefaction of God. For the holiness of the gnostic is, as it were, a kind of return upon providence, and a reciprocal goodwill on the part of the friend of God. For God is not good unwillingly, in the way that fire is hot; rather, the imparting of good things is voluntary with him, even if he anticipates the request. Nor again is the one who is saved saved unwillingly; for he is not without a soul, but, more than anything, will hasten toward salvation willingly and by deliberate choice. Therefore man received the commandments as having of himself an impulse toward whichever he might will of the things to be chosen and the things to be shunned. So then God does not do good by necessity, but does good by choice to those who turn of themselves. For the providence that comes to us from God is not a thing of servile ministry—as though proceeding from worse beings to better; but it is out of mercy toward our weakness that the nearer dispensations of providence are worked, just as is the case with the shepherds' care toward the sheep, and the king's toward his subjects, while we ourselves are obediently disposed toward our governors, those who orderly administer affairs according to the rank with which they were entrusted by God. They, then, are servants and ministers of the Divine who render the most free and most kingly service, that which is through devout judgement and knowledge.

that he may save his soul. And yet, even if you die for your neighbour out of love—and you suppose the Saviour to be our neighbour (for God, who saves, was called "the near one" to the one being saved)—you will die having chosen death for the sake of life, having suffered for your own sake rather than for his. And is it not for this that He is called "brother"—that the man who suffers out of love toward God suffers for his own salvation, while the man who dies for the sake of his own salvation endures it through love toward the Lord? For He too, being life, willed to suffer for those for whom He suffered, that by His suffering we might live. "Why do you call me, Lord, Lord," He says, "and do not do what I say?" For the people who love with the lips, but have the heart far from the Lord, are another people, persuaded by another, and have willingly sold themselves to him; but those who fulfil the commandments of the Saviour bear witness in every action, doing what He wishes, and consistently naming the Lord, and by deed bearing witness to the one they are persuaded is, those who have crucified the flesh with its desires and passions. "If we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit," He says. "He who sows to his own flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh; but he who sows to the Spirit shall reap eternal life from the Spirit."

And further, in what are called among them the processions of the gods, they carry round golden figures — two dogs, one hawk, and one ibis — and the four figures of the statues they call four letters. The dogs, then, are symbols of the two hemispheres, as it were going round and keeping watch; the hawk, of the sun, for it is fiery and destructive — thus they ascribe pestilential diseases to the sun; the ibis, of the moon, the dark parts likened to the black, the bright to the white, of its feathers. And there are some who hold that the tropics are signified by the dogs, which guard and keep the door of the sun's passage to the south and to the north; while the hawk shows forth the equator, which is high and scorched, just as the ibis the ecliptic. For the ibis seems above the other creatures to have furnished the Egyptians with the beginning of the conception of number and measure, as the oblique circle did of the circles.

Every place, then, is truly sacred in which we receive the conception of God, and every time. And when the man of good purpose, and grateful as well, asks through prayer, he in some way co-operates toward the receiving, gladly receiving what he longs for through the very things for which he prays. For when the Giver of good things receives our readiness, all the good things follow at once upon the very act of receiving. Indeed, through prayer the character is tested, how it is disposed toward what is fitting. And if voice and speech have been given us for the sake of understanding, how shall not God hear the soul itself and the mind—seeing that already soul perceives soul, and mind perceives mind? Whence God does not wait for the many-voiced tongues, as the interpreters among men do, but simply knows the thoughts of all; and what voice signifies to us, that our thought speaks to God, which thought, even before the creation, he knew would come into being. It is possible, then, not even to send forth one's prayer by voice, but only to strain all the spiritual part within toward the intelligible voice, in undistracted turning toward God. And since the dawn is an image of the day of birth, and from there the light increases, having first "shone forth out of darkness"—but also a day of the knowledge of the truth has risen, like the sun, upon those rolling about in ignorance—our prayers are toward the morning dawn. Whence too the most ancient of the shrines looked toward the west, that those standing face to face with the images might be taught to turn toward the east. "Let my prayer be set before you as incense," say the Psalms, "the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice."

To the wretched among men, the martyrdom through blood for the Lord seems to be the most violent death, not knowing that such a gate of death is the beginning of the truly existent life. And they are not willing to understand either the honours after death of those who have lived holily, or the punishments of those who have conducted themselves unjustly and lewdly—I do not say only from our Scriptures (for almost all the commandments make these things plain), but they are unwilling even to obey their own writers. For Theano the Pythagorean writes: "Life would indeed be a feast for the wicked who, having done evil, then die, if the soul were not immortal"; and Plato in the Phaedo: "For if death were a release from everything," and so on.

For the wicked among men, then, prayer is most hurtful, not only to others, but to themselves as well. If, indeed, they should ask and obtain even the things they call good fortune, the obtaining harms them, since they are ignorant of how to use them. For they pray to acquire what they do not have, and ask for the seeming goods, not the real ones. But the gnostic asks for the continuance of the things he has acquired, for fitness for the things he is to pass over to, and for the eternity of the things he will not receive; and he prays that the truly good things, those concerning the soul, may both be his and abide. In this way he does not even reach out for anything that is absent, being content with what is present. For he is not wanting in his own proper goods, being already sufficient to himself out of the divine grace and knowledge. Rather, having become self-sufficient and in need of nothing besides, knowing the almighty will, and at once possessing and praying, having drawn near to the all-powerful Power, and having striven to be spiritual, through love without bound he has been united to the Spirit. This is the high-minded man, the one who possesses, in his knowledge, the most precious of all and the best of all things—keen in the application to contemplation, and possessing in his soul an abiding power over the things contemplated, that is, the penetrating sharpness of knowledge. And this power he strives as far as possible to acquire, having become master "of the things that war against the mind," and unceasingly attending upon contemplation, having trained himself by discipline both in the holding back from pleasures and in the right doing of things to be done. Besides these, having made use of much experience in learning and in life, he has frankness of speech—not that power of an unbarred tongue, simply so called, but a power that uses plain speech, hiding none of the things that may be said at the fitting season, where it is most needful, neither for favour nor for fear.

It is not, then, according to the Telephus of Aeschylus, that one should think a single path leads to Hades; but many are the ways that lead off, the sins that lead far astray. These faithless men, it seems, Aristophanes mocks when he says:
Come, men of dim life, like the race of leaves, of little strength, things moulded of wax, shadowy tribes, feeble, wingless, creatures of a day.

And Epicharmus: "This is the nature of men—blown-up wineskins." But to us the Saviour has said: "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak"; for "the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God," the apostle explains, "for it does not submit to the law of God, nor indeed can it; and those who are in the flesh cannot please God." And, further explaining, he adds—lest anyone, like Marcion, should ungratefully take creation to be evil: "But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness." And again: "For if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; for I reckon that the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is going to be revealed in us, if indeed we suffer together, that we may also be glorified together, as joint heirs of Christ."

Having, then, grasped in a manner worthy of the subject the things concerning God, taught by the very truth in the mystic choir, he uses the word that exhorts toward the greatness of virtue—a word that displays virtue and what springs from it according to its worth—being made gnostically akin, with God-inspired uplifting of prayer, as far as may be, to things intelligible and spiritual. Whence he is ever gentle and mild, easy of access, easy to meet, patient of evil, fair-minded, of a good conscience, austere. This austerity of ours is directed not only toward incorruptibility, but toward freedom from temptation; for in no way does he show his soul yielding or capturable by pleasure and pain. He is a judge, if reason should call him to it, having become unbending, granting nothing whatever to the passions, walking unswervingly in the path where the just by nature proceeds—being well persuaded that all things are most nobly administered, and that the advance ever goes on toward the better for souls that have chosen virtue, until they come to the Good itself, having become, as it were, near to the great High Priest "at the doors" of the Father. This is, for us, the faithful gnostic, persuaded that the affairs of the world are administered in the best way. Indeed, he is well pleased with all that befalls.

"And we know that to those who love God all things work together for good, to those who are called according to His purpose. For those whom He foreknew He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom He predestined, these He also called; and those whom He called, these He also justified; and those whom He justified, these He also glorified." You see martyrdom taught through love. And if you would bear witness in return for goods, you will hear again: "For by hope we were saved; but hope that is seen is not hope; for what a man sees, why does he also hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through endurance." But "even if we suffer for righteousness' sake, blessed are we," says Peter. "And do not fear their fear, nor be troubled; but sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts, and be always ready for a defence to everyone who asks of you a reason for the hope that is in you, but with meekness and fear, having a good conscience, that in the thing in which you are spoken against, those who revile your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better, doing good, if the will of God should so will, to suffer than doing evil."

With good reason, then, he seeks none of the things in life that are convenient for necessary use, persuaded that God, who knows all things, furnishes good things even to those who do not ask, whatever may be profitable. For just as, I think, to the artisan things are rendered after the manner of the artisan, and to the heathen after the heathen manner, so to the gnostic each thing is rendered after the gnostic manner. And the one converting from among the heathen will ask for faith; the one ascending into knowledge, for "the perfection of love." But the gnostic, already at the summit, prays that contemplation may increase and abide, just as the common man prays for continuous health. Yes, and he will ask never to fall away from virtue, co-operating especially that he may remain unfallen. For he knows that some even of the angels, having slipped through sloth, fell again to the ground, not yet having wrung themselves wholly out of their fitness for double-mindedness into that one settled disposition. But for the one who has been trained from here below into the height of knowledge and the lofty pre-eminence of the complete man, all things in time and place go before him on the road—for the one who has chosen and practises to live unwaveringly, through the everywhere-monotonous steadfastness of his judgement. But for those in whom there is still left over some heavy corner inclining downward, the part raised up by faith is dragged down. For the man who has, by gnostic discipline, made virtue a thing that cannot be cast away, the settled disposition becomes a second nature; and just as weight belongs to the stone, so to him knowledge becomes a thing that cannot be cast off—not unwillingly, but willingly, established by a rational and gnostic and provident power.

And if anyone, mocking, should say, "And how is it possible for the weak flesh to set itself against the powers and the spirits of the authorities?"—let him recognize this, that, taking courage in the Almighty and the Lord, we set our citizenship against the rulers of darkness and against death. "While you are still speaking," it says, "He will say, 'Behold, I am here.'" See the unconquered helper, the one who shields us. "Do not be surprised, then," says Peter, "at the fiery trial among you that comes to test you, as though something strange were happening to you; but rejoice, in so far as you share in the sufferings of Christ, that you may rejoice exulting in the revelation of His glory also. If you are reproached in the name of Christ, blessed are you, for the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you"; as it is written: "For your sake we are put to death all the day long; we are reckoned as sheep for the slaughter. But in all these things we more than conquer through Him who loved us."

And since that which is not cast away through caution becomes, through good reasoning, a thing that cannot be cast away, he will hold fast to caution toward not sinning, and to good reasoning toward the irremovability of virtue. And knowledge seems to furnish good reasoning, teaching one to discern the things that can help toward the continuance of virtue. Greatest of all, then, is the knowledge of God. Therefore by it the irremovability of virtue is preserved. And he who has known God is holy and devout. The gnostic alone, then, has been shown by us to be devout. This man rejoices over the present goods, and exults over those promised, as already present. For they have not escaped him as though still absent, since through knowledge he has anticipated of what kind they are. Persuaded, then, by knowledge that each of the things to come is as it is, he possesses it. For that which is deficient and lacking is measured against what is fitting. If, then, he has acquired wisdom, and wisdom is divine, the one who partakes of that which needs nothing would himself be in need of nothing. For the imparting of wisdom does not come about by the activity and the partaker moving and holding back one another, nor by anything being taken away, nor by the giver becoming needy; rather, the activity is shown to be undiminished through the very imparting. So, then, the gnostic has all good things in respect of power, though not yet in respect of number—for otherwise he would be unchanging according to the God-inspired advances and dispensations that are due. With this man God too co-operates, having honoured him with a nearer oversight.
The things you wish to learn from my mind, neither by burning, nor by letting down terrible saws from the top of my head to my feet's ends, could you learn, nor if you should put all bonds upon me,
says a woman, playing the man fearlessly in tragedy. And Antigone too, despising the proclamation of Creon, boldly says:
For it was not Zeus who proclaimed these things to me;

but God proclaims to us, and we must obey Him. "For with the heart it is believed unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." So the Scripture says: "Everyone who believes in Him shall not be put to shame." With good reason, then, Simonides writes:

There is a saying that Virtue dwells upon rocks hard to climb, and that the swift, holy chorus of nymphs attends her; nor is she to be seen by the eyes of all mortals, save by the one in whom heart-biting sweat comes from within, and who reaches the summit by manliness.

For have not all things come to be for the sake of good men, and for their use and benefit—nay rather, for their salvation? He would not, then, take away from these the things that are theirs for the sake of virtue—they on whose account the things that are have come to be. For it is plain that he would honour their good nature and their holy purpose, since he breathes strength even into those who have undertaken to live well, for the rest of their salvation—exhorting some only, but to those who have become worthy of themselves giving his aid as well. For everything is an added gift to the gnostic, if indeed his end is to know and to do each thing knowingly. And as the physician furnishes health to those who co-operate toward health, so too God furnishes eternal salvation to those who co-operate toward knowledge and right action; and, together with our doing—since the things that the commandments enjoin are in our power—the promise too is fulfilled. And this, it seems to me, is also nobly said among the Greeks: a certain athlete, no mean man, in the days of old, having for a long time trained his poor body well toward manliness, went up to Olympia, and, looking toward the statue of Pisaean Zeus, said: "If, O Zeus, all things have been duly prepared by me for the contest, come, give me the victory in justice." For so it is with the gnostic too: when he has irreproachably and with a good conscience fulfilled all that lies in his own power, toward learning and toward training and toward well-doing and toward being well-pleasing to God, then the whole is brought together for his most perfect salvation. These things, then, are required of us: of the things in our power and of the things that pertain to us, both present and absent—choice and longing and acquisition and use and continuance.
And Pindar:
The cares of the young, whirled about with toils, find glory; and in time their works shine, kindled above the heavens.
Aeschylus too, laying hold of this thought, says:
To the one who toils there is due from the gods the offspring of his toil, glory.
For "greater deaths obtain greater portions," according to Heraclitus.
Who is a slave who has no thought of dying?

For God has not given us a spirit of slavery again unto fear, but of power and of love and of self-discipline. "Do not, then, be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me His prisoner," he writes to Timothy. Such a man would be the one who, according to the apostle, cleaves to the good, abhorring the evil, having unfeigned love; for he who loves the other has fulfilled the law. And if the God of hope is the one to whom we bear witness, as indeed He is, we confess our hope, hastening toward the hope; but they are "full of goodness," he says, "filled with all knowledge."

Therefore he who holds converse with God must have his soul undefiled and sincerely unstained—most of all, having wrought himself wholly good; or, if not, at least making progress toward knowledge and reaching out for it, but utterly drawn away from the works of vice. And it is fitting, too, that all prayers be made fairly, and in company with the fair; for it is perilous to be set down as a sharer in the sins of others. Concerning these things, then, the gnostic will pray together with those who have believed in the more common way, and concerning whom it befits him also to act together with them. And his whole life is a holy festival. His sacrifices, accordingly, are prayers and praises, and the readings from the Scriptures before the meal, and psalms and hymns during the meal and before sleep, and again prayers by night. Through these he unites himself to "the divine choir," set, out of the continual remembrance, into ever-mindful contemplation. What then? Does he not know also that other sacrifice—the giving, according to those in need, both of doctrines and of money? Yes indeed. But the prayer through the mouth he does not make with many words, having learned from the Lord what one ought to ask. In every place, then—yet not openly or visibly before the many—he will pray; while walking, in converse, in quietness, in reading, and in his works that are according to reason, he prays in every way.
