And even if in the very "storehouse" of the soul he is but thinking, and "with unspeakable groanings calls upon the Father," he who is near is present even while the man still speaks. And since there are three ends of every action, he works all things for the noble and the profitable; but the doing of a thing for the sake of pleasure he leaves to those who pursue the common life.

The philosophers of the Indians say to Alexander the Macedonian: "You will transfer bodies from place to place, but our souls you will not compel to do what we do not wish. Fire is for men the greatest instrument of torture; this we despise." Hence Heraclitus chose for himself one thing in place of all—glory—but the many, he says, glut themselves like cattle.
For the sake of the body are the many toils, for its sake have we found a sheltering house, and to dig out white silver, and to sow the earth, and all the other things that we know by names.

To the many, then, this vain toil is to be chosen; but to us the apostle says: "This we know, that our old man was crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be brought to nought, so that we should no longer be slaves to sin." Does not the apostle also plainly add those words, showing the disgrace of the faith among the many? "For I think God has set forth us apostles last, as men appointed to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world and to angels and to men; even to this present hour we hunger and thirst and are naked and are buffeted and have no fixed abode; persecuted, we endure; defamed, we entreat; we have become as the refuse of the world."

Such too are the things in Plato's Republic: even if the just man be racked, even if his two eyes be gouged out, he will be happy. The gnostic, then, will never have his end lying in fortune, but happiness and being blessed and being a royal friend of God would lie in himself. And even if a man should wrap him in dishonour and exile and confiscation, and over all in death, he will never be torn away from his freedom and his most sovereign love toward God, which "bears all things and endures all things." For love is persuaded that divine providence administers all things well.

"I beseech you, then, become imitators of me," he says. Now the first step of salvation is the teaching with fear, by which we abstain from injustice; the second is hope, by which we reach out toward the best things; and love perfects, as is fitting, educating now in a gnostic way. For the Greeks, having somehow given over the things that befall to an irrational necessity, confess that they obey unwillingly. Euripides, at any rate, says:
What I counsel, take this from me, woman. There is no mortal born who does not toil; he buries his children and sows new ones, and himself dies. And mortals are grieved at these things.
Then he adds:

There is set before those hastening toward perfection the rational knowledge, of which the foundation is the holy triad: faith, hope, love; but the greatest of these is love. Indeed, "all things are permitted, but not all things are profitable; all things are permitted, but not all things build up," says the apostle. And "let no one seek his own only, but also the other's," so as to be able both to do and to teach at once, building and building further. For that "the earth is the Lord's and its fullness" has been agreed; but the conscience of the weak is offended. By "conscience" I mean not one's own, but the other's. "For why is my freedom judged by another's conscience? If I share with thanks, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks? Whether, then, you eat or drink or do anything, do all to the glory of God." For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war according to the flesh; "for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but mighty before God for the casting down of strongholds, casting down reasonings and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of the Lord."

. . . as we noted long ago, we do not mean the discipline of each several school, but, what philosophy truly is — rightly, a skilled wisdom that furnishes the experience of the things of life; and the wisdom, a firm knowledge of things divine and human, being a certain sure and unshakeable apprehension, embracing the things that are and that have been and that shall be, which the Lord taught us both through his coming and through the prophets. And it is unshakeable by reason, being delivered to that very will by which also it is wholly true, as known through the Son. And the one is everlasting, the other useful in time; the one is one and the same, the others many and various; the one is without any passible movement, the other with a passible craving; the one is perfect, the other defective.
The gnostic, armed with these weapons, says: "O Lord, grant occasion and receive the display; let this terror come; I despise dangers for love of you,"
because virtue alone among the things of men takes its rewards not from outside, but itself has itself as the prize of its toils.

"Put on, then, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, long-suffering; and over all these put on love, which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body; and be thankful"—you who are still in the body, like the just men of old, reaping freedom from passion and tranquillity of soul;

This wisdom, then, philosophy craves — . . . of the soul, and of the rightness of reason, and of the purity of life, being disposed lovingly and affectionately toward wisdom, and doing all things for the sake of attaining it. And philosophers are called among us those who love the wisdom of the Maker and Teacher of all, that is, the knowledge of the Son of God; but among the Greeks, those who lay hold of the discourses about virtue. Philosophy would be the irreproachable doctrines of each of the schools (I mean those of philosophy), together with a manner of life in agreement, gathered into one chosen system. And these very things, stolen from the barbarian, God-given grace, have been adorned with Greek discourse; for of some they are thieves, and of some they heard amiss; and in the rest, some things they said as men moved, but did not work out perfectly, and some by human conjecture and reasoning, in which they also fall short. And they think they apply themselves to the truth perfectly; but as we apprehend them, only partially.

For of this world they know nothing more. And indeed, as geometry, dealing with measures and magnitudes and figures by the drawing of them on flat surfaces, and painting, which seems to take up the whole field of optics in scene-painting, deceives the sight in this way, using the points of the meeting of the optical lines according to its art (whence appearances and recessions and projections are preserved, and some things seem to stand out, others to sink in, others to be otherwise represented on the level and smooth surface) — so too do the philosophers, after the manner of painting, imitate the truth. And self-love is the cause of all sins for each man on every occasion. Wherefore one must not, choosing glory among men, be self-loving, but, loving God, become truly holy with prudence.

Now human continence—I mean the kind taught by the philosophers of the Greeks—professes to fight against desire and not to be subservient to it in action; but ours professes not to desire, so that a man may not endure while desiring, but may be continent even with respect to desiring. And it is not possible to obtain this continence otherwise than by the grace of God. For this reason He said, "Ask, and it shall be given you." This grace Moses too received, though clothed in a needy body, so that for forty days he neither hungered nor thirsted. As it is better to be healthy than for the sick man to discourse about health, so to be light is better than to talk about light, and the continence that is according to truth is better than that taught by the philosophers. For where there is light, there is no darkness; but where desire sits enthroned, even if it is quiet in its outward activity through the body, it consorts in memory with what is not present.

If, then, one chance to use the particular things as if they were universal, and honour the slave as lord and ruler, he falls away from the truth, not understanding what was said by David in confession: "Earth and ashes I ate as bread." And self-love and conceit are to him earth and error. But if this be so, knowledge and science come of learning. And learning being, one must seek the teacher. Cleanthes inscribes Zeno as his teacher, and Theophrastus Aristotle, and Metrodorus Epicurus, and Plato Socrates; but even if I come to Pythagoras and Pherecydes and Thales and the first wise men, I stand still seeking their teacher; and if you say Egyptians or Indians or Babylonians or the Magi themselves, I shall not cease asking for their teacher. And I lead you up to the first generation of men, and from there I begin to seek, who is the teacher? Of men, none; for they had not yet learned; nor any of the angels; for neither, as the angels make known in so far as they are angels, do men hear; nor, as we have ears, so have they a tongue. Nor could one assign to angels organs of voice — I mean lips and the parts near them, and throat and windpipe and inward parts and breath and stricken air. Far indeed is God from shouting aloud, separated by an unapproachable holiness even from the archangels themselves. And we have received that the angels too learned the truth, and the rulers over them; for they are begotten.

Let our discussion proceed generally, concerning marriage and food and the rest: to do nothing from desire, but to will only those things that are necessary. For we are not children of desire, but of will. And the man who has married for the sake of begetting children must practise continence, so as not even to desire his own wife, whom he ought to love, begetting children with a dignified and prudent will. For we have not learned to make provision for the flesh unto its desires, but, walking becomingly as in the day—in Christ, and in the luminous conduct of the Lord—not in revelling and drunkenness, not in chambering and lewdness, not in strife and jealousy.

It remains, then, that, ascending above, we crave the teacher of these. And since one is the unbegotten, God the Almighty, and one too is that which was begotten before, through whom all things came to be and without whom not one thing came to be (for "one is God in truth, who made the beginning of all things" — showing the first-born Son, Peter writes, having exactly understood the word, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth"); and since this one is called Wisdom by all the prophets, this is the teacher of all begotten things, the counsellor of God who foreknew all things. And he, from above, from the first foundation of the world, in many ways and in many parts both has instructed and brings to perfection. Whence with reason it was said, "Call no man teacher upon the earth." You see whence the true philosophy has its handles. And though the law be an image and shadow of the truth — yes, the law is a shadow of the truth — yet the self-love of the Greeks proclaims certain men teachers.

But indeed we ought to see continence not as concerning one single kind of thing, namely sexual matters, but also concerning the other things which our soul, given to luxury, desires, not being content with what is necessary, but fussing over extravagance. Continence is to despise money, to look down on luxury, possessions, and spectacles, to master the mouth, to rule over evil thoughts. Indeed, even certain angels, becoming incontinent and being seized by desire, fell down here from heaven. And Valentinus, in his epistle to Agathopus, says: "Enduring all things, Jesus was continent; He worked at being a god; He ate and drank in a manner of His own, not giving up His food; so great was the power of His continence that the food was not even corrupted within Him, since He had no corruption in Himself." We, then, for love toward the Lord and for the sake of the good itself, embrace continence, sanctifying the temple of the spirit; for it is good, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, to make oneself a eunuch of all desire, and to cleanse the conscience from dead works, in order to serve the living God.

As, then, every fatherhood runs up to God the Maker, so too the teaching of noble things, which justifies and leads by the hand to this and lays hold of it, runs up to the Lord. And if from some . . . some have, in whatever way, taken seeds of the truth and not nourished them, but, handing them over to a barren and rainless land, choked them with wild weeds — as the Pharisees turned aside from the law, bringing in human teachings — of these not the teacher is the cause, but those who chose to hear amiss. And those of them who are persuaded both by the Lord's coming and by the plainness of the Scriptures come into recognition of the law; as those too from philosophy, through the Lord's teaching, are established in the recognition of the true philosophy. "For the oracles of the Lord are pure oracles, silver tried by fire, purified for the earth sevenfold."

But those who, out of hatred toward the flesh, ungratefully long to be quit of the union according to marriage and of the partaking of suitable foods—they are both ignorant and godless, practising continence without reason, like most of the other nations. The Brahmans, at any rate, eat no living thing and drink no wine; but some of them take food daily, as we do, while some take it every three days, as Alexander Polyhistor says in his Indica. They despise death and count life as nothing; for they believe there is rebirth; and they worship Heracles and Pan. But the Indians called Semnoi live naked all their lives. These practise truth and foretell the future and worship a certain pyramid, beneath which they believe the bones of some god are laid. Neither the gymnosophists nor those called Semnoi have intercourse with women, for they think this contrary to nature and unlawful, and for this reason they keep themselves pure. The Semnai women too remain virgins. And they are thought to observe the heavenly bodies and, by the signs from them, to prophesy certain things to come.

Either, as silver often purified comes into a tested state, the just man becomes a coin of the Lord and receives the royal stamp; or, since Solomon too says, "The tongue of the just is silver tried by fire," he shows that the tested and wise teaching is praiseworthy and to be accepted, when it is richly purified "for the earth" — that is, when the gnostic soul is in many ways sanctified by the abstention from earthly fiery passions. And the body too, in which it dwells, is sanctified, made its own unto the sincerity of a holy temple. But the first purification of the soul in the body is this — the abstention from evils, which some hold to be perfection, and is simply the perfection of the common believer, both Jew and Greek; but of the gnostic, after the perfection reckoned by others, his righteousness goes forward into the working of good deeds. And to him in whom the intensity of righteousness has increased toward beneficence, to him perfection abides in an unchangeable habit of doing good, after the likeness of God. For some are the seed of Abraham, still slaves of God — these are the called; but sons of Jacob are his elect, those who have tripped up the working of evil.

If, then, we call Christ himself Wisdom, and his working through the prophets, by which it is possible to learn the gnostic tradition — as he himself, at his coming, taught the holy apostles — knowledge would be wisdom, being science and apprehension of the things that are and that shall be and that have been, sure and unfailing, as delivered and revealed by the Son of God. And indeed, if the end of the wise man is contemplation, the one still philosophizing craves the divine science, but does not yet attain it, unless he take up by learning the prophetic voice made plain to him, through which he receives the things that are and that shall be and that have been before, how they are and were and shall be. And this knowledge, delivered without writing by succession to a few from the apostles, has come down. Hence, then, one must train knowledge, or wisdom, into a habit of contemplation everlasting and unchangeable.

There are three things concerning speech: the names, which are symbols of the notions primarily, and consequently of the underlying things; second, the notions, which are likenesses and impressions of the underlying things (whence the notions are the same for all, because the same impression is produced in all from the underlying things, but no longer the names, on account of the differing tongues); and third, the underlying things, from which the notions are impressed upon us. The names, then, are reduced by grammar to the twenty-four universal elements; for the elements must be determinate, since of particulars, being infinite, there is no knowledge, and it is the property of knowledge to rest upon universal and determinate considerations: whence the particulars are reduced to the universals. And the work of the philosophers is occupied with the notions and the underlying things. And since the particulars of these are infinite, certain elements of these too have been found, under which everything sought is brought. And if it should appear to have crept under some one of the elements, or several, we shall declare that it exists; but if it should escape all, that it nowhere is. Of the things said, some are said with combination, as "man runs"; others are said without combination, as "man" and as "runs," and all that do not complete a discourse, nor have the true or the false. And of the things said without combination, some signify substance, others quality, others quantity, others relation, others where, others when, others to lie, others to have, others to do, others to be affected—which we also call the elements of the things that are in matter and that are after the beginnings. For these are contemplated by reason, but the immaterial things are grasped by mind alone, in the first application.

Of the things ranked under the ten categories, some are said in themselves, as the nine categories; others are relatives. And again, of the things under these ten categories, some are synonyms, as ox and man, in respect of being animal; for synonyms are those of which both the name is common—the "animal"—and the discourse is the same, that is, the definition, namely, an ensouled substance. Heteronyms are all those that, concerning the same underlying thing, are in different names, as ascent and descent; for the road is the same, whether upward or downward. But the other kind of heteronyms, as horse and black, having both name and discourse different from one another, and not sharing in the underlying thing—these must be called "others," not heteronyms. Polyonyms are those that have the same discourse but a different name, as sword, blade, brand. Paronyms are those named with reference to something else, as the brave man from bravery. And homonyms are those using the same name, but not having the same discourse, as "man" the animal and "man" the painted figure. And of homonyms, some are homonymous by chance, as Ajax the Locrian and Ajax the Salaminian; others by intention, and of these some by likeness, as "man" the animal and the painted; some by analogy, as "the feet of Ida" and our own feet, because of being lower; some by activity, as the foot of a ship, by which the ship sails, and our own foot, by which we are moved. Things are also called homonymous from the same thing and toward the same thing, as the book and the lancet are called "medical" from the physician who uses them and with reference to the same discourse, the medical.

Here those about Basilides, expounding this saying, say that the Archon himself, hearing the utterance of the ministering Spirit, was struck with astonishment both at the hearing and at the sight, having beyond hope received good tidings; and that his astonishment was called fear, becoming the beginning of a wisdom that distinguishes by classes, and discerns, and perfects, and restores. For not only the world, but also the election, the One over all, having distinguished, sends forth. And Valentinus too, in a certain letter, seems to have had such things in mind, writing in these very words: "And as though there came to be fear upon that creature among the angels, when it spoke greater things than its formation, on account of the one who had invisibly given in it a seed of the essence from above and who spoke with frankness; so too in the generations of worldly men the works of men became fears to those who made them — such as statues and images and all that hands accomplish in the name of God. For Adam, formed in the name of Man, gave fear of the pre-existing Man, as though he himself stood in him; and they were astounded, and quickly made the work vanish."

But there being one principle, as will be shown later, these men will appear to be inventing twitterings and warblings. And since it seemed good to God that men should be educated beforehand, through the Lord, from the law and the prophets, "the fear of the Lord is said to be the beginning of wisdom" — given by the Lord through Moses to the disobedient and hard-hearted; for those whom reason does not take, fear tames. Which the educating Word too, foreseeing from above, fitted as an instrument, in each of the two ways, cleansing fittingly toward godliness. Astonishment, then, is a fear from an unaccustomed impression, or at an unexpected impression — as also of a message; and fear is as at something that has come to be or is, or an excessive marvelling. They do not, then, perceive that they make passible, through astonishment, the greatest God, the one hymned even by them, and one who, before the astonishment, came to be in ignorance. And if ignorance preceded the astonishment, and the astonishment and the fear became the beginning of the wisdom of God, then ignorance is in danger of preceding causally the wisdom of God and the whole world-making, and indeed the restoration of the election itself.

Is the ignorance, then, of good things or of base? But if of good things, why does it cease at astonishment? And the minister is superfluous to them, and the proclamation and the baptism. But if of base things, how is the evil the cause of the noblest things? For unless ignorance had pre-existed, the minister would not have come down, nor would astonishment have taken the Archon, as they themselves say, nor would he have received a beginning of wisdom from the fear, for the distinguishing of the election and of the worldly things. And if the fear of the pre-existing Man made the angels plotters against their own creature — as though the seed of the essence from above were invisibly seated in the work — either by an empty supposition they were jealous, which is implausible, that angels should become slayers of a creation entrusted to them, like some child, being condemned of all ignorance; or, held in foreknowledge, they were moved, but then they would not have plotted, through what they attempted, against him whom they foreknew, nor would they have been astounded at their own work, having from foreknowledge perceived the seed from above; or, lastly, trusting in knowledge, they dared — which is itself impossible, that those who had learned the superior thing in the Man of the Fullness should plot against it, and further against that according to the image, in which they had received both the archetype and the incorruptible together with the rest of the knowledge.

The sophistic art, which the Greeks have zealously pursued, is a power of producing impressions, by means of words breeding false opinions as true. For it furnishes rhetoric for persuasion and eristic for contention; and these arts, if they are not joined with philosophy, would be more harmful than anything. Plato outright called sophistic a "base art," and Aristotle, following him, declares it a kind of thievery, inasmuch as it plausibly filches the whole work of wisdom and professes a wisdom it has not practised. To put it briefly: just as of rhetoric the beginning is the plausible, the work is the argument, and the end is persuasion; and of eristic the beginning is opinion, the work is the contest, and the end is victory; in the same way, of sophistic the beginning is the apparent, the work is twofold — the discursive part from rhetoric and the questioning part from dialectic — and its end is astonishment. And the dialectic harped on in the schools is shown to be the philosopher's exercise about the probable, for the sake of the power of arguing against; but nowhere in these things is the truth.

To these very men, then, and to certain others, but especially to those from Marcion, the Scripture cries out, though they do not hear: "But he who hears me shall rest in peace, trusting, and shall be at ease without fear from every evil." What, then, do they wish the law to be? Evil, indeed, they will not say, but just, distinguishing the good from the just. But the Lord, commanding to fear the evil, does not put away the evil by evil, but dissolves the contrary by the contrary. And evil is contrary to good, as just to unjust. If, then, he has called the abstinence from evils "fearlessness," which the fear of the Lord works, the fear is a good; and the fear from the law is not only just but also good, doing away with vice. And, by fear introducing fearlessness, not by passion impassivity, but by education it produces moderation of passion. When, then, we hear, "Honour the Lord, and you shall be strong; but besides him fear no other," we take it that to fear sinning, and to follow the commandments given by God, is the honour of God.

With reason, then, the noble Apostle, disparaging these superfluous arts of phrases, says: "If anyone does not come over to sound words, but is puffed up with some teaching while knowing nothing, but is sick about inquiries and battles of words, out of which come strife, envy, blasphemy, evil suspicions, the constant frictions of men corrupted in mind and robbed of the truth." You see how he is stirred against them, naming their logical art a "sickness," the art on which they pride themselves to whom this chattering base craft is dear, whether they be Greek or barbarian sophists. Most nobly, then, the tragic poet Euripides says in the Phoenician Women: "The unjust word, being sick in itself, has need of clever remedies." For the saving Word is called "sound," being itself truth; and the sound thing abides always immortal, while the separation from the sound and the divine is godlessness and a death-bringing passion. These are "ravening wolves hidden in sheep's clothing," enslavers of men and smooth-tongued seducers of souls, stealing secretly, but, when refuted, robbers, struggling to take captive, both by trickery and by force, us the unsophisticated — those, so to speak, less powerful in argument.

And dread is a fear of the divine. But even if fear is a passion, as some wish, because fear is a passion, not all fear is a passion. Superstition, at any rate, is a passion, being a fear of demons, both passion-ridden and passionate; but, on the contrary, the fear of the impassible God is impassible; for one fears not God, but the falling away from God; and he who dreads this — the falling into evils — fears and dreads the evils; and he who dreads the fall wishes himself to be incorruptible and impassible. "The wise man, fearing, turned away from evil; but the fool, trusting, mingles with it," says the Scripture; and again, "In the fear of the Lord is hope of strength," it says.

"Often a man caught in want of eloquence, though he has spoken what is just, fares worse than the eloquent. And now, with fluent mouths, they steal away the truest things, so that what ought to seem does not seem so" — so the tragedy says. Such are these eristics, whether they pursue heresies or train themselves in dialectic arts — these who "pull down the rigging and weave nothing," as the Scripture says, having pursued a vain labour, which the Apostle called "the dice-play of men" and "craftiness, fit for the method of error." "For there are many," he says, "insubordinate, vain talkers, deceivers of the mind." So it was not said to all, "You are the salt of the earth." For there are some, even of those who have heard the word, like the fish of the sea, which, though nourished from birth in brine, still need salt for their seasoning. I, for one, very much approve the tragedy that says: "O child, words well spoken may be false, and by the beauties of their phrases may conquer the truth; but this is not the most exact thing — rather, nature and the right; and he who conquers by fine speech is clever, but I reckon the facts ever stronger than the words." Never, then, must one be eager to please the many. For what pleases them, we do not practise; and what we know is far from their disposition. "Let us not become vainglorious," says the Apostle, "provoking one another, envying one another."

In this way the truth-loving Plato, as if inspired, says: "Such am I, as to obey nothing other than the reason which, on consideration, appears to me the best." He blames, at any rate, those who, without mind and knowledge, trust to opinions, as though, having left the right and sound reason in a way they should not, they trust the one who shares in falsehood. For to be deceived of the truth is an evil, but to speak truth and to hold opinions of the things that are is a good. Now of good things men are deprived against their will; yet they are deprived, all the same — either robbed, or bewitched, or forced, or persuaded. The man who has trusted willingly is thereby brought to waste; but he is robbed who is persuaded away and he who forgets, since of the one the time, of the other the argument, takes it away unnoticed; and often pain and grief, and again contentiousness and anger, force a man to change his opinion; and above all they are bewitched who have either been charmed by pleasure or terrified by fear. But all these changes are involuntary, and none of them would knowledge ever cast out.

But indeed not only the most reasoning of the Egyptians, but also, besides, those of the other barbarians who reached after philosophy, were zealous for the symbolic kind. They say, for instance, that Idanthura, the king of the Scythians, as Pherecydes of Syros records, when Darius had crossed the Ister and was threatening war, sent him, instead of a letter, a symbol — a mouse, a frog, a bird, an arrow, a plough. And when there was, as was likely, perplexity over these things, Orontopagas the captain of a thousand said they would surrender the rule, conjecturing from the mouse the dwellings, from the frog the waters, from the bird the air, from the arrow the arms, and from the plough the land. But Xiphodres interpreted it the opposite way; for he said: "Unless we fly up like birds, or burrow into the earth like mice, or dive under water like frogs, we shall not escape their arrows; for we are not masters of the country." And they say that Anacharsis the Scythian, while asleep, used to hold his private parts with his left hand and his mouth with his right, hinting that one ought to master both, but that it is a greater thing to master the tongue than pleasure.

And why should I linger over the barbarians, when I may set forth the Greeks themselves as having very much used concealment? Androcydes the Pythagorean, then, says that what are called the Ephesian letters — much-talked-of among many — have the rank of symbols, and that Askion signifies darkness, since this has no shadow; Kataskion light, since it lights up the shadow; Lix is earth, by an ancient appellation, and Tetrax the year, by reason of the seasons; and Damnameneus the sun, the subduer; and Aisia the true voice. The symbol, then, signifies that divine things are set in order — as darkness to light, and the sun to the year, and the earth to the begetting of every kind of nature. And Dionysius the Thracian, the grammarian, in his work On Indication, speaks thus, word for word, concerning the symbol of the wheels: "Some signified their acts not by speech alone, but also by symbols — by speech as in the Delphic precepts, 'Nothing too much' and 'Know yourself' and the like; by symbols as the wheel that is turned in the precincts of the gods, drawn from the Egyptians, and the giving of branches to those who worship." For Orpheus the Thracian says: "Of branches, as many works as men upon earth have a care for, none has one single lot in mind, but all wheel round about; and to stand still in one part is not lawful, but each one keeps, as he began, an equal share of the course." The branches, then, are a symbol either of the first food, or that the many may come to know that the fruits flower and grow throughout, abiding very long, while they themselves have obtained but a short span of life; for this reason they will have the branches given; and perhaps also that they may come to know that, as these are burned, so they too must quickly leave this life and become the work of fire.

Most useful, then, is the kind of symbolic interpretation, helping toward many things, and toward right theology, and toward piety, and toward the showing of understanding, and toward the practice of brevity, and toward the display of wisdom; "for it is the part of a wise man," says Didymus the grammarian, "to use the symbolic mode of speech with dexterity, and to recognize what is shown forth by it." Indeed the elementary teaching of children embraces the interpretation of the four elements. For the Phrygians call water bedy, as Orpheus too: "and bedy, the bright water of the nymphs, is poured down." But the priest Dion likewise appears to write: "And taking bedy, pour it over your hands and turn to the inspection of the sacrifice." On the other hand, Philyllius the comic poet knows bedy as the air, the giver of life, by these words: "I pray to draw in the saving bedy" — which is the greatest part of health, to draw in the air pure, not befouled.

In agreement with this opinion is Neanthes of Cyzicus also, when he writes that the priests of the Macedonians, in their prayers, call upon bedy to be gracious to them and to their children — which they interpret as air. And as for zaps, "fire," some have taken it, in their ignorance, from zesis, "boiling"; but the sea is called by this name, as Euphorion in his replies to Theodoridas: "And zaps, the destroyer of ships, works mischief upon the reefs." And Dionysius the Iambic likewise: "the briny zaps groans around the raging sea." So too Cratinus the younger, the comic poet: "the zaps casts forth shrimps and little fishes." And Simmias of Rhodes: "the briny zaps was mother of the Ignetes and the Telchines." And chthon is the earth, poured out into magnitude. And plēktron, "the striker," some take as the pole, others as the air that strikes and moves all things into nature and growth, or that which fills all things.

But these men had not read Cleanthes the philosopher, who downright calls the sun the striker; for in its risings, driving home its rays as it were striking the world, it leads the light into its harmonious course; and from the sun it gives sign also to the other stars. And the sphinx is not the binding-together of all things and the revolution of the world according to the poet Aratus, but perhaps it might be the pervading spiritual tension that holds the world together; though it is better to take it as the aether that holds and binds all things, as Empedocles too says: "But come, I will tell you first the sun, the beginning, from which were made plain all the things now beheld — earth, and the much-billowing sea, and the moist air, the Titan, and the aether that binds tight all things round in a circle." And Apollodorus of Cercyra says that these verses were uttered aloud by Branchus the seer, when he was cleansing the Milesians from a plague. For sprinkling the multitude with branches of laurel, he led off the hymn somewhat thus: "Sing, O children, of the Far-worker and the Far-worker's maid"; and the people, so to speak, struck up in answer: "bedy, zaps, chthōm, plēktron, sphinx; knaxzbich, thyptes, phlegmo, drōps." Callimachus too mentions the story in his Iambics. And knaxzbich is, by derivation, the disease, from knaiein, "to grate," and "to destroy," and thypsai, "to burn with lightning." Thespis, however, the tragedian, says that something else is signified by these, writing somewhat thus: "Lo, I pour you a libation of knaxzbich, white, pressed from the dugs of yellow goats; lo, for you thyptēs, cheese mingled with red honey, I set upon your holy altars, O horned Pan; lo, for you I pour Bromius' phlegmo." He hints, I think, at the first milky food of the soul that comes from the four-and-twenty elements; after which is the food now curdled into cheese, and last the blood of the vine of the Word, the fiery wine, which teaches the gladness that perfects the discipline. And drōps is the active Word, which from the first catechizing brings the man to growth, to the measure of his stature, kindling and enlightening the man.

But there is borne about also a third copy-line for boys: "Grasp, sphinx, thief, gratingly." It signifies, I think, by the management of the elements and of the world, that the way must lie for us toward the knowledge of the more perfect, since eternal salvation is won by force and toil. For "to grasp" is to apprehend; the sphinx is the harmony of the world; "gratingly" shows forth the difficulty; and "thief" shows at once the knowledge of the Lord that escapes notice, and the day. And again — does not Epigenes, in his work On the Poetry of Orpheus, setting forth the peculiar usages in Orpheus, say that "crook-fashioned shuttles" signify ploughs, and "warp-threads" the furrows; that the "thread" is allegorized as the seed, and "the tears of Zeus" show the rain; that the Fates, again, are the phases of the moon, the thirtieth, the fifteenth, and the new moon — wherefore Orpheus calls them "white-robed," being parts of the light? And again, "the flowery one" is the spring by reason of nature, "the shining one" is the night by reason of its rest, and "the Gorgon" is the moon by reason of the face in it; and "Aphrodite" is the season in which one ought to sow — these are said in the theologian.

Such things the Pythagoreans too hinted at, allegorizing the dogs of Persephone as the planets, and the sea as the tear of Cronos. And we should find ten thousand things upon ten thousand spoken in riddles by both philosophers and poets, seeing that whole books too show forth the hidden purpose of the writer — such as the book of Heraclitus On Nature, who for this very reason was surnamed "the Obscure." Like this book is the theology of Pherecydes of Syros. For the poet Euphorion, and the Causes of Callimachus, and the Alexandra of Lycophron, and such-like works, are set as an exercise in exegesis for the boys of the grammarians.

Far indeed should it be that the one examined in such piety should be ready either to lie or to swear an oath. For an oath is a determining acknowledgement with the additional taking-on of the divine. But the one who is once faithful—how could he show himself faithless, so as even to need an oath, and not rather make his very life a firm and fixed oath? He lives and conducts himself, and shows the trustworthiness of his confession in a life and a word that do not waver and are steadfast. And if doing wrong lies in the judgement of the one who acts and speaks, and not in the suffering of the one wronged, he will neither lie nor swear falsely, as one wronging the Divine, knowing that it is by nature unharmable; but neither, for his neighbour's sake, will he lie or transgress anything—him whom he has learned to love, even if he happen to be no acquaintance; and for his own sake, all the more, he will neither lie nor swear falsely, since he would never willingly be found unjust toward himself. But neither will he swear, having chosen to set, in assent, only the "yes," and in denial the "no," as his adverb. For to swear is to bring forward an oath, or to bring something forward, as it were, by way of an oath, affirmatively from the intention.

It is not unlikely, then, that the barbarian philosophy too, of which it is our purpose to speak, should in some places prophesy in a hidden way and through symbols, as has been shown. Such, for instance, are the things Moses enjoins — these common ones: "You shall not eat the swine, nor the eagle, nor the hawk, nor the raven." For the swine signifies the pleasure-loving and unclean desire for foods, and the lickerish craving for venery, and a defiled wantonness, ever itching, material and lying in the mire, fattened for slaughter and destruction. On the contrary, he permits the eating of what parts the hoof and chews the cud, signifying, says Barnabas, that one ought to cleave to those who fear the Lord, and to those who meditate in their heart on the distinction of the word which they have received, to those who speak the ordinances of the Lord and keep them, to those who know that meditation is a work of gladness, and who chew the cud upon the word of the Lord. And what is the parting of the hoof? That the just man both walks in this world and awaits the holy age. Then he goes on: "See how well Moses laid down the law. But how could they understand or grasp these things? But we, understanding the commandments rightly, speak as the Lord willed. For this reason he circumcised our ears and our hearts, that we might understand these things."

It suffices him, then, to add to his assent or his denial the words "I speak truly," for the setting-forth of his answer's firmness to those who do not discern it. For one ought, I think, to have toward outsiders a life worthy of trust, so that one is not even asked for an oath; and toward oneself and toward those who understand, fair-mindedness, which is voluntary righteousness. Accordingly, the gnostic keeps his oath well, yet is not prone to swearing, coming to swear but rarely, and even then in the manner we have described. And yet the speaking of truth under oath comes about with the accord of what is according to truth; the keeping of an oath, then, results according to the right doing of one's duties. Where, then, is there any further need of an oath for the man who lives at the height of truth? For the one who does not even swear is far indeed from swearing falsely; and the one who transgresses none of the things agreed upon would never even swear at all, seeing that the ratification both of transgression and of fulfilment lies in deeds—just as, indeed, lying and false swearing lie in speaking and in swearing contrary to duty. But the one who lives justly, transgressing none of his duties, where the judgement of truth is examined, keeps his oath in his deeds; superfluous, then, for him is the witness of the tongue. Persuaded, then, that God is everywhere always, and ashamed not to speak the truth, and knowing that lying is unworthy of himself, he is content with the divine conscience and his own alone; and in this way he neither lies nor does anything contrary to the agreements, and in this way too he neither swears an oath when required, nor ever denies—lest he lie—even though he should die under torture.

Indeed, when he says, "You shall not eat the eagle, the hawk, the kite, and the raven," he means: "You shall not cleave to, nor be made like, those men who do not know how to provide themselves food by toil and sweat, but live by plunder and lawlessness." For the eagle signifies plunder, the hawk injustice, and the raven greed. And it is written: "With the innocent man you shall be innocent, and with the elect you shall be elect, and with the perverse you shall be perverse." It is fitting, then, to cleave to the holy, because those who cleave to them shall be sanctified. Hence Theognis writes: "From the good you shall learn good things; but if you mingle with the evil, you shall lose even the mind you have." And again, when it says in the song, "He has been gloriously glorified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea," the many-limbed, brutish, impulsive passion — desire — together with the rider mounted upon it, the charioteer who has given the reins to pleasures, he has cast into the sea, hurling them into the disorders of the world.

So too Plato, in his treatise On the Soul, says that the charioteer and the horse that has revolted — the irrational part, which is cleft in two, into spirit and desire — fall down. By which the myth too hints that Phaethon fell through the unruliness of the colts. Indeed in the case of Joseph also: his brothers, in envy of him as a youth who saw further in the matter of knowledge, stripped off his many-coloured tunic, and taking him, cast him into a pit; and the pit was empty, it had no water. Spurning the varied knowledge of the earnest man that comes of love of learning, or using only the bare faith that is according to the law, they cast it into the pit empty of water, to sell it off into Egypt, the desert of the divine Word. And the pit is empty of knowledge, into which the man cast and stripped of his knowledge — the wise man who had escaped notice — seemed to his brothers like to themselves, naked of knowledge. By another signification the many-coloured garment might be desire, leading away into a yawning pit. "And if anyone open a pit, or hew one out," it says, "and do not cover it, and a calf or an ass fall in there, the owner of the pit shall pay money and give it to his neighbour; but the dead beast shall be his."

Here bring to my aid that prophecy: "The ox knew its owner, and the ass the manger of its master; but Israel did not know me." That none of these, then, falling into the knowledge taught by you, having become a hearer of the truth, may misunderstand and stumble, "Be safe," it says, "concerning the use of the word"; and toward those who come to it irrationally, shut up the living spring that lies in the deep, but hold out drink to those who thirst for the truth. Concealing yourself, then, from those who are not able to receive the depth of knowledge, cover the pit. The owner of the pit, then — the gnostic himself — will be punished, it says, undergoing the charge of him who is offended or swallowed up by the greatness of the word, while still small-minded, or of having moved the labourer over to contemplation and set him aside, by reason of his ill-prepared faith. And he shall give money, rendering account and answer to the all-sovereign will.

This, then, is the type of the law and the prophets up to John. But he — although he spoke more plainly, as no longer prophesying but already pointing to him who was symbolically announced from the beginning as now present — nevertheless says, "I am not worthy to loose the strap of the Lord's sandal." For he confesses that he is not worthy to baptize so great a power; for those who purify must loose the soul from the body and from its sins, as one looses the foot from the bond. And perhaps too he means the last operation of the Saviour toward us, the nearest one, that which comes through his presence, hidden under the riddle of prophecy; for he who by his own showing pointed out him who was prophesied of, who announced the presence as having come, that had journeyed from afar into manifestation, truly loosed the end of the oracles of the dispensation, uncovering the meaning of the symbols. And among the Romans the things done over wills have their order — those scales and asses and acts of redemption and the touchings of the ears that are done for justice' sake — some that they may be done justly, some for the apportioning of the honour, and one that the bystander, as though some weight were laid upon him, may stand and hear and take the rank of a witness.

since not only Aesopians and Macedonians and Laconians endured being racked, as Eratosthenes says in his work On Goods and Evils, but Zeno the Eleatic too, when compelled to tell something of the secret things, held out against the tortures, confessing nothing, but in the end bit out his tongue and spat it at the tyrant, whom some call Nearchus, others Demylus. Likewise too Theodotus the Pythagorean did, and Paulus the acquaintance of Lacydes, as Timotheus of Pergamum says in his work On the Courage of the Philosophers, and Achaeus in his Ethics. But Postumus the Roman too, taken by Peucetio, not only did not reveal any of the hidden things, but even, putting his hand upon the fire, let it melt like bronze with a wholly unchanged bearing. I pass over in silence the deeds of Anaxarchus, who cried out, "Pound the pouch of Anaxarchus; for Anaxarchus you do not pound," when he was being pounded by the tyrant with iron pestles.

Neither, then, the hope of happiness nor the love toward God is impatient at what befalls, but remains free, even if it should fall among the most savage beasts, even if into the all-devouring fire, even if it be slain by tyrannical tortures, hanging upon the divine friendship, unenslaved, it circles aloft, having handed over the body to those who alone are able to lay hold of it. The Getae, a barbarian nation not untouched by philosophy, choose each year an envoy to the hero Zamolxis; and Zamolxis was one of the acquaintances of Pythagoras.

So the man judged most worthy is slaughtered, to the grief of those who have studied philosophy but were not chosen, as having been rejected from a blessed service. But the whole Church is full of those who, throughout their lives, have practised the life-giving death into Christ—men, and likewise prudent women too. For it is possible for the one who conducts his life according to us to philosophize even without letters, whether he be barbarian or Greek, slave or old man or child or woman; for prudence is common to all men who have chosen it; and it has been agreed by us that each kind has the same nature and likewise has the same virtue.

The woman, then, does not appear to have one nature toward humanity and the man another, but the same; so that also the same virtue. And if a man's virtue is, of course, prudence and righteousness and all that are reckoned to follow upon these, is it fitting for a man alone to be virtuous, and for a woman to be licentious and unjust? But this is unseemly even to say. Prudence, then, and righteousness and all the rest of virtue must be cared for alike by a woman and alike by a man, by free and slave, since the same and one virtue belongs to the same nature. We do not say that the nature of the female is the same as that of the male in so far as it is female; for surely there had to be some difference between each of them, on account of which the one became female, the other male. We say, then, that conceiving and bearing belong to the woman, in so far as she happens to be female, not in so far as she is human; for if there were no difference between man and woman, each of them would do and suffer the same things.

In so far, then, as it is the same—according to the soul—it will arrive at the same virtue; but in so far as it is different—according to the peculiarity of the body—it inclines toward childbearing and housekeeping. "For I wish you to know," says the apostle, "that the head of every man is Christ, and the head of woman is the man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man. Nevertheless neither is woman without man nor man without woman in the Lord." For as we say the man must be prudent and superior to pleasures, so we would deem it right that the woman too be likewise prudent and practised in fighting against pleasures. I say, "Walk by the Spirit and you shall not fulfil the desire of the flesh," the apostolic commandment counsels; "for the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh." These, then, are set against each other not as evil against good, but as fighting beneficially. So he adds:

Since those who introduce the doctrine of indifference do violence to a few Scriptures and think they argue in favour of their own indulgence—and indeed that one, "Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under law but under grace" (and certain others of this kind, which it is not reasonable to recall on such occasions; for I am not fitting out a pirate ship)—come now, let us briefly cut through their attempt. For the noble apostle himself, in what he adds to the aforesaid saying, will dispel the charge: "What then? Shall we sin, because we are not under law but under grace? God forbid." Thus divinely and prophetically he at once overthrows the sophistical art of pleasure.

"that you may not do the things you wish. And the works of the flesh are plain, which are fornication, uncleanness, lewdness, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, strifes, jealousies, fits of anger, factions, dissensions, heresies, envyings, drunkennesses, revellings, and the like; of which I tell you beforehand, as also I told you before, that those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, long-suffering, kindness, continence, goodness, faith, meekness." By "flesh," I think, he means the sinners, as by "Spirit" the righteous. And indeed the quality of manliness is to be taken in the sense of good courage and endurance, so as to offer the other cheek to the one who strikes, and to yield even the tunic to the one who takes the cloak, mastering wrath strongly. For we do not train our women to be Amazons in manliness for war, since we wish even the men to be peaceful.

They do not understand, it seems, that we must all be made manifest before the judgement-seat of Christ, that each may receive, through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil—that each may receive back what he has done through the body. So that, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation, no longer sinful; the old things have passed away; we have washed away the old life; behold, things have become new—chastity instead of fornication, continence instead of incontinence, righteousness instead of unrighteousness. "For what fellowship has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what communion has light with darkness? And what agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what part has a believer with an unbeliever? And what concord has the temple of God with idols? Having, then, these promises, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God."

But I hear that the Sauromatian women practise war no less than the men, and others, the Sacian women, who shoot backwards, pretending to flee, equally with the men. I know too that the women near Iberia work and toil in a manly way, and even when they are about to give birth do not give up any of their tasks, but often in the very contest of their labours the woman, having given birth, takes up the infant and carries it home. Indeed, the bitches no less than the males both keep the house and hunt and guard the flocks.
The Cretan hound Gorgo ran upon the deer's track.
The women, then, must philosophize in a manner like the men, even if the males be better and take the first place in all things, except in so far as they grow soft.

For Paul too in the Epistles does not appear to disparage philosophy, but holds that one who partakes of the gnostic height should no longer run back to Greek philosophy, allegorizing it as the elements of the world, being a kind of elementary and preparatory teaching of the truth. Wherefore, writing to the Hebrews, those turning back to the law from faith, he says again, "You have need that someone teach you what are the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God, and you have become such as have need of milk and not solid food." Likewise too to the Colossians turning from among the Greeks: "See that no one shall lead you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elements of this world and not after Christ" — luring them back to run up again to philosophy, the elementary teaching. And if one say that philosophy was discovered by the Greeks by human understanding, yet I find the Scriptures saying that understanding is sent from God.
Education, then, and virtue are necessary for the whole race of men, if indeed they would hasten toward happiness. And somehow Euripides not in vain writes variously: at one time,
and at another, "For a prudent woman is the slave of her husband, but the imprudent one surpasses the man who is with her in folly."
For there is nothing greater and better than when a man and a woman keep house being of one mind in their thoughts.
The head, then, is the ruling part. And if the Lord is the head of the man, and the head of woman is the man, then the man is lord of the woman, being the image and glory of God.

The psalmist, at any rate, holds understanding the greatest gift, and asks for it, saying, "I am your servant; give me understanding." And does not David, asking for the manifold experience of knowledge, write, "Goodness and discipline and knowledge teach me, for I have believed in your commandments"? And the covenants have been confessed to be of supreme authority, and to be given to those held in greater honour. The psalm, at any rate, says again of God, "He has not done so to any nation, and his judgements he has not made plain to them." And the "he has not done so" shows that he did it, but not so. By comparison, then, the "so" is set against the surpassing measure that comes to us; for the prophet might surely have said simply "he has not done it," without the addition of "so." Yes, and Peter too in the Acts says, "In truth I apprehend that God is no respecter of persons, but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him."

Wherefore in the epistle to the Ephesians he writes: "Submitting yourselves to one another in the fear of God. Wives, to your own husbands as to the Lord, because the husband is the head of the wife, as also Christ is the head of the Church, He being the Saviour of the body. But as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let the wives be to their own husbands in everything. Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church"; so too the husbands ought to love their own wives as their own bodies. "He who loves his own wife loves himself; for no one ever hated his own flesh."

Not in time, then, is the impartiality of God, but from eternity; nor did his benefaction ever begin, nor is it bounded by places or by certain men; for his beneficence is not partial. "Open to me," it says, "the gates of righteousness; entering in by them I will confess to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the just shall enter in by it." And Barnabas, expounding the prophet's saying, adds: "Of many gates that are opened, this in righteousness is the one in Christ, in which all are blessed who have entered." And of the same thought is that prophetic saying too: "The Lord is upon many waters" — not of the different covenants only, but also of the modes of teaching, both those among the Greeks and those among the barbarians, leading to righteousness. And plainly already David too, witnessing to the truth, sings: "Let the sinners be turned into Hades, all the nations that forget God." They forget, plainly, him whom they formerly remembered, and whom, before they forgot him, they knew; this one they cast aside. There was, then, some dim knowledge of God even among the Gentiles.

And in the epistle to the Colossians: "Wives," he says, "be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and be not bitter against them. Children, obey your parents in all things, for this is well-pleasing to the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they be discouraged. Slaves, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh, not with eye-service as men-pleasers, but in simplicity of heart, fearing the Lord. And whatever you do, work from the soul as serving the Lord and not men, knowing that from the Lord you shall receive the recompense of the inheritance. For you serve the Lord Christ; for the unjust man shall receive back what he did unjustly, and there is no respect of persons. Masters, give to your slaves what is just and equal, knowing that you too have a Master in heaven, where there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free, but Christ is all and in all."

And let these things be so. But the gnostic must be of much learning; and since the Greeks say that, Protagoras having led the way, to every argument an argument is opposed, it is fitting that he be prepared even against such arguments. For the Scripture says, "He who says much shall also hear in turn." And "who shall understand a parable of the Lord, except the wise and understanding man, and he who loves his Lord?" Let such a man, then, be faithful; let him be able to declare knowledge; let him be wise in the discernment of words; let him be vehement in deeds; let him be pure. "For so much the more ought he to be humble-minded, the greater he seems to be," says Clement in the Epistle to the Corinthians. Such a one is able to obey that precept: "And some snatch out of the fire, but on the doubting have mercy." For instance, the pruning-hook is made chiefly for pruning, but with it we also separate the entwined shoots and cut away the thorns grown up with the vines, which it is not easy to approach. And all these have their reference to the pruning. Again, man was made chiefly for the recognition of God; but he also tills the soil, and does geometry, and philosophizes — of which the one is unto living, the other unto living well, and the other unto the practice of demonstrative reasoning.

The earthly Church is an image of the heavenly, for which we pray that the will of God may come to pass on earth too as in heaven: "having put on bowels of compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, long-suffering, bearing with one another and forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; as Christ also forgave us, so also we. And over all these is love, which is the bond of perfection. And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which also you were called in one body; and be thankful." For nothing hinders us from often setting down the same Scripture for the rebuke of Marcion, in case he should somehow change, being persuaded, having learned that the faithful man must be thankful to the Demiurge God who called us and brought us the good news in a body.

Yes, and those who say that philosophy sets out from the devil, let them attend to this too: that the Scripture says the devil transforms himself into an angel of light. To do what? Plainly, to prophesy. And if he prophesies as an angel of light, then he will say true things. And if he prophesies angelic and luminous and profitable things, then it is when he transforms himself by a likeness of working, even though he be other in respect of the substratum of apostasy. For how could he deceive anyone, unless by drawing the lover of learning, through true things, into familiarity, and so afterward dragging him down into falsehood? And besides, he will be found knowing the truth, and even if not apprehensively, at any rate not inexperienced of it. Not false, then, is philosophy, even if the thief and the liar, by a transformation of working, says true things; nor must one, on account of the speaker, ignorantly condemn beforehand the things spoken — which is to be observed too in the case of those now said to prophesy — but one must look at the things said, whether they hold to the truth.

From these things, then, it has been plainly shown to us what the unity from faith is, and who the perfect man is; so that, even against the will of some and though most things stand in the way, even if punishments be hung over them by the husband or the master, both the slave and the woman will philosophize. Yes, and the free man too, even if death be threatened him by a tyrant, even if he be led to courts and dragged into the extremest dangers and put in peril concerning all his possessions, will not in any way let go of piety. Nor will the woman ever despair, living with a worthless husband, nor the son if he has a worthless father, nor the slave if a wicked master, but they hold nobly to virtue. For as it is noble for a man to die for virtue and for freedom and for himself, so likewise for a woman; for this is not proper to the nature of males, but to that of the good.

And by now, saying with a universal word that all things necessary and useful to life come to us from God, we should not err; and that philosophy was given more especially to the Greeks, as a covenant of their own, being a substructure for the philosophy according to Christ — even though those who philosophize after the manner of the Greeks willingly turn deaf to the truth, despising the voice of the barbarians, or fearing the danger of death hanging over the believer by the civil laws. And as in the barbarian philosophy, so too in the Greek the tares were sown by the proper husbandman of tares. Whence the heresies too sprang up among us, together with the fruitful wheat; and those who proclaim the godlessness and pleasure of Epicurus, and whatever else has been sown contrary to right reason in Greek philosophy, are spurious fruits of the husbandry God-given to the Greeks.

Faithfully, then, the old man and the young and the slave, obeying the commandments, will both live and, if need be, die—which would be to be made alive through death. For we know that children and slaves and wives have often, against the will of fathers and masters and husbands, become most excellent. None the less, then, ought those who are about to live piously to be eager, when some seem to hinder them; but it is far more fitting, I think, to hasten and strive especially, that they may not, being overcome, fall away from the best and most necessary counsels. For I do not think it admits of comparison whether it is better to become a fellow-worshipper of the Almighty or to choose the darkness of the demons. For the things we do for the sake of others, we would do each time, trying to look toward those for whose sake they seem to be done, reckoning as our measure what is pleasing to them; but the things that are more our own than another's, these we would do with equal zeal, whether they seem to please some or not.

This the apostle calls the wisdom of this age, the pleasure-loving and self-loving, as teaching only the things of this world and about it, and consequently subject, by way of presidency, to the rulers here. Wherefore this partial philosophy is a kind of elementary thing, while the truly perfect science deals with the things beyond the world, the things of mind, and yet more, the things more spiritual than these — "which eye has not seen and ear has not heard, nor have they entered into the heart of man," before the teacher made plain to us the discourse about them, having revealed the holy of holies, and, by an ascent, the holier things still, to the genuine and not spurious heirs of the Lord's adoption. For we dare to say (for here is the gnostic faith) that the truly gnostic man is knowing of all things and embracing of all things, using a sure apprehension even in the things insoluble to us — such as were James, Peter, John, Paul, and the rest of the apostles. For prophecy is full of knowledge, as given by the Lord and again made plain by the Lord to the apostles. And knowledge is the peculiar property of a rational soul trained for this, that through knowledge it may be enrolled unto immortality. For both are powers of the soul, knowledge and impulse.

If, then, some of the indifferent things have obtained such honour that they seem to be choiceworthy even against the will of some, much more must virtue be reckoned worth fighting for, looking to nothing else but to the very thing that is able to be nobly done, whether it seem otherwise to some or not. Well, then, does Epicurus too write to Menoeceus: "Let no one, while young, delay to philosophize, nor when old grow weary of philosophizing. For no one is too young or too old to be healthy in soul. And the one who says that the time to philosophize has not yet come or has passed is like one who says that the time for happiness has not yet come or is no longer. So that both the young and the old must philosophize—the one, that growing old he may be young in good things through gratitude for what has been; the other, that he may be young and old at once, through fearlessness toward what is to come."

And impulse is found to be a movement following upon a certain assent; for he who has the impulse toward some action first takes the knowledge of the action, and second the impulse. And further, let us consider this: since the learning is older than the doing (for he who is to do a thing by nature first learns the thing he wishes to do), and knowledge comes of learning, but the doing of impulse; and impulse follows upon science, and after it the action; knowledge would be the beginning and maker of every rational action; so that with reason by this alone would the peculiar quality of the rational soul be characterized. For in truth impulse, like knowledge, is moved upon the things that are; but knowledge, this very thing, is a certain beholding of the soul, of the things that are, of some of them, or, when perfected, of all together.

And yet some say that the wise man is persuaded that there are certain incomprehensible things, so as to have some comprehension even about these, comprehending that the incomprehensible will be incomprehensible. Which is common even to those able to foresee a little; for such a one makes sure that there are certain incomprehensible things. But that gnostic of whom I speak comprehends the very things that seem incomprehensible to others, having believed that nothing is incomprehensible to the Son of God, and so nothing unteachable. For he who suffered out of love toward us would withhold nothing for the teaching of knowledge. This faith, then, becomes a sure demonstration, since truth follows upon the things delivered by God. And if one craves much experience, the disciple of wisdom knows the things of old and conjectures the things to come, understands the turnings of words and the solutions of riddles, foreknows signs and wonders, and the issues of seasons and times.

Of causes, some are antecedent, some sustaining, some co-operating, some "those-without-which." Antecedent are those that primarily furnish an occasion for something to come to be—as beauty does of love, to the intemperate; for, being seen by them, it produces only the amorous disposition, yet not by necessity. Sustaining are those which are also called, synonymously, self-complete, since they are of themselves sufficiently productive of the result. And next, all the causes must be shown in the case of the learner. The father is an antecedent cause of the learning; the teacher a sustaining cause; the nature of the learner a co-operating cause; and time holds the rank of the "those-without-which." And a cause is strictly said to be that which actively furnishes something, since we say that iron is cutting not only in the cutting, but also in the not cutting. So, then, "the thing that furnishes" signifies both: both that which is already acting, and that which is not yet, but possesses the power of acting.

Some, then, say that the causes are of bodies; others, of incorporeals. Some say that the body is strictly a cause, but the incorporeal so called by a misuse of terms and, as it were, in a cause-like way. Others reverse it, saying that incorporeals are strictly causes, and bodies only by misuse—as that the cutting, being an activity, is incorporeal, and is the cause of cutting, being an incorporeal activity; and of being cut, likewise, both to the knife and to the thing cut, which are bodies. The phrase "is a cause of certain things" is said in three ways: first, that which is the cause—as the statue-maker; second, that of which it is a cause—as of the statue's coming to be; third, that for which it is a cause, as for the matter; for to the bronze it is a cause of the statue's coming to be. The coming-to-be, then, and the being cut—the things of which it is a cause—being activities, are incorporeal. With reference to this account: causes are causes of predicates, or, as some say, of things-said (for Cleanthes and Archedemus call the predicates things-said); or, what is rather the case, some causes will be said to be of predicates, as of "is cut," whose noun-form is "the being cut," and others of propositions, as of "a ship comes to be," whose noun-form, again, is "the ship's coming to be." But Aristotle makes them causes of appellations, as of such things as house, ship, burning, cutting. And the noun-form is agreed to be incorporeal; for which reason too that sophism is solved thus: "What you say passes through your mouth"—which is true; "but you say 'house'; therefore a house passes through your mouth"—which is false. For we do not say the house, being a body, but the noun-form, being incorporeal, of which a house happens to be the case.

And we say that the builder builds, with reference to what is to come to be. Thus we say that a cloak is woven; for the thing that does is indicative of activity. And it is not the case that the thing that does is of one thing and the cause of another, but of the same; for inasmuch as it is a cause of coming-to-be, in that respect it is also productive of coming-to-be. The same thing, then, is both cause and productive. And if something is cause and productive, this is wholly also a "that-because-of-which"; but if something is a "that-because-of-which," it is not wholly also a cause. For many things run together toward one result, because of which the end comes to be, but not all are causes. For Medea would not have slain her children had she not been angered, nor would she have been angered had she not been jealous, nor this, had she not loved, nor this, had not Jason sailed to Colchis, nor this, had not the Argo been built, nor this, had not the timbers been cut from Pelion. For in all these, the "that-because-of-which" being present, not all are causes of the child-slaying, but only Medea. Therefore the thing that does not hinder is inactive; for which reason the thing that does not hinder is not a cause, but the thing that hinders. For in acting and doing something the cause is conceived.

Further, the thing that does not hinder is separated from the thing that comes to be (for the reason the thing is accomplished is that the thing able to hinder is not present), whereas the cause is toward the thing that comes to be; so that the thing that does not hinder would not be a cause. The cause is said in four ways: the thing that does, as the statue-maker; the matter, as the bronze; the form, as the impressed character; and the end, as the honour of the gymnasiarch. The bronze holds the rank of "those-without-which" toward the statue's coming to be, and is likewise a cause. For everything without which the result cannot come to be is by necessity a cause—but not a cause simply; for the "that-without-which" is not sustaining, but co-operating. Everything that acts furnishes the result with a fitness in the thing affected. For the cause disposes, and each thing is affected toward that for which it is by nature fitted, the fitness being furnishing and holding the rank of "those-without-which." The cause, then, is inactive without the fitness, but the fitness is not a cause, but a co-operator, since every cause is conceived in acting. And the earth would not make itself; so that it would not be a cause of itself. And it is ridiculous to say that the fire is not the cause of the burning, but the wood; nor the knife of the cutting, but the flesh; nor, of the athlete's being thrown, the strength of the opponent, but his own weakness. The sustaining cause needs no time; for the cautery, at the very instant of being pressed against the flesh, furnishes the pain. Of the antecedent causes, some need time until the result comes to be, others do not, as the fall in the case of a fracture. Surely, then, these are called timeless not by privation of time, but by diminution of it, as "the sudden" too, which itself does not come to be apart from time.

Every cause, as a cause, is grasped by a twofold understanding, since it is conceived both as of something and as toward something: of something, the result, as the knife of cutting; and toward something, the thing fitly disposed, as the fire toward the wood—for it will not burn the adamant. The cause is among relatives; for it is conceived in respect of its relation toward something else, so that we apply two things in order to conceive the cause as a cause. The same account holds also of the maker and producer and father. Nothing is itself a cause of itself, nor is anyone his own father, since then the first will become second. The cause acts and disposes; the thing that comes to be by the cause is affected and is disposed. But the same thing, taken with reference to itself, cannot at once act and be disposed, nor be son and father. And besides, the cause is prior in time, in respect of substance, to the thing that comes to be by it, as the knife to the cutting. But the same thing cannot, in the same respect, be both prior in time to the matter, in that it is a cause, and at the same time later and posterior in time, in that it is the work of the cause. And being differs from coming-to-be; so too the cause is of the thing that comes to be, the father of the son. For it is not possible for the same thing, in the same respect, both to be and to come to be at once. Nothing, then, is a cause of itself.

Causes are not causes of one another, but causes to one another. For the splenic disposition, lying beforehand, is not a cause of fever, but of the fever's coming to be; and the fever, lying beforehand, is not a cause of the spleen, but of the disposition's increasing. So too the virtues are causes to one another of not being separated, on account of their mutual implication; and the stones in an arch are causes to one another of the predicate "to remain," but are not causes of one another; and the teacher and the learner are causes to one another of the predicate "to advance." And things are said to be causes to one another sometimes of the same thing—as the merchant and the retailer are causes to one another of gaining; sometimes of one thing and another—as the knife and the flesh; for the one is to the flesh a cause of being cut, and the flesh to the knife a cause of cutting. "Eye for eye" and "life for life." For he who has struck someone a deadly blow is a cause to him of death, or of death's coming to be; but, struck back by him deadly, has him as a counter-cause—not in the same respect in which he became a cause to him, but in another. For he became to the man a cause of death; but it was not the death that in turn laid upon him the deadly counter-blow, but the man himself who was wounded; so that he himself became a cause of one thing, and had another as cause.
