And the one who has done wrong becomes a cause to the other of the wrong done to him; but the law that bids one be requited is a cause not of wrong, but to the one of vindication, and to the other of instruction. So that the causes are not causes of one another, as causes, but are causes to one another.

Further, it is inquired whether many causes, by concurrence of one result, become several causes. For the men who have come together are causes of the ship's being dragged down; but each is not a cause in his own right, but together with the rest—unless indeed the joint-cause too is a cause. Others say that, if there are many causes, each one in its own right becomes a cause of the one thing. Of being happy, at least, being one thing, the virtues, being many, are causes; and of being warmed and of feeling pain, likewise, the causes are many. Surely, then, the many virtues are one in power, and the things that warm and the things that cause pain are too. And the multitude of the virtues, being one in genus, becomes a cause of the one thing, being happy. But in truth several antecedent causes become causes of one thing, both in genus and in species: in genus, of falling ill in whatever way—as chilling, scorching, weariness, indigestion, drunkenness—and in species, of fever. But the sustaining causes are several in genus only, no longer also in species. For of being made sweet-smelling, being one in genus, the causes are many in species—as frankincense, rose, saffron, storax, myrrh, perfume; for the rose would not be so sweet-smelling as the myrrh.

And the same thing becomes a cause of contraries—sometimes in respect of the magnitude of the cause and its power, sometimes in respect of the fitness of the thing affected. In respect of the qualitative power: the same string, by tension or by slackening, gives back a high or a low note. In respect of the fitness of the things affected: honey is sweet to the healthy, but bitter to the feverish; and one and the same wine leads some toward anger, others toward relaxation; and the same sun melts the wax but dries the clay. Of causes, then, some are evident, taken by reckoning; others non-evident, taken by analogy. And of the non-evident, some are non-evident for a time—hidden at one season, but again at another seen plainly—and others non-evident by nature, never able to become evident at any season. And of the things non-evident by nature, some are apprehensible, which some called "not non-evident," being taken analogically through signs—as the proportion of the passages contemplated by reason; and others are inapprehensible, those that can in no way fall under apprehension, which indeed are called non-evident absolutely. And some causes are antecedent, others sustaining, others joint-causes, others co-operating; and some of that which is according to nature, others of that which is contrary to nature, others of disease; and, in respect of subordination, some of affections, others of their magnitude, others of times and seasons.

When, then, the antecedent causes are removed, the result remains; but a sustaining cause is one in whose presence the result remains, and on whose removal it is removed. And the sustaining is also called, synonymously, self-complete, since it is of itself sufficiently productive of the result. And if the self-complete cause is indicative of a self-complete activity, the co-operating signifies a service and a ministry along with another. If, then, it furnishes nothing, it will not even be called co-operating; but if it furnishes something, it becomes by all means a cause of that which it furnishes—that is, of the thing that comes to be through it. The co-operating, then, is that in whose presence the result came to be—an evident thing in the presence of an evident, a non-evident in that of a non-evident. And the joint-cause too is of the kind of the causes, just as the fellow-soldier is a soldier and the fellow-ephebe an ephebe. The co-operating cause, then, helps the sustaining toward the intensifying of that which comes to be through it; but the joint-cause is not of the same conception. For there can be a joint-cause even if something is not a sustaining cause; for the joint-cause is conceived along with another that is not itself able, in its own right, to produce the result—being a cause along with a cause. And the co-operating differs from the joint-cause in this: that the joint-cause furnishes the result with another that does not, in its own right, produce it; while the co-operating, not producing it in its own right, but coming to another that does produce it in its own right, co-operates with that other toward the result's coming to be more vehemently. And especially does the having become co-operating out of an antecedent set forth that the power of the cause extends to the co-operating.

Such fear, then, leads up both to repentance and to hope. And hope is the expectation of good things, the good hope of an absent good. Indeed, even . . . readiness-to-fall is taken into hope, which we have learned to lead by the hand toward love. And love would be a concord of the things according to reason and life and manner — or, to speak briefly, a fellowship of life, or an intensity of friendship and tender affection, with right reason, about the use of a companion. And the companion is a second self; whence we call brothers those reborn by the same word. And beside love lie hospitality, being a kind of fond skill about the use of strangers; and strangers are those to whom worldly things are strange. For we understand as worldly those who hope toward earth and the fleshly desires. "Be not conformed," says the Apostle, "to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of the mind, that you may approve what is the will of God, the good and well-pleasing and perfect." Hospitality, then, busies itself about what is profitable to strangers; and strangers are guests, and guests are friends, and friends are brothers: "dear brother," says Homer. And love of mankind, through which is tender affection too, being a friendly use of men; and tender affection, being a kind of fond skill about the cherishing of friends or kindred, accompany love.

And if the true man in us is the spiritual, then love of mankind is brotherly love toward those who have shared the same spirit. And cherishing, again, is the keeping of goodwill or of fondness; and fondness is a complete acceptance, and to love is to be pleased with the character, being led toward and away. And men are led into sameness through concord, which is the science of common goods; for concord too is a harmony of judgments. And "let love be unfeigned among us," he says, "and let us ourselves, abhorring the evil, become joined to the good in brotherly love," and the rest, down to "if possible, as far as in you lies, being at peace with all men." Then he says, "Be not overcome by the evil, but overcome the evil in the good." And the same Apostle confesses to bear witness of the Jews that "they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge; for, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God." For they neither knew nor did the will of the law, but what they themselves supposed, this they thought the law too wished; nor did they believe the law as prophesying, but followed it by bare word and fear, not by disposition and faith. "For the end of the law is Christ unto righteousness" — the one prophesied by the law — "to everyone who believes."

But some, thinking themselves well-endowed, claim that one should touch neither philosophy nor dialectic, nor even learn natural contemplation, but require faith alone and bare — as if they expected, having taken no care of the vine, to gather the clusters straightway from the beginning. And the Lord is allegorized as the vine, from which, with care and the husbandry that is according to the Word, the fruit is to be gathered. One must prune, dig, tie up, and do the rest; and there is need, I think, of the pruning-hook and the mattock and the other husbandman's tools for the care of the vine, that it may show us the edible fruit. And just as in husbandry and in medicine the man of good learning is the one who has touched the more varied studies, so as to be able to farm and to heal the better, so here too I call the man of good learning the one who refers all things to the truth, so that, gathering the useful from geometry and music and grammar and philosophy itself, he keeps the faith guarded against plots. And the athlete too is looked down upon, as has been said, yet contributes to the whole array.

Whence it is said to these by Moses: "I will provoke you to jealousy over what is no nation; over a nation without understanding I will anger you" — meaning, of course, the nation made ready for obedience. And through Isaiah he says: "I was found by those who did not seek me; I became manifest to those who did not ask after me" — before the coming of the Lord, that is; after which those prophesied things too are now fittingly said of Israel: "I stretched out my hands all the day to a disobedient and gainsaying people." You see the cause of the calling from the nations plainly stated by the prophet — the disobedience and gainsaying of the people? Then the goodness of God is shown even in these things; for the Apostle says: "But by their falling away salvation came to the nations, to provoke them to jealousy and to make them wish to repent." And the Shepherd, having put the saying simply about those who have fallen asleep, knows certain just men among the nations and among the Jews, not only before the coming of the Lord, but also before the law, according to their pleasing of God, like Abel, like Noah, like any other just man.

So we praise the pilot of much experience, "who saw the cities of many men," and the physician who has come to be in the experience of many — by which some even mould the empiric. And the man who refers each thing to the right life, bringing examples both from Greek and from barbarian sources, this man of much experience is a tracker of the truth and truly "of many counsels," being able, after the manner of the touchstone (the Lydian stone, believed to distinguish the spurious from the genuine gold), to separate — our man of much skill and gnostic — sophistic from philosophy, beautifying-art from gymnastic, cookery from medicine, and rhetoric from dialectic, and magic and the other heretical schools according to the barbarian philosophy from the truth itself. And how is it not necessary, for the man who longs to become a partaker of the power of God, to discourse, in philosophizing, about intelligible things? And how is it not useful to distinguish the ambiguous expressions and those uttered with the same name across the covenants? For it is by ambiguity that the Lord outwits the devil at the time of the temptation; and I, for one, no longer see here how the inventor of philosophy and of dialectic, as some suppose, is led astray, deceived in the manner of ambiguity.

So he says that the apostles and teachers who preached the name of the Son of God and fell asleep, in power and faith, preached to those who had fallen asleep before. Then he adds: "And they themselves gave them the seal of the preaching. They went down, then, with them into the water, and again came up. But these went down living and again came up living; while those who had fallen asleep before went down dead and came up living. Through these, then, they were made alive and came to know the name of the Son of God. For this reason they also came up together with them and were fitted together into the building of the tower, and were built in unhewn; for they fell asleep in righteousness and in great purity, only this seal they had not." "For when the nations that do not have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves," according to the Apostle.

And if the prophets and the apostles did not know the arts through which the exercises of philosophy are displayed, yet the mind of the prophetic and teaching Spirit, spoken in a hidden way because the understanding hearing is not of all, requires the arts of skill for the clearness of teaching. For the prophets and the disciples of the Spirit knew that mind securely; for it was from faith, and, as the Spirit has said, not easily. But it is not possible so to receive it for those who have not learned. "And write down the commandments," it says, "doubly, with will and knowledge, that you may answer words of truth to those who put questions to you." What, then, is the knowledge of answering? The same as that of asking; and this would be dialectic. And what — is not the saying also a work, and does the doing not come from reason? For if we did not act by reason, we would act unreasonably. And the rational work is accomplished according to God; and "nothing," it says, "came to be without him," the Word of God. Or did not the Lord too do all things by the Word? And the cattle too work, driven by the compelling of fear. And do not those called the orthodox-minded apply themselves to good works, not knowing what they do?

That the virtues follow one another reciprocally, what need is there to say, since it has already been shown that faith is upon repentance and hope, and caution upon faith, and that the abiding in these and the exercise, together with learning, are brought to completion in love, which in turn is perfected by knowledge? But this must of necessity be noted: that the divine alone must be conceived as wise by nature; wherefore wisdom too is the power of God that has taught the truth; and here, somewhere, the perfecting of knowledge has been taken. And the philosopher loves and is fond of the truth, being, from a genuine servant, already reckoned a friend through love. And the beginning of this is to wonder at the things that are, as Plato says in the Theaetetus, and as Matthias too, in the Traditions, advises: "Wonder at the things present," laying this down as the first step toward the knowledge beyond. So in the Gospel according to the Hebrews too it is written: "He who has wondered will reign, and he who has reigned will rest." It is impossible, then, for the unlearned, so long as he remains unlearned, to philosophize — at least the man who has not received a notion of wisdom, philosophy being a reaching after the truly existing and after the studies that tend toward this. And even if doing well is practised by some, yet the knowing how one must use and do must be worked out together, in respect of which one is also made like to God — to God, I mean, the Saviour — serving the God of the universe through the high-priestly Word, through whom are beheld the things that are truly noble and just. Reverence . . . is an action that follows and is consequent upon God.

But the gnostic dignity is heightened still further and more in the one who has taken up the presidency of teaching others, undertaking in word and deed the dispensation of the greatest good upon earth, through which he mediates conjunction and fellowship toward the Divine. And as those who do service to earthly things pray to the images as though they heard, making their firm agreements upon them, so, in the case of the living images—men—the true magnificence of the Word is received from the trustworthy teacher, and the benefit done to these is referred to the Lord himself, after whose image the man who is truly a man, in teaching, fashions and transforms anew unto salvation the man being catechized. For as the Greeks call iron "Ares" and wine "Dionysus," by a certain reference, so the gnostic, reckoning the benefit of his neighbours to be his own salvation, would reasonably be called a living image of the Lord—not in respect of the property of form, but in respect of the symbol of power and the likeness of his preaching.

Whatever, then, he has in mind, this he also carries upon the tongue toward those worthy to hear, out of assent, speaking from judgement and at the same time living it. For he both thinks true things and speaks the truth—except when, perchance, by way of treatment, like a physician toward the sick for the salvation of the suffering, he will lie, or speak a falsehood, as the sophists put it. Thus the noble Apostle circumcised Timothy, though he cried aloud and wrote that circumcision made with hands profits nothing; but lest, by tearing them all at once away from the Law toward the circumcision of the heart that is of faith, he should compel the Hebrew hearers, who were still unbridled, to break away from the synagogue—accommodating himself to the Jews, he "became a Jew, that he might gain all." He, then, who descends only as far as accommodation, for the sake of his neighbours' salvation—the bare accommodation for the salvation of those for whose sake he accommodates himself—partaking of no hypocrisy, because of the danger that hangs over the just from the jealous, this man is in no way compelled; but only for the benefit of his neighbours will he do certain things which he would not otherwise have done for their own sake, were he not doing them on their account. This man gives himself for the Church, for the friends whom he himself "begot" in faith, as an example to those able to take up the supreme dispensation of the man-loving and God-loving teacher—for the establishment of the truth of his words, for the operation of his love toward the Lord. He is unenslaved by fear, true in word, patient in toil, unwilling ever to lie even in the spoken word, and in this too always achieving sinlessness. For the lie itself, being spoken with a certain deceit, is no idle word, but works toward evil.

On every side, then, the gnostic alone bears witness to the truth, both in deed and in word; for he always does rightly in all things absolutely—in word and in act and in the very thought. This, then, to speak as in a running survey, is the godliness of the Christian. If indeed he does these things fittingly and according to right reason, he does them devoutly and justly. And if these things are so, the gnostic alone would be in truth devout and just and godly. The Christian, then, is not an atheist—for this was what was proposed to be shown to the philosophers—so that he will in no way ever do anything evil or shameful, which is unjust. Accordingly, neither is he impious, but he alone is in truth godly, holily and fittingly approaching, according to the true godliness, the God who truly is—the all-ruling and all-kingly and almighty—holily turning toward him.

But, as it seems, in my zeal for demonstration I have unawares digressed beyond what is needful. For life will fail me as I set forth the multitude of those who philosophized in symbols. For the sake, then, of memory, and of brevity, and of being stretched out toward the truth, such are the writings of the barbarian philosophy. For they will have the truly true philosophy and the true theology belong only to those who have often drawn near to these writings and have given proof in faith and in their whole life. Indeed, they will have us in need of some interpreter and guide; for thus, they reckoned, the worthy would the more give themselves to study and be benefited, and would not be deceived, receiving the teaching from those who well know. And besides, all things that show through some veil display the truth as greater and more august — as fruits gleaming through water, and forms through veils which lend them certain added showings. For things in full glare both prove deceptive and let only what is plain be perceived in a single way.

It is possible, then, to take many connected meanings, as indeed we do take them, from things said with concealment. And, this being so, the inexperienced and unlearned man goes astray, but the gnostic apprehends. For this very reason they did not wish all things to be set forth nakedly to the chance comer, nor the goods of wisdom to be made common to those who have not even in a dream had their soul cleansed; for it is not lawful to hold out to all comers the things won with so great toils, nor to declare the mysteries of the Word to the profane. They say, for instance, that Hipparchus the Pythagorean, being charged with having written down the doctrines of Pythagoras plainly, was cast out of the school, and a pillar was set up over him as over one dead. Hence in the barbarian philosophy too they call dead those who have fallen away from the doctrines and have subjected the mind to the passions of the soul. "For what fellowship has righteousness with lawlessness," according to the divine apostle, "or what communion has light with darkness? And what concord has Christ with Belial, or what part has a believer with an unbeliever?" For apart are the honours of the Olympians and of the dead. "Therefore come out from among them and be separate," says the Lord, "and touch no unclean thing; and I will receive you, and I will be a Father to you, and you shall be my sons and daughters."

It was not the Pythagoreans, then, and Plato alone who hid most of their teaching; the Epicureans too say that there are certain secret things even of his, and that they do not permit all to come upon these writings. And the Stoics too say that certain things were written by Zeno the first, which they do not readily permit the disciples to read, unless they have first given proof whether they philosophize genuinely. And the Aristotelians say that of his writings some are esoteric, and some common and exoteric. And those who established the mysteries, being philosophers, buried their own doctrines in myths, so that they should not be plain to all. If, then, these men, hiding away human opinions, kept the unlearned from coming upon them, was it not the more fitting that the truly holy and blessed contemplation of the things that really are should be concealed from everyone? Yet neither the things of the barbarian philosophy, nor the Pythagorean myths, nor even those in Plato — of Er the son of Armenius in the Republic, of Aeacus and Rhadamanthus in the Gorgias, of Tartarus in the Phaedo, of Prometheus and Epimetheus in the Protagoras, and besides these the myth of the war of the men of Atlantis and the Athenians in the Atlanticus — are to be allegorized outright in every name, but only so much of them as is significant of the general thought; and these things, indeed, we should find indicated through symbols under the veil of allegory.

Indeed the assembly of Pythagoras too, and his twofold fellowship with his hearers — calling the many "auditors," and certain others, who genuinely laid hold of philosophy, "mathematicians" — hinted that some things are to be spoken and some kept hidden from the many. And perhaps that twofold division of the Peripatetics too, called in their discourses the "probable" and the "scientific," is not free of a distinguishing of opinion from good repute and truth: "Let not the flower of glorious honour from mortals force you to take it up, on condition of speaking beyond what is holy." The Ionian Muses, at any rate, plainly say that the many and the seeming-wise "follow the singers of the people, and use the customs, knowing that many are bad, but few good; while the best pursue glory." For "the best choose one thing in place of all," it says, "everlasting glory among mortals; but the many are glutted like cattle," measuring happiness by the belly and the privy parts and the basest of the things within us. And the Eleatic Parmenides the great brings in a teaching of two ways, writing somewhat thus: "Both the unshaken heart of well-persuasive Truth, and the opinions of mortals, in which is no true faith."

Those who set themselves against the creation of God through their fair-named continence cite also those things spoken to Salome, which we mentioned earlier; they are reported, I think, in the Gospel according to the Egyptians. For they say that the Saviour Himself said: "I came to destroy the works of the female"—by "the female" meaning desire, and by its "works" generation and decay. What then would they say? Has this administration been destroyed? They would not say so; for the world remains under the same dispensation. But the Lord did not lie; for in truth He destroyed the works of desire—love of money, contentiousness, love of glory, madness for women, pederasty, gluttony, profligacy, and the like; of which the generation is the corruption of the soul, since we become dead through our trespasses; and this was the female—incontinence. But generation and decay in the creation must necessarily come about, as the primary thing, until the complete separation and the restoration of the elect, on account of which even the substances commingled with the world are assigned to their proper places.

Hence it is fitting that, when the Word had signified the consummation, Salome said: "Until when shall men die?" Now Scripture calls "man" in two ways: both the visible man and the soul; and again, the man who is saved and the one who is not. And the death of the soul is called sin. Therefore the Lord answers guardedly: "As long as women bear children"—that is, as long as the desires are active. "For this reason, as through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so death passed to all men, in that all sinned; and death reigned from Adam to Moses," says the apostle. But by a natural necessity of the divine dispensation death follows upon generation, and upon the union of soul and body there follows their dissolution. And if generation is for the sake of learning and knowledge, then dissolution is for the sake of restoration. And as woman is reckoned the cause of death because of bearing children, so for the same reason she shall be called the leader unto life.

So she who began the transgression was called "Life," because she becomes the cause of the succession both of those who are born and of those who sin—the mother alike of the righteous and of the unrighteous, since each of us makes himself righteous or, on the contrary, prepares himself for disobedience. Hence I, for my part, do not think the apostle loathes life in the flesh when he says: "But in all boldness, as always, now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. But if to live in the flesh—this too is for me the fruit of work; what I shall choose I do not know. I am hard pressed between the two, having the desire to depart and to be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake." For he showed clearly, I think, through these words, that the departure from the body is the perfection of love toward God, while the presence in the flesh is a thankful endurance for the sake of those who need to be saved.

But why do these men, who follow anything rather than the gospel rule that accords with truth, not bring forward also what follows in the words spoken to Salome? For when she said, "I did well, then, in not bearing children," as though it were not fitting to accept generation, the Lord answers, saying: "Eat every herb, but the one that has bitterness do not eat." For He signifies through these words too that it is in our power, and not by the constraint of a prohibiting commandment, to choose either continence or marriage; and further makes plain that marriage cooperates somewhat with the creation.

Let no one, then, count marriage according to reason a sin, unless he supposes the rearing of children to be bitter (for, on the contrary, to many childlessness is most grievous); nor, if the begetting of children seems bitter to anyone, drawing him away from divine things by its necessary occupations, let him who does not easily bear the solitary life desire marriage; for what is well-pleasing, when joined with prudence, is harmless, and each of us is master of the choice of whether to beget children. But I observe how some, on the pretext of marriage—those who have abstained from it not according to holy knowledge—have slid down into misanthropy, and love is gone from among them; while others, entangled in it and given to pleasure under the indulgence of the law, as the prophet says, have become like the beasts.

Concerning martyrdom the Lord has spoken expressly, and let us set in order the things written variously. "I say to you, everyone who confesses Me before men, the Son of Man too shall confess him before the angels of God; but the one who denies Me before men I shall deny before the angels. For whoever is ashamed of Me or of My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man too shall be ashamed of him when He comes in the glory of His Father with His angels. Everyone, then, who confesses Me before men, I also will confess him before My Father who is in heaven. And when they bring you into the synagogues and before the rulers and the authorities, do not be anxious beforehand how you shall make your defence or what you shall say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what must be said."

Heracleon, the most esteemed of the school of Valentinus, explaining this passage, says, word for word, that confession is of two kinds—the one in faith and conduct, the other in voice. The confession in voice, then, takes place also before the authorities, which alone, he says, the many wrongly suppose to be confession; and this confession the hypocrites too are able to make. But this saying will not be found to be spoken universally; for not all those who are saved made the confession through voice and so departed, among whom were Matthew, Philip, Thomas, Levi, and many others. And the confession through voice is not universal but partial. But the universal one, which He now speaks of, is the one in works and deeds corresponding to the faith in Him. And upon this confession there follows also the partial one, the one before the authorities, if it be necessary and reason require. For this man will confess also by voice, having rightly confessed beforehand in his disposition.

For such is the gnostic, that he meets only with those passions that come about for the maintenance of the body — such as hunger, thirst, and the like. But in the case of the Saviour, to say that the body demanded, as a body, the necessary ministrations for its maintenance, would be ridiculous; for he ate, not for the body's sake, held together by a holy power, but lest those with him should think otherwise about him — as indeed afterward some supposed that he had appeared in mere semblance; but he himself was downright impassible, into whom no passible movement entered, neither pleasure nor pain. And the apostles, having mastered, more gnostically, through the Lord's teaching, anger and fear and desire, did not so much as take on even the seeming goods among the passible movements — such as boldness, zeal, joy, cheerfulness — abiding in a fixed condition of mind, in no way changed at all, but ever remaining, after the Lord's resurrection, unaltered in the habit of discipline. For even if one should accept the aforesaid as goods when they come about with reason, yet in the case of the perfect man they are not to be admitted, who has neither boldness (for neither does he come to be in dread things, holding nothing in life dread, nor can anything draw him, even without this, from the love toward God), nor has need of cheerfulness (for neither does he fall into grief, persuaded that all things happen well), nor again is angered (for there is nothing to stir him to anger, ever loving God and being turned wholly toward him alone, and for this reason hating none of God's creatures); nor again is he jealous (for nothing is lacking to him for likeness to the noble and good); nor does he love anyone with this common love, but loves the Creator through the creatures.

And rightly, concerning those who confess, He said "in Me," but concerning those who deny He added "Me." For these, even if they confess Him by voice, deny Him by not confessing Him in deed. But those alone confess in Him who live in the confession and deed according to Him, in whom He too confesses, being clasped by them and held by them. Therefore they can never deny Him; but those deny Him who are not in Him. For He did not say "whoever denies in Me," but "Me"; for no one ever, being in Him, denies Him. And the "before men" applies likewise to those who are saved and to the Gentiles: before the former by conduct, before the latter by voice.

Neither, then, does he fall into any desire or craving, nor is he in want, as touching his soul, of any of the rest, dwelling already through love with the Beloved, to whom he is made akin by his choice, and by the habit that comes of discipline drawing nearer to him; being blessed by reason of the abundance of good things, so that for these things' sake he forces himself to be made like to the teacher unto impassibility. For the Word of God is intellectual, in respect of which the image of mind is seen in man alone, by which the good man is godlike and godlike in soul as to his soul, and again God is man-shaped; for the form of each is the mind, by which we are characterized. Wherefore those who sin against a man are both unholy and impious. For it is foolery too to say that the gnostic and perfect man ought not to be stripped of anger and boldness, as though without these he would neither rise up against difficulties nor endure dreadful things.

Thus far Heracleon; and in other respects he seems to hold the same opinion as we do in this passage, but he did not attend to this: that even if some have not confessed Christ before men in deed and in life, yet by confessing in voice in the courts and not denying Him even to death under torture, they show that they have believed from disposition. And a confessed disposition, especially one not turned aside even by death, makes a cutting-off, at one stroke, of all the passions that were begotten through bodily desire. For there is, so to speak, at the end of life a sudden repentance in deed and a true confession to Christ, the voice bearing witness. And if the Spirit of the Father bears witness in us, how are they still hypocrites, of whom He said that they bear witness by voice only? But to some it will be granted, if it be profitable, to make a defence, so that through both the martyrdom and the defence all may be benefited—those in the Church being strengthened, and those of the Gentiles who have inquired curiously into salvation being filled with wonder and led to faith, and the rest held fast by amazement.

But if we should take cheerfulness too from him, he would surely be confounded by grievous things, and so make a most wretched end of living. And if desire did not belong to him, as some have thought, he could not, they say, take a craving for the things like to the noble and good. If, then, all familiarity with the noble comes about with craving, how does he who craves the noble remain impassible? But these men, as it seems, do not know the divineness of love; for love is no longer a craving on the part of the lover, but an affectionate familiarity, which has restored the gnostic into the unity of the faith, having no further need of time or place. For he who has come to be, through love, already in the things in which he shall be, having grasped hope beforehand through knowledge, craves nothing, holding, so far as may be, the very thing craved. With reason, then, he abides in the one unchangeable habit, loving gnostically; nor will he be jealous to be made like to the noble, having beauty through love. And what further need has such a one of boldness and desire, who has received, through love, familiarity with the impassible God, and through love has enrolled himself among the friends?

So that one must confess in every case, for this lies in our power; but to make a defence is not in every case, for this too is not in our power. "But the one who endures to the end, he shall be saved." For who of those who think rightly would not choose to reign in God rather than to serve? Some, then, confess that they know God, according to the apostle, but by their works deny Him, being abominable and disobedient and reprobate toward every good work; while others, even if they confess only this, have accomplished at the end one good work. Martyrdom, then, seems to be a purifying of sins with glory. So at once the Shepherd says: "You shall escape the energy of the wild beast if your heart becomes pure and blameless." But the Lord Himself too says: "Satan asked to sift you; but I prayed for you."

We must, then, set apart for ourselves the gnostic and perfect man from every passion of the soul. For knowledge works training, and the training a habit or disposition, and such a state works impassibility, not moderation of passion; for the complete cutting out of desire reaps impassibility as its fruit. But neither does the gnostic partake of those much-talked-of goods — that is, the passible goods that lie beside the passions; I mean such as gladness (which lies beside pleasure) and dejection (for this is yoked to grief) and caution (for this has subsided from fear), nor yet of spirited anger (for this is ranked beside wrath).

The Lord, then, first drank the cup, for the purifying of the men who plotted against Him and of the unbelievers; in imitation of whom the apostles, as being truly gnostic and perfect, suffered for the churches which they founded. So then those gnostics too who walk in the apostolic footstep ought both to be sinless and, out of love toward the Lord, to love their neighbour too, so that, if the occasion should call, enduring the afflictions without stumbling for the Church's sake, they may drink the cup. And those who bear witness in deed throughout their life, and in word in the court—even if they look forward to a hope, even if they shrink in fear—these are better than those who confess salvation with the mouth only. But if anyone should go beyond, to love, he is truly blessed and a genuine martyr, having confessed perfectly both to the commandments and to God through the Lord, whom, loving, he recognized as brother, having given himself wholly out of love toward God, giving back, like a deposit, in a grateful and loving way, the man who was demanded back.

Even though some say that these are no longer evils, but already goods. For it is impossible that one once perfected through love, and feasting everlastingly and insatiably on the unfilled gladness of contemplation, should still take delight in small and groundling things. For what reasonable cause is left to such a one to run back to worldly goods, who has received the unapproachable light — even if not yet according to time and place, yet by that gnostic love, by which the inheritance and the complete restoration follow, the rewarder confirming by deeds what the gnostic, by gnostic choice through love, has grasped beforehand? For does he not, sojourning toward the Lord through love toward him — even though his tabernacle be beheld upon earth — not lead himself out of life (for that is not permitted him), but lead his soul out of the passions (for that is granted him), and live again, having mortified the desires, and no longer use the body, but only permit it to use the necessary things, lest he furnish the cause of its dissolution?

How, then, has such a one further need of courage, who does not come to be in dread things, being not present in them, but already wholly dwelling with the Beloved? And what need of temperance to one who has no need of it? For to have such desires as to need temperance for the restraining of them belongs not yet to the pure, but to the passible man; and courage is taken on by reason of fear and cowardice. For it is no longer fitting that the friend of God, whom God foreordained before the foundation of the world to be enrolled in the highest adoption, should fall into pleasures or fears and busy himself about the restraining of the passions. For I would dare to say: as he lies foreordained, by what he shall do, to attain what he shall attain, so too he himself holds foreordained, by what he has known, the one whom he loved, not having the future hard to conjecture, as the many live conjecturing, but having received, through gnostic faith, what to others is unseen.

And to him, through love, the future is already present; for he has believed, both through the prophecy and through the coming, in the God who does not lie; and what he has believed, he has and holds fast — the promise (and Truth is he who promised) — and the end of the promise, through the trustworthiness of him who promised, he has received surely, by science. And he who knows the sure apprehension of things to come, in the state in which he is, through love runs forward to meet the future. For instance, he who is persuaded that he shall attain the truly good things will not even pray to attain the things here, but rather to cling ever to the faith that hits the mark and sets things right. And besides these, he will pray that as many as may be become like to himself, unto the glory of God, which is perfected by recognition; for a saving thing is he who is made like to the Saviour, in so far as it is lawful for human nature to contain the image, setting straight, inviolably, the things according to the commandments. And he whose part it is to worship the divine through true righteousness, both of deeds and of knowledge —

of such a one the Lord does not wait for the voice in prayer, saying, "Ask, and I will do; think, and I will give." For, taken generally, in that which changes the unchangeable cannot take firm setting and standing; and in continual change, and therefore in an unstable ruling part, the steadying power is not preserved. For that which is ever altered by the things that creep in from without and fall upon it — how could it ever come to be in a habit and disposition, and, in a word, in the possession of science? And yet the philosophers too hold the virtues to be habits and dispositions and sciences. And that knowledge is not born together with men, but is an acquired thing, and the learning of it has need of attention in the beginning, and of nourishment and increase, and then, from unceasing study, comes into a habit — so, perfected into the mystic habit, it abides unfailing through love. For not only has he apprehended the first cause and the cause begotten by it, and holds firmly concerning these, having gotten abiding reasons abidingly, unfailing and unmoved; but also, concerning goods and evils, and concerning all becoming, and, in a word, concerning the things of which the Lord spoke, he holds the most exact truth, from the foundation of the world to the end, having learned it from the truth itself — not, if anywhere something appear plausible or compelling by Greek reasoning, choosing this before the truth itself, but having taken the things spoken by the Lord plain and manifest. And even if to others they are still hidden, he has already taken the knowledge of all things. And our oracles give their utterance concerning the things that are, that they are; concerning the things to come, that they shall be; and concerning the things that have come about, that they came about.

And in scientific matters, being alone the man of science, he will hold the first place and represent the doctrine of the Good, ever clinging to the things of mind, and from those archetypes above transcribing the ordering of his affairs among men — as those who sail and steer the ship toward the star — being prepared to hold himself ready for every fitting action, accustomed to look down on all things troublesome and dread, whenever he must endure, doing nothing rash nor out of tune, either with himself or with the common good, ever; being foreseeing, and unbending to pleasures both waking and in dreams. For accustomed to a frugal diet and to self-sufficiency temperately, he is well-girt with dignity, needing few of the necessary things for living, busying himself with nothing superfluous; nor admitting even these as chief things, but as necessary, by reason of fellowship in life, to the sojourn of the flesh, so far as is needful; for knowledge is his chief concern.

For this reason, then, the Saviour, having taken bread, first spoke and gave thanks; then, having broken the bread, set it forth, that we might eat rationally, and, recognizing the Scriptures, might order our life in obedience. And just as those who use a wicked word differ in nothing from those who use a wicked deed (for slander is the servant of the sword, and blasphemy breeds grief, from which come the overthrows of life — and these would be works of the wicked word), so too those who use a good word come near to those who accomplish the noble works. So the word too restores the soul and exhorts toward nobility; and "blessed is the man of ready hand on both sides." The benefactor, then, must not be reviled by the one able to speak well, nor must the one able to speak well be reviled by the one fit to do well; but let each act in that for which he is naturally fitted. What, then, the one shows by deed, the other speaks, as one preparing the way for the well-doing and leading the hearers to beneficence. For there is also a saving word, as there is a saving deed; righteousness, at any rate, is not established without the word.

Three things, then, does our own philosopher hold to: first, contemplation; second, the fulfilling of the commandments; third, the equipping of good men — which, coming together, complete the gnostic. And whatever of these is lacking, the things of knowledge go lame. Whence divinely the Scripture says: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: I am the Lord your God. According to the pursuits of the land of Egypt, in which you dwelt, you shall not do; and according to the pursuits of the land of Canaan, into which I bring you there, you shall not do; and in their customs you shall not walk. My judgments you shall do, and my ordinances you shall keep, to walk in them: I am the Lord your God. And you shall keep all my ordinances and do them. The man who does them shall live in them: I am the Lord your God."

And as the receiving of good is taken away, if we take away the doing of good, so obedience and faith are done away when neither the commandment nor the one who will make the commandment clear is taken along with it. But as it is, we are well supplied, for one another's sake, both with words and with deeds. But the eristic and sophistic art must be wholly declined, since the very phrases of the sophists not only bewitch and rob the many, but, forcing the issue, have sometimes carried off a Cadmean victory. For more than anything that psalm is true: "The righteous shall live unto the end, for he shall not see corruption, when he sees the wise dying." Whom, then, does it call wise? Hear from the wisdom of Jesus: "Wisdom is not the knowledge of wickedness." This he means, which the arts of speech and of dialectic have devised. "You will seek wisdom among the wicked and will not find it." And if you ask again, of what sort is this? "The mouth of the righteous," it will say to you, "will distil wisdom." But the sophistic art is called wisdom by the same name as the truth.

Whether, then, Egypt and the land of Canaan are a symbol of the world and of deceit, or of passions and vices, from which one must abstain, and what things are to be practised as divine and not worldly, the oracle shows us. And when it says, "The man who does them shall live in them," it calls life both the correction of the Hebrews themselves and the joint-exercise and advance of those near, of our very selves. For "those dead in trespasses are made alive together with Christ" through our covenant. And the Scripture, often repeating "I am the Lord your God," most turningly puts us to shame, teaching us to follow the God who gave the commandments; and it gently reminds us to seek God and to attempt to know him so far as may be — which would be the greatest contemplation, the higher vision, the science in truth, that which comes to be unwavering by reason. This alone would be the knowledge of wisdom, from which right action is never separated.

And it is, I think, with reason, set before me to live according to the Word and to understand the things signified, but, never being a zealot for fine speech, to be content only with hinting at what is meant. And by what name this is shown which I wish to present, I care nothing. For I know well that to be saved, and to lend a hand to those who long to be saved, is best, not to compose little phrases like ornaments. "And if you keep," says the Pythagorean in Plato's Statesman, "the not being in earnest about names, you will appear richer in prudence toward old age." And in the Theaetetus too you would find again: "And the easy use of names and verbs, not examined with exactness, is for the most part not ignoble, but rather its opposite is illiberal, though it is sometimes necessary." These things the Scripture brought out as briefly as may be, saying: "Be not much in words"; for the phrasing is like clothing on the body, but the matters are flesh and sinews. One must not, then, care for the clothing before the safety of the body. For not only a frugal diet, but also a discourse plain and without superfluity, must be practised by the man who has taken up the true life — if indeed we decline luxury as deceitful and prodigal, just as the ancient Spartans declined perfume and purple, supposing rightly — and naming them rightly — the garments "deceitful" and the unguents "deceitful," since neither is that a noble preparing of food which has more seasonings than nourishment, nor that an elegant use of speech which is able to delight the hearers rather than to benefit them. Pythagoras advises us to think the Muses sweeter than the Sirens, teaching to practise the parts of wisdom without pleasure, and refuting the rest of soul-leading as deceitful. To sail past the Sirens, one suffices; and to answer the Sphinx, another one; or, if you will, not even one.

We must not, then, ever broaden our phylacteries, being zealots for vainglory; it suffices the gnostic even if a single hearer be found. It is possible, at any rate, to hear Pindar the Boeotian too, writing: "Not to all is the ancient discourse to be broken open; sometimes the ways of silence are most trustworthy, and the prevailing word is a goad of battle." The blessed Apostle, then, very earnestly insists, exhorting us not to wrangle about words for nothing useful, to the overthrow of the hearers, but to shun the profane empty talkings; "for they advance further in impiety, and their word will have a spreading like a gangrene."

For knowledge is, so to speak, a kind of perfecting of man as man, completed through the science of things divine, in character and in life and in word—in accord and agreement with itself and with the divine Word. For through it faith is perfected, the believer becoming perfect in this way alone. Faith, then, is a kind of inward good, which, even without seeking God, confesses that he is and glorifies him as existing. Whence one must, being led up from this faith and increased in it by the grace of God, attain the knowledge concerning him, as far as may be. And we say that knowledge differs from the wisdom which comes into being through teaching: for wherever there is any knowledge, there is also, by all means, wisdom; but wherever there is any wisdom, there is not by all means knowledge—for it is only in the matter of the spoken word that the name of wisdom appears. Nevertheless, not to doubt concerning God, but to believe, is the foundation of knowledge; and both are Christ—both the foundation and the building upon it, through whom are both the beginning and the ends. And the extremes are not taught—the beginning and the end, I mean faith and love; but knowledge, handed down by tradition according to the grace of God to those who show themselves worthy of the teaching, is entrusted like a deposit, from which the worth of love shines forth, from light to light. For it is said, "to him who has it shall be added"—to faith, knowledge; to knowledge, love; and to love, the inheritance.

And this comes about whenever a man is hung upon the Lord through faith and through knowledge and through love, and ascends together with him to where the God and Guardian of our faith and love is. Whence at the end knowledge is handed down to those fit for it and approved—because there is need of more preparation and previous training, both toward the hearing of the things spoken, and toward the composure of life, and toward having advanced, by intensity, beyond the righteousness that is according to the Law. This knowledge leads us to the endless and perfect end, teaching us beforehand the manner of life we shall have, according to God, with gods, once we have been freed from all chastisement and punishment—which we endure, because of our sins, for our saving instruction. After this redemption the reward and the honours are rendered to those made perfect, when they have ceased from purification and ceased from all other ministry, even if it be holy and among holy ones. Then, having become pure in heart, in nearness to the Lord there awaits them, by the eternal contemplation, the restoration; and they are called by the name of "gods," being destined to be enthroned together with the other gods who are ranked first under the Saviour. Swift, then, unto purification is knowledge, and well suited to the welcome change toward the better.

Whence it easily transfers a man into that which is kindred to the soul—the divine and holy—and through a certain proper light leads him across, by his mystic advances, until it restores him to the highest place of rest, having taught the pure in heart to behold God face to face, with science and with comprehension. For here, in a manner, is the perfection of the gnostic soul: to come to be with the Lord, having passed beyond all purification and ministry, where it is in immediate subjection to him. Faith, then, is, so to speak, a compendious knowledge of the things that press upon us; but knowledge is a strong and firm demonstration of the things received through faith, built up upon faith through the Lord's teaching, conveying us on toward that which is unwavering and grasped with science. And there seems to me to be a first saving change—that from the heathen into faith, as I said before—and a second, that from faith into knowledge; and this last, passing on into love, thereupon presents the knower as a friend to the friend, the knowing to the known.

The first mode of the Lord's working is a token of the requital that I spoke of, which is according to godliness. Of many testimonies that there are, I shall set forth one summarily, spoken thus by the prophet David: "Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He that is innocent in hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain nor sworn deceitfully to his neighbour: this man shall receive a blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour. This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob." Concisely, I think, the prophet has indicated the gnostic; and, in passing, David has shown us, as it seems, that the Saviour is God, calling him "the face of the God of Jacob"—he who brought the good news and taught concerning the Father. Therefore the Apostle too named the Son "the express character of the Father's glory"—him who taught the truth concerning God, and stamped it that "God and Father is one" and alone the Almighty, "whom no one has known except the Son, and he to whom the Son reveals him." And that God is one is signified by the words "of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob," whom our Saviour and God characterizes as the "only" God, the Father, the "good." And the generation of those who seek him is "the elect race," that which seeks toward knowledge.

For this reason too the Apostle says: "I shall profit you nothing, unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching." And yet certain things are done rightly even by those who are not gnostic, but not according to reason—as in the case of courage. For some, being by nature high-spirited, and then having nourished this without reason, rush irrationally upon most things and do deeds like those of the courageous, so that sometimes they achieve the same things—such as enduring tortures easily; yet neither from the same cause as the gnostic, nor with the same purpose, not even "if they give up the whole body"; for "they have not love," in the Apostle's phrase, the love begotten through knowledge. Every action, then, done through the man of knowledge is a doing well, but that done through the man without knowledge is a doing ill, even if he keeps to his resolve—since he does not play the man out of reasoning, nor direct the action toward anything useful, toward virtue and away from virtue. And the same account holds of the other virtues, so that it holds proportionally of godliness too. Not only, then, is the gnostic such for us in respect of holiness, but consequent upon scientific godliness are also the professions concerning the rest of his conduct. For our purpose now is to describe the life of the gnostic, not to set forth the contemplation of doctrines, which we shall expound later at the fitting season, preserving at the same time the proper sequence.

With reason, then, the inspired apostle says: "By revelation was made known to me the mystery, as I wrote before in few words, by which, when you read, you may understand my insight into the mystery of Christ, which in other generations was not made known to the sons of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets." For there is a certain learning of the perfect, concerning which, writing to the Colossians, he says: "We do not cease to pray for you and to ask, that you may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding, to walk worthily of the Lord unto all pleasing, bearing fruit in every good work and growing in the knowledge of God, being strengthened with all power according to the might of his glory." And again: "according to the dispensation of God given to me," he says, "toward you, to fulfil the word of God, the mystery which has been hidden from the ages and from the generations, but now has been made manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make known what is the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles."

So that there are, on the one hand, the mysteries hidden until the apostles, and delivered by them as they received them from the Lord — hidden in the old covenant — which have now been made manifest to the saints; and, on the other hand, "the riches of the glory of the mystery among the Gentiles," which is faith and hope toward Christ, whom elsewhere he has called a foundation. And again, as it were ambitious to make knowledge plain, he writes somewhat thus: "Admonishing every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ." Not every man simply, since then there would be no unbeliever; nor again every believer perfect in Christ, but he says "every man," meaning, so to speak, the whole man, purified in body and in soul. For, that knowledge is not for all, he plainly adds: "knit together in love, and unto all the riches of the full assurance of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery of God in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Continue steadfastly in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving." And the thanksgiving is made not for the soul only and for spiritual goods, but also for the body and for the goods of the body.

And still more plainly he uncovers that knowledge is not for all, adding: "Praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which also I am bound, that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak." For there were certain things delivered without writing. To the Hebrews, for instance, he says: "And though you ought to be teachers by reason of the time" — that is, as having grown old in the old covenant — "you have need again that someone teach you what are the elements of the beginning of the oracles of God, and you have become such as have need of milk and not of solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unacquainted with the word of righteousness, for he is a babe, entrusted with the first lessons; but solid food is for the perfect, for those who through habit have their senses exercised to discern good and evil. Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us press on toward perfection."

But Barnabas too, who himself co-proclaimed the word with the apostle in the ministry to the Gentiles, says: "I write to you more simply, that you may understand." Then, a little later, already setting down a trace of the gnostic tradition more plainly, he says: "What says the other prophet, Moses, to them? 'Behold, thus says the Lord God: Enter into the good land which the Lord swore to give — the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob — and inherit it, a land flowing with milk and honey.' What does knowledge say? Learn. Hope, it says, upon him who is about to be made manifest to you in the flesh, Jesus; for a man is earth that suffers, since out of the face of the earth was the moulding of Adam. What then does it mean, 'into the good land, a land flowing with milk and honey'? Blessed be our Lord, brethren, who has set wisdom and understanding of his hidden things in us. For the prophet says, 'Who shall understand a parable of the Lord, except the wise and understanding man, and he who loves his Lord?'" — since it is given to few to contain these things. For "not out of envy," he says, "did the Lord proclaim, in a certain Gospel, 'My mystery is for me and for the sons of my house'" — making his election in safety and without anxiety, that the household of those he has chosen, having received what is proper to them, may become superior to envy. For he who has no knowledge of good is evil, since there is one good, the Father; and to be ignorant of the Father is death, as to know him is eternal life, by participation in the power of the incorruptible. And not to be corrupted is to partake of divinity, while corruption is brought on by the falling away from the knowledge of God.

Again the prophet: "And I will give you treasures hidden, dark, unseen, that they may know that I am the Lord God." The like to these David too sings: "Behold, you have loved truth; the obscure and hidden things of your wisdom you have made plain to me." "For day to day utters speech" — that which is plainly written — "and night to night declares knowledge" — that which is hidden mystically; "and there are no words nor speeches whose voices are not heard" by God, who said, "Shall a man do anything in secret, and I shall not see him?" For this reason discipleship has been called enlightenment, as making plain the hidden things, when the teacher alone uncovers the lid of the ark — contrary to what the poets say of Zeus, that he laid hold of the jar of goods but opened the jar of ills. "I know that, coming to you," the apostle says, "I shall come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ" — calling the spiritual gift and the gnostic tradition, which, present, he longs to impart to them present (for these things could not be made plain by letter), the "fullness of Christ," "according to the revelation of a mystery kept silent through eternal times, but now made manifest through the prophetic Scriptures, and, by the command of the eternal God, made known to all the Gentiles unto the obedience of faith" — that is, to those of the Gentiles who believe, that he is; but to few of these is it shown what these mysteries are.

With reason, then, Plato too, in the Letters, treating of God, says: "It must be told you in riddles, so that, if the tablet should suffer anything in the recesses of sea or land, he who reads it may not understand." For the God of all, who is above all voice and all conception and all thought, could never be handed down in writing, being unspeakable by his own power. And this very thing Plato has shown, saying: "Looking, then, to these things, take heed lest you ever repent of what now falls out unworthily. The greatest safeguard is not to write, but to learn by heart; for it is not possible — it is not — that what is written should not fall out." Brother to these things are the words of the holy apostle Paul, who keeps the prophetic and truly ancient concealment, from which the noble doctrines flowed to the Greeks: "We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age that come to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom."

Then, a little further on, he teaches the caution to be used in the going-out of words to the many, in some such fashion as this: "And I, brethren, could not speak to you as to spiritual men, but as to fleshly, as to babes in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able; but neither even now are you able, for you are still fleshly." If, then, the milk is said by the apostle to be the food of babes, and the solid food the nourishment of the perfect, milk will be understood as the catechizing, the first food, as it were, of the soul, and the solid food as the contemplation that beholds — these are flesh and blood of the Word, that is, the apprehension of the divine power and substance. "Taste and see that the Lord is good," it says; for thus he imparts himself to those who partake more spiritually of such food, when the soul now nourishes itself, according to Plato the lover of truth. For the eating and drinking of the divine Word is knowledge of the divine substance. Therefore Plato too says, in the second book of the Republic: "Having sacrificed, not a swine, but some great and hard-to-find offering, we must thus inquire about God." And the apostle writes: "For our Passover has been sacrificed, even Christ" — a hard-to-find offering in truth, the Son of God being consecrated for us.

Who are the "two or three gathered in the name of Christ," among whom the Lord is in the midst? Does He not mean by "the three" husband and wife and child, since a wife is joined to a husband by God? But even if a man wishes to be unencumbered, not choosing the begetting of children because of the distraction of begetting children, "let him remain unmarried," says the apostle, "as I also am." They interpret the Lord as meaning that with the many is the Demiurge, the God who makes generation, but with the one, the elect, is the Saviour, who is plainly the Son of another God, the Good. But this is not so; rather, God is by His Son with those who marry prudently and beget children, and the same God likewise is with the man who is continent according to reason. But the "three" might also be otherwise—wrath, desire, and reason; or flesh, soul, and spirit, by another account.

And perhaps the aforesaid triad hints at the calling first, the election second, and third the class ranked into the first honour; with whom is the all-overseeing power of God, divided without division. He, then, who uses in due measure the natural activities of the soul desires the things that are suitable and hates the things that harm, as the commandments enjoin: "You shall bless the one who blesses, and curse the one who curses," it says. But when, rising above even these—wrath and desire—he loves the creation in deed for the sake of the God and Maker of all, he will live in a gnostic way, having acquired the effortless habit of continence in his likeness to the Saviour, having united knowledge, faith, and love, being one from this point on in his judgement, and truly spiritual, wholly and altogether unreceptive of the reasonings of wrath and desire—the man who is being perfected after the image of the Lord by the very Craftsman, the perfect man, already worthy to be called brother by the Lord, friend and son at once. So the two and the three are gathered together into the same thing—the gnostic man.

The concord of the many, too, might be reckoned from the three with whom the Lord is: the one Church, the one man, the one race. Or was it not that with the one—the Jew—the Lord was a lawgiver, and prophesying even then, sending Jeremiah to Babylon, but also calling those of the Gentiles through prophecy, He gathered the two peoples; and a third was created out of the two, one new man, in whom indeed He walks about and dwells, in that very Church? Law and prophets together with the gospel are gathered, in the name of Christ, into one knowledge. So those who do not marry out of hatred, or who use the flesh indifferently out of desire, are not in the number of those saved ones with whom the Lord is.

And when, on the contrary, He says, "When they persecute you in this city, flee to the other," He does not counsel flight as though being persecuted were evil, nor does He command us to shun it by flight as though fearing death; rather He wishes us to become to no one a cause or fellow-cause of any evil, whether to themselves or to the persecutor or to the slayer. For in a way He commands us to keep clear of it, and the man who disobeys is rash and reckless.

And if the man who kills a man of God sins against God, the one who brings himself to the court becomes guilty also of the deed of the man who kills him. This would be the man who does not keep clear of persecution, but offers himself to be taken through rashness. As far as in him lies, he becomes a fellow-worker in the wickedness of the persecutor; and if he should provoke besides, he is wholly the cause, calling forth the beast. And likewise, if he should provide some cause of strife or loss or enmity or lawsuit, he has begotten an occasion of persecution. For this reason it has been commanded us to hold to nothing of the things in this life. But even to the man who takes the cloak we are to give the tunic besides, not only that we may remain free from passionate attachment, but that, not contending, we may not enrage those who claim things against us, and through us stir up blasphemy against the name.

As a consequence, then, he gives himself also to the studies that train him toward knowledge, taking from each subject what is suited to the truth: from music, pursuing the proportion in things harmonized; in arithmetic, marking the increases and decreases of numbers, and their relations to one another, and how the most things fall under a certain proportion of numbers; in geometry, contemplating substance itself by itself, and accustoming himself to conceive a continuous extension and an unchangeable substance, other than these bodies; and from astronomy too, lifted from the earth by the mind, he will be raised on high with the heaven, and will go round in company with the revolution, ever observing the divine things and their harmony with one another — from which, setting out, Abraham mounted up to the knowledge of the Maker. And the gnostic will use dialectic too, choosing the division of the genera into species, and will take the discernment of the things that are, until he lays hold of the first and simple things. But the many, like children fearing the bugbears, so fear the Greek philosophy, fearing lest it lead them away.

But if their faith (for I would not call it knowledge) is such as to be dissolved by plausible speech, let it be dissolved; for thereby above all they confess that they have not the truth, since "the truth is unconquerable," it says, "but false opinion is dissolved." For instance, we choose out purple by setting it against other purple. So that if one confesses that he has not the heart well-jointed, he has not the table of the money-changers, nor the criterion of words. And how is this man still a money-changer, not being able to test and to discern the genuine coin from the counterfeit? And David cries out, "Because for ever the just man shall not be shaken" — neither by deceitful speech nor by misleading pleasure, whence neither shall he be shaken from his own inheritance. "From an evil report, then, he shall not be afraid" — neither, then, of empty slander, nor of false opinion concerning himself; nor will he fear the crafty words, being one able to discern these, both to ask rightly and to answer. For dialectic is, as it were, a coping that the truth be not trodden down by the sophists. For we who praise in the holy name of the Lord, according to the prophet, must make glad the heart, seeking the Lord. "Seek him, then, and be strengthened; seek his face continually in every way." For having spoken in many parts and in many ways, he is not known simply.

Not, then, as if using these as virtues will the gnostic be of much learning, but as certain helpers, and in distinguishing the common and the proper he will draw near the truth; for the cause of all error and false opinion is the not being able to discern in what the things that are share with one another and in what they differ. And if one should not go along the path of the argument according to the distinctions, he will, unawares, confound the common and the proper; and this coming about, he must of necessity fall into a trackless way and error. And the distinction of names and of things, even in the Scriptures themselves, engenders a great light in souls; for it is necessary to attend both to the words that signify several things, and to the several words, when they signify one and the same thing; whence comes the power of answering rightly. But the great uselessness must be declined, that busies itself about things of no concern; and the gnostic uses the studies as, so to speak, contributory preliminary exercises, both toward the exact delivery of the truth, so far as may be, and undistractedly, and toward the warding off of the ill-contrived arguments that aim at the cutting out of the truth.

He will not, then, be left behind those who advance in the encyclical studies and in the Greek philosophy; yet not according to the chief account, but according to the necessary and second and circumstantial; for those things which they who labour according to the heresies use cunningly, these the gnostic will use to good. Since, then, the truth that appears in the Greek philosophy is partial, the truly real truth, as the sun, shining upon the colours, both the white and the black, shows of what kind each of them is — so too does it refute every sophistical plausibility. With reason, then, was it proclaimed beforehand even to the Greeks: "Beginning of great virtue, queen, Truth."

But the knowledge of the reputed wise — whether they be barbarian heresies or the philosophers among the Greeks — "puffs up," according to the Apostle. But faithful is the knowledge which is a scientific demonstration of the things handed down according to the true philosophy. And we would say that it is a reasoning which furnishes faith for the things in dispute out of the things agreed upon. And faith being twofold, the one scientific, the other based on opinion, nothing hinders us from naming demonstration twofold, the one scientific, the other based on opinion — since knowledge too, and foreknowledge, are called twofold, the one having its own nature made exact, the other deficient. And surely the demonstration that is among us would alone be true, as being supplied from the divine Scriptures, the sacred writings, and the God-taught wisdom, according to the Apostle. Learning, at any rate, is also the obeying of the commandments, which is to believe God. And faith is a certain power of God, being a strength of the truth.

So it says: "If you have faith as a grain of mustard, you will remove the mountain"; and again, "According to your faith be it to you"; and the one is healed, having received the cure through his faith, and the other, who is dead, is raised through the strength of him who believed that he would rise. But the demonstration based on opinion is human, and comes from rhetorical arguments or dialectical syllogisms. For the highest demonstration, which we hinted to be scientific, sets faith in the souls of those who long to learn, through the setting-out and opening of the Scriptures — which would be knowledge. For if the things taken up toward the thing inquired are taken as true, as being divine and prophetic, it is plain that the conclusion drawn from them will, in consequence, be brought in as true; and rightly would knowledge be a demonstration for us.

"This wisdom of the world, then, is folly with God; and the Lord knows the reasonings of these wise men, that they are vain." Let no one, then, boast, holding himself up in human understanding. For well is it written in Jeremiah: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, and let not the strong man boast in his strength, and let not the rich man boast in his riches; but let him who boasts boast in this, to understand and to know that I am the Lord who does mercy and judgment and righteousness upon the earth, for in these is my will, says the Lord." "That we may not be trusting in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead," says the Apostle, "who delivered us from so great a death, that our faith may not be in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God. For the spiritual man examines all things, but is himself examined by no one." And I attend to those words of his too: "And this I say, that no one may deceive you with persuasive speech, nor that the spoiler come stealing in." And again: "See, then, that there be no one who carries you off as spoil through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ" — not all philosophy, but the Epicurean, which Paul also mentions in the Acts of the Apostles, slandering it as doing away with providence and deifying pleasure, and any other that has over-honoured the elements without setting over them the efficient cause, and has not imagined the Creator.

So when the memorial of the heavenly and divine food was commanded to be consecrated in a golden jar, "the gomor," it says, "was the tenth of the three measures." For in us ourselves three measures, three criteria, are indicated: perception of things of sense; of things said, both names and words, reason; and of things of thought, mind. The gnostic, then, will abstain from the sins that are according to reason and according to thought and according to perception and activity, having heard how "he who looked toward desire committed adultery," and having taken to mind that "blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God," and knowing that too, that "not the things that enter into the mouth defile the man, but those that come out through the mouth, these defile the man; for out of the heart come the reasonings." This, I think, is the true and just measure according to God, by which the things measured are measured — the decad that holds the man together, which, in summary, the aforesaid three measures showed. And it would be body and soul, and the five senses, and the vocal power and the seminal, and the rational or spiritual — or however you wish to call it.

But the Stoics too — whom he also mentions — say, not rightly, that God is a body and pervades the basest matter. By "human tradition" he means the logical quibbling.
