And so he writes those things as well: "Flee the newer inquiries, for such contentions are childish." But virtue is not a lover of boyish things, says the philosopher Plato; and our contest, according to Gorgias of Leontini, needs two virtues, boldness and wisdom: boldness, to endure the danger; wisdom, to know the riddle. For the Word, like the proclamation at Olympia, calls whoever is willing, but crowns the one who is able. The Word, then, does not want the believer to be unmoved toward truth and truly idle. "Seek," it says, "and you will find." But it brings the seeking to a finding, having driven out the empty chatter and approving the contemplation that fortifies our faith. "I say this," says the Apostle, "that no one may deceive you with persuasive speech" — meaning, of course, those who have learned to discern what is said by them, and have been taught to meet the objections brought forward.

And one must, so to speak, mounting up above all the others, stand upon the mind — just as, indeed, in the world, having leaped over the nine portions, the first being that of the four elements set in one region because of their equal change, and then the seven wandering and the eighth unwandering — coming to the perfect number above the nine, the tenth portion, to arrive at the knowledge of God, longing, in a word, after the Maker, after the creation. For this reason the tithes both of the ephi and of the victims were brought to God, and the feast of the Passover began from the tenth, being a passing over from every passion and every thing of sense. The gnostic, then, is fixed in faith; but the man of conceited wisdom willingly does not touch the truth, using unstable and unsettled impulses. With reason, then, it is written: "And Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Naid over against Eden"; and Naid is interpreted "tossing," Eden "delight." And faith and knowledge and peace are the delight, from which the man who disobeys is cast out; but the man of conceited wisdom from the beginning does not even wish to hear the divine commandments, but, like a self-taught one who has thrown off the rein, willingly removes into the surging tossing, going down to mortal and generated things from the knowledge of the ungenerated, holding now one opinion, now another. "And those who have no guidance fall like leaves." Reason and the governing part, remaining unstumbling and leading the soul, is called its pilot; for in truth the approach to the unchangeable is by the unchangeable.

"As, then, you received Jesus Christ the Lord, walk in him, rooted and built up in him, and made firm in the faith" — and persuasion is the making firm of faith — "see that there be no one who carries you off as spoil from the faith that is in Christ, through philosophy and empty deceit," the kind that does away with providence, "according to the tradition of men." For the philosophy that is according to the divine tradition establishes providence and makes it firm, and, this being done away, the whole dispensation concerning the Saviour appears a fable, since we are then borne along "according to the elements of the world and not according to Christ." For the teaching that follows Christ both deifies the Creator and brings providence down to particular things, and knows the nature of the elements to be changeable and generated, and teaches us to live a civic life in the power that makes us like to God, and to admit the dispensation as the governing principle of all instruction. As elements men worship — Diogenes the air, Thales water, Hippasus fire, and those who lay down the atoms as first principles, putting on the name of philosophy: certain godless little men, lovers of pleasure.

So Abraham was "standing before the Lord, and, drawing near, said"; and to Moses it is said, "But you, stand here with me." But those about Simon wish to be made like in their manner to the "Standing One" whom they revere. Faith, then, and the knowledge of the truth ever make the soul that has chosen them to be in the same condition and after the same manner. But akin to falsehood are change and turning aside and departure, as to the gnostic belong stillness and rest and peace. As, then, conceit and self-opinion have slandered philosophy, so too false knowledge — called by the same name — has slandered knowledge; concerning which the Apostle, writing, says: "O Timothy, keep the deposit, turning away from the profane empty talkings and oppositions of the falsely-named knowledge, which some, professing, have missed the mark concerning the faith." Convicted by this saying, those from the heresies reject the Epistles to Timothy. Come, then: if the Lord is truth and wisdom and the power of God, as indeed he is, it would be shown that the man who has known him, and the Father through him, is in truth a gnostic; for he perceives along with the one who says: "The lips of the just know lofty things."

"For this reason I pray," he says, "that your love may yet more and more abound in full knowledge and in all perception, that you may approve the things that differ." For "when we were infants," says the same Apostle, "we were enslaved under the elements of the world. And the infant, even if he is an heir, differs in nothing from a slave until the time set by the father." Infants, then, are the philosophers too, unless they are made men by Christ. For if "the son of the handmaid will not inherit with the son of the freewoman," yet he is at least a seed of Abraham, though he has received what is his own not by promise, but as a gift. "But the solid food is for the perfect," for those who, by their habit, have their faculties of perception exercised for the discernment of good and evil. "For everyone who partakes of milk is without experience of the word of righteousness" — being an infant, not yet knowing the word according to which he has believed and acts, nor able to render the reason for it within himself. "Test all things," says the Apostle, "and hold fast the good" — speaking to the spiritual, who examine all that is said according to truth, whether it merely seems so, or truly holds to the truth.

"But education unexamined goes astray"; and "blows and reproofs give the discipline of wisdom" — reproofs made with love, of course; "for the upright heart seeks out knowledge," since "he who seeks God will find knowledge with righteousness, and those who have rightly sought him have found peace." "And I will know," he says, "not the speech of those who are puffed up, but the power" — writing to rebuke those who are reputed wise and think themselves so, but are not. "For the kingdom of God is not in word" — the true word — but, by assumption, in the plausible: "but in power," he said; for truth alone is power. And again: "If anyone thinks he has known something, he has not yet known as he ought to know." For truth is never mere opinion; the assumption of knowledge puffs up and fills with conceit, but love builds up, since it busies itself not about opinion but about truth. Hence: "If anyone loves, this man is known."

Concerning the universe, then, he has formed a true and magnificent conception, as one who has made room for divine teaching. Beginning, accordingly, from wonder at the creation, bringing from his own resources a token that he is able to receive knowledge, he becomes an eager disciple of the Lord; and straightway, on hearing of God and providence, he believed, out of the things at which he wondered. Setting out, then, from this point, in every way he co-operates toward learning, doing all those things through which he will be able to receive the knowledge of the things he longs for (and the longing is established when, in the advance of faith, it is mingled with inquiry)—and this is to become worthy of so great and so high a contemplation. In this way the gnostic will taste the will of God; for he presents not his ears, but his soul, to the things signified by what is spoken. Receiving, then, through the words the very substances and the things themselves, he reasonably leads his soul also to what is fitting, taking the "You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill" in the special sense in which it is spoken to the gnostic, not as it is understood by the rest.

He proceeds, then, training himself in scientific contemplation, to contend with the things said more universally and more magnificently—knowing well that "he who teaches man knowledge," according to the prophet, "is the Lord," the Lord working through a human mouth; for which cause too he took on flesh. Reasonably, then, he never chooses the pleasant before the profitable—not even if a fair woman, having got him beforehand into some circumstance, should challenge him, forcing him after the manner of a courtesan—since not even did the master's wife avail to lead Joseph aside from his resolve; but he stripped off his tunic to her as she held him by force, becoming naked of sin, but clothing himself with the orderliness of character. For even if the master's eyes did not see Joseph—the Egyptian's, I mean—yet those of the Almighty were watching. For we hear the voice and behold the bodies; but God examines the thing from which the speaking and the seeing proceed. Consequently, then, even if disease comes upon the gnostic, or some adverse circumstance, and indeed most of all the most fearful thing, death, he remains unchanged in his soul, knowing that all such things are a necessity of creation, and that even so, by the power of God, they become a "medicine of salvation," benefiting through chastisement those who are being refashioned more harshly—being apportioned according to worth by the providence that is truly good.

Using created things, then, whenever reason chooses, and so far as it chooses, he is made master also of his enjoyment of them, in giving thanks to the Creator. He never remembers a wrong, he is harsh toward no one, even though that one happens to be worthy of hatred for what he does; for he reveres the Maker, and loves the partner of his life, pitying him and praying for him because of his ignorance. And indeed he suffers along with the body, being bound to it, which is by nature subject to passion; yet he does not suffer first in respect of the passion. According to the involuntary circumstances, lifting himself up from the toils to the things that are his own, he is not carried away together with the things alien to him, but accommodates himself to his necessary needs only so far as the soul is kept unharmed. For he does not wish to be faithful in mere supposition, nor even in seeming, but in knowledge and truth—that is, in firm deed and active word. Accordingly he not only praises noble things, but forces himself to be noble, passing from "the good and faithful servant" through love into "a friend," on account of the perfection of his settled disposition, which he acquired purely out of true learning and much joint discipline.

As one, then, who forces his way to the height of knowledge—adorned in character, restrained in bearing, having all those advantages that belong to the gnostic according to the truth, looking toward the noble images: the many patriarchs who set things right before him, the very many prophets, the angels beyond all our reckoning by number, and the Lord over all, who taught and showed that it is possible to acquire that supreme life—for this reason he does not love all the ready things of the world that are called noble, lest he remain on the ground, but rather the things hoped for—or rather the things already known, but hoped for in respect of attainment. For this reason he endures toils and tortures and afflictions—not, as the courageous among the philosophers do, in hope that present pains will cease and that he will again partake of pleasures, but because knowledge has begotten in him a most firm conviction of the attainment of the things to come. Therefore he despises not only the chastisements here, but also all the pleasures. They say, indeed, that the blessed Peter, when he beheld his own wife led off to death, rejoiced because of her calling and her conveyance home, and called to her, very encouragingly and consolingly, addressing her by name: "Remember, you there, the Lord."

Such was the marriage of the blessed, and their perfect disposition toward those most dear. In this way too the Apostle: "he who marries" should be "as though not marrying," judging that marriage should be free from passion and "undistracted" from the love toward the Lord—which love the true husband exhorted his wife to hold to, as she departed from life toward the Lord. Was not their faith in the hope after death plainly manifest, in those who gave thanks to God in the very heights of the chastisements? For firm, I think, was the faith they had acquired, upon which the faithful works too followed. The soul of the gnostic, then, is in every circumstance vigorous, like the body of an athlete established in the height of good condition and strength. For it is of good counsel concerning the affairs of men, deliberating what must be done by the just, taking its starting points from God above, and, toward the divine assimilation, having gained for itself mildness toward bodily pleasures and pains; and it rises up against fears with good courage and trust in God. Simply, then, the gnostic soul is an earthly image of divine power, adorned with perfect virtue, having grown together out of all these at once—nature, discipline, reason. This beauty of soul becomes "a temple of the Holy Spirit," when it acquires a disposition agreeing with the Gospel throughout the whole of life.

Such a man, then, rises up against every fear and every terror—not only death, but also poverty and disease and ill repute, and all that is akin to these—becoming unconquered by pleasure and master of the irrational desires. For he knows well what must and must not be done, having known with full strength both the things that are truly fearful and the things that are not. Whence he undergoes, with knowledge, the things that reason dictates as needful and befitting to him, discerning with knowledge the things that are truly to be confidently embraced (that is, the goods) from the things that merely seem so, and the things that are fearful from the things that merely appear so—such as death and disease and poverty, which cling to opinion rather than to truth. This is the truly good man, the one outside the passions, who, by the settled disposition of his virtuous soul, has passed beyond the whole life subject to passion. To this man "all things are bound up in himself" toward the acquisition of the end. For the things called fortuitous evils are not fearful to the diligent man, because they are not evils; but the things that are truly fearful are alien to the Christian gnostic, going diametrically opposite to the goods, since they are evils—and it is impossible that contraries should meet in the same person at the same point and at the same time. Blamelessly, then, "playing his part in the drama of life," whatever God grants him to contend in, he recognizes both the things to be done and the things to be endured.

Surely, then, if cowardice is constituted by ignorance of the things fearful and not fearful, the gnostic alone is confident, knowing the present goods and the goods to come, and knowing together with these, as I said, the things that are not truly fearful—since, knowing vice alone to be hostile and destructive of those who advance toward knowledge, fenced about with the weapons of the Lord, he wars it down. For if anything is constituted through folly and through the working—or rather the co-working—of the devil, this is not on that account at once devil or folly (since no activity is prudence, for prudence is a settled disposition, and no activity is a disposition); so neither is the action constituted through ignorance already ignorance, but vice through ignorance, yet not ignorance; for neither are the passions, nor sins, vices, even though they are carried along from vice. No one, then, who is irrationally courageous is gnostic; otherwise let a man call even children courageous, who undertake fearful things through ignorance of the dangers (they take hold even of fire); and let them call the beasts that go straight against the spears virtuous, being irrationally courageous. And perhaps they will likewise call the conjurers courageous, who tumble onto the swords, working their evil craft out of a certain experience, for a sorry wage. But the truly courageous man, having the danger plain before him because of the jealousy of the many, with good courage takes up all that comes. In this he is distinguished from the rest called martyrs: that some, providing occasions for themselves, throw themselves into dangers—I know not how (for it is right to speak well of them)—while others, hedging themselves about according to right reason, then, when God truly calls, give themselves up eagerly, and "confirm their calling" out of being conscious of nothing rash in themselves, and offer their courage to be examined in the truly rational courage.

The sacrifice acceptable to God is the unrepenting separation from the body and from its passions. This is the true godliness indeed. And is it not perhaps with reason that philosophy was for this cause called by Socrates a study of death? For he who in his thinking neither brings the sight to his aid nor draws in any other of the senses, but meets the realities with the pure mind itself, pursues the true philosophy. This, then, is what the silence of five years means to Pythagoras too, which he enjoins upon his disciples, that, turning away from things of sense, they might behold the divine with the bare mind. . . . The chief men of the Greeks philosophized such things from Moses. For he enjoins that the whole burnt-offerings be flayed and divided into limbs, since the gnostic soul, become bare of its material hide, without the bodily babble and all the passions which empty and false suppositions bring about, having stripped off the fleshly desires, must be consecrated to the light.

Neither, then, enduring the lesser evils through fear of the greater, as the rest do, nor again, suspicious of the blame that comes from their equals and like-minded, do they remain in the confession of their calling; but through love toward God they willingly obey the calling, having chosen no other aim than the being well-pleasing to God, and not on account of the prizes of their toils. For some, through love of glory, others through dread of another and sharper chastisement, and others through certain pleasures and gladnesses that come after death, endure—children in the faith: blessed indeed, yet not yet become men in love toward God, as the gnostic has. For there are, there truly are—just as in the gymnastic contests, so also in the Church—crowns of men and of children. But love itself is to be chosen for its own sake, not for the sake of anything else. Nearly, then, in the gnostic, with knowledge the perfection of courage grows out of the joint discipline of life, since he has practised always to master the passions. Love, then, anointing and training, makes ready its own athlete to be fearless and undismayed and trusting in the Lord, just as righteousness furnishes him with the speaking of truth through the whole of his life. For it was an epitome of righteousness to say: "Let your yes be yes and your no, no." And the same account holds also of temperance. For neither through love of honour (as the athletes, for the sake of crowns and good repute), nor through love of money (as some pretend to be temperate, pursuing the good with a grievous passion), nor again through love of the body for the sake of health—nor, indeed, through boorishness, is anyone, abstaining and untasted of pleasures, truly temperate (for indeed, having tasted of pleasures, those who lead the laborious working life very quickly break the unbending of their continence into pleasures). And such too are those held back by law and fear; for, getting an occasion, they steal aside, they steal from the law, running away from the noble things. But temperance, chosen for its own sake, ever perfected and abiding according to knowledge, makes the man lord and self-ruler, so that the gnostic is temperate and free from passion, untouched by pleasures and pains, as they say the adamant is by fire.

But most men, putting on the mortal like snails, and rolling themselves up into a ball about their own intemperances like hedgehogs, hold such opinions about the blessed and incorruptible God as they hold about themselves. It has escaped them — even though they chance to be near us — that God has bestowed on us ten thousand things of which he himself has no share: birth, being himself unbegotten; nourishment, being himself without need; growth, being himself in equality; a good old age and a good death, being himself immortal and ageless. Hence let no one suppose that hands and feet and mouth and eyes and goings-in and goings-out and wraths and threatenings are said by the Hebrews to be passions of God — by no means; but rather that certain of these names are allegorized in a more holy way, which indeed, as the discourse goes forward, we shall make plain in their own season. "Wisdom is the all-healing remedy of all things," Callimachus writes in his epigrams. "And one man is wise from another, both of old and now," says Bacchylides in his Paeans; "for not even is it the easiest of things to find the gates of words unspoken."

The cause of these things, then, is the most holy and most sovereign of all knowledge—love. For through the service of the best and most excellent—which is characterized by the One—it makes the gnostic at once friend and son, having grown into "a perfect man, to the measure of stature" in truth. But also concord is an agreement about the same thing, and the same thing is one; and friendship is brought to completion through likeness, the community lying in the One. The gnostic, then, being a lover of the one true God, is truly a perfect man and a friend of God, enrolled in the rank of a son. For these are names of nobility and knowledge and perfection, according to the vision of God, which the gnostic soul receives as its supreme advance, having become utterly pure—counted worthy, it is said, to behold eternally "face to face" the almighty God. For, having become wholly spiritual, and having made its way to that which is akin to it, it abides in the spiritual Church, unto the rest of God.

Well, then, does Isocrates in the Panathenaicus, having put the question "Whom, then, do I call educated?", go on: "First, those who use well the matters that befall them day by day, and have a judgement that hits the occasions and is able, for the most part, to aim at the expedient; next, those who associate becomingly and justly with all who draw near, who bear easily and lightly the unpleasantnesses and grievousnesses of others, and present themselves to their companions as inoffensive and moderate as may be; further, those who master their pleasures, and are not too much overcome by their misfortunes, but bear themselves manfully in them and worthily of the nature we share; fourth — and this is greatest — those who are not corrupted by good fortune, nor stand outside themselves, nor become proud, but abide in the rank of the right-minded." Then he adds the coping-stone of the discourse: "Those who have the disposition of their soul well-attuned, not toward one of these only, but toward all of them — these I call both prudent and perfect men, and possessed of all the virtues." Do you see how the Greeks too deify the gnostic life, although they know not how one ought to know? But what knowledge is, they do not know even in a dream.

If, then, it is agreed among us that knowledge is rational food, blessed truly, according to the Scripture, are those who hunger and thirst after the truth, since they shall be filled with everlasting food. Very wonderfully Euripides, the philosopher of the stage, is found to be in tune with what we have said before, hinting, I know not how, at Father and Son together: "To you, the ruler of all, I bring libation and cake — Zeus or Hades, by whatever name you would be called — receive from me an offering without fire, full of all manner of fruits, an outpouring." For Christ is a whole-burnt-offering for us, an offering without fire. And that he speaks of the Saviour himself without knowing it, he makes plain by adding: "For you, among the gods of heaven, wield the sceptre of Zeus, and you share with Hades the rule of the world below." Then he says outright: "Send up to the light the souls of the dead, for those who wish to learn beforehand whence their toils sprang, what is the root of evils, and which of the blessed ones one must propitiate to find a respite from troubles." Not unfittingly, then, the rites among the Greeks too begin with purifications, just as among the barbarians with the washing.

These things having been shown thus, come, let us now set down how many Scriptures are opposed to these sophists of the heresies, revealing the rule of the continence kept according to reason. And the discerning man, choosing for each of the heresies the Scripture properly opposed to it, will use it in season for the overthrow of those who lay down doctrines contrary to the commandments. From of old, then, the law, as we have said before, declared beforehand "You shall not covet your neighbour's wife," anticipating the closely related saying of the Lord under the new covenant, when the same Lord says in His own person: "You have heard the law commanding, 'You shall not commit adultery'; but I say, 'You shall not covet.'" That the law wished men to use their wives prudently and for the begetting of children alone is plain from its forbidding the unmarried man to mingle at once with a captive woman, but permitting him, if he has once desired her, to mourn thirty days, having shaved her hair too; and if even so his desire did not wither, then to beget children, the impulse that had mastered him having been tested over the appointed length of time and shown to be a reasonable appetite.

After these come the lesser mysteries, which have some groundwork of teaching and of preparation for what is to come; and the greater concern the whole, where there is no longer anything left to learn, but only to behold and to view in the mind both nature and the realities. We may take the purifying mode as confession, and the contemplative as analysis, advancing toward the first conception, making our beginning, by way of analysis, from the things that underlie it — taking away from the body its natural qualities, stripping off the dimension into depth, then that into breadth, and after these that into length. For what is left is a point, a unit, so to speak, having position; and if we take away its position, the unit is conceived. If, then, taking away all that belongs to bodies and to what are called incorporeals, we cast ourselves into the greatness of Christ, and thence advance by holiness into the boundless, we should come, in some way or other, to the conception of the Almighty — knowing not what he is, but what he is not. Shape and motion, or standing-still, or a throne, or place, or right hand, or left hand of the Father of all things, are not at all to be conceived, even though these too are written; but what each of them is meant to show forth shall be set out in its own place. The first cause, then, is not in place, but above place and time and name and conception. Therefore Moses too says, "Show yourself to me," hinting most clearly that God is not teachable by men, nor speakable, but knowable only by the power that comes from himself. For the inquiry is formless and invisible, but the grace of the knowledge comes from him through the Son.

Hence you could not show, according to Scripture, any one of the men of old approaching a pregnant woman; but later, after the pregnancy and after the suckling of the child that was born, you would find the wives again being known by their husbands. You will find, for instance, that Moses' father too kept this aim, leaving a space of three years after the birth of Aaron before begetting Moses. And again, the tribe of Levi, keeping this law of nature from God, entered the promised land fewer in number than the others; for a race does not easily increase to a multitude when the men who have undertaken marriage according to the laws sow seed, but wait not only for the pregnancy but also for the suckling.

Most plainly does Solomon witness to us, saying somewhat thus: "Prudence of man is not in me, but God gives me wisdom; and holy things I know." Take, for instance, how Moses, allegorizing the divine prudence, named it a tree of life planted in paradise — which paradise may also be the world, in which all things from creation grow. In this the Word too flowered and bore fruit, becoming flesh, and made alive those who tasted of his kindness; since not even apart from the tree did he come to our knowledge, for our life was hung upon our faith. And Solomon again says: "It is a tree of immortality to those who lay hold of it." For this cause it says: "Behold, I set before your face life and death, to love the Lord your God, and to walk in his ways, and to hear his voice, and to believe in the life; but if you transgress the ordinances and the judgements I have given you, you shall surely perish. For this is your life and the length of your days, to love the Lord your God."

Hence with good reason Moses too, leading the Jews little by little toward continence, ordered them, when they had abstained from sexual pleasure for three days in succession, to listen to the divine words. We, then, are temples of God, as the prophet said: "I will dwell in them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people," if we conduct ourselves according to the commandments, whether each of us severally or the whole Church together. "Therefore come out from their midst and be separated," says the Lord, "and touch no unclean thing; and I will receive you, and will be to you a Father, and you shall be to me sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty." Not, as they say, from those who have married, but from the Gentiles who still live in fornication, and moreover from the aforesaid heresies, He commands us prophetically to be separated, as from those who are unclean and godless.

Again: "Abraham, having come to the place which God told him, on the third day, lifting up his eyes, sees the place from afar." For the first stage is the longing for noble things through sight; the second is the soul's desire for the best; and on the third the mind discerns spiritual things, when the eyes of the understanding are opened by the teacher who rose on the third day. And the three days might be the mystery of the seal, by which the truly existent God is believed. With reason, then, he sees the place from afar; for hard to seize is the country of God — which Plato called "the country of ideas," having taken from Moses that it is a place, as being that which contains all things and the whole. But it is fittingly seen from afar by Abraham, because he was still in the world of becoming, and at hand he is initiated through an angel.

Hence Paul too, aiming at men like those mentioned, says: "Having, then, these promises, beloved, let us cleanse our hearts from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God; for I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." Now the Church does not marry another, having gained her Bridegroom; but each of us has the authority to marry, according to the law, whichever woman he wishes—I mean the first marriage. "But I fear lest somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness, your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is toward Christ"—very carefully and didactically the apostle has spoken.

Hence the apostle says, "We see now as through a mirror, but then face to face" — by those pure and incorporeal applications of the understanding alone. And it is possible, even in discourse, to divine concerning God, if one attempts, apart from all the senses, by means of reason to rush toward what each thing is, and not to stand off from the realities, until, ascending to the things that lie above, he should grasp, by intelligence itself, the very Good — coming to be at the very end of the intelligible, according to Plato. Again, Moses, not permitting altars and precincts to be built in many places, but founding one temple of God, proclaimed a world only-begotten, as Basilides says, and the one God — as Basilides no longer thinks. And since the gnostic Moses does not enclose the unenclosable in place, he set up no image in the temple, showing that God is to be reverenced as invisible and uncircumscribed, yet bringing the Hebrews, in some measure, to the conception of God through the honour of the name attached to the temple. But indeed the Word, forbidding the building of temples and all sacrifices, hints that the Almighty is not in any place, by these words: "What house will you build me? says the Lord. Heaven is my throne," and the rest. And concerning sacrifices likewise: "Blood of bulls and fat of lambs I do not want," and all that the Holy Spirit forbids besides these things through the prophet.

Wherefore the admirable Peter too says: "Beloved, I exhort you as sojourners and pilgrims to abstain from the fleshly desires, which war against the soul, keeping your conduct good among the nations; because this is the will of God, that by doing good you should silence the work of foolish men; as free, and not having your freedom as a cloak for wickedness, but as servants of God." Likewise Paul too writes in the epistle to the Romans: "We who died to sin, how shall we still live in it? For our old man was crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be brought to nought"—down to "and do not present your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin."

Most beautifully, then, does Euripides too sing in tune with these things, writing: "What house, fashioned by the hands of builders, could enclose the divine frame within the folds of walls?" And concerning sacrifices he likewise says: "For God, if he is truly God, has need of nothing; these are the wretched tales of bards." For God did not make the world out of need, that he might reap honours from men and from the other gods and the spirits, says Plato, gathering, as it were, some revenue from the world of becoming — from us, smoke, and from gods and spirits their proper ministries. Most instructively, then, does Paul say in the Acts of the Apostles: "The God who made the world and all things in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in temples made with hands, nor is he served by human hands as though he needed anything, himself giving to all breath and life and all things."

And having come to this point, I think I should not leave it unremarked that the apostle proclaims the same God through the law and the prophets and the gospel; for the "You shall not covet," written in the gospel, he attaches to the law in the epistle to the Romans, knowing that the Father who proclaimed through the law and the prophets and the Father who through Himself was preached as good news are one. For he says: "What then shall we say? Is the law sin? God forbid. But I did not know sin except through the law; for I would not have known desire if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet.'" And even if the heterodox who set themselves against us suppose that Paul went on to speak in opposition to the Creator in what follows, "For I know that there does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh—any good," let them read the things said before and the things that follow; for he had said before, "But the sin that dwells in me," on account of which it was consistent to say that "no good dwells in my flesh."

And Zeno too, the founder of the Stoic school, says, in his book On the Republic, that one ought neither to make temples nor images; for no work is worthy of the gods. And he does not shrink from writing in these very words: "There will be no need to build temples; for a temple is not to be thought worth much, nor holy; and no work of builders and artisans is worth much or holy." With reason, then, Plato too, knowing the world to be a temple of God, marked off for the citizens a place of the city in which the images were to be set up, but privately forbade anyone to possess statues of the gods. "Let no one," he says, "consecrate sacred things to the gods in any other way; for gold and silver, in other cities, both privately and in temples, is an invidious possession; ivory, from a body that has left its soul, is no holy offering; iron and bronze are instruments of wars; but of wood let a man set up what he will, of one piece, and likewise of stone, for the common shrines."

Consistently with this he added: "But if I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who work it, but the sin that dwells in me, which, warring against the law of God and of my mind, takes me captive in the law of sin that is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" And again (for he never tires of helping in any way whatever) he does not hesitate to add: "For the law of the Spirit has freed me from the law of sin and death, since through His Son God condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." Besides this, still clarifying what he has said, he cries out: showing that the body is "dead because of sin," in that it is no longer a temple but is still a tomb of the soul—for whenever it is sanctified to God, the Spirit will raise it. "He who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, who will also give life to your mortal bodies through His Spirit that dwells in you."

With reason, then, in the great letter he says: "There is no way to speak of it, as of other lessons; but out of much fellowship with the matter itself, and out of living together with it, suddenly, as a light kindled from a leaping fire, it comes to be in the soul and thenceforth nourishes itself." Are not these things like to those spoken by Zephaniah the prophet? "And the Spirit took me up and carried me to a fifth heaven, and I beheld angels called lords, with their diadem set upon them in the Holy Spirit; and the throne of each of them was sevenfold the light of the rising sun; and they dwelt in temples of salvation and hymned the unspeakable Most High God."

Again, then, rebuking the lovers of pleasure, he adds these things: "For the mind of the flesh is death; for those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, and the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God, for it does not submit to the law of God. And those who are in the flesh"—not, as some lay it down as doctrine, but as we have said before—"cannot please God." Then, by way of distinction from these, he says to the Church: "But you are not in the flesh but in the spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone has not the Spirit of Christ, he is not His. But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. So then, brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh; for if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you shall live. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God." And against the nobility and freedom contemptibly introduced by the heterodox who boast in their lewdness, he adds, saying: "For you did not receive a spirit of slavery again unto fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, in which we cry, 'Abba, Father'"—that is, we received it for this, that we might know Him to whom we pray, the one who is truly Father, the only Father of all that is, who chastises unto salvation as a Father, and... fear He threatens.

"Yes," they say, "if God cares for you, why are you persecuted and killed? Or does He Himself give you over to this?" But we do not suppose that the Lord wished us to fall into these circumstances; rather, He foretold prophetically the things that were going to come to pass, namely, that on account of His name we shall be persecuted, killed, impaled. So that He did not wish us to be persecuted, but foretold what we should suffer, training us by the foretelling of what was to come into endurance, to which He promised the inheritance. And yet we are not punished alone, but along with many. "But those," they say, "being evildoers, justly undergo punishment."

So then unwillingly they bear witness to our righteousness, who are unjustly punished for the sake of righteousness. But the injustice of the judge does not touch providence. For the judge must be lord of his own judgement, not pulled by strings like lifeless instruments, perhaps receiving merely occasions from the cause outside. So he is put to the test in his judging, just as we are in the choice of what is choiceworthy and in endurance; and even if we do no wrong, yet the judge looks on us as though we did wrong. For he does not know our affairs, nor does he wish to learn, but is carried away by an empty prejudice—and therefore he too is judged. They persecute us, then, not because they have found us to be unjust, but supposing, by the mere fact of our being Christians, that we do wrong to our life, both ourselves conducting ourselves thus and urging others to choose the like life.

"But why," they say, "are you not helped when persecuted?" For in what are we wronged, as regards ourselves, being released by death to the Lord, and undergoing, as it were, a change of age, so too an alteration of life? But if we are of sound mind, we shall be thankful to those who have furnished the occasion of a swift departure, . . . if we bear witness out of love. But if we did not seem to the many to be worthless men, and they too knew the truth, all would leap upon the road, and there would be no election. But our faith, being the light of the world, convicts unbelief. "For Anytus and Meletus might indeed kill me, but harm me they could in no way; for I do not think it lawful that the better should be harmed by the worse." So that each of us takes courage to say: "The Lord is my helper, I will not fear; what shall man do to me?" For "the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment shall touch them."

As, then, in astronomy we have for an example Abraham, so in arithmetic the same Abraham. For when he heard that Lot had been taken captive, having numbered his own household, three hundred and eighteen, and gone out, he overcame a very great number of the enemy. They say, then, that the three-hundredth letter, in respect of its shape, is a type of the Lord's sign, and the iota and the eta signify the Saviour's name; so that it is shown that Abraham's household, who took refuge in the sign and the name, became masters of those who took captive, and of the very many unbelieving nations that followed them. Now the number three hundred is a triad in the hundreds, and the decad is confessed to be all-perfect; and the eight, the first cube, the equality in all the dimensions — length, breadth, depth. "The days of men," it says, "shall be a hundred and twenty years." And the number is, from the monad by composition, the fifteenth; and the moon on the fifteenth day becomes full of light.

And in another way the hundred and twenty is a triangular number, and is made up of the equality of the sixty-four, of which the composition by parts begets squares — 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15 — and out of the inequality of the fifty-six, seven of the even numbers from the dyad, which beget the oblongs — 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. And by another signification again the hundred and twenty is made up of four: of one triangle, the fifteenth; of another, a square, the twenty-fifth; of a third, a pentagon, the thirty-fifth; of a fourth, a hexagon, the forty-fifth. For according to the same proportion the five is taken in each kind: of the triangles, from the monad, the five gives the fifteenth; of the squares, the twenty-fifth; and of the rest proportionately. Yes, and the number twenty-five, being five from the monad, is said to be a symbol of the Levitical tribe; and the thirty-five itself holds of the arithmetical and geometrical and harmonical diagram of the doubles — 6, 8, 9, 12 — of which the composition begets the thirty-five; in which days the Jews say the seven-months' children are formed. And the forty-five holds of the diagram of the triples — 6, 9, 12, 18 — of which the composition begets the forty-five; and in these days likewise they say the nine-months' children are formed.

This, then, is the form of the arithmetical example. And let there be for a witness of geometry the tabernacle that was set up, and the ark that was framed, by certain most rational proportions, fashioned by divine devices, by a gift of understanding, leading us from the things of sense to the things of mind — or rather, from these to the holy things, and from the holy things to the holy of holies. For the four-square pieces of wood, by the four-square figure standing firm on every side, completing right angles, show forth security. And the length of the structure was three hundred cubits, the breadth fifty, the depth thirty; and it is brought up to a cubit at the top, the ark being tapered from its broad base after the manner of a pyramid, a symbol of those purified and tested through fire. And this geometrical proportion is furnished for the conveyance of those holy abodes, whose differences the differences of the numbers set down make plain.

And the proportions borne in are sixfold, as the three hundred to the fifty; and tenfold, as the three hundred is tenfold the thirty; and the proportion two-and-a-third, for the fifty is two-and-a-third the thirty. And there are some who say that the three hundred cubits are a symbol of the Lord's sign; the fifty, of hope and of the remission at the Pentecost; and the thirty — or, as in some, twelve — they record to show forth the preaching, because in his thirtieth year the Lord preached, and twelve were the apostles; and that the structure is brought up to a cubit, the advance of the just ending in unity and in the oneness of the faith. And the table in the temple was made of six cubits, and the four feet each a cubit and a half. So they gather the whole to twelve cubits, in agreement with the winding of the twelve months in the yearly circle, according to which all things grow and bear fruit, the earth being made familiar with the four seasons. And the table, I think, shows an image of the earth, resting on four feet — summer, autumn, spring, winter — through which the year travels. Wherefore it says too that the table has twisted wave-mouldings, either because all things are wheeled round by the periods of the seasons, or perhaps it showed forth the earth surrounded by ocean.

Further, let David, singing at once and prophesying, hymning God tunefully, be set forth as an example of music. And it well suits the enharmonic genus to the Dorian harmony, and the diatonic to the Phrygian, as Aristoxenus says. The harmony, then, of the barbarian psaltery, showing forth the dignity of the melody, being most ancient, becomes an example above all to Terpander, who hymns Zeus to the Dorian harmony somewhat thus: "Zeus, beginning of all, leader of all, Zeus, to you I send this beginning of hymns." And the psalmist's lyre might be allegorized: by the first signification the Lord; by the second, those who closely strike the souls under the Lord as leader of the muses. And if the people that is saved be called a lyre, it is heard, by the inspiration of the Word and by the recognition of God, glorifying musically, being struck unto faith by the Word. And you might take in another way too the ecclesiastical musical concord, of law and prophets together with apostles and the Gospel, and the under-running concord, that according to each prophet, in the leaps from person to person.

But, as it seems, the most of those who inscribe themselves with the name, like the comrades of Odysseus, go after the discourse boorishly, passing by, not the Sirens, but the rhythm and the melody, stopping their ears with want of learning, since they know they will not be able, having once submitted their hearing to the Greek studies, thereafter to attain the return home. But for him who culls the useful for the benefit of the catechumens, and especially when they are Greeks ("for the Lord's is the earth and the fulness thereof"), the love of learning is not to be abstained from, after the manner of irrational animals; but as many helps as may be must be gathered for those who hear. Yet one must in no way linger over these, except only for the useful thing from them, so that, having taken this and acquired it, one may be able to go away home to the true philosophy, having procured for the soul a sure pledge of security from all sides. One must, then, take hold of music for the adorning and ordering of character.

For instance, even over the cup we pledge one another in singing, charming our desiring part, and glorifying God for the ungrudging gift of human enjoyments, of the foods supplied everlastingly both for the increase of the body and for that of the soul. But excessive music must be spat out, that breaks down souls and casts them into variety, now dirge-like, now wanton and luxurious, now bacchic and frenzied. The same account holds also of astronomy; for this, after the history of things on high, concerning the shape of the whole and the motion of the heaven and the movement of the stars, bringing the soul nearer to the creating power, teaches it to be quick-sensed concerning the seasons of the year, the change of the airs, the risings of the stars; since both navigation and husbandry are full of the use of it, as architecture and building of geometry. And this study makes the soul, as far as may be, attentive, discerning of the true and refuting of the false, finding out agreements and proportions, so as to track down the like in the unlike; and it leads us up to find a breadthless length and a depthless surface and a partless point, and transfers us from the things of sense to the things of mind.

The studies, then, are helpers of philosophy, and philosophy itself toward the apprehension of truth. For instance, the cloak was at first a fleece, then it was carded and became woof and warp, and then it was woven. The soul, then, must be prepared and variously worked, if it is to be made best; since of the truth one part is gnostic, the other practical, and this has flowed from the contemplative, and has need of training and much joint exercise and experience. But of the contemplative too one part is toward one's neighbours, the other as toward oneself. Wherefore education too must be so prepared as to be fitted to both. It is possible, then, for one who has sufficiently learned the things that hold together what leads to knowledge to remain thenceforth in quiet, at rest, directing his actions toward contemplation; but on account of the benefit of his neighbours — some pressing on to write, some setting out to deliver the word — both the other education is useful, and the reading of the Lord's Scriptures is necessary for the proof of what is said, and most of all if those who hear are led up from the Greek education.

Such a church does David describe: "The queen stood at your right hand, in a garment of woven gold, clad in things of many colours" — that is, with the Greek and superfluous studies — "in golden fringes, clad in things of many colours." But the truth is through the Lord. "For who has known your counsel," it says, "unless you have given wisdom and sent your Holy Spirit from on high? And so were the paths of those upon the earth set straight, and men were taught the things pleasing to you, and were saved by wisdom." For the gnostic, according to the Scripture, knows the things of old and conjectures the things to come, understands the turnings of words and the solutions of riddles, foreknows signs and wonders and the issues of seasons and times, as we said before.

Do you see the spring of the studies setting out from wisdom? But to those who object, "What profit is it to know the causes of how the sun moves, for instance, and the rest of the stars, or to have studied the geometrical theorems or the dialectical, and each of the other studies, for these are of no profit toward the rendering of what is fitting; and that the Greek philosophy is human understanding, for it does not teach the truth" — to these those things are to be said: first, that they stumble even about the greatest of the things that are — that is, the free choice of the mind. "For those who guard holily the holy things," it says, "shall be sanctified, and those who have been taught them shall find a defence." For the gnostic alone will do, with reason and holily, all the things to be done, as he has learned, having received it through men by the Lord's teaching. And again one may hear: "For in his hand" — that is, in his power and wisdom — "are both we and our words, and all prudence and the science of crafts. For God loves nothing but the man who dwells with wisdom." And next — have they not read what was said by Solomon? For, treating of the construction of the temple, he downright says, "And wisdom, the craftswoman, built it; and your providence, O Father, steers it."

And how is it not unreasonable to think philosophy worse than carpentry and shipbuilding? Perhaps too the Lord fed that multitude reclining on the grass over against Tiberias with the two fishes and the five barley loaves, hinting at the preliminary education of Greeks and Jews before the divine wheat of the food husbanded according to the law; for the barley is riper toward the summer season than the wheat. And the Greek philosophy, born and borne about upon the Gentile wave, the fishes show forth, given for stretched-out nourishment to those still lying on the ground; not increasing, as did the fragments of the loaves, but, having partaken of the Lord's blessing, breathing in the resurrection of divinity through the power of the Word. But if you are also curious, take the one of the fishes to be the encyclical learning, and the other to show forth that very philosophy which has mounted higher, both being akin to the Lord's Word; and "a chorus of voiceless fishes plashed about," the tragic muse has said somewhere. "And I too must be lessened, but the Lord's Word alone increase," into which the law is brought to its end, the prophet John has said.

Understand now for me the mystery of the truth, granting pardon if I shrink from going further in the working-out, proclaiming only this: "All things came to be through him, and without him not one thing came to be." Indeed, he is called a corner-stone, "in whom every building, fitly framed together, grows into a holy temple of God," according to the divine apostle. I am silent now of the parable in the Gospel that says, "The kingdom of heaven is like to a man who cast a net into the sea, and out of the multitude of the fishes taken makes a choice of the better ones." And now too our wisdom plainly proclaims the four virtues somewhat thus, so that the springs of these too were given to the Greeks from the Hebrews. This one may learn from these words: "And if anyone love righteousness, the labours of this are virtues; for she teaches temperance and prudence, righteousness and courage, than which nothing is more useful in the life of men." But above all they ought to have known this too: that by nature we have come to be fit for virtue, yet not so as to have it from birth, but suited to the acquiring of it.

And faith, like time, being twofold, we would find two virtues dwelling with both. For of time, to the past belongs memory, to the future hope; and we believe that the past has come to be and that the future will be; and again we love, persuaded by faith that the past is so, and awaiting the future by hope. For through all things love has gone forth to the gnostic who knows one God; and, "behold, all things which he has made are very good," he knows and marvels at. And "godliness adds length of life, and the fear of the Lord adds days." As, then, the days are a portion of the life that is by ascent, so too fear is the beginning of love, becoming, by increase, faith, then love — but not as I fear the wild beast and hate it (fear being twofold), but as I dread the father too, whom I both fear and love at once. Again, fearing lest I be punished, I love myself, choosing the fear; but he who fears to offend the father loves him. Blessed, then, is he who becomes faithful, mingled of love and fear; for faith is strength unto salvation, and power unto eternal life.

Again, prophecy is foreknowledge, and knowledge is the understanding of prophecy — that is, knowledge of the things foreknown to those men by the Lord who makes all things plain beforehand. The knowledge of the things foretold, then, shows their issue to be threefold: either having come to pass long ago, or already present, or to be in the future. Then the extremes have fallen under faith — of things accomplished or of things hoped for; but the present activity furnishes conviction for the confirmation of both extremes. For if, prophecy being one, the one part is now accomplished and the other fulfilled, from this both the hoped-for is trustworthy and the past is true. For first it was present, then it has passed for us, so that the faith of past things is an apprehension of a past thing, and the hope of future things an apprehension of a future thing. And the assents — not only those from Plato, but also those from the Stoa — say are in our power.

But since the tradition is not common and public — at least to one who has perceived the greatness of the Word — the wisdom spoken in a mystery, which the Son of God taught, must be kept hidden. So already Isaiah the prophet has his tongue cleansed by fire, that he might be able to tell the vision; and not the tongue alone, but our ears too must be purified, if indeed we try to be partakers of the truth. These things hindered me from writing, and even now I am cautious, as it is said, of "casting the pearls before swine, lest they trample them with their feet, and turn and tear you." For it is hard to display the truly pure and translucent words concerning the true light to swinish and uneducated hearers; for there are scarcely any things more laughable to the many than these, nor, on the other hand, more marvellous and inspiring to the well-endowed.

Every opinion, then, and judgment and assumption and learning, by which we live and are ever in company with the race of men, is an assent; and this would be nothing other than faith. And unbelief too, being a departure from faith, shows assent and faith to be possible; for a privation of a non-existent thing could not be spoken of. And if anyone considers the truth, he will find man by nature ill-disposed toward assent to falsehood, but having occasions toward faith in the truth. The virtue that holds the Church together, as the Shepherd says, is faith, through which the elect of God are saved; and that which plays the man is self-control. And there follow upon these simplicity, knowledge, harmlessness, gravity, love. And all these are daughters of faith. And again: "Faith leads the way, fear builds up, and love perfects." "One must fear the Lord, then," he says, "unto building up, but not the devil unto overthrow." And, on the contrary: "the works of the Lord — that is, the commandments — must be loved and done, but the works of the devil feared and not done"; for the fear of God educates and restores to love, but the works of the devil have hatred as their housemate. And the same author says that repentance is great understanding; for he who repents of what he has done no longer does or says it, but, torturing his own soul for the things in which he sinned, works good. Forgiveness of sins, then, differs from repentance, but both show the things in our power.

"But the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him." And "the wise do not bring out of their mouth what they reason in council." But "what you hear in the ear," says the Lord, "proclaim upon the housetops" — bidding us receive the hidden traditions of true knowledge, interpreted in a high and excellent way, and, just as we have heard in the ear, so to hand them on to those for whom it is fitting, but not to give out unreservedly to all the things spoken to them in parables. But the outline of these memoranda is in truth such that they have the truth scattered here and there and strewn in, so that it may escape those who, like jackdaws, pick up seeds. And whenever it meets with a good husbandman, each of them will spring up and bring the wheat to light.

These things, then, are thus. And being so disposed toward body and soul, and toward his neighbours—whether one be a household servant, or made an enemy by law, or whosoever he may be—the gnostic is found equal and alike toward all. For he does not look down upon his brother, who by the divine law is of one father and one mother. Indeed, when his brother is afflicted he lightens his burden with consolations, with encouragements, helping him in the necessities of life, giving to all who are in need—yet not alike, but justly and according to worth; and besides, even to the one who persecutes and hates him, if he have need of this, caring little for those who say that the man gave to him through fear—if it be not through fear, but that he does this for the sake of helping. For if men are free from love of money and forgetful of wrongs toward their enemies, how much more loving toward their own household? Such a man proceeds from this to know exactly to whom one should especially give, and how much, and when, and how. And who would reasonably be an enemy to a man who in no way furnishes any cause of enmity? And just as, in the case of God, we say that God is set against no one and is the enemy of no one (for he is the Creator of all, and there is none of the things that exist which he does not will), but we say that the disobedient, and those who do not walk according to his commandments, are his enemies—as being at enmity with his covenant—in the same way we would find it also in the case of the gnostic. For he himself would never in any way become an enemy to anyone; but those who turn to the opposite road would be conceived of as enemies to him—especially since the disposition of giving is called among us righteousness; but the disposition that discerns according to worth, toward the more and the less, in the cases where it befits one to act according to knowledge, is a form of the highest righteousness. There are, indeed, some things that are set right even out of mere ordinary habit by certain men—such as continence in pleasures. For just as among the heathen, both from not being able "to obtain the things one loves" and from fear of men, and there are some who, for the sake of greater pleasures, abstain from the pleasures at their feet—so too in the faith some practise continence either through a promise or through fear of God.

But such continence is a foundation of knowledge, and a kind of approach toward the better, and an impulse toward the perfect. For "the beginning of wisdom," it is said, "is the fear of the Lord." But the perfect man, through love, "bears all things, endures all things, as pleasing not man, but God." And yet praise too follows him as a consequence—not toward his own benefit, but toward the imitation and use of those who praise him. And continent is said also in another sense—not only the one who masters the passions, but the one who has become master of the goods and has firmly acquired the great things of knowledge, from which he bears the fruit of activities according to virtue. In this way the gnostic, when a circumstance arises, never departs from his own settled disposition. For firm and unchangeable is the scientific acquisition of the good, being a science of things divine and human. Knowledge, then, never becomes ignorance, nor does the good change into evil. Therefore he eats and drinks and marries—not as a primary aim, but of necessity; and "to marry" I say of the one whom reason chooses, and as it befits. For, having become perfect, he has the apostles for images. And a man is shown to be truly a man not by choosing the solitary life, but he "surpasses men" who has trained himself, without pleasure-seeking and without grief, in marriage and the begetting of children and the care of his household—having become, with the care of the household, inseparable from the love of God, and rising up against every trial brought through children and wife and household servants and possessions. But to the man without a household it has happened, for the most part, to be without trial. Caring, then, only for himself, he is surpassed by the one who falls short of him as regards his own salvation, but excels in the management of life—who simply preserves a small image of the providence that is according to truth. But we, at least, must exercise the soul in every way, as variously as possible.

that he may become a good worker toward the reception of knowledge. Do you not see how wax is softened and bronze cleansed, that they may receive the impress that comes upon them? Indeed, as death is "a separation of the soul from the body," so knowledge is, as it were, a rational death, leading and separating the soul away from the passions and bringing it forward into the life of well-doing, so that it may then say with frankness to God: "As you will, I live." For he who chooses "to please men cannot please God," since the many choose not what profits, but what delights; but he who pleases God becomes well-pleasing, as a consequence, also to the diligent among men. How then could the things concerning food and drink and sexual pleasure still be delightful to such a man, when he looks with suspicion even upon a word that brings a certain pleasure, and upon a movement of thought and a pleasing act? For "no one can serve two masters, God and mammon." He does not say this simply of money, but of the supplying, out of money, toward the various pleasures. For in truth it is not possible for one who has known God greatly and truly to be a slave to the opposing pleasures.

One alone, then—the Lord, the lover of mankind, who for our sakes also became man—is from the beginning free from desire; but as many as strive to be made like to the stamp given by him force themselves, through discipline, to become free from desire. For he who has desired and then mastered himself is, like the widow who through self-control becomes again a virgin... This is the reward of knowledge to the Saviour and Teacher, which he himself asked for: abstinence from evils and the working of well-doing, through which salvation is won. As, then, those who have learned the arts provide their food through the things in which they were trained, so the gnostic, providing his life through the things he knows, is saved. For he who would not cut out the passion of the soul has killed himself. But, as it seems, ignorance is the soul's starvation, and knowledge its nourishment. These are the gnostic souls, which the Gospel likened to the sanctified virgins who awaited the Lord. For they are virgins as having abstained from evils, and they await the Lord through love, and they kindle their own proper light unto the contemplation of things—prudent souls, saying, "We long for you, O Lord, to receive you at last. We have lived according to what you commanded, transgressing none of your charges; therefore we ask for the promises, and we pray for the things that profit, not the things that please, since it befits us to ask the most beautiful things from you. And all things we shall receive as for our profit, even if the trials that come upon us should seem grievous—the exercises which your dispensation brings upon us for the training of our steadfastness."

The gnostic, then, through excess of holiness, is more ready to fail in obtaining when he asks, than to obtain without asking. For his whole life is a prayer and a converse with God; and if he be pure of sins, by all means he will obtain what he wills. For God says to the just man, "Ask, and I will give to you; think it, and I will do it." If, then, the things be profitable, he will receive them at once; but things unprofitable he will never ask, and therefore will not receive. So shall it be as he wills. And if anyone should say to us that some even of sinners obtain things according to their requests, we reply that this happens rarely, by reason of the just goodness of God, and is given to those able to benefit others as well. Whence the gift comes about not for the sake of the one who asked; but the dispensation, foreseeing the one who is to be saved through him, makes the bestowal just on its own account. And to as many as are worthy, the truly good things are given even when they do not ask. Whenever, then, a man is just not by necessity or fear or hope, but by deliberate choice, this is called the kingly road, which the kingly race travels; but the other branchings-off are slippery and precipitous. If, then, one were to take away fear and honour, I do not know whether even the noble among the philosophers who boast of their frankness would still hold out under their afflictions.

Desires and the other sins are called "thorns and prickles." The gnostic, then, works in the vineyard of the Lord, planting, pruning, watering, being a truly divine husbandman of those planted unto faith. They, then, who have not done evil think it right to receive a reward for their idleness; but he who has done good out of bare deliberate choice claims his reward as a good worker. Indeed, he will receive double—both for the things he did not do, and in return for the benefits he did. This gnostic is tempted by no one, except where God should permit it, and this for the benefit of those with him. For they are strengthened toward faith, being encouraged by his manly endurance. Indeed, for this reason too the blessed Apostles were brought to the fixing and confirming of the Churches, for the trial and witness of perfection. Having, then, ever ringing in his ears the voice that says, "Whom I shall strike, do you have mercy," the gnostic asks even of those who hate him that they may repent. For the punishment of evildoers carried out in the arenas is a thing for even children not to look upon. For there is no way the gnostic could ever be instructed or delighted by such men, having trained himself by deliberate choice to be noble and good, and in this way become impervious to pleasures; never falling under sins, he is not instructed by the examples of the evils of others. Far indeed is such a man from being well pleased with earthly pleasures and spectacles—he who has set even the worldly promises, divine though they are, at nothing. "Not everyone, then, who says 'Lord, Lord' shall enter into the kingdom of God, but he who does the will of God." This would be the gnostic worker—he who masters "the worldly desires" while still in the very flesh, but is exactly persuaded concerning the things he has known, the things to come and still unseen, so as to count these more present than the things at his feet.

This is the worker well-suited—rejoicing over the things he has known, but drawing himself in over the things in which he is rolled about by the necessity of life, not yet counted worthy of the active partaking of what he has known. In this way he uses this present life as a thing alien, only so far as the portion of necessity requires. He knows also the riddles of the fast of these days—of the fourth day and of the day of preparation, I mean. For the one is named after Hermes and the other after Aphrodite. Accordingly, he fasts in his life from love of money and from love of pleasure together—out of which all the vices spring up. For we have often before set forth, after the Apostle, the three highest distinctions of fornication: love of pleasure, love of money, idolatry.

He fasts, then, both according to the Law, from base deeds, and according to the perfection of the Gospel, from wicked thoughts. To him the trials too are brought—not for his purification, but, as we said, for the benefit of his neighbours: if, having made trial of toils and pains, he has despised them and let them pass. And the same account holds of pleasure. For it is the greatest thing, having come into the experience of a thing, then to abstain from it. For what is great if a man controls himself in things he does not know? This man, having carried out the commandment that is according to the Gospel, makes that day a Lord's day, when he casts off a base notion and takes on a gnostic one, glorifying the resurrection of the Lord within himself. And further, when he receives the grasp of a scientific principle, he thinks that he sees the Lord, directing his eyes toward the unseen things; and even if he seems to see what he does not wish to see, he chastises the faculty of sight, when he becomes aware of himself taking pleasure in the application of the eyes—since he wishes to see and to hear only that which befits him. Indeed, contemplating the souls of the brethren, he beholds the beauty of the flesh too by the soul itself, that soul accustomed to look only on the noble apart from fleshly pleasure.

And they are truly brothers, according to the chosen creation, and according to likeness of character, and according to the substance of their works—doing and thinking and speaking the same things, holy and noble works, which the Lord willed them, being elect, to hold in mind. For faith is in choosing the same things; knowledge, in having learned and thought the same; and hope, in longing for the same. And even if, for the necessity of life, he be occupied for a little while of the hour about his food, he thinks himself defrauded, distracted by the business. In this way he never even in a dream sees what does not befit the elect. Simply, "a stranger and a sojourner" in all this life is every such man—who, dwelling in a city, has despised the things of the city that are admired by others, and lives in the city as in a desert, that the place may not compel him, but that his deliberate choice may show him just. This gnostic, to speak briefly, fills up the absence of the apostle by living rightly, knowing exactly, benefiting the fit, "removing the mountains" of his neighbours and casting away the unevennesses of their souls. And yet each of us is his own vineyard and his own worker. And the man who, even while doing the best things, wishes to escape the notice of men—persuading the Lord and himself at once that he lives according to the commandments, choosing these things out of those by which he has come to believe (for "where a man's mind is," it is said, "there is his treasure too")—this man impoverishes himself, so as never to overlook a brother who has come into affliction, on account of his perfection in love, knowing especially that he himself will more easily bear his own want than his brother's.

"For to find the Father and Maker of this whole is a task, and having found him, to declare him to all is impossible. For there is no way to speak of it, as of other lessons," says the truth-loving Plato. For he had heard very well how the all-wise Moses, going up into the mountain — through the holy contemplation to the summit of the things of mind — by necessity charges that not all the people go up with him; and when the Scripture says, "And Moses entered into the thick darkness where God was," this makes plain, to those able to understand, that God is invisible and unspeakable, and that the darkness is, in truth, the unbelief and ignorance of the many, set before the gleam of the truth. And Orpheus the theologian, again, profited from this source, when he said: "He is one, self-complete, and from one are all things sprung (or 'grown,' for so it is also written)," and adds: "Nor does any of mortals behold him, but he himself sees all." And still more plainly he goes on: "But him I do not behold, for round about him a cloud is fixed; for in all mortals are mortal pupils in their eyes, small, since flesh and bones are grown into them."

Indeed, he reckons that man's pain his own pain; and if, out of his own want, providing through well-doing, he suffers something hard, he is not vexed at it, but increases his benefaction yet more. For he has unmixed faith concerning these matters, praising the Gospel by works and contemplation. And so it is "not the praise from men, but from God" that he reaps, doing the very things the Lord taught. This man, distracted by his own hope, does not taste the noble things in the world, despising all things here—pitying those who after death are instructed through chastisement, confessing unwillingly; with a good conscience toward the departure, and ever ready, as "a sojourner and a stranger" to the things here, mindful only of his own inheritances, and counting all things here as alien. Not only does he marvel at the commandments of the Lord, but, so to speak, through knowledge itself he is a partaker of the divine will, being truly the household of the Lord and of the commandments, chosen out as just. And he is governing and kingly, as gnostic—looking down upon all the gold on the earth and beneath the earth, and upon a kingdom reaching from one end of the ocean to the other, so as to cling to the service of the Lord alone. Therefore, even eating and drinking and marrying—if reason should choose it—and even seeing dreams, he does and thinks the holy things; and in this way he is ever pure for prayer. And he prays in company with angels, as being already "equal to the angels," and is never outside the holy guard; and even if he prays alone, he has the choir of the saints standing with him. He knows a twofold faith: the one, the activity of the believer; the other, the worthy pre-eminence of the one believed in—since righteousness too is twofold.

The partners who by agreement, for a season, give themselves to prayer—this is a teaching of continence. For he added "by agreement," so that no one should dissolve the marriage; and "for a season," so that the married man, not practising continence by necessity, should not at some time slip into sin, sparing his own consort but falling into another's desire. By this same reasoning he said that the man who thinks he behaves unseemly in keeping his daughter a virgin does well to give her in marriage. And the purpose of each—both of the man who has made himself a eunuch and of the man who has joined himself in marriage for the begetting of children—ought to remain firm, never yielding to the worse. For if he is able to intensify his life, he will gain for himself a greater worth in God's eyes, being continent at once purely and with reason; but if, having transgressed the rule he chose for greater glory, he then... falls away from his hope. For just as celibacy has, so too does marriage have, its own services and ministries pertaining to the Lord—I mean the care of children and of a wife.
