For it seems that to the man perfect in marriage the intimacy of the union becomes a pretext—he who has undertaken the care of all things in the common household.

For He says that bishops must be appointed who have practised presiding over their own household and over the whole Church. Let each, then, in the work to which he was called, fulfil his ministry, that he may become free in Christ, receiving the appropriate reward of his ministry.

The apostle will bear witness to what has been said, saying, "I know a man in Christ caught up to the third heaven, and thence into paradise, who heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter" — thus hinting at the unspeakableness of God; not adding the "it is not lawful" by reason of any law or fear of some charge, but showing that the divine is unutterable by human power, since beyond the third heaven it begins to be spoken, as is right, by those who there initiate the chosen souls into the mysteries. For I know that even in Plato (for the examples from the barbarian philosophy, being many, the discourse now postpones, awaiting their occasion according to its first promises) many heavens are conceived. At any rate, being in doubt in the Timaeus whether one ought to think there are more worlds than this one, he is indifferent about the names, calling world and heaven synonymously; and the words run thus: "Have we, then, rightly spoken of one heaven, or would it be more correct to say many and infinite? One, if indeed it is to have been fashioned according to the pattern."

The one is through love, the other through fear. It is said, accordingly: "The fear of the Lord, pure, abiding for ever and ever." For those who turn from fear toward faith and righteousness abide for ever. Fear, indeed, works abstinence from evils; but love, building up toward the voluntary, urges toward well-doing, that a man may hear from the Lord: "No longer do I call you servants, but friends," and may now approach the prayers with confidence. And the very form of the prayer is thanksgiving—both for the things gone before, and for things present, and for things to come, as already present through faith. And before this comes the having received knowledge. And further, he asks so to live the appointed life in the flesh as a gnostic, as though without flesh, and to obtain the best things, but to flee the worse. He asks also for relief concerning the things in which we have sinned, and for conversion unto recognition; so swiftly following the one who calls him at the departure, as the other calls, going forward, so to speak, by reason of his good conscience, hastening to give thanks even there, having come to be with Christ. Having shown himself worthy through purity, he holds, by a kind of fusion, the power of God which is supplied through Christ. For he does not wish to be warm by participation in warmth, nor luminous by participation in fire, but to be wholly light. This man knows exactly the saying: "Unless you hate father and mother, and besides also your own life, and unless you bear the sign..." For he has hated the fleshly attachments that hold so much of the charm of pleasure, and he despises all things that are proper to the begetting and nourishment of the flesh; and he rises up against the bodily soul as well, putting a bit upon the irrational spirit when it grows unbridled, because "the flesh lusts against the spirit." But "to bear the sign" is "to carry death about," renouncing "all things" while still living, since the love of the one who sowed the flesh is not equal to that of the one who created the soul unto knowledge.

And again, discoursing about the law and using an allegory: "For the married woman," he says, "is bound by law to her living husband," and so on. And again: "The wife is bound for as long a time as her husband lives; but if he dies, she is free to be married, only in the Lord; but she is happier if she remains so, according to my judgement." But in the former passage he says, "You were put to death to the law"—not to marriage—"so that you might become another's, His who was raised from the dead"—a bride and a Church, who must be pure both from the inward thoughts that are contrary to the truth and from those who tempt from without; that is, from those who pursue the heresies and persuade her to fornicate away from the one husband, God Almighty—lest, as the serpent deceived Eve, the so-called Life, we too, through the lecherous craftiness of the heresies, transgress the commandments. But the second passage establishes monogamy. For it is not to be supposed, as some have interpreted, that the binding of a woman to a man indicates the entanglement of the flesh with corruption; for he is accusing the notion of godless men who attribute the invention of marriage outright to the devil—a notion through which the lawgiver is in danger of being blasphemed.

But in the Epistle of the Romans to the Corinthians it is written of "an ocean boundless to men, and the worlds beyond it." Consistently, then, the noble apostle cries out again: "O depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!" And was not this perhaps what the prophet hinted at, bidding men make unleavened cakes baked in ashes — showing that the truly sacred Word, initiate concerning the Unbegotten and his powers, ought to be kept hidden? Confirming these things, the apostle has openly said, in the Epistle to the Corinthians: "We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age that come to nothing; but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom." And again elsewhere he says: "unto the knowledge of the mystery of God in Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge." Our Saviour himself sets his seal to these things, saying somewhat thus: "To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven." And again the Gospel says that our Saviour spoke the word to the apostles in a mystery; for the prophecy too says of him: "He will open his mouth in parables, and will utter things hidden from the foundation of the world." And by the parable of the leaven too the Lord shows the concealment; for he says, "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal, until the whole was leavened." For either the threefold soul is saved by obedience, through the spiritual power hidden in it by faith; or because the strength of the Word given to us, being intense and powerful, draws to itself, secretly and unseen, everyone who has received it and gotten it within himself, and gathers his whole frame into unity.

This man, having come into a disposition of well-doing, benefits others more swiftly than he speaks nobly—praying that the sins of the brethren may be shared by him, unto the confession and conversion of his kinsmen, and eager to share his own goods with those dearest to him; and they in turn are thus his friends. Increasing, then, the seeds laid up within him according to the husbandry the Lord commanded, he remains free from sin, and becomes self-controlled, and passes his life with those like him in spirit, among the choirs of the saints, even while still held upon earth. This man, through the whole day and night, speaking and doing the charges of the Lord, rejoices exceedingly—not only when he has risen in the morning and at midday, but also when walking and lying down, when putting on his clothes and putting them off. And he teaches his son, if he have a son by birth, being inseparable from the commandment and the hope, giving thanks ever to God, like those creatures of praise allegorized by Isaiah, patient toward every trial. "The Lord," he says, "gave; the Lord has taken away." For such was Job too, who, even when his outward goods were taken away together with the health of his body, laid all aside beforehand through his love toward the Lord. "For he was," it is said, "just, holy, abstaining from all wickedness." And "holy" signifies the things just toward God according to the whole dispensation, which, knowing them, he was a gnostic. For one must neither, if the things be good, cling fast to them, being human things, nor again, if evil, be set against them; but be above both—treading the one underfoot, and passing the other on to those in need. And the gnostic is safe in accommodation, lest the accommodation should escape him and become a settled disposition.

It is Tatian the Syrian, I think, who dared to lay down such doctrines. He writes, at any rate, in so many words in his work On Perfection according to the Saviour: "Agreement, then, is suited to prayer; but communion in corruption dissolves the intercession." Indeed, very shamefully, through his concession, he forbids it; for, having conceded that they may come together again because of Satan and incontinence, he declares that the one who will be persuaded is going "to serve two masters"—through agreement, God; through disagreement, incontinence and fornication and the devil. He says this in interpreting the apostle; but he sophistically subverts the truth, fabricating a lie out of what is true. For we too confess that incontinence and fornication are devilish passions; but agreement mediates in prudent marriage, leading continently to prayer and joining in wedlock, with dignity, for the begetting of children. "Knowing" is even named as the proper season of begetting children by the Scripture, when it says: "Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth; for God has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel." Do you see against whom they blaspheme, those who loathe the prudent sowing of seed and attribute generation to the devil? For not just "a god" did he address, who by prefixing the article indicated the Almighty.

Basilides, in the twenty-third book of his Exegetica, concerning those punished in martyrdom, says, in these very words: "For I say that all who fall into the so-called afflictions—either, having sinned in other faults that escape notice, are led to this good thing by the kindness of the one who leads them about, being truly accused of other things than those for which they really suffer, so that they may not suffer as condemned for confessed evils, nor reviled as the adulterer or the murderer, but because they are by nature Christians—which will console them so that they do not even seem to suffer. And even if anyone, having altogether not sinned, should come to suffer—rare though this be—yet not even this man will suffer anything by the plotting of a power, but will suffer as the infant suffers that seems not to have sinned."

Most wisely, then, was this written by Solon concerning God: "Hardest of all is it to perceive the unseen measure of judgement, which alone holds the bounds of all things." For "the divine," says the poet of Acragas, "cannot be approached so as to be reached by our eyes, nor laid hold of with the hands, by which the greatest highway of persuasion falls into the minds of men." And John the apostle: "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten God, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him" — calling the invisible and unspeakable the "bosom" of God. And from this some have called him "the Depth," as having embraced and taken to his bosom all things, unreachable and boundless. Indeed this is the most unmanageable discourse about God. For since the beginning of every matter is hard to find, surely the first and most ancient beginning, which is the cause to all the rest of their coming-to-be and of being once come to be, is hardest to point out. For how could that be spoken of which is neither genus nor difference nor species nor individual nor number, nor yet an accident, nor that to which anything accrues? Nor could one rightly call him "whole"; for "whole" is ranked under magnitude, and he is the Father of wholes. Nor are any parts of him to be spoken of; for the One is indivisible, and for this reason also infinite — conceived not in respect of being unable to be gone through, but in respect of being without dimension and having no boundary; and therefore shapeless and nameless.

And the apostle's addition, "that you may come together again, because of Satan," cuts off beforehand the danger of ever being turned aside to other desires; for the temporary agreement, putting the natural appetites to shame, does not altogether repel them, and on their account he again introduces the union of marriage—not for incontinence and fornication and the work of the devil, but so that one may not fall under incontinence and fornication and the devil. And Tatian too separates the old man and the new, but not as we say. We agree with him in saying that the old man is the law and the new is the gospel; only not in the way he wishes, abolishing the law as belonging to another God. But the same Man and Lord, renewing the old, no longer permits polygamy (for then God required it, when it was necessary to increase and multiply), but introduces monogamy for the sake of begetting children and of the care of the house, for which the woman was given as a helper. And if to anyone, because of incontinence and burning, the apostle grants a second marriage by way of indulgence, this man too does not sin against the covenant (for it is not forbidden by the law), yet he does not fulfil the heightened perfection of the conduct that is according to the gospel; but he gains for himself a heavenly glory who remains by himself and keeps undefiled the union that has been dissolved by death, and who obeys the dispensation in a well-pleasing manner, since by it he has become undistracted in the service of the Lord. Nor indeed does the divine providence through the Lord now command, as of old, that one be baptized after the marriage-bed; for the Lord did not, by binding the believers, compel them to abstain from begetting children, He who through one baptism washed away the whole of intercourse for ever—the same Lord who in one baptism comprised the many washings of Moses.

Then, going on a little, he again adds: "As, then, the infant, having not sinned beforehand—or, actively, having sinned in nothing, but having in itself the capacity to sin—when it is subjected to suffering, is benefited, gaining many hard things; so likewise too, even if a perfect man should happen to have sinned in nothing by deed, yet, whatever he suffers, this he suffered in a manner like the infant. For, having in himself the capacity to sin, but not having received occasion to have sinned, he did not sin. So that his not having sinned is not to be reckoned to his credit. For as the man who wishes to commit adultery is an adulterer, even if he does not succeed in committing adultery, and the man who wishes to do murder is a murderer, even if he is unable to kill, so likewise too, even if I see the sinless man of whom I speak suffering, even if he has done nothing evil, I will call him evil for his wishing to sin. For I will say anything rather than call providence evil."

And if at any time we name it, calling it, not properly, either One or the Good, or Mind, or the Existent itself, or Father, or God, or Creator, or Lord — we do not speak as uttering his name, but, out of perplexity, we make use of noble names, that the understanding may have these to lean upon, and not wander among other things. For no one of these things by itself is significant of God, but all together are indicative of the power of the Almighty. For things spoken are spoken either out of what belongs to them, or out of their relation to one another; and none of these can be taken concerning God. Nor again is he grasped by demonstrative knowledge; for this is established out of things prior and more knowable, and nothing exists before the Unbegotten. It remains, then, by divine grace and by the Word alone that comes from him, to conceive the unknown — even as Luke too, in the Acts of the Apostles, records Paul saying: "Men of Athens, in all things I behold you as more than ordinarily religious; for as I went about and surveyed the objects of your worship, I found even an altar on which was inscribed, 'To an unknown God.' Whom, then, you worship in ignorance, this one I proclaim to you."

From of old, then, the law, prophesying our regeneration through carnal generation, attached baptism to the seminal deposit of seed, not loathing the generation of man; for what shows itself as a begotten man, this the deposit of seed can produce. So not many acts of intercourse make for fruitfulness, but the womb's reception declares the generation, the seed being shaped into an embryo in nature's workshop. And how can marriage be old and merely a discovery of the law, while the marriage according to the Lord is of a different kind, the same God being kept by us? For what God has joined together, man could never reasonably put asunder. Much more shall the Son too keep the things that the Father commanded. And if the same is both lawgiver and evangelist, He never contends with Himself. For the law lives, being spiritual and understood in a gnostic way. But we were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, that we might become another's, His who was raised from the dead, who was prophesied by the law, that we might bear fruit to God.

Then, going on, he speaks even outright concerning the Lord, as though concerning a man: "If, however, leaving aside all these arguments, you come to abash me by means of certain persons, saying perhaps, 'So-and-so, then, sinned, for so-and-so suffered'—if you permit me, I will say, he did not sin, but was like the suffering infant; but if you should force the argument more vehemently, I will say that any man whom you may name is a man, but God is just. For 'no one is clean,' as someone said, 'from filth.'" But the hypothesis of Basilides says that the soul, having sinned beforehand in another life, undergoes punishment here—the elect soul honourably through martyrdom, the other being purified by its own appropriate punishment. And how is this true, since the confessing and being punished, or not, lies in our power? For on the man who will deny, the providence according to Basilides is undone.

Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. We were put to death, then, to the law—that is, to the sin indicated by the law, which the law reveals but does not generate, by its commanding of the things to be done and its forbidding of the things not to be done, convicting the underlying sin, that sin might appear. But if marriage according to the law is sin, I do not know how anyone can claim to have known God while saying that the ordinance of God is sin; but since the law is holy, marriage is holy. This mystery, then, the apostle refers to Christ and the Church. As what is born of the flesh is flesh, so what is born of the spirit is spirit, not only as regards the birth but also as regards the learning. So the children are holy—the things well-pleasing to God—when the words of the Lord have wedded the soul. Fornication, then, and marriage are distinct, since the devil stands far off from God. "And you too were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, that you might become another's, His who was raised from the dead." For there is also understood, by close connection, that we became obedient, since indeed, according to the truth of the law, we obey the same Lord who exhorts us from afar.

I ask him, then, concerning the confessor who has been seized: will he bear witness and be punished according to providence, or not? For if he denies, he will not be punished. But if he should say, from the result, that this man too ought not to be punished, he will unwillingly bear witness besides to the destruction of those who deny as coming from providence. And how, then, is the most glorious reward laid up in heaven for the one who has borne witness, because of his bearing witness? And if providence did not allow the man with a capacity to sin to come to sinning, it becomes unjust on both counts—both not rescuing the man who is dragged to punishment for righteousness' sake, and rescuing the man who wished to do wrong, the one having done the things he willed, the other being one who hindered the deed and did not justly attend to the man capable of sin.

And perhaps it is concerning such men that the Spirit fittingly says outright: "In later times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and to teachings of demons, in the hypocrisy of liars, seared in their conscience, and forbidding to marry and to abstain from foods, which God created to be partaken of with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified through the word of God and intercession." We must not, then, forbid marriage by way of constraint, nor the eating of meat or the drinking of wine; for it is written: "It is good not to eat meat nor to drink wine, if one eats with offence"; and "It is good to remain as I also am"—but let both the one who uses with thanksgiving and the one who does not use, himself also with thanksgiving,

And how is he not godless, deifying the devil, and daring to call the Lord a man capable of sin? For the devil tempts, knowing what we are, but not knowing whether we shall endure; but, wishing to shake us from the faith and to draw us to himself, he tempts—which alone has been permitted to him, both because we must be saved by ourselves, having received occasions from the commandment, and because of the shame of the tempter who has been tempted and failed, and because of the strengthening of those in the Church, and because of the conscience of those who have wondered at the endurance. But if martyrdom is a recompense through punishment, then faith and teaching too, on account of which the martyrdom comes, are fellow-workers of the punishment—than which what greater absurdity could there be? But against those doctrines, whether the soul is reincarnated, and concerning the devil, it shall be spoken at the proper times; for now let us add to what has been said these things too: where any longer is faith, if martyrdom comes as a recompense for sins committed beforehand? Where is the love toward God that is persecuted and endures for the truth's sake? Where is the praise of the confessor or the blame of the one who denies? To what end is right conduct any longer useful—the mortifying of the desires and the hating of none of the creatures?

live according to reason, with continent enjoyment. And in general all the epistles of the apostle, teaching prudence and continence, and containing thousands of commandments concerning marriage and the begetting of children and the management of a house, nowhere reject prudent marriage; but, preserving the continuity of the law, they accept, in accordance with the gospel, both the man who uses marriage with thanksgiving to God and prudence, and the man who lives in celibacy as the Lord wishes, each as he was called, having chosen without stumbling and perfectly. "And the land of Jacob was praised above all the land," says the prophet, glorifying the vessel of His Spirit. But someone runs down generation, calling it corruptible and perishing, and forces the point, saying that with reference to the begetting of children the Saviour said, "Do not lay up treasure on earth, where moth and rust destroy," and is not ashamed to add the prophet's words to these: "You shall all grow old as a garment, and the moth shall eat you." But neither do we contradict the Scripture, that our bodies are corruptible and by nature in flux; only, perhaps he was prophesying corruption to those to whom he spoke as sinners. But the Saviour did not speak about the begetting of children; rather, urging toward the sharing of communion, He spoke to those who wish only to acquire a superfluity of wealth, and are unwilling to help the needy.

And if, as Basilides himself says, we have supposed one part of what is called the will of God to be the having loved all things, because they preserve a relation to the whole of all, and another to desire nothing, and a third to hate not one thing, then by the will of God the punishments too will be—which is impious to think. For neither did the Lord suffer by the will of the Father, nor are the persecuted persecuted by the will of God; since, of two, one: either persecution will be something good by the will of God, or those who afflict and oppress are guiltless. But indeed nothing among all things is without the will of the Lord of all. It remains, then, to say briefly that such things come about because God does not prevent them; for this alone preserves both the providence and the goodness of God.

Wherefore He says: "Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which abides unto eternal life." Likewise they bring forward also that saying: "The sons of that age neither marry nor are given in marriage." But if anyone considers carefully that this question is about the resurrection of the dead, and those who asked it, he will find that the Lord does not reject marriage, but heals the expectation of carnal desire in the resurrection. And "the sons of this age" He did not say by way of contrast with sons of some other age, but as equivalent to "those who have come to be in this age, being sons through generation, beget and are begotten"—since no one will come into this life without generation; but this generation, which admits of like corruption, no longer awaits the one who has once been separated from this life. "One, then, is your Father who is in heaven"—but He is also the Father of all by virtue of creation. "Call no one your father on earth," He says—meaning, do not regard as the cause the one who sowed you by carnal sowing as the substance of your being, but as a fellow-cause of generation, or rather a minister of generation.

We must not, then, suppose that He actively brings about the afflictions—for far be it to think this—but it is fitting to be persuaded that He does not prevent those who bring them about, and that He turns the rash deeds of the adversaries to good use ("I will throw down the wall, then," He says, "and it shall be for trampling under foot"), since such providence is an educative art—in the case of others on account of each man's own sins, but in the case of the Lord and the apostles on account of ours. So at once the divine apostle says: "For this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire, even as the Gentiles too who do not know the Lord; that no one go beyond and defraud his brother in the matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as also we told you before and testified. For God did not call us to uncleanness, but in sanctification. Therefore the one who rejects this rejects not man, but God, who also gave His Holy Spirit unto you." For the sake of this sanctification of ours, then, the Lord was not prevented from suffering.

So He wishes us, when we have turned, to become again as little children, recognizing the true Father, having been born again through water, this being another sowing than the sowing in creation. "Yes," he says, "the unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord; but the married man, how he may please his wife." What of it? Is it not permitted, even to the wife, while pleasing according to God, to give thanks to God? Is it not granted even to the married man, together with his consort, to be anxious about the things of the Lord? But just as the unmarried woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and in spirit, so too the married woman is anxious about the things of her husband and the things of the Lord, in the Lord, that she may be holy in body and in spirit; for both are holy in the Lord, the one as a wife, the other as a virgin. And to abash and check those prone to a second marriage, the apostle harmoniously strikes a higher note and at once says: "Every sin is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body."

If, then, one of them, making a defence, should say that the martyr is punished for the sins before this embodiment, but will receive back in turn the fruit of his conduct during this life, for so the dispensation has been arranged—we shall ask him whether the recompense comes from providence. For if it should not be of the divine dispensation, then the dispensation of purifications is gone, and their hypothesis has fallen; but if the purifications are from providence, then the punishments too are from providence. And though providence, as they say, begins to be set in motion from the Archon, yet it was sown into the substances, along with the generation of the substances, by the God of all. This being so, they are forced to confess either that the punishment is not unjust (and those who condemn and persecute the martyrs act justly), or that the persecutions too are wrought by the will of God. Therefore the toil and the fear, as they themselves say, no longer supervene upon things as rust upon iron, but come upon the soul from its own will.

But if anyone dares to call marriage fornication, again, running back to the law and the Lord, he blasphemes. For just as covetousness is called fornication, being opposed to contentment, and just as idolatry is the apportioning out from the one God to many gods, so fornication is a falling away from the one marriage into many; for fornication and adultery are taken in three ways by the apostle, as we have said. Concerning these the prophet says: "You were sold for your sins"; and again: "You were defiled in a strange land"—accounting defiled the communion that is entangled with another's body, and not that which is given in wedlock for the begetting of children. Wherefore the apostle too says: "I wish, then, that the younger women marry, bear children, manage their households, giving no occasion to the adversary for reviling; for some have already turned aside after Satan."

Yes, and he heartily approves of the husband of one wife, whether he be presbyter or deacon or layman, who uses marriage blamelessly; "and she shall be saved through child-bearing." And again the Saviour, calling the Jews a wicked and adulterous generation, teaches that, not having known the law as the law intends, but having followed the tradition of the elders and the commandments of men, they "commit adultery against the law," not having received it as a husband and lord of their virginity. And perhaps He knows them to be enslaved to strange desires, on account of which, being continually enslaved to sins, they were sold to the foreigners—since among the Jews women were not appointed common, but adultery too was forbidden. And the man who said, "I have married a wife and cannot come to the supper," was a divine example for the refutation of those who, for pleasures' sake, fall away from the divine commandment; since, by this reasoning, neither those who were righteous before the coming nor those who married after the coming—even if they be apostles—shall be saved. And if they again bring forward this, that the prophet too says, "I have grown old among all my enemies," let them understand by "enemies" their sins; and there is one such sin—not marriage, but fornication—since otherwise let them call generation too sin, and the Creator of generation.

By which account is solved the difficulty raised against us by the heretics, whether Adam was moulded perfect or imperfect. But if imperfect, how is the work of the perfect God imperfect — and most of all, man? But if perfect, how does he transgress the commandments? For they shall hear from us too that he did not come to be perfect in his constitution, but fit for the receiving of virtue; for it makes a difference, surely, to have been made fit for virtue with a view to the acquiring of it. And he wills us to be saved out of ourselves. This, then, is the nature of the soul, to be moved out of itself; next, being rational, philosophy being rational, we have a certain kinship with it; and the fitness is a bearing toward virtue, but not virtue. All men, then, as I said, are by nature fit for the acquiring of virtue; but one goes forward more, another less, both in learning and in training; wherefore some have held out to perfect virtue, others have reached only to a certain point, and some, again, being neglected, even though otherwise of good natural parts, have turned aside to the contrary. And much more is the knowledge that differs in greatness from all studies and in truth most grievous to acquire, and is won with much labour.

But, as it seems, they have not known the mysteries of God: that God created man unto incorruption, and made him an image of his own peculiar being, according to which peculiar being of him who knows all things the gnostic, being just and holy with prudence, hastens to come to the measure of perfect manhood. And that not the deeds and the thoughts only, but the words too, are pure in the gnostic — "You have tried my heart, you have visited it by night," it says; "you have proved me by fire, and no injustice was found in me, so that my mouth shall not speak the works of men." And what does it mean by "the works of men"? It makes known sin itself, not as drawn back to repentance (for this is common to the rest of believers too), but what sin is. For neither does it condemn this or that sin, but simply all sin; nor what someone has done amiss, but it shows forth what is not to be done. Whence repentance too is twofold: the one common, over the having stumbled; the other, having learned the nature of sin, persuades to stand apart from the very sinning, by a chief account, upon which follows the not sinning.

Let them not, then, say that he who acts unjustly and sins sins by the working of spirits; since then he would be guiltless. But choosing, in sinning, the same things as the spirits, being unstable and light and changeable in his desires, like a spirit, the man becomes spirit-driven. For instance, the evil man by nature, having become given to sin through evil, is base, holding what he willingly chose; and being given to sin, he also errs in his deeds; but, on the contrary, the earnest man sets things right. Wherefore we call not only the virtues, but also the noble actions, goods; and of goods we know that some are to be chosen for their own sake, as knowledge (for we hunt nothing else from it, when it is present, than its very presence, and our being in unceasing contemplation, and our struggling toward it and through it), but others for the sake of other things, as faith, for the sake of the escape from chastisement that comes of it and the benefit that comes from the recompense. For fear is the cause of not sinning to the many, and the promise the occasion of pursuing obedience, through which is salvation.

Most perfect, then, is knowledge as a good, being chosen for its own sake; and consequently the things following through it are noble. And chastisement, to the one chastised, is the cause of correction; and to those able to foresee from afar it becomes an example, by which they cut off the falling together with those like them. Let us, then, receive knowledge, not craving the results, but embracing it for the sake of knowing itself. For the first benefit is the gnostic habit, furnishing harmless pleasures and gladness both now and hereafter. And the gladness they say is cheerfulness, being a reasoning upon the virtue that is according to truth, through a certain feasting and outpouring of the soul. And the works that partake of knowledge are the good and noble deeds. For true wealth is the abundance in the deeds according to virtue, and poverty is the want according to worldly desires. For the possessions and uses of necessary things have not their quality harmful, but their quantity beyond measure.

Wherefore the gnostic circumscribes his desires, both in possession and in use, not overstepping the bound of necessities. Holding, then, the living here to be necessary for the joint increase of science and the procuring of knowledge, he will set, not the living, but the living well above all things; preferring neither children, nor again marriage, nor parents, to the love toward God and the righteousness in life. And the wife, after the bearing of children, is judged by him a sister, as being of the same Father, then only being reminded of her husband whenever she looks upon her children, as one who shall truly be a sister even after the putting off of the flesh, which separates and divides the knowledge of spiritual things by the peculiarity of the forms. For the souls, by themselves, are equal; the souls are neither, neither male nor female, when they neither marry nor are given in marriage. And is not the woman thus translated into the man, becoming unwomanish and manly and perfect alike?

This, then, was the laughter of Sarah, when the birth of a son was announced to her, not disbelieving the angel, I think, but ashamed of that intercourse, through which she was about to become the mother of a son. And was it not from then that Abraham, when he was in danger before the king of Egypt on account of Sarah's beauty, properly called her sister and of the same father, but not yet of the same mother? To those, then, who have repented of sins, and have not firmly believed, God grants their requests through their prayers; but to those who live sinlessly and gnostically, he gives upon their merely thinking. For instance, to Anna, upon her merely thinking of the child, was granted the conception of Samuel. "Ask," says the Scripture, "and I will do; think, and I will give." For we have received that God is the knower of hearts, not conjecturing, as we men do, from the movement of the soul, nor again from the result (for it is ridiculous so to think); nor, as the architect, when the work was made, praised it, so did God, having so made the light, then, having seen it, say it was good; but he, even before making it, knowing what it would be, praised this; and "it came to be" by the power of him who makes it good from above, through the beginningless purpose, the thing that should be good in actuality. For instance, he said beforehand that the thing to come should already be good, the phrase, by the inversion of order, hiding the truth.

The gnostic, then, prays even in thought every hour, being made familiar with God through love. And first he will ask remission of sins; and after the no longer sinning, the being able yet to do good and to understand the whole creation and dispensation of the Lord, that so, being pure in heart, he may be initiated, through the recognition that is through the Son of God, into the blessed vision face to face — having hearkened to the Scripture that says, "Fasting with prayer is good." And fastings show forth abstentions from all evils whatsoever, both in deed and in word and in the very thought. As it seems, then, righteousness is four-square, equal and like on every side — in word, in deed, in abstention from evils, in beneficence, in gnostic perfection, in no way at all limping, lest it appear unjust and unequal. As, then, one is just, this man is altogether faithful too; but as faithful, he is not yet also just — I mean the righteousness that is by advance and perfection, according to which the gnostic is called just.

For instance, to Abraham, having become faithful, it was reckoned for righteousness, when he had advanced to the greater and more perfect thing than faith. For not he who only abstains from the evil deed is just, unless he work besides both the doing good and the knowing on what account some things are to be abstained from and others done. "Through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left," says the apostle, the just man is conveyed to the highest inheritance, hedged about by the one and working by the other. For the mere shelter of the whole armour and the abstention from sins is not sufficient for perfection, unless it take besides the work of righteousness, the working unto beneficence. Then the ambidextrous and gnostic among us is revealed in righteousness, glorified already even here, as Moses was in his face — which, in what went before, we said is the characteristic property of the just soul. For as the styptic of the dye, abiding in the wool, gives it its peculiarity and its difference from the rest of the wool, so too in the case of the soul the labour has passed by, but the noble remains; and the sweet is left behind, but the shameful is wiped off. For these are the characteristic qualities of either soul, by which the one is known as glorified, the other as condemned.

Yes, and as upon Moses, from his righteous doing and his continual converse with the God who spoke to him, a certain glorified tint settled upon his face, so too upon the just soul a certain divine power of goodness, in respect of oversight and of prophecy and of governing energy, drawing near, as it were the radiance of an intellectual light, like the warmth of the sun, leaves its mark — a manifest seal of righteousness, a light united to the soul through undivided love, the soul being borne of God. Here the likeness to the saving God springs up to the gnostic, in so far as is lawful for human nature, he becoming perfect "as the Father," it says, "in the heavens." It is he who said, "Little children, yet a little while I am with you"; since God too, not in respect of his being good by nature, in this remains blessed and incorruptible, neither having troubles nor giving them to another; but working good in his own way, being God truly and the good Father, being and becoming in unceasing beneficences, he abides inviolably in the sameness of goodness. For what profit is there of a good thing that does not work nor do good?

He who has received the forgiveness of sins, then, must no longer sin. For upon the first and only repentance of sins (this would be of the sins that pre-existed in the gentile and first life, the one in ignorance, I mean) there is set forth at once, to those called, the repentance that cleanses the place of the soul from offences, that faith may be founded. And the Lord, being a knower of hearts and foreknowing the things to come, both the changeableness of man and the shiftiness and craftiness of the devil, foresaw from the very beginning above how the devil, being jealous over the forgiveness of the man's sins, would fasten certain causes of sins upon the servants of God, working evil prudently, that they too might fall away together with him.

Truth, then, being one (for falsehood has ten thousand byways), the schools of philosophy, both the barbarian and the Greek, like the Bacchae tearing apart the limbs of Pentheus, each boasts of the part it has obtained as though it were the whole truth; but all things, I think, are lit by the rising of the light. All, then, both Greeks and barbarians, who have reached after the truth, may be shown to hold some part — some not a little, others, perhaps, only a portion — of the discourse of truth. For the age of time brings together in a moment the future and the present, and indeed the past as well; but truth is far more powerful than the age in gathering its own seeds, even if they have fallen into foreign ground. For we should find very many of the opinions dogmatized among the schools (all that have not been wholly deafened, nor cut off from the natural sequence, like the men whom the women's quarters have castrated of reason) — even if they seem unlike one another, yet agreeing in their kind and with the whole truth; for they are joined into one, either as a limb, or as a part, or as a species, or as a genus. The highest string, indeed, is opposite to the lowest, yet both are one harmony; and among numbers the even differs from the odd, yet both agree in arithmetic, as in figure the circle and the triangle and the square, and all the figures that differ from one another. And in the whole universe too all the parts, even if they differ from one another, preserve their kinship with the whole. So, then, the barbarian and the Greek philosophy have made a kind of rending of the eternal truth — not the rending of the mythology of Dionysus, but of the theology of the ever-existing Word. And the man who puts together again what is divided and unifies it will, be assured, behold the truth, the perfect Word, without danger.

He gave, then, yet another repentance, a second, to those who, even in the faith, fall into some offence, being very merciful, that, if anyone be tempted after the calling, but forced and over-reached by craft, he may receive still one repentance not to be repented of. For "if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there is no longer left a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a zeal of fire that is about to devour the adversaries." But the continual and repeated repentances upon sins differ in nothing from those who have not believed at all, except only in the perceiving that they sin; and I do not know which of the two is worse — to sin knowingly, or, having repented of the sins, to offend again. For by either way the sin is shown by conviction: the one condemned at the doing by the worker of lawlessness, the other by the man who, foreknowing the thing to be done as base, attempts it. And the one perhaps gratifies anger and pleasure, not ignorant whom he gratifies; but the other, repenting of what he gratified, then running back again to pleasure, is joined to the one who from the beginning willingly sins; for he who does again that of which he repented, doing what he has condemned,

It is written, at any rate, in Ecclesiastes: "And I added wisdom beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem; and my heart saw many things — wisdom and knowledge; I came to know parables and understanding. For this too is a preference of the spirit, that in the abundance of wisdom is the abundance of knowledge." And the man experienced in wisdom of every kind, he would properly be the gnostic. So it is written: "The abundance of the knowledge of wisdom will give life to the man who has it from her." And again this saying more clearly confirms what has been said: "All things are plain to those who understand" (and "all things" are both Greek and barbarian, but the other things are no longer "all"), "and straight to those who wish to carry off perception. Choose education and not silver, and knowledge above tested gold; and choose perception above pure gold; for wisdom is better than precious stones, and nothing of worth is equal to her."

does it willingly. He, then, who from the nations and from that former life rushed to faith, once obtained forgiveness of sins; but he who, even after these things, has sinned, then repents, even if he meet with pardon, ought to be ashamed, no longer washing himself unto forgiveness of sins. For he must leave behind not only the idols which he formerly deified, but also the works of his former life — the man not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, but reborn in spirit; which would be not to repent of the same offence into which he has been carried. For to repent often is, on the contrary, a practice of sins, and an aptitude toward readiness, from want of training.

To ask pardon often for the things in which we often offend is, then, a semblance of repentance, not repentance. "But righteousness cuts straight blameless ways," cries the Scripture. And again: "The righteousness of the harmless will set straight his way." Indeed, "as a father pities his sons, so the Lord pitied those who fear him," David writes. "Those, then, who sow in tears," of those who in repentance make confession, "will reap in gladness; for blessed are all who fear the Lord." You see the blessing that resembles those in the Gospel? "Fear not," it says, "when a man becomes rich, and when the glory of his house is multiplied; for in his dying he will not take all things, nor will his glory go down with him. But I, in your mercy, will enter into your house; I will worship toward your holy temple in your fear. Lord, lead me in your righteousness." Now impulse is a movement of the mind toward something or away from it; and passion is an excessive impulse, or one overstraining the measures according to reason, or an impulse carried away and disobedient to reason. So passions are a movement of the soul contrary to nature, in the disobedience toward reason. (And the departure and the standing-out and the disobedience are in our power, as obedience too is in our power; wherefore the voluntary things are judged.) And indeed if one should go through each of the passions one by one, one would find them irrational appetites.

He never remembers those who have sinned against him, but forgives. Therefore too he justly prays, saying, "Forgive us; for we too forgive." For this also is one of the things God wills: to desire nothing, to hate no one. For all men are the work of one will. And does not our Saviour, willing the gnostic to be "perfect as the heavenly Father"—that is, as himself—who says, "Come, children, hear from me the fear of the Lord," will that this man should no longer be in need of help through angels, but should receive, having become worthy of himself, and should have the guard from himself through obedience? Such a man demands from the Lord, and does not merely ask. And in the matter of needy brethren, the gnostic will not ask for an abundance of money for himself for distribution, but will pray that the supply of what they need may come to them. For thus the gnostic both gives his prayer to those in need, and provides what comes through prayer, at once without their knowing and without ostentation.

They say in the traditions that Matthias the apostle said at each point: "If the neighbour of an elect man sins, the elect man has sinned; for if he had borne himself as the Word dictates, the neighbour too would have stood in such awe of his life as not to sin." What, then, should we say concerning the gnostic himself? "Or do you not know," says the Apostle, "that you are a temple of God?" The gnostic, then, is divine and already holy, God-bearing and borne by God. Indeed, Scripture, showing that to sin is alien, sells off those who fall away to men of another race; and saying, "Do not look with desire upon another's wife," it plainly calls sin alien and contrary to the nature of the temple of God. And a temple there is, the great one, like the Church, and the small, like the man who preserves the seed of Abraham. Therefore he who has God resting in him will not desire anything else. Indeed, leaving behind all that is in the way and despising all the matter that distracts him, he cuts through heaven by knowledge, and, passing through the spiritual substances and every principality and authority, he lays hold of the highest thrones, pressing on toward that alone which alone he has known. Having mingled, then, the serpent with the dove, he lives at once perfectly and with a good conscience, having tempered faith with hope toward the awaiting of the future. For he is aware of the gift he has received, having become worthy to attain it, and, transferred from slavery into adoption, he performs the things that follow upon knowledge ("having known God—or rather having been known by him"), displaying his activities in a manner worthy of the grace. For the works follow upon knowledge as the shadow upon the body.

Everything, then, that falls under a name is begotten, whether they will it or no. Whether, then, the Father himself draws to himself everyone who has lived purely and has passed into the conception of the blessed and incorruptible nature; or whether the freedom of will in us, having come to the knowledge of the Good, leaps and bounds beyond the bars, as the trainers say — yet not without the special grace does the soul take wings and rise and is lifted up above the things that lie above, casting off all that weighs it down and rendering it to its kindred. And Plato too, in the Meno, says that virtue is God-given, as these words show: "From this reasoning, then, Meno, virtue appears to come to those to whom it comes by a divine portion." Does it not seem to you that the gnostic habit, which does not come to all, is hinted at as a divine portion? And more plainly he adds: "If now we, in all this discourse, have inquired well, virtue would be neither by nature nor taught, but coming by a divine portion, without intelligence, to those to whom it comes." God-given, then, is wisdom, being a power of the Father, which rouses our free will, and welcomes faith, and rewards with the highest fellowship the attentiveness of the elect choice.

On no account, then, is he reasonably disturbed by anything that happens, nor does he suspect anything of the things that come about in the dispensation for our profit, nor is he ashamed to die, having a good conscience to be seen by the authorities, since he has cleansed away, so to speak, all the stains of his soul—he who knows very well that things will be better for him after his departure. Whence he never prefers the pleasant and the profitable to the dispensation, training himself through the commandments, that he may become both well-pleasing to the Lord in all things and praiseworthy toward the world, since all things rest upon the one almighty God. "To his own," it is said, "the Son of God came, and his own received him not." Therefore, in the use of worldly things, he not only gives thanks and marvels at the creation, but, using them as is fitting, he is praised—since his end is brought, through gnostic activity according to the commandments, into contemplation. From here already, reaping through knowledge the provisions for the journey of contemplation, and having received with high-mindedness the greatness of the knowledge, he advances to the holy requital of the translation. For he has heard the psalm that says: "Go round about Zion and encompass her; recount in her towers." For it hints, I think, that those who have received the Word loftily will be lofty as towers, and will stand firm both in faith and in knowledge.

And indeed I will set Plato before you, downright requiring men to believe in the children of God. For, having made his discourse concerning gods visible and begotten, in the Timaeus, he says: "But to speak of the other spirits, and to know their generation, is beyond us; but we must trust those who spoke before, being, as they said, offspring of gods, and clearly somehow knowing their own forefathers. It is impossible, then, to disbelieve children of gods, even though they speak without probable and necessary proofs." I do not think the Saviour and those anointed unto prophecy could be more plainly attested to by Greeks — the former proclaimed children of God, but the Lord his genuine Son — that they are true witnesses concerning divine things; wherefore he added that one must believe them, since they are divinely inspired. And though one should say, in more tragic vein, that he disbelieves — "for it was not Zeus who proclaimed these things to me" — yet let him know that it was God himself, through the Son, who proclaimed the Scriptures. And he is trustworthy who announces what is his own, since "no one," says the Lord, "knew the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son reveals him."

Belief, then, must be given to this one, even according to Plato, even if without probable and necessary proofs he is proclaimed and spoken of, through both the old and the new covenant. "For unless you believe," says the Lord, "you shall die in your sins"; and on the contrary, "He who believes has eternal life." Blessed, then, are all who have trusted in him. To have trusted is more than to believe; for when one knows that the Son of God is our teacher, he has trusted that his teaching is true. And as learning, according to Empedocles, increases the mind, so trust in the Lord increases faith. We say, then, that it belongs to the same men to blame philosophy and to run down faith, to praise injustice and to count the life of desire happy.

Now faith, even if it is a voluntary assent of the soul, is yet a worker of good things and a foundation of righteous action. And though Aristotle reason technically — teaching that "making" is ranked among the irrational creatures and among lifeless things too, but "acting" belongs to men only — let him set right those who say that God is the maker of all things. But the thing to be done, he says, is either as good or as necessary. To act unjustly, then, is not good (for no one acts unjustly except for the sake of something else), and of necessary things none is voluntary; to act unjustly, then, is voluntary, so that it is not necessary. And the earnest men differ above all from the base both in their choices and in their seemly desires. For every depravity of soul is accompanied by intemperance, and he who acts through passion acts through intemperance and depravity. It comes to me, then, to marvel at every turn at that divine voice: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter by the door into the fold of the sheep, but climbs up another way, that man is a thief and a robber; but he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep; to him the doorkeeper opens." Then, explaining himself, the Lord says: "I am the door of the sheep."

It is necessary, then, having learned the truth through Christ, to be saved, even if one chance to have philosophized in the Greek philosophy; for now it has been plainly shown — what in other generations was not made known to the sons of men — now it has been revealed. For there was always, in all who were right-minded, a natural conception of one God, the Almighty; and most men, even those who had not utterly lost their shame before the truth, laid hold of the everlasting benefaction according to the divine providence. Generally, at any rate, Xenocrates of Chalcedon does not despair of the conception of the divine even in the irrational creatures; and Democritus, though he wish it not, will confess it, by the consequence of his own doctrines; for he made the same images fall upon men and upon the irrational creatures from the divine substance. Far indeed is man from being without a share in the divine conception, who has been recorded as partaking too of the inbreathing at his creation, having received a purer substance than the other creatures.

Hence the school of Pythagoras say that the mind comes to men by a divine portion, as Plato and Aristotle too confess. But we say that the Holy Spirit is breathed upon him who has believed; whereas the school of Plato place the mind in the soul as an effluence of a divine portion, and the soul in the body. For plainly, through Joel, one of the twelve prophets, it is said: "And it shall come to pass after these things, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy." But the Spirit is not in each of us as a part of God. And how this distribution comes about, and what in the world the Holy Spirit is, will be shown by us in the books On Prophecy and On the Soul. But "to hide the depths of knowledge is good unbelief," according to Heraclitus; "for by unbelief it escapes being known."

And concerning these things the discussion is long, which we shall reserve to consider later, treating it at the proper time. But Valentinus, in a certain homily, writes, word for word: "From the beginning you are immortal, and you are children of eternal life, and you wished to apportion death among yourselves, that you might spend it and use it up, and that death might die in you and through you. For when you dissolve the world but yourselves are not dissolved, you are lords over the creation and over all corruption." For he too, like Basilides, supposes a kind saved by nature, and that this different kind has come down from above to us here for the destruction of death, and that the generation of death is the work of the one who created the world. Wherefore he understands that Scripture too thus: "No one shall see the face of God and live"—of God as the cause of death. Concerning this God he hints those things, writing in these very words: "By however much the image is inferior to the living face, by so much is the world inferior to the living aeon."

XIV. We must add what comes next, and now set forth more plainly the Greek theft from the barbarian philosophy. For the Stoics say that God is a body and spirit in substance, just as, indeed, the soul also is. All these things you will find downright in the Scriptures. For do not think now of their allegories as the gnostic truth delivers them, since these, while showing one thing, signify another, like skilful wrestlers. But while they say that God pervades all substance, we call him Maker only, and Maker by the Word. And they were led astray by what is said in Wisdom, "It pervades and passes through all things by reason of its pureness," since they did not understand that these things are said of the Wisdom that was first-created by God. "Yes," they say, "but the philosophers lay down matter among the first principles — both the Stoics and Plato and Pythagoras, and Aristotle the Peripatetic too — and not one principle." Let them know, then, that what is called matter is said by themselves to be without quality and without shape, and, more daringly still, has been called by Plato "not-being." And does not Plato, knowing most mystically that the one truly existing principle is one, say in the Timaeus, in these very words: "Now, then, let our position be thus: concerning the beginning, or beginnings, of all things, or however we are minded about these matters, it must not now be spoken of, for no other reason than this, that it is hard, in the present manner of the exposition, to make plain what seems good."

What, then, is the cause of the image? The majesty of the face that provided the type to the painter, that it might be honoured through His name; for the form was not found authentically, but the name filled up what was lacking in the moulding. And the invisibility of God too contributes toward the faith of the thing moulded. For the Demiurge, called god and father, he addressed as image of the true God and as prophet, but Sophia as painter, of whom the moulded thing is the image, unto the glory of the invisible—since whatever comes forth from a conjugal pairing is fullnesses, but whatever from a single one is images. And since the visible part of him is not the soul from the middle state, there comes the "different" element, and this is the in-breathing of the different spirit, which is breathed into the soul, the image of the spirit. And, in general, the things spoken concerning the Demiurge who came to be after the image, these, they say, were prophesied in Genesis, in the rank of a perceptible image, concerning the generation of man. And indeed they transfer the likeness to themselves too, handing down that the insertion of the different spirit came about unknown to the Demiurge.

And besides, that prophetic saying, "And the earth was invisible and unfurnished," supplied them with starting-points for a material substance. Indeed, to Epicurus the smuggling-in of chance came from not following the meaning; whence "vanity of vanities, all is vanity." And Aristotle was able to bring providence down only as far as the moon, from this Psalm: "O Lord, your mercy is in the heaven, and your truth reaches to the clouds." For the showing-forth of the prophetic mysteries was not yet uncovered before the coming of the Lord. And again, the punishments after death, and the chastisement by fire, the whole poetic muse, and the Greek philosophy too, filched from the barbarian philosophy. Plato, at any rate, in the last book of the Republic, says in these very words: "There, then, savage men, fiery to look upon, standing by and marking the utterance, took some apart and led them away; but Aridaeus and the others they bound, hands and feet and head, and threw down and flayed, and dragged them along the way outside, carding them upon thorns." For the fiery men he means to be angels, who take the unjust and chastise them; "he makes," it says, "his angels winds, and his ministers a flaming fire."

With such things Julius Cassianus too, the founder of the Docetic doctrine, makes his attempt. In his work On Continence, or On Celibacy, at any rate, he says in so many words: "And let no one say that, because we have such parts—so that the female is shaped one way and the male another, the one for receiving, the other for sowing—intercourse is therefore permitted by God. For if this arrangement were from God, toward whom we hasten, He would not have called the eunuchs blessed, nor would the prophet have said that they are not a fruitless tree"—transferring the figure from the tree to the man who by free choice makes himself a eunuch of such a notion.

Whenever, then, we treat of the one God being the one proclaimed through the law and the prophets and the gospel—and we shall discourse on this too (for the argument is fundamental)—but for the present we must answer the pressing point. If the different kind comes for the destruction of death, then it is not Christ who has destroyed death, unless He too be said to be of the same substance with them; but if He destroyed it to this end, namely, that He might not touch the different kind, then it is not these counterfeits of the Demiurge who destroy death—those who breathe into the soul from the middle state, their own image, the life from above according to the heresy of their doctrine, even if they say this comes about through the mother. But even if they should say that they wage war together with Christ against death, let them confess the hidden doctrine, that they dare to run down the divine power of the Demiurge, setting right His creation as though they were better, attempting to save the psychic image which He Himself had not the power to deliver from corruption. The Lord too, then, would be better than the Demiurge God; for the Son would never contend with the Father, and that among gods.

And it follows upon these that the soul is immortal. For that which is chastised or instructed, being in sensation, lives, even though it be said to suffer. And again — does not Plato know of rivers of fire and the depth of the earth, calling, in poetic fashion, what is named by the barbarians Gehenna "Tartarus," and bringing in Cocytus and Acheron and Pyriphlegethon and certain such places of chastisement for the bringing of men to soberness through instruction? And of the little ones, according to the Scripture, and the least, the angels who behold God, and moreover the oversight that comes to us through the appointed angels — showing these things, he does not shrink from writing: "When all the souls had chosen their lives, as they had drawn lots, they went up in order to Lachesis; and she sent with each, as a guard of his life and a fulfiller of what he had chosen, that spirit which he had chosen." And perhaps the divine sign hinted some such thing to Socrates too.

And still contending for the godless opinion, he adds: "How would one not reasonably also blame the Saviour, if He refashioned us and freed us from error and from the communion of the parts and the appendages and the genitals?"—laying down doctrines like Tatian's in this. But he came out of the school of Valentinus. For this reason Cassianus says: "When Salome asked when the things she inquired about would be known, the Lord said, 'When you have trampled on the garment of shame, and when the two become one, and the male with the female is neither male nor female.'"

But that this one is the Father of the Son, the Demiurge of all things, the Lord Almighty, we have postponed to that examination in which we promised to discourse against the heresies, showing that this is the only one proclaimed by Him. But for us the apostle, writing for the endurance of afflictions, says this too is from God: "Because to you it was granted in behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer in His behalf; having the same conflict which you saw in me and now hear of in me. If, then, there is any encouragement in Christ, any consolation of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any bowels and compassions, fulfil my joy, that you be of the same mind, having the same love, joined in soul, minding the one thing." And if "he is poured out upon the sacrifice and ministry of the faith, rejoicing and rejoicing together with all"—and he calls those to whom the apostle's discourse is addressed, the Philippians, "sharers in the grace"—how does he call them "joined in soul" and "psychic"? Likewise, writing concerning Timothy and himself: "For I have no one like-souled," he says, "who will genuinely care for the things concerning you; for all seek their own things, not the things of Jesus Christ."

Indeed, that the world is begotten, the philosophers laid down as a doctrine taking it from Moses. And Plato downright says: "Was it always, having no beginning of generation, or has it come to be, beginning from some beginning? It has come to be; for it is visible and tangible, and being tangible has a body." And again, when he says, "Now the Maker and Father of this whole it is a task to find," he not only showed the world to be begotten, but signifies that it came to be from him as a son, and that he is called its Father, as having come from him alone and subsisted out of what was not. And the Stoics too lay it down that the world is begotten. And the devil so noised abroad by the barbarian philosophy, the ruler of the spirits, Plato in the tenth book of the Laws calls an evil-working soul, in these words: "Must we not say that a soul ordering and dwelling in all things that move every way orders the heaven too? Surely. One soul, or more? More — I will answer for you both. Let us lay down not fewer than two, the one beneficent, and the other able to work the contrary."

First, then, in the four gospels handed down to us we do not have this saying, but in the Gospel according to the Egyptians. Next, he seems to me to be ignorant that by "male" it hints at the impulse of wrath, and by "female" desire, which, when acted upon, are followed by repentance and shame. So whenever a man, gratifying neither wrath nor desire—which, indeed, increased by custom and bad nourishment, overshadow and veil the reason—but having stripped off the mist that comes from these, ashamed through repentance, unites spirit and soul in obedience to the Word, then, as Paul too says, "there is in you neither male nor female." For the soul, departing from this form by which male and female are distinguished, is transferred into unity, being neither of the two. But this noble fellow holds, in a rather Platonic way, that the soul, being divine and from above, made female by desire, comes down here into generation and decay.

Let not, then, the aforesaid call us "psychic" in the way of reproach—nor the Phrygians; for these too already call those who do not attend to the new prophecy "psychic," against whom we shall discourse in the books On Prophecy. The perfect man, then, must practise love, and from this hasten toward the divine friendship, fulfilling the commandments out of love. And to love one's enemies does not mean to love the evil, nor impiety or adultery or theft, but the thief and the impious and the adulterer—not in so far as he sins and defiles by his particular activity the appellation of "man," but in so far as he is a man and a work of God. To be sure, the sinning lies in activity, not in substance; therefore it is not a work of God either.

And likewise in the Phaedrus he writes thus: "There are indeed other evils too; but some spirit has mingled with most of them, in the immediate present, a pleasure." But in the tenth book of the Laws, too, he downright shows forth that apostolic saying, "Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the spiritual hosts in the heavens," writing somewhat thus: "Since, then, we have granted among ourselves that the heaven is full of many goods, and of their opposites too, but of the latter the more, there is, we say, such a battle undying, and needing wondrous watchfulness." And the barbarian philosophy, again, knows the world to be intelligible on the one hand, and sensible on the other; the one an archetype, the other the image of what is called the pattern; and it dedicates the one to the monad, as being intelligible, and the sensible to the hexad. For among the Pythagoreans the hexad, as being a generative number, is called marriage. And in the monad it sets up an invisible heaven and an unseen earth and intelligible light; "for in the beginning," it says, "God made the heaven and the earth; and the earth was invisible."

The sinners are called enemies of God, having become enemies of the commandments which they have not obeyed, just as those who have obeyed are called friends—the one set named for their kinship, the others for the estrangement that comes of their own choice; for neither enmity nor sin exists without the enemy and the sinner. And "to desire nothing" does not teach us to have no longing, as though the objects of desire were alien to us—as those have supposed who lay down as doctrine that the Creator is other than the first God—nor as though generation were abominable and evil, for these opinions are godless; but we say the things of the world are "alien," not as being out of place, nor as not belonging to God the Lord of all, but because we do not abide among them for all eternity, they being, by way of possession, alien and belonging to the line of succession, but by use, the proper things of each of us, for whose sake they came to be—only in so far as it is necessary for them to be present with us. We must use, then, in accordance with natural appetite, the things not forbidden, nobly, declining every excess and passionate attachment.

Then it goes on: "And God said, Let there be light; and there was light." And in the sensible cosmogony he fashions a solid heaven (and the solid is sensible) and a visible earth and a light that is seen. Does it not seem to you that hence Plato leaves the ideas of living creatures in the intelligible world, and fashions the sensible kinds according to the intelligible genera? With reason, then, Moses says that the body was moulded out of earth — which Plato calls an "earthy tabernacle" — and that the rational soul was breathed in from above by God into the face. For here, they say, the ruling part is seated, interpreting the entrance of the soul through the senses in the case of the first-moulded man; wherefore man came to be after the image and likeness. For the image of God is the divine and royal Word, the man free from passion; and the image of the image is the human mind. And if you wish to take the assimilation by another name, you would find it called, in Moses, a divine "following"; for he says, "After the Lord your God you shall walk, and his commandments you shall keep." And followers, I think, and worshippers of God are all the virtuous.

Hence the Stoics have said that the end of philosophy is to live in agreement with nature, and Plato, to be made like God (as we set forth in the second book of the Stromateis). And Zeno the Stoic, taking from Plato, and Plato from the barbarian philosophy, says that all good men are friends of one another. For Socrates says, in the Phaedrus, that it is not fated for evil to be friend to evil, nor good not friend to good — which he showed sufficiently in the Lysis too, that in injustice and wickedness friendship could never be preserved. And the Athenian stranger likewise says that there is an act dear to and in accordance with God, holding one ancient principle, when the like is friend to the like, it being measured, but the unmeasured is friend neither to the unmeasured nor to the measured.

And God would be for us the measure of all things. Then, a little after, he adds again: "For every good man is like to every good man, and in this is like also to God, and is friend both to every good man and to God." Coming to this point, I called to mind that other saying; for at the end of the Timaeus he says that one ought to liken the thinking part to the thing thought, according to the ancient nature, and, having made it like, to attain the end of the best life set before man by the gods, both for the present and for the time to come. For these have the same force as those words: "He who seeks will not cease until he finds; and having found, he will be amazed; and being amazed, he will reign; and having reigned, he will rest." And again — do not those sayings of Thales hang upon these? For the "being glorified unto the ages of ages" and the being called among us "the knower of hearts" he plainly interprets. Thales, at any rate, being asked what the divine is, said, "That which has neither beginning nor end." And when another inquired whether the divine escapes a man's notice when he does anything, "How," he said, "when it does not escape him even when he thinks?" Indeed the barbarian philosophy knows only the noble to be good, and virtue to be sufficient for happiness, when it says: "Behold, I have set before your eyes the good and the evil, life and death; choose life." For the good it calls life, and the choice of it noble, but the choosing of the contrary it calls evil. And of good and of life there is one end, to become a lover of God; "for this is your life and your length of days, to love what is toward the truth."

And those words have it still more plainly. For the Saviour, having charged us to love God and our neighbour, says that on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets. These doctrines the Stoics noise abroad, and before them Socrates, in the Phaedrus, praying: "O Pan and you other gods, grant that I may be beautiful within." And in the Theaetetus he says outright: "For he who speaks beautifully is beautiful and good." And in the Protagoras he confesses to his comrades that he met one fairer than Alcibiades, if indeed the wisest is the fairest; for he said virtue is the beauty of the soul, and, on the contrary, vice the ugliness of the soul. And Antipater the Stoic, having written three books on the point that, according to Plato, the noble alone is good, shows that, according to him too, virtue is sufficient for happiness, and sets down many other doctrines in accord with the Stoics. And to Aristobulus, who lived under Ptolemy Philometor, whom the writer of the epitome of the books of the Maccabees mentions, there belong sufficient books, in which he shows that the Peripatetic philosophy depends upon the law according to Moses and upon the other prophets.

And let these things be so. But that we are brethren, as being of one God and one teacher, Plato too somewhere appears to declare, somewhat thus: "For you are all brethren in the city, as we shall say to them, telling our tale; but God, in moulding you, mingled gold in the begetting of those of you who are fit to rule, wherefore they are most honoured; and silver in the auxiliaries; and iron and bronze in the husbandmen and the other craftsmen." Hence, he says, there is need to welcome and to love these things, in which knowledge is, but those others, in which opinion is.
