Perhaps he divines this elect nature that reaches after knowledge — unless, supposing three natures, he is sketching three polities, as some have taken it, of the Jews the silver, of the Greeks the third, and of the Christians, in whom the royal gold, the Holy Spirit, has been mingled. And, setting forth the Christian life, he writes in these very words in the Theaetetus: "Let us speak of the chief men. For why should one speak of those who pass their time meanly in philosophy? These men know neither the way to the market-place, nor where the court is, nor the council-chamber, nor any other common gathering of the city; laws and decrees written they neither see nor hear. The eagernesses of partisans, and assemblies, and revels with flute-girls — to do such things does not occur to them even in a dream. And whether anyone in the city has been born well or ill, or what evil has befallen anyone from his forefathers, escapes them more than the proverbial pints of the sea. And he does not even know that he does not know all this; but in truth his body alone lies and sojourns in the city, while he himself, according to Pindar, flies about, measuring out the heavens above and the earth beneath, doing astronomy, and searching out all nature on every side."

Again, to the Lord's saying, "Let your yes be yes, and your no, no," that other is to be likened: "But to me it is in no way lawful either to grant a falsehood or to do away with the truth." And with the prohibition of swearing this saying in the tenth book of the Laws agrees: "Let praise and oath be far from everything." And, in sum, Pythagoras and Socrates and Plato, when they say they hear the voice of God, beholding the framework of the whole accurately made by God and held together unceasingly, have heard Moses saying, "He said, and it came to be" — describing the word of God as a work. And standing upon the moulding of man out of dust, the philosophers at every turn proclaim the body earthy; and Homer does not shrink from setting, by way of curse, the words: "But may you all become water and earth," just as Isaiah says, "And tread them down as clay."

And Callimachus plainly writes: "That was the year in which both the winged thing, and that in the sea, and the four-footed, so spoke, as the Promethean clay." And again the same: "If Prometheus moulded you, and you are come of clay and of no other thing." And Hesiod says concerning Pandora: "And he bade the renowned Hephaestus, as quickly as might be, to mix earth with water, and to set in it a man's voice and mind." The Stoics define nature as a craftsmanlike fire, going by a way toward generation; but God and his Word are allegorized by the Scripture as fire and light. And again — does not Homer too, paraphrasing the separation of the water from the earth, and the plain uncovering of the dry land, say of Tethys and Oceanus: "For already a long time they have held apart from one another the bed of love"? Again, the most learned among the Greeks ascribe to God omnipotence in all things — Epicharmus (and he was a Pythagorean) saying, "Nothing escapes the divine; this you must know: he himself is our watcher, and nothing is impossible to God."

And the lyric poet: "And it is possible for God, out of black night, to raise an unstained light, and with dark cloudy gloom to cover the pure brightness of the day" (for the one who alone, while day is present, can make night, this, he says, is God); and in the work entitled Phaenomena, Aratus, having said, "Let us begin from Zeus," whom, O men, we never leave unspoken, adds: "and full of Zeus are all the streets, and all the gatherings of men, full too the sea and the harbours; everywhere we all have need of Zeus. For we are also his offspring" — that is, his creation; "and gentle to men he gives favourable signs, and stirs the peoples to work; and these signs he fixed in the heaven, distinguishing the stars; and he looked out, against the year, for stars that should most surely signify to men the things of the seasons, that all might grow firm; and him men ever propitiate first and last: hail, Father, great wonder, great help to men." And before him Homer too, fashioning the world after Moses upon the shield wrought by Hephaestus, says: "On it he made the earth, and on it the heaven, and on it the sea, and on it all the constellations with which heaven is crowned." For the Zeus sung of in the poems and in the prose writings carries the conception up to God.

And already, as one might say, in the light of day, Democritus writes that there are a few of mankind who, lifting up their hands toward what we Greeks now call the air, say, "Zeus debates all things, and this one knows all things and gives all things and takes them away, and this is king of all." And more mystically the Boeotian Pindar, being a Pythagorean, hands down: "One is the race of men, one of gods, and from one mother do we both draw breath" — that is, of matter — and one Maker of these, whom he calls "the most excellent craftsman, the Father," who has furnished even the advances, according to desert, toward divinity. For I pass over Plato; he downright, in the letter to Erastus and Coriscus, appears, I know not how, to show forth Father and Son out of the Hebrew Scriptures, charging in these words: "Calling to witness, in earnest and not without the grace of the Muses, and with discipline, the sister of earnestness, the God who is the cause of all, and the Lord, the Father of the leader and cause, whom, if you philosophize rightly, you shall know." And the address in the Timaeus calls the Creator Father, saying somewhat thus: "Gods of gods, of whom I am Father and Maker of works."

So that even when he says, "About the king of all are all things, and he is the cause of all noble things; and the second is about the second things, and the third about the third things," I for my part understand it in no other way than that the holy Trinity is signified: for the third is the Holy Spirit, and the Son the second, through whom all things came to be according to the will of the Father. And the same Plato, in the tenth book of the Republic, mentions Er the son of Armenius, by race a Pamphylian, who is Zoroaster. Zoroaster himself, at any rate, writes: "These things I, Zoroaster son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by race, having died in war, learned from the gods while I was in Hades." This Zoroaster Plato says came to life again, lying twelve days upon the pyre. Perhaps, then, he hints at the resurrection; or perhaps at this, that the way is made for souls, through the twelve signs of the zodiac, to the ascent; and he says the same descent is made even to birth. And in this way one must understand that the labours of Heracles too came to be twelve, after which the soul obtains its release from this whole world. Nor do I pass over Empedocles, who in his physical way speaks of the taking-up of all things, as if a change were to come at some time into the substance of fire.

And most plainly Heraclitus of Ephesus is of this opinion, approving the view that one world is everlasting, and another is perishing — knowing that the world taken in respect of its arrangement is not other than the former, considered in a certain state. But that he knew the world, peculiarly qualified out of all substance, to be everlasting, he makes plain by speaking thus: "This world, the same for all, neither any of the gods nor of men made; but it ever was and is and shall be, an ever-living fire, kindled in measures and quenched in measures." And that he held it also to be begotten and perishable, the words that follow show: "The turnings of fire: first the sea; and of the sea, the half is earth, and the half the fiery storm-cloud." For in effect he says that fire, by the Word and God who orders the whole, is turned through air into the moisture which is as the seed of the world's ordering, which he calls "sea"; and out of this in turn come earth and heaven and all that they contain. And how it is again taken up and burned, he plainly shows by these words: "The sea is poured out and measured into the same proportion as it was before it became earth." And concerning the other elements the same things hold likewise.

The most reputed of the Stoics dogmatize in a like manner, treating both of the conflagration, and of the world's ordering, and of the peculiarly-qualified world and man, and of the further continuance of our souls. And again Plato, in the seventh book of the Republic, has called the day here "nocturnal" (on account, I think, of the world-rulers of this darkness), and the soul's descent into the body "sleep" and "death," in agreement with Heraclitus. And perhaps the Spirit foretold this, concerning the Saviour, through David, saying: "I lay down and slept; I awoke, because the Lord will sustain me." For it allegorizes not the resurrection of Christ alone as a rousing from sleep, but the Lord's descent into the flesh too as a sleep.

He, then, who has first moderated his passions and trained himself toward impassibility, and grown into the beneficence of gnostic perfection, is equal to the angels here; and being already luminous, and shining as the sun by reason of his good-doing, he hastens, through just knowledge, by love of God, to the holy abode, like the apostles — who became apostles not because they were elect by any peculiar excellence of nature (since Judas too was chosen with them), but because they were such as could become apostles, being chosen by him who foresees even the ends. For instance, Matthias, who was not chosen with them, having shown himself worthy to become an apostle, is set in the room of Judas.

The same Saviour, for instance, charges: "Watch" — that is, "Practise living, and try to separate the soul from the body." And the Lord's day Plato divines in the tenth book of the Republic, by these words: "And when seven days had passed for each in the meadow, on the eighth they must arise and depart thence, and arrive on the fourth day after." The meadow, then, is to be understood as the fixed sphere, as a gentle place and a kindly, and the region of the holy; and the seven days as each motion of the seven, and all the workful craft hastening to the end of rest. But the journey after the wandering stars leads to heaven — that is, to the eighth motion and day. And he says the souls go away "on the fourth day," showing the journey through the four elements.

It is possible, then, even now for those who have trained themselves in the Lord's commandments, having lived perfectly and gnostically according to the Gospel, to be enrolled in the election of the apostles. Such a one is truly an elder of the church and a true deacon of the will of God, if he do and teach the things of the Lord — not ordained by men, nor counted just because he is an elder, but enrolled in the presbytery because he is just; and even if here on earth he be not honoured with the first seat, he shall sit on the four-and-twenty thrones, judging the people, as John says in the Revelation. For one in truth is the saving covenant, reaching from the foundation of the world to us, supposed to be different in the giving according to different generations and times. For it follows that there is one unchangeable gift of salvation, from one God through one Lord, benefiting in many ways; for which cause the middle wall is taken away that divides the Greek from the Jew, into a peculiar people.

But the seventh day, too, is held sacred not only by the Hebrews but by the Greeks, according to which the whole world of all things that are quickened and grow goes round. Hesiod, then, speaks of it thus: "First the new moon and the fourth, and the seventh, a holy day." And again: "On the seventh again the bright light of the sun." And Homer: "On the seventh thereupon came the holy day." And: "The seventh was holy." And again: "It was the seventh day, and on it all was accomplished." And again: "On the seventh dawn we left the stream from Acheron." Indeed Callimachus the poet too writes: "On the seventh dawn, and on it all things were fashioned." And again: "Among good things is the seventh, and the seventh is the birthday." And: "The seventh is among the first, and the seventh is perfect." And: "Seven were all the things made in the starry heaven, appearing in their circles as the years come round."

And so both come into the unity of the faith, and the election out of both is one. And of the elect, it says, the more elect are those who, by the perfect knowledge, are culled out of the church itself and honoured with the most magnificent glory, judges and governors alike, of Jews and of Greeks, the four-and-twenty, the grace being doubled. Since the advances here in the church, of bishops, elders, deacons, are imitations, I think, of angelic glory, and of that dispensation which the Scriptures say awaits those who, following in the footsteps of the apostles, have lived in perfection of righteousness according to the Gospel. These, caught up in clouds, the apostle writes, shall first minister, then be enrolled in the presbytery by advance of glory (for glory differs from glory), until they grow into perfect manhood.

But the elegies of Solon too greatly deify the hebdomad. And again — is it not like the Scripture that says, "Let us take away the just man, because he is troublesome to us," when Plato, all but prophesying the saving dispensation, says in the second book of the Republic, somewhat thus: "Thus disposed, the just man shall be scourged, racked, bound, have both his eyes burned out, and at last, having suffered all evils, shall be impaled"? And Antisthenes the Socratic, paraphrasing that prophetic voice, "To whom have you likened me? says the Lord," says that God is like to no one; wherefore no one can learn him thoroughly from an image. And Xenophon the Athenian says the like, in these words: "He, at any rate, who shakes all things and brings them to rest, that he is some great and powerful one is plain; but of what form he is, is unseen; nor does the sun, who seems all-radiant, even he, seem to allow himself to be looked upon, but if anyone gazes at him shamelessly, he takes away the sight." For "what flesh can with its eyes behold the heavenly and true immortal God, who dwells in the sky? Nay, men, mortal-born, cannot stand even over against the rays of the sun," the Sibyl foretold.

Well, then, does Xenophanes of Colophon, teaching that God is one and incorporeal, add: "One God, greatest among gods and men, in no way like to mortals, neither in body nor in mind." And again: "But mortals think that the gods are born, and have their own raiment and voice and shape." And again: "But if oxen or lions had hands, so as to draw with their hands and accomplish such works as men, then horses would draw the forms of gods like horses, and oxen like oxen, and would make their bodies such as each itself had."

Let us hear again Bacchylides the lyric poet speaking of the divine: "They are untamed of unseemly diseases, and unharmed, in no way like to men." And Cleanthes the Stoic, having written these things about God in a certain poem: "You ask me what the Good is like? Hear, then: ordered, just, holy, pious, master of itself, useful, beautiful, fitting, austere, downright, ever profitable, fearless, painless, advantageous, free of grief, beneficial, well-pleasing, secure, friendly, honoured, consistent, . . . of good repute, free of conceit, careful, gentle, strong, lasting, blameless, ever-abiding."

And the same poet, in what he leaves unsaid, censuring the idolatry of the many, adds: "Unfree is everyone who looks to opinion, as though he should obtain from it some good." We must, then, no longer suppose things concerning the divine according to the opinion of the many. For neither do I think it secret — "putting on the shape of a malefactor of light, to come to your bed, like a man, to Zeus's chamber" — Amphion says to Antiope. And Sophocles plainly writes: "For Zeus wedded the mother of this man, not gold-shaped nor wrapped in the feather of a swan, as he made pregnant the Pleuronian maid, but as a man through and through." Then, coming on, he adds: "And swift the adulterer set foot upon the nuptial steps." Upon which, still more plainly, he describes the incontinence of the fabled Zeus, somewhat thus: "And he, touching neither feast nor lustral water, went to the bed, his heart stung; and all that night he raged with lust." Let such things, then, be left to the follies of the theatres. But Heraclitus says outright: "Though this Word is true forever, men prove uncomprehending, both before they hear it and when first they have heard it."

And the lyric poet Melanippides, singing, says: "Hear me, O Father, wonder of mortals, ruler of the ever-living soul." And the great Parmenides, as Plato says in the Sophist, writes of the divine somewhat thus: "very many things, as that it is unbegotten and imperishable, whole and only-begotten and unshaken and unbegotten." And Hesiod too: "For he himself is king and lord of all the immortals; and against your might no other has matched himself." Indeed tragedy too, drawing men away from the idols, teaches them to look up to heaven.

Sophocles, as Hecataeus, who composed the histories, says in his work On Abraham and the Egyptians, cries out plainly upon the stage: "One in very truth, one is God, who made the heaven and the broad earth, and the grey-green swell of the sea, and the strength of the winds. But we mortals, many, wandering in heart, set up for ourselves a comfort in our pains — images of the gods made of stones, or of bronze, or of figures wrought of gold or ivory; and decking these with sacrifices and vain festivals, we think thus we are pious."

And Euripides, playing the tragedian upon the same stage, says: "Do you behold this boundless aether on high, and the earth held round in its moist embraces? This deem to be Zeus; this hold to be God." And in the play Pirithous the same poet also sings these things in tragic vein: "You, the self-grown, who have woven the nature of all things in the aetherial whirl, around whom light, and round whom dusky night of changing hue, and the countless throng of stars unceasingly dance." For here by "the self-grown" he means the creative Mind, and what follows is ranked of the world, in which are the oppositions of light and darkness. And Aeschylus, the son of Euphorion, says of God most solemnly: "Zeus is the aether, Zeus is the earth, Zeus is the heaven; Zeus, indeed, is all things, and whatever is higher than these."

I know that Plato too bears witness to Heraclitus, who writes: "The one wise alone is unwilling and willing to be called by the name of Zeus." And again: "It is law also to obey the counsel of one." And if you should wish to refer that saying, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear," you would find it indicated somewhat thus by the Ephesian: "The uncomprehending, when they have heard, are like the deaf; the saying bears them witness that, being present, they are absent." But do you long to hear of one beginning even from the Greeks? Timaeus the Locrian, in his work on nature, will witness to me thus, word for word: "There is one beginning of all things, unbegotten; for if it had come to be, it would no longer be a beginning, but that from which the beginning came to be." For from that source flowed the true opinion: "Hear, O Israel; the Lord your God is one, and him alone you shall serve." "This one, behold, is plain to all, unwandering," as the Sibyl says.

And already Homer too appears to speak of Father and Son, by these words, having hit upon a happy divining: "If, then, no one forces you, being alone, it is in no way possible to escape the malady of great Zeus; for the Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus the aegis-bearer." And before him Orpheus, bearing upon the matter before us, has said: "Son of great Zeus, Father of Zeus the aegis-bearer." And Xenocrates of Chalcedon, calling the one Zeus highest and the other lowest, leaves a showing of Father and Son. And, most marvellous of all, Homer appears to know the divine, though he brings in the gods as subject to human passion — which not even Epicurus reverences thus.

He says, at any rate: "Why, son of Peleus, do you pursue me with swift feet, yourself being mortal, a god immortal? Have you not yet known that I am a god?" For he has made plain that the divine is not to be caught nor grasped by a mortal, neither with feet nor with hands nor with eyes, nor at all with the body. "To whom have you likened the Lord? Or with what likeness have you likened him?" says the Scripture. "Has a workman made an image, or a goldsmith, having melted gold, gilded it over?" — and the things that follow.

And the comic poet Epicharmus speaks plainly of the Word in his Republic, somewhat thus: "Life has very great need for man of reckoning and number; we live by number and reckoning, for these save mortals." Then he downright adds: "Reason governs men, and saves them in their measure." Then: "If there is reckoning in man, there is also a divine reason. The one in man is born for the conduct of life; but the divine reason attends upon all the arts, itself teaching men what they must do for their advantage. For man did not find out an art, but God brings it; and the reason in man is sprung from the divine reason."

Indeed, when the Spirit cries out through Isaiah, "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord; I am full of whole-burnt-offerings of rams, and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls I do not want"; and a little after adds, "Wash yourselves, become clean, take away the wickednesses from your souls," and the things that follow — Menander the comic poet writes in these very words: "If anyone, O Pamphilus, bringing a sacrifice — a multitude of bulls or of kids, or, by Zeus, of other such things, or fashionings, having made golden cloaks or purple ones, or figures of ivory or emerald — thinks to make God well-disposed, he is deceived and has a feather-light mind. For a man must be of use, not corrupting maidens nor committing adultery, not stealing and slaughtering for the sake of money. Nor covet even the thread of a needle, friend; for God sees you, being present near at hand." "I am a God who draws near, and not a God afar off; or shall a man do anything in secret, and I shall not see him?" he says through Jeremiah.

And again Menander, paraphrasing that Scripture, "Sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness, and hope upon the Lord," writes somewhat thus: "Never covet, dearest, even a needle that belongs to another; for God delights in righteous deeds, and not in unjust ones, and suffers the man who toils to lift up his own life, ploughing the earth night and day. To God sacrifice continually, being righteous, not splendid in your cloaks so much as in your heart. If you hear thunder, do not flee, conscious of no evil within yourself, O master; for God sees you, being present near at hand." "While you are still speaking," says the Scripture, "I will say, Behold, I am here."

Again Diphilus the comic poet discourses thus concerning the judgement: "Do you think, Niceratus, that the dead, who have partaken of all luxury in life, have escaped the divine as though unobserved? There is an eye of Justice that sees all things. For we believe there are two paths in Hades — one of the just, the other of the impious. And if the earth shall cover both for all time, then go off and plunder, steal, despoil, throw all into confusion; but be deceived in nothing — there is a judgement even in Hades, which God will hold, the master of all, whose name is fearful, and which I would not even name. He gives to those who sin a long span of life. And if any mortal thinks that, doing some evil by day, he has escaped the gods, he is convicted of thinking wickedly, and of being so, whenever Justice chances to have leisure. Look, all you who think there is no God: there is, there is. And if any man, being evil by nature, does well, let him gain the time; for in time, afterward, he will pay the penalty." And tragedy sings in tune with these things by these words: "For there shall be, there shall be, that time of the age, when the golden-faced aether shall let loose its treasury full of fire, and the nursed flame, raging, shall burn up all things upon earth and on high."

And a little after he goes on again: "But when the whole shall fail, all the deep of the waves shall be gone, and the earth bereft of its seats, and the air, set on fire, shall no longer bear up the winged tribes; and then it shall save all that it formerly destroyed." The like to these we shall find in the Orphic writings too, written somewhat thus: "For having hidden all, again into the gladdening light he brought them up from his holy heart, doing dreadful deeds." But if we live our lives in holiness and righteousness, we are blessed here, and more blessed after our departure hence, having our happiness not for some time only, but able to rest in eternity, "fellow-hearth with other immortals, and at their tables, free from the woes of men, unworn," as the philosophic poetry of Empedocles says. Not even among the Greeks, then, shall anyone be so great as to overstep Justice, nor so small as to escape her.

The same Orpheus says these things too: "Looking to the divine Word, attend upon it, guiding straight the intelligent vessel of your heart; and walk well in the path, and gaze upon the immortal Ruler of the world alone." And again concerning God, calling him invisible, he says he was made known to one only, a Chaldean by race — whether he means Abraham, or his Son — by these words: "Except one only, a scion sprung from the stock of the Chaldeans from above; for he knew the path of the star, and the movement of the sphere round the earth, how it revolves in a circle, evenly upon its own axle, and he guides the winds about the air and about the stream."

Then, paraphrasing, as it were, "The heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet," he goes on: "But he himself, again, is fixed upon the great heaven on a golden throne, and the earth has gone beneath his feet; and his right hand he has stretched out to the bounds of Ocean; and the base of the mountains trembles within at his wrath, nor can it bear his mighty force. And he is everywhere heavenly, and on earth he accomplishes all things, himself holding beginning and middle and end. In no other way is it lawful for you to speak; and my limbs tremble in my mind. From on high he sways," and the rest. For by these things he has shown forth all those prophetic words: "If you open the heaven, trembling shall seize the mountains from before you, and they shall melt, as wax melts before the face of fire."

And the words through Isaiah: "Who measured the heaven with a span, and the whole earth with a handful?" Again, when he says: "Lord of aether and Hades, of sea and earth, who with your thunders shakes the strong dwelling of Olympus; before whom the spirits shudder, and the throng of gods is afraid; whom the Fates obey, inexorable though they are; imperishable one, mother-and-father, by whose passion all things are stirred; you who move the winds, and cover all with clouds, cleaving the broad aether with your lightnings; yours is the order among the stars, running upon unchangeable behests; and beside your fiery throne stand the much-toiling angels, whose care it is that all things be accomplished for mortals; yours is the spring that shines new with purple flowers; yours the winter that comes on with chill clouds; your fruits the reveller Bromius once distributed."

Then he adds, downright naming God Almighty: "Imperishable, immortal, utterable only to the immortals. Come, greatest of all gods, with strong necessity, dread, unconquerable, great, imperishable, whom aether crowns." By the "mother-and-father" he has not only shown forth the coming-to-be out of what is not, but has also given handles to those who bring in the emanations — perhaps even to conceive a consort of God. And he paraphrases those prophetic Scriptures: that through Hosea, "I am he that fixes fast the thunder and creates the wind, whose hands founded the host of heaven"; and that through Moses, "See, see, that I am, and there is no other God beside me. I will kill and make alive; I will smite, and I will heal; and there is none who shall deliver out of my hands." "But he himself plants evil for mortals out of good, and chilling war and tearful pains," according to Orpheus.

Such things Archilochus of Paros too says: "O Zeus, Father Zeus, yours is the rule of heaven, and you behold the works of men, both lawless and unrighteous." Again let Orpheus the Thracian sing for us: "And his right hand he has stretched out to the bound of Ocean, and the earth has gone beneath his feet." These things are plainly taken thence: "The Lord shall save inhabited cities, and shall lay hold of the whole world with his hand like a nest; the Lord who made the earth in his strength," as Jeremiah says, "and set up the world in his wisdom." And besides these, Phocylides, calling the angels spirits, presents some of them as good and some as base, by these words — since we too have received that some are apostates: "But indeed there are spirits upon men, now these, now those; some, when evil comes on, to deliver men from it."

Well, then, does Philemon the comic poet also cut down idolatry, by these words: "There is for us no Fortune that is a god, there is none; but the chance thing that comes to pass for each as it happens is called fortune." And Sophocles the tragedian: "Not even for the gods," he says, "are all things self-willed, save for Zeus; for he holds the end and the beginning." And Orpheus: "One power, one spirit there came to be, a great one, kindling heaven; and one are all things made, in which all these things wheel round — fire and water and earth."

And the things that follow. And Pindar the lyric poet is, as it were, carried away as in a bacchic frenzy, saying outright: "What is God? That which is the whole." And again: "God who fashions all things for mortals." And when he says: "What do you hope of wisdom? Little it is that a man has over a man. To search out the counsels of the gods with a mortal mind is hard; and one is born of a mortal mother" — thence he drew the thought: "Who knew the mind of the Lord? Or who became his counsellor?" But Hesiod too, by what he writes, sings in tune with the foregoing: "There is no seer among earth-dwelling men who could know the mind of Zeus the aegis-bearer." With reason, then, Solon the Athenian, in his elegies, following Hesiod too, writes: "Wholly hidden to men is the mind of the immortals."

Again, when Moses prophesied that the woman, on account of the transgression, should bring forth into toils and pains, a poet of no mean note writes: "Never by day shall they cease from toil and grief, nor by night, hard pressed; and grievous cares the gods will give." Further, Homer, having said, "And the Father himself stretched out the golden scales," shows forth God as just. And Menander the comic poet, interpreting God as good, says: "For every man at his very birth a spirit stands beside, a good guide of his life; for one must not think there is an evil spirit harming a good life." Then he adds: "And every god is good" — either saying that every god is good, or, what is rather the meaning, that in all things God is good.

Again, Aeschylus the tragedian, setting forth the power of God, does not shrink from calling him Most High too, by these words: "Set God apart from mortals, and do not think him to be fleshly, like to yourself. You do not know him: now he appears as fire, an unapproachable rush; now as water; now as gloom. And he becomes like to beasts, to wind and cloud and lightning, thunder and rain. And sea and rocks serve him, and every spring and gatherings of water. And the mountains and the earth tremble, and the monstrous deep of the sea, and the great height of the mountains, when he casts upon them the dread eye of the Master. For all-powerful is the glory of the Most High God." Does it not seem to you that he is paraphrasing the saying, "From before the face of the Lord the earth trembles"?

Besides these, Apollo, the most oracular, witnessing to the glory of God, is constrained to speak concerning Athena, at the time when the Medes were marching against Hellas, how she besought and supplicated Zeus on behalf of Attica. The oracle runs thus: "Pallas cannot propitiate Olympian Zeus, though she entreat with many words and shrewd counsel; but many temples of the immortals he will give over to the devouring fire — temples that even now, perhaps, stand streaming with sweat, quaking with terror," and the rest.

And Thearidas, in his work On Nature, writes: "The beginning of the things that are — the beginning truly and indeed true — is one; for that, in the beginning, is one and only." "Nor is there any other apart from the great King," says Orpheus. Persuaded by him, the comic poet Diphilus most sententiously says: "Him who is the Father of all, this one alone honour continually, the finder and founder of so many goods." With reason, then, Plato too trains the best natures to come to the lesson which we said before is the greatest — to behold the Good and to mount that ascent. "And this, as it seems, is no mere turning round of a shell, but a turning-about of the soul, from a kind of nocturnal day to the true ascent into being, which we shall say is true philosophy." And those who have shared in this he judges to be of the golden race, saying, "You are all brethren," but those of the golden race the most exactly and in every way. Of the Father, then, and Maker of all things, all creatures lay hold, by nature and untaught, on every side: lifeless things sympathizing with the living; of living things, some already immortal, working day by day; of those still mortal, some in fear, even while borne in the womb of their mother; others by free will — and of men, all, both Greeks and barbarians. And there is no race anywhere, whether of husbandmen or of nomads, nor even of city-dwellers, that can live without being first possessed by faith in a higher being. Therefore every nation that touches the eastern shores, and every one that touches the western, the northern and all that lie toward the south, holds one and the same preconception concerning him who appointed the rule, if indeed the most universal of his works have passed alike upon all things.

And much more did the busy inquirers among the Greeks, setting out from the barbarian philosophy, give the prerogative to him who is invisible and alone and most powerful and most skilful and most causative of the noblest things — not knowing the consequences of these things, unless they had been instructed by us, nor knowing even how God himself is naturally to be conceived, but only, as we have often said, by a true periphrasis. With reason, then, the apostle says, "Is he the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Greeks?" — not only saying prophetically that those of the Greeks who believe shall come to know God, but also signifying this, that in power the Lord and God of all might be, and is in truth Almighty; but in respect of knowledge he is not the God of all. For they know neither what he is, nor how he is Lord and Father and Maker, nor the rest of the dispensation of the truth, not having been taught by it.

In the same way the prophetic words too have the same force as the apostolic word. For Isaiah says: "But if you say, 'Upon the Lord our God we have trusted,' now mingle with the Lord, my king of the Assyrians." And he adds: "And now, have we come up against this country to war against it without the Lord?" And Jonah, himself also a prophet, hints at the same thing by these words: "And the captain came to him and said to him, 'Why do you snore? Arise, call upon your God, that he may save us, and we perish not.'" For the "your God" he said to him who knew by recognition; but by the "that he may save us" God showed the common consciousness of those of the Gentiles who had set their minds upon the Almighty, but had not yet believed. And again the same: "And he said to them, 'I am a servant of the Lord, and I fear the Lord, the God of heaven.'"

And again the same: "And they said, 'By no means, Lord; let us not perish for the soul of this man.'" And Malachi the prophet downright shows God saying: "I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands, because from the rising of the sun to its setting my name has been glorified among the Gentiles, and in every place sacrifice is offered to me." And again: "Because I am a great king, says the Lord Almighty, and my name is glorious among the Gentiles." What name? Among those who have believed, the Son revealing the Father; but among the Greeks, "God the Maker." And Plato shows forth free will by these words: "Virtue is without a master; and as each man honours or dishonours it, so he shall partake more or less of it. The fault is the chooser's; God is faultless." For God is never the cause of evils. "O war-loving Trojans," says the lyric poet, "Zeus who rules on high, who sees all things, is not to the cause of great woes for mortals; but it lies in the midst, for all men to attain, holy Justice, the companion of pure Order and of prudent Right; happy are the children of those who find her for their housemate."

And Pindar downright brings in Zeus the Saviour too, dwelling with Themis, the king, the saviour, the just, interpreting somewhat thus: "First the well-counselling heavenly Themis, with golden horses, beside the streams of Ocean, the Fates led up to the august stairway of Olympus, along the shining way, to be the ancient consort of Zeus the Saviour; and she bore the gold-crowned, bright-fruited, true Hours." He, then, who is not persuaded by the truth, but puffed up with human teaching, is ill-fated and wretched, and, according to Euripides, "he who, beholding these things, perceives not God, and has cast far off the crooked deceits of those who babble of things on high, whose ruinous tongue casts at random concerning the unseen, having no share of judgement."

He, then, who is come to the true learning, if he will, let him hear Parmenides the Eleatic promising: "You shall know the aetherial nature, and all the signs in the aether, and the unseen works of the pure torch of the bright sun, and whence they came to be; and you shall learn the wandering works of the round-eyed moon and its nature; and you shall know also the heaven that holds all round, whence it grew, and how Necessity, leading it, bound it to hold the bounds of the stars." And Metrodorus, though he was an Epicurean, has said these things divinely inspired: "Remember, Menestratus, that, born mortal and having received a fixed span of life, you ascended in your soul up to the age and the infinity of things, and beheld both 'the things that are to be and that have been before.'" Then, "in company with the blessed choir," according to Plato, "we shall view the blessed sight and vision, following — we with Zeus, and others with other gods — being initiated, as it is lawful to say, into the most blessed of mysteries, which we celebrate, ourselves whole and untouched by the evils that awaited us in a later time; and beholding, as initiates and viewers, whole and unshaken visions in pure light, being ourselves pure and unmarked by this which now, carrying it about, we call body, bound to it after the manner of an oyster."

The Pythagoreans call the heaven the counter-earth, the earth concerning which it is said through Jeremiah: "I will set you among the children, and will give you a chosen land, the inheritance of God Almighty," which those who inherit it shall be kings of the earth. And ten thousand things upon ten thousand more flow in upon me to set down; but for the sake of due proportion the discourse must now be brought to a stop, lest we ourselves suffer the fate the tragedian Agathon speaks of: "treating what is by the way as the main work, and labouring at the main work as though it were by the way."

Now that it has been plainly shown, as I think, how it is to be understood that the Greeks were called thieves by the Lord, I willingly leave aside the doctrines of the philosophers. For if we should go through their very words, we should not have done — gathering together what a multitude of notes — in showing that all the wisdom among the Greeks is borne from the barbarian philosophy. Upon which contemplation we shall lay hold again none the less, as it becomes necessary, when we collect the opinions concerning first principles that are current among the Greeks. But this too comes quietly before us to consider, from what we have said — in what way one who is able to swim through the waves in them must meet the Greek books. "Blessed," as it seems, then, is he, according to Empedocles, "who has won the wealth of divine thoughts, but wretched he whose care is a dim opinion concerning the gods." Divinely he showed forth knowledge and ignorance as the bounds of happiness and of misery. "For philosophic men must be inquirers into very many things," according to Heraclitus; and in truth one who seeks to be good must of necessity wander much.

It is, then, plain to us from what has been said before, that the beneficence of God is everlasting, and that the natural righteousness, equal downright to all from a beginning that has no beginning, comes to each according to the desert of its kind, never having begun. For God took no beginning of being Lord and good, being always what he is; nor shall he ever cease from doing good, even though he bring each thing to its end. And each of us partakes of his beneficence according as he will, since the difference of election is wrought by the soul's choice and joint exercise, become worthy. Thus, then, let our fifth book of the gnostic notes, according to the true philosophy, the Stromateis, be brought to a close.

The Greeks say that, after Orpheus and Linus and the most ancient of the poets among them, the first to be admired for wisdom were the seven called the Sages. Of these, four were from Asia: Thales of Miletus, Bias of Priene, Pittacus of Mitylene, and Cleobulus of Lindos; and two from Europe: Solon of Athens and Chilon of Sparta. As for the seventh, some say he was Periander the Corinthian, some Anacharsis the Scythian, and some Epimenides the Cretan — whom the Apostle Paul mentions in the Epistle to Titus, saying thus: "One of them, their own prophet, said: 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle bellies'; and this testimony is true." You see how, even to the prophets of the Greeks, he grants something of the truth, and is not ashamed, when speaking for edification and for shaming, to make use of some Greek verses. So, to the Corinthians — for it is not only here — discoursing on the resurrection of the dead, he has made use of a tragic iambic line, saying: "What profit is it to me, if the dead are not raised? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. Be not deceived: bad company corrupts good morals." Some reckoned Acusilaus the Argive among the seven sages; others, Pherecydes the Syrian. And Plato, in place of Periander, as unworthy of wisdom because he had been a tyrant, sets in his stead Myson of Chenae.

That the sages among the Greeks came somewhat below the age of Moses will be shown a little later; but the manner of their philosophy, as being Hebraic and enigmatic, must now be examined. They welcomed, at any rate, the hortatory brevity of speech, the most useful kind. Plato, for instance, says that this manner was of old in vogue, commonly among all the Greeks, but especially among the Spartans and the Cretans, who had the best laws. Now the "Know yourself" some have supposed to be Chilon's, but Chamaeleon, in his work On the Gods, ascribes it to Thales, and Aristotle to the Pythia. It may, then, urge us to pursue knowledge; for it is not possible to know the parts without the essence of the whole. One must, then, busy oneself with the genesis of the world, through which it will also be possible to learn thoroughly the nature of man.

The involuntary, then, is not judged (and this is twofold: the one coming about with ignorance, the other by necessity); for how could you give judgment about the things said to be sinned according to the involuntary modes? For either a man was ignorant of himself, as Cleomenes and Athamas who went mad; or of the thing he does, as Aeschylus, who, having uttered the mysteries on the stage, was judged in the Areopagus and so released, having shown himself not initiated; or one might be ignorant of the person about whom it is done, as the man who let go the adversary and killed his own instead of the enemy; or of that wherein it is done, as the man who, exercising with spears tipped with balls, and killing someone when the spear cast off its ball; or of the manner — as the man in the stadium who killed his antagonist (for he contended not for death but for victory); or of that for the sake of which it is done — as the physician who gave a wholesome antidote and killed, yet gave it not for this, but to save.

Again, to Chilon the Spartan they refer the "Nothing too much." Strato, in his work On Discoveries, attaches the saying to Sodamus of Tegea; Didymus assigns it to Solon, just as he assigns to Cleobulus the "Measure is best." And the "Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand" — Cleomenes, in his work On Hesiod, says was uttered before by Homer in these words: "Worthless are the pledges of worthless men, to be pledged for." But the followers of Aristotle think it Chilon's, while Didymus says the advice is Thales'. Then next, the "All men are bad," or "Most men are bad" (for the same saying is uttered in two ways), the followers of Sotades of Byzantium say is Bias'; and they wish "Practice accomplishes everything" to be Periander's; likewise the advice "Know the right moment" they hold to be Pittacus'. Solon, then, gave laws to the Athenians, Pittacus to the Mitylenaeans. And it was late that Pythagoras, the disciple of Pherecydes, first proclaimed himself a "philosopher."

The law of that time held even the involuntary slayer, as it held the involuntary one with an issue, but not on a par with the voluntary. And yet he too will be punished as for a voluntary thing, if one transfer the passion to the truth; for in truth he is to be punished who cannot control the seminal reason. Which is itself an irrational passion of the soul, going near to babbling; but the faithful man has chosen to hide matters with discretion. The things of choice, then, are judged; "for the Lord searches hearts and reins"; and "he who looked toward desire is judged." Wherefore "You shall not even desire," it says; and "This people honours me with the lips," it says, "but their heart is far from me." For God looks to the very judgment, since he left Lot's wife too, who turned, willingly only, toward the worldly vice, without perception, having shown her as a pillar of salt and fixed her so as not to advance — not a foolish and useless image, but one to season and to give pungency to the man able to discern spiritually.

After the men already mentioned, then, there arose three successions of philosophy named from the places where they spent their time: the Italic, from Pythagoras; the Ionic, from Thales; and the Eleatic, from Xenophanes. Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, was a Samian, as Hippobotus says; but as Aristoxenus, in his Life of Pythagoras, and Aristarchus and Theopompus say, he was a Tyrrhenian; and as Neanthes says, a Syrian or a Tyrian — so that, according to most, Pythagoras was a barbarian by race. Thales too, as Leander and Herodotus relate, was a Phoenician, though some have supposed him a Milesian. He alone is thought to have associated with the prophets of the Egyptians; but no teacher of his is on record, just as none of Pherecydes the Syrian, whose pupil Pythagoras was.

The Pythagorean philosophy, the Italic, grew old at Metapontum in Italy. Anaximander, son of Praxiades, the Milesian, succeeds Thales; him Anaximenes, son of Eurystratus, the Milesian; after whom Anaxagoras, son of Hegesibulus, of Clazomenae. This man transferred the school from Ionia to Athens. Him Archelaus succeeds, whose pupil Socrates was. "From these he turned aside, the stone-cutter, the babbler about laws, the enchanter of the Greeks," says Timon in the Silloi, because he turned aside from natural philosophy to ethics. Having heard Socrates, Antisthenes practised the Cynic way, and Plato withdrew to the Academy. Aristotle, having philosophized under Plato, passed over to the Lyceum and founded the Peripatetic school. Him Theophrastus succeeds, him Strato, him Lyco, then Critolaus, then Diodorus. Speusippus succeeds Plato; him Xenocrates, him Polemo. Hearers of Polemo were Crates and Crantor, in whom the Old Academy from Plato came to an end. Arcesilaus had part with Crantor, and from him, down to Hegesinus, the Middle Academy flourished.

Then Carneades succeeds Hegesinus, and those after him. And Zeno of Citium, who began the Stoic school, becomes a pupil of Crates. Him Cleanthes succeeds, him Chrysippus and those after him. Of the Eleatic conduct Xenophanes of Colophon is the head, who, Timaeus says, lived in the time of Hiero, lord of Sicily, and of Epicharmus the poet; while Apollodorus says he was born about the fortieth Olympiad and lasted down to the times of Darius and Cyrus. Parmenides, then, becomes a hearer of Xenophanes, and of him Zeno, then Leucippus, then Democritus. Hearers of Democritus were Protagoras of Abdera and Metrodorus of Chios, whose pupil was Diogenes of Smyrna, whose pupil Anaxarchus, and of him Pyrrho, of whom Nausiphanes. Some say Epicurus was a pupil of this man. Such, then, is the succession of the philosophers among the Greeks, given as in a summary; and the times of those who first began their philosophy must next be told, so that by comparison we may show the philosophy among the Hebrews to be older by many generations.

Concerning Xenophanes, who began the Eleatic philosophy, it has been said. And Eudemus, in his Astrological Histories, says that Thales foretold the eclipse of the sun which occurred at the time when the Medes and the Lydians joined battle with one another, in the reign of Cyaxares, the father of Astyages, over the Medes, and of Alyattes, the father of Croesus, over the Lydians. And Herodotus agrees with him in his first book. The time is about the fiftieth Olympiad. Pythagoras is found in the time of Polycrates the tyrant, about the sixty-second Olympiad. Mnesiphilus is recorded as an admirer of Solon, with whom Themistocles associated. Solon, then, flourished about the forty-sixth Olympiad. For Heraclitus, the son of Blyson, persuaded Melancomas the tyrant to lay down his rule. This man disdained Darius, who invited him to come to Persia.

And let these things, by way of seed, be said as briefly as may be concerning the gnostic, to the Greeks. But it must be understood that, even if the believer should set right one of these things, or even a second, yet not all together, nor indeed with the highest knowledge, as the gnostic does. And concerning that freedom from passion, so to speak, which belongs to the gnostic—according to which the perfecting of the believer, advancing through love "to a perfect man, to the measure of stature," arrives at being made like to God, having become truly "equal to the angels"—many other testimonies from Scripture come to mind to be set forth; but I think it better to defer such ambition on account of the length of the discourse, leaving it to those who are willing to toil and to work further at the doctrines by selection from the Scriptures. But of one I shall make mention as briefly as may be, so as not to leave the place without note. For the divine Apostle says in the former Epistle to the Corinthians: "Dares any of you, having a matter against another, go to law before the unjust, and not before the saints? Or do you not know that the saints shall judge the world?"—and what follows. The passage being very large, using the relevant apostolic phrases, very briefly and in a cursory way, as it were paraphrasing the saying, we shall set forth the meaning of the Apostle's words, according to which he sketches the perfection of the gnostic. For he sets the gnostic alone not merely in the position of being wronged rather than wronging, but teaches him also to bear no malice, not permitting him even to pray against the one who wronged him; for he knows that the Lord too plainly charged us to "pray for our enemies." For "to go to law before the unjust," he says of the one who has been wronged, means nothing but to seem to wish to render back, and to be willing to wrong in return as a second thing, which is alike to wrong oneself as well.

And the willing of certain men "to go to law before the saints" shows those who ask, by prayer, that their wronging may be requited upon those who wronged them—and that the latter are better than the former, but not yet free from passion, unless, having become wholly without malice according to the teaching of the Lord, they pray even for their enemies. It is good, then, that they should partake also of a good mind out of repentance unto faith. For even if the truth seems to gain enemies in those who provoke it, yet it is not itself at enmity with anyone. For "God makes his sun to shine upon the just and the unjust," and indeed sent the Lord himself upon just and unjust; and the man who forces himself toward being made like to God, through much absence of malice "forgiving seventy times seven" (signifying, as it were, through the whole of life and through the whole worldly circuit, reckoned in sevens), deals kindly with everyone, even if someone wrongs the gnostic throughout all this time he lives in the flesh. For the diligent man does not think fit to commit merely the judgement of those who have wronged him to others, but wishes the just man to ask of those judges the remission of sins for those who have offended against him—and reasonably; if indeed it is only the outward thing and that which concerns the body, even if it goes as far as death, in which those who set out to wrong him have the advantage—none of which is proper to the gnostic. And how could a man judge the apostate angels, having himself become an apostate from that absence of malice which is according to the Gospel? "Why," he says, "are you not rather wronged? Why are you not rather defrauded? But you wrong and defraud"—praying, that is, against those who offend through ignorance—"and you defraud," as far as in you lies, those against whom you pray, of the love and goodness of God. "And this, your brethren"—not those according to faith only, but the proselytes too, he means. For even if the one now at enmity will afterwards believe...

...we do not yet know. From which it is plainly gathered that, even if they are not all our brethren, yet they ought, in our judgement, to be our brethren—and indeed that all men, being the work of one God and clothed with one image upon one substance, even if some happen to be more fouled than others, the man of knowledge alone recognizes; and he worships also the activity of the creatures, through which, again, he worships the will of God. "Or do you not know that the unjust shall not inherit the kingdom of God?" He wrongs, then, who wrongs in return, whether in deed or in word or in the very thought of willing it—which thought the Gospel circumscribes after the tutelage of the Law. "And such were some of you"—of such a kind, that is, as those still happen to be whom you yourselves do not pardon. "But you were washed"—not simply as the rest, but with knowledge you scoured off the passions of the soul, toward being made like, as far as may be, to the goodness of the providence of God, both through patience of evil and through absence of malice, shining, like the sun, "upon just and unjust" with the kindliness of word and deed. Whether, then, the gnostic shall gain this through greatness of mind, or through imitation of the better; and the third cause is the "Forgive, and it shall be forgiven you," the commandment, as it were, forcing toward salvation through excess of goodness. "But you were sanctified." For to the one who has come to this settled disposition it belongs to be holy, falling in no way whatever into any of the passions.

But as to one already without flesh and become holy above this earth. Therefore, "you were justified," he says, "by the name of the Lord"; you were made, so to speak, by him to be just, as he is; and "by the Holy Spirit" you were, as far as may be in your power, fused into one. For surely it is not the case that "all things are lawful for me, but I shall not be brought under the power" of anything—he says—so as to do or think or speak anything contrary to the Gospel? "But meats for the belly, and the belly for meats"—which "God will bring to nothing"—that is, those who reckon and live in this way, as though they had come into being for the sake of eating, and not rather eating in order that they may live, as a consequence, but as their primary aim attending upon knowledge. And does he not say that such men are, as it were, the flesh of the holy body? And the Church of the Lord is allegorized as a body, the spiritual and holy choir; and of these, those who have only called upon the name, but do not live according to reason, are flesh. "But this body" is spiritual—that is, the holy Church—which "must in no way and by no means be made akin to fornication," nor to the apostasy from the Gospel toward the heathen life.

For he plays the fornicator against the Church and against "his own body" who conducts himself in the Church after the heathen manner—whether in deed, or in word, or in the very thought. "He who is joined to this harlot"—the activity contrary to the covenant—becomes another body, not holy, "into one flesh" and a heathen life and another hope. "But he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit"—a spiritual body, the race distinct from that union. This man is wholly a son, a holy man, free from passion, gnostic, perfect, formed by the teaching of the Lord, that he may, in deed and word and in the very spirit, drawing near to the Lord, receive that abode which is owed to the man thus brought to manhood. The hint is enough for those who have ears. For one must not roll out the mystery, but indicate only so much as serves for recollection to those who have partaken of knowledge—who will also understand how it has been said by the Lord: "Become perfect as your Father," perfectly forgiving sins, bearing no malice, and passing their lives in the settled disposition of freedom from passion. For as we speak of a perfect physician and a perfect philosopher, so too, I think, of a perfect gnostic; yet none of these things, great though it be, is taken up into likeness to God. For we do not, like the Stoics, most impiously say that the virtue of man and of God is the same. Surely, then, ought we to become perfect as the Father wills? For it is impossible and out of all reach for anyone to become perfect as God is; but the Father wills us, living according to the obedience of the Gospel, to become perfect blamelessly. If, then, the saying being spoken by way of ellipsis, we supply the missing part toward the filling-out of the passage—left to be grasped by those able to understand—we shall both recognize the will of God, and shall conduct ourselves, in a manner worthy of the commandment, at once devoutly and high-mindedly.

Indeed he forces Paul to say that generation consists from the deceit, through these words: "But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve, your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is toward Christ." But the Lord too came confessedly to the things that had gone astray; yet they had not gone astray from above into this present generation (for generation is created, and a creation of the Almighty, who would never bring a soul down from better to worse), but the Saviour came to us who had gone astray in our minds, which were corrupted by our disobedience to the commandments, through our love of pleasure—perhaps because our first-formed father anticipated the proper time and reached out for the grace of marriage before the hour, and so erred, since "everyone who looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her," not having awaited the time of God's will.

The same, then, was the Lord, even then, who judged the desire that anticipated marriage. Whenever, then, the apostle says, "Put on the new man, who is created according to God," he speaks to us who were fashioned by the will of the Almighty as we were fashioned; and by "old" and "new" he speaks not with reference to generation and regeneration, but with reference to the life that is in disobedience and the life that is in obedience. But Cassianus holds that the "coats of skin" are the bodies; concerning which we shall later show that he, and those who hold the like doctrines, are in error, when we take up, in due course, the explanation of the generation of man, after the necessary preliminaries. He says further: "Those who are ruled by earthly things both beget and are begotten; but our citizenship is in heaven, from which also we await a Saviour." We too know that this is well said, since we ought to conduct ourselves as strangers and pilgrims: those who marry as though not marrying, those who possess as though not possessing, those who beget children as begetting mortals, as though about to leave their possessions behind, as though about to live even without a wife if need be—using the creation without passionate attachment, but with all thanksgiving and high-mindedness.

And how great too is the kindness! "Love your enemies," He says, "bless those who curse you, and pray for those who despitefully use you," and the like; to which He adds: "that you may become sons of your Father who is in heaven," hinting at the likeness to God. And again He says: "Be of good will toward your adversary quickly, while you are in the way with him." Now the adversary is not the body, as some would have it, but the devil (and those who make themselves like him), who journeys with us through men who are zealous for his works in this earthly life. It is not possible, then, for those who confess themselves to be of Christ but spend their time in the works of the devil not to suffer the most hateful things; for it is written: "Lest he hand you over to the judge"—and the judge to the servant of the rule of the devil.

"For I am persuaded that neither death"—the one that comes by the assault of the persecutors—"nor life"—the one according to this present life—"nor angels"—the apostate ones—"nor principalities" (and a principality belongs to Satan, namely the life he chose; for such are the principalities and authorities of darkness according to him); "nor things present, in which we are during the time of life, as the soldier's hope, the merchant's gain; nor height nor depth, nor any other creature acting according to its own activity against the man who chooses faith" (and a creature is called, by the same name, also an activity, being our own work); "such an activity will not be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." You have the summary of the gnostic martyr.

Such men, according to David, shall rest in the holy mountain of God, the highest church, in which are gathered the philosophers of God, the true Israelites, the pure in heart, in whom is no guile — who have not remained in the hebdomad of rest, but have looked over, by the good-doing of divine likeness, into the inheritance of the beneficence of the ogdoad, giving themselves to the pure beholding of insatiable contemplation. "There are also other sheep," says the Lord, "which are not of this fold" — held worthy of another fold and abode, in proportion to the faith. "But my sheep hear my voice," understanding gnostically the commandments; and this is to receive them high-mindedly and worthily, together with the recompense and the joint sequence of the works. So that, when we hear "Your faith has saved you," we do not take him to say that those who have in any way believed shall be saved, unless the works too follow. For instance, he spoke this voice to Jews only, who had lived lawfully and blamelessly, to whom faith in the Lord alone was lacking.

Such a one, then, could not be faithful with intemperance; but even if he should not go out from the flesh, he must put off his passions, that he may be able to come into his own abode. And it is more to know than to believe, as indeed it is more, after being saved, to be held worthy of the highest honour. The believer, then, through much instruction having put off the passions, passes over to the abode better than the former, bearing as his greatest chastisement the peculiar mark of repentance for what he sinned after the baptism. For he is grieved yet the more, either at not yet, or at not at all, attaining what he sees others have partaken of. And besides, he is ashamed of his stumblings, which indeed are the greatest chastisements to the believer. For good is the righteousness of God, and just is his goodness. And even if the punishments cease somewhere, upon the paying out of the requital and the cleansing of each, those found worthy of the other fold have a great abiding grief — the grief at not being together with those glorified for righteousness.

For instance, Solomon, calling the gnostic wise, says this concerning those who marvel at the dignity of the abode: "For they shall see the end of the wise, and shall not understand what the Lord purposed concerning him, and for what he secured him; and over his glory they shall say, 'This was he whom we once had for a laughing-stock and for a byword of reproach, we the foolish; we reckoned his life madness and his end dishonourable. How was he counted among the sons of God, and is his lot among the saints?'" Not only the believer, then, but the Gentile too is judged most justly. For since God knew, being foreknower, that this man would not believe, none the less, that he might receive the perfection that lay within his own reach, he gave him philosophy, but before faith; and he gave the sun and the moon and the stars for worship, which God made for the Gentiles, says the law, that they might not, becoming utterly godless, be utterly destroyed. But those who, even in this commandment, became thankless, giving heed to carved images, are judged, unless they repent — some because, being able, they were not willing to believe in God, others because, willing, they did not work it out to become faithful;

yes, and those too who, from the worship of the stars, did not run back up to the maker of them. For this was the way given to the Gentiles, to look up to God through the worship of the stars. But those who would not abide upon these stars given to them, but fell away even from these to stones and wood, "were reckoned as chaff," it says, "and as a drop from a bucket" — superfluous unto salvation, those cast off from the body. As, then, the merely saving is of the middle things, but the rightly and fittingly is a setting-right, so too every act of the gnostic is a setting-right, but of the merely faithful a middle act, not yet performed according to reason, nor yet set right according to attention; but every act of the Gentile, on the contrary, is sinful. For not the merely faring well, but the making one's acts toward a certain aim and the working with reason, the Scriptures set forth as fitting.

As, then, lyres are not to be handled by those inexperienced in lyre-playing, nor flutes by those inexperienced in flute-playing, so neither are affairs to be handled by those who have not received knowledge and do not know how to use them throughout their whole life. The contest for freedom, then, is contended not only in wars by the athletes of war, but also in symposia and on the bed and in the law-courts by those anointed with the Word, ashamed to become captives of pleasure: "Never will I exchange virtue for unjust gain." And unjust gain outright is pleasure and grief, longing and fear, and, in a word, the passions of the soul, whose present delight is grievous for the time to come. "For what profit, if you gain the world," it says, "but lose your soul?" It is plain, then, that those who do not accomplish the noble deeds do not even know what is profitable to themselves. And if this be so, neither are they able rightly to pray and to receive from God the good things, being ignorant of the truly good things; nor, if they received them, would they perceive the gift, nor would they enjoy worthily that which they did not know, both from inexperience of the using well of what is given, and from the great unlearning, not yet having known how the divine gifts are to be used. And unlearning is the cause of ignorance.

And it seems to me to be the boast of a boastful soul, yet a soul of good conscience, to declare to the things that befall by circumstance: "Against these let them contrive what they will; for the good is with me, and the just shall be my ally, and I shall never be caught doing noble deeds." And this good conscience preserves both holiness toward God and righteousness toward men, keeping the soul pure with august thoughts and pure words and just deeds. Thus, having received the Lord's power, the soul practises to be God, holding that nothing else is evil except ignorance and the working that is not according to right reason, and ever giving thanks for all things to God, through just hearing and divine reading, through true inquiry, through holy offering, through blessed prayer; praising, hymning, blessing, singing. Such a soul is never at any season separated from God. With reason, then, it was said, "And those who trust in him shall understand truth, and the faithful in love shall abide with him." You see what things wisdom discourses concerning the gnostics.

Proportionately, then, the abodes too are various according to the worth of those who have believed. For instance, Solomon: "For there shall be given him the choice grace of faith, and a lot in the temple of the Lord, more pleasing." For the comparative shows the things that lie beneath in the temple of God, which is the whole church; and leaves us to conceive also the superlative, where the Lord is. And these three elect abodes the numbers in the Gospel hint at — the thirty and the sixty and the hundred. And the perfect inheritance belongs to those who come to perfect manhood, according to the image of the Lord; but the likeness is not, as some hold, that according to the human shape (for godless is this notion), nor again that according to virtue, which is toward the first cause (for impious too is this rendering, of those who expect the same virtue to belong to man and to God the Almighty); "you supposed," it says, "lawlessness, that I shall be like you." But "it is enough for the disciple to become as the teacher," says the teacher. According to the likeness of God, then, he who has been ranked into adoption and friendship of God comes to be, by the joint inheritance, of the lords and gods, if, as the Lord himself taught, he be perfected according to the Gospel.

And the voluntary is either according to appetite, or according to choice, or according to thought. So these stand somehow beside one another: error, mishap, wrongdoing. And there is error — say, to live luxuriously and licentiously; mishap — to strike a friend as an enemy through ignorance; and wrongdoing — grave-robbing or sacrilege. And erring is constituted from not knowing how to judge what one must do, or from being unable to do it; just as, indeed, a man falls into a pit either through ignorance or through being unable to leap over it because of weakness of body. But in our power, at all events, are both our standing toward our education and our obedience toward the commandments.

And if we should not wish to share in these, giving ourselves over to anger and desire, we shall err, or rather we shall wrong our own soul. For that Laius in the tragedy says: "None of these things of which you admonish me has escaped me; yet, though I have judgment, nature forces me" — that is, his having become given over to the passion. And Medea too likewise cries out on the stage: "And I understand what evils I am about to do, but my anger is stronger than my counsels." Nor is Ajax silent, but, about to slay himself, cries out: "No grief so gnaws the soul of a free man as dishonour. So have I suffered, and a deep stain, welling up from the depths, turns me back, goaded with the bitter spurs of madness."

These, then, anger sets in tragedy; but desire, ten thousand others — Phaedra, Antheia, Eriphyle, "who received precious gold for her dear husband." For that comic Thrasonides, another stage says: "A cheap little slave-girl has enslaved me." Mishap, then, is an error contrary to reason; and error is an involuntary wrongdoing, but wrongdoing a voluntary vice. Error, then, is mine, involuntary. Wherefore he says: "For sin shall not have lordship over you; for you are not under law but under grace" — speaking to those who have already believed, that "by his stripe we were healed." And misfortune is an involuntary action of another upon me; but wrongdoing alone is found voluntary, whether mine or another's.

These differences of sins the Psalmist hints at, calling blessed those whose lawlessnesses God has wiped out, and whose sins he has covered, and the others he has not reckoned, and the rest he has forgiven. For it is written: "Blessed are those whose lawlessnesses are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin, nor is there guile in his mouth." This blessing came upon those chosen by God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For love covers a multitude of sins; but he wipes them out who chooses the repentance of the sinner rather than his death.

Such are the times of the most ancient sages and philosophers among the Greeks. And that most of them were barbarians by race and were educated among barbarians — what need to say it, since Pythagoras was shown to be a Tyrrhenian or a Tyrian, Antisthenes a Phrygian, and Orpheus an Odrysian or a Thracian? For most make Homer an Egyptian. Thales, being a Phoenician by race, is said to have associated with the prophets of the Egyptians, as did Pythagoras with these same men, for whose sake he even had himself circumcised, that he might go down into the inner sanctuaries and learn thoroughly the mystic philosophy from the Egyptians; and he kept company with the best of the Chaldeans and the Magi, and his "common hearing-place" hints at what is now so called, the church. Plato does not deny that he imports the noblest things for philosophy from the barbarians, and confesses that he came to Egypt. So in the Phaedo he says the philosopher can be helped from every quarter, writing: "Great is Greece, O Cebes, in which there are everywhere good men, and many too are the races of the barbarians."

And those sins are not reckoned which are not constituted according to choice; for "he who desired has already committed adultery," it says. And the enlightening Word forgives sins; and "in that time," says the Lord, "they will seek the iniquity of Israel, and it shall not be, and the sins of Judah, and they shall not be found; for who is like me? And who shall stand against my face?" You see one God announced, good, both apportioning according to worth and forgiving sins. And John too, in the greater Epistle, plainly teaches the differences of sins in these words: "If anyone sees his brother sinning a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and he will give him life" — speaking of those who sin not unto death; "for there is a sin unto death; not concerning that do I say that anyone should ask." "All unrighteousness is sin,"

Thus Plato thinks that some of the barbarians too are philosophers, while Epicurus, on the contrary, supposes that the Greeks alone are able to philosophize. And in the Symposium Plato, praising the barbarians as having practised it surpassingly, says they alone truly philosophize, and "many others in many places, both among Greeks and barbarians, in whose honour many shrines have already arisen on account of such children." And the barbarians are clearly seen to have honoured surpassingly their lawgivers and teachers, calling them gods. For they suppose, according to Plato, that good souls, leaving the place above the heaven, have endured to come into this tartarus, and, taking on a body, to share in all the evils of generation, caring for the race of men — souls that have laid down laws and proclaimed philosophy, "than which no greater good ever came, or will come, to the race of men from the gods."

and there is a sin not unto death. But David too, and before David Moses, show forth the knowledge of the three doctrines in these words: "Blessed is the man who walked not in the counsel of the impious" — as the fishes go in darkness into the depths; for those that have no scales, which Moses forbids to touch, feed at the bottom of the sea — "nor stood in the way of sinners" — as those who seem to fear the Lord sin like the pig; for, when hungry, it cries out, but when filled does not recognize its master — "nor sat in the seat of the pestilent" — as the winged creatures ready for plunder. And Moses advised: "You shall not eat the pig, nor the eagle, nor the sharp-winged, nor the raven, nor any fish that has not a scale in itself." This is from Barnabas. But I, for one, have heard a wise man interpret such things, saying that the "counsel of the impious" is the nations, and taking the "way of sinners" to be the Jewish supposition, and the "seat of the pestilent" the heresies.

And it seems to me that, having perceived the great benefit conferred through the wise, they both revered those men and philosophized publicly. The Brahmans all, and the Odrysae and the Getae and the race of the Egyptians, treated their own matters as theology with exactness; the Chaldeans too, and the Arabians called blessed, and all who inhabited Palestine, and not the least part of the Persian race, and ten thousand other races besides. And Plato is plainly found always honouring the barbarians, remembering that both he and Pythagoras learned most of their doctrines, and the noblest, among the barbarians. For this reason he spoke of "the races of the barbarians," knowing the races of barbarian philosophers; and in the Phaedrus he shows the Egyptian king to be wiser even than Thoth, whom he knows to be Hermes. And in the Charmides he is seen to know certain Thracians, who are said to make the soul immortal.

But another said, more authoritatively, that the first blessing is set upon those who did not follow after the wicked judgments — those that apostatized from God; the second upon those who do not abide in the broad and wide way — whether those reared in the law, or those from the nations who have repented; and the "seat of the pestilent" would be the theatres and the law-courts; or, rather, the following after the wicked and ruinous authorities, and the fellowship in their works. "But his will is in the law of the Lord" — Peter, in the Preaching, called the Lord both law and Word.
