And the legislator seems, in another way too, to teach the abstinence from sin in three modes: from those in word, through the voiceless fishes (for there is in truth a place where silence is better than word; there is also a guerdon of silence, free of danger); from those in deed, through the rapacious and flesh-eating birds; . . . the pig delights in mire and dung;

It is recorded that Pythagoras was a pupil of Sonchis, the Egyptian arch-prophet; Plato of Sechnuphis of Heliopolis; and Eudoxus of Cnidos of Conuphis, who was also an Egyptian. And in the work On the Soul Plato . . . is again seen to recognize prophecy, bringing in as a prophet the spokesman of the word of Lachesis, who announces and foretells to the souls being allotted their lots. And in the Timaeus he brings in the most wise Solon learning from the barbarian. The words run thus: "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children, and there is no aged Greek; for you have no learning grown grey with time." For Democritus made the "Babylonian discourses" his own ethical writings; for he is said to have arranged in his own compositions the inscription of Acicarus, when it had been translated, and one can note from him, "These things says Democritus," where he writes. And indeed, glorying over himself for his wide learning, he says somewhere: "Of the men of my time I wandered over the most land, inquiring into the farthest things, and saw the most climates and lands, and heard the most learned men, and in the composition of lines with demonstration no one yet surpassed me, not even the Egyptians called rope-stretchers, with whom in all I lived eighty years in foreign lands." For he travelled over Babylon and Persia and Egypt, learning from the Magi and the priests. And Pythagoras zealously followed Zoroaster the Persian Magus; and those who follow the school of Prodicus boast that they possess secret books of this man.

and one must not even have the conscience defiled. With reason, then, the prophet says: "Not so the impious, not so, but as the chaff which the wind drives from the face of the earth. For this reason the impious shall not rise in judgment" (those already condemned, since "he who does not believe is already judged"), "nor sinners in the counsel of the just" (those already condemned not to be united with those who have lived unstumbling), "for the Lord knows the way of the just, and the way of the impious shall perish." Again the Lord shows plainly that both the trespasses and the offences are in our power, laying down modes of cure corresponding to the passions, wishing us to be set right by the shepherds, through Ezekiel, blaming certain of them, I think, for the things in which they did not keep the commandments: "The weak you did not strengthen," and the rest, down to "and there was none who sought after nor who turned back"; "for there is great joy with the Father over one sinner saved," says the Lord. By this Abraham is the more praiseworthy, that "he went as the Lord spoke to him."

Alexander, in his work On Pythagorean Symbols, relates that Pythagoras was a pupil of Zaratus the Assyrian (whom some think to be Ezekiel, though he is not, as will afterward be shown), and would have it that Pythagoras besides heard the Galatians and the Brahmans. And Clearchus the Peripatetic says he knew a certain Jew who associated with Aristotle. For Heraclitus says that the future was shown to the Sibyl not in human fashion, but with God. They say, at any rate, that at Delphi, near the council-chamber, a certain rock is shown, on which the first Sibyl is said to have sat, who came from Helicon and was reared by the Muses. But some say she came from the Malians, being a daughter of Lamia, who was the daughter of Poseidon. And Sarapion, in his verses, says that even in death the Sibyl did not cease from prophecy; and that the part of her that passed into air after her death is what prophesies in rumours and omens, while from the body that was changed into earth grass naturally sprang up, and whatever cattle, feeding in that place, grazed upon it, showed to men, through their entrails, the exact disclosure of the future, as he writes; and he thinks her soul is the face that appears in the moon.

From this one of the sages among the Greeks drew the "Follow God." "And the godly," says Isaiah, "took intelligent counsel." And counsel is an inquiry about how we might carry ourselves rightly in present matters, and good counsel is prudence toward deliberations. And what? Does not God too, after the pardon over Cain, in consequence, not much later bring in Enoch the penitent, showing that repentance naturally begets pardon? And pardon is constituted not according to forgiveness, but according to cure. And the same thing happens also in the calf-making of the people under Aaron. From this one of the sages among the Greeks uttered, "Pardon is better than punishment" — just as, indeed, the "Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand" is from the voice of Solomon, which says: "My son, if you give surety for your friend, you will hand over your hand to an enemy; for a man's own lips are a strong snare to him, and he is caught by the words of his own mouth." And more mystically still, the "Know yourself" is taken from there: "You have seen your brother, you have seen your God."

So much concerning the Sibyl. Numa, the king of the Romans, was a Pythagorean; and, helped by the writings of Moses, he forbade the Romans to make any image of God in the form of man or beast. So in the first hundred and seventy years, though they built temples, they made no statue, either moulded or painted. For Numa showed them, under a veil, that it is not possible to lay hold of the Best in any other way than by the mind alone. Philosophy, then, a thing of much benefit, flourished of old among the barbarians, shedding its light over the nations, and afterward came down to the Greeks also. At its head stood the prophets of the Egyptians, the Chaldeans among the Assyrians, the Druids among the Galatians, the Samanaeans among the Bactrians, the philosophers of the Celts, and the Magi of the Persians (who by their magic foretold the birth of the Saviour, coming into the land of Judaea led by a star), and among the Indians the gymnosophists, and other barbarian philosophers besides. Of these there are two kinds: some of them are called Sarmanae, others Brahmans. And of the Sarmanae those called the "forest-dwellers" neither inhabit cities nor have roofs, but are clothed in the bark of trees and feed on acorns and drink water with their hands; they know neither marriage nor the begetting of children, like those now called the Encratites. And there are among the Indians those who follow the precepts of Buddha, whom, for his surpassing solemnity, they have honoured as a god.

In this sense, somehow, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself"; "on these commandments," he says, "the whole law and the prophets hang and depend." In harmony with these are those words too: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be fulfilled. And this is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you." "For the Lord is merciful and compassionate, and good is the Lord to all." And more clearly, commending the "Know yourself," Moses says often: "Take heed to yourself." By alms, then, and by faith are sins cleansed away; and "by the fear of the Lord everyone turns away from evil." And "the fear of the Lord is education and wisdom."

Anacharsis too was a Scythian, and he is recorded as surpassing many of the philosophers among the Greeks. And Hellanicus relates that the Hyperboreans dwell beyond the Rhipaean mountains, and are taught righteousness, not eating flesh but using acorns and the like; and those of sixty years they lead outside the gates and make away with. And among the Germans too there are the so-called holy women, who, gazing at the eddies of rivers and the windings and noises of streams, divine and foretell what is to come. These, at any rate, did not allow them to join battle with Caesar before the new moon shone. Of all these the race of the Jews is by far the most ancient; and that their philosophy, committed to writing, preceded the philosophy among the Greeks, the Pythagorean Philo shows at length, as do also Aristobulus the Peripatetic and very many others — that I may not waste time going through them by name. Most plainly the historian Megasthenes, who lived with Seleucus Nicator, writes thus in the third book of his Indica: "All that has been said about nature by the ancients is said also among those who philosophize outside Greece — some things among the Indians by the Brahmans, and some in Syria by those called Jews."

Some say, more in the manner of myth, that certain wise men, the so-called Idaean Dactyls, were the first; to whom is referred the discovery both of the so-called Ephesian letters and of the rhythms of music; for which cause the "dactyls" among the musicians have taken their name. And the Idaean Dactyls were Phrygians and barbarians. Herodorus relates that Heracles, having become a seer and a natural philosopher, received the pillars of the universe from Atlas the barbarian, the Phrygian — the myth hinting that he succeeded to the knowledge of heavenly things by learning. And Hermippus of Berytus calls Chiron the Centaur "wise," concerning whom the author of the Titanomachy too says that he was the first to lead the race of mortals into righteousness, by showing oaths and glad sacrifices and the figures of Olympus. Under him is educated Achilles, who marched against Ilium; and Hippo, the daughter of the Centaur, dwelling with Aeolus, taught him natural philosophy, the science of her fathers. Euripides too bears witness concerning Hippo, somewhat thus: "who first prophesied things divine by clear oracles, at the risings of the stars." Under this Aeolus Odysseus is entertained as a guest, after the capture of Ilium. Observe for me the times, for comparison with the age of Moses and with the most ancient philosophy of his time.

And since it is fitting to make a defence against the charges brought against us by Greeks and Jews, and since in some of the perplexities the heresies concerning the true teaching join in, like those mentioned before, it would be well, first to clear away the obstacles, and then, well prepared for the solutions of the perplexities, to proceed to the next Book of the Miscellanies. First, then, they bring against us this very thing, saying that one ought not to believe, because of the discord of the heresies—for with whom is the truth, when different men hold different doctrines? To these we say that both among you Jews and among the most approved of the philosophers of the Greeks there have arisen very many sects, and yet you surely do not say that, on account of the discord of your sects with one another, one ought to shrink from philosophizing or from Judaizing. And further, that heresies would be sown beside the truth—just as "the tares" beside the wheat—was foretold prophetically by the Lord, and it is impossible that what was foretold should not come to pass; and the cause of this is that blame follows upon every noble thing.

Surely, then, even if a man should transgress agreements and pass over the confession made to us, are we, on account of the one who has belied his confession, to keep away from the truth ourselves? Rather, just as the fair-minded man must speak truth and annul nothing of what he has promised, even if some others transgress agreements, so too it befits us in no way to transgress the rule of the Church—and especially the confession concerning the greatest things, which we keep, while they transgress it. We must therefore believe those who hold firmly to the truth. And it is possible already, using this defence broadly, to say to them that physicians too, holding contrary opinions according to their own schools, treat their patients equally in practice. Surely, then, a man sick in body and needing treatment does not refuse to admit a physician on account of the schools in medicine; nor, then, would the one diseased in soul and full of idols, for the sake of being healed and turned to God, ever plead the heresies as a pretext. Indeed it is said, "the heresies are for the sake of the approved." By "the approved" it means either those who come to faith with more discernment, approaching the Lord's teaching after the manner of approved money-changers, distinguishing the genuine coin of the Lord from the counterfeit; or those who have already become approved in the very faith, both in life and in knowledge.

For this very reason, then, we need more care and forethought in the examination of how one ought exactly to live, and what the truly existing godliness is. For it is plain that, the truth being difficult and hard to work out, the inquiries arose on this account—from which spring the self-loving and glory-loving heresies, of men who have not truly learned or received, but have taken to themselves a mere opinion of knowledge. With greater care, then, must the truth that truly is be searched out—which alone is concerned with the God who truly is. And upon toil there follows sweet discovery and remembrance. We must, then, strip for the toil of discovery on account of the heresies, but must not utterly stand off. For if fruit lies before us, one part true and ripe, the other made of wax as like as possible, we must not abstain from both on account of the resemblance, but discern the true from the apparent both by the comprehending contemplation and by the most sovereign reasoning. And just as, of roads, one being the kingly highway, and many others—some leading to a precipice, some to a rushing river or a sea sheer-deep—a man would not shrink from travelling on account of the discord, but would use the safe and kingly and public way; so, when different men say different things about truth, we must not stand off, but must hunt more carefully for the most exact knowledge concerning it. Since even in cultivated vegetables weeds spring up together—do the husbandmen then abstain from the care of the garden? Having, then, many starting-points by nature toward examining the things said and discovering the consistency of the truth, we ought to do so. Therefore too we are reasonably judged, when we do not assent to those we ought to obey, when we do not distinguish the contentious and unseemly and unnatural and false from the true and consistent and seemly and natural—these being the starting-points which we ought to use toward the recognition of the truth that truly is.

Vain, then, is this pretext of the Greeks. For to those who will, it shall be possible even to find the truth; but for those who put forward irrational excuses, the judgement is without excuse. For do they do away with demonstration, or do they grant that there is such a thing? I think all would agree, except those who do away with the senses. And demonstration existing, it is necessary to descend into the inquiries, and through the very Scriptures to learn demonstratively how the heresies went astray, and how in the truth alone and in the ancient Church there is both the most exact knowledge and the truly best school of thought. But of those who turn aside from the truth, some try to deceive only themselves, others their neighbours as well. Those, then, who are called wise in their own conceit—who think they have found the truth, having no true demonstration whatever—deceive themselves, thinking they have come to rest; and of these there is no small multitude, who turn aside from the inquiries on account of the refutations, and flee even from the teachings on account of the condemnation. But the others, those who deceive those that approach, are exceedingly crafty: who, even while themselves aware that they know nothing, nevertheless darken the truth with plausible arguments. And the nature of plausible arguments is, I think, one thing, and that of true ones another. And we know that the name of "heresies" must be spoken by way of contrast to the truth; from which the sophists, tearing off certain parts to the ruin of men, and burying them in the human arts they have devised for themselves, boast that they preside over a school rather than over a Church.

Again, when he says, "It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication let each man have his own wife," he then, as it were explaining, says again: "lest Satan tempt you." For he does not say this to those who use marriage continently for the begetting of children only, on account of incontinence, but to those who desire to go beyond the begetting of children, lest the adversary, blowing strongly, should stir up appetite as a wave into other men's pleasures. Or perhaps, since the adversary opposes those who live righteously out of envy and contends against them, wishing to draw these too into his own band, he means to give them occasions for a laborious continence.

With good reason, then, he says, "It is better to marry than to burn"—so that the husband may render to the wife her due, and the wife to the husband, and they may not deprive one another of the help given for generation through the divine dispensation. And: "Whoever does not hate," they say, "father or mother or wife or children, cannot be my disciple." He does not exhort us to hate our kindred; for He says, "Honour father and mother, that it may be well with you." Rather He says: do not be led away by irrational impulses, nor join yourself to civic customs; for a household is composed of a family, and cities of households, just as Paul too said that those who are busied with marriage seek to please the world. Again the Lord says: "Let him who has married not cast her out, and let him who has not married not marry"—he who, according to a purpose of celibacy, has confessed that he will not marry, let him remain unmarried.

"And we know that we all have the knowledge"—the common knowledge in common things, and that there is one God; for he was writing to believers; whence he adds: "but the knowledge that is handed down among the few is not in all." And there are those who say that the knowledge concerning things sacrificed to idols is not present in all . . . "lest somehow this authority of yours become a stumbling-block to the weak; for the weak man is destroyed by your knowledge." And though they assert that "everything sold in the meat-market one must buy," bringing in, by way of question, "asking no question," on a par with "asking no question," they will set forth a ridiculous interpretation. For the apostle says: "All the other things buy from the meat-market, asking no question"—with the exception of the things made plain, by way of an exception, in the catholic epistle of all the apostles, with the good pleasure of the Holy Spirit, the one written in the Acts of the Apostles and conveyed to the believers by the very ministry of Paul. For they made known that it is necessary to abstain from things sacrificed to idols and from blood and from things strangled and from fornication, by keeping themselves from which they would do well. It is, then, another thing that is said by the apostle: "Have we not the right to eat and to drink? Have we not the right to take about a sister, a wife, as also the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas? But we did not use this right," he says, "but we bear all things, that we may give no hindrance to the gospel of Christ"—whether carrying burdens about, when one ought to be free and ready for all things, or becoming an example to those who wish to be continent, who are built up unto eating fearlessly what is set before them and conversing with the wife as occasion serves; but especially is it fitting that those entrusted with so great a stewardship should be set forth as an undefiled example to the learners.

To both, then, the same Lord, through the prophet Isaiah, gives the appropriate promises, speaking in some such way as this: "Let not the eunuch say, 'I am a dry tree.' Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: If you keep my Sabbaths and do all that I command, I will give you a place better than sons and daughters." For celibacy alone does not justify, nor indeed the eunuch's Sabbath, if he does not do the commandments. And to those who have married He adds, saying: "My elect shall not toil in vain, nor beget children for a curse, for they are a seed blessed by the Lord." For to the man who has begotten children according to reason, and reared them, and educated them in the Lord, as also to the one who has begotten through true instruction, there is laid up a reward, as also to the elect seed. But others take the begetting of children to be a curse, and do not understand that the Scripture speaks against those very people. For the truly elect of the Lord do not lay down such doctrines, nor do they beget children unto a curse, as the heresies do.

"For though I am free from all, I have made myself a slave to all," he says, "that I might gain all"; and "everyone who competes is continent in all things." But "the earth is the Lord's and its fullness." For the sake of conscience, then, one must abstain from what one must abstain. By "conscience" I mean not one's own, for it is gnostic, but the other's, lest he be badly built up, imitating in ignorance what he does not know, becoming a despiser instead of high-minded. "For why is my freedom judged by another's conscience? If I share with thanks, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks? Whatever, then, you do, do to the glory of God"—whatever it has been granted to do under the rule of faith.

So a eunuch is called not the man who has been forced in his members, nor indeed the unmarried man, but the man barren of truth. Such a one was formerly a dry tree; but having obeyed the Word and kept the Sabbaths by abstaining from sins and having done the commandments, he will be more honoured than those who are educated by mere reason without right conduct. "Little children," He says, "yet a little while I am with you"—the Teacher. Wherefore Paul too, writing to the Galatians, says: "My little children, for whom I again travail in birth until Christ be formed in you." And again, writing to the Corinthians: "For though you have countless tutors in Christ," he says, "yet not many fathers; for in Christ, through the gospel, I begot you." For this reason the eunuch shall not enter into the Church of God—the man barren and fruitless both in conduct and in word; but those who have made themselves eunuchs of all sin for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, these are blessed, who fast from the world.

The gnostic, then, takes the closer likeness — the mind of the teacher; which the teacher, conceiving, both enjoined and counselled upon the prudent and temperate, understanding it as the teacher willed, and having taken up privately the magnificent conception — having taught worthily upon the housetops those able to be built up loftily, and having begun the working of the things said according to the example of his manner of life. For he enjoined things possible; and the kingly and Christian man must in truth be ruling and leading, since we have been appointed to be lords not over the wild beasts without only, but also over the savage passions within ourselves. By attention, then, as it seems, to the evil and the good life the gnostic is saved, understanding and working more than the scribes and Pharisees. "Bend the bow, and prosper, and reign," David writes, "for the sake of truth and meekness and righteousness, and your right hand shall guide you wonderfully" — that is, the Lord. "Who, then, is wise and shall understand these things? Prudent, and shall know them? For straight are the ways of the Lord," says the prophet, showing that the gnostic alone is able to understand and make plain the things said hiddenly by the Spirit. "And he that is prudent shall keep silence at that season," says the Scripture — plainly, from declaring them to the unworthy; for the Lord says, "He that has ears to hear, let him hear," saying that the hearing and understanding belong not to all.

For instance, David writes, "Dark water in the clouds of the airs"; "from the brightness before him the clouds passed through, hail and coals of fire" — teaching that the holy words are hidden. And he shows that to the gnostics they are sent down from God transparent and far-shining, like harmless hail; but dark to the many, like coals quenched out of fire, which, unless one kindle and rekindle them, will not flame nor give light. "The Lord, then," it says, "gives me a tongue of discipline, to know in season when it is needful to speak a word" — not in martyrdom only, but also that by question and answer; "and the discipline of the Lord opens my mouth." It belongs to the gnostic, then, both to know how to use the word, and when, and how, and to whom.

And already the apostle too, saying "after the elements of the world and not after Christ," delivers the Greek teaching to be elementary, but that according to Christ perfect, as we showed before. For instance, the wild olive is grafted into the fatness of the olive, and indeed grows of the same kind with the cultivated olives; for the thing implanted uses the tree in which it is planted instead of earth; and all the plants together have sprung up from a divine command. Wherefore, even if the wild olive be a wild thing, yet it crowns the Olympic victors; and the elm, leading the vine up to a height, teaches it to bear good fruit. And we see now the wild trees drawing more nourishment to themselves through their not being able to digest. The wild, then, are less digestive than the cultivated, and the cause of their being wild is the lack of digestive power.

The grafted olive, then, takes more nourishment, by reason of the wild thing being implanted; but, being of this kind, it is accustomed to digest the nourishment, being made like to the fatness of the cultivated. So too the philosopher, likened to the wild olive, having much that is undigested, by reason of being inquisitive and easy to follow up and craving the fatness of the truth — if he take besides the divine power through faith, planted in the kindly and cultivated knowledge, like the wild olive grafted into the truly noble and merciful Word, both digests the nourishment delivered and becomes a good olive. For the grafting makes the worthless noble, and forces the unfruitful to become fruitful, by the husbandman's art and the gnostic science.

They say, then, that the grafting comes about in four ways: one, by which the thing grafted must be fitted between the wood and the bark, as the unlearned of the Gentiles are catechized, receiving the word on the surface; another, when, having split the wood, they thrust into it the noble shoot, which happens in the case of those who have philosophized — for, their doctrines being cleft, the recognition of truth comes about in them; thus too, the old Scripture being opened to the Jews, the new and noble shoot of the olive is grafted in. The third grafting touches the wild and the heretics, who are brought over to the truth by force; for, having shaved off each side with a sharp knife to a wedge, until they bare the pith, but do not wound it, they bind them to one another. And a fourth manner of grafting is that called inoculation; for from a noble stem an eye is taken off, with the bark around it cut round about, about a hand's-breadth in length; then the stem is shaved off, at an eye equal to the cut round about, and so the eye is set in, bound about with cords and smeared with clay, the eye being kept unhurt and undefiled. This is a kind of gnostic teaching, able to look through into things; and indeed this kind is most useful even in the case of cultivated trees.

And the grafting spoken of by the apostle, into the good olive, may be into Christ himself, the savage and unbelieving nature being planted into Christ — that is, into those who believe in Christ; but it is better that the faith of each be grafted into the very soul. For the Holy Spirit too is somehow thus transplanted, distributed according to the circumscription of each without circumscription. And concerning knowledge Solomon, discoursing, says this: "Bright and unfading is wisdom, and easily beheld by those who love her; she anticipates those who desire her, to be known beforehand. He who rises early to her shall not labour; for to have thought about her is the perfection of prudence, and he who has watched for her sake shall quickly be free of care; for she goes about seeking those worthy of her" (for knowledge is not for all), "and in their paths she shows herself to them graciously." And the paths are the conduct of life and the manifold variety according to the covenants. For instance, he adds:

"and in every thought she meets them," being beheld variously — through every kind of education, plainly. Then he adds, setting forth the perfecting love, by a syllogistic argument and true premises, most demonstrative and true, bringing on somewhat thus the conclusion: "For her most true beginning is the craving of education" (that is, of knowledge), "and the care of education is love, and love is the keeping of her laws, and the giving heed to her laws is the confirmation of incorruption, and incorruption makes one near to God. The craving of wisdom, then, leads up to a kingdom." For he teaches, I think, that true education is a craving of knowledge, and the practice of education is established through love of knowledge. And love is the keeping of the commandments that lead up to knowledge, and the keeping of them is the confirmation of the commandments, through which incorruption comes about; and incorruption makes one near to God. If, then, love of knowledge makes incorruptible and leads up the kingly man near to God the King, one must seek knowledge unto discovery. And inquiry is an impulse toward apprehension, finding out, by certain signs, the thing that lies before it; and discovery is the end and rest of inquiry, having come to be in apprehension — which is knowledge. And this is properly discovery, being the apprehension of inquiry. And a sign they say is the leading or accompanying or following.

Of the inquiry, then, concerning God, the discovery is the teaching that comes through the Son; and a sign that our Saviour himself is that very Son of God are the prophecies that went before his coming, proclaiming him, and the testimonies concerning him that accompanied his sensible birth, and besides these the powers proclaimed and openly shown after his ascension. A proof, then, that the truth is among us, is the very fact that the Son of God himself taught. For if in every inquiry these universals are found, person and thing, the truly real truth is shown to be among us alone, since the person of the truth that is shown is the Son of God, and the thing is the power of faith, which abounds over everyone whatsoever that opposes, even over the whole world standing in array. But since this has been confessed to be confirmed by everlasting deeds and words, and is already manifest, everyone worthy of chastisement, not of contradiction, who thinks there is no providence and is truly godless — but it lies before us, by doing what and living in what manner we may come to the recognition of God the Almighty, and how, honouring the divine, we may become causes of salvation to ourselves; having learned and known, not from the sophists, but from God himself, the thing well-pleasing to him, we set our hand to do the just and holy thing. And our being saved is well-pleasing to him; and salvation comes about through good-doing and through knowledge, of both of which the Lord is teacher.

If, then, even according to Plato it is only possible to learn the true thing either from God or from the offspring of God, with reason, culling our testimonies from the divine oracles, we boast to be taught the truth through the Son of God, prophesied first and afterward made plain; and the things that help toward the discovery of the truth are not themselves to be rejected. Philosophy, at any rate, proclaiming providence, and the recompense of the happy life and the chastisement of the unhappy, theologizes in a comprehensive way, but no longer keeps the things to exactness and in particular. For neither concerning the Son of God nor concerning the dispensation according to providence does it treat as we do; for it did not know the worship that is according to God. Wherefore the heresies of the barbarian philosophy, even if they speak of one God and hymn Christ, speak comprehensively, not to the truth; for they both invent another God and receive Christ not as the prophecies deliver him. But their false doctrines are nothing against us, so long as they oppose the conduct according to the truth.

For instance, Paul circumcised Timothy on account of those who believed from among the Jews, that the catechumens from the law should not fall away from the faith while he was dissolving the things assumed too fleshly out of the law, knowing exactly that circumcision does not justify; for he confessed to become all things to all men, by accommodation preserving the authoritative doctrines, that he might gain all. And Daniel bore the collar before the king of the Persians, not overlooking the affliction of the people. Liars, then, in truth are not those who accommodate themselves through the dispensation of salvation, nor those who err about some particular matter, but those who fall away in the most authoritative things and reject the Lord as far as in them lies, robbing the Lord of his true teaching, those who do not speak and deliver the Scriptures worthily of God and the Lord. For a deposit rendered to God is the understanding and joint training, according to the Lord's teaching through his apostles, of the godly tradition; "and what you hear in the ear" (hiddenly, that is, and in a mystery; for such things are allegorized as being spoken into the ear), "preach upon the housetops," it says — receiving them high-mindedly and delivering them loftily, and making the Scriptures plain according to the rule of truth. For neither the prophecy nor the Saviour himself uttered the divine mysteries simply so, as to be easily caught by the chance comer, but discoursed in parables.

The apostles, at any rate, say of the Lord that he spoke all things in parables, and without a parable spoke he nothing to them. And if all things came to be through him, and without him not one thing came to be, then prophecy and the law too came to be through him, and were spoken in parables through him. "But all things are right before those who understand," says the Scripture — that is, before all those who, receiving the interpretation of the Scriptures made plain by him according to the ecclesiastical rule, preserve it. And the ecclesiastical rule is the concord and the symphony of the law and the prophets with the covenant delivered at the Lord's coming. Knowledge, then, is followed by prudence, and temperance by prudence. For let it be said that prudence is a divine knowledge, and exists in those made gods; but temperance is mortal, and exists in men who philosophize, but are not yet wise. For instance, if virtue is divine, the knowledge of it is divine too; but temperance is, as it were, an imperfect prudence, craving prudence, and working laboriously and not contemplatively — as righteousness too, being human, is a common thing, and has subsided below holiness, which is the divine righteousness. For to the perfect man righteousness is not in civil contracts nor in the prohibition of the law, but from his own proper doing and from the love toward God.

For many causes, then, the Scriptures hide the sense: first, that we may be inquirers and ever wakeful to the discovery of the saving words; next, because it was not fitting for all to understand, lest they be harmed by taking otherwise the things spoken savingly by the Holy Spirit. Wherefore the holy mysteries of the prophecies, kept for the elect of men and for those approved from faith unto knowledge, are veiled in the parables. For the character of the Scriptures is parabolic, since the Lord too, not being of the world, came among men as one of the world. For he wore all virtue, and was about to lead up the man bred together with the world, through knowledge, to the things of mind and authoritative, from world to world. Wherefore too he used the metaphorical Scripture; for such is the parable, a discourse, from something not the chief thing, but like to the chief thing, leading the understanding one to the true and chief thing — or, as some say, a phrasing that sets forth, through other things, with energy, the things properly said.

And by now too the whole dispensation prophesied concerning the Lord seems, in truth, a parable to those who have not known the truth, when one says, and others hear, that the Son of God, of him who made all things, having taken flesh and been carried in a virgin's womb (in respect of which his sensible little body has come to be), and consequently, in respect of his having become this, having suffered and risen — to the Jews a stumbling-block, to the Greeks foolishness, as the apostle says. But the Scriptures, opened, and showing to those who have ears the very truth, namely what the flesh suffered which the Lord took up, proclaim the power and wisdom of God. And above all, the parabolic kind of Scripture, being most ancient, as we set forth, with reason abounded especially among the prophets, that so the Holy Spirit might show that the philosophers among the Greeks and the wise men among the other barbarians had been ignorant of the coming of the Lord that should be, and of the mystic teaching that should be delivered by him. With reason, then, the prophecy, proclaiming the Lord — that it might not seem, by speaking against the suppositions of the many, to blaspheme to some — shaped the things signified by voices able to lead also to other thoughts. For instance, all the prophets who foretold the coming of the Lord, and with it the holy mysteries, were persecuted and slain, as the Lord himself too, making plain their Scriptures, and his acquaintance who proclaimed the word, likewise after him hazarded their life.

Whence Peter too, in the Preaching, speaking of the apostles, says: "But we, having unrolled the books of the prophets which we had, some through parables, some through riddles, and some authoritatively and in so many words naming Christ Jesus, found both his coming and his death and the cross and all the other chastisements which the Jews wrought against him, and his rising and his ascension into the heavens before Jerusalem was founded — even as all these things were written, what he must suffer, and what shall be after him. Having recognized these things, then, we believed in God through the things written concerning him." And a little after he adds again, setting forth that the prophecies came about by divine providence, thus: "For we knew that God truly ordained them, and we say nothing apart from Scripture."

And the dialect of the Hebrews has, then, some other peculiarities too, as each of the rest, containing a certain principle that shows forth a national character. For they define a dialect as a speech wrought out by a national character. But it is not by those dialects that the prophecy is made known. For among the Greeks the so-called changes of figure make their concealments on purpose, after the image of the prophecies among us — being referred . . . except that it is shown to be a voluntary turning-aside from the straight, made in metrical or extemporaneous phrasing. For a figure is a phrasing transferred from its proper to its improper sense, for the sake of construction and for the usefulness of the phrasing in the discourse. But the prophecy does not at all pursue the figures of speech for the beauty of the phrasing; rather, because the truth is not for all, it is concealed in many ways, raising the light only upon those initiated unto knowledge, those who seek the truth through love.

There is said, then, to be a kind of prophecy, the proverb, according to the barbarian philosophy; and the parable too is so called, and the riddle besides these. But also it is called wisdom, and, as something different from it, education; and again "words of prudence" and "turnings of words" and "true righteousness"; and again "teaching of how to set straight a judgement," and "cunning" coming to the guileless by education, and "perception" and "thought" coming to the newly catechized. "He who has heard these prophets," it says, "being wise, shall be the wiser, and the intelligent shall acquire governance, and shall understand a parable and a dark saying, and the sayings of the wise, and riddles." And if it came about that the Greek dialects were named from Hellen the son of Zeus, surnamed of Deucalion, it is easy to see, from the times which we set forth above, by how many generations the dialects current among the Greeks are later than the Hebrew tongue.

And as the Scripture goes forward, marking the aforesaid figures used by the prophet at each section, we shall set them forth, showing, with art, the gnostic conduct according to the rule of truth. For did not, in the vision, the power, appearing to Hermas in the figure of the church, give the book to be transcribed, which she willed to be announced to the elect? And this he transcribed letter by letter, he says, not finding how to complete the syllables. And it showed, then, that the Scripture is plain to all, taken according to the bare reading, and that this is the faith, holding the order of the elements; wherefore too the reading "to the letter" is allegorized. But the gnostic unfolding of the Scriptures, when the faith has already advanced, we take to be likened to the reading according to the syllables. But Isaiah the prophet too is bidden to take a new book and write certain things, the Spirit prophesying that the holy knowledge, through the interpretation of the Scriptures, would later be — being, up to that season, unwritten, because not yet known; for it had been spoken from the beginning only to those who understand. For instance, when the Saviour had taught the apostles, the tradition, unwritten of the written, is now delivered even to us, written on new hearts according to the renewing of the book, by the power of God.

So the most learned of the Greeks consecrate to Hermes, whom indeed they say is the Word, on account of the interpretation, the fruit of the pomegranate; for the Word holds much within. With reason, then, Joshua the son of Nun saw Moses, when he was taken up, double — the one with angels, the other deemed worthy of burial upon the mountains, about the ravines. And Joshua saw this sight below, lifted up in spirit, together with Caleb. But both did not behold alike; for the one came down the more quickly, drawing much weight with him; but the other, having come down after, recounted the glory he had beheld, being able to look through more than the other, as being also purer — the history showing, I think, that knowledge is not for all, since some look upon the body of the Scriptures, the words and the names, as the body of Moses; while others look through to the meanings and the things shown forth by the names, inquiring after the Moses who was with angels. For instance, of those who called upon the Lord himself, the most said, "Son of David, have mercy on me," but few knew him as Son of God, like Peter, whom he blessed, because flesh and blood revealed not the truth to him, but his Father in heaven — showing that the gnostic recognizes the Son of the Almighty, not through his flesh that was conceived, but through the very power of the Father. Not only, then, to those who chance simply upon it is the acquiring of the truth difficult, but even to those whose own the science is — to these too the contemplation is not given all at once, the history about Moses teaches, until, accustomed to look back, as the Hebrews looked at the glory of Moses, and the saints of Israel at the visions of angels, so too we may be able to look at the flashings of the truth.

Here again the accusers fasten on, calling joy and grief passions of the soul. For they render joy a reasonable elation, and to exult, to rejoice over noble things; and pity, grief over one suffering ill undeservedly; and they say that such things are changes and passions of the soul. But we, as it seems, do not cease understanding the Scriptures in a fleshly way, and, raising ourselves from our own passions, awaiting the will of the impassible God in likeness to our own motions; supposing that, as we are able to hear, so it is with the Almighty, we wander godlessly. For it was not possible to speak of the divine as it is; but as it was possible for us, fettered in the flesh, to hear, so the prophets spoke to us, the Lord bearing himself with us in a saving way toward the weakness of men.

Since, then, it is the will of God that the man obedient to the commandments be saved, and the man who repents of his sins, and we rejoice over our salvation, the Lord, who spoke through the prophets, made our gladness his own, just as in the Gospel he says, lovingly toward mankind: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I thirsted, and you gave me to drink; for what you did to one of these least, you did to me." As, then, he is fed without being fed, because the one whom he wishes has been fed, so he rejoiced without being changed, because the one who repented has come to be in joy, as he wished. And since God, being good, has mercy richly — giving the commandments through the law, . . . through the prophets, and now more closely through the coming of the Son, saving and having mercy, as has been said, on those who have obtained mercy — and properly the greater has mercy on the lesser; and man would not be greater than man, in so far as he is man by nature, but God is greater than man in all things; if, then, the greater has mercy on the lesser, God alone will have mercy on us. For man becomes social through righteousness and shares what he received from God, both through natural goodwill and relation, and through the commandments which he obeys;

Not of philosophy only, but of nearly every art, the barbarians are the inventors. The Egyptians, at any rate, first brought astrology to men, and likewise the Chaldeans. The Egyptians again first showed how to burn lamps, and divided the year into twelve months, and forbade intercourse with women in the temples, and laid it down by law that men should not enter the temples after being with a woman without bathing; and the same men became the inventors of geometry. And there are those who say the Carians devised foretelling through the stars. The Phrygians were the first to observe the flights of birds, and the Tuscans, neighbours of Italy, perfected the art of inspecting victims. The Isaurians and the Arabians worked out augury, as the Telmesians did divination through dreams. The Tyrrhenians devised the trumpet, and the Phrygians the flute; for Olympus and Marsyas were Phrygians.

but God has no natural relation toward us, as the founders of the heresies wish (neither if he should make us from things that are not, nor if he should fashion us from matter — since the one is not at all, and the other is in all respects other than God) — unless one should dare to call us a part of him and of the same essence as God. And I do not know how anyone who has known God will endure to hear this, when he looks at our life, in how many evils we are entangled. For in this way God would be — what it is not even lawful to say — sinning in part, if indeed the parts of the whole are parts and complementary of the whole; and if they are not complementary, neither would they be parts. But, being by nature rich in mercy, through his own goodness God cares for us, though we are neither portions of him nor by nature his children.

Cadmus was a Phoenician, the inventor of letters for the Greeks, as Ephorus says; whence Herodotus writes that the letters were called "Phoenician." But some say the Phoenicians and the Syrians were the first to devise letters. Medicine they say Apis, an Egyptian aboriginal, invented before Io came to Egypt, and that afterward Asclepius increased the art. Atlas the Libyan first built a ship and sailed the sea. Celmis again and Damnameneus, the Idaean Dactyls, first found iron in Cyprus, and Delas, another Idaean, found the tempering of bronze, though Hesiod says it was a Scythian. The Thracians, indeed, were the first to find the so-called harpe (a curved sword), and the first to use bucklers on horseback. Likewise the Illyrians invented the so-called parma. Further, they say the Tuscans devised modelling, and Itanus (he was a Samnite) first made the oblong shield. For Cadmus the Phoenician found out the cutting of stone and devised the gold mines around Mount Pangaeus. And yet another nation, the Cappadocians, first found the so-called nabla, as the Assyrians did the two-stringed instrument. The Carthaginians first built a quadrireme, and Bosporus built it offhand.

And indeed this is the greatest proof of the goodness of God, that, we being so disposed toward him and by nature wholly estranged, he yet cares for us. For the tender affection toward children is natural to the animals, and the friendship from custom toward those of like mind; but the mercy of God toward us is rich, who belong to him in nothing — I mean by our essence or nature, or by the power proper to our essence — but only by our being the work of his will. And indeed the man who, willingly, with exercise and teaching, has taken up the knowledge of the truth, he calls into adoption, the greatest advance of all. "But lawless deeds hunt down a man, and each is bound fast by the cords of his own sins"; and God is without responsibility. And in truth "blessed is the man who is afraid of all things through caution."

Medea, the daughter of Aeetes, the Colchian, first devised the dyeing of hair. The Noropes too (a Paeonian nation, now called Norici) were the first to work bronze and to refine iron. Amycus, the king of the Bebryces, first found the thongs for boxing. In music, Olympus the Mysian skilfully wrought the Lydian harmony; and those called the Troglodytes found the sambyke, a musical instrument. They say also that Satyrus the Phrygian found the transverse pipe; that Agnis, himself too a Phrygian, found likewise the three-stringed lyre and the diatonic harmony; that Olympus, likewise a Phrygian, found the strokes; as also that Marsyas, of the same country as those just named, found the Phrygian, the mixophrygian, and the mixolydian harmonies; and that Thamyris the Thracian devised the Dorian. We have heard, too, that the Persians were the first to make the carriage and the couch and the footstool, and the Sidonians to build the three-banked ship. The Sicels, near Italy, first found the phorminx, not much inferior to the lyre, and devised the castanets. In the time of Semiramis, king of the Egyptians, they relate that linen garments were found. And Hellanicus says that Atossa, who reigned over the Persians, was the first to compose letters.

Scamon of Mitylene, then, and Theophrastus of Eresus, and Cydippus of Mantinea, and besides Antiphanes and Aristodemus and Aristotle, and besides these Philostephanus, and Strato the Peripatetic too, in his works On Discoveries, related these things. I have set down a few of them to establish the inventive and life-benefiting nature among the barbarians, from whom the Greeks profited in their pursuits. And if anyone disparages the barbarian tongue — "To me," says Anacharsis, "all the Greeks speak Scythian." This was the man admired among the Greeks, who said: "My covering is a cloak, my supper milk and cheese." You see philosophy among the barbarians professing deeds, not words.

And the Apostle says thus: "You too, if you do not give an intelligible word through the tongue, how will what is spoken be known? For you will be speaking into the air. There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none without meaning. If, then, I do not know the force of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to the speaker, and the speaker a barbarian to me. And let him who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret." Indeed, it was late that the teaching and writing of discourses came to the Greeks. Alcmaeon, son of Perithus, of Croton, first composed a treatise on nature. And some relate that Anaxagoras, son of Hegesibulus, of Clazomenae, was the first to publish a book in writing. Terpander of Antissa first set melody to verse and put the laws of the Spartans into song; Lasus of Hermione devised the dithyramb; Stesichorus of Himera the hymn; Alcman the Spartan the choral dance; Anacreon of Teos the songs of love; Pindar the Theban the hyporcheme. And Timotheus of Miletus was the first to sing the laws in chorus and with the lyre.

Indeed, Archilochus of Paros devised the iambus, and Hipponax of Ephesus the limping iambus; Thespis the Athenian devised tragedy, and Susarion of Icaria comedy. The times of these the sons of the grammarians hand down; but it would be a long matter to set them out with exactness, since Dionysus himself, on account of whom the Dionysiac spectacles are held, is shown presently to be later than Moses. They say also that Antiphon of Rhamnus, son of Sophilus, first found out the discourses of the schools and the rhetorical idioms, and first pleaded for pay, writing a forensic speech for publication, as Diodorus says. And Apollodorus of Cyme first introduced the name of "grammarian" instead of "critic," and was called a grammarian; though some say it was Eratosthenes of Cyrene, since he published two books entitled Grammatica. But the first to be called "grammarian," as we now use the term, was Praxiphanes, son of Dionysophanes, of Mitylene. And Zaleucus the Locrian is recorded as the first to lay down laws, though some say it was Minos, the son of Zeus, in the time of Lynceus. He comes eleven generations above, from Inachus and Moses, after Danaus, as we shall show a little further on. And Lycurgus, who lived many years after the capture of Ilium, gives laws to the Spartans a hundred years before the Olympiads; for we have already stated the times of Solon.

Draco too, himself a lawgiver, is found to have lived about the thirty-ninth Olympiad. And Antilochus, who treated of the men of learning from the age of Pythagoras to the death of Epicurus . . . on the tenth of Gamelion at its beginning, brings the whole to three hundred and twelve years. Further, they say that Phanothea, the wife of Icarius, found the hexameter heroic verse, though some say Themis, one of the Titanides. And Didymus, in his work On Pythagorean Philosophy, relates that Theano of Croton was the first of women to philosophize and to write poems. Greek philosophy, then, as some hold, lays hold of the truth somewhat by chance, but dimly and not the whole of it; but as others would have it, it takes its movement from the devil. And some have supposed that certain inferior powers inspired the whole of philosophy. But even if Greek philosophy does not comprehend the greatness of the truth, and besides is too weak to do the commandments of the Lord, yet it does at least prepare the way beforehand for the most kingly teaching, in some way bringing to soberness and shaping the character in advance, and disposing toward the reception of the truth the man who glorifies providence.

But those ready to toil over the noblest things will not stop seeking the truth before they take the demonstration from the Scriptures themselves. Now there are certain criteria common to all men, like the sense-organs; but the others belong to those who have willed and trained themselves in the truth—the criteria, wrought through mind and reasoning, of words true and false. And the greatest thing is to lay aside opinion, taking one's stand midway between exact knowledge and rash conceit of wisdom, and to know that he who hopes for the eternal rest knows also that the entrance to it is toilsome and "narrow." And he who has once been told the good news and "has seen the salvation," at whatever hour he recognizes it, let him not "turn back, like Lot's wife," nor turn to the former life that clings to the things of sense, nor run back to the heresies; for they contend in a manner, not knowing the God who is. For "he who loves father or mother more than me"—the true Father and Teacher of the truth, who regenerates and refashions and nurses the chosen soul—"is not worthy of me," he says, worthy of being a son of God and a disciple of God, and at once a friend and a kinsman. "For no one who looks back, and lays his hand upon the plough, is fit for the kingdom of God." But, as it seems, to the many it still appears even now that Mary is a woman in childbed by reason of the birth of the child, though she is not in childbed; for some say that, after giving birth, when examined by the midwife, she was found a virgin.

And such, for us, are the scriptures of the Lord—bringing forth the truth and remaining virgins, with the hiding of the mysteries of the truth. "She has brought forth, and has not brought forth," says the Scripture, as having conceived of herself, not from union. Therefore the Scriptures have conceived for the gnostics; but the heresies, not having learned them, are dismissed as not having conceived. And though all men have the same judgement, some, following the reason that chooses, make their acts of faith; but others, having given themselves over to pleasures, force the Scripture toward their desires. And there is need, I think, for the lover of truth of a certain vigour of soul; for those who set their hands to the greatest matters must of necessity err most greatly, unless they have received from the truth itself the rule of the truth. Such men, accordingly, as having fallen from the right road, in most particulars also go astray, reasonably—through not having a criterion of true and false, exactly trained to choose what is needful. For if they had acquired it, they would obey the divine Scriptures.

As, then, if a man should become a beast out of a man, like those drugged by Circe, so the one who has kicked against the tradition of the Church and leaped away into the opinions of human heresies has destroyed his being a man of God and his remaining faithful to the Lord. But he who has run back from this deceit, having heard the Scriptures and committed his own life to the truth, is made, as it were, a god out of a man. For we have the beginning of the teaching—the Lord, leading the way of knowledge from the beginning to the end through the prophets and through the Gospel and through the blessed apostles, "in many ways and many parts." And if anyone should suppose that the beginning needs something else, then it would no longer be truly preserved as a beginning. He, then, who of himself is faithful to the Lord's Scripture and voice is reasonably trustworthy, as being worked through the Lord toward the benefit of men. Indeed, we use it as a criterion toward the discovery of things; but everything judged is still untrustworthy until it has been judged—so that what needs judgement is not a beginning. Reasonably, then, having grasped by faith the indemonstrable beginning, and having received in abundance the demonstrations concerning the beginning from the beginning itself, we are trained by the voice of the Lord toward the recognition of the truth. For we would not give heed to men who simply make pronouncements, against whom it is equally open to pronounce in turn. And if it is not enough simply to state one's opinion, but the thing said must be confirmed, we do not wait for the testimony from men, but confirm the matter in question by the voice of the Lord, which is more to be trusted than all demonstrations—or rather, which alone is demonstration. According to this knowledge, those who have only tasted the Scriptures are faithful; but those who have advanced further are exact judges of the truth—the gnostics. Since even in the affairs of life the craftsmen have something more than the laymen, and shape the better thing beyond the common conceptions.

So, then, we too, demonstrating perfectly concerning the Scriptures from the Scriptures themselves, are persuaded out of faith demonstratively. And even if those who pursue the heresies dare to make use of the prophetic Scriptures—first, they do not use all; then, they use them imperfectly, nor as the body and texture of the prophecy dictate, but choosing out the things said ambiguously and transferring them to their own opinions, culling a few phrases here and there, not considering what is signified by them, but using the bare wording. For in nearly all the texts they bring forward you would find them clinging to the names only, altering the things signified, neither knowing them as they are spoken, nor using them as they are by nature, in the very selections they adduce. But the truth is not found in transposing the things signified (for so they will overturn all true teaching), but in considering what is wholly proper and fitting to the Lord and the almighty God, and in confirming each of the things demonstrated according to the Scriptures, again from the like Scriptures themselves. Neither, then, are they willing to turn back toward the truth, being ashamed to lay down the advantage of their self-love; nor have they any way to arrange their own opinions, forcing the Scriptures. Having anticipated us by bringing forth false doctrines to men, they fight openly with nearly all the Scriptures, and being always refuted by us who contradict them, even now they continue—partly not admitting some of the prophetic Scriptures, and partly slandering us, as though we, being of another nature, were unable to understand the things proper to those Scriptures—and sometimes, when their own doctrines are refuted, they deny them, ashamed to confess openly the things they boast of teaching in private.

For thus one may see throughout all the heresies, going over the wickedness of their doctrines. For whenever they are overturned by us, who show them plainly opposing the Scriptures, one or other of two things may be seen happening among the leaders of the doctrine: for they despise either the consistency of their own doctrines, or the prophecy itself—or rather, their own hope—and choose in each case what seems to them more evident than what was spoken by the Lord through the prophets, and witnessed and confirmed by the Gospel, and besides by the apostles. Seeing, then, that the danger for them is not about a single doctrine, but about preserving the heresies—not about finding the truth (for they despised, as cheap, the things that lie open and ready among us); and being eager to overstep the common ground of the faith, they have stepped outside the truth. For not having learned the mysteries of the knowledge that is of the Church, nor made room for the greatness of the truth, having shrunk through sloth from going down to the depth of things, reading superficially they dismissed the Scriptures.

Lifted up, then, by conceit of wisdom, they pass their lives in contention, having shown themselves to be more concerned for seeming than for philosophizing. Accordingly, laying down for themselves no necessary principles of things, and being moved by human opinions, then necessarily working out for themselves a conclusion that follows upon them, they brawl, on account of the refutations, against those who handle the true philosophy; and they endure all things, and, as they say, "move every cable," even though they are about to be impious through their unbelief toward the Scriptures, rather than change—out of love of glory for their heresy, and for the much-talked-of first seat in their assemblies, for the sake of which they embrace also that banqueting first couch of the love that is falsely named. But among us the recognition of the truth furnishes faith to those not yet faithful out of those already faithful—faith which is established, so to speak, as the very substance of demonstration. But, as it seems, every heresy has ears that do not hear the things profitable, but are open only to the things toward pleasure. Since indeed even one of them might be healed, if only he would consent to be persuaded by the truth. There is a threefold treatment of conceit, as of every passion: the learning of the cause, and of how it may be removed, and, third, the training of the soul and the habituation toward being able to follow the things rightly judged.

"For with the heart it is believed unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." So the Scripture says: "Everyone who believes in Him shall not be put to shame." This is the word of faith which we preach, that "if you confess the word with your mouth, that the Lord is Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you shall be saved." He plainly outlines a perfect righteousness, filled with both work and contemplation. We must, then, bless the persecutors: "Bless and do not curse." For "this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience, that in holiness and sincerity we have known God"—through this small occasion displaying the work of love—"that not in fleshly wisdom, but in the grace of God we have conducted ourselves in the world."

For just as an eye troubled, so too the soul, fouled by doctrines contrary to nature, is unable to discern exactly the light of the truth, but overlooks even the things at its feet. They say that in turbid water even eels are caught, being blinded. And just as wicked children shut out the tutor, so these men keep the prophecies out of their own Church, suspicious of them on account of refutation and admonition. Indeed, they patch together very many falsehoods and fabrications, that they may seem with good reason not to admit the Scriptures. In this way, then, they are not devout, being displeased with the divine commandments—that is, with the Holy Spirit. And just as almonds are called empty, not those in which there is nothing, but those in which what is within is useless, so we say that the heretics are empty of the counsels of God and of the traditions of Christ—being bitter in truth, like the wild almond, as the begetters of doctrines, except for so much as, through the evidence of the truths, they have been unable to lay aside and hide.

"Cursed be the day on which I was born, and let it not be longed for," says Jeremiah—not calling generation simply cursed, but in despair over the sins of the people and their disobedience. He adds, at any rate: "Why was I born to see toils and pains, and that my days have been spent in shame?" For indeed all who proclaim the truth were persecuted and endangered because of the disobedience of their hearers. "Why did not the womb of my mother become my tomb, that I might not see the trouble of Jacob and the toil of the race of Israel?" says Esdras the prophet. "No one is clean from filth," says Job, "not even if his life be one day." Let them tell us where the newborn infant has fornicated, or how the one who has done nothing has fallen under the curse of Adam. It remains for them, it seems, to say consistently that generation is evil—not only that of the body, but also that of the soul, for the sake of which the body too exists. And when David says, "In sins was I conceived, and in iniquities did my mother bear me in the womb," he speaks prophetically of his mother Eve; but Eve became the mother of the living, and even if he was conceived in sin, yet he himself was not in sin, nor was he sin.

These things the apostle says concerning knowledge; but the common teaching of faith he called "the fragrance of knowledge" in the second epistle to the Corinthians. "For until this present day the same veil remains for the many at the reading of the old covenant, not being unveiled in their turning to the Lord." For this reason too He showed resurrection to those able to see clearly, the resurrection that, while still in the flesh, comes from the life of the thing that creeps upon its belly. Hence too He called such men "offspring of vipers"—the lovers of pleasure, those who serve belly and genitals, and who cut off one another's heads for the sake of worldly desires. "Little children, let us not love in word nor in tongue," says John, teaching them to be perfect, "but in deed and in truth. In this we shall know that we are of the truth." And if God is love, then piety too is love; "there is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. This is the love of God, that we keep His commandments." And again, to the gnostic who longs to come into being it is written: "But become a pattern of the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity"; for the perfection of faith, I think, is distinguished from the common faith.

As, then, in war the soldier must not leave the post which the general appointed to him, so too one must not leave the post which the Word gave—the Word whom we have received as ruler of knowledge and of life. But the many have not even examined this: whether one ought to follow anyone, and whom this is, and how. For of what kind the Word is, of such kind it befits the believer's life also to be, so as to be able "to follow God," who from the beginning brings all things "to a straight end." But whenever a man transgresses the Word, and through this God, if indeed through some impression suddenly falling upon him he has grown weak, he must make the rational impressions ready to hand; but if, overcome by the habit that has previously held him, he has become (as Scripture says) "common," the habit must be made to cease utterly, and the soul must be trained to contradict it. And if doctrines at war with one another seem to draw certain men, these must be taken out of the way, and one must go to the "peacemakers" among doctrines, who lull with chants of the divine Scriptures the timid among the inexperienced, making the truth plain through the consistency of the covenants. But, as it seems, we incline rather toward the things of reputation, even if they happen to be contrary, than toward the truth; for it is austere and grave. And there being three dispositions of the soul—ignorance, conceit, and knowledge—those in ignorance are the heathen, those in knowledge the true Church, and those in conceit those who follow the heresies.

And if every man who turns from sin to faith turns from the sinful custom, as from a mother, to life, one of the twelve prophets will bear witness for me, who says: "Shall I give my firstborn for impiety, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?" He does not slander the one who said, "Increase and multiply," but calls the first impulses from generation, in accordance with which we do not know God, "impieties." But if anyone on this ground calls generation evil, let him also, on that other ground, call it good, in that in it we come to know the truth: "Awake righteously, and do not sin; for some have ignorance of God"—plainly those who sin; since our struggle is not against blood and flesh, but against the spiritual powers, and the world-rulers of darkness are able to make trial of us, on account of which the pardons exist.

For this reason Paul too says, "I buffet my own body and bring it into subjection," because "everyone who competes is continent in all things"—instead of "is continent unto all things," not abstaining from all things, but using continently the things he has chosen—"those, indeed, that they may receive a corruptible crown, but we an incorruptible one," conquering in the struggle, and not being crowned without dust and effort. Already some even prefer the widow to the virgin in respect of continence, since she has despised the pleasure of which she has had experience.

And indeed the divine apostle sets forth a rule of the gnostic through such words, on the one hand writing: "For I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content. I know both how to be abased and how to abound; in everything and in all things I have been initiated, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer want; I can do all things in Him who strengthens me." And on the other hand, discoursing for the rebuke of others, he does not hesitate to say: "Remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great struggle of sufferings—partly being made a spectacle by reproaches and afflictions, and partly becoming sharers with those so treated. For you both suffered together with my bonds, and accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have for yourselves a better and abiding possession. Do not cast away, then, your boldness, which has a great recompense. For you have need of endurance, that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a little while, the coming One shall come and shall not tarry. But my righteous one shall live by faith; and if he draw back, my soul has no pleasure in him. But we are not of those who draw back unto destruction, but of faith unto the gaining of the soul."

Nothing, indeed, is clearer to see than that those who know affirm with confidence about the things they know, while those who merely opine do so about the things they opine—at least so far as concerns affirming without demonstration. They despise one another, then, and laugh at one another; and it comes about that the same intelligence is among some most honoured, and among others convicted of madness. And yet we have learned that pleasure is one thing, which must be assigned to the heathen; that contention is another, which must be allotted to the heresies; that joy is another, which must be made proper to the Church; and that gladness is another, which must be rendered to the gnostic according to the truth. And just as, if a man attend to Ischomachus, he will make him a husbandman, and Lampis a shipmaster, and Charidemus a general, and Simon a horseman, and Perdix a huckster, and Crobylus a cook, and Archelaus a dancer, and Homer a poet, and Pyrrho a wrangler, and Demosthenes an orator, and Chrysippus a logician, and Aristotle a natural philosopher, and Plato a philosopher; so the man who is obedient to the Lord, and has followed the prophecy given through him, is perfectly perfected after the image of his Teacher, a god walking about in the flesh. They fall away, then, from this height who do not follow God wherever he leads; and he leads according to "the God-inspired Scriptures." For though the things men do be ten thousand in number, there are nearly two starting-points of all sin: ignorance and weakness—both of which are in our power, since we neither wish to learn nor again to master desire. And of these, through the one men judge not nobly, and through the other they have not the strength to follow the things rightly judged. For neither would a man, deceived in his judgement, be able to do well, even if he be wholly able to do the things known; nor would one with strength to judge what is fitting show himself blameless in his deeds, being weak in action.

Then he sets before you a swarm of divine examples. "For was it not by faith," he says, "through endurance, that those triumphed who took a trial of mockings and scourgings, and besides of bonds and prison? They were stoned, they were tested, they died by the slaughter of the sword; they went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being in want, afflicted, ill-treated, of whom the world was not worthy, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth. And all these, having been borne witness to through faith, did not receive the promise of God." It remains to understand the word spoken by way of silence: "alone."

Accordingly, two kinds of training are handed down, suited to each of the two sins: to the one, knowledge and the clear demonstration of the testimony from the Scriptures; to the other, the discipline that is according to reason, trained up by faith and fear. And both increase together unto perfect love. For the end of the gnostic, here at least, is, I think, twofold: in some cases the scientific contemplation, in others the action. May it be, then, that these heretics too, having learned from these notes, may be brought to soberness and turn to the almighty God. But if, like "the deaf serpents," they "give no ear to the new-spoken but most ancient song," then at least let them be instructed by God, enduring the fatherly admonitions before the judgement, until, put to shame, they repent—and not, bearing themselves by harsh disobedience into the final judgement, cast themselves there. For there are also certain partial chastisements, which they call punishments, into which many of us, of those of the Lord's people who have come into transgression, slip and fall; but, as children by the teacher or the father, so we are chastised by providence. For God does not take vengeance—since vengeance is a returning of evil for evil—but he chastises for the profit, both in common and in private, of those chastised.

So at any rate he adds: "God having foreseen something better concerning us"—for He was good—"that they should not be made perfect apart from us. Therefore we too, having so great a holy and translucent cloud of witnesses surrounding us, laying aside every weight and the sin that so easily besets us, let us run with endurance the contest set before us, looking to the author and perfecter of faith, Jesus." That, then, he speaks of one salvation in Christ, of the righteous and of us, he has said plainly before; and none the less, speaking of Moses too, he adds: "esteeming the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the recompense. By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured as seeing the Invisible." The divine Wisdom says concerning the martyrs: "They seemed in the eyes of the foolish to have died, and their departure was reckoned an affliction, and their going from us a destruction; but they are in peace. For even if in the sight of men they are punished, their hope is full of immortality."

These things, then, I have set forth, wishing to turn the lovers of learning away from the readiness to fall into the heresies; and longing to make those of the prevailing—whether one must call it ignorance, or stupidity, or ill condition, or whatever it should be named—cease, and trying to win over and to bring to the truth those at least who are not altogether incurable, I have used these arguments. For there are some who do not even endure at the first to hear those who exhort them toward the truth; and indeed they attempt to talk nonsense, pouring out blasphemous words against the truth, conceding to themselves that they know the greatest of beings, though they have not learned, not inquired, not toiled, not found the consistency. These a man might pity, or hate, for such perversity. But if anyone happens to be curable, able to bear, like fire or iron, the frankness of the truth that cuts away and burns out their false opinions, let him hold out the ears of his soul. And this will be, if they do not, hastening to be slothful, thrust away the truth, or, grasping after reputation, force themselves to innovate.
