For they are slothful who, when it is possible to provide from the Scriptures themselves the demonstrations proper to the divine Scriptures, choose instead what comes to hand and joins with their pleasures; and they desire reputation, as many as willingly play the sophist, with other tamperings, against the things akin to the God-inspired words handed down by the blessed apostles and teachers, setting human teachings against the divine tradition for the sake of establishing their heresy. For what argument, in truth, was left over for Marcion, say, or Prodicus and the like, who did not walk the right road, among men so great—I mean according to the knowledge that is of the Church? For they did not surpass in wisdom the men before them, so as to find out something besides the things truly said by those men; rather, it would have been enough for them, if they could but learn the things handed down before.

Then it adds, teaching that martyrdom is a glorious purification: "And having been disciplined a little, they shall be greatly benefited, because God tested them"—that is, He allowed them to be tested, for a proving and for the shaming of the tempter—"and found them worthy of Himself," plainly, to be called sons. "As gold in the furnace He proved them, and as a whole-burnt sacrifice of offering He received them. And in the time of their visitation they shall shine forth, and as sparks in stubble they shall run to and fro. They shall judge nations and have dominion over peoples, and the Lord shall reign over them for ever."

The gnostic alone, then, for us, having grown old in the very Scriptures, preserving the apostolic and ecclesiastical right division of the doctrines, lives most rightly according to the Gospel, finding out, sent back by the Lord to the Law and the prophets, whatever demonstrations he may seek. For the gnostic's life, I think, is nothing else but deeds and words that follow the tradition of the Lord. But "knowledge is not in all." "For I would not have you ignorant, brethren," says the Apostle, "that all were under the cloud, and all partook of spiritual food and drink"—plainly establishing that not all who heard the Word had received the greatness of the knowledge in deed and word. Therefore he added: "But not in all of them was he well pleased." Who is this? The one who said: "Why do you call me Lord, and do not the will of my Father?"—that is, the teaching of the Saviour, which is our spiritual food and a drink that knows no thirst, "the water" of gnostic "life." "Yes," they say, "knowledge is said to puff up." To these we reply: perhaps the knowledge that seems such is said to puff up, if one should take the phrase to mean to be inflated. But if—what is more—the Apostle's voice signifies thinking greatly and truly, then the difficulty is solved; and, following the Scriptures, let us confirm what was said.

"Wisdom," says Solomon, "has puffed up her children." For surely the Lord did not produce conceit in the youths by his teaching, but the being confident upon the truth; and he prepares one to be high-minded in the knowledge handed down through the Scriptures, and to be contemptuous of the things that drag down into sin—which is what the word "puffed up" signifies, namely, that wisdom has implanted greatness of mind in the children who learn, through the things she teaches. Indeed the Apostle says: "And I shall know, not the word of those who are puffed up, but the power"—that is, if you understand the Scriptures high-mindedly (which is to understand them truly, and nothing is greater than truth). For here is the power of the children of wisdom who have been puffed up. As though to say: I shall know whether you justly think greatly of your knowledge. For "known," according to David, "is God in Judaea"—that is, among the Israelites according to recognition. For "Judaea" is interpreted "confession." Reasonably, then, it has been said by the Apostle: "The 'You shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not covet,' and any other commandment, is summed up in this word: You shall love your neighbour as yourself." For one must never, as those who pursue the heresies do, commit adultery against the truth, nor steal the rule of the Church, gratifying one's own desires and loves of glory unto the deceit of one's neighbours—whom, more than anything, while they love us, it befits us to teach to cling to the truth itself. For it has been said plainly: "Declare among the nations his doings," that they may not be judged, but may be converted—those who have heard beforehand. But as many as "deal deceitfully with their tongues," they have their penalties written.

And let the Decalogue, by the way, be set forth for us as an example for gnostic clearness. And that the decad is holy, it is superfluous now to say. And if the tables that were written are a work of God, they will be found showing forth the natural creation; for "the finger of God" is understood as the power of God, by which the creation of heaven and earth is perfected, of both of which the tables are to be understood as symbols. For the writing and shaping of God, laid up in the table, is the creation of the world. And the Decalogue, after a heavenly image, contains sun and moon, stars, clouds, light, wind, water, air, darkness, fire. This is the natural decalogue of heaven. And the image of earth contains men, cattle, creeping things, beasts, and of the things in the water, fishes and sea-monsters; and again, of the winged things likewise, both the flesh-eating and those that use mild food; and of plants likewise the fruit-bearing and the unfruitful. This is the natural decalogue of earth. And the ark that contained these would be the knowledge of things divine and human, and wisdom. And perhaps these two tables might be the prophecy of two covenants.

They were renewed, then, mystically, ignorance and sin at the same time abounding. Twice over, as it seems, the commandments are written for two spirits — the ruling and the subject — since the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. And there is also a certain decad about the man himself: the five senses, and the faculty of speech, and the faculty of generation, and this eighth, the spiritual one in respect of the moulding; the ninth, the ruling part of the soul; and the tenth, the characteristic property of the Holy Spirit that comes through faith. And besides these, the legislation appears to enjoin upon ten parts of man: the sight and the hearing and the smell, the touch and the taste, and the organs that minister to these, being twofold — hands and feet. For this is the moulding of man.

And the soul is brought in besides, and the ruling part is brought in besides, by which we reason, not begotten by the casting down of the seed; so that even without this the number ten is made up, through which the whole working of man is accomplished. For in order man, immediately upon coming to be, takes the beginning of life from the passible parts. The reasoning, then, and ruling part we say is the cause of the constitution of the living creature, and also of the irrational part being ensouled and being a portion of it. For instance, the vital power, in which is contained the nutritive and the growth-giving and, in general, the moving — this the fleshly spirit has obtained, being quick-moving, and going everywhere through the senses and the rest of the body, and feeling first through the body; but the ruling part has the deliberative power, about which are inquiry and learning and knowledge. But the reference of all is ranked into one — the ruling part; and through that man lives and lives in a certain manner.

Through the bodily spirit, then, man perceives, desires, takes pleasure, is angered, is nourished, grows; and indeed too through this he goes to the actions according to thought and reasoning; and when the ruling part masters the desires, it reigns. The "you shall not desire," then, says, "You shall not be a slave to the fleshly spirit, but shall rule over it"; since the flesh lusts against the spirit and rises up to act disorderly, against nature, and the spirit prevails against the flesh, unto the conduct of man according to nature. And was not man, then, with reason said to have come to be after the image of God — not as to the shape of the constitution, but since God by the Word creates all things, and the man who has become gnostic accomplishes the noble deeds by the rational part? With reason, then, the two tables are said to show forth the commandments given to the two spirits — that delivered to the moulded part, and that to the ruling part, before the law — said elsewhere; and the movements of the senses are both stamped in respect of thought and made manifest in respect of the working from the body; for from both is the apprehension.

And again, as sense is to the sensible, so is intellection to the intelligible. And the actions too are twofold — some according to thought, some according to working. And the first commandment of the Decalogue sets forth that there is one only God Almighty, who led the people out of Egypt through the wilderness to the fatherland, that they might apprehend his power, as they were able, through the divine workings, and stand apart from the idolatry of begotten things, having all their hope upon the God who truly is. And the second word showed that one must not take, nor bring, the great might of God (which is the name; for this alone they had room to learn, as still now the many do) — that one must not bring the calling upon it to begotten and vain things, which the craftsmen among men have made, among which the Existent is not ranked; for in unbegotten sameness the Existent is alone, himself only. And the third word is that which shows that the world came to be by God, and that he gave us rest, a seventh day, on account of the suffering in life; for God is unwearied and impassible and unneedy, but we who bear flesh have need of rest.

The seventh day, then, is proclaimed a rest, by abstention from evils preparing the primal day, our true rest — which indeed is the first true birth of light, in which all things are beheld together and all things inherited. From this day the first wisdom and knowledge is shed upon us; for the light of truth is true light, shadowless, the Spirit of the Lord partitioned without partition unto those sanctified through faith, holding the rank of a lamp unto the recognition of the things that are. Following it, then, throughout our whole life, we are made impassible; and this is to be at rest. Wherefore Solomon too says that wisdom came to be before heaven and earth and all the things that are, with the Almighty, the participation in which (the participation according to power, I mean, not according to substance) teaches one to be apprehensively a knower of things divine and human. And being come to this point, these things too must be recalled, by the way, since the discourse came in about the hebdomad and the ogdoad. For the ogdoad runs the risk of being properly the hebdomad, and the hebdomad a hexad, as touching the apparent; and the one is properly the sabbath, but the hebdomad a worker. For the cosmogony is completed in six days, and the movement of the sun from turning to turning is accomplished in six months, in which now the plants shed their leaves, now bud forth, and the seeds come to their perfection.

And they say too that the embryo is completed to exactness in the sixth month — that is, in a hundred and eighty days and two and a half over — as Polybus the physician records in his work On Eight-months' Children, and Aristotle the philosopher in his work On Nature. And the Pythagoreans, hence, I think, from the becoming of the world according to the prophet, hold the number six perfect, and call it "midway-straight," and "marriage," because it is in the middle of the straight number — that is, of the ten and the two; for it appears equidistant from both. And as marriage begets from male and female, so the six is begotten from the odd, three, said to be a male number, and the even, two, held to be female; for twice three is six. So many, again, are the most generic movements, by which all becoming is borne — up, down, to the right, to the left, forward, backward.

With reason, then, they reckon the number seven motherless and childless, interpreting the sabbath and allegorizing the kind of rest, according to which men neither marry nor are given in marriage any longer; for neither, taken from any number to any other, does seven come about, nor, taken to any other, does it produce another of those within the decad. And the ogdoad they call a cube, counting in, with the seven planets, the fixed sphere, through which the great year comes about, as it were a certain period of the recompense of the things promised. For instance, the Lord, having ascended the mountain fourth, becomes sixth, and is surrounded with spiritual light, having laid bare the power from himself, so far as it was possible for those chosen to see to behold it, proclaimed by a seventh, the voice, to be the Son of God — that some might be at rest, persuaded concerning him, and he, through the birth which the hexad showed forth, being the notable letter, might appear an ogdoad, God in a little body showing forth the power, numbered as a man, but hidden as to who he was. For in the order of the numbers the six too is counted in, but the sequence of the letters knows the notable letter that is not written.

Here, according to the numbers themselves, each unit is preserved in its order into the hebdomad and ogdoad; but according to the number of the letters, the zeta becomes sixth, and the eta seventh. But, the notable letter having crept in, I know not how, into the writing, if we follow thus, the hebdomad becomes sixth and the ogdoad seventh. Wherefore too on the sixth man is said to have been made, who, having become faithful to the notable letter, straightway receives the rest of the Lord's inheritance. Such a thing too does the sixth hour of the saving dispensation show forth, in which man was perfected. Yes, and of the eight the middle terms become seven, and of the seven the intervals appear to be six. For that is another account, when the hebdomad glorifies the ogdoad, and "the heavens declare to the heavens the glory of God." The sensible types of these are the vowel letters among us. So too the Lord himself is called Alpha and Omega, beginning and end, "through whom all things came to be, and without whom not one thing came to be." Not, then, as some suppose, has God, by his rest, ceased from making; for, being good, if he should ever cease from doing good, he would cease too from being God — which it is not lawful even to say.

But to have ceased is to have ordered that the order of the things made be preserved inviolably for all time, and that each of the creatures has ceased from the old disorder; for the creations according to the different days had received, by a greatest sequence, as it were the honour from the earlier, all the things made being to have order, created together with the thought, but not being of equal honour. Nor would the becoming of each have been shown by a voice, the creation having been said to be made all at once; for it was needful to name something first too. Wherefore the first things were prophesied, out of which the second, all things together coming to be from one substance by one power; for one, I think, is the will of God in one sameness. And how could the creation come to be in time, when time too came to be along with the things that are? And by now too in hebdomads the whole world is wheeled round, of all the things quickened and that grow.

For seven are the first-born rulers of the angels, who have the greatest power; and seven too the wandering stars, the men of the sciences say, that accomplish the management of the earth, by whom the Chaldeans think, by sympathy, all the things of mortal life come to be — wherefore they promise too to say certain things about the future. And of the fixed stars, seven are the Pleiades, and seven-starred the Bears, by which husbandry and navigation are brought to their end; and the moon takes its changes of figure through seven days. In the first hebdomad, then, it becomes half; in the second, full; in the third, from the waning, again half; and in the fourth it vanishes. But it too, as Seleucus the mathematician records, changes its figure seven times. For out of lightless it becomes crescent, then half, then gibbous and full, and at the waning again gibbous, and likewise half, and crescent.

"With seven-toned lyre we shall sing new hymns," a poet of no mean note writes, teaching too that the old lyre was seven-noted. And seven too are the organs of the senses set about our face — two of the eyes, two of the channels of hearing, two of the nostrils, and the seventh that of the mouth. And that the changes of the ages come about by hebdomads, the elegies of Solon make plain, somewhat thus: "A boy, while still a child, ungrown, having grown the hedge of his teeth, casts the first within seven years; and when God has completed the second seven years, he shows forth the tokens of coming youth; in the third, while his limbs are growing, his chin is downed, his skin changing its bloom; and in the fourth, every man is greatest in strength, which men hold for the tokens of manhood; in the fifth, it is time for a man to be mindful of marriage, and to seek a generation of children thereafter; in the sixth, the mind of a man is fitted in all things, and he no longer wishes to do vain deeds; and in the seventh, he is greatest in mind and tongue, and in the eighth — fourteen years in both; in the ninth, he is still able, but his body and strength are more moderate toward great virtue; and in the tenth, when God has completed seven years, he would not be untimely in having his portion of death."

Again, in diseases the seventh and the fourteenth day are critical, in which nature contends against the causes of disease. And ten thousand such things, hallowing the number, Hermippus of Berytus sets down in his work On the Hebdomad. And plainly the blessed David delivers the mystic discourse about hebdomad and ogdoad to those who know, singing somewhat thus: "Our years were studied as a spider. The days of our years among them are seventy years; but if in strength, eighty years." . . . And that we may be taught the world to be begotten, and not suppose that God makes in time, the prophecy adds: "This is the book of the becoming, and of the things in them, when it came to be; in the day in which God made the heaven and the earth." For the "when it came to be" shows an indefinite and timeless bringing-forth; and the "in the day in which God made" — that is, in and through which he made all things, and without which not one thing came to be — shows the working through the Son, of whom David says, "This is the day which the Lord made; let us be glad and rejoice in it" — that is, let us feast on the divine banquet delivered through the knowledge that is through him. For "day" is called the Word that lights the hidden things, and through whom each of the creatures passed into light and becoming. And in sum the Decalogue, through the letter iota, shows forth the blessed name, setting forth Jesus, who is the Word.

And the fifth word in order is about the honour of father and mother. And it plainly calls God Father and Lord. Wherefore too it proclaims those who have recognized him sons, and gods. The Lord, then, and Father is the Creator of all; and the mother is not, as some hold, the substance out of which we came to be, nor, as others have rendered it, the church, but the divine knowledge and wisdom — as Solomon says, calling wisdom the "mother of the just." And it is to be chosen for its own sake. And all that is noble and august is known from God through the Son. Upon this follows the word about adultery. And it is adultery if one, leaving the ecclesiastical and true knowledge and the grasp concerning God, comes over to a false opinion that is not fitting — either making a god of some begotten thing, or making an idol of some non-existent thing, into a transgression, or rather a going-out of knowledge. And the false opinion is foreign to the gnostic, as the true is his own and his consort.

Wherefore too the noble apostle calls idolatry one of the kinds of fornication, following the prophet who says: "It committed adultery with the wood and the stone; to the wood it said, 'You are my father,' and to the stone, 'You begot me.'" Then the word about murder follows. And murder is a violent taking-away. He, then, who wishes to take away the true word about God and his everlastingness, that he may rank in the falsehood — saying either that the whole is without providence, or that the world is unbegotten, or anything against the sure things of the true teaching . . . is most pernicious. And after this is the word about theft. As, then, he who steals the things of others, greatly doing wrong, with reason falls into the evils he deserves, so he who appropriates to himself the divine works, by the art either of moulding or of painting, and says that he is the maker of the animals and plants — likewise too those who counterfeit the true philosophy — are thieves. And whether one be a husbandman or a father of a child, he is a minister of the casting down of seeds; but God, furnishing the increase and perfecting of all things, brings the things that come to be into the state according to nature.

But the most, together with the philosophers, attribute the increases and turnings to the stars, by the chief account, robbing, as far as in them lies, the Father of all of his unwearied power. And the elements and the stars — that is, the governing powers — were appointed to accomplish the things suited to the dispensation, and they themselves obey and are led by the things set over them, wherever the word of the Lord leads, since the divine power is by nature wont to work all things hiddenly. He, then, who says that he has devised or made something of the things that tend to the creation, shall undergo correction for his impious daring. And the tenth is the word about all desires. As, then, he who desires the things that are not fitting is corrected, in the same way it is not permitted to desire false things, nor to suppose that of the things in becoming the ensouled are able of themselves, while the soulless absolutely are not able, to save or to harm; and if one say that the antidote is not able to heal nor the hemlock to destroy, he is unawares quibbling. For none of these things works without him who uses the herb and the drug, as neither does the axe work without him who cuts, nor the saw without him who saws. As, then, they do not work of themselves, but have certain natural qualities that contribute, by the working of the craftsman, to the proper work, so too by the universal providence of God the effective working is distributed, through the things more immediately moved, by descent, into the particular things.

As, then, knowledge is a state that makes one know, from which the knowing comes about, and the apprehension by it is unwavering by reason, so too ignorance is a yielding impression, changeable by reason; and the changeable, like the thing trained by reason, is in our power. And beside knowledge lie experience and acquaintance, understanding and conception and knowledge. And acquaintance would be a knowledge of universals according to kind; experience a comprehensive knowledge, so as to busy oneself with what each thing is; conception a knowledge of the intelligible; and understanding a knowledge of the comparable, or an unwavering comparison, or a comparative power of the things of which prudence and knowledge are — both of one and of each and of all the things that come into one account; and knowledge a science of the being itself, or a science in harmony with the things that come to be; and truth a knowledge of the true, and the state of the truth a knowledge of true things.

And knowledge is constituted through reason and is unwavering by another reason. The things we do not do, we either do not do through not being able, or through not wishing, or through both. We do not fly, then, since we neither can nor wish; and we do not, say, swim just now, since we can but do not wish; and we are not as the Lord, since we wish but cannot. For "no disciple is above the teacher; and it is enough if we become as the teacher" — not in essence, for it is impossible for what is so by position to be equal in existence to what is so by nature, but in having become eternal, and in having known the contemplation of the things that are, and in being called sons, and in beholding the Father from the things proper to himself alone. To will, then, leads before all things; for the rational powers are by nature ministers of willing. "Will," it says, "and you will be able." And of the gnostic, the will and the judgment and the exercise are the same. For if the purposes are the same, the doctrines too and the judgments are the same, so that his words and his life and his manner are in keeping with his stand. "And an upright heart seeks out knowledge" and attends to those things. "God has taught me wisdom, and I have known the knowledge of holy things."

Yes, they say, it is written: "All who came before the coming of the Lord are thieves and robbers." Now all who are in the Word — those, that is, before the incarnation of the Word — are understood more generally. But the prophets, sent and inspired by the Lord, are not thieves, but servants. So the Scripture says: "Wisdom sent her own servants, summoning with high proclamation to the bowl of wine." But philosophy was not sent by the Lord; rather, it came, it says, stolen, or given by a thief. So some power or angel, having learned something of the truth and not having remained in it, inspired and taught these things, having stolen them — not without the Lord's knowledge, who both knows the ends of things to be before the foundation of the world, and that each thing should be, but having not prevented it. For the theft, coming then to men, had a certain benefit, not because the thief looked to what was advantageous, but because providence guided the outcome of his daring toward what was advantageous.

I know that many continually fasten upon us and say that what does not prevent is a cause; for they say that the cause of a theft is the man who did not guard against it, or did not prevent it — as the cause of a fire is the man who did not quench the danger at its beginning, and of a shipwreck the pilot who did not take in the sail. So indeed those responsible for such things are punished by the law; for to the man who had the power to prevent is also attached the cause of what happens. We say, then, to them, that the cause is conceived as residing in doing and acting and effecting, but that what does not prevent is, in this respect, inactive. Further, the cause is bound up with the activity — as the shipwright with the building of the ship, the builder with the building of the house — but what does not prevent is separated from what comes to be. For this very reason it is accomplished, that the one who could prevent does not act, nor prevent. For what does the man who does not prevent effect? Indeed, the argument leads them into absurdity, if of the wound they will blame, not the arrow, but the shield that did not prevent the arrow from passing through; for so they would blame, not the thief, but the man who did not prevent the theft.

So let them say that it was not Hector who burned the ships of the Greeks, but Achilles, because, being able to prevent Hector, he did not prevent him. Yet Achilles, through wrath (and it was in his power both to be wrathful and not), did not keep off the fire, and perhaps was a joint cause; but the devil, being self-determining, was able both to repent and to steal, and is himself the cause of the theft, not the Lord who did not prevent it. But neither was the gift harmful, that the prevention should be passed over. And if we must speak exactly to them, let them know that what does not prevent — which we say happened in the case of the theft — is not at all a cause; but that what does prevent is liable to the charge of being a cause. For the man who holds his shield before another is the cause to the one shielded of his not being wounded, by preventing his being wounded; and to Socrates the divine sign was a cause not by not preventing, but by turning away, even if it did not urge on. Neither praises nor blames, neither honours nor punishments, are just, if the soul does not have the power of impulse and of holding back.

But since vice is involuntary, the man who prevents is a cause, while the man who does not prevent judges the soul's choice justly — that, most of all, God may remain to us not the cause of vice. And since moral choice and impulse begin the sins, and a mistaken assumption sometimes prevails — an assumption that is ignorance and lack of learning, from which we make light of departing — he would rightly punish. (For a fever too is involuntary; but when a man falls into fever through himself and through intemperance, we blame him.) And vice is involuntary; for no one chooses evil as evil, but, carried away by the pleasure that attends it, supposing it good, he thinks it something to be grasped. This being so, to be freed from ignorance and from the base and delightful choice, and, before these things, not to assent to those deceitful impressions, lies in our power. And the devil is called a robber and a thief, having mingled false prophets among the prophets, as tares among the wheat. "All, then, who came before the Lord are thieves and robbers" — not simply all men, but all the false prophets, and all who were not properly sent by him.

The false prophets too had the theft, the prophetic name, being prophets, but of the liar. For the Lord says: "You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a man-slayer from the beginning, and has not stood in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks the lie, he speaks of his own, because he is a liar and the father of it." And among their falsehoods the false prophets spoke some true things, and indeed these prophesied in ecstasy, as servants of the apostate. And the Shepherd too, the angel of repentance, says to Hermas concerning the false prophet: "For he speaks some true words; for the devil fills him with his own spirit, to see whether he can break any of the righteous." All things, then, are ordered from above for good, "that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known," according to the foreknowledge of the ages, "which he wrought in Christ." And to God nothing is opposed, nor does anything stand against him, since he is Lord and Almighty.

But the counsels and activities of those who have apostatized, being partial, arise indeed from an evil disposition, like the diseases of the body; yet they are steered by the universal providence to a wholesome end, even though the cause be disease-producing. The greatest work of the divine providence, indeed, is not to let the vice that has sprung from a voluntary apostasy remain useless and unprofitable, nor to let it become in every respect harmful. For it is the work of the divine wisdom and virtue and power not only to do good (for this is, so to speak, the nature of God, as of fire to heat and of light to give light), but especially this too: through the evils devised by certain ones to bring about some good and wholesome end, and to use to advantage the things that seem base — as the witness of martyrdom, which comes from temptation.

There is, then, even in philosophy — stolen, as it were, by Prometheus — a little fire, usefully rekindled to a light fit for its purpose: a certain trace of wisdom and a movement toward God. In this way the philosophers among the Greeks would be thieves and robbers, having, before the coming of the Lord, taken parts of the truth from the Hebrew prophets, not with full knowledge, but appropriating them as their own doctrines, and falsifying some, and, through over-curiosity, ignorantly sophisticating others, and even finding out some. For perhaps they too had a spirit of perception. And Aristotle agreed with the Scripture, calling sophistic a thievery of wisdom, as we have indicated before. But the Apostle says: "Which we also speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit." For concerning the prophets he says: "We all received of his fullness" — meaning, of course, of Christ. So the prophets are not thieves. And "My teaching is not mine," says the Lord, "but his who sent me, the Father." But concerning the thieves: "He who speaks of himself," he says, "seeks his own glory." Such are the Greeks: lovers of self and boasters. And the Scripture, calling them "wise," does not slander the truly wise, but those reputed wise.

But if generation is evil, then let the blasphemers say that the Lord, who partook of generation, is in evil, and that the virgin who bore Him is in evil. Alas for these evils! They blaspheme the will of God and the mystery of the creation by slandering generation. For these reasons there is Docetism for Cassianus; for these reasons there is also, for Marcion, and yes, for Valentinus too, the "psychic body"; because they say: "Man was made like the beasts when he came to copulation." But it is when a man, truly enraged, wishes to mount another's bed, that such a one is then made bestial in truth: "They became horses mad for the female; each neighed after his neighbour's wife." And even if the serpent took the practice of intercourse from the irrational animals and persuaded Adam to consent to the union with Eve as a matter of chance—as though the first-formed had not used this by nature, as some claim—still the creation is again blasphemed, as having made men weaker than the nature of the irrational creatures, whom the first-formed of God followed.

But if nature led them, as it leads the irrational creatures too, to the begetting of children, yet they were moved sooner than was fitting, being still young, led astray by deceit—then the judgement of God is just upon those who did not await His will, but generation is holy, through which the world is established, through which the substances are, through which the natures, through which the angels, through which the powers, through which the souls, through which the commandments, through which the law, through which the gospel, through which the knowledge of God. "And all flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass; and the grass withers and the flower falls; but the word of the Lord abides"—the word that anointed the soul and united it with the Spirit. And how, without the body, would the dispensation according to the Church among us reach its completion?—seeing that He Himself, the Head of the Church, came indeed in the flesh, but formless and without comely shape, teaching us to look toward the formless and incorporeal nature of the divine cause. "For a tree of life," says the prophet, "comes to be in good desire," teaching that the desires that are in the living Lord are noble and pure.

But further they wish that the intercourse of husband with wife in marriage, called "knowing," should be a sin; for this, they say, is indicated by the eating of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the figure "knew" teaching the transgression of the commandment. But if this is so, then the knowledge of the truth too is an eating of the tree of life. It is possible, then, for prudent marriage to partake of that tree as well; and it has been said before by us that marriage can be used both well and badly, and this is the tree of knowledge—if we do not transgress the law of marriage. What? Did not the Saviour heal the body of its passions just as He healed the soul? But He would not, if the flesh were the enemy of the soul, have fortified it against the soul by restoring it to health. "But this I say, brothers, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption"; for sin, being corruption, cannot have communion with incorruption, which is righteousness. "Are you so foolish?" he says; "having begun in the spirit, are you now being perfected in the flesh?"

Yes, and in the epistle to the Corinthians the apostle Clement too, himself sketching for us a kind of pattern of the gnostic, says: "For who that has sojourned among you has not proved your all-virtuous and steadfast faith? And has not marvelled at your prudent and gentle piety in Christ? And has not proclaimed the magnificent character of your hospitality? And has not counted blessed your perfect and secure knowledge? For you did all things without respect of persons, and walked in the ordinances of God," and so on. Then more plainly: "Let us fix our eyes, then, on those who perfectly served His magnificent glory. Let us take Enoch, who, being found righteous in obedience, was translated; and Noah, who, having believed, was saved; and Abraham, who, for faith and hospitality, was called the friend of God and the father of Isaac. For hospitality and piety Lot was saved from Sodom; for faith and hospitality Rahab the harlot was saved; for endurance and faith, in goatskins and sheepskins and woven camel's hair, they went about, proclaiming the kingdom of Christ—I mean Elijah and Elisha, Ezekiel and John, the prophets."

For indeed Abraham, called the friend of God on account of his free faith, was not lifted up by the glory, but, moderating his feeling, said: "But I am earth and ashes." And concerning Job it is thus written: "Job was righteous and blameless, true and god-fearing, abstaining from every evil." This is the man who conquered the tempter through endurance and bore witness, and was at the same time borne witness to by God; he holds to humility and says: "No one is clean from filth, not even if his life be one day." Moses, the faithful servant in his whole house, said to the one who spoke from the bush: "Who am I, that you send me? But I am of feeble voice and slow of tongue"—to minister the voice of the Lord through a human tongue. And again: "But I am a vapour from a pot." For "God sets Himself against the proud, but gives grace to the humble."

Those, then, who touch upon impious words, and who lead others on as well, not using the divine words well but with error, neither enter themselves into the kingdom of heaven, nor allow those whom they have deceived to attain the truth. But, not having the key of the entrance themselves, but a false one, and, as the common phrase is, a counterfeit key—through which they do not throw open the outer court, as we enter through the tradition of the Lord, but, having cut a side-door and dug secretly through the little wall of the Church, overstepping the truth—they set themselves up as initiators of the soul of the impious. For that they made these human gatherings later than the Catholic Church there is no need of many words. For the teaching of the Lord at his coming, beginning from Augustus and Tiberius Caesar, is completed in the middle of the times of Augustus; and that of his apostles, down to the ministry of Paul, is completed under Nero; while it was lower down, about the times of Hadrian the king, that those who devised the heresies arose, and they continued down to the age of Antoninus the elder—such as Basilides, even though he inscribes Glaucias as his teacher, the interpreter of Peter (as they themselves boast). Likewise they say that Valentinus heard Theudas; and this man had been an acquaintance of Paul.

Yes, and David too, concerning whom the Lord says, bearing witness: "I found a man after my own heart, David the son of Jesse; with holy oil I anointed him." But he too says to God: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my transgression. Wash me more thoroughly from my lawlessness, and cleanse me from my sin; for my lawlessness I acknowledge, and my sin is ever before me." Then, hinting at the sin that does not fall under the law, in gnostic moderation of feeling he adds: "Against you only have I sinned, and done the evil before you." For the Scripture somewhere says: "The spirit of the Lord is a lamp, searching the chambers of the belly." And the more a man, doing righteously, becomes gnostic, the more closely is the luminous Spirit present to him. So the Lord draws near to the righteous, and none of the thoughts and reasonings that we make escapes Him—I mean the Lord Jesus, who, by the will of the Almighty, is the overseer of our heart, whose blood was sanctified for us.

For Marcion, being of the same age as these, associated with younger men as an old man with juniors; and after him Simon, for a little while, gave ear to Peter when he was preaching. These things being so, it is plain that, in comparison with the most ancient and most true Church, these later heresies, and those still later in time, were newly coined and adulterated. From what has been said, then, it is, I think, manifest that the true Church is one—the one that is truly ancient—into which are enrolled those who are just according to purpose. For there being one God and one Lord, on this account too that which is supremely honourable is praised in respect of its being alone, as being an imitation of the one Beginning. The one Church, then, is allotted to the nature of the One—the Church which they force to cut up into many heresies. Both in substance, then, and in conception, and in beginning, and in pre-eminence, we say that the ancient and Catholic Church is alone—gathering, "into the unity of one faith," that which is according to the proper covenants, or rather according to the one covenant in different times, by the will of one God through one Lord, those already ordained—whom God foreordained, having known before the foundation of the world that they would be just. But also the pre-eminence of the Church, just as the beginning of its constitution, is according to the Monad, surpassing all other things and having nothing like or equal to itself.

Let us, then, reverence those who lead us and respect them; let us honour the presbyters; let us educate the young in the education of God. For blessed is he who teaches and does the things of the Lord according to worth; and he is of a high-minded mind and contemplative of the truth. "Let us set right our women toward the good. Let them display the lovely character of purity," he says; "let them show forth the sincere will of their meekness; let them make manifest, through their silence, the gentleness of their tongue; let them give their love not according to partialities, but holily and equally to all who fear God. Let our children share in the education that is in Christ; let them learn what humility avails before God, what pure love can do before God, how the fear of the Lord is good and great, saving all who conduct themselves holily in it with a pure heart." For He is a searcher of thoughts and reflections, whose breath is in us, and when He wills, He will take it away.

These things, then, also for later. But of the heresies, some are named from a name, like that from Valentinus and Marcion and Basilides—even though they boast of bringing forward the opinion of Matthias; for the teaching of all the apostles was one, just as the tradition was also one. Others are named from a place, like the Peratici; others from a nation, like that of the Phrygians; others from an activity, like that of the Encratites; others from peculiar doctrines, like that of the Docetae and that of the Haematites; others from suppositions and from the men they have honoured, like the Cainists and those called Ophites; and others from the lawless things they practised and dared, like those of the Simonians who are called Entychites.

And all these things the faith in Christ confirms. "Come, children," says the Lord, "hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man that wills life, that loves to see good days?" Then He adds the gnostic mystery of the hebdomad and the ogdoad: "Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit; turn aside from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it." For through these things He hints at knowledge, teaching that one is perfected both by abstinence from evils and by the activity of good, in deed and in word. "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears toward their petition; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth."

"The righteous cried, and the Lord heard him, and delivered him out of all his afflictions." "For many are the scourges of sinners, but mercy shall encircle those who hope in the Lord." He says that the one who genuinely hopes is encompassed by a multitude of mercy. For in the epistle to the Corinthians it is written: "Through Jesus Christ our foolish and darkened mind springs up anew into the light. Through Him the Master willed that we should taste of the immortal knowledge." And, displaying more expressly the property of knowledge, he added: "Since, then, these things are plain to us, and we have peered into the depths of the divine knowledge, we ought to do all things in order, all that the Master commanded us to accomplish at appointed times. Let the wise man, then, display his wisdom not in words only, but in good works; let the humble-minded bear witness not to himself, but let him allow himself to be witnessed to by another; let the man pure in the flesh not boast, knowing that it is another who supplies him his continence. Consider, brothers, that by however much more knowledge we have been deemed worthy, by so much the more are we exposed to danger."

But, as it seems, the philosophers of the Greeks, naming God, do not know him, since they do not worship God as God. And the things they philosophize among themselves, according to Empedocles, "having passed through the tongue of many mouths in vain, are poured out, since they saw little of the whole." For as the light from the sun is by art conducted, through a glass vessel full of water, into fire, so too philosophy, having taken the spark from the divine Scripture, is faintly seen among a few. Yes, and as all living creatures breathe the same air, but some in one way, some in another, and to a different end, so too the more part pursue the truth — or rather the discourse about the truth. For they say nothing about God, but, referring their own passions to God, expound them. For their life has become a seeking of the plausible, not of the true; and truth is not taught from imitation, but from learning. For it is not that we may seem to be good that we believe in Christ — just as neither do we pass into the sun for the sake of merely appearing, being in the sun, but here for the sake of being warmed; but there, for the sake of being noble and good, we force our way to be Christians, since most of all the kingdom is of those who force their way, who, out of inquiry and learning and perfect joint training, reap the becoming a king.

He, then, who imitates the seeming, beguiles the preconception too. But when one, having taken a kindling of a matter, kindles this within in the soul by longing and learning, he sets all things in motion thereupon, to come to the recognition of it. For what one does not lay hold of, neither does he long for, nor embrace the benefit from it. The gnostic, then, afterward, at the end of his right-doings, imitates the Lord, so far as is attainable by men, having taken a certain Lordly quality unto the likeness of God. But those who do not know knowledge are not able even to canon out the truth. To partake, then, of the gnostic theorems is not possible, unless we empty ourselves of the former thoughts. For simply thus truth is said commonly of everything of mind and of sense. For instance, it is possible to behold the truth of painting too, as against the vulgar, and the dignity of music as against the wanton. And of philosophy too, then, there is a certain truth as against the other philosophers, and a true beauty as against the adulterated. We must not, then, busy ourselves about the partial truths, of which the truth is predicated, but about the truth itself, not seeking to learn names; for the matter of God is not one, but ten thousand; and it makes a difference to seek God or the things about God. And, to speak generally, about each thing one must distinguish the substance from the accidents.

And it is enough for me to say that the Lord is God of all. And I say "of all" downright, with nothing left over by way of exception. Since, then, there are two kinds of truth — the names and the things — some speak of the names, those who busy themselves about the beauties of words, the philosophers among the Greeks; but the things are with us, the barbarians. For instance, the Lord did not without cause will to use a lowly form of body, that no one, praising the comeliness and marvelling at the beauty, should stand apart from the things said, and, cleaving to the things left behind, be cut off from the things of mind. We must not, then, dwell upon the phrasing, but upon the things signified. To those, then, who lay hold of the phrasing, and are not moved toward knowledge, the word is not believed; since the crows too imitate human voices, having no conception of the thing they say; but intellectual apprehension holds of faith. So too Homer said "father of men and of gods," not knowing who the Father is and how the Father.

And as to him who has hands belongs by nature the taking, and to him who has sound eyes the seeing of light, so to him who has received faith it is proper by nature to partake of knowledge, if he would work in besides and build up besides gold, silver, precious stones upon the foundation laid down. He does not, then, promise to be willing to partake, but begins; nor to be about to, but it is fitting for him to be kingly and luminous and gnostic, and not in name, but in deed, to be willing to lay hold of the things. For God, being good through the ruling part of all creation, willing this to be saved, turned to making the rest too, furnishing them from the beginning this first benefaction — the coming to be; for that being is much better than not being, everyone would confess. Then, as it was possible for each to have of nature, it came to be, and comes to be, advancing toward its own better.

So that it is not absurd that philosophy too was given by the divine providence, preparatory to the perfecting that is through Christ — unless philosophy be ashamed, being disciple to the barbarian knowledge, to advance toward truth. But "the hairs are numbered," and the small movements; and how is philosophy not in the account? And yet to Samson too the power was given in his hairs, that he might understand that the rejected arts of life — those that lie and remain on the ground after the soul's departure — were not given without the divine power. For instance, it says, "providence from above, from the leading things as from a head, pervades all, as the ointment," it says, "that comes down upon the beard of Aaron and upon the hem of his garment" (that is, of the great high priest, "through whom all things came to be, and without him not one thing came to be") — not into the adorning of the body, but, outside the people, philosophy, like a garment.

The philosophers, then, who have trained themselves toward their own perceiving by a perceptive spirit, when they busy themselves, not with a part of philosophy, but with philosophy itself absolutely, truth-lovingly and without conceit bearing witness to the truth, even among the heterodox in the things well said, advance toward understanding, according to the divine governance, the unspeakable goodness that on every occasion leads the nature of the things that are toward the better, as far as may be; and then, having associated not only with Greeks but also with barbarians, they are led, from common joint training, to a private understanding, unto the faith; and having received the foundation of the truth, they take besides power to go forward to inquiry, and thence, having become disciples, they love, and craving knowledge, they hasten toward salvation. So the Scripture says that "a spirit of perception was given to the craftsmen by God"; and this is nothing but prudence, a contemplative power of the soul concerning the things that are, discerning the consequent, the like and the unlike, and again composing and commanding and forbidding, and conjecturing the things to come. And it stretches not only to the arts, but to philosophy itself.

Why, then, is the serpent too called prudent? Because even in evil-doings one may find a certain sequence and discernment and composition and conjecture of the things to come. And the most of wrongs escape notice for this reason, that the wicked make their dispositions beforehand for themselves, to escape the punishments wholly and in every way. And prudence, being of many parts, stretched through the whole world and through all human affairs, changes its name in each of them: and when it applies to the first causes, it is called intellection; when it confirms this by demonstrative reasoning, it is named knowledge and wisdom and science; and when it comes to be in the things that tend to godliness, and, without contemplation, receives the ruling word, in respect of the keeping of the working in it, it is called faith; and in the things of sense, having made sure of what seems, as among these, most true, it is right opinion; and again in the actions with handiwork, it is art; and where, without contemplation of the first causes, by keeping of the like and by transition it makes a certain impulse and constitution, it is called experience. And that is the proper and truly authoritative and ruling thing, which over and above all the believer takes, after the sure faith, the holy Spirit, by oversight.

Philosophy, then, having partaken of a more excellent perception, as has been shown from the foregoing, partakes of prudence. For instance, the rational going-through of the things thought, with choice and assent, is called dialectic, confirmatory of the things said about truth by demonstration, and beating off the difficulties brought against it. Those, then, run a risk who say that philosophy did not come here from God, of saying that it is impossible for God to know all the particular things, nor to be the cause of all noble things, even though each of the particulars chance to be one of them. For nothing of the things that are could have stood from the beginning, God being unwilling; but if of his will, then philosophy is from God, he having willed it to be such as it is, on account of those who will not abstain from evils except thus. For God knows all things, not only the things that are, but also the things that shall be, and how each shall be; and foreseeing the particular movements, he beholds all things and hears all things, seeing the soul bare within, and holds the thought of each of the particulars through eternity; and that which happens in the theatres, and in the parts of each man, by inlooking and surveying and joint-looking, this happens in the case of God. For he beholds all things at once, and each in part, by one application — yet not all in respect of the leading attention.

By now, then, many of the things in life take their becoming through some human reasoning too, having received the spark from God. For instance, health through medicine, and good condition through the trainer's art, and wealth through money-getting, take becoming and presence according to the divine providence, but with human co-working. And understanding too is from God. For instance, the free choice of good men chiefly obeys the will of God; wherefore many of the advantages are common to good and to evil men, but become profitable only to the good and earnest, for whose sake God made them; for to the use of good men the power of the God-given things is by nature. But the thoughts too of virtuous men come about by divine inbreathing, the soul being somehow disposed, and the divine will being distributed into the human souls, the particular divine ministers contributing to such services. For the protectorships of the angels are distributed by nations and cities, and perhaps too certain are assigned to some of the particular men.

The shepherd, at any rate, cares too for each of the sheep; and his oversight is most immediate to those who are eminent in their natures and able to help the multitudes. And these are the leading and educative men, through whom the working of providence is most plainly shown, whenever, either through education or through some rule and management, God wills to do good to men. And he wills it always; wherefore he stirs the fit to the profitable working-out of the things that tend toward virtue and peace and beneficence. And every virtuous thing is both from virtue and is referred to virtue, and either is given toward the becoming earnest, or, in those who are so, toward the using of the advantages according to nature; for it co-works both in the things universal and in the particular.

How, then, is it not absurd, attributing disorder and injustice to the devil, to make him the giver of a virtuous thing, philosophy? For he runs the risk of having become more kindly to the Greeks, toward the becoming of good men, than the divine providence and purpose. But, on the contrary, I think, it is proper to law and to all right reason to render to each what is fitting and proper and what falls to him. For as the lyre belongs to the lyre-player alone, and the flute to the flute-player, so the advantages are possessions of good men; and as it is the nature of the good-doer to do good, as of fire to warm and of light to give light, an evil thing the good man would not do, as neither would light darken nor fire chill. So, on the contrary, evil would not do anything virtuous; for its working is to do evil, as it is of darkness to confound the sight. Not, then, is philosophy a work of evil, since it makes men virtuous. It remains, then, that it is of God, whose work alone is to do good; and all things that are given by God are nobly both given and received. Yes, and the use of philosophy is not of evil men; but if it has been given to the best of the Greeks, plainly whence it has been bestowed — from the providence that renders to each what is fitting according to worth. With reason, then, to the Jews the law, to the Greeks philosophy, until the coming; and from then the universal calling, gathering into a peculiar people of righteousness, according to the teaching that is by faith, through the one Lord, the only one God of both, of Greeks and of barbarians, or rather of the whole race of men.

We have often said that we call philosophy the attaining, according to philosophy, of the truth, even though it chance to be partial; and now the goods in the arts too, as in arts, have their beginning from God. For as the doing of anything by art is comprehended in the theorems of the art, so the doing of anything prudently is ranked under prudence; and prudence is a virtue; and it is proper to it to know the other things, and much more, first, the things concerning itself. And wisdom, being a power, is nothing else than the science of things divine and human good things. And "the Lord's is the earth and the fulness thereof." The Scripture, teaching that good things come to men from God, has said it by a divine power and might, the distribution coming down unto human help. For instance, there are three modes of all benefit and imparting to another from another: the one according to accompaniment, as the trainer shapes the boy; another according to likeness, as he who exhorts another to advance by advancing first, and the one co-works with the learner, the other co-benefits the receiver. And a third mode is that according to command, when the trainer, no longer moulding the learner nor showing through himself the wrestling-feat for imitation by the boy, as one now more practised, commands him the wrestling-feat by name.

The gnostic, then, having received from God the being able to help, profits some by shaping them by accompaniment, some by exhorting them by likeness, some by educating and teaching them by command. And indeed he himself too is benefited by the like things from the Lord. So, then, the benefit reaching to men from God becomes known, the angels co-exhorting; for through angels too the divine power furnishes good things, whether seen or unseen. Such too is the mode according to the manifestation of the Lord. And at times too, according to the thoughts of men and their reasonings, the power inbreathes something and sets in their hearts strength and a more exact perception, furnishing might and the boldness of eagerness toward the inquiries and toward the works. And there lie set out for us, for imitation and likeness, truly marvellous and holy examples of virtue, through the recorded deeds. And indeed too the mode of command is most manifest, both through the Lord's covenants and through the laws among the Greeks, and through the things enjoined according to philosophy. And, in a word, all benefit unto life, according to the highest account, is accomplished by God the Almighty, the Father who guides all, through the Son — who for this reason too is "the Saviour of all men," says the apostle, "but most of all of the faithful" — and according to the immediate, by those immediate to each, according to the command and enjoining of the one immediate to the first cause, the Lord.

Plain, then, are all the other virtues too, recorded in Moses, that furnished to the Greeks the beginning of the whole ethical sphere — I mean courage and temperance and prudence and justice, and steadfastness and endurance, and gravity and self-control, and the reverence that is upon these. But reverence is plain to everyone, teaching to reverence and honour the highest and most ancient cause. And the law itself presents justice, educating prudence both through the abstinence from the idols of sense and through the allotment to the Maker and Father of the universe, from which opinion, as from a spring, all understanding grows.

"For the sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of those who walk straight are acceptable with him." Since such too are the things in Isaiah: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?" says the Lord, and the whole passage. "Loose every bond of injustice"; "for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a contrite heart that seeks its Maker." "Deceitful balances are an abomination before God, but a just weight is acceptable to him." From this Pythagoras advises not to step over the balance. And the profession of the heresies is called a deceitful justice; and "the tongue of the unjust will be utterly destroyed, but the mouth of the just distils wisdom." Yet they call the wise and prudent base. But it would be a long matter to set out testimonies concerning these virtues, since all the Scripture hymns them. Since, then, they define courage as the knowledge of things terrible and not terrible and the things between, and temperance as a state preserving, in choice and avoidance, the judgments of prudence, there lie beside courage both endurance, which they call steadfastness, a knowledge of things to be abided in and not to be abided in, and magnanimity, a knowledge that rises above the things that befall; and beside temperance lies caution, being an avoidance with reason.

And the keeping of the commandments, being a harmless observance of them, is the gaining of safety in life. And it is not possible to be steadfast without courage, nor self-controlled without temperance. And the virtues follow one another reciprocally; and in whom are the sequences of the virtues, in him is also salvation, being the keeping of the good condition. With reason, then, having further treated of these virtues, we would have considered all of them, since he who has one virtue gnostically has all through the reciprocal following. So self-control is a disposition not to be overstepped of the things that appear according to right reason. And he is self-controlled who holds back the impulses that are against right reason, or who holds himself so as not to be impelled against right reason. And this temperance is not without courage, since it comes about from the commandments, following upon what is ordained . . . by God — prudence and the justice that imitates the divine disposition, according to which, being self-controlled, we are arrayed, pure, toward reverence and the action that consequently follows God, being made like to the Lord so far as is possible for us who are by nature perishable.

And this is to become just and holy with prudence. For the divine is without need and impassible; whence it is not, properly speaking, self-controlled, for it never falls under passion, that it should master it. But our nature, being passionate, needs self-control, through which, being trained toward the condition of small need, it tries to draw near in disposition to the divine nature. For the earnest man is of small need, on the borderland of immortal and mortal nature, having neediness both through the body and through generation itself, but having been taught to need few things through rational self-control. For what reason has it that the law forbids a man to put on the covering of a woman? Or does it not wish us to be manly, made effeminate neither in body and works nor in thought and reason? For it wishes the man who is at leisure for truth to be made masculine in endurances and steadfastnesses, in life and manner and reason and exercise, by night and by day, and, if there should overtake him the need of a martyrdom that goes through blood.

Again, if anyone, it says, having lately built a house, has not had time to dwell in it, or, having worked a newly-planted vineyard, has not yet partaken of the fruit, or, having betrothed a virgin, has not yet married her, the law that loves mankind orders these to be released from the campaign — in a generalship-like way, that we may not, distracted toward our desires, serve the war unwillingly (for those are free in their impulses who, without pretext, strip for the dangers); and in a way that loves mankind, since the things of wars are uncertain, having reckoned it unjust that the one should not enjoy his own labours, while another should take, without toil, the things of those who have laboured.

And the law seems also to show forth the courage of the soul, legislating that the planter should enjoy the fruit, and the builder should dwell, and the betrothed should marry; for it will not make the hopes incomplete to those who have exercised themselves according to the gnostic reason. For of a good man, dead or living, the hope does not perish. "I," it says, "love those who love me," wisdom says; "and those who seek me will find peace," and the rest. And what? Did not the women of the Midianites, warring against the Hebrews by their own beauty, bring them out of temperance, through incontinence, into godlessness? For, having made them their companions out of the grave exercise into harlot-pleasures, and lured them by beauty, they drove them mad toward the sacrifices of the idols and toward foreign women; and, overcome at once by women and by pleasure, they departed both from God and from the law; and well-nigh the whole people had become subject to the enemy by a woman's stratagem, until fear, admonishing, reined them in as they were in danger.

So those who were left, taking up, in love of danger, the contest for reverence, became masters of the enemy. "The beginning of wisdom, then, is the reverence of God, and the understanding of holy things is forethought, and to know the law belongs to a good understanding." Those, then, who supposed the law to be productive of a passionate fear neither understood as good men nor truly conceived the law. "For the fear of the Lord makes life. But the wanderer will be pained in toils which knowledge does not inspect." Indeed, mystically, Barnabas: "But God, who is Lord of the whole world," he says, "may he give to you too wisdom and understanding, science, knowledge of his ordinances, endurance. Become, then, taught of God, seeking out what the Lord seeks from you, that you may find it in the day of judgment." Those who attain these things he called gnostically children of love and of peace. And concerning sharing and fellowship, there being many discourses, it is enough to say only this: that the law forbids lending to a brother (calling "brother" not only one sprung from the same parents, but anyone who is of the same nation and of like mind and has shared the same reason), thinking it not just to exact interest on money, but to give to those in need with open hands and judgments. For God is the Creator of such a grace; and indeed the man who shares receives notable interest too — the most precious things among men: gentleness, kindness, magnanimity, good report, good fame.

Does not this precept seem to you to be of love for mankind, as does that one too — to pay the wage of the poor man the same day? It teaches that the wage for services must be paid without delay; for the eagerness of the poor man, who has gone without food, is paralyzed, I think, toward the morrow. Again, it says, let not the creditor stand at the door of the debtor's house, to take a pledge by force, but let the one bid the pledge be brought outside, and let the one who has it not refuse. And in the harvest it forbids the owners to gather up the sheaves that fall, just as in the reaping it advises that something be left uncut, by this very well training the owners toward fellowship and magnanimity, through letting go some of their own to those in need, and furnishing to the poor an occasion of nourishment.

You see how the legislation announces at once the justice and the goodness of God, who supplies the nourishment to all ungrudgingly? And again, in the vintage, it has forbidden going over again to gather the things left, and to collect the grapes that fall; and the same things it ordains for those who gather olives. Indeed, the tithes too of both the fruits and the flocks taught reverence toward the divine, and not to be wholly lovers of gain, but to share love of mankind with the neighbours too. For from these first-fruits, I think, the priests too were nourished. Do we now understand that we are educated by the law toward reverence and toward fellowship and toward justice and toward love of mankind? Is it not so? Does it not, through the seventh year, command the land to be left idle, and bid the poor freely use the fruits that grow up according to God, nature farming for those who wish? How, then, is the law not good and a teacher of justice? And again, in the fiftieth year, it commands the same things to be accomplished as in the seventh, restoring to each his own, if anyone in the meantime, through some circumstance, was deprived of a plot — limiting the desire of those who long to acquire by a measured time of enjoyment, and having mercy on those who paid the penalty of long poverty and were punished through life. "Alms and faiths are kingly safeguards, and a blessing is upon the head of him who shares"; and "he who has mercy on the poor will be blessed," because he shows love toward his like, through the love toward the Creator of the race of men.

The aforesaid things have also other, more natural interpretations, concerning rest and the receiving back of the inheritance, but they are not to be told at present. And love is conceived in many ways: through gentleness, through kindness, through endurance, through ungrudgingness and freedom from jealousy, through freedom from hatred, through freedom from remembering wrongs. It is undivided in all things, undiscriminating, social. Again, if you see, it says, the beast of burden of your kindred or friends, or in general of men whom you know, wandering in the desert, lead it away and restore it. And if the master happens to be far off, keep it safe with your own until he recovers it, and restore it. Through natural fellowship it teaches to reckon the find as a deposit, and not to remember wrongs against the enemy.

"And of these," it says, "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will set aside." So the Apostle adds: "Where is the wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputer of this age?" — setting, in contrast to the scribes, the seekers of this age, that is, the philosophers from among the nations. "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?" — the same as to say he showed it to be foolish and not true, as they supposed. And if you ask the cause of their reputed wisdom, he will say it is through the hardening of their heart. "Since, in the wisdom of God" — that is, proclaimed through the prophets — "the world by wisdom" — the wisdom that speaks through the prophets — "did not know him," namely God, "it pleased" this God, "through the foolishness of the proclamation" — the foolishness it seems to the Greeks — "to save those who believe. Since the Jews," he says, "ask for signs" toward faith, "and the Greeks seek wisdom" — the so-called compelling arguments and the other syllogisms — "but we proclaim Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling-block," because, knowing the prophecy, they do not believe its fulfilment, "and to the Greeks foolishness"; for the reputed wise think it a fable that the Son of God should speak through a man, and that God should have a Son, and that this Son should have suffered. Hence the prepossession of their conceit persuades them to disbelieve; for the coming of the Saviour did not make them foolish and hard-hearted and unbelieving, but understanding and obedient and, beyond that, faithful. And those who did not wish to obey were shown, by the voluntary inclination of those who obeyed, to be set apart as without understanding and unbelieving and foolish; but to the called themselves, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

"The command of the Lord is a spring of life," truly, "making one turn away from the snare of death." And what? Does it not command us to love the sojourners, not only as friends and kindred, but as ourselves, both in body and in soul? Indeed, it has honoured the nations too, and does not remember evil against those who have done evil. Plainly, then, it says: "You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in Egypt" — calling "Egyptian" either the gentile or the whole worldly man. And the enemies, even if they are already standing at the walls trying to take the city, are not yet to be reckoned enemies, until, sending heralds, they summon them to peace. Indeed, with the captive woman too it commands one to consort not for outrage, but, having allowed her to mourn whom she wishes for thirty days, and afterward changing her clothes, "come together with her by law as with a wife"; for it deems that intercourse should come about neither for outrage nor for hire, as with a harlot, but only for the begetting of children.

Should we not, then — and this is better — take "Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?" as a denial, equivalent to "He did not make it foolish," so that the cause of their hard-heartedness may not appear to have come to them from God, the one who made the wisdom foolish? For, on the contrary, though they were wise, they came under the greater charge for not believing the proclamation; for both the choice and the turning aside from the truth are voluntary. But by "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise" he means that it is outshone by the comparison with the despised and overlooked barbarian philosophy — just as the lamp, outshone by the sun, is said to have perished by not performing an equal activity. All men, then, being called, those who chose to obey were named "the called." For there is no injustice with God. So those of either race who believed, these are a peculiar people. And in the Acts of the Apostles you would find, word for word: "Those, then, who received his word were baptized; but those who would not obey set themselves apart, plainly."

You see love of mankind with self-control? To the man who has fallen in love, become master of the captive, it does not permit gratifying his pleasure, but checks the desire by a measured interval, and besides shaves off the captive's hair too, that it may put to shame the outrageous love; for if reasoning persuades to marry, he will hold to her even when she has become unsightly. Then, if anyone, having become sated with the desire, no longer deems it worthy to consort with the captive, it ordains that it is not permitted to sell her, nor even to have her any longer as a handmaid, but wishes her to be free and to be released from servitude, lest, another woman coming in, she suffer something incurable from jealousy.

To these the prophecy says: "If you are willing and listen to me, you will eat the good things of the earth" — proving that both the choice and the turning aside lie with us. And the Apostle called "the wisdom of God" the teaching that is according to the Lord, that he might show the true philosophy handed down through the Son. But indeed the reputed wise man too has certain exhortations, those in the Apostle that bid us "put on the new man, created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of the truth. Therefore, putting away falsehood, speak truth; do not give place to the devil. Let him who steals steal no more, but rather let him labour, working the good." And to work is to toil further while seeking the truth — together with rational well-doing, "that you may have to share with the one in need" both of worldly abundance and of divine wisdom. For he wants the word to be taught and the silver, exactly tested, to be put on the bankers' tables for lending out. Hence he adds: "Let no rotten word come out of your mouth" — a rotten word is this, the word from conceit — "but if there be any good word for the building up of the need, that it may give grace to the hearers." And of necessity the word of the good God is good. And how is the one who saves not good?

And what? Does it command us to help lift and raise up the burden-bearing beasts of enemies too, the Lord teaching us from afar not to welcome rejoicing over evil, nor to take pleasure in the misfortunes of enemies, that, having exercised ourselves in these things, he may teach us to pray for the enemies? For it befits us neither to envy nor to grieve over the goods of the neighbour, nor yet to reap pleasure over the evils of the neighbour. "And if you find a wandering beast of some enemy," it says, "leaving aside the fuel of the quarrel, lead it away and restore it." For upon the forgetting follows nobility, and upon this the dissolution of the enmity. From this we are fitted toward concord, which leads by the hand to happiness. And if you suppose someone an enemy from habit, and overtake him reasoning unreasonably, whether through desire or also through anger, turn him toward nobility.
