Does it now appear that the law is loving of mankind and good, the schoolmaster toward Christ, and that the God who is the same is good with justice, having dealt fittingly, from beginning to end, with each race unto salvation? "Have mercy," says the Lord, "that you may obtain mercy; forgive, that it may be forgiven you; as you do, so it will be done to you; as you give, so it will be given to you; as you judge, so you will be judged; as you show kindness, so kindness will be shown to you; with what measure you measure, it will be measured back to you." Further, it forbids those who serve for food to be dishonoured, and to those enslaved by debts it gives, in the seventh year, a release from everything. But it also forbids handing over suppliants to punishment. So more than anything that oracle is true: "As gold and silver are tried in the furnace, so the Lord chooses the hearts of men." And "the merciful man is long-suffering, and in everyone who takes thought there is wisdom; for thought will fall upon the man of understanding, and, being thoughtful, he will seek life"; and "he who seeks God will find knowledge with righteousness, and those who have rightly sought him found peace."

And it seems to me that Pythagoras too took the gentleness toward the irrational animals from the law. So he forbade abstaining from the immediate enjoyment of the young born among the flocks and the herds of goats and oxen — not even taking them on the pretext of sacrifices — both for the sake of the offspring and of the mothers, rearing man toward gentleness from below, from the irrational animals. "Grant, then," it says, "to the mother her offspring, even the first seven days." For if nothing comes about without cause, and milk is showered upon those who have given birth for the nourishment of the offspring, the man who drags the newborn away from the dispensation of the milk dishonours nature. Let the Greeks, then, be put to shame, and anyone else who runs down the law, if the one shows kindness even toward irrational animals, while they expose even the offspring of men, though the law, from afar and prophetically, reins in their savagery through the aforesaid commandment. For if it forbids the offspring of the irrational to be separated from the mother before the giving of milk, much more, in the case of men, does it heal beforehand the cruel and untamed mind, that, even if not nature, they may at least not despise learning.

For to take one's fill of kids and lambs is permitted, and there is perhaps some excuse for the man who separated the offspring from the mother; but what cause has the exposing of a child? For he ought not to have married at all who neither longs to beget children, nor, through incontinence of pleasure, to have become a child-killer. Again, the good law forbids sacrificing offspring and mother on the same day. Hence the Romans too, even if some pregnant woman is condemned to death, do not allow her to undergo the punishment before she has given birth. Plainly, then, of those animals too that are pregnant the law does not permit the slaughtering until they have given birth, restraining from afar the readiness of those who do wrong toward man. Thus it extended the fairness even to the irrational animals, that, having exercised ourselves among the kinds unlike us, we may use, with much abundance of love of mankind, toward the kinds like us.

But those who, kicking the bellies of certain animals before the birth, that they may feast on flesh mixed with milk, have made the womb, created for generation, a grave of the things carried in it, though the legislator plainly commands: "But you shall not boil a lamb in the milk of its mother"; for, it says, let not the nourishment of the living thing become a seasoning of the slain animal, nor let the cause of life become a co-worker in the consuming of the body. And the same law ordains not to muzzle the ox that threshes; for the worker too must be deemed worthy of food. And it forbids yoking together for the ploughing of the earth an ox and an ass, perhaps aiming at what is unsuited in the animals, but showing at the same time that one must wrong none of the other nations and bring them under the yoke, having nothing to charge except the difference of race, which is without responsibility, springing neither from vice nor from vice. And it seems to me that the allegory also indicates that one must not share the husbandry of the Word equally with the clean and the unclean, the faithful and the unfaithful, because the one is clean, the ox, but the ass has been reckoned among the unclean.

And, lavishing love of mankind, the good Word teaches that it is not fitting to cut down even those trees that are of cultivated stock, nor to reap the ear unto ruin before the harvest, nor at all to destroy cultivated fruit, neither that of the earth nor that of the soul; for it does not even allow cutting down the country of the enemy. Indeed, husbandmen too have been benefited by the law in these things; for it commands that the newly-planted trees be tended for three years in succession, cutting off the superfluous growths, that they be not weighed down and pressed, and that the nourishment, being not broken up into pieces, not become weak through want, and to mound them up and dig round them, that nothing growing beside hinder the increase. And it does not allow the fruit to be gathered incomplete from the incomplete, but, after three years, in the fourth, to consecrate the first-fruits to God, after the tree has been perfected.

And this type of husbandry would be a manner of teaching, teaching that one must cut off the side-growths of the sins, and the vain weeds of thought that spring up beside the fruitful fruit, until the shoot of faith be perfected and become firm. For in the fourth year — since there is need of time too for the one securely catechized — the tetrad of the virtues is consecrated to God, the third dwelling now joining on toward the fourth foundation of the Lord. "And a sacrifice of praise is above whole burnt-offerings. For he," it says, "gives you strength to do power. And if matters be enlightened for you, having received and acquired strength in knowledge, do power." For it shows by these things that the good things and the gifts are supplied from God, and that we must, having become ministers of the divine grace, sow the well-doings of God and equip those near us to be noble and good, that as much as possible the temperate man may render the self-controlled, and the courageous the noble, and the prudent and just the understanding and just.

The righteousness, then, and the harmony of the Saviour's teaching, which is dignified and sure, some have strained, as we have shown, receiving continence blasphemously, with all godlessness—although it is possible to choose celibacy according to the sound rule, with piety, giving thanks for the grace given, not hating the creation nor despising those who have married; for the world is created, and celibacy too is created, and let both give thanks in the state in which they were appointed, if they know also for what purposes they were appointed. But others, kicking against the rein, have run riot, becoming in truth "horses mad for the female," neighing after their neighbours' wives, pouring themselves out without restraint and persuading their neighbours to love pleasure—wretchedly attending to those Scriptures, "Cast in your lot among us, and let us all have one purse, and let there be one bag for us all."

On account of these men the same prophet, counselling us, says: "Do not go in the way with them; turn aside your foot from their paths; for not unjustly are nets stretched out for the birds; for they, partaking of bloodshed, lay up evils for themselves"—that is, laying claim to uncleanness and teaching their neighbours the like; "warriors, strikers, with their tails," according to the prophet—which the Greeks call "stings." And those whom the prophecy hints at might be: the licentious, the incontinent, who are "warriors with their tails," children of darkness and of wrath, murderers of themselves and slayers of their neighbours. "Cleanse out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump," the apostle cries to us. And again, vexed with certain such men, he ordains that we are not to associate, "if any one called a brother be a fornicator or covetous or an idolater or a reviler or a drunkard or a robber—with such a one not even to eat." "For I through the law died to the law," he says, "that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ; and I no longer live"—as I lived according to the desires—"but Christ lives in me," through obedience to the commandments, purely and blessedly; "so that then I lived in the flesh fleshly, but the life I now live in the flesh, I live in faith"—the faith of the Son of God.

"Do not go off into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter into a city of the Samaritans," the Lord says, turning us away from the contrary manner of life, since "the destruction of lawless men is evil. And these are the ways of all who accomplish lawless things." "Woe to that man," says the Lord; "it were good for him if he had not been born, rather than that he should offend one of my elect; it were better for him that a millstone be hung about him and that he be sunk into the sea, than that he pervert one of my elect"; for the name of God is blasphemed because of them. Wherefore the apostle nobly writes: "I wrote to you in the epistle not to associate with fornicators"—down to—"But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body." And, to show that he does not call marriage fornication, he adds: "Or do you not know that he who is joined to a harlot is one body?" Or will anyone call a virgin a harlot before she marries? "And do not deprive one another," he says, "except by agreement for a season"—by the word "deprive" indicating the debt of marriage, the begetting of children, which he made plain in what went before, saying, "Let the husband render to the wife her due, and likewise the wife to the husband."

After which creation, by virtue of housekeeping and faith in Christ, she is a helper; and still more plainly he says: "To those who have married I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not be separated from her husband (but if she is separated, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband), and that a husband should not put away his wife. But to the rest I say—I, not the Lord: if any brother..."—down to—"but now they are holy." What do those say to these things who run down the law and marriage, as if it were permitted only according to the law, and not also according to the new covenant? What can those say to these ordinances who loathe sowing and generation? Since indeed he legislates that the bishop who presides well over his house should lead the Church, and he establishes the household of the Lord by the wedlock of one wife.

"All things, then, are pure to the pure," he says; "but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and their conscience are defiled." And concerning pleasure that is contrary to the rule, "Do not be deceived," he says: "neither fornicators nor idolaters nor adulterers nor effeminate nor sodomites nor covetous nor thieves, no drunkards, no revilers, no robbers, shall inherit the kingdom of God. And such were some of us, but we were washed"—we who had been in these things. But others, washing into this lewdness, baptize from prudence into fornication, laying down as doctrine the gratifying of pleasures and passions, teaching men to become incontinent instead of prudent, and resting their hope on the shamelessness of the genitals; making their pupils outcasts of the kingdom of God, and not enrolled, having undertaken, under the name of falsely-called knowledge, the journey into the outer darkness. "Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever dignified, whatever just, whatever pure, whatever lovely, whatever of good report; if there be any virtue and if any praise, think on these things. The things you have both learned and received and heard and seen in me, these do; and the God of peace shall be with you."

Having, then, pointed out a small opening "to those who love the contemplation of the truth," from the law concerning sacrifices, regarding both the common Jews and the heresies—as unclean, being mystically distinguished from the divine Church, by the law of clean and unclean animals—let us bring the discourse to a close. For the Scripture hands down as clean and acceptable to God those of the sacrificial animals that part the hoof and chew the cud, as figuring that the just make their journey toward the Father and toward the Son through faith (for this is the steadfastness of the cleft-footed)—those who "meditate on the oracles of God night and day," and ruminate them in the receptacle of the soul that holds learning. Which gnostic exercise the law allegorizes as the cud-chewing of the clean animal. But those that have neither of these, or one without the other, it sets apart as unclean. Accordingly, the things that chew the cud but do not part the hoof hint at the many Jews, who have the oracles of God upon their lips, but do not have faith, and the foundation that conveys, through the Son, to the Father, leaning upon the truth. Whence the race of such cattle is also slippery, as not being cloven-footed nor leaning upon the double support of faith. "For no one," it is said, "knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son shall reveal him." And, again, unclean in like manner are those that part the hoof but do not chew the cud. For these signify the heretics, who have set foot upon the name of Father and Son, but are too weak to work fine and to grind smooth the exact clearness of the oracles, and besides who pursue the works of righteousness more grossly, not more exactly—if indeed they pursue them at all.

And Peter in his epistle says the like: "So that your faith and hope are toward God, having purified your souls in obedience to the truth, as children of obedience, not conformed to the former desires in your ignorance, but as He who called you is holy, be you also yourselves holy in all your conduct; because it is written, 'You shall be holy, for I am holy.'" But indeed the controversy with the falsely-named pretenders to knowledge, having become necessary, has led us beyond what is needful and stretched out our discourse to a great length. Wherefore this is where the third of our notebooks of gnostic memoranda concerning the true philosophy, the Stromateus, comes to its end.

To certain such the Lord says: "Why do you call me 'Lord, Lord,' and do not the things I say?" And altogether unclean are those that neither part the hoof nor chew the cud. "But you, O Megarians," says Theognis, "are neither third nor fourth nor twelfth, neither in account nor in number," but rather "like the chaff which the wind drives away from the face of the earth," and "like a drop from a bucket." Now that these things have been brought to an end for us, and the ethical division has been sketched as in summary, having sown in here and there—scattered and dispersed, as we promised—the live coals of the doctrines of true knowledge, so that it may not be easy for the chance uninitiated reader to find out the holy traditions, let us pass on to our promise.

The dignified and pure conduct of our love of mankind, according to Clement, seeks the common benefit—whether it bears witness or educates, in deed and in word, and this in a twofold way, both unwritten and written. This is love—to love God and one's neighbour. This leads up to the unspeakable height: "Love covers a multitude of sins"; love bears all things, suffers long with all; love joins us to God; love does all things in concord. In love all the elect of God were perfected; without love nothing is well-pleasing to God. "Of its perfection there is no explanation," he says. "Who is fit to be found in it, save those whom God Himself deems worthy?" So at once the apostle Paul says: "If I give over my body"—and have not love—"I am sounding brass and a clanging cymbal"; unless from elect disposition, through gnostic love, I bear witness, he says—but through fear.

The Miscellanies are somewhat like, not those parks set in order with trees planted in rows for the pleasure of the eye, but rather like some shady and thick-grown hill planted with cypresses and plane-trees, with laurel and ivy, and at the same time with apple-trees and olives and figs—the planting deliberately mingled of fruit-bearing and unfruitful trees together, on account of those who dare to filch and steal the ripe fruit; the writing willing to lie hid. From which the husbandman, transplanting and re-grafting, will set in order a fair park and a delightful grove. The Miscellanies, then, aim neither at arrangement nor at style, since indeed on purpose both the diction is not such as the Greeks would have it, and the sowing-in of the doctrines has been made secretly and not according to the plain truth—preparing the readers, if any chance to be such, to be lovers of toil and discoverers. For many and various are the baits, by reason of the differences among the fish. And now, after this seventh Book of our Miscellanies, we shall make the discourse of what follows from another beginning.

If, then, even with a reward expected, beating my lips toward the testimony of the Lord, I confess the Lord, I am a common man, sounding "the Lord," not knowing Him. For there is the people that loves with the lips, and there is another who gives over his body to be burned. And "though I distribute all my goods," he says—not according to the law of loving fellowship, but according to the law of recompense, either from the man benefited or from the Lord who promised—"and though I have all faith, so as to remove mountains" and cast off the passions that overshadow, "but be not made faithful to the Lord through love, I am nothing"—being reckoned, in comparison with the man who bears witness gnostically, in the multitude and in the realm of what makes no difference. And all the generations from Adam to this present day have passed away; but those perfected in love, according to the grace of God, have a place among the pious, who shall be made manifest at the visitation of the kingdom of Christ.

Love does not permit one to sin; but if a man fall unwillingly into some such circumstance, through the assaults of the adversary, imitating David, he will sing: "I will confess to the Lord, and it shall please Him better than a young bullock that has horns and hoofs. Let the poor see and be glad." For He says: "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Lord; and call upon me in the day of your affliction, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me"; for "a sacrifice to God is a broken spirit." Love, then, God too is called, being good. He whose love works no harm to the neighbour, neither wronging nor ever requiting wrong, but doing good to all without exception, after the image of God. The fullness of the law, then, is love, as Christ is—that is, the presence of the Lord who loves us, and our loving teaching and conduct according to Christ. By love, then, the not committing adultery and the not coveting the neighbour's wife are perfected, which were before forbidden by fear. The same deed, then, has a difference, whether done through fear or accomplished through love, and whether wrought through faith or gnostically.

With good reason, then, their prizes too are different. For the gnostic there are prepared the things "that eye has not seen nor ear heard nor have entered into the heart of man"; but to the one who has simply believed He bears witness of a hundredfold of what he has left behind—a promise that has happened to fall within the comprehension of men. Having come to this point, I was reminded of a certain man who called himself a gnostic. For, explaining the words "But I say, the one who looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery," he held that the bare desire is not judged, but only if to the desire the deed corresponding to it, going beyond the desire, is accomplished in it; for "if it be in a dream, through imagination, it already misuses the body too."

So those who composed the histories tell of such a judgement of Bocchoris the just. A young man in love with a courtesan persuades the girl, for a fixed price, to come to him on the next day. But, his desire having been satisfied beforehand by a dream beyond his hope, when his beloved came according to agreement, he barred her from entry; and she, having learned what had happened, demanded the price, saying that she had in this way fulfilled the desire of the lover. They came, then, to the judge. He, ordering the young man to hold out the purse of the price in the sun, commanded the courtesan to take hold of its shadow—gracefully bidding her receive an image of payment for an image of intercourse.

So a man dreams when the soul consents to the imagination; but the man who looks toward desire dreams waking—not only, as that supposed gnostic said, if together with the sight of the woman he conceive in thought the intercourse (for this is already a work of desire as desire), but if anyone, reason says, look toward the beauty of a body, and the flesh seem to him beautiful for desire, he is judged, having looked carnally and sinfully, by the very thing at which he wondered. For, on the contrary, the man who looks at beauty through pure love does not regard the flesh as beautiful, but the soul, marvelling, I think, at the body as at a statue, and through whose beauty sending himself on to the Craftsman and to the truly beautiful, displaying to the angels set over the ascent a holy symbol, the luminous character of righteousness—I mean the anointing of well-pleasing, the quality of the disposition that lies upon the soul made bright by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit.

This glory that shone upon the face of Moses the people were not able to look upon, wherefore he took a veil of the glory toward those who looked carnally. For those who bring along anything of the worldly things, the ones who demand the toll hold fast, weighed down by their own passions; but the man who is bare of the things subject to the toll, but full of knowledge and of the righteousness that comes from works, they send on with their prayers, counting the man blessed together with his work. "And his leaf shall not fall off"—the leaf of the tree of life, the tree nourished by the channels of the waters; for the righteous man is likened to fruit-bearing trees, not only to those in the offering of the things raised on high . . . in the sacrifice. And in the offerings of the sacrifices under the law there were inspectors of the victims for blemishes. The men skilled in these matters, then, distinguish appetite from desire, and they assign desire, which is concerned with pleasures and licence, to the irrational; but appetite, which is concerned with the necessary things according to nature, they reckon a rational motion.

And our gnostic ever spends his time in the most authoritative things; and if anywhere there be leisure and a season of relaxation from the chief things, instead of other idleness, he lays hold of the Greek philosophy too, as a kind of sweetmeat eaten as a relish after dinner, not neglecting the better things, but taking these too, so far as is fitting, and for the reasons I said before. But those who craved the unnecessary and superfluous things of philosophy, and gave themselves to the contentious sophisms alone, were left behind the necessary and most authoritative things, downright pursuing the shadows of words. It is good, then, to know all things; but for him whose soul is too weak to stretch itself toward the much-learned experience, he will choose only the leading and better things. For the truly real science, which we say the gnostic alone has, is a sure apprehension, leading up, through true and sure reasonings, to the knowledge of the cause; and he who is scientific of the true about anything whatsoever is forthwith scientific too of the false about the same. And indeed that argument seems to me well enough: "If one must philosophize, one must philosophize; for the thing follows upon itself. But even if one must not philosophize — for no one could condemn anything not having first known this. One must philosophize, then."

These things being so, the Greeks must learn, through law and prophets, to worship one only God, who is the truly existent Almighty; and then must be taught this through the apostle: "To us there is no idol in the world," since no likeness of God can be among begotten things; and must be taught besides that not even of the things which they worship would the images be the likenesses; for not at all is the kind of souls such, in respect of shape, as the Greeks mould the carved figures. For souls are invisible, not only the rational, but also those of the irrational animals; and their bodies never become parts of the souls, but instruments, of some seats, of some chariots, and of others, in another way, possessions.

But not even the images of the instruments is it possible to imitate clearly; since let one mould the sun, as it is seen, and liken the rainbow by its colours. But when they leave the idols, then they shall hear the Scripture: "Unless your righteousness exceed more than that of the scribes and Pharisees" — who are justified by abstention from evils — "by the being able, together with the perfection in these things, to love the neighbour too and to do good, you shall not be kingly." For the intensity of the righteousness according to the law shows the gnostic. Thus one, ranked according to the ruling part of his own body, the head, having advanced to the height of faith, knowledge itself, about which all the senses are, shall likewise attain the highest inheritance. And the ruling part of knowledge the apostle plainly shows to those able to look through, writing thus to those Greekish Corinthians: "But having hope, as your faith increases, to be magnified among you according to our rule unto abundance, to preach the good news to the parts beyond you" — not meaning the extension of the preaching according to place (since he himself says that the faith abounded even in Achaia,

and it is recorded too in the Acts of the Apostles that he preached the word in Athens too), but he teaches knowledge, which is the perfecting of faith, to abound beyond the catechizing, according to the magnificence of the Lord's teaching and the ecclesiastical rule. Wherefore too, a little after, he adds: "And though rude in speech, yet not in knowledge." But let those of the Greeks who boast at having apprehended the truth tell us from whom, having learned, they make their vaunt. From God, indeed, they would not say; from men they confess. And if this be so, then either, having learned it from themselves late — as indeed some of them, puffed up, boast — or from others like themselves. But men, speaking about God, are not trustworthy teachers, in so far as they are men; for one who is a man is not of weight to speak even the true things about God — the weak and perishable about the unbegotten and incorruptible, the work about him who made it.

Then, he who is not able to speak the true things about himself — is he not the less to be believed about the things of God? For as much as a man falls short of the power of God, by so much also his word fails, even if he speak not God, but the things about God and the divine word. For the human word is by nature weak and unable to declare God — I do not mean the name (for to name it is common, not to philosophers only, but to poets too), nor the substance (for that is impossible), but the power and the works of God. And yet those who inscribe God as their teacher hardly come to a conception of God, the grace co-helping them unto a certain recognition — accustomed, as it were, to behold the will by the will and the Holy Spirit by the Holy Spirit; for "the Spirit searches the deep things of God, but the natural man receives not the things of the Spirit." Only, then, the wisdom among us is God-taught, from which all the springs of wisdom hang, as many as aim at the truth. For instance, as the Lord was to come to men, the one who should teach us, there were ten thousand signallers, heralds, preparers, forerunners, from above, from the foundation of the world, by deeds, by words, foretelling, prophesying that he should come, and where and how, and what the signs.

For instance, from afar the law and the prophecy practise beforehand, and then the forerunner shows him present, and after him the heralds, teaching the power of the manifestation, declare it. . . . to a few only, and not even to all of these, did the philosophers please; but to Plato Socrates was pleasing, and Plato to Xenocrates, and Aristotle to Theophrastus, and Zeno to Cleanthes, who persuaded their own sectaries only. But the word of our teacher remained not in Judaea alone, as philosophy in Hellas, but was poured out over the whole inhabited earth, persuading Greeks and barbarians together, by nation and village and every city, whole houses and each privately of those who hearkened — yes, and not a few of the philosophers themselves — bringing them over already to the truth. And if any chance ruler hinder the Greek philosophy, it perishes forthwith; but our teaching, from then, together with the first proclamation, kings and tyrants and the particular rulers and governors, with all their hirelings, and besides the countless men, hinder, warring against us and trying as far as may be to root it out; but it flourishes the more. For it does not die as a human teaching, nor wither as a weak gift (for no gift of God is weak), but abides unhindered, prophesied to be persecuted to the end.

Then, concerning poetry, Plato writes, "A poet is a light thing and holy, and not able to make until he becomes inspired and out of his senses." And Democritus likewise: "Whatever a poet writes with enthusiasm and a holy breath is very noble." And we know what kind of things poets say. But the prophets of God the Almighty — would not one be struck with awe at them, having become instruments of the divine voice? As, then, having moulded a statue of the gnostic, we have already shown what manner of man he is, having made plain, as in a sketch, the greatness and the beauty of his character; but what manner of man he is in respect of contemplation in things natural will be shown after these things, when we begin to treat of the becoming of the world.

That the Greeks too are testified to dogmatize some true things, one may consider from this as well. Paul, in the Acts of the Apostles, is recorded as saying to the Areopagites: "I see that you are more religious. For, going through and observing the objects of your worship, I found an altar on which was inscribed: 'To the unknown God.' Whom, then, you worship in ignorance, this one I proclaim to you. God, who made the world and all things in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, dwells not in temples made with hands, nor is served by human hands as though he needed anything, himself giving to all life and breath and all things; and he made of one every race of men to dwell over all the face of the earth, having determined appointed seasons and the boundaries of their dwelling, that they should seek the divine, if perhaps they might feel after it or find it, though it is not far from each one of us. For in him we live and move and have our being, as some too of your own poets have said: 'For we are also his offspring.'" From which it is plain that, using also poetic examples from the Phaenomena of Aratus, he approves what has been well said among the Greeks, and through the "unknown God" he hinted that the Creator God was honoured by the Greeks by a periphrasis, but that he must be received and learned with full knowledge through the Son.

"For this reason, then, I have sent you to the nations," he says, "to open their eyes, that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a portion among those sanctified by faith in me." These eyes of the blind, then, that are opened, are the knowledge of the Father through the Son, the grasping of the Greek periphrasis; and to turn from the power of Satan is to change from sin, through which the slavery had come about. We do not, however, simply accept all philosophy, but that of which Socrates too, in Plato, speaks: "For there are, as those concerned with the rites say, many bearers of the thyrsus, but few bacchants" — hinting that the called are many, but the chosen few. So he adds clearly: "These, in my opinion, are none other than those who have philosophized rightly. And of these I too, so far as I could, left nothing undone in my life, but strove in every way to become one. Whether I strove rightly and accomplished anything, we shall know clearly, when we have come there, if God will, a little later."

Does he not seem to you, from the Hebrew Scriptures, to be making plain the hope of the just man after death? And in the Demodocus — if indeed the work is Plato's — he says that this is not philosophizing: to live stooping over the arts, nor being a man of much learning, but something else; "since I, for one, thought it even a reproach." For he knew, I think, that "much learning does not teach one to have understanding," according to Heraclitus. And in the fifth book of the Republic he says: "Shall we, then, set down all these, and others of such sort, as mathematicians and as philosophers of the little arts? By no means, I said, but as like to philosophers. And whom, he said, do you call the true ones? Those, I said, who love to behold the truth." For philosophy is not in geometry, which has its postulates and hypotheses, nor in music, which is conjectural, nor in astronomy, crammed with physical and flowing and probable accounts, but is the knowledge of the Good itself and of the truth — those other things being distinct from the Good, but ways toward the Good. So not even he grants that the cyclic education of itself accomplishes anything toward the Good, but that it works together to rouse and to exercise the soul toward the objects of thought.

Whether, then, they say that the Greeks uttered some sayings of the true philosophy by chance, the chance is of the divine dispensation (for no one will deify the spontaneous through his ambition toward us); or whether by coincidence, the coincidence is not without providence; or whether, again, one should say the Greeks had a natural notion — we know the Maker of nature to be one, in the sense in which we have called righteousness too natural; or whether, indeed, they had a common mind, let us consider who is the father of this and of the righteousness that comes according to the apportioning of mind. For if one speaks of a foreannouncement and alleges a joint utterance, he speaks of kinds of prophecy. Indeed, others wish that some things were said to the philosophers by a reflection of the truth. The divine Apostle, then, writes concerning us: "For we now see as through a mirror" — knowing ourselves by reflection in it, and contemplating, so far as we can, the efficient cause from the divine within us. For "You have seen your brother," it says, "you have seen your God." The Saviour, I think, is called God to us now; but after the laying aside of the flesh, "face to face," then at last definitely and comprehensibly, when the heart has become pure. And by reflection and through a medium those who have exactly philosophized among the Greeks discern God; for such are the true impressions seen through weakness, as an image is seen in the waters, and as we see through transparent and translucent bodies.

Well, then, does Solomon say: "He who sows righteousness works faith. And there are those who, sowing their own, make more." And again: "Take care of the green things in the field, and you will shear grass; and gather the ripe hay, that you may have sheep for clothing." You see how one must take thought for the covering and the guarding from outside. "And you will know with knowledge the souls of your flock." For "when the nations that do not have the Law do by nature the things of the Law, these, not having the Law, are a law to themselves" — the uncircumcision keeping the ordinances of the Law, according to the Apostle, both before the Law and before the coming. And the discourse, as if making a comparison of those from philosophy with those called heretics, says very plainly: "Better is a friend near than a brother dwelling far off; and he who leans upon falsehoods, this man herds the winds and pursues winged birds." I do not think the discourse means philosophy here. Indeed, in many things philosophy attempts what is probable and is persuasive; but it rebukes the heresies. So it adds: "For he has left the ways of his own vineyard, and has wandered from the tracks of his own tillage." And these are they who forsake the Church that is from the beginning. So the man who has fallen into heresy passes through a waterless desert, having left the truly existing God; bereft of God, seeking waterless water, coming upon the uninhabited and thirsty land, gathering barrenness with his hands.

"And to those wanting in understanding I give command, saying" — says wisdom, meaning, of course, those about the heresies — "Touch with pleasure the hidden loaves and the sweet stolen water." By "bread and water" the Scripture plainly means none other than the heresies that use bread and water in the offering not according to the rule of the Church. For there are some who give thanks even with bare water. "But spring away; do not linger in her place" — calling the synagogue a "place," and not, by the same name, a church. Then it cries out: "For so you will cross over strange water" — reckoning the heretical baptism not proper and genuine water — "and you will pass over a strange river" that carries along and drags down into the sea, into which the man who has turned aside from the steadfastness that is according to truth is poured out, swept away again into the worldly and disordered waves of life.

This is the man according to the image and likeness, the gnostic, who imitates God so far as is possible, leaving out nothing of what tends to the attainable likeness — being self-controlled, enduring, living justly, reigning over the passions, sharing what he has, doing good both in word and in deed so far as he can. "This man," it says, "is greatest in the kingdom, who shall do and teach," imitating God by giving graces like his own; for the gifts of God are for the common benefit. "But whoever undertakes to do anything with arrogance, provokes God," it says; for boastfulness is a vice of the soul, from which, and from the other vices, it commands men to repent, fitting their life out of disharmony toward the better change, through these three: mouth, heart, hands.

And these would be a symbol: the hands of action, the heart of counsel, and the mouth of speech. Well, then, was that oracle spoken concerning the penitent: "You have chosen God today to be your God, and the Lord has chosen you today to become a people to him." For God makes his own the man who hastens to serve the Being, being a suppliant. And even if he be one in number, he is honoured on a par with the people; for, being a part of the people, he becomes a completion of it, restored from that whence he was; and the whole is also named from a part. And this nobility is shown in the choosing and the joint-exercise of the noblest things. For what did his so great nobility profit Adam? And his father is no mortal; for he himself is the father of men in generation. The shameful things he eagerly chose, following the woman, but the true and noble he neglected; for which he changed a mortal for an immortal life — yet not unto the end.

But Noah, who did not become as Adam, is saved by divine oversight; for, bringing himself, he offered himself up to God. And Abraham, who begot children by three women, not for the enjoyment of pleasure, but, I think, for the hope of multiplying the race in the beginning — one alone succeeds as heir of the ancestral goods, while the others were settled apart from the kindred. And of twins born from him, the younger inherits, having become well-pleasing to the father, and receives the prayers, while the elder serves him; for the greatest good for the base man is not to be his own master. And this dispensation is both prophetic and typical. And that all things belong to the wise man, he plainly indicates, saying: "Because God has had mercy on me, I have all things." For he teaches that one must reach after one thing, through which all things have come to be, and who apportions the promised things to the worthy.

He records, then, the earnest man, who has become heir of the kingdom, as a fellow-citizen, through the divine wisdom, of the just men of old too, who lived lawfully both under the law and before the law, whose actions have become laws for us. And again, teaching that the wise man is king, he makes those not of the same nation say to him: "You are a king from God among us" — the ruled, by willing judgment, obeying the earnest man through zeal for virtue. And Plato the philosopher, setting happiness as the end, says it is likeness to God so far as possible — whether running together somehow with the doctrine of the law (for great natures, bare of passions, somehow hit upon the truth, as the Pythagorean Philo says, expounding the things of Moses), or being instructed by certain learned men of that time, as one ever thirsting for learning. For the law says: "After the Lord your God shall you walk, and my commandments shall you keep." For the law names the being-made-like "following"; and such following makes like according to power. "Become," says the Lord, "merciful and compassionate, as your heavenly Father is compassionate."

From this the Stoics too dogmatized that the end is to live in accordance with nature, having unbecomingly renamed God into nature, since nature extends even to plants and to crops and to trees and to stones. Plainly, then, it is said: "Bad men do not understand law, but those who love law set up for themselves a wall. For the wisdom of the cunning will recognize its ways, but the folly of the foolish is in wandering." "For upon whom shall I look but upon the meek and quiet and him who trembles at my words?" the prophecy says. And we are taught three kinds of friendship; and of these the first and best is that according to virtue, for firm is the love from reason; the second and middle is that according to return — and this is social and giving and useful for life, for common is the friendship from grace; and the last and third we call that from custom, but others that according to pleasure, changeable and variable.

And it seems to me that Hippodamus the Pythagorean writes most nobly: "Of friendships, the one is from the knowledge of the gods, the one from the giving of men, the one from the pleasure of animals." So the one is the friendship of a philosopher, the one of a man, the one of an animal. For in truth man, doing good, is an image of God, in which he is himself also benefited; for as the pilot at once saves and is saved, so for this reason, when one happens to be asking, one does not say to the giver, "You have given well," but "You have received well." So the giver receives, and the receiver gives. "And the just pity and have mercy; and the kind will be inhabitants of the earth, and the harmless will be left upon it; but the lawless will be utterly destroyed from it." And it seems to me that Homer, foretelling the faithful man, said: "Give to a friend." One must share with a friend, that he may remain still more a friend; and one must aid an enemy, that he may not remain an enemy; for by aid goodwill is bound and enmity dissolved. But if eagerness is set forth, "it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one has not." "For it is not that to others there be relief and to you affliction, but out of equality in the present time," and the rest. "He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness abides forever," says the Scripture. For by the "according to the image and likeness," as we said before too, what is according to the body is not meant — for it is not lawful for a mortal to be made like to the immortal — but what is according to mind and reasoning, upon which the Lord fittingly seals the likeness both toward doing good and toward ruling; for rulings are set right not by the qualities of bodies, but by the judgments of the mind. For "by the counsels of holy men cities are well governed, and a house well ordered."

Of this perfection, then, it is possible to partake alike for a man and alike for a woman. At once, it was not Moses alone who, hearing from God: "I have spoken to you once and twice, saying, I have seen this people, and behold, it is stiff-necked; let me utterly destroy them, and I will blot out their name from under heaven, and I will make you a great and wonderful nation, far more than this"—answers, entreating, not looking to his own advantage, but to the common salvation: "By no means, Lord; forgive the sin to this people, or blot me too out of the book of the living." How great the perfection of the man who wished to die together with the people rather than be saved alone! But Judith too, perfected among women, when the city was besieged, having begged the elders, goes out into the camp of the foreigners, despising every danger, giving herself over to the enemies for her country's sake, in faith of God; and at once she receives the reward of her faith—a woman who triumphed over the enemy of the faith, having become mistress of the head of Holofernes.

And again, Esther, perfect in faith, delivering Israel from the tyrannical power and from the cruelty of the satrap, a single woman, afflicted with fastings, set herself against ten thousand armed right hands, undoing through faith the tyrannical decree; and indeed she tamed the one, and held back Haman, and through her perfect prayer to God kept Israel unharmed. For I pass over Susanna and the sister of Moses—how the one was fellow-general with the prophet, taking the lead of all the women renowned among the Hebrews for wisdom; and the other, by surpassing dignity, holding out even to death when condemned by her licentious lovers, remained, unwavering, a martyr of purity.

Yes, and Dio the philosopher records that a certain woman, Lysidice, out of excess of modesty bathed in her very tunic; and Philotera, whenever she was about to enter the bath, quietly drew up the tunic as far as the water covered her bare parts, and then, rising up again little by little, put it on once more. And did not Leaena the Athenian too bear tortures manfully? She, being privy to the plot of Harmodius and Aristogeiton against Hipparchus, did not in any way tell of it, though well tortured. And they say too that the Argive women, with Telesilla the poetess leading them, merely by appearing routed the Spartans, valiant in war, and gained for those women fearlessness of death. The author of the Danaid says the like concerning the daughters of Danaus:
And then swiftly the daughters of Danaus armed themselves before the fair-flowing river of lord Nile,

and so on. And the rest of the poets sing of Atalanta's swiftness in the hunt, and of the tender love of Anticleia, and of Alcestis' love of her husband, and of the good courage of Macaria and of the Hyacinthides. And what? Did not Theano the Pythagorean come to such a height of philosophy that, when a man, looking at her inquisitively, said, "A fair arm," she answered, "But not a public one"? Of the same dignity is reported also this saying: for, being asked on what day a woman goes down to the Thesmophoria after being with a man, she said, "From her own, at once; but from another's, never." Yes, and Themisto of Lampsacus, the wife of Leonteus of Lampsacus, philosophized in the Epicurean way, as did Myia the daughter of Theano in the Pythagorean way, and Arignote who wrote the things concerning Dionysus; for the daughters of Diodorus, surnamed Cronus, all became dialecticians, as Philo the dialectician says in the Menexenus, whose names he sets down as follows: Menexene, Argeia, Theognis, Artemisia, Pantacleia. I remember too a certain Cynic woman, called Hipparchia, the Maronite, the wife of Crates, in whose honour he even celebrated the "dog-wedding" in the Stoa Poikile.

And Arete of Cyrene, the daughter of Aristippus, educated Aristippus surnamed the Mother-taught. And with Plato there philosophized Lasthenia the Arcadian and Axiothea the Phliasian. For of Aspasia the Milesian, of whom the comic poets too write much, Socrates made use for philosophy, and Pericles for rhetoric. I pass over the others, then, for the length of the discourse, neither cataloguing the poetesses—Corinna and Telesilla and Myia and Sappho—nor the women painters, such as Eirene the daughter of Cratinus and Anaxandra the daughter of Nealces, of whom Didymus speaks in the Symposiaca.

And the daughter of Cleobulus the wise man and monarch of the Lindians was not ashamed to wash the feet of her father's guests; just as Sarah, the wife of Abraham, that blessed woman, herself prepared the cakes for the angels, and royal maidens among the Hebrews tended the sheep, whence too Nausicaa in Homer went to the washing-places. The prudent woman, then, would choose first to persuade her husband to be her partner in the things that lead to happiness; but if she is unable, let her hasten toward virtue alone—obedient to her husband in all things, so as never to do anything against his will, except in so far as it is judged to make a difference toward virtue and salvation. But even if anyone should hinder a woman, or a maidservant too, who unfeignedly sets out toward such a disposition, the man who does this then plainly does nothing other than purpose to lead her away from righteousness and prudence, and to make his own household at once unjust and licentious.

It is not possible, then, for a man or a woman to become noteworthy in anything whatever without using learning and practice and training; and we say that virtue depends on nothing else so much as on ourselves. Other things one may hinder by warring against them, but the things in our power not at all, even if one should especially set himself against them; for the gift is god-given and not subject to anything else. Hence licence would be reckoned the evil of none other than the man who is licentious, and prudence the good of the man who is able to be prudent.

As the many men who drag down the ship would not be said to be many causes, but, of many men, one cause (for each is not a cause of the ship's being dragged down, but together with the others), so philosophy too, being a search for truth, contributes to the grasping of the truth, not being a cause of the grasping, but, together with the others, a cause and a co-worker. And perhaps the joint cause is a cause. And as, happiness being one, the virtues that are its causes are several; and as of being warmed the sun and the fire and the bath and clothing are causes; so, truth being one, many are the things that contribute to the search for it, but the finding is through the Son. If, then, we consider, virtue is one in power, but it has come about that, when present in these matters, it is called prudence, in these temperance, in these courage or righteousness. By the same account, then, truth too being one, in geometry there is the truth of geometry, in music that of music, and in right philosophy there would be Greek truth. But this sovereign truth alone is not to be tampered with, in which we are educated by the Son of God.

In this way we say that one and the same drachma, when given to the shipmaster, is called fare; to the tax-collector, toll; rent to the landlord; wage to the teacher; and earnest-money to the seller. And each thing, whether virtue or truth, called by a synonymous name, is the cause only of the result that belongs to it. And by the joint use of these comes about the living happily (for let us not be happy merely in names), when we call the right life happiness, and call happy the man whose soul is virtuously ordered. And if philosophy contributes, even from afar, to the finding of truth — reaching, by its various attempts, toward the knowledge that is according to us, which touches truth nearly — yet it does contribute to the man who has been earnest to lay hold of knowledge by attempting it rationally. But Greek truth is separated from ours, even if it has shared the same name, both in the greatness of knowledge and in the more authoritative demonstration and in the divine power and the like. For we are taught of God, being instructed in the truly sacred letters by the Son of God; whence, too, they do not move souls in the same way, but by a different teaching.

And if, for the sake of the fault-finders, we must make a distinction, then in calling philosophy a joint cause and a co-worker of the true apprehension, being a search for truth, we shall confess it to be a preliminary education of the gnostic, not setting down the joint cause as a cause, nor the co-worker as something that holds together, nor philosophy as a thing without which there is nothing. For nearly all of us, without the cyclic education and Greek philosophy — and some even without letters — moved by the divine and barbarian philosophy, have received by faith, in power, the word concerning God, educated by self-acting wisdom. And what acts with another, being incomplete to act of itself, we call a co-worker and a joint cause, named from being a cause together with a cause, or from becoming a cause by coming together with another, but not able of itself to furnish the result that is according to truth. And yet philosophy of itself once justified the Greeks, not unto the universal righteousness, toward which it is found a co-worker (just as the first and second step are to the man going up to the upper room, and the writing-master is to the one who is to be a philosopher); nor as though, by its removal, the universal account would be deficient or the truth done away. For sight contributes, and hearing and voice, toward truth, but it is the mind that recognizes it of itself. But of the co-workers some bring greater, some less power. So clearness is a co-worker toward the handing down of the truth, and dialectic toward not falling before the heresies that run riot.

Self-complete, then, and in need of nothing, is the teaching that is according to the Saviour, being the power and wisdom of God; and Greek philosophy, coming to it, does not make the truth more powerful, but, by rendering powerless the sophistical attempt against it and beating back the treacherous plots against the truth, it has fitly been called a fence and a wall of the vineyard. And the truth that is according to faith is necessary for life, as bread; while the preliminary education is like a relish and a dessert — "a sweet morsel at the close of dinner," according to Pindar the Theban. The Scripture has plainly declared: "The harmless man, understanding, will become more cunning, and the wise man will receive knowledge." And "he who speaks of himself seeks his own glory," says the Lord, "but he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him is true, and there is no unrighteousness in him." On the contrary, then, he does wrong who appropriates the things of the barbarians and boasts of them as his own, increasing his own glory and falsifying the truth. This man is called a thief by the Scripture. So it says: "My son, do not become a liar; for the lie leads to theft." And the thief truly has what he has stolen, whether it be gold or silver or speech or doctrine. In part, then, the things they have stolen are true, but they know them by conjecture and by the necessities of argument. Once discipled, then, they will recognize them comprehensibly.

And steadfastness too itself forces its way toward the divine likeness, reaping, through endurance, impassivity — if anyone has ringing in his ears the things recorded about those around Ananias, of whom one was Daniel the prophet, filled with divine faith. Daniel dwelt in Babylon, just as Lot in Sodom, and Abraham, who a little after became the friend of God, in the land of the Chaldeans. The king of the Babylonians, then, brought down Daniel into a pit full of beasts, but the king of all, the faithful Lord, brought him up unharmed. This endurance the gnostic, as gnostic, will gain; he will bless when tested, like the noble Job; he will pray, like Jonah, when swallowed by the whale;

and faith will restore him, prophesying to the Ninevites; and if he be shut up with lions, he will tame the beasts; and if he be cast into fire, he will be bedewed and not be burned up. He will witness by night, he will witness by day; in word, in life, in manner he will witness; being a housemate of the Lord, a familiar and a table-companion according to the spirit, he will remain pure in the flesh, pure in the heart, sanctified in the word. "To this man," it says, "the world is crucified, and he himself to the world." This man, bearing about the cross of the Saviour, follows the Lord "in the track, as of a god," having become a holy one of the holy.

The divine law, then, making mention of every virtue, anoints man especially toward self-control, laying this down as the foundation of the virtues; and indeed it educates us beforehand toward the gaining of self-control by the use of the animals, forbidding us to partake of all that are by nature fat, like the race of swine, which happens to be very full-fleshed; for such use is supplied to those given to luxury. It is said, at any rate, that one of the philosophers, etymologizing, said the sow (hys) is "for sacrifice" (thyein), as fit only for slaughter and killing; for soul has been given to this animal for nothing else than that its flesh might be plump. Likewise it forbade partaking of the fishes, restraining our desires of those that have neither fins nor scales; for these differ from the other fishes in plumpness and fatness.

From this, I think, the one who found the rites too forbids touching not only certain animals, but there are also parts even of the sacrificed victims which he excludes from use, for reasons which the initiates know. If, then, one must master the belly and the parts below the belly, it is plain that from above we have received from the Lord, through the law, to cut out desire. And this would come about perfectly, if we should, without dissembling, condemn the fuel of desire — pleasure, I mean. And they say that the notion of it is a smooth and gentle motion with a certain perception. Enslaved to this, they say, Menelaus, after the capture of Ilium, having set out to kill Helen as having become the cause of so many evils, yet was not able to do it, overcome by her beauty, through which he came to the recollection of pleasure.

Whence, mocking, the tragic poets cried out reproachfully at him: "But you, when you saw the breast, casting away the sword, received a kiss, fawning on the traitorous bitch." And again: "Are swords, then, made dull by beauty?" But I welcome Antisthenes, who says: "Aphrodite I would even shoot down, if I caught her, because she has corrupted many noble and good women of ours." And he calls love a vice of nature; "and the wretched, being weaker than it, call the disease a god." For it is shown by these things that the more unlearned are overcome, through ignorance, by pleasure, which one must not welcome, even if it be called a god — that is, even if it happens to have been given from God toward the need of begetting children. And Xenophon too, plainly calling pleasure a vice, says: "O wretched one, what good do you know, or what noble thing do you regard? You who do not even await the desire of pleasant things, eating before you are hungry, drinking before you are thirsty; and, that you may eat pleasantly, contriving cooks; and, that you may drink pleasantly, preparing costly wines, and in summer running about seeking snow; and, that you may sleep pleasantly, preparing not only soft couches but also stools for the couches."

Whence, as Ariston said, against the whole tetrachord — pleasure, grief, fear, desire — there is need of much exercise and battle: "For these, these go within the entrails and disturb the heart of men." For even of those who are thought grave, pleasure makes the spirits "waxen," according to Plato, because "each pleasure and grief nails the soul to the body" of the man who does not separate and cross himself off from the passions. "He who has lost his own soul," says the Lord, "will save it" — either giving it over recklessly for the Saviour, as he himself has done for us, or releasing it from fellowship with the accustomed life. For if you should wish to release and remove and separate (for this is what the cross signifies) the soul from the delight and pleasure that is in this life, you will have it found and at rest in the expected hope.

And this would be the practice of death, if, with the appetites measured according to nature alone, defining nothing beyond the things according to nature toward the more or contrary to nature — where the sinful springs up — we should wish to be content. One must, then, put on the whole armour of God, that we may be able to stand against the methods of the devil, "since the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful with God for the pulling down of strongholds, casting down reasonings and every high thing that lifts itself up against the knowledge of God, and taking captive every thought into the obedience of Christ," says the divine Apostle. There is need of a man who will use, without marvelling and without confusion, the things from which the passions are set in motion — such as wealth and poverty, glory and ill repute, health and disease, life and death, toil and pleasure. For that we may use indifferently the indifferent things, we have need of much discrimination, as having been beforehand harmed by much weakness, and beforehand distorted by bad upbringing and nourishment together with ignorance.

The simple account, then, of our philosophy says that all the passions are imprints upon the soft and yielding soul, and, as it were, seals impressed by the spiritual powers, against which is our wrestling. For it is the work, I think, of the maleficent powers to try to effect, at each turn, something of their own state, toward overcoming and making their own those who have renounced them. And it follows fittingly that some are thrown down; but those who handle the contest in more athletic fashion, having contended in the all-in struggle and advanced even to the crown, the aforesaid powers, in much gore, then give out, marvelling at the victors. For of the things that move, some are moved by impulse and impression, as the animals, and some by transference, as the lifeless things. And they say that of the lifeless things too the plants are moved by transference toward growth, if one will grant the plants to be lifeless.

Of state, then, are the stones; of nature, the plants; and of impulse and impression, and again of the two aforesaid, the irrational animals too partake. But the rational power, being proper to the human soul, ought not to be impelled in the same way as the irrational animals, but to discern the impressions and not to be carried away together with them. The powers, then, of which we have spoken, hold out beauties and reputations and adulteries and pleasures and certain such alluring impressions to the easily-led souls, just as those who drive cattle shake green boughs before them; then, having over-reached those unable to discern the true from the false pleasure, and the perishable and outrageous from the holy beauty, they lead them away, having enslaved them. And each deceit, continually pressing upon the soul, imprints in it its image; and so the soul, unawares, bears about the image of the passion, the cause arising both from the bait and from our assent.

Those about Basilides are wont to call the passions "appendages," and to say that these are certain spirits existing in essence, appended to the rational soul according to a certain original disturbance and confusion; and that other bastard and heterogeneous natures of spirits grow upon these — such as of wolf, ape, lion, goat — whose properties, appearing about the soul, they say make the desires of the soul like to the animals. For of whatever properties they bear, the works of these they imitate; and they not only become akin to the impulses and impressions of the irrational animals, but they emulate even the motions and beauties of plants, because they bear the properties of plants too appended,

and further the properties of state too, such as the hardness of adamant. But against this doctrine we shall discourse later, when we treat of the soul; now only this must be noted, that the Basilidean man preserves the image of a certain Trojan horse, according to the poetic myth, having enfolded in one body an army of so many different spirits. Indeed, Isidore himself, the son of Basilides, perceiving the doctrine in his work On the Adventitious Soul, as though accusing himself, writes word for word thus: "For if you give anyone a conviction that the soul is not single-part, but that the passions of the worse come about by the violence of the appendages, the base among men will have no ordinary pretext to say: 'I was forced, I was carried off, I acted unwillingly, I worked without wishing it' — they themselves having led the desire of the evils, and not having fought with the violences of the appendages."

"But one must, having become superior by the reasoning part, appear to master the lesser creation in us." For he too supposes two souls in us, like the Pythagoreans, about whom we shall consider later. But Valentinus too, writing to certain ones, says in these very words concerning the appendages: "There is one good, whose frank manifestation is through the Son, and through him alone the heart can become pure, every wicked spirit being thrust out of the heart. For the many spirits dwelling in it do not allow it to be pure, but each of them accomplishes its own works, outraging it in many ways with desires not fitting. And it seems to me that the heart suffers something like the inn; for that too is bored through and dug up, and often filled with dung by men who lodge in it licentiously and take no forethought for the place, as being another's. In this way the heart too, so long as it has no forethought, is unclean, being a dwelling of many demons; but when the only good Father visits it, it is sanctified and shines with light; and so blessed is the man who has such a heart, for he will see God."

What, then, is the cause of such a soul's not being provided for from the beginning, let them tell us. For either it is not worthy (and how, then, does the providence approach it, as though from repentance?); or it happens to be a nature saved, as he himself wishes, and then it must from the beginning, being provided for through kinship, give no entrance to the unclean spirits, unless it be forced and convicted of weakness. For if he grants that, having repented, it chooses the better things, this is what he will say unwillingly, the very thing which the truth among us dogmatizes — that salvation comes from an obedient change, and not from nature. For as the exhalations both from the earth and from marshes are constituted into mists and cloudy gatherings, so the risings of the fleshly desires bring an ill state upon the soul, scattering the images of pleasure before the soul.

They darken, at any rate, the intellectual light, the soul drawing on the risings from desire and thickening the gatherings of the passions by the continuance of pleasures. But a lump of gold is not lifted from the earth, but, being boiled down, is filtered; then, having become pure, it is called gold — earth cleansed. "For ask, and it will be given you," is said to those able of themselves to choose the noblest things. And how we say that the activities of the devil and the unclean spirits sow themselves into the soul of the sinner, I need not many words to present, having set out as witness the apostolic Barnabas (and he was of the seventy and a fellow-worker of Paul), saying somewhat thus, word for word: "Before we believed in God, the dwelling-place of our heart was corruptible and weak, truly a temple built by hand; for it was full of idolatry and was a house of demons, through the doing of all that was contrary to God."

He says, then, that the sinners accomplish the activities corresponding to the demons, but does not say that the spirits themselves dwell in the soul of the unbeliever. For this reason he adds: "Take heed, that the temple of the Lord be built gloriously. How? Learn. Having received the forgiveness of sins, and having hoped upon the name, let us become new, again created from the beginning." For not the demons are driven out of us, but the sins, he says, are forgiven, which we accomplished, like them, before believing. With reason, then, he set over against this what follows: "Wherefore in our dwelling-place God truly dwells in us. How? His word of faith, his calling of the promise, the wisdom of the ordinances, the commandments of the teaching." I know that I met with a certain heresy, and the one who presided over it asserted, through the use of pleasure, that one must fight pleasure by pleasure — this noble gnostic (for he asserted himself to be a gnostic too) deserting to pleasure through a pretended fight; since, he said, it was no great thing to abstain from pleasure for one who had not tried it, but, being in it, not to be mastered; whence one must exercise through it within it.

But the wretch, over-reaching himself by the pleasure-loving art, escaped his own notice. To this opinion, evidently, Aristippus of Cyrene too inclined, the sophist who boasted of the truth. Reproached, at any rate, for continually consorting with the Corinthian courtesan, he said: "For I have Lais, and am not had by her." And such too are those who assert themselves to follow Nicolaus, bringing forward a saying of the man, by perversion, that one must abuse the flesh. But the noble man showed that one must cut short both the pleasures and the desires, and by this exercise wither away the impulses and assaults of the flesh. But they, poured out unto pleasure like goats, outraging the body as it were, give themselves to soft living, not knowing that the body wastes away, being by nature in flux, while their soul is buried in the mire of vice — pursuing the doctrine of pleasure itself, and not that of an apostolic man. For in what do these differ from Sardanapallus, whose life the epigram shows: "These I have, all that I ate and outraged and the pleasant things I suffered with love; but those many and blessed things are left behind. For I too am ashes, who reigned over great Ninus." For in general the passion of pleasure is not necessary, but a consequence of certain natural needs — hunger, thirst, cold, marriage.

If, then, without it one could drink, or take nourishment, or beget children, it would be shown that there is no other need of it. For pleasure is neither an activity nor a disposition, nor any part of us, but came into life for the sake of service, as they say salt does for the sake of the digesting of food. And pleasure, having thrown off the rein and mastered the house, begets the first desire, which is an irrational longing and appetite for what is pleasing to it — which persuaded even Epicurus to set pleasure as the end of the philosopher. He deifies, at any rate, "the stable condition of the flesh and the trustworthy hope concerning it." For what else is luxury but pleasure-loving daintiness and a superfluous excess toward soft living of men given over to it? Plainly Diogenes writes in a certain tragedy: "Those who, in the unmanly and beslimed luxury, stuffed in heart with pleasures, are unwilling to toil even a little." And the things upon these, as many as are shamefully said, yet worthily of the pleasure-lovers.

Wherefore it seems to me that the divine law necessarily hangs fear over us, that, by caution and attention, the philosopher may gain and keep freedom from anxiety, remaining unstumbling and sinless in all things. For peace and freedom are not otherwise won than through the unceasing and unresting counter-struggle against our passions . . . For these antagonists are stout and Olympic, sharper, so to speak, than wasps — and especially pleasure, which not only by day but also by night, in the very dreams, plots and bites alluringly with sorcery. How, then, are the Greeks any longer just in running down the law, when they themselves too teach the enslaving of pleasure by fear? Socrates, at any rate, commands to guard against the things that persuade us to eat when not hungry and to drink when not thirsty, and the glances and kisses of the beautiful, as fit to inject a venom worse than that of scorpions and spiders.

And Antisthenes too chooses rather to go mad than to feel pleasure; and Crates the Theban says: "But of these be master by a soul exulting in character, neither enslaved by gold nor by love that melts with longing, nor if there be any companion of outrage." And in sum he adds: "Unenslaved and unfulled by slavish pleasure, they love the immortal kingdom and freedom." The same man writes elsewhere outright that the poultice for the uncontrollable impulse toward the things of love is hunger, and, if not, a noose. And to Zeno the Stoic the comic poets bear witness of his teaching, though deriding it, somewhat thus: "For this man philosophizes a new philosophy: he teaches hunger and gets disciples; one loaf, dried figs for relish, and water to drink upon them."

All these, then, are not ashamed plainly to confess the benefit that comes from caution. But the true and not irrational wisdom, trusting not in bare oracles and divinations, but in shelters that cannot be wounded and in effective mysteries, the divine commandments, . . . practising itself by joint-exercise and joint-training, receives a divine power according to the part of it that is inspired by the Word. So already they write of the aegis of the poetic Zeus that it is terrible, "about which on all sides Fear is wreathed; in it is Strife, in it Valour, in it chilling Pursuit; and in it the Gorgon head of the dread monster, terrible and grim, the portent of aegis-bearing Zeus."

To those able rightly to discern the saving thing, I do not know if anything will appear dearer than the gravity of the law and its daughter, caution. But when it is said to sing "too high a pitch" — as the Lord too sang to certain ones, that none of those who emulate him might sing out of pitch and off the string — I understand it thus: not as too high a pitch, but to those unwilling to take up the divine yoke it is too high a pitch. For to the slack and weak the moderate seems too high, and to the unjust the fitting seems extremely just. For all whom pardon enters in because of their friendly disposition toward sins, these suppose the truth to be harshness, and the austerity severity, and the man who neither sins with them nor is dragged down with them, merciless.

Well, then, does the tragedy write concerning Hades: "And to what a god you will come, as to a Love that knew neither fairness nor grace, but cherished only bare justice." For even if you are not yet able to do the things commanded by the law, yet, perceiving that the noblest examples lie before us in it, we can nourish and increase the love of freedom; and here too we would be benefited, more eagerly, according to our power, in some things calling ourselves on, in some imitating, in some too being put to shame. For neither were the just men of old, who lived according to the law, "from oak of olden tale or from rock"; but by their willing to philosophize genuinely, bearing themselves whole, they offered themselves up to God, and it was reckoned unto faith.

Most nobly Zeno said of the Indians that he would rather see one Indian roasted than learn all the demonstrations about pain. But to us there are ungrudging springs of witnesses, beheld every day before our eyes, roasted, impaled, having their heads cut off. All these the fear from the law, having schooled them toward Christ, trained to display their caution even through bloods. "God stood in the assembly of gods, and in the midst he will judge gods." Who are these? Those superior to pleasure, those who surpass the passions, those who know each thing they do, the gnostics, those greater than the world. And again, "I said, you are gods, and all sons of the Most High." To whom does the Lord speak? To those who decline, so far as may be, all that is human. And the Apostle says: "For you are no longer in the flesh, but in the spirit." And again he says: "Being in the flesh, we war not according to the flesh; for flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does corruption inherit incorruption; but behold, you die as men" — the Spirit has said this, convicting us.
Euripides sketches a husband-loving woman with dignity, counselling:
She must seem to speak well, when he says something, even if he does not speak, and to work out what she means to say so as to please the man who is with her.
And again somewhere, the like to these:
And it is sweet, if he fares ill in anything, for the wife to be downcast together with her husband, and to have her share in common of grief and pleasure.
And showing the gentle and tender-loving spirit somehow thus, he adds, even in misfortunes:
But I, when you are sick, will be sick along with you and endure, and I will bear your evils with you, and nothing is bitter to me;
for with friends
one must
fare well and fare ill; for what else is friendship but this?

One must, then, train oneself toward caution about the things that fall under the passions, banishing, as the true philosophers do, the foods that lead to passion, and the slack relaxation at the bed, and luxury and the passions toward luxury, . . . a heavy contest to others, but to us no longer; for self-control is the greatest gift of God. For he himself has said, "I will not loose you, nor will I forsake you," having judged us worthy on account of our genuine choice. So, when we try to approach cautiously, the good yoke of the Lord will receive us, "from faith to faith," one charioteer driving each of us, according to advance, toward salvation, that the fitting fruit of happiness may result. And, according to Hippocrates of Cos, exercise is not only of the body, but also of the soul: "health is freedom from sluggishness in toils, freedom from satiety in food."

So marriage too is sanctified when it is perfected according to reason, if the union submits to God and is administered with a true heart in fullness of faith, the hearts being purified from an evil conscience and the body washed with pure water, and holding the confession of hope; for faithful is He who promised. And the happy marriage must be judged neither by wealth nor by beauty, but by virtue. "No woman," says the tragedy,
Then, as though giving counsels, she says:
