First of all, this holds: even if the husband be unshapely, he must seem to be shapely to the woman who has got a mind. For it is not the eye that judges, but the mind that sees,
and the things following. For very properly the Scripture said that the woman was given to the man by God as a helper.

It is plain, then, I think, that she will choose to heal by reason, with persuasion, each of the grievous things that befall from the husband in the housekeeping; but if he should not obey, then she will try, as far as is possible for human nature, to lead a sinless life—whether she must die with reason or live—reckoning God to be the helper and partner of such conduct, who is truly her support and saviour both for the present and for the future, having made Him the general and leader of every action, considering prudence and righteousness her work, and making love of God her end.

Gracefully, then, in the epistle to Titus, the apostle says that the elder women must be in a state befitting holiness, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, that they may train the young women to be husband-lovers, child-lovers, prudent, pure, keepers of the house, good, subject to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed. "But rather," he says, "pursue peace with all men, and sanctification, without which no one shall see the Lord, looking carefully lest anyone be a fornicator or profane, as Esau, who for one meal gave up his birthright; and lest any root of bitterness springing up cause trouble, and by it the many be defiled."

Then, as though setting a coping-stone on the question concerning marriage, he adds: "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled; but fornicators and adulterers God shall judge." And, one aim and one end having been shown to man and woman, what the perfect thing is, Peter says in his epistle: "Though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials, that the proof of your faith, far more precious than perishing gold yet tested through fire, may be found unto praise and glory at the revelation of Jesus Christ; whom not having seen you love, in whom now, though not seeing Him, yet believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory, receiving the end of faith, the salvation of souls." Wherefore Paul too boasts that he has been, for Christ's sake, in labours more abundantly, in stripes above measure, in deaths often.

Concerning the fashioning of the doctrines of the philosophers from the Hebrews, we shall treat a little later; but first, as was the next thing, we must now speak of the times of Moses, by which it will be shown beyond dispute that the philosophy of the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. These matters have been treated exactly by Tatian in his Against the Greeks, and also by Cassian in the first book of his Exegetica; yet the present work requires that we too run over what has been said on the subject. Apion the grammarian, then, surnamed Pleistonices, in the fourth book of his Egyptian Histories — though he was hostile in disposition toward the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by race, so that he even composed a book against the Jews — mentioning Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the deeds done in his time, cites as witness Ptolemy of Mendes. And his words run thus: "Amosis razed Auaris, living in the time of Inachus the Argive, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his Chronicles." And this Ptolemy was a priest, who, setting out the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, says that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the journey of the Jews out of Egypt took place under the leadership of Moses; from which it is seen that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of Greek matters are the Argive, those from Inachus I mean, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. Younger than these by forty generations are the Attic matters, those from Cecrops, the two-natured and earth-born, as Tatian says word for word; and by nine generations the Arcadian, those from Pelasgus — he too is said to be earth-born. And by another two generations younger than these are the Phthiotic matters, those from Deucalion. From Inachus to the time of the Trojan War twenty generations, or one more, are reckoned, and, so to speak, four hundred years and beyond. And if the Assyrian matters are, by many years, older than the Greek, from what Ctesias says, the departure of Moses from Egypt, under Amosis the Egyptian and under Inachus the Argive, will appear to fall in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire, and in the thirty-second year of the dynasty of Belochus the eighth. And in Greece there were, under Phoroneus who came after Inachus, the flood in the time of Ogyges and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Europs, then of Telchis — and the kingdom of Cres in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man; whence the author of the Phoronis too said that he was "the father of mortal men."

From this Plato, following Acusilaus, writes in the Timaeus: "And once, wishing to draw them on to discourse about the ancient things, he tries to tell the most ancient things of this city, concerning Phoroneus, said to be the first, and Niobe, and the things after the flood." Under Phorbas was Actaeus, from whom Attica is called Actaea. Under Triopas were Prometheus and Atlas and Epimetheus and the two-natured Cecrops and Io. Under Crotopus was the conflagration in the time of Phaethon and the deluge in the time of Deucalion. Under Sthenelus were both the kingdom of Amphictyon and the coming of Danaus to the Peloponnese, and the founding of Dardania by Dardanus, whom "first," says Homer, "the cloud-gatherer Zeus begot," and the carrying back of Europa from Phoenicia to Crete. Under Lynceus were the rape of the maiden and the founding of the precinct at Eleusis, and the husbandry of Triptolemus, and the coming of Cadmus to Thebes, and the kingdom of Minos. Under Proetus was the war of Eumolpus against the Athenians. Under Acrisius were the crossing of Pelops from Phrygia, and the arrival of Ion at Athens, and the second Cecrops, and the deeds of Perseus and of Dionysus, and Orpheus and Musaeus.

And in the eighteenth year of the kingdom of Agamemnon Ilium was taken, in the first year of the reign at Athens of Demophon, son of Theseus, on the twelfth of the month Thargelion, as Dionysius the Argive says; but Agias and Dercylus say on the eighth from the end of the month Panemus; for Hellanicus says on the twelfth of the month Thargelion. And some of those who have written the Attic histories say on the eighth from the end, in the last year of the reign of Menestheus, when the moon was full. "It was midnight," says the author of the Little Iliad, "and the bright moon was rising." Others say on the same day of the month Scirophorion. And Theseus, being a rival of Heracles, is older than the Trojan matters by one generation. For Homer mentions Tlepolemus, who was a son of Heracles, as having marched against Ilium.

Moses, then, is shown to be earlier than the deification of Dionysus by six hundred and four years, if indeed Dionysus was made a god in the thirty-second year of the reign of Perseus, as Apollodorus says in his Chronicles. And from Dionysus to Heracles and the chiefs about Jason who sailed in the Argo, sixty-three years are reckoned together; and Asclepius and the Dioscuri sailed with them, as Apollonius of Rhodes testifies in his Argonautica. And from the reign of Heracles in Argos to the deification of Heracles himself and of Asclepius thirty-eight years are reckoned, according to the chronographer Apollodorus. From that point to the deification of Castor and Polydeuces, fifty-three years. And somewhere here is the capture of Ilium. And if we must trust Hesiod the poet too, let us hear him: "To Zeus the Atlantid Maia bore glorious Hermes, the herald of the immortals, having mounted the holy bed; and the Cadmean Semele bore him a shining son, having joined in love, Dionysus the bringer of much joy."

Cadmus, the father of Semele, comes to Thebes in the time of Lynceus and becomes the inventor of Greek letters; and Triopas is contemporary with Isis in the seventh generation from Inachus (and they say Isis is the same as Io, because she went, wandering, through the whole earth); and Ister, in his work On the Egyptian Colony, says she was the daughter of Prometheus. And Prometheus, under Triopas, is in the seventh generation after Moses, so that Moses is shown to have flourished even before the origin of mankind according to the Greeks. And Leon, who treated of the gods of Egypt, says that Isis is called Demeter by the Greeks, who comes in the time of Lynceus, in the eleventh generation later than Moses. And Apis, the king of Argos, founds Memphis, as Aristippus says in the first book of his Arcadica. And Aristeas the Argive says that this man was surnamed Sarapis, and that this is the one whom the Egyptians worship; while Nymphodorus of Amphipolis, in the third book of the Customs of Asia, says that the bull Apis, having died and been embalmed, was laid in a coffin (soros) in the temple of the honoured deity, and that from this he was called Soroapis, and later, by a certain habit of the natives, Sarapis.

And Apis is the third from Inachus. Leto, indeed, is in the time of Tityus, for "Leto he dragged, the glorious consort of Zeus"; and Tityus was contemporary with Tantalus. With reason, then, the Boeotian Pindar too writes: "And in time Apollo was born" — and no wonder, since he is found serving Admetus, together with Heracles, for a great year. And Zethus and Amphion, the inventors of music, lived about the age of Cadmus. And if anyone tells us that Phemonoe first delivered oracles to Acrisius, let him know that twenty-seven years after Phemonoe came Orpheus and Musaeus and Linus, the teacher of Heracles. And Homer and Hesiod are much younger than the Trojan matters; and after them, much younger still, are the lawgivers among the Greeks, Lycurgus and Solon, and the seven sages, and those about Pherecydes the Syrian and Pythagoras the great, who lived somewhere low down about the Olympiads, as we have shown. So Moses is proved to be older than most of the gods among the Greeks, and not only than the so-called sages and poets.

And not he alone, but the Sibyl too is older than Orpheus; for there are several accounts both of her surname and of the oracles ascribed to her — that, being a Phrygian, she was called Artemis, and that she, coming to Delphi, sang: "O Delphians, servants of the far-shooting Apollo, I have come to deliver the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus, being wroth with my own brother Apollo." And there is another, the Erythraean, called Herophile; Heraclides of Pontus mentions these in his work On Oracles. I pass over the Egyptian and the Italian, who dwelt at the Carmalum in Rome, whose son was Evander, the founder of the shrine of Pan in Rome called the Lupercal.

It is worthwhile here to inquire also into the times of the other prophets among the Hebrews after Moses. After the end of Moses' life, Joshua succeeds to the leadership of the people, making war for sixty-five years, and resting in the good land another twenty-five. But, as the book of Joshua contains, the man just named succeeded Moses for twenty-seven years. Then, the Hebrews having sinned, they are handed over to Chusachar, king of Mesopotamia, for eight years, as the book of Judges relates; and afterward, having besought God, they receive as leader Gothoniel, the younger brother of Caleb, of the tribe of Judah, who, having killed the king of Mesopotamia, ruled the people for fifty years in succession. And again, having sinned, they were handed over to Eglom, king of the Moabites, for eighteen years; and when they turned back, Aod led them again for eighty years, an ambidextrous man of the tribe of Ephraim; this is the man who slew Eglom.

And when Aod had died, having sinned again, they were handed over to Jabim, king of Canaan, for twenty years. In his time Deborah prophesies, the wife of Lapidoth, of the tribe of Ephraim; and the high priest was Ozius, the son of Riesus. Under her leadership of the army, Barak, the son of Benner, of the tribe of Naphtali, having drawn up against Sisera, the commander-in-chief of Jabim, conquered; and from this Deborah ruled the people, judging, for forty years. And when she had died, the people, having sinned again, is handed over to the Midianites for seven years. After these, Gideon, of the tribe of Manasseh, the son of Joas, having gone out to war with three hundred men, and having destroyed a hundred and twenty thousand of them, ruled for forty years. After him his son Abimelech for three years. Him succeeds Bolea, son of Bedan, son of Charran, of the tribe of Ephraim, who ruled twenty-three years. After him, the people, having sinned again, is handed over to the Ammonites for eighteen years.

And when they had repented, Jephthah the Gileadite, of the tribe of Manasseh, leads them, and ruled six years; after him ruled Abatthan of Bethlehem, of the tribe of Judah, seven years; then Hebron the Zebulonite, eight years; then Eglom of Ephraim, eight years. But some join Hebron's eight years to Abatthan's seven. And after this the people, having sinned again, comes under the foreign Philistines for forty years. And when they had turned back, Samson, of the tribe of Dan, leads them, having conquered the foreigners in war. He ruled for twenty years. And after him, there being no rule, Eli the priest judged the people for forty years. Him Samuel the prophet succeeds, with whom Saul reigned, holding rule for twenty-seven years. This Samuel also anointed David.

And Samuel died two years before Saul, under the high priest Abimelech. He anointed Saul as king, who was the first to reign over Israel after the judges, of whom the whole number, down to Samuel, comes to four hundred and sixty-three years and seven months. Then, through the first book of Kingdoms, the years of Saul are twenty, since, being renewed, he reigned. And after the death of Saul, David, the son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah, reigns the second time, in Hebron, for forty years, as the second book of Kingdoms contains; and the high priest was Abiathar, the son of Abimelech, of the kindred of Eli; and Gad and Nathan prophesy in his time. So from Joshua the son of Nun until David took over the kingdom there are, as some say, four hundred and fifty years; but, as the chronography here set forth shows, five hundred and twenty-three years and seven months are reckoned together, down to the death of David.

And after these things Solomon, the son of David, reigned forty years. In his time Nathan continues prophesying, who also exhorted him concerning the building of the temple; likewise Achias of Shilom prophesies; and both kings, David and Solomon, were prophets. And Sadon the high priest was the first to perform priestly service in the temple which Solomon built, being the eighth from Aaron the first high priest. So from Moses to the age of Solomon there are, as some say, five hundred and ninety-five years; but, as others say, five hundred and seventy-six. And if one should reckon together with the four hundred and fifty years from Joshua to David the forty years of Moses' campaign and the other eighty years which Moses had lived before the exodus of the Hebrews from Egypt came about, and should add to these the forty years of the reign of David, he will bring the whole to six hundred and ten years.

But our chronography proceeds more exactly, if to the five hundred and twenty-three years and seven months down to the death of David one should add the hundred and twenty years of Moses and the forty of Solomon; for the whole, down to the death of Solomon, will come to six hundred and eighty-three years and seven months. Hiram gives his own daughter to Solomon at the time when, after the capture of Troy, Menelaus came to Phoenicia, as Menander of Pergamum and Laetus say in their Phoenician histories. And after Solomon, Rehoboam his son reigns seventeen years, and the high priest was Abimelech, the son of Sadok. In his time, the kingdom being divided, Jeroboam, of the tribe of Ephraim, the servant of Solomon, reigns in Samaria; and there still prophesy Achias the Shilonite and Samaias the son of Ailam, and the man who came from Judah against Jeroboam and prophesied at the altar.

After him Abium his son reigns three years, and likewise his son Asa forty-one; this man, in his old age, suffered from gout; and in his time Iu, the son of Ananias, prophesies. After him Jehoshaphat his son reigns twenty-five years; in his time prophesy Elijah the Tishbite and Michaias the son of Iebla and Abdias the son of Ananias. And in the time of Michaias there was also a false prophet, Sedekias the son of Chanaan. These are followed by the reign of Joram the son of Jehoshaphat, for eight years, in whose time Elijah prophesies, and after Elijah, Elisha the son of Saphat. In his time those in Samaria ate dove's dung and their own children. And the time of Jehoshaphat extends from the last things of the third book of Kingdoms to the fourth. And in the time of Joram, Elijah was taken up, and Elisha the son of Saphat began to prophesy for six years, being forty years old. Then Ochozias reigned one year, in whose time Elisha still prophesies, and with him Abdadonaeus.

After him Gotholia, the mother of Ozias, reigns eight years, having killed the children of her own brother; for she was of the family of Ahab. But Josabaia, the sister of Ozias, stole away Joas, the son of Ozias, and afterward set the kingdom upon him. In the time of this Gotholia Elisha still prophesies, after whom reigns, as I said before, Joas, who was saved by Josabaia, the wife of Jodae the high priest; and the whole comes to forty years. So from Solomon to the death of Elisha the prophet there are, as some say, a hundred and five years; but, as others say, a hundred and two; but, as the chronography here set forth shows, from the reign of Solomon, a hundred and eighty-one years.

From the Trojan matters to the birth of Homer is, according to Philochorus, a hundred and eighty years, after the Ionian colony. But Aristarchus, in his Notes on Archilochus, says he flourished about the Ionian colony, which took place a hundred and forty years after the Trojan matters. And Apollodorus says it was a hundred years after the Ionian colony, when Agesilaus the son of Doryssaeus reigned over the Spartans, so that Lycurgus the lawgiver, still a young man, overlapped with him. But Euthymenes, in his Chronicles, says he flourished together with Hesiod, in the time of Acastus, and was born in Chios about the two-hundredth year after the capture of Ilium. Of this opinion too is Archemachus in the third book of his Euboica; so that he and Hesiod are even younger than Elisha the prophet. And if anyone wishes to follow the grammarian Crates and says that Homer lived about the return of the Heraclidae, eighty years after the capture of Ilium, he will again be found later than Solomon, in whose time was the coming of Menelaus to Phoenicia, as has been said. And Eratosthenes sets the age of Homer after the hundredth year from the capture of Ilium. Indeed, Theopompus, in the forty-third book of his Philippica, relates that Homer was born five hundred years after those who marched against Ilium. And Euphorion, in his work On the Aleuadae, places him in the time of Gyges, who began to reign from the eighteenth Olympiad, and whom he says was the first to be called "tyrant." And Sosibius the Laconian, in his register of times, sets Homer in the eighth year of the reign of Charillus, the son of Polydectes. Now Charillus reigns sixty-four years, after whom his son Nicander reigns thirty-nine; and in the thirty-fourth year of his reign, he says, the first Olympiad was established; so that Homer is some ninety years before the establishment of the Olympic games.

After Joas, Amasias his son succeeds to the kingdom for thirty-nine years; him Ozias likewise, his son, for fifty-two years, and this man died a leper; and in his time prophesy Amos and Isaiah his son, and Hosea the son of Beeri, and Jonah the son of Amathi, of Geth Chober, who preached to the Ninevites, the one who came forth from the whale. Then Jonathan, the son of Ozias, reigns sixteen years; in his time Isaiah still prophesies, and Hosea and Micah the Morasthite and Joel the son of Bathuel.

Him succeeds his son Ahaz, for sixteen years; in whose fifteenth year Israel was led away to Babylon, and Salmanasar, the king of the Assyrians, removed those in Samaria to the Medes and to Babylon. Again, Ahaz is succeeded by Hosea for eight years, then Hezekiah for twenty-nine years. To this man, for his holiness, near the end of his life, God grants through Isaiah to live another fifteen years, by the going-back of the sun. Down to this time Isaiah and Hosea and Micah continue prophesying. And these are said to have lived after the age of Lycurgus the lawgiver of the Spartans; for Dieuchidas, in the fourth book of his Megarica, sets the flourishing of Lycurgus about the two hundred and ninetieth year after the capture of Ilium. And Isaiah, from the reign of Solomon, in whose time Menelaus was shown to have come to Phoenicia, in the three-hundredth year, is found still prophesying, and Micah with him, and Hosea, and Joel the son of Bathuel.

After Hezekiah his son Manasseh reigns fifty-five years, then his son Amos two years, after whom Josiah his son, the most law-abiding, thirty-one years. This man set the limbs of men upon the limbs of the idols, as it is written in Leviticus. In his eighteenth year the Passover was kept, which had not been performed since Samuel, nor in the time between. Then too Chelkias the priest, the father of the prophet Jeremiah, having lighted upon the book of the Law laid away in the temple, read it and died. In his time prophesy Oldas and Sophonias and Jeremiah. And in the time of Jeremiah Ananias becomes a false prophet. This Josiah, having disregarded Jeremiah the prophet, was slain by Nechao, king of Egypt, at the river Euphrates, having gone to meet him as he set out against the Assyrians.

Josiah is succeeded by Jechonias, also called Joachas, his son, for three months and ten days. Nechao, king of Egypt, having bound him, led him away to Egypt, setting up in his place as king his brother Joakim, on tribute of the land, for eleven years. After him his namesake Joakim reigns three months, then Sedekias eleven years. And down to this time Jeremiah continues prophesying; and there prophesy also Buzi and Urias the son of Samaeus, and Ambacum with him; and the line of the Hebrew kings comes to an end. So from the birth of Moses to this captivity there are, as some say, nine hundred and seventy-two years; but, according to the exact chronography, a thousand and eighty-five years, six months, ten days; and from the reign of David to the captivity that came about under the Chaldeans, four hundred and fifty-two years and six months; but, as our exactness of the times reckons it, four hundred and eighty-two years, six months, ten days.

And in the twelfth year of the reign of Sedekias, Nebuchadnezzar, seventy years before the rule of the Persians, marched against the Phoenicians and the Jews, as Berossus says in his Chaldean histories. And Juba, writing about the Assyrians, confesses that he took the history from Berossus, bearing witness to the man's truth. Nebuchadnezzar, then, having blinded Sedekias, leads him away to Babylon and removes all the people (and the captivity lasts seventy years), except a few, who fled into Egypt. And in the time of Sedekias too there still prophesy Jeremiah and Ambacum; and in the fifth year of his reign Ezekiel prophesies in Babylon, after whom Naum the prophet, then Daniel; and again, after him, prophesy Aggaeus and Zacharias, in the time of Darius the First, for two years; after whom the Messenger among the Twelve.

And after Aggaeus and Zacharias, Nehemiah, the chief cup-bearer of Artaxerxes, the son of Acheli the Israelite, builds the city of Jerusalem and repairs the temple. In this captivity are Esther and Mardochaeus, of whom a book is current, as also that of the Maccabees. During this captivity Misael, Ananias, and Azarias, unwilling to serve the image, are cast into a furnace of fire and saved by the appearance of an angel. Then Daniel, cast into a lions' den on account of the dragon, fed by the providence of God through Ambacum, is brought safe on the seventh day. Here too the sign of Jonah came about; and Tobias, through Raphael the angel, takes Sarah to wife, the demon of hers having killed her seven first suitors; and after the marriage of Tobias his father Tobit recovers his sight.

Here Zorobabel, having conquered his rivals by wisdom, obtains from Darius, having bought it, the renewal of Jerusalem, and with Esdras returns to the land of his fathers; through him come about the redemption of the people, the recognition and renewal of the inspired oracles, the keeping of the saving Passover, and the dissolution of foreign marriages. Cyrus too had proclaimed beforehand the restoration of the Hebrews; and when the promise was fulfilled under Darius, the feast of the dedication is kept, as also at the time of the tabernacle. And the whole of the years, together with those of the captivity, down to the restoration of the people, comes, from the birth of Moses, to one thousand one hundred and fifty-five years, six months, ten days; and from the reign of David, as some say, five hundred and fifty-two years, but, more exactly, five hundred and seventy-two years, six months, ten days.

From the captivity, then, that came about under Jeremiah the prophet, when it was carried to Babylon, were fulfilled the things spoken by Daniel the prophet, which run thus: "Seventy weeks have been cut short upon your people and upon the holy city, to finish sin, and to seal up sins, and to wipe out the iniquities, and to make atonement, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal vision and prophet, and to anoint the Holy of Holies. And you shall know and understand, that from the going forth of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem until Christ the leader are seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and it shall return and the street and the wall be built, and the times shall be emptied. And after the sixty-two weeks the anointing shall be utterly destroyed, and there is no judgment for it; and the city and the holy place he shall destroy together with the leader who comes; they shall be cut off in a flood; and to the end of the war, cut short, with desolations. And he shall make firm a covenant for many for one week; and in the half of the week my sacrifice and libation shall be taken away; and upon the temple the abomination of the desolations, and until the consummation of time a consummation shall be given upon the desolation. And in the half of the week he shall cause to cease the incense of sacrifice and of the pinnacle of desolation, until the consummation and the haste of the order of desolation."

That the temple, then, was built in seven weeks, this is plain; for it is written in Esdras. And so Christ became king of the Jews, the leader, in the fulfilment of the seven weeks, in Jerusalem; and in the sixty-two weeks all Judaea was at rest and was without wars; and our Lord Christ, the Holy of the holy, having come and fulfilled the vision and the prophet, was anointed in the flesh by the spirit of his Father, in these sixty-two weeks, as the prophet said. And in the one week, the half of which week Nero held when he was reigning, and in the holy city Jerusalem set up the abomination; and in the half of the week he himself was slain, and Otho and Galba and Vitellius; but Vespasian prevailed and tore down Jerusalem and laid waste the holy place. And that these things are so, it is plain to the one able to understand, as the prophet too has said.

In the fulfilment of the eleventh year, then, at the beginning of the following one, when Joakim was reigning, the captivity to Babylon comes about under King Nebuchadnezzar, in his seventh year of reigning over the Assyrians, while Vaphres reigned over the Egyptians in his second year, and Philip was archon at Athens in the first year of the forty-eighth Olympiad; and the captivity remained for seventy years, ending in the second year of Darius the son of Hystaspes, who became king of the Persians and Assyrians and Egyptians, in whose time, as I said before, Aggaeus and Zacharias and the Messenger among the Twelve prophesy, and the high priest was Jesus the son of Josedek. And in the second year of the reign of Darius, whom Herodotus says broke the rule of the Magi, Zorobabel the son of Salathiel is sent to raise and adorn the temple in Jerusalem.

But Epicurus, setting the happiness equal to the gods in the not being hungry nor thirsty nor cold, uttered, speaking impiously, "In these things I would fight even with father Zeus" — dogmatizing a blessed victory of dung-eating pigs, and not of rational and philosophic beings. For of those who begin from pleasure . . . are the Cyrenaics and Epicurus; for these say outright that the end is to live pleasantly, and that pleasure alone is the perfect good. And Epicurus says that the removal of pain too is pleasure; and he says that to be chosen is what first, of itself, draws toward itself, being plainly in motion. And Dinomachus and Calliphon said the end is to do all that depends on oneself for the sake of attaining and obtaining pleasure; and Hieronymus the Peripatetic said the end is to live without disturbance, but the final good is happiness alone. And Diodorus likewise, being of the same school, declares the end to be to live without disturbance and nobly.

The times of the Persians too, then, are reckoned together thus: Cyrus thirty years, Cambyses nineteen, Darius forty-six, Xerxes twenty-six, Artaxerxes forty-one, Darius eight, Artaxerxes forty-two, Ochus eight, Arses three. . . . The whole of the Persian period comes together to two hundred and thirty-five years. And Alexander the Macedonian, having overthrown this Darius, begins to reign in the years above set out. Likewise, then, the times of the Macedonian kings are brought down thus: Alexander eighteen years, Ptolemy the son of Lagus forty years, Ptolemy Philadelphus twenty-seven years, then Euergetes twenty-five years, then Philopator seventeen years, after whom Epiphanes twenty-four years; him Philometor succeeds and reigns thirty-five years, after whom Physcon twenty-nine years, then Lathurus thirty-six years, then the one surnamed Dionysus twenty-nine years.

Epicurus, then, and the Cyrenaics say the first thing proper is pleasure; for virtue, they say, came in for the sake of pleasure and produced pleasure. But according to those about Calliphon, virtue entered in for the sake of pleasure, but afterward, in time, having beheld the beauty about it, presented itself as of equal honour with the beginning — that is, with pleasure. But those about Aristotle render the end to be living according to virtue, but say that neither happiness nor the end is present to everyone who has virtue; for the wise man, when tortured and falling into unwished-for fortunes, and on account of these willingly wishing to escape from life, is neither blessed nor happy. For virtue too needs some time; for it does not result in one day, and it is constituted in a perfect being, since, as they say, a child is never happy; and the perfect time would be the human life. Happiness, then, is filled up out of the threefold kind of goods. So neither the poor, nor the obscure, nor the sickly, nor, if anyone be a slave, is happy, according to them. . . .

After all these Cleopatra reigned twenty-two years, after whom the kingdom of Cleopatra's children of eighteen days. The times of the Macedonian kings, then, come together to three hundred and twelve years and eighteen days. So those who prophesied in the time of Darius the son of Hystaspes, in the second year of his reign — Aggaeus and Zacharias and the Messenger among the Twelve, who prophesied in the first year of the forty-eighth Olympiad — are shown to be older than Pythagoras, who is placed about the sixty-second Olympiad, and than the oldest of the sages among the Greeks, Thales, who lived about the fiftieth Olympiad. And those reckoned with Thales among the sages were his contemporaries, as Andron says in his Tripod. For Heraclitus, being later than Pythagoras, mentions him in his treatise.

Again, Zeno the Stoic holds the end to be living according to virtue; Cleanthes, living in agreement with nature; and Diogenes held the end to lie in good reasoning, which he took to lie in the choosing of the things according to nature. And Antipater, his pupil, supposes the end to lie in continually and inviolably choosing the things according to nature and rejecting the things contrary to nature. And Archedemus again thus expounded the end to be, living, choosing the greatest and most authoritative things according to nature, which it is not possible to overstep. Besides these, Panaetius declared the end to be living according to the occasions given us from nature. And above all, Posidonius declared the end to be living, contemplating the truth and order of the universe, and helping to constitute it so far as possible, being led in nothing by the irrational part of the soul. And some of the younger Stoics rendered it thus: that the end is to live in keeping with the constitution of man. Why should I reckon up Ariston for you? He said the end is indifference; but the indifferent simply leaves the indifferent. Or should I bring into the midst the things of Herillus? He sets the end to be living according to knowledge. For some hold that the younger ones from the Academy render the end to be the secure withholding of judgment toward the impressions. Indeed, Lyco the Peripatetic said the true joy of the soul is the end, as Leucimus said the joy over noble things. And Critolaus, himself too a Peripatetic, said it is the perfection of a life flowing well according to nature, indicating the threefold perfection filled up out of the three kinds.

Hence, beyond dispute, older than the age of the prophets just mentioned, together with the so-called seven sages, would be the first Olympiad, which is also shown to be later than the Trojan matters by four hundred and seven years. It is easy, then, to see that Solomon, who lived in the time of Menelaus (and Menelaus was in the time of the Trojan matters), is older by many years than the sages among the Greeks. And by how many years Moses again is earlier than Solomon, has been shown by us in what went before. And Alexander, surnamed Polyhistor, in his treatise On the Jews, recorded certain letters of Solomon to Vaphres the king of Egypt and to the king of the Tyrians of Phoenicia, and theirs to Solomon, by which it is shown that Vaphres sent him eighty thousand Egyptian men for the building of the temple, and the other an equal number, together with a Tyrian master-builder of a Jewish mother, of the tribe of David, named, as it is there written, Hyperon.

We must not, then, stop, contenting ourselves with these things, but must be as ambitious as possible to set out also the things dogmatized by the natural philosophers about the matter before us. For they say that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae said that the end of life is contemplation and the freedom that comes from it; and Heraclitus of Ephesus, well-pleasing. And Heraclides of Pontus relates that Pythagoras handed down that the science of the perfection of the numbers of the soul is happiness. But the Abderites too teach that there is an end: Democritus, in his work On the End, cheerfulness, which he also called "well-being" (and he often adds: "For delight and lack of delight are the boundary of things at their height"); and Hecataeus, self-sufficiency; and Apollodotus of Cyzicus, leading of the soul, as Nausiphanes, freedom from astonishment — for this, he said, was called by Democritus "freedom from amazement." Further, besides these, Diotimus declared the all-completeness of goods, which is named "well-being," to be the end. Again, Antisthenes said freedom from conceit; and those called Annicereans, from the Cyrenaic succession, set down no defined end of the whole life, but said that of each action the proper end is the pleasure that results from the action. These Cyrenaics reject Epicurus' definition of pleasure — that is, the removal of pain — calling it the condition of a corpse; for we rejoice not only over pleasures, but also over companionships and ambitions. But Epicurus thinks that all joy of the soul comes about upon the flesh as primarily affected.

Here I find "the perfect" taken in many ways, according to the man who succeeds in each virtue. One is perfected, then, both as devout and as patient and as continent and as a worker and as a martyr and as a gnostic; but perfect in all things at once I do not know if any man is, while still being a man, save only the One who put on man for our sake. And yet by the bare law a man might be perfect, the law that professes abstinence from evils; but this is a road both to the gospel and to good-doing. But the gnostic perfection of the man under the law is the taking on of the gospel, that the man under the law may become perfect; for so Moses, who was under the law, foretold that one must hear, that we might receive, according to the apostle, Christ the fullness of the law. And in the gospel the gnostic already advances, not using the law merely as a step, but understanding it and perceiving it as the Lord who gave the covenants handed it down to the apostles. And even if he should conduct himself rightly (as indeed it is impossible for knowledge to follow upon evil-doing), and be moreover a martyr, having most rightly confessed out of love—he would receive greater worth, as among men; yet not even thus will he be reckoned "perfect" while still in the flesh, since the consummation of life has anticipated this appellation, the gnostic martyr having already anticipated the displaying and presenting authentically of the perfect work through gnostic love, the spirit being sent forward when the blood is offered with thanks.

Indeed, Onomacritus the Athenian, whose are said to be the poems ascribed to Orpheus, is found in the time of the rule of the Pisistratids, about the fiftieth Olympiad. And Orpheus, who sailed with Heracles, was the teacher of Musaeus. For Amphion precedes the Trojan matters by two generations; and Demodocus and Phemius, after the capture of Ilium (the one among the Phaeacians, the other among the suitors), were of good repute for their playing of the lyre. And the oracles ascribed to Musaeus they say are Onomacritus'; the Krater of Orpheus is Zopyrus' of Heraclea, and the Descent into Hades is Prodicus' of Samos. Ion of Chios, in his Triagmoi, relates that Pythagoras too referred some things to Orpheus. And Epigenes, in his work On the Poetry Ascribed to Orpheus, says that the Descent into Hades and the Sacred Discourse are by Cercops the Pythagorean, and the Peplos and the Physica by Brontinus. Indeed, some make Terpander archaic; Hellanicus, at any rate, relates that he lived in the time of Midas, while Phanias, setting Lesches the Lesbian before Terpander, makes Terpander younger than Archilochus, and says Lesches contended with Arctinus and conquered. And Xanthus the Lydian says Thasos was founded about the eighteenth Olympiad (but Dionysius says about the fifteenth), so that it is evident that Archilochus was already known after the twentieth Olympiad. He mentions, at any rate, the destruction of the Magnesians as recently happened. Simonides, then, is placed in the time of Archilochus; but Callinus is older by not much, for Archilochus mentions the Magnesians as destroyed, while Callinus mentions them as prosperous. And Eumelus the Corinthian, being older, is said to have overlapped Archias, the founder of Syracuse.

And Metrodorus, in his work On the fact that the cause in ourselves toward happiness is greater than that from things, says: "What good of the soul is there other than the stable condition of the flesh and the trustworthy hope concerning it?"

Blessed, then, would he be from this point, and rightly proclaimed perfect, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God and not from us, as the apostle says; only let us preserve the power of choice and the love, "being afflicted in everything, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed." For those who hasten toward consummation must, according to the same apostle, "give no offence in anything, but in everything commend themselves," not to men, but to God. And let it be, as a consequence, that we obey men too; for this too is reasonable on account of the slanderous blasphemies. And the commendation is "in much endurance, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings, in purity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned love, in the word of truth, in the power of God," that we may be temples of God, "cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit"; "and I," He says, "will receive you, and will be to you a Father, and you shall be to me sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty." "Let us perfect, then," he says, "holiness in the fear of God." For though fear begets grief, "I rejoice," he says, "not that you were grieved,

And these things we have been led to say, because the poets of the Cycle especially are placed among the very ancient. And already among the Greeks too many oracle-mongers are said to have arisen, like the Bacides (one a Boeotian, the other an Arcadian), who foretold many things to many. And by the counsel of the Athenian Amphilytus, Pisistratus too established his tyranny, when the man had pointed out the moment for the attack. For let there be silence about Cometes the Cretan, Cinyras the Cypriot, Admetus the Thessalian, Aristaeus the Cyrenian, Amphiaraus the Athenian, Timoxenus the Corcyrean, Demaenetus the Phocaean, Epigenes the Thespian, Nicias the Carystian, Ariston the Thessalian, Dionysius the Carthaginian, Cleophon the Corinthian, and Hippo the daughter of Chiron, and Boeo and Manto, and the multitude of the Sibyls — the Samian, the Colophonian, the Cymaean, the Erythraean, Phyto, Taraxandra, the Macetian, the Thessalian, the Thesprotian — and Calchas again and Mopsus, who lived in the time of the Trojan matters; but Mopsus is older, as having sailed with the Argonauts.

but that you were grieved unto repentance; for you were grieved according to God, that you might suffer loss in nothing through us. For godly grief works repentance unto a salvation not to be repented of; but the grief of the world works death. For behold, this very thing, your being grieved according to God, what diligence it has wrought in you—nay, what defence, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what avenging! In everything you have commended yourselves to be pure in the matter." These are the preliminary exercises of gnostic training. And since the Almighty God Himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as shepherds and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints unto the work of ministry, unto the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ—we must hasten to come to maturity in a gnostic way and to be perfected, as much as possible while still remaining in the flesh, having practised, from the perfect like-mindedness here, to run together with the will of God unto the restoration of the truly perfect nobility and kinship, unto the fullness of Christ, the thing perfectly completed out of the perfecting. We already see in what way and how and when the divine apostle speaks of "the perfect," and how he shows the differences of the perfect. And again, to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is profitable. "For to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith in the same Spirit, to another gifts of healings in the same Spirit, to another workings of powers, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of tongues; but all these things the one and the same Spirit works, dividing severally to each as He wills."

And they say that Battus the Cyrenian compiled the so-called Mantike of Mopsus; and Dorotheus, in the first book of his Pandect, relates that Mopsus understood the kingfisher and the crow. And Pythagoras the great too always attended to foreknowledge, and Abaris the Hyperborean and Aristeas of Proconnesus and Epimenides the Cretan, who came to Sparta, and Zoroaster the Mede and Empedocles of Acragas and Phormion the Laconian, indeed Polyaratus the Thasian and Empedotimus the Syracusan, and besides these, especially, Socrates the Athenian. "For there is for me," he says in the Theages, "beginning from childhood, by a divine lot, a daemonic sign that comes upon me; and this is a voice, which, when it comes, restrains me from what I am about to do, but never urges me on." And Execestus, the tyrant of the Phocians, wearing two enchanted rings, by the sound they made against each other perceived the right moments for his actions; yet he died, treacherously slain, even though the sound had given warning beforehand, as Aristotle says in his Constitution of the Phocians.

This being so, the prophets are perfect in prophecy, the righteous in righteousness, the martyrs in confession, and others in preaching—not without share in the common virtues, but succeeding in the things in which they were appointed. For who that thinks rightly would say the prophet is not righteous? And what? Did not the righteous too, like Abraham, prophesy?
For to one God gave warlike works, to another the dance, to another the lyre and song,
says Homer. But each has his own gift from God, this one in this way, that one in that; but the apostles were filled in all things.

But there were also, among the Egyptians, men who were once living and afterward became gods by human opinion: Hermes the Theban and Asclepius of Memphis; and again Tiresias and Manto at Thebes, as Euripides says; and Helenus too and Laocoon and Oenone, the daughter of Cebren, at Ilium. For Crenus too, one of the Heraclidae, is recorded as a notable seer, and another Iamus in Elis, from whom come the Iamidae, and Polyidus at Argos and at Megara, whom the tragedy mentions. Why should I reckon up for you Telemus, who, being a seer of the Cyclopes, prophesies to Polyphemus the things of the wandering of Odysseus; or Onomacritus at Athens; or Amphiaraus, who is recorded as being older by one generation than the capture of Ilium, having been among the seven who marched against Thebes; or Theoclymenus in Cephallenia, or Telmessus in Caria, or Galeus in Sicily? And there would be others besides these: Idmon, who was with the Argonauts; Phemonoe the Delphian; Mopsus the son of Apollo and Manto, in Pamphylia and Cilicia; Amphilochus the son of Amphiaraus, in Cilicia; Alcmaeon, among the Acarnanians; Anius, in Delos; and Aristander of Telmessus, who was with Alexander. And already Philochorus relates that Orpheus too became a seer, in the first book of his work On Divination.

You will find, then, if you wish, from their deeds and writings, the knowledge, the life, the preaching, the righteousness, the purity, the prophecy. And yet one must know that, even though Paul is younger in time, having flourished immediately after the Lord's ascension, still his Scripture hangs upon the old covenant, breathing and speaking from there; for the faith in Christ and the knowledge of the gospel are an explanation and a fulfilment of the law. And for this reason it was said to the Hebrews: "Unless you believe, you shall not understand"—that is, unless you believe the one prophesied through the law and decreed by the law, you shall not understand the old covenant, which He Himself explained at His own coming.

And Theopompus and Ephorus and Timaeus record a certain Orthagoras as a seer, as does Pythocles of Samos, in the fourth book of his Italica, Gaius Julius Nepos. But these are all thieves and robbers, as the Scripture says, having foretold most things from observation and from probabilities, like the physicians and seers who judge by physiognomy; while others were moved by demons, or disturbed by waters and incenses and a certain quality of air. But among the Hebrews the prophets prophesied by the power of God and his inspiration: before the Law, Adam, foretelling concerning the woman and concerning the naming of the animals; and Noah, proclaiming repentance; and Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, plainly showing forth not a few of the things to come and already present. And with the Law, Moses and Aaron, after whom prophesy Joshua the son of Nun, Samuel, Gad, Nathan, Achias, Samaias, Iu, Elijah, Michaias, Abdiu, Elisha, Abdadonai, Amos, Isaiah, Hosea, Jonah, Joel, Jeremiah, Sophonias, Buzi, Ezekiel, Urias, Ambacum, Naum, Daniel, Misael (the author of the syllogisms), Aggaeus, Zacharias, and the Messenger among the Twelve.

And the prophets in all are thirty-five. And of women (for these too prophesied), Sarah and Rebecca and Mariam and Deborah and Olda. . . . Then, about the same times, John prophesies down to the saving baptism; and after the birth of Christ, Anna and Symeon; for Zacharias too, the father of John, is said in the Gospels to prophesy even before the child. Let us, then, from the beginning, from Moses, gather together the chronography according to the Greeks. From the birth of Moses to the exodus of the Jews out of Egypt are eighty years, and the other forty down to his death; the exodus takes place in the time of Inachus, before the Sothiac period, Moses having gone out of Egypt three hundred and forty-five years earlier. And from the leadership of Moses and Inachus to the flood of Deucalion — the second deluge, I mean — and to the conflagration of Phaethon, which fall in the time of Crotopus, forty generations are counted; but to a hundred years three generations are reckoned. And from the flood to the conflagration of Ida and the finding of iron and the Idaean Dactyls, seventy-three years, as Thrasyllus says. And from the conflagration of Ida to the rape of Ganymede, sixty-five years.

From this to the expedition of Perseus, when Glaucus too established the Isthmian games in honour of Melicertes, fifteen years. From the expedition of Perseus to the founding of Ilium, thirty-four years. From this to the sailing of the Argo, sixty-four years. From this to Theseus and the Minotaur, thirty-two years; then to the seven against Thebes, ten years; to the contest at Olympia, which Heracles established in honour of Pelops, three years; and to the expedition of the Amazons against Athens and the rape of Helen by Theseus, nine years. From this to the deification of Heracles, eleven years; then to the rape of Helen by Alexander, four years; then to the capture of Troy, twenty years. And from the capture of Troy to the return of Aeneas and the founding of Lavinium, ten years; to the rule of Ascanius, eight years; and to the return of the Heraclidae, sixty-one years; and to the Olympiad of Iphitus, three hundred and thirty-eight years.

And Eratosthenes records the times thus: from the capture of Troy to the return of the Heraclidae, eighty years; from this to the founding of Ionia, sixty years; the things next after these, to the guardianship of Lycurgus, a hundred and fifty-nine years; to the year preceding the first Olympiad, a hundred and eight years; from that Olympiad to the crossing of Xerxes, two hundred and ninety-seven years; from that to the beginning of the Peloponnesian War, forty-eight years; and to its end and the defeat of the Athenians, twenty-seven years; and to the battle at Leuctra, thirty-four years; after which, to the death of Philip, thirty-five years; and after these, to the passing of Alexander, twelve years. Again, from the first Olympiad some say that to the founding of Rome are reckoned twenty-four years. From this to the abolition of the kings, when there came to be consuls, two hundred and forty-three years; and from the abolition of the kings to the death of Alexander, a hundred and eighty-six years.

From this to the victory of Augustus, when Antony slew himself in Alexandria, two hundred and ninety-four years, when Augustus was consul for the fourth time. From which time to the contest which Domitian established in Rome, a hundred and fourteen years; and from the first contest to the death of Commodus, a hundred and eleven years. And there are those who reckon together, from Cecrops to Alexander the Macedonian, one thousand eight hundred and twenty-eight years; from Demophon, one thousand two hundred and fifty; and from the capture of Troy to the return of the Heraclidae, a hundred and twenty years, or a hundred and eighty. From this to the archon Euaenetus, in whose time they say Alexander crossed into Asia, as Phanias says seven hundred and fifteen years, as Ephorus seven hundred and thirty-five, as Timaeus and Cleitarchus eight hundred and twenty, as Eratosthenes seven hundred and seventy; and as Duris, from the capture of Troy to the crossing of Alexander into Asia, a thousand years. From this to Euaenetus, the archon at Athens, in whose time Alexander dies, eleven years. From this to the rule of Germanicus Claudius Caesar, three hundred and sixty-five years; from which time the years down to the death of Commodus, however many are reckoned together, also become plain.

And after the Greek matters, we must render an account also from the times among the barbarians, according to the greatest intervals. From Adam to the flood are reckoned together two thousand one hundred and forty-eight years, four days; from Shem to Abraham, one thousand two hundred and fifty years; from Isaac to the giving of the inheritance, six hundred and sixteen years. Then from the judges to Samuel, four hundred and sixty-three years, seven months. And after the judges, the years of the kings, five hundred and seventy-two years, six months, ten days. After which times, the years of the Persian kingdom, two hundred and thirty-five; then of the Macedonian, down to the slaying of Antony, three hundred and twelve years, eighteen days. After which time, the kingdom of the Romans, down to the death of Commodus, two hundred and twenty-two years. And again, from the seventy-year captivity and the restoration of the people to the land of their fathers, to the captivity under Vespasian, are reckoned together four hundred and ten years; and lastly, from Vespasian to the death of Commodus, are found a hundred and twenty-one years, six months, twenty-four days.

And Demetrius says, in his work On the Kings in Judaea, that the tribe of Judah and Benjamin and Levi were not led captive by Sennacherim, but that from this captivity to the last, which Nebuchadnezzar made out of Jerusalem, are a hundred and twenty-eight years, six months. And from the time when the ten tribes became captive out of Samaria, down to Ptolemy the Fourth, five hundred and seventy-three years, nine months; and from the time out of Jerusalem, three hundred and thirty-eight years, three months. And Philo too himself recorded the kings of the Jews, at variance with Demetrius. And further, Eupolemus, in a similar work, says that the whole of the years from Adam to the fifth year of the reign of Demetrius, when Ptolemy was reigning the twelfth year over Egypt, come together to five thousand one hundred and forty-nine years. And from the time when Moses led the Jews out of Egypt to the aforesaid term, are reckoned together one thousand five hundred and eighty years. And from this time down to the consuls in Rome, Gnaeus Domitius and Asinius, are gathered together a hundred and twenty years.

And Ephorus and many other historians say that there are seventy-five nations and tongues, having heard the voice of Moses, which says: "And all the souls from Jacob, those who went down to Egypt, were seventy-five." And according to the true account too the generic dialects appear to be seventy-two, as our Scriptures hand down; while the other many come about by the sharing of two or three or even more dialects. And a dialect is a manner of speech that shows the proper character of a place, or a manner of speech that shows the proper or common character of a nation. And the Greeks say that the dialects among them are five — the Attic, the Ionic, the Doric, the Aeolic, and fifth the Common — but that the tongues of the barbarians, being innumerable, are not called dialects but languages.

And Plato assigns even to the gods a certain dialect, judging especially from dreams and oracles, and also from those possessed by demons, who utter not their own voice or dialect, but that of the demons that have entered them. And he thinks there are dialects even of irrational animals, which those of the same kind understand. When an elephant, for instance, fell into the mud and cried out, another that was present and saw what had happened turned back and, after no long while, brings with him a herd of elephants and saves the one that had fallen in. And they say that in Libya a scorpion, if it cannot reach to strike a man, goes off and returns with several others, and, fastening one to another like a chain, in this way contrives to get the start in carrying out the plot — the irrational animals surely not using some unseen nod, nor indicating to one another by gesture, but, I think, by their own dialect. And certain others say that if a fish drawn up escapes when the line has broken, no fish of the same kind will any longer be found in the same place that day. But the first and generic dialects, though barbarian, have their names by nature, since men too confess that the prayers spoken in the barbarian tongue are more powerful. And Plato, in the Cratylus, wishing to interpret "fire," says the name is barbarian; he testifies, at any rate, that the Phrygians so call it, with a small variation.

And I think it no worse, in addition to these things, to set out also the times of the Roman kings, for the showing of the birth of the Saviour: Augustus forty-three years, Tiberius twenty-two years, Gaius four years, Claudius fourteen years, Nero fourteen years, Galba one year, Vespasian ten years, Titus three years, Domitian fifteen years, Nerva one year, Trajan nineteen years, Hadrian twenty-one years, Antoninus twenty-three years, and likewise again Antoninus and Commodus thirty-two years. The whole, from Augustus to the death of Commodus, is two hundred and twenty-two years; and from Adam to the death of Commodus, five thousand seven hundred and eighty-four years, two months, twelve days. Some, however, record the times of the Roman kings thus: Gaius Julius Caesar three years, four months, six days, after whom Augustus reigned forty-six years, four months, one day; then Tiberius twenty-six years, six months, nineteen days, whom Gaius Caesar succeeds, three years, ten months, eight days; him Claudius, thirteen years, eight months, twenty-eight days; Nero thirteen years, eight months, twenty-eight days; Galba seven months, six days; Otho five months, one day; Vitellius seven months, one day; Vespasian eleven years, eleven months, twenty-two days; Titus two years, two months; Domitian fifteen years, eight months, five days; Nerva one year, four months, ten days; Trajan nineteen years, seven months, fifteen days; Hadrian twenty years, ten months, twenty-eight days; Antoninus twenty-two years, three months, seven days; Marcus Aurelius Antoninus nineteen years, eleven days; Commodus twelve years, nine months, fourteen days. From Julius Caesar, then, to the death of Commodus there are two hundred and thirty-six years, six months. And all the years from Romulus, the founder of Rome, to the death of Commodus, are reckoned together as nine hundred and fifty-three years, six months.

Our Lord was born in the twenty-eighth year, when the first census was ordered to be made under Augustus. And that this is true is written in the Gospel according to Luke thus: "And in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar the word of the Lord came upon John the son of Zacharias." And again in the same Gospel: "And Jesus was coming to the baptism about thirty years of age." And that he had to preach for only one year, this too is written thus: "He has sent me to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." This both the prophet said and the Gospel. The fifteen years of Tiberius, then, and the fifteen of Augustus — so are fulfilled the thirty years, down to the time when he suffered. And from the time he suffered to the destruction of Jerusalem there are forty-two years, three months; and from the destruction of Jerusalem to the death of Commodus, a hundred and twenty-two years, ten months, thirteen days. So from the time when the Lord was born to the death of Commodus, the whole is a hundred and ninety-four years, one month, thirteen days. And there are those who, more curiously, add to the birth of our Saviour not only the year but also the day, which, they say, was the twenty-fifth of Pachon, in the twenty-eighth year of Augustus.

And those of the school of Basilides keep also the day of his baptism as a feast, passing the night beforehand in readings. And they say that the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar is the fifteenth of the month Tybi, but some again the eleventh of the same month. And, dealing exactly with his passion, some bring it, in the sixteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, on the twenty-fifth of Phamenoth, others on the twenty-fifth of Pharmuthi; and others say the Saviour suffered on the nineteenth of Pharmuthi. Indeed, some of them say he was born on the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth of Pharmuthi. And these too must be rendered to the chronography — the days, I mean, at which Daniel hints, from the desolation of Jerusalem . . . the years of Vespasian, seven, eleven months. For the two years are added to the seventeen months and eight days of Otho and Galba and Vitellius, and so come to three years and six months, which is the half of the week, as Daniel the prophet has said. He said that two thousand three hundred days come about from the time the abomination was set up by Nero in the holy city until its destruction. For so the appended text shows: "Until when shall the vision stand — the sacrifice taken away, and the sin of desolation that is given, and the power and the holy place be trodden down together? And he said to him: Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days; and the holy place shall be cleansed." These two thousand three hundred days, then, come to six years, four months, of which the half Nero held while reigning, and it became the half of a week; and the other half Vespasian, together with Otho and Galba and Vitellius. And for this reason Daniel says: "Blessed is he who comes to the one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days." For down to these days was the war, and after these it ceased.

And this number too is shown from the appended passage, which runs thus: "And from the time of the changing of the continual sacrifice, and the giving of the abomination of desolation, a thousand two hundred and ninety days. Blessed is he who endures and comes to the one thousand three hundred and thirty-five days." And Flavius Josephus the Jew, who composed the Jewish histories, bringing down the times, says that from Moses to David are five hundred and eighty-five years; from David to the second year of Vespasian, one thousand one hundred and seventy-nine. Then from this to the tenth year of Antoninus, seventy-seven years; so that from Moses to the tenth year of Antoninus the whole is one thousand eight hundred and thirty-three years. And others, reckoning down to the death of Commodus from Inachus and Moses, said the years come to one thousand eight hundred and forty-two; but others, one thousand and twenty-one. And in the Gospel according to Matthew the genealogy from Abraham is carried down to Mary the mother of the Lord; for, it says, from Abraham to David are fourteen generations, and from David to the removal to Babylon fourteen generations, and from the removal to Babylon to Christ likewise another fourteen generations — three mystical intervals, completed in six weeks.

Indeed, Plato the philosopher says the end is twofold: the one participable and primary, existing in the very forms — which he also names "the Good"; and the one participating in that and receiving the likeness from it, which comes about among men who lay claim to virtue and the true philosophy. Wherefore Cleanthes too, in the second book On Pleasure, says that Socrates taught at every turn that the same man is both just and happy, and cursed the first man who divided the just from the advantageous, as having done an impious thing; for in truth impious are those who separate the advantageous from the just that is according to law. And Plato himself says that happiness is "to have the daimon well" (eu ton daimona echein), and that the governing part of our soul is called daimon, and that happiness is the most perfect and fullest good. And sometimes he calls it a life that is in agreement and harmony, and sometimes the most perfect according to virtue; and this he sets in the knowledge of the Good and in the being made like to God — declaring the likeness to be to become just and holy with prudence. For is it not so that some of our own people take it that man received the "according to the image" straightway at his generation, but is to receive the "according to the likeness" later, at his perfecting?

So Plato, teaching that this likeness will come to the virtuous man with humility, somewhere interprets that saying: "Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted." He says, at any rate, in the Laws: "God, then, as the ancient saying too has it, holding the beginning and the middle and the end of all things, brings them to fulfilment by a straight course, going round according to nature; and upon him there ever follows Justice, the avenger of those who fall short of the divine law." You see how he too brings caution toward the divine law? So he adds: "To which the man who is to be happy clings and follows, humble and adorned." Then, having joined the things that follow upon these, and having admonished by fear, he adds: "What action, then, is dear to and follows God? One, and having one ancient saying: that the like is dear to the like, being measured; but the unmeasured is dear neither to one another nor to the measured. The man, then, who is to become dear to God must of necessity become, so far as possible, such a one himself."

And according to this account the temperate man among us is dear to God, for he is like; and the man not temperate is unlike and different. Having said that this doctrine is ancient, he hinted at the teaching that came to him from the law. And in the Theaetetus, having granted that the evils about mortal nature and this place go round of necessity, he adds: "Wherefore one must try to flee from here to there as quickly as possible; and the flight is likeness to God so far as possible; and the likeness is to become just and holy with prudence." And Speusippus, the nephew of Plato, says that happiness is a perfect state in those who are according to nature, or a state of goods, of which condition all men have appetite, but the good aim at freedom from disturbance. And the virtues would be productive of happiness. And Xenocrates of Calchedon renders happiness the possession of one's own virtue and of the power that serves it. Then, as that in which it comes to be, he plainly says the soul; as that by which, the virtues; as that out of which, as of parts, the noble actions and the earnest states and dispositions and motions and relations; and as those without which it is not, the bodily and external things. For Polemo, the pupil of Xenocrates, plainly wishes happiness to be self-sufficiency in all goods, or in the most and greatest. He dogmatizes, at any rate, that without virtue happiness can never exist, but that, apart from the bodily and external things, virtue is self-sufficient toward happiness.

And let these things be so; but the refutations of the opinions stated will be set down in due time. For us ourselves it is set forth to come to an endless end, obeying the commandments — that is, God — and having lived according to them blamelessly and with knowledge, through the knowledge of the divine will. And the likeness, so far as possible, to right reason is the end; and the restoration, through the Son, to the perfect adoption, which ever glorifies the Father through the great High Priest, who deigned to call us brothers and joint-heirs. And the Apostle, briefly describing the end in the Epistle to the Romans, says: "But now, freed from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit unto sanctification, and the end eternal life." And, knowing hope to be twofold — the one expected, the other received back — he teaches that the restoration of hope is already the end; "for endurance," he says, "works proof, and proof hope; and hope does not put to shame, because the love of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us." On account of which love is also the restoration to the hope, which he elsewhere says is laid up for us as a rest.

The like you would find in Ezekiel too, running thus: "The soul that sins, it shall die. And a man who becomes just and does judgment and righteousness, who has not eaten upon the mountains, and has not lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, and has not defiled his neighbour's wife, and has not approached a woman in the separation of her uncleanness" (for he does not wish the sowing of man to be outraged), "and, it says, has not oppressed a man, will restore the debtor's pledge, will not seize plunder, will give his bread to the hungry, and will clothe the naked, will not give his money at interest, and will take no excess, will turn his hand from injustice, will do true judgment between a man and his neighbour, will walk in my ordinances and has kept my ordinances to do truth — he is just, he shall surely live, says the Lord Adonai." And Isaiah, exhorting the believer toward gravity of life, but the gnostic toward attention, presenting that the virtue of man and of God is not the same, says thus: "Seek the Lord, and in finding him call upon him; and when he draws near to you, let the impious leave his ways, and the lawless man his ways, and let him turn to the Lord, and he will obtain mercy,"

The man who understands and is keen-sighted, this is the gnostic. And his work is not the abstinence from evils (for this is a stepping-stone to the greatest advancement), nor indeed the doing of any good thing either through fear (for it is written: "Where shall I flee, and where shall I hide from your face? If I go up into heaven, you are there; if I depart to the ends of the sea, there is your right hand; if I go down into the depths, there is your Spirit"), nor through hope of the promised honour (for it is said: "Behold, the Lord, and His reward is before His face, to give back to each according to his works"—"things which eye has not seen nor ear heard nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him"), but only the good-doing through love, which is choiceworthy for the gnostic for the sake of the good itself.

"for your thoughts are far from my thought." We, then, according to the noble Apostle, await from faith the hope of righteousness. "For in Christ neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love." "And we desire each of you to show the same diligence toward the full assurance of hope," down to "having become, according to the order of Melchizedek, a high priest forever." The like to Paul the all-virtuous Wisdom too says: "But he who hears me will dwell upon hope, trusting"; for the restoration of hope is called, by the same name, "hope"; wherefore to the word "will dwell" it most nobly added "trusting," showing that such a one is at rest, having received back the hope which he hoped; wherefore it adds: "and he will be at ease, without fear, from every evil." And plainly the Apostle, in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, says outright: "Become imitators of me, as I also am of Christ" — that that might come about: "if you are mine, and I am Christ's, then become imitators of Christ, and Christ of God." The being made like to God, then, so far as was possible — to become just and holy with prudence — he lays down as the aim of faith, and as the end the restoration of the promise that is upon faith. From these, then, gush the springs of those who dogmatized about the end, which we have spoken of before. But enough of these.

At once it is said to the Lord, in the person of God: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance"—teaching Him to ask the most royal request, the salvation of men, without reward, that we ourselves may inherit and possess the Lord. For, on the contrary, to long for the knowledge concerning God for the sake of some need—that this may happen to me and that may not—is not proper to the gnostic; rather, the knowledge itself suffices him as a cause of contemplation. For I would dare to say that the man who pursues knowledge for the sake of the divine science itself will not choose knowledge for the sake of wishing to be saved. For thinking, by exercise, is stretched out into ever-thinking; and ever-thinking, becoming the substance of the knower by an undivided commingling, abides as an eternal contemplation, a living subsistence. If, then, one should set before the gnostic, by way of hypothesis, which he would wish to choose—the knowledge of God or eternal salvation—and these were separated (though they are most of all in identity), he would, without any hesitation whatever, choose the knowledge of God, judging that to be choiceworthy for its own sake which is the property of the faith that has ascended through love into knowledge.

This, then, is the first good-doing of the perfect man, when it comes about not for the sake of any need of the things that tend toward himself, but, judging that it is good to do good, the activity, carried out earnestly, does good in every action—not in some things but not in others, but established in the habit of good-doing, no longer for the sake of glory or, as the philosophers say, of good repute, nor for the sake of a reward, whether from men or from God; . . . that he may carry out his life after the image and likeness of the Lord. And if, while doing good, something contrary should meet him, he will, as a good recompense, send it forth without remembering wrong, becoming just and good to the just and the unjust. To such men the Lord says: "Be as your Father, perfect." For such a man the flesh has died, and he himself alone lives, having consecrated the tomb into a holy temple to the Lord, having turned the old sinful soul toward God.

This man is no longer continent, but has come into the habit of freedom from passion, awaiting to put on the divine form. "If you do alms," it says, "let no one know; and if you fast, anoint yourself, that God alone may know, and of men not one"—but neither ought the man who does the mercy himself to know that he is doing mercy; for so he will be sometimes merciful and at other times not. But when he does the beneficent thing in habit, he will imitate the nature of the good; and the disposition will be both nature and training. One must not, however, be lifted up and transported, but, walking, arrive where one must, having passed through the whole of the narrow road; for this is to be drawn by the Father—to become worthy to receive the power of grace from God and to run up unhindered. And even if some hate the elect man, he knows their ignorance, pitying the mind of their stupidity.

With good reason, then, this knowledge loves even those who are ignorant, and teaches and educates the whole creation to honour the Almighty God. And if it has learned to love God, this man will in no way have his virtue cast away, neither waking nor sleeping nor in any imagination; since the habit never goes out of itself, falling away from being a habit, whether knowledge be called a habit or a disposition. For, by never letting in differing notions, the ruling part, remaining unaltered, does not take on any alteration of imaginations, dreaming the image-makings that come from the daytime motions. For this reason indeed the Lord commands us to keep awake, so that not even in a dream may our soul ever suffer passion, but He bids us preserve the conduct even of the night, as wrought in the day, pure and unspotted. For this is the likening to God, as far as is possible—to keep the mind in the same relation. And this is the relation of mind as mind; but the varied disposition comes about through the passionate attachment to material things.

So that they seem to me to have called the night "the kindly time" [euphrone], since at that season the soul, having ceased from the senses, inclines toward itself and shares more in understanding. For this reason too the initiations are held mostly by night, signifying the night-time contraction of the soul from the body. "Let us, then, not sleep as the rest, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep by night, and those who are drunk are drunk by night; but let us, being of the day, be sober, having put on the breastplate of faith and love, and for a helmet the hope of salvation."

And the things they say concerning sleep, the same must be understood concerning death too. For each shows the withdrawal of the soul, the one more, the other less; which is also to be got from Heraclitus: "Man in the kindly night kindles a light for himself, dead, his eyes being quenched; living, he touches the dead while sleeping, his eyes being quenched; awake, he touches the sleeper." For "blessed are those who know the season," according to the apostle, that "it is now the hour for you to be raised from sleep; for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed. The night is far advanced, and the day is at hand. Let us, then, put away the works of darkness, and put on the weapons of light." By "day" he allegorizes the Son and light, and again the commandments as the "weapons of light" metaphorically. So they say one must come washed to the sacred rites and the prayers, pure and bright.

And this—the being adorned and purified outwardly—is done for the sake of a symbol; but purity is to think holy things. And indeed an image of baptism would be the one handed down to the poets from Moses in some such way:
And she, having washed herself, having clean garments on her flesh,
Penelope comes to her prayer; and Telemachus,
having washed his hands in the grey sea, prayed to Athena.
This was a custom of the Jews, as also the frequent washing themselves after the bed. Well, then, is that also said:
Know that you are pure not by washing, but by the mind.
