For perfect purity, I think, is that of the mind and of the works and of the thoughts, and besides the sincerity of words, and, lastly, sinlessness in dreams.

And it is sufficient, I think, as a purification for a man, an exact and sure repentance, if indeed, having condemned ourselves for our former deeds, we put away the past, and after these things having understood, and having drawn the mind up out of both the things that delight according to sense and the former errors. If, then, one must give the etymology of "knowledge" [epistēmē], and must take its application from "standing" [stasis], because it sets [histēsi] our soul among the things, the soul that before was carried now this way, now that, then likewise faith [pistis] must be etymologized as the standing of our soul about that which is. But we long to learn of the man who is always and in all things just—who, neither fearing the punishment from the law, nor being cautious of the hatred of evil felt by those who are present and who pursue evildoers, nor suspecting the danger from the wronged men themselves, remains just; for the man who, on account of these things, abstains from doing anything unjust is not willingly good, but good through fear. And Epicurus too says that the wise man according to him does not wish to do wrong for the sake of some gain; for he cannot get assurance of escaping notice. So that, if he should be persuaded he will escape notice, he will do wrong, according to him.

And such are the dark doctrines. But if, in hope of the recompense from God for the just, a man should abstain from doing wrong, this man too is not willingly good; for as fear justified the one, so a reward justifies this man—or rather, makes him seem to be just. But the hope after death—that it is good for the good and the contrary for the base—not only those who pursue the barbarian wisdom know, but the Pythagoreans too; for they too laid down hope as the end for those who philosophize. So that Socrates too in the Phaedo says that the good souls depart hence with a good hope, and again, blaming the base, he sets against them: "For they live with an evil hope." With this Heraclitus too plainly agrees, in what he says discoursing about men: "Things await men, when they have died, which they neither expect nor suppose."

Divinely, then, Paul writes outright to the Romans: "Affliction works endurance, and endurance proof, and proof hope, and hope does not put to shame." For endurance is for the sake of the hope to come; but "hope" is also called, by the same name, the giving-back and the restoration of hope, which also "does not put to shame," being no longer reproached. But the man who obeys the bare call, in so far as he has been called, hurries on toward knowledge neither through fear nor through pleasures; for he does not look around whether any profitable gain or enjoyment follows him from outside, but, drawn by love of the truly existent Beloved and led toward what is fitting, he is pious.

Hence not even if, by hypothesis, he should receive authority from God to do the forbidden things without punishment, nor even if he should receive the promise of receiving, as a reward for these, the goods of the blessed—nay, not even if he should be persuaded that he will escape the notice of God in the things he does, which is impossible—would he ever wish to do anything contrary to right reason, having once chosen the truly good and choiceworthy of itself, and on this account lovely. For we have understood that the good does not lie
in the food of the belly.

But that man has heard that "food does not commend us, nor indeed marriage, nor again abstinence from marriage in ignorance, but the gnostic work according to virtue"—since the dog too, the irrational animal, might be called continent, that fears the man lifting the staff and on this account abstains from the meat. And of such men, know well, that when the promise made beforehand has been taken away, and the threatened fear circumscribed, and the impending danger removed, their purpose is convicted.

Let what has been thus variously recorded by many concerning the times, and set forth by us, so stand. And they say that the Scriptures, both those of the Law and the prophetic, were interpreted from the dialect of the Hebrews into the Greek tongue in the reign of Ptolemy the son of Lagus, or, as some say, of the one surnamed Philadelphus, who brought the greatest ambition to this task, Demetrius of Phalerum having dealt exactly with the matters of the interpretation. For while the Macedonians still held Asia, the king, being ambitious to adorn with all writings the library founded by him in Alexandria, requested the men of Jerusalem to interpret their prophecies into the Greek dialect.

And they, as being still subject to the Macedonians, chose out from the most approved among them seventy elders, experienced in the Scriptures and skilled in the Greek dialect, and sent them to him, together with the divine books. And when each had interpreted each prophecy separately, by himself, all the interpretations, compared together, agreed both in their sense and in their words; for it was a purpose of God studied for Greek ears. Nor is it strange that, by the inspiration of God who gave the prophecy, the interpretation too should be wrought, as it were, a Greek prophecy, since in the captivity under Nebuchadnezzar too, when the Scriptures had been destroyed, in the times of Artaxerxes the king of the Persians, Esdras the Levite, the priest, becoming inspired, prophesied, renewing again all the ancient Scriptures.

And Aristobulus, in the first book of his work addressed to Philometor, writes word for word: "And Plato too followed our legislation, and is plainly seen to have worked carefully through each of the things said in it. And before Demetrius it had been interpreted by others, before the conquest of the Persians by Alexander — both the things concerning the leading of the Hebrews, our fellow-citizens, out of Egypt, and the manifestation to them of all that had happened, and the mastery of the land, and the exposition of the whole legislation; so that it is quite plain that the aforesaid philosopher took much from it (for he became a man of much learning), just as Pythagoras too transferred many of our things into his own doctrine-making." And Numenius the Pythagorean philosopher writes outright: "For what is Plato but Moses speaking Attic?" This Moses was a theologian and prophet, and, as some say, an interpreter of sacred laws. His race and his deeds and his life the Scriptures themselves, worthy of trust, proclaim; yet we too must speak of them, as briefly as may be.

Since marriage seems to fall under pleasure and desire, we must treat of this too. Marriage, then, is the first union of man and woman according to law, for the sowing of legitimate children. So the comic poet Menander says: "For the begetting of legitimate children I give you my own daughter." And we inquire whether one should marry, which is one of the things named as somehow "in relation to something." For who should marry, and being in what condition, and whom, and being in what condition? For neither should everyone marry, nor at all times; but there is a time in which it is fitting, and a person to whom it befits, and an age up to which. So neither should everyone marry every woman, nor at all times, nor at all, nor without restraint, but the man in a certain condition, and such a woman as he ought, and when he ought, and for the sake of children, and one in all respects like-minded, and not loving the husband by force or necessity.

Whence Abraham says concerning his wife, pretending her to be his sister: "She is my sister by my father, but not by my mother; and she became my wife also" — teaching that those of the same mother must not be taken in marriage. Let us run over the history in brief. Plato sets marriage among the external goods, providing for the immortality of our race and a kind of continuance, as it were, handed down like a torch through children's children. But Democritus declines marriage and the begetting of children, on account of the many unpleasantnesses from them and the distractions from more necessary things. And Epicurus too is ranged with him, and all who set the good in pleasure and freedom from disturbance, and further in freedom from grief. Further, according to those from the Stoa, marriage and child-rearing are indifferent, but according to those from the Peripatos a good. In sum, these, having brought their doctrines as far as the tongue, were enslaved to pleasures — some using concubines, some courtesans, and most of them boys. And that wise tetrad in the garden, with the courtesan, gloried in pleasure by their works.

So they would not escape the Buzygian curse, all who, not approving certain things as advantageous to themselves, enjoin upon others to do these, or, again, the contrary. This the Scripture has shown briefly, saying: "What you hate, you shall not do to another." But those who approve marriage say: Nature has made us well-fitted for marriage, as is plain from the constitution of the bodies, both of the males and of the females; and they continually cry out the "Increase and multiply." And even if these things are so, yet let it seem shameful to them that man, fashioned by God, should be more incontinent than the irrational animals, which do not mingle with many and without restraint, but with one and of their own kind — such as the wild pigeons and the ring-doves and the race of turtle-doves and the like. Further, they say, the childless man falls short of the perfection according to nature, as not having set in his own place a successor of his own; for the perfect man is one who has made from himself the like, or rather, when he sees that one too having done the same — that is, when he has set the begotten into the same nature as the begetter.

One must, then, by all means marry, both for the sake of the fatherland, and for the succession of children, and for the completing of the world, so far as in us lies. Since the poets too pity a certain marriage that is half-finished and childless, but bless the one with both parents flourishing. And the bodily diseases especially show marriage to be necessary; for the care of the wife and the intensity of her staying-by seem to surpass the perseverances of the other kindred and friends, by as much as she chooses to differ in sympathy and to attend most of all; and in truth, according to the Scripture, she is a necessary helper.

So the comic poet Menander, having run down marriage, but setting against it also the useful things, answers the one who said: "I am ill-disposed toward the matter." "B: For you take it the wrong way." Then he adds: "You see in it the troublesome things and those that will grieve you, but you do not look upon the goods," and the rest. And marriage helps also in the case of those advanced in time, presenting the wife who cares, and rearing the children from her as nurses of old age. "And children, to a man who has died, are tokens of fame; like corks they hold up the net, saving the spun line of flax from the deep," according to the tragic Sophocles. And the lawgivers do not allow those who have not married to seek the greatest offices. So the lawgiver of the Spartans set a penalty not only for celibacy, but for bad marriage and late marriage and solitary living. And the noble Plato commands that the man who has not married pay the maintenance of a wife to the public treasury, and render the fitting expenses to the magistrates. For if men who do not marry will not beget children, they will, so far as in them lies, make a scarcity of men, and dissolve both the cities and the world that is from them.

And such a thing is impious, of men dissolving the divine generation. And it is, besides, unmanly and weak to flee the common life with wife and children. For of that whose loss is an evil, the possession is altogether a good; and so it is with the rest too. But indeed the loss of children is among the greatest evils, they say. The possession of children, then, is a good. And if this, then marriage too. "And without a father," he says, "there could never be a child, and without a mother not even the conception of a child."

And marriage makes a father, as a man makes a mother. So Homer too sets it as the greatest prayer, "a husband and a house" — but not simply, but "with noble like-mindedness"; for the marriage of others is of one mind toward soft living, but that of those who philosophize leads to the concord according to reason — the marriage that bids the women adorn not their form but their character, and does not enjoin the men to use their wives as mistresses, having made the outrage of bodies their aim, but to win marriage as a help in the whole of life and the best temperance. For of wheat, I think, and of barley too, cast down at their proper seasons, more precious is the man who is sown, for whom all things grow; and those seeds the husbandmen cast down sober. Everything filthy and defiled in conduct, then, must be purified away from marriage, that we be not reproached with the union of the irrational animals as agreeing more with nature than human wedlock, according to the agreed definition.

Some of them, at any rate, having mounted at the season commanded, straightway depart, leaving the creation to the administration. And by the tragic poets Polyxena, though she is being slaughtered, is recorded — even dying, yet to have taken much forethought to fall decently, "hiding what must be hidden from the eyes of males." And for her too the calamity was a marriage. To fall under, then, and to yield to the passions is the utmost slavery, just as, indeed, to master these is the only freedom. So the divine Scripture says that those who transgress the commandments are "sold to strangers" — that is, to sins unsuited to nature — until, turning back, they repent.

Marriage, then, must be kept pure, like some sacred image, from the things that defile it — by those who rise from sleep with the Lord, and go to sleep with thanksgiving and prayer, "both when you lie down and when the holy light comes," calling the Lord to witness throughout the whole of our life — having gained godliness in the soul, and bringing temperance even to the body. For it is in truth dear to God to lead orderliness by the hand from the tongue to the works; and the way to shamelessness is shameful speech, and the end of both is shameful deed. And that the Scripture counsels marrying, and never permits departing from the wedlock, it plainly legislates: "You shall not put away your wife, except for the matter of fornication"; and it reckons it adultery to marry again while either of the separated is living.

And it shows a woman unsuspected of slander by her not adorning herself, nor decking herself beyond what is fitting, but devoting herself earnestly to prayers and supplications; guarding against the many goings-out of the house, and shutting herself off so far as possible from the sight of those to whom she does not belong, holding housekeeping more important than untimely chatter. "And he who takes a divorced woman commits adultery," it says; "for if anyone puts away his wife, he makes her commit adultery" — that is, he forces her to be adulterated. And not only the man who puts her away becomes the cause of this, but also the man who takes her in, furnishing the woman an occasion of sinning; for if he did not receive her, she would turn back to her husband.

What, then, does the law do? For the checking of the proneness of the passions, it commands the adulteress, when convicted of this, to be put to death; and if she be a priest's daughter, it commands her to be given over to fire. And the adulterer too is stoned, but not in the same place, that not even their death be common. The law does not, then, fight with the Gospel, but agrees with it. For how should it not, the supplier of both being one, the Lord? For she who has played the harlot lives indeed to sin, but has died to the commandments; while she who has repented, as though reborn through the turning of her life, has a regeneration of life, the old harlot having died, and the woman born according to repentance having come again into life. The Spirit bears witness to what has been said, through Ezekiel, saying: "I do not wish the death of the sinner, so much as his turning back." So they are stoned, as having died, through hardness of heart, to the law which they did not obey; but for the priest's daughter the punishment is intensified, because "to whom more was given, of him will also more be required." Let this second Miscellany too be here circumscribed for us, on account of the length and multitude of the chapters.

For they do not become familiar with the very nature of the thing, so as truly to grasp gnostically that all things created for our use are good—as, for example, marriage and the begetting of children received with prudence—but that it is better than good to become free from passion and virtuous through the likening to the divine. But, being drawn by the external things, useful or unuseful, they abstain from some and not from others; and indeed the things from which they hold off, they plainly loathe, slandering the creation and the Demiurge, and in their seeming to conduct themselves faithfully they have an unholy judgement. But "You shall not covet" needs neither the necessity that comes from fear, which forces abstinence from pleasant things, nor the reward which by promise persuades one to check the impulses; nor is the obedience for the sake of the commandment. But those who have obeyed God for the sake of the promise choose it for the sake of the promise, having been chosen by the lure of pleasure;

nor would the turning away from perceptible things consequently produce the familiarity with the intelligible; rather, on the contrary, the familiarity with the intelligible produces a natural turning of the gnostic from the perceptible, when he has chosen the good gnostically by an election of the noble things—marvelling at the generation and sanctifying the Maker, and sanctifying the likening to the divine. "But I will free myself from desire," he will say, "for the sake of my familiarity with you, O Lord. For good is the dispensation that was created, and all things are well administered; nothing comes about without cause. I must be among your things, Almighty; and even if I am here, I am with you. I wish to be free of fear, that I may be able to draw near to you, and to be content with little, practising your just election of the noble things from the like things."

Most mystically and most holily the apostle, teaching us the truly thankful election—an election not by way of rejection of the others as base, but of making nobler things out of noble ones—indicated this when he said: "So that both the one who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and the one who does not give her in marriage does better, toward what is seemly and waits well upon the Lord without distraction." And we know that the things hard to procure have, in the love of the good, been made by God not necessary, and the necessary things easy to procure. Wherefore Democritus says well that nature and teaching are nearly the same; and he has briefly added the reason: "for teaching reshapes a man, and reshaping makes his nature, and it differs in nothing whether one was moulded such by nature or remodelled in time and by learning." But the Lord has provided both—the one according to creation, the other according to the re-creation and renewal from the covenant. And the thing profitable to the more sovereign is the more choiceworthy; and most sovereign of all is the mind. To the man, then, to whom the truly noble things appear most pleasant, he procures from himself the fruit he longs for, the stability of the soul. "But he who hears me," it says, "shall rest in peace, confident, and shall be quiet, fearless of every evil. Be confident, with your whole heart and your mind, in God." By this way it is possible for the gnostic already to become a god: "I said, You are gods, and sons of the Most High."
And Empedocles too says that the souls of the wise become gods, writing in some such way:

Man, then, simply, is moulded thus according to the form of the spirit that is congenital with him; for he is fashioned neither shapeless nor formless in the workshop of nature, where mystically the generation of man is accomplished, the craft and the substance being common. But the particular man is characterized according to the impress that comes into the soul of the things he has chosen. Hence we say that Adam was perfect as regards his moulding; for none of the things that characterize the form and shape of man was lacking to him. But that which he was to receive in the becoming—the perfection, and to be justified through obedience—this was the thing laid upon him, namely, to come to maturity. But of him who chose by his own cause, and still more chose the forbidden, God is not the cause; for generation is twofold—the one of things begotten, the other of things coming to be.

Moses, then, being a Chaldean by descent, is born in Egypt, his forefathers having migrated from Babylon to Egypt on account of a long-lasting famine. Born in the seventh generation and reared royally, he met with such a circumstance as this. The Hebrews having increased to a great multitude in Egypt, the king of the country, fearing a plot from their number, ordered them to rear the females among the children born of the Hebrews (for a woman is weak for war), but to destroy the males, suspicious of a vigorous youth. The child being of noble birth, his parents reared him hidden three months in succession, natural affection conquering the tyrannical cruelty; but afterward, fearing they might perish together with the child, having made a kind of vessel from the native papyrus and placed the child in it, they expose him by the banks of the river, which was marshy; and the child's sister watched, standing at a distance, for what would come about.

And the manliness [andreia] of man, who is by substance subject to passion, makes, they say, the one who partakes of it fearless and unconquerable; and wrath is the spear-bearer of the mind in endurance and steadfastness and the like; and over desire are ranked prudence and saving practical wisdom. But God is free of passion, free of wrath and free of desire; and He is not fearless in the sense of avoiding terrors, nor prudent in the sense of ruling over desires; for neither could the nature of God fall into any terror, nor does God flee cowardice, just as neither will He desire, so as to rule over desire. So mystically, concerning us, the Pythagorean saying was uttered, that man too must become one, since the high priest himself is one, there being one God, according to the unchangeable habit of the good ever running on.

Here the daughter of the king, who for a long time had not conceived but desired children, comes on that day to the river to use it for bathing and sprinkling; and hearing the child wailing, she orders it to be brought to her, and, taking pity, sought a nurse. Then the child's sister, running up, said that she could present to her, if she wished, a Hebrew woman who had given birth not long before, to be a nurse; and when she had agreed and asked her, she brought the mother, who was to be the child's nurse, as though she were some other woman, for a fixed wage. Then the queen gives the child the name Moses, fitly, because she took it up out of the water (for the Egyptians call water mou), into which it had been exposed to die. For they call Moses one who has breathed out his life in the water.

So at once the Saviour, along with desire, took away wrath too, wrath being a desire of vengeance; for, in general, the passible part . . . to every kind of desire; but the man who is made divine into freedom from passion becomes purely monadic. As, then, those at sea, drawn taut from an anchor, draw the anchor, but do not drag it to themselves, but rather themselves to the anchor, so those who, in the gnostic life, draw God to themselves, unawares are themselves led toward God; for the man who serves God serves himself. In the contemplative life, then, a man takes care of himself, worshipping God, and through his own sincere purification he beholds the holy God holily; for prudence, conceived as standing by and watching over itself and contemplating itself unceasingly, is likened, as far as possible, to God.

It is plain, then, that in the earlier time, when the child was circumcised, his parents gave him a name; and he was called Joacheim. And he had also a third name in heaven, after his assumption, as the initiates say, Melchi. And when he came of age, he was taught arithmetic and geometry, rhythm and harmony, and besides metric and music, by the most distinguished of the Egyptians, and further the philosophy through symbols, which they display in the hieroglyphic letters. And the rest of the cyclic education the Greeks taught in Egypt, as for a royal child, as Philo says in his Life of Moses; and he learned besides the letters of the Assyrians and the science of heavenly things both from the Chaldeans and from the Egyptians, whence in the Acts he is said to have been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. And Eupolemus, in his work On the Kings in Judaea, says that Moses was the first wise man, and the first to hand down grammar to the Jews, and that the Phoenicians received it from the Jews, and the Greeks from the Phoenicians. And, having sprung up to the nature of men, he strained his understanding, zealously following his kindred and ancestral education, until he even struck and killed the Egyptian who had unjustly attacked the Hebrew.

And the initiates say that he slew the Egyptian by a word alone, just as later Peter, in the Acts, is recorded as having killed by a word those who had embezzled the price of the land and lied. Artapanus, at any rate, in his work On the Jews, relates that Moses, having been shut up in prison by Chenephres the king of the Egyptians, for petitioning that the people be released from Egypt, when the prison was opened by night according to the will of God, came forth and, going to the palace, stood over the sleeping king and roused him; and the king, astonished at what had happened, ordered Moses to tell the name of the God who had sent him; and Moses, bending to his ear, told it; and the king, hearing it, fell speechless, but, held up by Moses, came to life again.
Concerning the rearing of Moses, Ezekiel too, the poet of the Jewish tragedies, will sing in tune with us, in the drama entitled Exagoge, writing thus in the person of Moses:

"For seeing our race grown numerous enough, King Pharaoh devised much guile against us, torturing some mortals at the brick-making and the heavy buildings, and walling cities, for the sake of his own ill-fated ends. Then he proclaimed to us, the race of the Hebrews, to cast the males into the deep-flowing river. Here my mother who bore me hid me three months, as she said; but, not escaping notice, she put me secretly away, having wrapped a covering about me, by the river's edge, in the deep, shaggy marsh. And Mariam my sister kept watch nearby; and then the king's daughter came down with her maids, to brighten her young skin with bathing. And seeing me at once, and pitying me, she took me up, and knew that I was a Hebrew; and Mariam my sister, running up, says this to the princess: 'Do you wish that I find for you quickly a nurse for this child from among the Hebrews?' And she urged on the girl. And going, she told my mother, and quickly she was present, my mother herself, and took me in her arms. And the king's daughter said: 'Nurse this one, woman, and I will give you your wage.' And she named the name Moses, for the reason that she took me up from the watery river-bank. And when the time of infancy had passed for me, my mother brought me to the princess's halls, having told me everything in story and recounted to me my father's race and the gifts of God. And so, as long as we had the time of childhood, she promised everything by royal rearings and trainings, as though from her own womb. But when the full circle of days was at hand, I went out of the royal house."

Then, having narrated the struggle of the Hebrew and the Egyptian, and the burial of the Egyptian in the sand, he says thus of the second fight: "'Why do you strike one weaker than yourself?' And he said: 'Who sent you here as a judge or overseer over us? Will you not kill me as you did the man yesterday?' And, afraid, I said: 'How did this become known?'" So he flees from there and tends sheep, being taught beforehand for leadership by the shepherd's craft. For shepherding is a preliminary exercise of kingship for the man who is to preside over the gentlest flock of men, just as hunting is for those naturally inclined to war. And from there God leads him to the command of the Hebrews.

Then the Egyptians, who were often without understanding, are often admonished; and the Hebrews became spectators of the evils which others endured, learning thoroughly, without danger, the power of God. And further, the Egyptians, not accepting by hearing the effects of the power, the infants disbelieving through folly, then, as has been said, "the infants knew the deed when it was done"; and afterward, going out, the Hebrews carried off much spoil of the Egyptians and departed — not through love of money, as their accusers say (for God did not persuade them to covet others' things), but, first, receiving the necessary wage for what they had served the Egyptians during all that time; and then, in a manner, requiting and paying back the money-loving Egyptians by the carrying off of the spoil, just as those had paid back the Hebrews by their enslavement. So whether one should say this happened as in war — they thought it right to carry off the enemy's things by the law of the conquerors, as stronger over weaker (and the cause of the war was just: the Hebrews came as suppliants to the Egyptians on account of famine; but the Egyptians, having enslaved the strangers, forced them to serve them in the manner of captives, not even paying the wage) — or whether as in peace, they took the spoil as wage from the unwilling, who for a long time did not pay it but defrauded them.

So at once the thing in our power is that of which we are equally lords, both of it and of its opposite—as the philosophizing or not, and the believing or disbelieving. Through our being equally lords of either of the opposites, the thing in our power is found possible. And indeed the commandments are such as can be both done and not done by us, upon which there reasonably follows praise and blame; and again those who are punished on account of the sins committed by them are punished for these alone; for the things done have passed away, nor could the thing done ever become undone. So the sins before faith are forgiven by the Lord, not that they should not have come to pass, but as not having come to pass. Yet not all of them, Basilides says; only the involuntary and those in ignorance are forgiven, as if it were a man, but not God, who provided so great a gift. To this man the Scripture says: "You supposed, lawless one, that I would be like you." But even if we are punished for the voluntary ones, we are punished, not that they should not have come to pass, having come to pass, but because they came to pass. And punishment does not profit the sinner toward his not having done it, but toward his no longer sinning, nor any other man falling into the like.

Here, then, the good God educates for these three causes: first, that the one being educated may become better than himself; next, that those able to be saved through examples may be checked beforehand, being admonished; and third, that the wronged man may not be easily despised and fit to be wronged. And two are the modes of correction—the one didactic, the other punitive, which we have called also educative. One must know, however, that those who fall into sins after the washing are the ones being educated; for the things done before were forgiven, but the things supervening are purged out. Concerning the unbelievers it was said that they are reckoned "as dust, which the wind drives from the face of the earth, and as a drop from a bucket."

Moses, then, is to us prophetic, legislative, skilled in tactics, in generalship, in statesmanship, a philosopher. How he was prophetic will be told afterward, when we treat of prophecy. The tactical part would be a part of the generalship, and the generalship of the kingly part; and again the legislative part would be a part of the kingly, as also the judicial. And of the kingly part one portion is divine, that which is according to God and his holy Son, from whom both the goods that come from the earth and the external goods and perfect happiness are supplied; for, "Ask," it says, "for the great things, and the small shall be added to you." And a second kind of kingship, after the pure rational and divine administration, is that which uses for kingship the spirited part of the soul alone — the kind by which Heracles reigned over Argos and Alexander over the Macedonians. And a third is that which aims at the one thing, to conquer and subdue only (and to make the victory toward evil or toward good does not belong to such a one) — which the Persians, marching against Greece, used. For of the spirited part one element is merely contentious, having made its power for the sake of mastering itself; the other is honour-loving, when the soul uses the spirited part for the noble end.

And fourth, the worst of all, is set down the kingship that is according to the desires, like that of Sardanapallus and of those who make their end in the desires, to gratify as much as possible. And of the kingly art — both that which conquers by virtue and that which conquers by force — the instrument is the tactical; but it is one for one nature and matter, another for another. In arms and the fighting animals, through living and lifeless things, the soul and mind are what marshal; but in the passions of the soul, over which we prevail by virtue, reasoning is the tactical part, setting its seal upon self-control and temperance together with holiness, and good knowledge with truth, referring its end to the reverence of God. For to those who so use virtue, prudence is the marshalling power: in things divine, wisdom; in things human, statesmanship; in all things together, kingship. A king, then, is one who rules according to laws, who has the science of ruling the willing — such as is the Lord, welcoming those who believe in him and through him. For God has handed over all things and subjected all things to Christ our king, that "in the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is to the glory of God the Father."

And the conduct of a campaign is held in three forms: the safe, the hazardous, and the mixed of these; and each of these is composed of three: either by word, or by deeds, or by both of these together. And it will be possible to accomplish all these either by persuading, or by forcing, or by doing wrong in self-defence; among which are included either doing what is just, or lying, or telling the truth, or using some of these together at the same time. And all these, and how one must use each of them, the Greeks, having taken from Moses, have profited by. For the sake of a model I shall mention one or even two examples of generalship. Moses, having led out the people, suspecting that the Egyptians would pursue, left the short and direct road and turned toward the desert, and used the night for the most part of the journey. For there was another dispensation, according to which the Hebrews were being educated through much desert and long time, being accustomed, by sober endurance, to believing only that God is.

The generalship of Moses, then, teaches that, before the dangers, one must perceive what is useful, and so set about it. Indeed, what he suspected came about; for the Egyptians pursued on horses and chariots, but perished quickly when the sea broke and flooded over them, horses and chariots together, so that not even a remnant of them was left. And after these things a pillar of fire following (for it led on before them) led the Hebrews by night through trackless places, exercising and training them, in toils and journeyings, toward manliness and toward endurance, that the things of the land too might appear good after the trial of what seemed terrible, the land into which he was conducting them out of the pathless region.

Indeed, having routed the enemies who sat before the country, he killed them, attacking them from a desert and rough road (for such is the virtue of the general). For it was the work of experience and generalship to take the country of the enemy. Perceiving this, Miltiades, the general of the Athenians, who conquered the Persians in the battle at Marathon, imitated this manner: he led the Athenians by night, going through trackless places and eluding the barbarians who watched him. For Hippias, having revolted from the Athenians, brought the barbarians into Attica, and, having seized beforehand the opportune places, kept guard, because he had experience of the country. It was a task, then, to escape Hippias' notice; whence Miltiades, fittingly making use of a trackless way and the night, and attacking the Persians, whom Datis led, accomplished the victory in the contest with those whom he himself led.

But for Thrasybulus too, when he was bringing back those who had been driven out from Phyle and wished to escape notice, a pillar became a guide, as he went through untrodden places. To Thrasybulus, by night, when the weather had become moonless and stormy, a fire was seen going before, which, having conducted them without stumbling along Munychia, vanished where now the altar of the Light-bearer is. Let our things, then, be made credible to the Greeks even from this, that it is possible for the almighty God to make, going before the Hebrews by night, a pillar of fire, which also led the way for them on the road. And it is said too in a certain oracle: "A pillar to the Thebans is Dionysus, bringer of much joy" — from the history among the Hebrews. But Euripides too, in the Antiope, says: "and within the chambers of the herdsmen, a pillar of the Euian god, crowned with ivy." And the pillar signifies the imagelessness of God; and the lighted pillar, besides signifying the imagelessness, shows the standing and abiding nature of God, and his unchangeable and figureless light.

So, before the postures of statues were made exact, the ancients, setting up columns, worshipped these as images of God. So the author of the Phoronis writes: "Callithoe, key-bearer of the Olympian queen, Argive Hera, who first adorned with fillets and tassels the long column round the queen." But the author of the Europia too relates that the statue of Apollo at Delphi is a column, in these words: "that we might hang for the god a tithe and first-fruits from the most holy stalls and from the lofty column." Apollo, however, mystically understood by way of privation of the many, is the one God. But that fire which was like a pillar, and the fire that was in the bush, is a symbol of the holy light that passes over from earth and runs up again to heaven through the wood, through which the seeing intelligibly too has been granted to us.

Blessed is the man who has gained learning of inquiry, neither setting out to the harm of the citizens nor toward unjust deeds, but beholding the ageless order of immortal nature, in what way it came together, and where and how. To such men there never clings the practice of shameful deeds.

With good reason, then, Plato too says that the contemplator of the ideas will live a god among men; "and mind is the place of the ideas, and mind is God." He said, then, that the contemplator of the invisible God lives a god among men; and in the Sophist Socrates named the Eleatic stranger, who was a dialectician, "a god"—"such gods, like strangers from abroad, who visit cities." For when the soul, having risen above generation, is by itself and converses with the forms, like the chief one in the Theaetetus, having become as it were an angel, it shall be with Christ, being contemplative, ever beholding the will of God; truly "alone wise, but the others flit about as shadows"; for "the dead bury their own dead." Whence Jeremiah says: "I will fill her with dead, earth-born men, whom my wrath has struck."

God, then, being indemonstrable, is not an object of scientific knowledge; but the Son is wisdom and knowledge and truth and all else akin to this, and indeed has demonstration and exposition. And all the powers of the Spirit, becoming together one thing, are summed up unto the same, the Son; but He is uncircumscribed by the notion concerning each of His powers. And indeed He becomes neither absolutely one as one, nor many as parts, the Son, but as all things one. Whence also all things; for He is a circle of all the powers rolled up and unified into one.

For this reason the Word is called Alpha and Omega, of whom alone the end becomes beginning, and again ends at the upper beginning, taking no separation anywhere. Therefore to believe in Him and through Him is to become monadic, unified without distraction in Him; while to disbelieve is to be in doubt and to stand apart and to be divided. For this reason the Lord says these things: "Every alien-born son, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh"—that is, unclean in body and spirit—"shall not enter the holy place, from among the aliens in the midst of the house of Israel, but only the Levites." And by "aliens" He meant those who have not wished to believe, but choose to disbelieve.

Only those, then, who live purely are truly priests of God. For this reason, though all the tribes were circumcised, the tribes that anoint the high priests and kings and prophets were reckoned holier. Whence too He bids them not even touch the dead nor enter to the departed—not as though the body were defiled, but because sin and disobedience are fleshly and embodied and dead, and therefore abominable. To the father alone, and to the mother and son and daughter who have died, is the priest permitted to enter, because these alone are kindred of flesh and seed, from whom the priest too has received the immediate cause of his entry into life. And these too are purified for seven days, the number through which generation is completed; for on the seventh the rest is worshipped, and on the eighth he offers propitiation, as it is written in Ezekiel, according to which propitiation it is possible to receive the promise.

And the perfect purification, I think, is the faith that comes through the law and the prophets unto the gospel; and the propitiation is the purity that comes through all obedience, together with the putting off of the worldly things, unto the thankful giving-back of the tabernacle at the release of the soul. Whether, then, it be the time which, through the seven periods numbered, restores into the highest rest, or the seven heavens, which some reckon by ascent, or even the fixed region that borders on the intelligible world, which is called the ogdoad—still he says the gnostic must rise up out of generation and sin. So at any rate on the seven days the victims for sins are sacrificed, for there is still caution about turning, and the seventh revolution too is touched.

And Job the just himself says: "Naked I came out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I depart thither"—naked not of possessions (for that is a small and common thing), but, as a righteous man, he departs naked of vice and sin and of the formless image that follows those who have lived unjustly; for this was the thing said, "Unless you turn and become as the little children," pure in the flesh, holy in the soul through abstinence from evil works—God showing that He wishes us to be such as He has begotten us from the womb of water; for generation, succeeding generation by way of advancement, wishes to make us immortal, but "the lamp of the impious shall be quenched."

Yes, and the purity in body and soul which the gnostic pursues, the all-wise Moses, using the repetition fittingly, indicated, describing the incorruption of the body and of the soul in the case of Rebecca thus: "But the virgin was fair, she was a virgin, no man had known her." And Rebecca is interpreted "the glory of God"; and the glory of God is incorruption. This is the truly righteous thing—not to have advantage in either part, but to be a wholly sanctified temple of the Lord. Righteousness, then, is peace of life and stability, to which the Lord released, saying, "Depart in peace"; for Salem is interpreted "peace," of which our Saviour is recorded as king, whom Moses calls "Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God," the one giving the wine and the bread, the sanctified food, as a type of the Eucharist. And indeed Melchizedek is interpreted "righteous king"; and there is a synonymy of righteousness and peace.

But Basilides supposes Righteousness and her daughter Peace to be subsistent beings, abiding ranked in the ogdoad. We must pass over, then, from the more natural matters to the more manifest ethical ones; for the discussion concerning those things will follow after the work in hand. The Saviour Himself, then, plainly, as in the tragedy, leads us into the mysteries,
seeing those who see, and gives the sacred rites.
And if you ask:
And these rites—of what form are they to you?
you will hear again:
Things not to be spoken, for mortals uninitiated to know.
And if anyone busily inquires of what kind they are, let him hear again:
It is not lawful for you to hear, but they are worthy to know: the rites hate the man who practises impiety against God.

God is without beginning, the wholly complete beginning of all things, the maker of the beginning. In so far, then, as He is substance, He is the beginning of the natural realm; in so far as He is the good, of the ethical; in so far again as He is mind, of the rational and judging realm. Whence too the Word alone is teacher, the Son of the Father-mind, the one who educates man.

And Plato the philosopher, helped by the things of Moses concerning legislation, censured the polity of Minos and Lycurgus, as looking to courage alone, but praised, as more venerable, that which says some one thing and ever inclines toward one doctrine; for he says that it is more fitting, by strength and venerableness and prudence, that we should philosophize toward the dignity of heaven, using without change the same judgment about the same things. Does he not, then, interpret the things according to the Law, looking to one God and enjoining the doing of justice? And of the statesman he says there are two kinds, the one named "legal," the other "political" by the same name; and as "political" in the proper sense he hints at the Creator, in the book of that name, and those who look to him and live actively and justly, together with the contemplation, he names "political"; but the "political" called on a par with the "legal" he divides both into a worldly magnanimity and into a private arrangement, which they have named orderliness and harmony and temperance — when rulers are fitting to the ruled, and the ruled become obedient to the rulers, which the work according to Moses is earnest to bring about.

And further, that the legal pertains to generation, but the political to friendship and concord — Plato, being helped, in the Laws set down the philosopher in the Epinomis, the man who knows the course of all generation through the wandering stars; and another philosopher, the Timaeus, who is astronomical and a contemplator of their motion and of their sympathy and fellowship with one another, he joins, in due order, to the Republic; and then . . . For the end, I think, both of the statesman and of the man who lives according to law is contemplation. It is necessary, then, to take part rightly in civic life, but best to philosophize. For the man who has mind would live having strained all that is his own toward knowledge, having set straight his life by good works, and dishonoured the contrary, and pursued the studies that contribute toward truth. And law is not the things customary (for neither are the things seen sight), nor is it every opinion (for not the worthless), but law is good opinion, and the good is the true, and the true is that which finds the being and attains it. "He who is has sent me," says Moses. By which some, following, of course, the good opinion, called law right reason, enjoining what is to be done and forbidding what is not to be done.

Not reasonably, then, do those run down the moulding and disparage the body, not perceiving that the structure of man was made upright for the contemplation of heaven, and that the organization of the senses tends toward knowledge, and the limbs and parts toward the good, not fitted out for pleasure. Hence this dwelling becomes receptive of the soul most precious to God and of the Holy Spirit, through the sanctification of soul and body, being deemed worthy and perfected by the equipping of the Saviour. And indeed the reciprocal sequence of the three virtues is found in connection with the gnostic man, who busies himself ethically and naturally and rationally about the divine. For wisdom is the knowledge of divine and human things; righteousness is the harmony of the parts of the soul; and holiness is the service of God. And if anyone should assert that the flesh, and through it generation, is slandered, citing Isaiah, who says, "All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass; the grass withered and the flower fell off; but the word of the Lord abides for ever," let him hear the Spirit interpreting the thing inquired into through Jeremiah: "And I scattered them like dry twigs blown by the wind into the desert.

This is the lot and portion of your disobeying, says the Lord; because you forgot me and hoped in lies, I too will uncover your hinder parts to your face, and your dishonour shall be seen, your adultery and your neighing," and so on. For this is the flower of the grass—both walking according to the flesh and being fleshly, according to the apostle, being in sins. The soul, it has been agreed, is better than the man, and the body inferior; but neither is the soul good by nature nor again the body evil by nature, nor is that which is not good straightway evil. For there are indeed certain middle things, and among the middle things things preferred and things rejected. The composition of man, then, having come into being among perceptible things, had to be constituted of different things, but not of opposites—of body and soul.

So the good deeds, then, are always, as better, attached to the better part, the spiritual; but the pleasure-loving and sinful ones are assigned to the inferior, the sinful part. So at once the soul of the wise and gnostic man, as though lodging as a guest in the body, conducts itself toward it gravely and honourably, not with passionate attachment, ready, whenever the time of departure should call, to leave the tabernacle. "A sojourner," it says, "in the land, and a pilgrim am I with you." And from this Basilides took to say that the election is a stranger to the world, as being by nature supramundane. But it is not so. For all things are of one God, and no one would be by nature a stranger to the world, the substance being one and the God one; but the elect man conducts himself as a stranger, knowing all things as things to be possessed and things to be given up.

And all the things the Peripatetics wish to be threefold goods, he uses, even the body too, as a man setting out on a far journey uses inns and the dwellings by the road—taking care of and adorning the place where he lodges, but leaving the dwelling and the possession, like its use, without passionate attachment, readily following the one who leads him away from life, in no way turning back for any cause whatever, having given thanks for the sojourning, but blessing his departure, embracing the abode in heaven. For "we know that, if our earthly house of the tabernacle is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For indeed in this we groan, longing to be clothed upon with our dwelling from heaven, if indeed, being clothed, we shall not be found naked; for we walk by faith, not by sight," as the apostle says. "But we are willing rather to be away from the body and at home with the Lord." Now the "rather" is in comparison; and comparison is among things that fall under likeness, as the more courageous is more courageous than the courageous, and most courageous of the cowardly.

Hence the law is rightly said to have been given through Moses, being a rule of just and unjust things. And this we may properly call an ordinance, the one handed down by God through Moses. For it has the leading toward the divine. And Paul too says: "The law was added for the sake of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom it was promised." Then, as if explaining further the meaning, he adds: "But before faith came we were kept guarded under the law, shut up" — by fear, that is, from sins — "toward the faith that was about to be revealed. So that the law became our schoolmaster toward Christ, that we might be justified by faith." And the legislator is one who assigns what is fitting to each part of the soul and to its works; and Moses, to speak briefly, was a living law, governed by the good Word.

Whence he added: "Wherefore we are ambitious, whether at home or away, to be well-pleasing to Him"—plainly to the one God, of whom all things are work and creation, both the world and the things above the world. I admire Epicharmus when he plainly says:
The man pious in mind would suffer no evil when he is dead; the spirit abides above in heaven;
and the lyric poet when he sings:
The souls of the impious flit below heaven over the earth in murderous pains, under inescapable yokes of evils; but the souls of the pious dwell in heaven, singing in hymns the great Blessed One.

The soul, then, is not sent down hither from heaven to the worse things—for God works all things toward the better—but the soul that has chosen the best life exchanges, by the righteousness of God, the earth for heaven.

He administered, at any rate, a good polity; and this is the noble nourishment of men in fellowship. So he handled the judicial art, which is a science correcting the things sinned, for the sake of justice. And of the same row with it is the punitive, which is a science of the measure in punishments. And punishment, being just, is a correction of the soul. And, to speak generally, the whole conduct of Moses is educative of those able to become noble and good men, and a hunting of such men, which would be generalship. And the wisdom that uses, in due manner, those hunted by reason, would be the legislative; for to acquire and to use this belongs to the most kingly art. For the philosophers proclaim the wise man alone king, legislator, general, just, holy, dear to God. And if we should find these things about Moses, as is shown from the Scriptures themselves, we might declare, with very full conviction, that Moses was truly wise.

With good reason, then, Job, having become possessed of knowledge, said: "Now I know that you can do all things, and that nothing is impossible for you. For who reports to me things I did not know, great and marvellous things which I did not understand? But I despised myself, reckoning myself to be earth and ashes." For the man who is in ignorance is sinful and earth and ashes; but the man established in knowledge, made like to God so far as he can be, is already spiritual and on this account elect. And that the Scripture calls the foolish and disobedient "earth," Jeremiah the prophet will make plain, speaking against Joachim and his brothers: "O earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord; write this man down as a man banished by proclamation."

As, then, we say that the shepherd's art is to take forethought for the sheep — "the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" — so we shall say that the legislative art is to bring about the virtue of men, rekindling the human good according to its power, being a thing that presides over and cares for the herd of men. And if the flock allegorized by the Lord is nothing other than a certain herd of men, the same will be both shepherd and good legislator of the one herd of the sheep that hear him — the one guardian, who seeks out and finds the lost by law and by reason, if indeed the law is spiritual and leads to happiness; for the man who has become spiritual by the Holy Spirit is spiritual. And this is the legislator in truth, who not only professes good and noble things but also knows them. And his law — the law of the one who has the knowledge — is the saving command; or rather, the law is the command of knowledge, for the Word of God is power and wisdom. And he himself again is the expounder of laws, through whom the law was given, the first expounder of the divine commands, the only-begotten Son who expounds the bosom of the Father.

And again another prophet says: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth"—calling understanding the "hearing," and the soul of the gnostic, who has taken upon himself the contemplation of heaven and of divine things, and in this way has become an Israelite, the "heaven"; for, on the contrary, he called the man who has chosen ignorance and hardness of heart "earth," and the "give ear" he addressed from the organs of hearing, the ears, assigning the fleshly things to those who cleave to the perceptible things. These are they concerning whom Micah the prophet says: "Hear, O peoples, the word of the Lord, you who dwell among pains." And Abraham said, "By no means, Lord, you who judge the earth"—since the man who has disbelieved is, according to the saving voice, already judged.

Then those who obey the law, by having some knowledge of it, can neither disbelieve nor be ignorant of the truth; but those who disbelieve, and have least of all wished to be among the works, are confessed, if any others, to be ignorant of the truth. What, then, is the unbelief of the Greeks? Is it not their unwillingness, somehow, to obey the truth which says that the law was given by God through Moses — when they themselves, out of their own, honour Moses? For they relate that Minos received his laws from Zeus every ninth year, going to the cave of Zeus; and Plato and Aristotle and Ephorus write that Lycurgus was educated in legislation by continually going to Delphi to Apollo; and Chamaeleon of Heraclea, in his work On Drunkenness, and Aristotle, in his Constitution of the Locrians, record that Zaleucus the Locrian received his laws from Athena. But those who, exalting the trustworthiness of the legislation among the Greeks, so far as they can, toward the divine, after the image of the prophecy according to Moses, are without sense, in that they do not at once confess both the truth and the archetype of the things recorded among them.

And it is written too in Kingdoms, the judgement and the decree of the Lord being thus: "God hears the righteous, but the impious He does not save, because they do not wish to know God; for the Almighty will not accomplish absurd things." What against this voice do the heresies still utter, when the Scripture proclaims the Almighty to be a good God and guiltless of vice and injustice—if indeed ignorance arises through not knowing, but God does nothing absurd? For "this is our God," it says, "and there is none beside Him who saves"; for "there is no injustice with God," according to the apostle. And still more plainly the prophet teaches the counsel of God and the gnostic advancement through these words: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, but to fear the Lord your God and to walk in all His ways and to love Him and to serve Him alone?" This He asks of you, who have the authority to choose salvation.

What, then, did the Pythagoreans intend when they bade men pray aloud with the voice? It seems to me, not that they supposed the divine could not hear those who speak softly, but that they wished the prayers to be just—such as one would not be ashamed to make with many witnesses. But concerning prayer we shall treat at the proper season as the discourse proceeds; and as for works, we ought to have them crying aloud, walking as in the day: "For let your works shine." "And behold, the man and his works are before his face." "For behold, God and His works." One must imitate God, as far as is possible for the gnostic. And to me it seems that the poets too call the elect among themselves "godlike" and "divine" and "like to the gods" and "equal to Zeus in counsel" and "having counsels like the gods" and "godlike in form"—nibbling, as it were, at the "according to the image and likeness."
Euripides, then, says:
Golden wings indeed are about my back,
and:
and the lovely sandals of the Sirens are fitted on, and I shall go, lifted high into the vast aether, to mingle with Zeus.

But I would pray that the Spirit of Christ might wing me into my own Jerusalem; for the Stoics too say that heaven properly is a city, but the things here on earth are no longer cities—they are called so, but are not; for a city is something earnest, and a people a noble assembly and a multitude of men governed by law, as the Church is by reason—an unbesieged, untyrannized city upon earth, a divine will upon earth as in heaven. The poets too create images of this city in their writings; for the Hyperborean and the Arimaspian cities and the Elysian plains are commonwealths of the just. And we know too Plato's city, laid up as a pattern in heaven.

Let no one, then, run down the law on account of the punishments, as though it were not noble and good. For the man who removes a disease of the body will be thought a benefactor, and shall not the man who tries to free the soul of injustice be all the more its guardian, by as much as the soul is more honourable than the body? But for the health of the body we submit to incisions and cauteries and the drinking of drugs, and the one who applies these is called a saviour and a physician — not out of any grudge or ill-will toward the patient, but as the reason of the art dictates — even cutting off certain parts, that the healthy may not be corrupted along with them; and no one would charge the physician's art with wickedness. And shall we not, for the soul's sake, likewise submit, whether it be banishment, or the paying of penalties, or bonds, if only one is ever to gain righteousness out of injustice? For the law, caring for its subjects, educates toward the reverence of God and dictates what is to be done, and keeps back each of the sins, imposing penalties on the moderate ones; but whenever it sees someone so disposed as to seem incurable, driving on to the extreme of injustice, then at last, caring for the others, that they may not be corrupted by him, as though cutting off a part of the whole body, it puts such a one to death in the most wholesome way.

"And being judged by the Lord," says the Apostle, "we are disciplined, that we may not be condemned with the world." For the prophet said before: "Disciplining, the Lord disciplined me, but to death he did not hand me over." "For, in order to teach you his righteousness," it says, "he disciplined you and tested you and made you hunger and made you thirst in a desert land, that all his ordinances and judgments might be known in your heart, all that I command you today; and you shall know in your heart that, as a man might discipline his son, so the Lord our God will discipline you." And that the example brings to soberness, it says at once: "The cunning man, seeing the wicked man punished severely, is himself disciplined."

For "the fear of the Lord is the offspring of wisdom." And it is the greatest and most perfect good, when one is able to bring someone over from acting badly to virtue and well-doing — which the law accomplishes. So that even when one falls into some incurable evil, having been seized by injustice and greed, he would be benefited by being put to death; for the law is a benefactor, able both to make the unjust just, if only they will hearken to it, and to free the others from present evils. For it promises immortality to those who have chosen to live temperately and justly. And to know the law belongs to a good understanding. And again: "Bad men do not understand the law, but those who seek the Lord will have understanding in every good thing." The administering providence must, then, be both sovereign and good. For by both the power administers salvation: the one bringing to soberness by punishment, as sovereign; the other showing kindness through well-doing, as benefactress. And it is possible not to be a son of disobedience, but to pass over from darkness to life, and, having set one's ear to wisdom, to be by law a servant of God — at the first a slave, then a faithful attendant, fearing the Lord God; and if one should advance, to be reckoned among the sons, and, when love covers a multitude of sins, having grown in love, to await the perfecting of the blessed hope, the man enrolled in the elect adoption that is called the friend of God, already singing the prayer and saying: "Let the Lord become to me a God."

And the Apostle has shown the beneficence of the law, through the passage about the Jews, writing somewhat thus: "But if you are surnamed a Jew and rest upon the law and boast in God and know his will and approve the things that differ, being instructed out of the law, and have persuaded yourself that you are a guide of the blind, a light to those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, having the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law." For it is confessed that the law can do these things, even if those who do not order their lives according to the law boast as though living in the law. "And blessed is the man who has found wisdom, and the mortal who has seen prudence; and from her mouth" — that is, of wisdom — "righteousness goes forth, and she bears law and mercy upon her tongue." For of one Lord, who is the power and wisdom of God, is the activity, both the law and the Gospel; and the fear which the law begot, this is merciful unto salvation. "And let not mercies and faith and truth fail you, but fasten them about your neck."

And, like Paul, the prophecy reproaches the people as not understanding the law: "Destruction and misery are in their ways, and the way of peace they have not known; there is no fear of God before their eyes. Professing to be wise, they were made foolish." "And we know that the law is good, if one uses it lawfully; but those who wish to be teachers of the law," says the Apostle, "understand neither what they say nor concerning what they affirm; and the end of the commandment is love out of a pure heart and a good conscience and unfeigned faith."

The philosophy according to Moses, then, is divided into four parts: into the historical and the properly so-called legislative, which would be the proper concerns of ethical treatment; the third into the part concerning sacred service, which already belongs to natural contemplation; and fourth, above all, the theological kind, the higher vision, which Plato says is of the truly great mysteries, and which Aristotle calls the kind that comes "after the natural things" (the metaphysical). And the dialectic according to Plato, as he says in the Statesman, is a certain science discovering the disclosure of the things that are; and it is to be acquired by the temperate man, not for the sake of saying or doing anything toward men, as the dialecticians now do who busy themselves about sophistical things, but for being able both to say what is pleasing to God and to do what is pleasing to him, the whole according to one's power.

And the true dialectic, being mixed with the true philosophy, examining the things and testing the powers and authorities, ascends up to the essence most sovereign of all, and dares beyond, to the God of the universe, professing not experience of mortal things but knowledge of things divine and heavenly, with which there follows also the proper use of human things, both in words and in actions. With reason, then, the Scripture too, wishing us to become such dialecticians, exhorts thus: "Become approved bankers, rejecting some things, but holding fast the good." For this is in truth the dialectic — a prudence that divides about the objects of thought, and shows each of the things that are unmixed and pure in its underlying nature, or a power that divides about the genera of things, descending to the most particular, presenting each of the things that are pure, such as it is, to appear.

Wherefore this alone leads by the hand to the true wisdom, which is a divine power, knowing the things that are as they are, having the perfect, freed from all passion — not without the Saviour, who, by the divine Word, has drawn off from the seeing part of our soul the misty ignorance poured over it by base conduct, and given back the best, "that we might know well both god and man." This is he who has in truth shown how one must know oneself; this is he who uncovers the Father of the universe to whomever he wishes, so far as human nature can hold it. "For no one knew the Son but the Father, nor the Father but the Son and he to whom the Son reveals him."

With reason, then, the Apostle says that by revelation he came to know the mystery: "As I wrote before in brief, by which, when you read, you can perceive my understanding in the mystery of Christ." "By which you can," he said, since he knew that some had received milk only, and not yet solid food — and indeed not simply milk. And we must take the meaning of the law in three ways: either as showing forth a sign, or as confirming a commandment toward right conduct of life, or as prophesying as prophecy. And I know well that to discern and to tell such things belongs to men; for the whole of Scripture is not, for understanding, "one Myconos," as the proverb-makers say; but one must approach it as dialectically as possible, hunting for the sequence of the divine teaching.

Hence most nobly the Egyptian priest in Plato: "O Solon, Solon," he said, "you Greeks are always children, having in your souls not a single ancient opinion through old hearing, and there is no aged Greek" — calling "aged," I think, those who know the more ancient things, that is, our things, just as, on the contrary, "young" those who know the newer things and the things practised by the Greeks, the things that happened yesterday and lately, but who record them as old and ancient. So he added: "learning grown grey with time," we using the metaphor in a certain barbarian way, unaffected and not over-precise. So the well-disposed approach the whole figure of the interpretation simply. And of the Greeks he says that their conceit differs little from children's stories; for we must not understand children's fables, nor yet the fables made for children; and he called the very fables "children," as if the reputed wise among the Greeks saw but little, hinting at "the grey learning," the truth most ancient among the barbarians; to which word he opposed "child's fable," refuting the fabulous character of the attempt of the newer men, as having, like children, nothing older — presenting both their fables and their discourses together as childish.

Divinely, then, the power that speaks the visions to Hermas by revelation says that both the visions and the revelations are for the sake of the double-minded, who reason in their hearts whether these things are or are not. And likewise the demonstrations that come from the abundance of wide learning strengthen and make firm and ground the demonstrative arguments, as far as their minds, being still young, flutter. "A lamp, then, is a good commandment," according to the Scripture, "and the law is a light of the way; for education reproves the ways of life." "Law, the king of all, both mortals and immortals," says Pindar. And I understand by this the one who established the law; and the saying of Hesiod too I take to have been spoken of the God of all, even if it was said by the poet conjecturally and not comprehensibly: "This law the son of Cronus ordained for men: for fishes and beasts and winged birds, to devour one another, since there is no justice among them; but to men he gave justice, which is far the best."

Whether, then, he means the law given together with generation, or the one given afterward — yet from God is both the law of nature and the law of learning, being one, as Plato too in the Statesman says there is one legislator, and in the Laws one who will understand the things of music, teaching by these that the Word is one and God is one. And Moses is plainly seen calling the Lord a covenant: "Behold," he says, "my covenant is with you"; since he had said before "covenant," . . . not to seek it in writing. For there is a covenant which God, the cause of the universe, establishes; and "God" is named from "establishing" (thesis) and ordering, the arrangement of the world. And in the Preaching of Peter you would find the Lord called both law and Word. But let this first Miscellany of gnostic notes according to the true philosophy be here circumscribed for us.
